This innovative platform will deliver audio, text message alerts, and images to subscribers, keeping them informed about the latest developments in the region. The service will be available in both English and French, catering to a wide audience.

To subscribe to the service, users simply need to send the word "JOIN" via WhatsApp to +44 7702 348 651, after saving the number in their phone's contacts. Those who wish to unsubscribe can send the word "STOP" to the same number. It is essential to note that subscribers should not attempt to take audio, pictures, or videos and send them to the BBC via WhatsApp, as this may put them at risk of exposure to Ebola.

The WhatsApp service is part of the BBC's extensive response to the Ebola crisis, which includes special radio, online, and TV content, as well as social media updates on Twitter and Facebook. The BBC is utilizing the popularity of WhatsApp, the largest "chat app" in Africa, to reach people directly through their mobile phones. Additionally, users can access Ebola public health information in audio form via the MXIT app, available on a range of devices, including smartphones and feature phones.

The BBC's Ebola response is its largest health information drive since its reporting on HIV/AIDS in the 1980s and 1990s. With the WhatsApp service and other initiatives, the BBC aims to provide accurate and timely information to help combat the spread of Ebola. Users can also access the latest Ebola stories on the BBC's social media accounts and on the BBC News website, bbc.com/ebola. Remember, safety is paramount, and users should never endanger themselves or others while seeking information.

A proposed electrification project for the Midland Mainline could bring significant economic benefits to the East Midlands region, but it comes with a hefty price tag of potentially £1.5 billion. Leicester South MP John Ashworth revealed the estimated cost during discussions with the Department for Transport. The project aims to replace diesel trains with electric ones, joining the already electrified East and West Coast mainlines.

Transport Minister Theresa Villiers expressed the government's support for the "progressive electrification" of the rail network, citing its importance for transport and environmental policy. Mr Ashworth emphasized the project's vital role in stimulating the regional economy, creating jobs, and promoting economic growth in cities like Leicester, Derby, Nottingham, and Sheffield.

Transport analyst Christian Wolmar noted that electrified lines would enable cleaner, more energy-efficient, and faster trains. He believes the major cities in the East Midlands would greatly benefit from the project. Currently, electric trains only run on the Midland Mainline up to Bedford, with diesel engines taking over thereafter. Network Rail has suggested that electrification of the London to East Midlands route could be completed by the end of the decade. The government is expected to announce further details on its rail industry plans in July.

Alan Pardew has expressed his desire to remain as Crystal Palace manager, stating that he hopes to sign a new contract once the team's safety in the Premier League is secured. Pardew, who took over as Palace boss in January 2015, led the team to a 10th place finish last season. However, this campaign has been marked by a significant slump, with the team dropping from fifth to 17th place. Despite this, Palace recently secured a much-needed win against Norwich, moving them 10 points clear of the relegation zone. Pardew acknowledged that the team's form has been disappointing in the second half of the season, but is hopeful that their recent victory will boost confidence and alleviate nervousness. With a crucial match against Everton upcoming, Pardew will be looking to build on this momentum and guide Palace to a stronger finish.

Controversy Surrounds Revised Wales Bill as it Proceeds through House of Lords

The Wales Bill, which aims to grant the Senedd new powers, has been revised following concerns that it may inadvertently reduce the assembly's authority. Despite these revisions, Professor Richard Wyn Jones has expressed "serious problems" with the bill, stating that he is confident Assembly Members (AMs) will consider blocking its passage. The Wales Office has announced that discussions with the Welsh Government will continue as the bill progresses through the House of Lords.

The Wales Bill has already undergone debate in the House of Commons and is currently being scrutinized by the House of Lords as part of the legislative process. The committee stage, scheduled to commence on Monday, will provide an opportunity for further examination and potential amendments. Professor Jones, speaking on BBC Radio Wales' Sunday Supplement program, emphasized that the bill falls short of its intended purpose, failing to "fulfil the original intentions of settling devolution."

Criticism of the bill is widespread, with Professor Jones noting that it is "genuinely hard to find people who aren't directly involved on the UK government side with a good word to say about this legislation." The proposed law's detail has been particularly problematic, with many experts pointing to fundamental flaws. The initial consensus among parties to adopt a reserved powers model has given way to disappointment, as the enactment of this intention has been marred by errors.

Professor Jones stressed that critics of the bill are not motivated by a desire to see it fail but rather by a desire to address the shortcomings of the current devolution settlement. The Welsh Government, National Assembly presiding office, and other stakeholders have offered constructive suggestions for change, yet the legislation is being pushed through Parliament with only minor concessions. The Wales Office, while consultative, lacks the institutional clout to drive more powerful departments towards a more sensible position.

First Minister Carwyn Jones has expressed "considerable concern" over unresolved issues, including the establishment of a Welsh legal jurisdiction and the scope of reservations. The Lords Constitution Committee has also warned that the bill may create a "recipe for confusion," potentially leading to more Welsh bills being challenged in the courts.

In response to these concerns, a Wales Office spokesperson emphasized that the Wales Bill presents a "historic opportunity" for the Welsh Assembly to secure greater powers and create a more robust devolution settlement. The spokesperson confirmed that discussions with the Welsh Government will continue as the bill progresses through Parliament, with opportunities for further debate and amendments in the coming weeks.

As the Wales Bill proceeds through the House of Lords, it remains to be seen whether the UK government will address the concerns raised by Professor Jones, the Welsh Government, and other stakeholders. The outcome of this process will have significant implications for the future of devolution in Wales and the balance of power between the Senedd and Westminster.

Search Efforts Continue for Missing 18-Year-Old Sarah Goldie

A massive search operation is underway in the River Clyde for 18-year-old Sarah Goldie, who was reported missing from her home in Renfrew on Friday night. Police from the specialist marine unit are scouring the river, and an appeal has been made for anyone with information to come forward.

According to police, Ms Goldie left her home at around 11:00 on Friday and took a taxi from Glasgow to Renfrew, where she was dropped off in the Torridon Drive area at about 18:00. Later that evening, at around 19:40, a call was made to emergency services regarding a young woman in the River Clyde near the Broomielaw and George V Bridge.

Despite a thorough search by emergency services, including a helicopter, and two men entering the water, the woman could not be found. Chief Inspector Mark Sutherland of Police Scotland said, "Our inquiry to trace Sarah Goldie continues, and I would like to thank the public for their positive response to our appeals for information."

Through CCTV evidence and witness accounts, police have been piecing together Ms Goldie's movements on Friday in both Renfrew and Glasgow. They have spoken to several people who witnessed an incident close to the King George V Bridge in Glasgow and now believe that the young woman seen in the water is indeed Sarah Goldie.

Ms Goldie's family has been kept updated throughout the inquiry, and police have confirmed that no one else is believed to have been involved in the incident that led to her entering the water. The police are continuing to appeal for anyone with information to contact Glasgow City Centre Police.

Sarah Goldie is described as white, 5ft 6in tall, of medium build, with brown eyes and sandy/strawberry blond straight hair. She was last seen wearing a khaki green Parka-type jacket with a fur hood and carrying a cherry-red handbag. Her bag was found near the river, prompting concerns for her safety. The search for Ms Goldie is ongoing, and police are urging anyone with information to come forward to help bring her home.

Astronomers have made a groundbreaking discovery in the search for nascent planetary systems, using a network of radio telescopes in Chile to identify a forming ice giant planet located 176 light-years from Earth. The findings, set to be published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, provide new insights into the diversity of planetary systems and the formation of Neptune-like icy giants.

The planet, which is thought to be similar to Uranus or Neptune in our Solar System, is orbiting a young star called TW Hydrae, estimated to be around 10 million years old. This star is one of the closest young stars to Earth, making it an ideal candidate for study. The fact that its axis of rotation points towards Earth also allows astronomers to get a face-on view of the developing planetary system.

Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (Alma) in northern Chile, a team of researchers led by Takashi Tsukagoshi at Ibaraki University, Japan, was able to take a close look at the planet formation site. Alma, which consists of 66 high-precision antennas, captured and concentrated radio waves from the astronomical source, allowing the team to see through the dust that obscures parts of the sky from visible light telescopes.

The team found that the young star is surrounded by a disc made of tiny dust particles, with variations in the signal received by Alma allowing them to estimate the size of these dust grains. Smaller, micrometre-sized dust particles dominate the most prominent gap in the disc, which has a radius of 22 astronomical units (AU). The researchers believe that gravitational interactions and friction between gas and dust have probably pushed the larger dust out of the gap.

By calculating the mass of the unseen planet based on the width and depth of the 22 AU gap, the team found that the planet is probably slightly more massive than Neptune. "Combined with the orbit size and the brightness of TW Hydrae, the planet would be an icy giant planet like Neptune," said Dr Tsukagoshi.

This discovery sheds new light on the formation of Neptune-like icy giants and the diversity of planetary systems. Over the past two decades, astronomers have discovered that planetary systems do not necessarily follow the familiar template set by the eight planets that orbit the Sun. The findings of this study contribute to our understanding of how this diversity emerges and provide valuable insights into the formation of planetary systems beyond our own.

Legal proceedings are ongoing over a proposed John Lewis store, initially planned for Sprucefield near Lisburn. Director Paul McMahon emphasized the need for clarity on planning policies. He expressed concerns that costly legal battles would deter businesses, sending the wrong message about Northern Ireland. McMahon advocated for a policy prioritizing town centers, which would bring John Lewis to Belfast, the capital city. He stressed the importance of a clear policy to attract businesses and promote investment in the region. The issue will be discussed on BBC Radio Ulster and Radio Foyle's Inside Business on Sunday at 13:30 BST.

A 29-year-old man, Michael Williams, has pleaded guilty to manslaughter over the death of 42-year-old Maxine Showers in Liverpool. However, prosecutors rejected the plea, and he will stand trial for murder on March 21. Williams was remanded in custody after Showers' body was found with blunt force head trauma in an alleyway last September.

Former Leeds United manager Neil Warnock has expressed sympathy for Aston Villa striker Ross McCormack, who was left out of the Scotland squad to face Malta on Sunday. Despite Celtic's Leigh Griffiths withdrawing from the squad due to injury, McCormack was not called up, a decision that Warnock believes is a dilemma for head coach Gordon Strachan.

Warnock, who managed McCormack during his time at Leeds United, understands the challenges of incorporating the striker into a team. "It was very difficult to find a system to suit Ross McCormack," Warnock said. "I couldn't play him up front because he wasn't big enough or good enough in the air, and I couldn't play him wide because I've got better wingers." As a result, Warnock often played McCormack in the "hole" behind the striker, a role that allowed him to utilize his creative skills.

McCormack has a proven track record of scoring goals, having netted 23 times for Fulham last season. Warnock believes that the striker will continue to score regularly, predicting that he will score 20 goals in the Championship this year. However, he acknowledges that McCormack's style of play can be difficult to incorporate into a team, making it challenging to find a winning formula.

Despite this, Warnock thinks that McCormack could be a valuable asset to the Scotland squad, particularly in games where a goal is needed against a stubborn opponent. "You could always do with a Ross involved," Warnock said. "If you are going to need a goal against a team like Malta, Ross can always give you that little bit different and create a chance." Ultimately, Warnock believes that McCormack's omission from the squad is a difficult decision, but one that Strachan had to make.

A Fatal Accident Inquiry (FAI) is underway at Glasgow Sheriff Court to investigate the death of Margaret Gilchrist, a 50-year-old woman with severe learning difficulties and epilepsy. Ms Gilchrist, who was also registered blind, passed away at her home in Carntyne Road, Glasgow, on September 26, 2013. The inquiry heard that on the night of her death, Ms Gilchrist was put in the bath by her carer and left alone for about an hour before being found unresponsive.

Tragically, it was revealed that Ms Gilchrist had suffered scalding injuries prior to her death. The FAI also examined a previous incident in 1998, in which Ms Gilchrist was scalded while being cared for by another worker, Georgina McDougall. Mrs McDougall testified that she had run a bath for Ms Gilchrist, checked the temperature, and then left the room briefly. She returned to find Ms Gilchrist standing in the bath with the water running, having apparently turned on the hot tap herself.

Following the 1998 incident, Mrs McDougall said she never left Ms Gilchrist alone in the bath for more than 10 minutes. The inquiry, led by Sheriff Lindsay Wood, is continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ms Gilchrist's death. The court will examine the care and supervision provided to Ms Gilchrist, particularly in relation to her bathing, to determine whether any failures or shortcomings contributed to her tragic passing.

Former England manager Sam Allardyce has been cleared of any wrongdoing by the City of London Police. The 62-year-old left his post after just one game in charge following a newspaper investigation that claimed he offered advice on how to bypass player transfer rules. Allardyce welcomed the police confirmation, stating he was always confident of being cleared due to a lack of evidence. He urged the Football Association to resolve the matter quickly, allowing him to move on. Despite his brief tenure, Allardyce expressed pride in having managed the England team. The police confirmation paves the way for the FA, English Football League, and Premier League to proceed with their own investigations into the matter. Allardyce's exit sparked a wave of controversy, but he can now begin to rebuild his reputation. The outcome is a significant development in the ongoing saga surrounding English football.

MOSCOW MOURNS NEMTSOV: QUEST FOR JUSTICE CONTINUES

It's been years since the brutal murder of Boris Nemtsov, a former Russian deputy prime minister and vocal critic of President Vladimir Putin. Nemtsov was shot dead in February 2015, just a stone's throw away from the Kremlin. The killing sent shockwaves across the nation, with many demanding justice for the slain politician.

Five Chechen men are currently on trial, accused of carrying out the killing in exchange for cash. However, all defendants deny the charges, leaving many to wonder if the true masterminds behind the murder will ever be brought to justice. Nemtsov's relatives fear that the case will follow a familiar pattern in Russia, where hitmen are prosecuted but those who ordered the killing remain at large.

Nemtsov, 55, was a prominent figure in Russian politics, having served as first deputy prime minister under President Boris Yeltsin. However, after falling out of favor with Putin, he became a fierce opposition leader, criticizing the government on various issues, including corruption and the war in Ukraine. His murder was widely condemned, with President Putin describing it as "vile and cynical." Despite assurances of a thorough investigation, many remain skeptical about the pursuit of justice in this high-profile case. The site of Nemtsov's murder remains marked with flowers, a poignant reminder of the quest for truth and accountability that continues to this day.

Nigeria's Super Eagles Coach, Samson Siasia, has confirmed that former players Vincent Enyeama and Emmanuel Emenike will not be returning to the team. The duo had retired from international football last October after a disagreement with former coach Sunday Oliseh. Following Oliseh's resignation, Siasia had reached out to the pair, asking them to reconsider their decision, but they have chosen to stick with their retirement.

Enyeama, the former goalkeeper, had been stripped of the team's captaincy by Oliseh, leading to his retirement. In a recent interview with Brila FM, he stated that his decision to retire still stands and he does not wish to discuss the matter further. Emenike, a striker, had followed Enyeama's lead and also quit the team.

Siasia has respected the players' decisions, stating that Nigeria has a wealth of talented footballers and the team must focus on the future. The coach, along with his assistants Salisu Yusuf and Emmanuel Amunike, is set to finalize the squad for the upcoming game against Egypt. When asked about the potential return of other players, such as Obafemi Martins, Victor Moses, and John Mikel Obi, Siasia remained tight-lipped, emphasizing that the team's focus is on the crucial matches against Egypt. He called for the support of everyone, saying that the players who are committed to giving their all for the country will be crucial in achieving success.

Millions of Syrians Flee to Safety as US Increases Refugee Resettlement Efforts

The ongoing conflict in Syria has led to a massive exodus of refugees, with over 4.2 million individuals fleeing their homeland in search of safety and security. Initially, many sought refuge in UN-run camps in neighboring countries, but in recent months, a growing number have embarked on perilous sea journeys to Europe, sparking a migration crisis on the continent.

In response to mounting pressure, the Obama administration announced plans to increase the number of Syrian refugees allowed to resettle in the US over the next year. As of now, 2,370 Syrian refugees have arrived in the US, with the majority being under the age of 20. The demographic breakdown of these refugees reveals that 55.69% are under 20, while 30.73% fall between the ages of 21 and 40. Women make up 47.05% of the arrivals, while men account for 52.95%.

The process of resettling in the US is a lengthy and rigorous one. Refugees must first leave their home country and register with the UNHCR, which then determines their eligibility for international resettlement. Those referred to the US undergo a thorough security screening process, which can take up to two years to complete. If cleared, they are then assisted by one of nine NGOs in finding a new home in the US.

The US government has come under scrutiny for its handling of the refugee crisis, with many arguing that it is not doing enough to provide a safe haven for those fleeing war-torn countries. The recent announcement to increase resettlement efforts is seen as a step in the right direction, but much work remains to be done to address the scale and complexity of the crisis. As the situation continues to unfold, it is clear that a comprehensive and coordinated approach will be necessary to provide protection and support to those affected by the conflict in Syria.

Mental Health Care Under Scrutiny in North Wales After Patient's Death

The family of a 49-year-old woman from Anglesey who struggled with depression and a personality disorder has spoken out about their concerns regarding the mental health care she received at a hospital in north Wales. Petra Jones, who had been treated at the Hergest mental health unit at Ysbyty Gwynedd, was found dead in her garage just hours after being released from the hospital in April 2015.

According to her daughter, Ffion Jones, Petra had been admitted to the hospital several times and had attempted to harm herself on multiple occasions. Despite the family's requests to have her sectioned, Petra was released from the hospital, and Ffion claims that her warnings about her mother's intentions to harm herself were not taken seriously by hospital staff.

Ffion recounted a disturbing phone call with a staff member at the hospital, in which she expressed her concerns about her mother's well-being. "My mother told me over the phone that once she was home, she'd go to the garage and kill herself," Ffion said. "I phoned Hergest and told this to one of the staff, and she said, 'well, I understand your concern, but the psychiatrist will say whether or not she's allowed to go home'."

Tragically, Petra was released from the hospital, and just a few hours later, she was found dead. Ffion has since filed a complaint with the community health council, citing concerns about the care her mother received and the lack of attention given to her warnings.

Ffion's story is not an isolated incident. Other families have come forward with similar concerns about mental health care in north Wales, and the community is calling for improved services and more support for families affected by mental illness. Clwyd West Conservative AM Darren Miller has identified two major problems with the current system: a lack of strong leadership and management, and a shortage of beds and staff.

In response to these concerns, Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board has stated that mental health services have undergone significant changes over the past year and that patient feedback is taken "extremely seriously." A spokesman for the health board said, "We are fully focused on improving the way mental health services are delivered across north Wales."

However, for Ffion and her family, the changes come too late. "I know this won't bring mum back," Ffion said, "but we know this has happened to a lot of families – the same situation. So, we've made a complaint so it doesn't happen again in the future and to get a bit more help for families." As the community continues to grapple with the issue of mental health care, Ffion's story serves as a poignant reminder of the need for improved services and support for those struggling with mental illness.

Malaysian Authorities Arrest 14 Suspects Planning Terror Attacks

Malaysian Home Minister Zahid Hamidi announced the arrest of 14 suspects, aged between 14 and 44, who were planning to attack police stations and army bases to gather weapons. Two of the suspects had recently returned from Syria, according to police. The group was also allegedly planning to kidnap high-profile individuals, although the targets were not named.

Notes were found describing how to make bombs, written by an Indonesian executed for his role in the 2002 Bali bomb attacks. Two of those arrested were members of the army, raising concerns about the extent of militant influence within the country. The arrests come as the government prepares to debate new anti-terrorism laws in parliament, which have been met with controversy and opposition from human rights groups.

The new laws would permit indefinite detention without trial and the revocation of passports for individuals suspected of terrorist activities. Prime Minister Najib Razak has defended the measures as necessary to combat militant Islamist cells and "lone wolf" attacks. However, critics argue that the laws could be used to stifle political dissent, particularly given the government's history of using the sedition law to silence opponents. The sedition law has been controversial due to its broad definition of sedition, which can include speech or actions deemed critical of the government, and its potential for abuse.

A motion has been tabled to the council by Vicky Davidson, representing Selkirkshire, to halt the routine deployment of armed officers in the Borders. Davidson argued that the region is a safe place and that carrying side arms is not necessary. She called for an immediate stop to the practice, which was adopted by Police Scotland last year, and for consultations to be held in each council area before restarting. The move has sparked concerns from various parties, including independent MSP John Finnie and Highland councillors, who question the need for armed officers in areas with low crime rates. The issue is set to be debated, with many calling for a more tailored approach to policing in different regions.

Pope Francis Brings Message of Hope and Unity to Egypt

In a historic visit to Egypt, Pope Francis brought a message of hope and unity to the Christian community, who have felt under siege in recent weeks. The Pope's visit comes just three weeks after the devastating attack on two Egyptian churches by the so-called Islamic State, which killed at least 45 people. Despite the somber mood, the Pope's arrival at Cairo's Air Defence Stadium was met with jubilation, as thousands of worshippers waved flags and released balloons.

As the Pope made his way through the stadium in an unprotected "popemobile", he was greeted with rapturous applause. In his address, he began by referencing the disciples' despair and disappointment following Christ's crucifixion, but went on to emphasize the transformative power of the resurrection. The Pope then turned to a theme that has been a hallmark of his visit: the importance of compassion and charity in religious faith.

"God is pleased only by a faith that is proclaimed by our lives," he said. "The only fanaticism believers can have is that of charity. Any other fanaticism does not come from God and is not pleasing to Him." These words echoed his earlier speech at al-Alzhar University, where he spoke to a largely Muslim audience and argued that hatred and violence have no place in religion.

The Pope's message was a challenge to both Christians and Muslims in Egypt to re-examine their faith and to strive for a more compassionate and engaged approach. As the country navigates a three-month state of emergency, the Pope's visit was a rare opportunity for the Christian community to come together and celebrate in the open air. The event was a powerful reminder of the importance of unity and solidarity in the face of adversity, and the Pope's words will undoubtedly resonate with people of all faiths in Egypt and beyond.

Monument Valley Creators Bask in Glory After BAFTA Wins and Presidential Endorsement

The team behind the critically acclaimed puzzle game Monument Valley is still reeling from their recent BAFTA wins and an unexpected endorsement from the President of the United States. Daniel Gray, a representative from UsTwo, the company behind the indie hit, beamed with pride on the red carpet, stating, "We feel like we've won, just for being nominated, especially for best game." Although the game missed out on the top category to Destiny, it took home the awards for best British game and best mobile game.

But the team's excitement wasn't just about the BAFTAs. They revealed that the game had been featured in an episode of the Netflix original series House of Cards, with President Frank Underwood, played by Kevin Spacey, playing the game in the White House. Gray explained that the show's producers had contacted them six months prior to ask for permission to use the game, to which they readily agreed.

The exposure has had a significant impact on the game's downloads, with Gray stating that they saw an eight-fold increase in downloads last week. "It's insane, we never thought it would have that kind of effect," he said. The game has already been downloaded around 2.5 million times, generating over $5.8 million in revenue.

Despite the game's massive success, Gray insists that it was not just luck that contributed to its popularity. "A lot of hard work went into coming up with an idea and a concept that we thought would really resonate with people," he said. The game's unique design and engaging gameplay have earned it numerous awards, including an Apple Design Award and iPad Game of the Year.

UsTwo Games has also been working on new projects, including a design for in-car displays. Gray hinted that the company is committed to surprising people with their innovative designs, stating, "The idea that the creators of Monument Valley can produce something beautiful for cars is going to surprise you every single time." With their BAFTA wins and presidential endorsement, the team behind Monument Valley is certainly basking in glory, and their future projects are eagerly anticipated.

Tensions Run High at JNU as Students Protest Sedition Charges Against Union Leader

The Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) campus is abuzz with passion and protest as hundreds of students gather near the main administrative block to demand the release of their union leader, Kanhaiya Kumar. The air is filled with slogans such as "Free Kanhaiya Kumar" and "Long live revolution" as students express their outrage over the sedition charges levelled against him. The police arrested Mr. Kumar on Saturday, alleging that he organized an event commemorating the hanging of 2001 Parliament attacks convict Afzal Guru, where "anti-India slogans" were raised.

The students are adamant that Mr. Kumar is innocent and that the charges against him are baseless. They claim that he had nothing to do with the anti-India slogans raised at the event and that he is being unfairly targeted. Many students are visibly agitated and are demanding that the charges against Mr. Kumar be dropped. However, they are also fearful of speaking out, with many refusing to speak on camera citing concerns for their safety.

Student activist Shreya Ghosh spoke of the fear prevailing inside the university, stating that many students have been sleeping in different rooms every night to avoid arrest. Another student activist, Deepshita, claimed that ideological politics lies at the heart of Mr. Kumar's arrest, suggesting that right-wing students are trying to increase their foothold in the university and are using the sedition charges as a means to silence their opponents.

The protests have been marked by fiery speeches, with many speakers attacking Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his BJP party. Professor Ajith Kanna, one of the speakers, told the cheering crowd that if Kanhaiya is anti-national, then he is also anti-national. He pleaded with the students to remain peaceful and not pay attention to rumors, which are flying across the tension-filled campus.

Not everyone is protesting, however. Some students, such as PhD students Bibas Sewa and Bijay Thapa, condemn the arrest of Mr. Kumar but agree that the protests have disrupted their studies. They just want to get on with their work, unaffected by the politics that has gripped the campus.

In a separate interview, Saurabh Kumar, a member of the right-wing student group Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), stated that the law will decide whether Mr. Kumar is guilty or not, but they will not tolerate anti-India activities inside the campus. The ABVP has been at odds with the JNU student union, which is dominated by left-wing groups.

As the protests continue, it remains to be seen how the situation will unfold. The JNU administration has called for calm and has urged the students to refrain from violent protests. The police have also increased their presence on campus, leading to fears of further clashes. One thing is certain, however - the students of JNU will not back down without a fight, and the controversy surrounding Kanhaiya Kumar's arrest will continue to simmer for some time to come.
