Reforms to the Judicial Pension Scheme are set to reduce the generosity of the scheme, bringing it more in line with other public sector pensions. The changes, which will come into effect in 2015, will affect new and younger judges, who will receive lower pensions and will no longer be eligible for large lump sums upon retirement.

However, judges who were within 10 years of retirement as of April 2012 will be exempt from the changes, and will continue to receive the more generous pension benefits. This means that many older judges will be spared the reductions, while their younger colleagues will face a less generous retirement package.

According to the Ministry of Justice, the current scheme is one of the most generous in the country, offering judges a pension of half their final salary after just 20 years of service, plus a lump sum of two and a quarter times their annual pension. For example, a High Court judge who retired after 20 years could currently receive an annual pension of £86,500, plus a lump sum of £173,000 after tax.

Under the new scheme, however, this would be reduced to £75,000 per year, with no lump sum. Additionally, judges will have to pay an annual allowance tax charge of £11,000 per year, due to the rate at which their pension pot builds up exceeding the forthcoming limit of £40,000 per year.

The changes are part of a broader effort to reform public sector pensions, which have been criticized for being too generous. The government has argued that the reforms are necessary to ensure the long-term sustainability of the pension system, and to bring public sector pensions more in line with those offered in the private sector.

Justice Minister Chris Grayling has defended the changes, saying that the new pension arrangements will "continue to provide a good way of saving for retirement" and that the judicial pension scheme will remain "among the most generous in the public sector." However, the reforms are likely to be unpopular with many judges, who will see their pension benefits reduced as a result of the changes.

The normal pension age for judges will also rise in line with the state pension age, to 66, 67, and eventually 68 in the coming decades. However, judges will no longer have their pension accrual capped at 20 years, and will be credited with pension for as many years as they work. Despite the reductions, the judicial pension scheme will still be considered one of the most generous in the public sector, and will continue to provide a good level of retirement benefits for judges.

Around 1,700 jobs were lost when SSI went into liquidation. Some staff remain to maintain the site, including coke ovens. Additional fuel supplies have been purchased, and the official receiver is in talks with interested parties about the site's future, keeping hopes of production restart alive.

Wigan Warriors' Hooker Waterworth is set to make his first team debut on Monday if selected. Meanwhile, Hull KR has been hit with injuries, losing Chris Clarkson, James Green, Albert Kelly, and Josh Mantellato. They have been replaced by Will Oakes, Kieran Moran, Joe Wardill, and Joe Cator, who has impressed in training sessions. Cator has been handed a squad number after his performances for the City of Hull Academy. Both teams have announced their 19-man squads, with Wigan's including Bateman, Tomkins, and Sarginson, and Hull KR's featuring Allgood, Blair, and Boudebza. The match is expected to be intense with both teams looking for a win.

Yr Ysgwrn, the former home of renowned Welsh poet Hedd Wyn, has been secured for the nation thanks to grants from the Welsh government and the National Heritage Memorial Fund (NHMF). The Grade II* listed building, located near Trawsfynydd, is a significant cultural and historical landmark, and its preservation is a major achievement.

Hedd Wyn, whose real name was Ellis Humphrey Evans, was a celebrated bard who tragically lost his life in World War I. His poem, "Yr Arwr" (The Hero), was posthumously awarded the prestigious Black Chair at the National Eisteddfod in 1917. The chair, which is housed at Yr Ysgwrn, is a poignant reminder of the poet's talent and sacrifice.

The house, which has been lovingly maintained by Hedd Wyn's nephew, Gerald Williams, will now be looked after by the Snowdonia National Park Authority. The authority plans to develop a heritage centre and agricultural unit on the site, which will showcase the life and work of Hedd Wyn, as well as the history and culture of rural Wales during the early 20th century.

First Minister Carwyn Jones announced the news on St David's Day, saying, "Hedd Wyn, his work and his tragic death give him a special place in both the history and culture of our nation." He added that the preservation of Yr Ysgwrn is particularly significant as the country approaches the 100th anniversary of the start of World War I.

Dr. Manon Williams, NHMF trustee for Wales, described the project as "very important," saying, "Like so many, Hedd Wyn paid the ultimate price and came to symbolise the loss of an entire generation." She added that his poetry, along with other writing inspired by his death, stands as a poignant testament to the culture of his age.

Gerald Williams, who had promised his grandmother to keep the door open as a way of paying respect to his uncle's bravery and success, welcomed the news. "By transferring Yr Ysgwrn to the careful care of the park authority, I know that my promise to my grandmother will be kept and respected, and that Yr Ysgwrn and the Gadair Ddu will stay together as a unit," he said.

The Snowdonia National Park Authority plans to develop the heritage centre, which will focus on the life of Hedd Wyn, World War I, poets and writers from the period, social life in rural Wales, and sustainable land management practices. The centre will also highlight the importance of biodiversity and the unique cultural heritage of the area.

Around 3,000 people visit Yr Ysgwrn each year, by appointment only. The park authority plans to continue this arrangement for at least the next four years, while finalizing plans for the future development of the site. The preservation of Yr Ysgwrn is a significant achievement, and it will ensure that the legacy of Hedd Wyn and his remarkable poetry continues to inspire future generations.

Nigeria's Super Eagles Overcome Adversity to Top World Cup Qualifying Group

The Nigerian national football team, led by captain Mikel, has once again demonstrated its resilience and determination in the face of adversity. Despite arriving in Zambia just 22 hours before their crucial 2018 World Cup qualifier on October 9, the team managed to secure a hard-fought 2-1 victory, solidifying their position at the top of Group B.

This is not the first time the Super Eagles have had to contend with challenging circumstances. At the 2016 Olympics in Brazil, the team arrived in Manaus just hours before their first match due to transport issues, yet still managed to win the bronze medal. Mikel, who was a key member of that Olympic team, reflected on the experience, saying, "I don't think anything can beat the problems that we faced at the Olympics. I think it's a miracle that we performed the way we did."

While the team's unorthodox journey to Olympic bronze was a remarkable achievement, Mikel acknowledges that the current situation is different, but the underlying issues remain the same. "I wouldn't say it's the same problem we are facing now, but it is still the same issues that need to be sorted out," he said.

As a seasoned veteran with 72 appearances for Nigeria, Mikel is well aware of the importance of hitch-free preparations in ensuring the team's success. "For us to succeed, we need to put things in place as early as possible and let the players focus on football, and not dealing with issues like flight and other things off the pitch," he emphasized.

Mikel's experience and leadership have been instrumental in keeping the team focused and motivated, despite the challenges they face. He has taken it upon himself to shield his teammates from the distractions and controversies that often surround Nigerian teams, including pay rows and bonus disputes. "I try to take in all the problems, I deal with it myself and I only speak to the players when there is good news," he revealed.

As the most experienced player in the current squad, Mikel is determined to use his influence to avert any potential conflicts and ensure that the team remains united and focused on their goal of qualifying for the 2018 World Cup. With his guidance, the Super Eagles are well-placed to clinch the group's sole ticket to Russia, and Mikel is confident that his team can overcome any obstacle that comes their way.

The victory over Zambia has given Nigeria a significant boost in their qualifying campaign, and Mikel is eager to build on this momentum. With his wealth of experience and leadership, he is well-equipped to navigate the challenges that lie ahead and lead his team to success. As he looks to the future, Mikel remains committed to his role as captain and is determined to make a positive impact on the team's fortunes.

Inmates in several high-security prisons across the UK have been found in possession of al-Qaeda's publication Inspire, according to the Ministry of Justice. The extremist magazine was discovered in prisons in Durham, London, Manchester, and Milton Keynes over the past five years. Justice minister Sam Gyimah stated that the government will not tolerate such material in prisons, and each copy was promptly removed. The possession of Inspire can be a criminal offense under the Terrorism Act 2006 or the Offender Management Act 2007. The figures were released in response to a parliamentary question, revealing instances of discovery at Belmarsh Prison, HMP Manchester, HMP Woodhill, and HMP Frankland between 2011 and 2015. The government has reaffirmed its commitment to preventing the spread of extremist ideology in prisons.

A comical mix-up has ensued after Kent Police released a suspect image in connection with a robbery, only to be met with ridicule from the public. The image, posted on the force's Facebook page, appears to show a man with an exaggerated "extra sideburn" and a resemblance to a Stone Age character, prompting humorous comments from viewers.

The image was released in relation to a robbery that occurred on September 26 in Cliftonville, Margate, where a 75-year-old man was targeted in an alleyway. Despite the seriousness of the incident, the public's response to the suspect image has been largely lighthearted, with many joking about the suspect's apparent prehistoric appearance. Over 100 people have shared the image, with dozens leaving amusing comments, including comparisons to the Flintstones character Fred Flintstone. Kent Police has declined to comment on the response, but the incident serves as a reminder of the challenges faced by law enforcement in releasing accurate and helpful suspect images. The investigation into the robbery remains ongoing.

British Superbike Championship contender Christian Iddon has expressed his interest in making the switch to road racing, with the Ulster Grand Prix being his preferred starting point. The 32-year-old, who currently rides for the Tyco BMW team, has been considering a move to road racing for some time and believes that the Ulster circuit would be an ideal introduction to the sport.

Iddon, a former 10-times British Supermoto champion, is drawn to the thrill and excitement of road racing, citing the "immense" buzz he gets from competing on circuits. He is keen to experience the unique challenge of racing on public roads, but is also mindful of his commitments to the British Superbike Championship. With a strong desire to win a title in the series, Iddon must weigh up the potential benefits of competing in road racing events against the potential distraction from his short circuit goals.

Should Iddon decide to make the jump to road racing, he could have the backing of one of the most successful teams in the sport, Tyco TAS. The team, owned by Philip and Hector Neill, has enjoyed numerous successes at the Ulster Grand Prix with riders such as Ian Hutchinson, Guy Martin, and Bruce Anstey. Iddon believes that with Tyco's support, he would be in "seriously good hands" and would have a strong chance of success on the roads.

However, it remains to be seen whether Iddon will be given the green light to compete in the Ulster Grand Prix. While Hector Neill is reportedly keen for Iddon to make his road racing debut, Philip Neill is more cautious, preferring Iddon to focus on the short circuits. Ulster Grand Prix Clerk of the Course Noel Johnston is optimistic that Iddon will make the switch, commenting that he would be "very, very quick" on the roads and would be a great addition to the paddock.

With his talent and experience on short circuits, Iddon has the potential to be a top contender in road racing. If he can secure the backing of Tyco TAS and balance his commitments to the British Superbike Championship, he could be a major player in the sport. As the racing world waits with bated breath to see if Iddon will make the switch, one thing is certain - he would be an exciting addition to the road racing scene.

Uber Secures Funding from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund

In a significant move to expand its operations in the Middle East, Uber has secured a substantial investment from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. The funding, which values Uber at $62.5 billion, will be used to further establish the company's presence in the region, particularly in Saudi Arabia where 80% of its users are women. Notably, women are currently banned from driving themselves in the country, making ride-hailing services like Uber a vital mode of transportation.

As part of the investment, Yasir al-Rumayyan, a managing director of the Public Investment Fund, will join Uber's board. The company has announced plans to invest $250 million in the Middle East, where it has been aggressively expanding its services. The investment is part of Uber's latest fundraising round and demonstrates the company's commitment to growing its user base in the region.

The move comes as the European Commission warns against restrictions on "sharing economy" services like Uber and Airbnb. The Commission emphasizes that any restrictions should be proportionate to the public interest and only used as a last resort. With significant investments from various backers, including carmakers Toyota and Volkswagen, Uber is poised for continued growth and expansion in the global market.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi concluded his three-day visit to the UK with a tour of the Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) facility in the West Midlands. The plant, owned by India's Tata Motors, is producing the new Jaguar XE sports saloon. Modi was impressed by the "focus on technology, quality and innovation" at the facility.

Earlier in the day, Modi unveiled a statue of 12th Century Indian philosopher Basaveshwara on the bank of the River Thames. He also addressed the recent terror attacks in Paris, condemning them as "barbaric" and expressing his strongest opposition.

The visit was largely focused on trade, with the UK seeking to capitalize on India's rapid economic growth. India is now the fastest growing large economy in the world, and British Prime Minister David Cameron is eager to secure a share of the market. Modi, on the other hand, is promoting his "Make in India" policy, encouraging British firms to invest in his country.

The visit has seen the unveiling of £9bn worth of commercial deals between India and the UK. Modi was greeted with cheers from a 60,000-strong crowd at Wembley stadium, where he appeared on stage with Cameron. He also had lunch with the Queen at Buckingham Palace.

However, the visit has not been without controversy. Modi has faced protests over his record as chief minister of Gujarat, where he is accused of failing to prevent the 2002 religious riots that resulted in the deaths of over 1,000 people, mostly Muslims. Modi has consistently denied these allegations.

Despite the protests, Modi's visit is expected to enhance the partnership between India and the UK. The Indian Prime Minister will hope that the positive coverage of his visit, including his appearances at Buckingham Palace and Wembley stadium, will help improve his image back home, following a recent defeat in the state election in Bihar.

Redruth secured their largest win of the season and first away victory, scoring 10 tries. Coach Churcher praised the team, saying "the boys were awesome." Despite the impressive performance, Churcher expressed slight disappointment, citing high standards. The bonus-point win propelled Redruth to fourth in the division, seven points behind leaders Taunton. Churcher emphasized the importance of the away win, noting the team's successful execution of a fast and physical game plan from the start, achieving their desired style of play. This victory marks a significant milestone for the team.

Sir Fynwy: Sut i Fwrw ymlaen â'r Pwysau ar y Farchnad Dai

Mae Cynghorydd Peter Fox yn dweud bod angen i Sir Fynwy "gwrdd â'r her" o fod yn lle poblogaidd i fyw. Gyda thollau Pont Hafren yn disgwyl eu haneru yn 2018, mae prisiau tai yn y sir wedi bod yn cynyddu wrth i bobl o Fryste brynu tai yno. Mae Mr Fox yn gweld hyn fel cyfle enfawr i bobl a busnesau sir Fynwy, ond hefyd fel her i'w hwynebu.

Wrth i'r ardal ddod yn boblogaidd ac yn ddymunol, bydd pwysau ar farchnad dai ac ein isadeiledd. Mae Bryste, heblaw am Lundain, yn yr economi sydd yn tyfu fwyaf ym Mhrydain, ac mae prisiau tai yn codi yn gynt yno nag unrhywle arall yn y DU. Mae ardaloedd yn Sir Fynwy felly yn dod yn llefydd poblogaidd i bobl sydd yn fodlon cymudo. Mae gwerthwyr tai yn yr ardal yn dweud bod 80% o'r prynwyr bellach yn dod o ardal Bryste.

Mae ffigyrau'n awgrymu bod prisiau tai yn yr ardal wedi cynyddu'n gynt na'r cyfartaledd ar draws Cymru. Mae Mr Fox yn dweud: "Wrth i brisiau tai gynyddu bydd yn rhaid i ni allu darparu mwy o dai fforddiadwy er mwyn gwneud yn siŵr bod ein pobl ifanc lleol yn gallu aros yma. Mae hynny yn bryder." Mae angen isadeiledd ychwanegol fel meddygfeydd, ysgolion a ffyrdd mwy bydd yn cael eu hariannu gan y datblygwyr.

Mae yna gynlluniau i adeiladu tai yn hen ardal y dociau yng Nghas-gwent a ger yr ysbyty, tra bod stad o dai newydd am gael ei hadeiladu ger Magwyr. Gobaith Mr Fox yw y bydd y lleihad yn y tollau yn denu busnesau yn ôl i'r sir, a bydd pobl ifanc yn penderfynu aros yno. "Rwy'n gynhyrfus ynglŷn â'r swyddi ychwanegol o bosib y byddwn ni yn gallu creu," meddai. "Rydyn ni eisiau i'n plant gael y cyfleoedd i aros yma, i fagu teulu yma, a chael swyddi gyda chyflogau da yma, yn hytrach na'u bod yn gorfod gadael y sir i wireddu eu dyheadau."

Somerset all-rounder Craig Overton has been handed a suspension after being reported for a Level One offence during a Championship game. Umpires Alex Wharf and Ian Gould made the report, which has resulted in a three-point penalty. This is Overton's third such offence, triggering an automatic ban. He will miss Somerset's final County Championship match against Warwickshire and their first Championship game next summer. Teammate Rory Kleinveldt, who was also reported for a Level One offence, received a reprimand as it was his first breach. Overton's suspension comes at a crucial time, with Somerset still needing seven points to ensure safety. They face Warwickshire at home next week, with the visitors currently one place above them in the standings. Despite the setback, Overton was recently named in England's Performance Programme and Lions squad for the upcoming winter tour.

Drainage Work to Begin on A55 in Autumn

Drainage work is set to commence on a stretch of the A55 between junction 12, Tal-y-Bont, and junction 13, Abergwyngregyn, this autumn. The work, which is contingent upon landowner agreements, aims to alleviate flooding issues that have plagued the area, including a notable incident on Boxing Day that forced the closure of the road.

First Minister Carwyn Jones announced the plans during a visit to the Traffic Management Centre in Conwy, where he emphasized the importance of improving the road's resilience to flooding. A separate £1.9m flood alleviation scheme in Tal-y-Bont is also slated to begin in the spring, with completion expected before next winter.

The Tal-y-Bont scheme was promised by Mr. Jones during a visit to the village in January, where residents had been affected by flooding over Christmas. At the time, residents expressed frustration after Mr. Jones drove through the village without stopping, despite their expectations of a meeting. He later apologized, stating he was unaware of their expectations.

Regarding the A55 work, Mr. Jones acknowledged that the project requires careful planning due to its scale. He reassured motorists that the goal is not to create perpetual roadworks, but rather to ensure the tunnels are safe for the future. The A55 was originally built on a limited budget, and Mr. Jones noted that modern road construction standards would prioritize better design and resilience. With these improvements, the road will be better equipped to withstand flooding and other challenges, providing a safer and more reliable route for drivers.

Wales' Sporting Success Marred by Participation Concerns

Wales has celebrated a record-breaking haul of 10 medals at the Rio Olympics, surpassing the seven medals won at London 2012. However, despite this success, concerns have been raised about the nation's sporting participation and investment in grassroots sports. Baroness Tanni Grey-Thompson, a renowned Paralympic athlete, has expressed her doubts about Wales being a true "sporting nation," suggesting that it is more a nation that enjoys watching sports rather than actively participating in them.

In an interview with BBC Radio Wales' Sunday Supplement, Baroness Grey-Thompson emphasized the need for investment in schools and community facilities to encourage people to engage in sports. She noted that while events like Wimbledon may inspire people to take up tennis, sustaining their interest beyond the summer months is a significant challenge. "People call us a sporting nation, but I think we are a nation that really likes watching sport," she said. "But we can't change that and get people active without investment in places like schools."

Newport East AM and cabinet minister John Griffiths agreed that investment is crucial, stating that "money wins medals" and that elite athletics can inspire others to participate. However, he also stressed the importance of balancing investment in elite sports with community-focused initiatives to get more people physically active. Griffiths highlighted the need for schools to open their facilities to the public in the evenings and weekends, allowing more people to access sports facilities.

Meanwhile, Baroness Grey-Thompson has expressed her concerns about the upcoming Paralympics in Rio, citing budget cuts and logistical challenges that may impact the event's success. Despite assurances that the event will go ahead as planned, she fears that the cuts will hinder the Paralympics' ability to promote disability sports globally. "I'm not sure it will move the Paralympics movement on around the world," she said. "It won't change the world as I hoped it would." With the Paralympics just around the corner, Wales will be watching with bated breath, hoping that its athletes can build on their Olympic success and inspire a new generation of sports enthusiasts.

Advocate General for Scotland, Richard Keen QC, is facing charges for allegedly breaching the Firearms Act 1968. The incident occurred on December 31 last year at his home in Ann Street, Edinburgh, after a reported break-in. According to court papers, Lord Keen, 62, failed to safely secure a 12-bore shotgun, contravening the conditions of his firearms certificate.

The charge states that shotguns must be stored securely to prevent unauthorized access. A spokesman for Lord Keen expressed regret over the "inadvertent breach of licence conditions," describing it as a "one-off error." Lord Keen has held a firearms licence for many years and has always adhered to the conditions, as evidenced by multiple police inspections.

The case is scheduled to be heard at Edinburgh Sheriff Court on March 1. Police Scotland initially responded to a report of a housebreaking at Lord Keen's property, leading to the discovery of the alleged offence. A Police Scotland spokeswoman confirmed that a 62-year-old man had been reported to the procurator fiscal for a firearms licensing offence.

Lord Keen is a prominent figure in Scottish law, having served as the Dean of the Faculty of Advocates and being appointed Advocate General in May 2015. He recently represented the UK government in the Supreme Court hearing on triggering Article 50, successfully arguing that the Scottish Parliament's consent was not required before Brexit negotiations began. Lord Keen has also represented high-profile clients, including al-Amin Khalifa Fhima, who was acquitted of the Lockerbie bombing.

The UK government has stated that it is aware of the matter and is satisfied that it will not impact Lord Keen's ability to perform his ministerial duties. Despite the charge, Lord Keen remains in his position as Advocate General for Scotland. The incident highlights the importance of adhering to firearms licensing conditions, even for experienced licence holders like Lord Keen. The outcome of the case will be determined at the upcoming hearing in Edinburgh Sheriff Court.

Wikileaks Releases Thousands of Saudi Government Documents, Including Letter Regarding Bin Laden's Death

In a massive leak, Wikileaks has released over 60,000 Saudi government documents, including a letter from the US embassy in Saudi Arabia regarding the death of Al-Qaeda leader Osama Bin Laden. The letter, written by Consul General Glen Keiser in 2011, informs Abdullah Bin Laden, Osama's son, that a death certificate for his father cannot be provided.

The letter, dated September 9, 2011, explains that it is consistent with US practice not to issue death certificates for individuals killed in military operations. Instead, Keiser provides US court records that confirm Bin Laden's death, along with an Arabic translation as a "courtesy." The reason behind Abdullah Bin Laden's request for a death certificate is not specified.

The release of these documents is part of a larger leak, dubbed the "Saudi Cables," which Wikileaks claims will eventually include over 500,000 papers from the Saudi foreign ministry. The majority of the documents released so far are in Arabic, and they touch on a range of topics, including Iranian nuclear talks and the Egyptian revolution.

The leak is reminiscent of Wikileaks' 2010 release of US State Department cables, which first brought the organization to prominence. The release of the "Saudi Cables" comes three years to the day that Wikileaks founder Julian Assange sought refuge at the Ecuadorian Embassy in London, where he remains to this day, avoiding extradition to Sweden on rape and sexual assault charges.

It is not clear how Wikileaks obtained the documents, but the organization references a hack of the Saudi foreign ministry by the Yemeni Cyber Army in May 2015. Over the next month, Wikileaks plans to release hundreds of thousands of additional documents, shedding further light on the inner workings of the Saudi government.

A recent patrol operation targeting "collision hotspots" in the region resulted in 57 warnings and 43 fines for speeding. Two motorists were fined for driving at excessive speeds, 54mph and 52mph, in a 30mph zone. The operation focused on rural roads, including the A84/A85/A82 corridor, and stopped over 120 motorists. Two cars were seized due to lack of insurance, and additional fines were issued for invalid MOTs and unpaid vehicle tax. Sgt Adam Weir emphasized the goal of promoting road safety to reduce collisions and casualties, and warned that authorities will continue to address dangerous behavior by all road users.

A British Columbia court has sentenced Brandon and Gail Blackmore to a combined 19 months in jail for their role in taking a 13-year-old girl across the border to marry the leader of a fundamentalist Mormon sect. The pair, who are former spouses, were convicted in February of transporting a minor for sexual purposes.

Brandon Blackmore, 71, received a 12-month jail sentence, while Gail Blackmore was given seven months. Both were also handed 18 months' probation. The girl was married to Warren Jeffs, the 60-year-old leader of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, which is based in Bountiful, British Columbia.

Jeffs, who refers to himself as a prophet, has been sentenced to life in prison in the US for sexually assaulting underage girls. The sect, which has approximately 10,000 members, believes polygamy is the key to heaven and has been the subject of controversy and scrutiny in recent years.

The Blackmores' case dates back to 2004, when they brought the 13-year-old girl to Utah to marry Jeffs. The sect's practices were exposed in 2008, when police raided their Texas compound and found numerous underage girls who were pregnant or had given birth. Polygamy is illegal in Canada and the Western world, and the Blackmores' sentencing serves as a reminder of the consequences of such actions.

Sweden's Supreme Court has upheld the arrest warrant for WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange, issued in 2010 for allegations of sexual assault. Assange, 43, has been residing at the Ecuadorean embassy in London since June 2012, seeking to avoid extradition. The court's decision means Swedish investigators will likely proceed with plans to question Assange in London.

Assange denies the allegations, claiming they are part of a plot to extradite him to the US due to WikiLeaks' publication of classified documents. However, he has not been charged with any crime in the US, and no extradition request has been made. Assange's lawyer, Per Samuelson, expressed disappointment with the court's decision, stating that it was made without allowing them to fully argue their case.

The ruling comes as no surprise, as the court saw no reason to lift the warrant with plans already in place to question Assange in London. The Australian-born Assange has been living in a small suite of rooms at the embassy since requesting asylum in 2012. The allegations against him stem from a trip to Sweden in August 2010, where two women accused him of sexual assault.

A man from Pembrokeshire is appealing a court decision after he fell 20ft from a hotel balcony in Tenerife while trying to reach his room to let his wife use the toilet. Philip Clay, from Milford Haven, was on a Thomson package holiday with his family at the 4-star Guayarmina Princess hotel in July 2011. After a night of drinks with his parents on their balcony, Mr. Clay and his wife, Valerie, found themselves locked out, and she urgently needed to use the bathroom.

In an effort to avoid embarrassment, Mr. Clay, who was wearing only his pyjama bottoms, attempted to climb to his own balcony next door, where he knew the door was unlocked. However, he misjudged a decorative cornice, thinking it was a solid concrete ledge, and fell two floors to the ground below. The cornice, made largely of polystyrene, collapsed under his weight, leaving him knocked unconscious and lying in a pool of blood for 30 minutes.

Mr. Clay, a fire safety and security officer, has since recovered from his injuries. He is now appealing a decision by Cardiff County Court, which dismissed his claim for damages against TUI UK Ltd, the company that operated the hotel. The court had ruled that the cornice was not part of the balcony and did not require a warning sign. However, Mr. Clay argues that the hotel breached safety standards and that the cornice should have been weight-bearing or featured a warning sign.

The case was heard at the Court of Appeal in London, where Lady Justice King reserved her judgment. Mr. Clay's lawyer argued that the hotel had a responsibility to ensure the safety of its guests, and that the decorative cornice posed a significant risk. The court will deliver its ruling at a later date, which will determine whether Mr. Clay is entitled to damages for his injuries. The case highlights the importance of hotel safety and the need for clear warnings and safeguards to prevent accidents.

Emma Rice, the newly appointed artistic director of the London theatre, has spoken out about the harsh criticism she has faced since taking on the role in January. According to a report by The Stage, Rice expressed her frustration with the negative press she has received, stating that critics do not use the same language when discussing male directors. She made these comments during a panel discussion at the Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, organized by Tonic Theatre, which aimed to celebrate successful female theatremakers.

Rice's remarks came in response to a suggestion by Tonic founder Lucy Kerbel that she had received an unusual amount of negative coverage compared to other new artistic directors. Rice acknowledged that she had been protected from the worst of the criticism due to her decision to avoid social media and limit her reading of reviews. However, she emphasized the importance of developing a thick skin and trusting one's instincts in the face of adversity.

The criticism Rice has faced has been fierce, with some reviewers accusing her of "wrecking" the Globe's success story. When asked if she believed that loud and opinionated women attracted more criticism, Rice denied being either loud or opinionated, stating that she was simply doing her job to the best of her ability. She questioned whether the same criticism would be leveled against a male director, highlighting the double standard that often exists in the industry.

Rice also shared a personal anecdote about being referred to as "naughty" by a figure high up in the arts, which she felt was a patronizing and sexist comment. She wondered if the same word would be used to describe a male director, further emphasizing the need for greater equality and respect in the industry.

Despite the challenges she has faced, Rice remains committed to her vision and artistic direction. When asked what advice she would give to directors who may receive similar criticism, she emphasized the importance of perseverance and self-belief. She noted that every great artist has faced criticism at some point in their career and that it is a natural part of the creative process.

Rice's comments have sparked a wider conversation about the treatment of women in the arts and the need for greater equality and respect. As a prominent figure in the industry, Rice's experiences and insights serve as a reminder of the challenges that many women face in achieving success and recognition in their field. By speaking out and sharing her story, Rice hopes to inspire and empower other women to pursue their passions and push against the boundaries of what is expected of them.

Doncaster Belles manager Andy Butler's departure was reported by BBC Sport. The team, promoted last season, currently sits bottom of the Women's Super League One after three losses. They face Notts County on June 26 following a month-long break, seeking to turn their season around after defeats by top teams.

Hearts Ready to Take on Aberdeen After Recovering from Gastroenteritis Outbreak

Hearts head coach Robbie Neilson has confirmed that his team is ready to face Aberdeen on Friday evening after a bout of gastroenteritis left the Edinburgh club with "few fit players" earlier in the week. The illness forced the postponement of their previous match, but Neilson is confident that his players have fully recovered and are raring to go.

The team's Riccarton training base was closed on Tuesday and Wednesday to prevent the bug from spreading further, with players instead doing individual workouts at their own gyms. Despite the disruption to their preparation, Neilson is optimistic about his team's chances against Aberdeen, who are currently 12 points ahead of third-placed Hearts.

Hearts have a game in hand over Aberdeen, and Neilson believes that if they can win on Friday, they can overhaul the Dons and challenge for second place. "It's a huge game," he said. "Aberdeen are desperate to win to keep close to Celtic and we're desperate to win to keep close to Aberdeen." The return of full-back Callum Paterson from a shoulder injury is also a boost to the team. With a full house expected at Tynecastle, Neilson is confident that his team will have the energy and momentum to take on Aberdeen and come out on top.

Scotland Edges Out Namibia in Rain-Affected World Cricket League Match

The World Cricket League match between Scotland and Namibia was halted twice by rain on Sunday, but the home team managed to secure a win. Scotland finished their innings on 268-5, with Richie Berrington scoring an impressive 110, his highest score in a one-day international. Namibia, who opted to field first after winning the toss, reached 26-0 before play was abandoned due to rain.

The match resumed on Monday, with Namibia scoring 217 from 39.4 overs. Zhivago Groenewald top-scored for the visitors with 42 before being caught by Calum MacLeod. Scotland captain Kyle Coetzer praised Berrington's performance, saying it was a "fine knock" and that the team's batting and bowling lineup is showing promise. Coetzer noted that Berrington's achievement was even more impressive given the challenging weather conditions, which forced him to come on and off the field multiple times.

The two teams will meet again on Tuesday at Edinburgh's Grange for their second WCL match. Scotland will be looking to build on their win, while Namibia will aim to bounce back from their defeat. With a strong batting and bowling lineup, Scotland is poised to make an impact on the international scene. The team's captain is confident in their abilities, citing a "pack of bowlers" and batters who are coming into their prime.

A Mother's Desperate Plea: Terminally Ill Candidate Highlights Healthcare Crisis in Northern Ireland

In a powerful display of determination and conviction, Melanie Kennedy, a mother of two from County Down, ran as an independent candidate in last week's election, polling an impressive 1,246 first preference votes in North Down. Despite her terminal cancer diagnosis, Kennedy felt compelled to take a stand against the state of the health service and the lack of stable government in Northern Ireland.

Kennedy's journey into politics began when she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2013. Initially optimistic about her recovery, she was later told that the cancer had spread to her liver, leaving her with a terminal prognosis. However, it was the discovery that patients in Northern Ireland cannot access the same specialist drugs as those in England that drove her to take action. "For someone in my situation who is on quite harsh treatment, I was driven to this - it took a lot for me to act and create a campaign, but I felt I had to try and fight for justice for cancer patients," she explained.

Kennedy's campaign highlighted the critical issues affecting the health service, including the lack of access to cancer drugs, lengthy waiting lists, and inadequate mental health support. Her message resonated with many, who share her concerns about the future of healthcare in Northern Ireland. "With no government and no health minister, it makes me feel like there's no one there to fight my corner. It's heartbreaking," she said.

The ongoing political impasse in Northern Ireland has prevented vital health and social care decisions from being made, leaving patients like Kennedy feeling abandoned. Health organizations have warned that the continued lack of government is having a devastating impact on the healthcare system, with many patients being denied access to life-saving treatments.

Kennedy's experience has given her a unique perspective on the healthcare crisis, and she is adamant that something needs to change. "The health service in Northern Ireland was already behind other parts of the UK, there was a lack of long-term stability and strategy, and now we're back to square one. It is the ordinary people like me who are suffering," she said.

As Kennedy faces her own mortality, she is desperate to see action taken to address the healthcare crisis. "Time is a luxury that I and other people who are terminally ill cannot afford. The reason I started all this was that I asked myself, 'where do I turn?' I could be told in the next couple of months, there's no more treatment for me, and I should go home and make my plans and say goodbye to my children," she said, her voice filled with emotion.

Kennedy's plea is simple: she wants to see a comprehensive cancer strategy implemented, one that prioritizes early treatment and access to specialist drugs. "Early treatment is critical - it can mean the difference between getting well and going on with your life and ending up in my shoes. I don't want anyone else ending up in my shoes," she said.

As the people of Northern Ireland await the formation of a new government, Kennedy's story serves as a poignant reminder of the human cost of political indecision. Her bravery and determination have inspired many, and her message will undoubtedly continue to resonate with those who are fighting for a better healthcare system.

Tragedy Strikes Mount Manaslu as Avalanche Claims Lives of Climbers

A devastating avalanche on Mount Manaslu has resulted in the recovery of two bodies, with a further seven spotted by rescue pilots. The avalanche struck a base camp near the summit on Saturday, catching climbers off guard as they prepared to ascend to the 8,156m high peak. Among the dead is a Spanish national, according to the Spanish foreign ministry, while four of the deceased and three of the missing are French nationals.

At least five climbers have been rescued and flown to hospitals by rescue helicopters, with two of them being French nationals. However, deteriorating weather conditions have hindered further air searches, with police officials forced to suspend operations on Sunday. The climbers were hit at an altitude of 7,000m (22,960ft) as they were preparing to head towards the summit.

The avalanche has highlighted the dangers of climbing in the Himalayas, with Manaslu considered one of the most treacherous mountains in the world. Dozens of deaths have occurred on the mountain in recent years, and the autumn climbing season, which began this month, has gotten off to a tragic start. Hundreds of foreign climbers flock to Nepal every year to tackle the country's eight highest mountains, including Mount Everest. As the search for missing climbers continues, the incident serves as a sobering reminder of the risks involved in high-altitude climbing.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has announced a temporary reprieve for citizens who have been subject to a controversial tax decree. The decree, which was adopted in 2015, requires individuals who work fewer than 183 days per year to pay a tax of approximately $250 as compensation for lost tax revenues. However, Lukashenko stated that those who fall into this category will not be liable for the tax in 2017.

The decision comes after mass protests erupted last month, with more rallies planned for March. Lukashenko emphasized that the decree will not be scrapped, but rather adjusted during March. He also announced that individuals who paid the tax in 2016 will be fully compensated if they find employment next year.

Despite the concession, Lukashenko warned that authorities will take a "tough reaction" to organizers of future street protests against the decree. The move is seen as an attempt to quell dissent and maintain control in a country where little opposition is tolerated. Lukashenko has been in power since 1994 and has been described by some as "Europe's last dictator." However, he has recently sought to improve ties with the West and reduce dependence on Russia. The tax decree has been a major point of contention, with only 50,000 of the 470,000 eligible individuals having paid the tax so far.

Libertarian Gary Johnson sparked controversy when asked about the crisis in Aleppo, responding with "What is Aleppo?" He later admitted to having a lapse in knowledge, but isn't the first White House candidate with knowledge gaps, raising questions about their preparedness for the role.

Violence Erupts in Kashmir as Militants Ambush Military Convoy

A standoff between security forces and militants in Kashmir has resulted in the deaths of two army captains, two other soldiers, and a civilian. The violence began on Saturday when up to four attackers ambushed a military convoy, before taking refuge in a government-run training institute. Despite efforts to dislodge them, the militants have continued to exchange gunfire with security forces, with part of the building catching fire.

About 100 students and staff were evacuated from the building on Saturday as it was encircled by troops. Security forces are preparing for a final assault on the institute, using reconnaissance drones to gather intelligence. The militants, described as "suspected anti-India rebels," had told civilians in the complex to move to a nearby hostel as they broke into the premises.

The region of Kashmir has been a flashpoint for over 60 years, with both India and Pakistan claiming it in its entirety. The two countries have fought two wars over the region, and intermittent exchanges of fire near the building could still be heard late on Sunday afternoon. Eyewitnesses report that as many as five gunmen may be holed up in the institute, with security forces working to bring the situation under control.

**Grenfell Tower Fire: Cladding Concerns Raised as Investigation Continues**

A devastating fire that engulfed the 24-storey Grenfell Tower in west London has raised concerns about the safety of the building's exterior cladding, which was installed during a recent renovation. According to BBC Newsnight, the cladding used on the tower had a polyethylene core, a type of plastic, instead of a more fire-resistant mineral core.

The renovation, which was completed in 2015 at a cost of nearly £9 million, included the installation of new cladding, replacement windows, and additional homes using vacant space in the building. Rydon, the company that completed the renovations, stated that the work met all fire regulations and building control and safety standards. However, experts have questioned the use of cladding with a polyethylene core, citing its potential to spread fires quickly.

Christopher Miers, managing director of specialist architects Probyn Miers, told Newsnight that the core of the cladding was "critical" in determining its fire safety. "I think attention on the cladding is because we've seen in the reports and the photographs, burning exterior of the building," he said. "And we've seen enormous areas where the exterior is destroyed." Matt Wrack, general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union, added that residents have the right to ask whether the cladding compromised the safety of the building and called for an "absolutely thorough investigation."

The cladding used on Grenfell Tower was sold under the brand Reynobond, which offers two different versions of the cladding - one with a plastic core and one with a mineral core. Newsnight understands that the version with a plastic core was used on the west London tower. Similar cladding has been linked to fires in high-rise buildings in France, the UAE, and Australia.

Residents of Grenfell Tower had previously raised concerns about the fire risk of the building, with the local Grenfell Action Group claiming that the block constituted a fire risk. They also warned that site access for emergency vehicles was "severely restricted". As recently as last weekend, residents were told to remain in their flats in the event of a fire, advice that has been called into question by the Fire Brigades Union.

The Kensington and Chelsea Tenant Management Organisation, which manages the tower on behalf of the council, stated that it is too early to speculate on the cause of the fire and its spread. However, the organisation has pledged to cooperate fully with the investigation. As the inquiry into the tragedy continues, concerns about the safety of similar buildings and the use of potentially flammable cladding are likely to grow.

Harley Facades, the company that fitted the panels to the building, has denied any link between the fire and the exterior cladding, stating that they are not aware of any connection. However, experts and residents are demanding answers about the safety of the building and the materials used in its renovation. The Grenfell Tower fire has raised important questions about building safety and the need for rigorous fire safety standards, and it is essential that a thorough investigation is conducted to determine the cause of this tragic event.

The FTSE 100 has kicked off the new year on a high note, rising 0.5% to close at 7,177.89 on the first trading day of 2017. This follows a record close of 7,142.83 on the final trading day of 2016. According to Neil Wilson at ETX Capital, "there are no January blues for equity markets" as traders return to their desks in an optimistic mood, carrying momentum from last week's Santa rally.

Banks and financial companies led the charge, with Hargreaves Lansdown surging 5% and Barclays up 3.78%. Changes to broker ratings also drove significant moves, with Intercontinental Hotels Group rising 1.3% after Barclays upgraded its rating to "overweight". Conversely, Halfords and Next were hit by downgrades from Deutsche Bank, falling 5.6% and 4.2% respectively.

Italian Prime Minister Matteo Renzi is facing a daunting year ahead, with his own political future hanging in the balance. Known for his bold ambitions to reform the Italian state, Renzi has set his sights on overhauling the country's parliament, aiming to streamline the system, cut costs, and bring about more stable government. However, his plans may ultimately lead to his own downfall.

At the heart of Renzi's reform efforts is a referendum scheduled to take place later this year, which seeks to reduce the powers of the Italian Senate. The prime minister has pledged to resign if the vote does not go in his favor, a promise that is starting to look increasingly realistic. With the UK's David Cameron having recently fallen victim to a referendum defeat, Renzi is not alone in putting his fate on the line in a public vote.

Renzi's rise to power in February 2014 was marked by a relatively easy first two years in office, during which he successfully commanded the center ground of Italian politics. However, the country is now experiencing a shift away from the center, with the populist Five Star movement gaining significant traction. Founded by comedian Beppe Grillo in 2009, Five Star has won support for its anti-establishment views, and recent opinion polls show that it has surpassed Renzi's center-left Democratic Party as the most popular party in Italy.

The Five Star movement's success has been bolstered by its victories in the mayoral elections in Rome and Turin, and it has now caught the referendum fever, calling for a vote on leaving the eurozone. While a general election is not expected until 2018, Italy's struggling economy and troubled banking sector may make it difficult for the country to reach that point in good shape.

The Italian economy is growing slowly, but its banks are struggling with a staggering €360 billion in bad loans. Monte dei Paschi di Siena, the country's oldest bank, is particularly troubled, and eurozone rules dictate that it cannot be bailed out by the Italian state unless its bondholders take losses first. Renzi has suggested that he will find a way around these rules, but it remains to be seen whether he will be able to navigate this complex situation successfully.

As Renzi faces numerous challenges, both self-inflicted and otherwise, his ability to push through his reform agenda and maintain his position as prime minister is increasingly uncertain. With the referendum on the horizon, the Italian people will soon have their say on Renzi's plans, and the outcome may ultimately determine the prime minister's own fate. Will Renzi be able to overcome the obstacles ahead and emerge victorious, or will his bold ambitions ultimately lead to his own downfall? Only time will tell.

Tragedy Strikes Esher Community as Mother and Daughter Found Dead

A devastating discovery was made in a gated community in Esher on Monday, as the bodies of 47-year-old Lisa Anthony and her 14-year-old daughter Ava were found at their residence. A post-mortem examination revealed that Mrs. Anthony died from a compression to the neck, while further tests are being conducted to determine the cause of Ava's death.

The news has sent shockwaves through the community, with Ava's head teacher, Fiona Boulton, describing her as a "wonderful, charming girl" with a "love of life that enriched everyone around her." Ava was a talented student, particularly excelling in drama and the performing arts. She was remembered as a warm, generous, and popular student who was a delight to be with.

Concerns had been raised about the mother and daughter's whereabouts after they had not been seen for nearly two weeks. The last confirmed sighting was on June 17. The case has been referred to the Independent Police Complaints Commission due to a call made to Surrey Police on June 24 by someone who knew Mrs. Anthony, expressing concerns for her welfare. Historic Strutt's Mills in Belper are facing a severe crisis due to significant water damage and disrepair. According to historian Roger Shelley, the mills are leaking badly, with missing window panes, blocked downpipes, and a leaking roof. The damage is extensive, and the costs of repair are multiplying by the day. 

Amber Valley Borough Council has expressed concern over the state of the buildings and is considering a compulsory purchase order to protect the Grade I listed North Mill and the Grade II listed East Mill. The council's report highlights the "significant damage" suffered by the mills, which were built by Jedediah Strutt, a key figure in the industrial revolution, in the 18th Century.

Despite the challenges, the owners, First Investment, claim to have a strategy in place to convert the mills into a mix of flats and retail space. However, Mary Smedley, a trustee of the Strutt's North Mill Trust, emphasizes the need for "serious TLC" to make the buildings viable for conversion. With the mills' rich history and UNESCO World Heritage Status, it is essential that a collaborative effort is made to restore them to their former glory.

Northern Ireland's World Cup qualifying campaign has been dealt a blow with the news that Stuart Dallas has returned to his club due to a calf injury. Laura Robson, the 19-year-old British tennis sensation, has made a triumphant return to the US Open, defeating Lourdes Dominguez Lino 7-5 6-0 in the first round. However, Robson's determination and skill ultimately paid off, as she secured a spot in the second round against Frenchwoman Caroline Garcia.

Robson will now face Caroline Garcia, who defeated American Shelby Rogers 6-3 6-2, in the second round. A 45-year-old man from Cwmbran has denied killing his daughter, Amelia Jones, who was left paralyzed and critically injured after an alleged attack in November 2012. Mark Jones, the defendant, was taking care of Amelia at the time of the incident in Pontnewydd. According to the prosecution, the attack may have been motivated by Jones's strong dislike for Amelia's father, Ian Skillern.

British cyclist Becky James is set to make her return to the international stage this weekend as she competes for Great Britain at the Track World Cup in New Zealand. "The nationals were only three weeks ago and obviously I'm looking forward to being back in the World Cup. **Bullying in Welsh Schools: A Persistent Problem**

A recent report has highlighted the ongoing issue of bullying in Welsh schools, with many institutions failing to effectively address the problem. According to Sally Holland, the Children's Commissioner for Wales, some schools are reluctant to tackle bullying due to fear of being perceived as having a problem. This reluctance has resulted in a lack of consistency in handling complaints, leaving some children feeling isolated and unsupported.

The report, titled "Sam's Story," gathered the experiences of 2,000 children and young people, as well as the views of 300 professionals. The findings revealed that children are often bullied due to differences such as ethnicity, poverty, disability, and gender stereotyping. Furthermore, many parents are unresponsive to their children's experiences of bullying, exacerbating the problem.

Dr. Holland expressed frustration that despite previous warnings from the schools inspectorate Estyn three years ago, the issues of confusion over what constitutes bullying and a lack of consistent recording remain unaddressed. "Some things have changed, but yes, there are some fundamentals we still need to get right," she said. "We do need to be recording bullying and make sure the best practice, which we know is out there, is available to schools."

The Welsh Government has stated that all forms of bullying should be tackled vigorously and that a school behavior policy should be in place by law. However, Dr. Holland argued that more needs to be done to ensure that schools are effectively addressing the issue. She has called on the government to place a statutory duty on schools to record all incidences and types of reported bullying, as well as to develop a clear definition of bullying.

Dr. Holland emphasized the importance of schools having an honest conversation with their students and the wider community about how they are tackling bullying. "Let's not keep it in the corner as an embarrassing aspect of school life," she said. "Let's accept that it happens and positively move forward to tackle it." She also stressed that everyone, including parents, teachers, and the wider community, needs to be involved in addressing the issue of bullying.

The Welsh Government has stated that it will consider Dr. Holland's report as part of its review of anti-bullying guidance. A spokesman said, "We do not tolerate any bullying in the Welsh education system. We expect schools and education services to make it clear that all forms of bullying are entirely unacceptable and to tackle all incidents vigorously, ensuring that pupils are properly supported."

While the government's commitment to addressing bullying is welcome, Dr. Holland's report highlights the need for more concrete action to be taken. The fact that anti-bullying guidance often sits on shelves in schools, unread and unimplemented, is a stark reminder of the work that still needs to be done to ensure that all children in Wales feel safe and supported in their schools. By working together, schools, parents, and the wider community can help to create a culture where bullying is not tolerated and all children can thrive.

Violence Erupts Between Wolves and Birmingham City Fans After Match

A clash between Wolverhampton Wanderers and Birmingham City fans near Wolverhampton railway station on Friday night has sparked a police investigation. The incident occurred after Wolves' 2-1 defeat, with West Midlands Police reporting that officers were forced to intervene to quell disorder. According to the police, Wolves supporters threw bottles, seats, and coins following Birmingham City's second goal, prompting a response from law enforcement.

Thirteen arrests were made on the night, with eight men believed to be Birmingham City supporters and five thought to be Wolves fans. However, a Birmingham fan who witnessed the incident has raised concerns about the use of force by police officers. Nick Glynn, a former police officer with 30 years of experience, claimed to have filmed "potentially unlawful violence" by officers. He stated that he saw an officer striking a fan with a baton, which he believes was excessive and unjustified.

Glynn, who has trained police in the use of force, said that the threat level required to justify such action is very high and that the officers' response seemed disproportionate. "Somebody could've died from getting struck on the head with a baton, and my question would be, for what? For maybe not walking quite quickly enough to a railway station?" he asked.

West Midlands Police match commander, Chief Inspector Nick Rowe, defended the officers' actions, saying that they had issued several warnings to no avail and used "proportionate force" to prevent further clashes and protect fans. He stated that the incident was "isolated" and that officers had to take action to maintain order. The police have launched an investigation into the two incidents and will review any complaints received.

The force is also working to identify those responsible for throwing missiles inside the stadium and those involved in trouble near the station. The incident has raised concerns about fan safety and the use of force by police officers. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) will be consulted as part of the investigation, and any complaints will be reviewed by the West Midlands Police professional standards department.

UK Borrowing Falls to Lowest May Total Since 2007, But Economists Remain Cautious

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) has announced that public sector borrowing, excluding support for state-owned banks, has fallen to £9.7 billion in May, the lowest total for the month since 2007. This figure is down £0.4 billion from the same month last year, but slightly higher than the forecasted £9.5 billion by economists.

Despite this decrease, borrowing for the financial year so far, covering April and May, has reached £17.9 billion, which is £0.2 billion higher than the same period last year. The ONS has also revised down its estimate of the amount borrowed in the 2015-16 financial year to £74.9 billion.

The government's total current expenditure rose, but receipts from income, corporation, and VAT taxes in May were all higher than a year earlier. The total public sector net debt, excluding banks, stood at £1.606 trillion by the end of May, equivalent to 83.7% of gross domestic product (GDP).

While annual borrowing has been falling in general since the peak reached in the 2009-10 financial year, economists remain cautious about the government's ability to meet its projections. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) has estimated that the public sector will borrow £55.5 billion during the financial year to March 2017, a reduction of about £20 billion from the previous financial year.

Chancellor George Osborne has pledged to fix the public finances and return a budget surplus by 2020. However, the Treasury and Bank of England have warned that the economy has been hit by uncertainty ahead of the EU referendum. Scott Bowman, an economist at Capital Economics, said that the chancellor "still has a long way to go" to meet his projections, but noted that GDP growth could rebound in the second half of the year if the UK votes to remain in the EU.

Ross Campbell, public sector director at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW), criticized the chancellor for "taking his eye off the economic ball." He emphasized the need for a comprehensive strategy to kick-start a faltering economic recovery, regardless of the outcome of the EU referendum. As the UK awaits the results of the referendum, it remains to be seen how the government will respond to the challenges facing the economy and whether it can meet its ambitious targets for reducing borrowing and achieving a budget surplus.

Aberdeen Manager Derek McInnes Hopes to Retain Niall McGinn Beyond Summer

I think it's just maybe weighing up more what he wants to do next, whether he wants to stay for a bit longer, which we certainly hope is the case, or whether he wants to try something different."

McGinn has consistently expressed his love for the club and has enjoyed his time at Aberdeen. McInnes is hopeful that this affection, combined with the club's contract offer, will be enough to persuade McGinn to stay. "He's quite within his rights and we respect that," McInnes said. "What is clear is Niall has never at any point said that he wants to leave. He's always indicated his love for the club and how much he's enjoying it."

McGinn's performances on the pitch continue to impress, and his individual display in Aberdeen's 3-0 win over Dundee was a testament to his skill and dedication. The forward scored two goals and laid on the other, showcasing his quality and importance to the team. McInnes praised McGinn's first goal, describing it as "top drawer" and a "fantastic piece of individual play."

The win over Dundee moved Aberdeen up to second in the Premiership, and McInnes was pleased with his team's overall performance. "We had to wait longer than we hoped to get in front, but once we made the breakthrough, we brought some real quality," he said.

In contrast, Dundee manager Paul Hartley was left to lament his team's defensive shortcomings. "The start was promising, but after that, we didn't defend properly," Hartley said. "For us tonight, not to defend balls coming in, they seemed to switch off and not do their jobs. We've got to do the basics properly. For me, we've got to try and make it as difficult as possible. We didn't do that."

Hartley also acknowledged the challenges his team faces in terms of recruitment, citing financial constraints as a major obstacle. "We want to try and bring some players in, but it's not going to be easy," he said. "Financially, it's going to be difficult. We've enquired about some players, but we can't get them because of the financial side of it. We want to add quality, and we need to add quality."

As the transfer window remains open, McInnes and Aberdeen will be eager to resolve McGinn's contract situation and ensure the player remains at the club beyond the summer. With McGinn's talent and dedication, the Dons will be keen to retain his services and build on their current success in the Premiership.

Kiribati, a Small Island Nation with a Big Challenge

Located in the South Pacific, Kiribati, pronounced Kiribas, is a small island nation that gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1979. With a population of approximately 103,000 people, Kiribati is home to the largest marine reserve in the South Pacific. However, the country faces a significant challenge due to its low-lying atolls, which are at risk from rising sea levels caused by global warming.

To address this issue, the Kiribati government has taken proactive measures, including purchasing land in Fiji with the permission of the Fijian government. This move aims to ensure food security and provide a possible refuge for its citizens in the event of a climate-related disaster. The country's economy is largely dependent on exports of copra and coconuts, as well as fishing licenses, foreign aid, and remittances from workers abroad.

Kiribati's history dates back to the 11th century when Samoans, Fijians, and Tongans migrated to the islands. The country was named the Gilbert Islands in 1820, after British naval captain Thomas Gilbert, who visited the islands in 1788. In 1892, Britain declared a protectorate over the Gilbert Islands and the neighboring Ellice Islands, which later became the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony in 1916.

The country has a relatively stable political system, with President Taneti Mamau elected in March 2016. Freedom of speech and media is generally respected, with a government-run radio station and newspaper offering diverse views. The country has a trust fund set up with revenues from phosphate mines on the island of Banaba, which was depleted in 1980, causing significant economic hardship for Kiribati.

Despite the challenges it faces, Kiribati remains a significant player in the Pacific region. With its stunning marine reserve and rich cultural heritage, the country is working to balance its economic development with environmental sustainability. As the world grapples with the impacts of climate change, Kiribati's story serves as a reminder of the urgent need for global action to protect vulnerable island nations and their communities.

Abbot Cuthbert Madden of Ampleforth Abbey has denied any wrongdoing amid allegations of misconduct dating back to the 1990s. The 61-year-old Benedictine monk, who has been at the abbey for over 30 years, was voluntarily interviewed under caution by North Yorkshire Police. The allegations involve four pupils at Ampleforth College, the school attached to the abbey, where Abbot Madden previously taught. 

In a statement, the abbey said Abbot Madden will cooperate fully with the investigation and denied any wrongdoing. The police investigation, which was triggered by reports made in August, is ongoing and has led to safeguarding measures being put in place. Abbot Madden was elected as abbot in 2005 and re-elected in 2013. The abbey has chosen to be transparent about the situation, informing the Ampleforth community and friends about the current investigation. North Yorkshire Police confirmed that the investigation is continuing, with no further details released at this time.

A court challenge brought by Vue Cinemas against the City of York Council's decision to approve an expanded cinema at the Monks Cross stadium site has been dismissed. The council had initially approved a 12-screen design, but later gave permission for a 13th screen and 400 extra seats. The judge found that the decision-making process was correct, paving the way for the development to proceed.

The stadium, which is expected to become home to York City FC and York City Knights Rugby League Club, has suffered numerous delays since it was first proposed in 2009. The project was initially forecast to cost £37m and open in spring 2017, but is now expected to cost an additional £7m and will not be operational until next year.

The council has welcomed the court decision, describing it as a "great step forward" for the development. The stadium will also feature leisure, retail, office, and community facilities, in addition to the cinema and sports facilities. Vue Cinemas has not commented on the decision. Despite the setbacks, the council remains committed to seeing the project through to completion.

Tragedy of Young Father's Drowning Highlights Dangers of Swimming in Open Water

It's been over a decade since 21-year-old Dale Alexander tragically lost his life while swimming with friends in the River Mourne at Sion Mills. The young father, whose wife was pregnant at the time, was an experienced swimmer and angler, having spent his youth exploring the river. However, despite his knowledge of the water, Dale fell victim to the bitterly cold temperatures, with his body going into shock as he swam back across the river.

Brendan Winters, chairman of Strabane Lifford anglers and a childhood friend of Dale's, remembers the incident vividly. "Dale had swum across the river, got out of the water, and spoken to people on the far side. But as he was swimming back, his body went into shock," he said. "It just goes to show you that regardless of how well you think you know the water, it's really dangerous. You should never become complacent."

The tragedy has prompted warnings from Northern Ireland Water and the Quarry Products Association, urging people to stay away from areas that are not usually open to the public. Michael Bergin of NI Water emphasized the importance of taking precautions, stating that "while a reservoir may look like the perfect place to cool down, it can be very dangerous. You may swim well in a warm indoor pool, but that does not mean that you will be able to swim in cold water."

A 2010 inquest into Dale's death heard that his life could have been saved had life-saving equipment, such as life ropes and rings, been in place. Brendan Winters echoed this sentiment, saying that the absence of these safety measures may have contributed to the tragic outcome. Dale's legacy lives on through his two young sons, who were born after his passing and will never get to know their father. As Brendan poignantly noted, "Dale is never far from my thoughts. I wouldn't wish that on any other family or for anyone else to have to lose a friend like that."

Revolutionary Solar Cell Technology Takes to the Skies, Paving Way for Future Space Exploration and Renewable Energy

A groundbreaking solar cell, developed by the UK Space Agency and the Algerian Space Agency, is currently orbiting the Earth, generating electricity and offering a glimpse into a future where space-based solar power could become a reality. The tiny satellite, measuring just 30cm by 10cm by 10cm, is equipped with a solar cell that is a mere 0.1mm thick, making it significantly smaller than conventional solar cells.

The device is flying at an altitude of 450 miles (724km) and travelling at a staggering 17,000mph (27,359km), completing one orbit around the globe every 90 minutes. According to Dr Dan Lamb, from Swansea University's College of Engineering's Solar Energy Research Centre, the project has the potential to revolutionize space exploration and provide a renewable source of energy on Earth.

The solar cell's thin design and compact size make it an attractive option for space missions, where every kilogram of weight counts. With the cost of launching payloads into orbit running into thousands of pounds per kilogram, this new approach to space solar power could offer significant cost reductions. Over the course of the satellite's estimated year-long life, Dr Lamb and his team will be monitoring the amount of electricity generated by the solar cell, as well as its ability to withstand radiation and extreme temperature fluctuations in space.

The advantages of space-based solar cells are numerous. With approximately 30% more sunlight available in orbit, the cell can generate more energy than its ground-based counterparts. Additionally, the cell spends less time in darkness, making it a more efficient source of power. However, the team is still uncertain about how the complex solar materials will hold up to the sun's radiation without the protection of the Earth's atmosphere.

If the experiment is successful, the technology could have far-reaching implications for space exploration. Dr Lamb believes that it could be used to power future manned lunar or Mars bases, as well as provide electric propulsion for spacecraft. Moreover, the technology could also be used to create orbiting solar arrays that beam electricity back to Earth, providing a green and renewable source of energy.

The test satellite was launched from Southern India on 26 September and has already begun transmitting data back to scientists in Swansea and their collaborators at the University of Surrey and Qioptiq Space Technology Ltd. By this time next year, the team hopes to have a better understanding of the technology's potential and be one step closer to making space-based solar power a reality. As Dr Lamb noted, the project is already offering a tantalizing glimpse into the future, and its success could pave the way for a new era in space exploration and renewable energy.

New Research Sheds Light on the Formation of the Moon

For decades, scientists have believed that the Moon was formed from debris left over after a massive collision between the early Earth and a planet-sized object approximately 4.5 billion years ago. However, this theory, known as the giant impact hypothesis, has been challenged by the fact that the Earth and Moon have surprisingly similar chemical compositions. Recently, two new studies published in the journal Science have proposed innovative solutions to this long-standing conundrum.

One team, led by Matija Cuk from the Seti Institute, suggests that the early Earth may have been spinning much faster than it does today, with a rotation period of just a few hours. Using advanced simulations, the researchers found that this rapid rotation would have allowed debris from the Earth's mantle to be ejected into orbit, forming a Moon with a chemical composition similar to that of our planet. Over time, the gravitational interaction between the Sun and the Moon would have slowed the Earth's rotation to its current 24-hour period.

Another team, led by Robin Canup from the Southwest Research Institute, took a different approach. Their simulations involved larger impactors colliding with a smaller Earth at lower speeds. The results showed that this scenario could also produce a Moon with a chemical composition similar to that of the Earth. These new findings provide a significant breakthrough in our understanding of the Moon's formation and offer a fresh perspective on the giant impact hypothesis.

The giant impact hypothesis was first proposed in the 1970s and suggests that the Moon formed from debris kicked into orbit after a massive collision between the early Earth and a smaller proto-planet. While this theory has been widely accepted, it has been difficult to reconcile with the fact that the Earth and Moon have identical oxygen isotope compositions. The new research provides a compelling explanation for this similarity and offers a new avenue for exploring the early history of our solar system.

UK's Top Spy Agency Partners with Private Firms to Boost Online Security

In a bid to strengthen the country's online security, the UK's most secretive agency, GCHQ, has partnered with several private companies to launch a new cyber security hub in Cheltenham. The GCHQ Cyber Accelerator, which was launched on Wednesday, will provide a platform for start-ups to work closely with the agency's staff and resources to develop innovative solutions to combat cyber threats.

Among the companies selected for the program are StatusToday, which uses artificial intelligence to monitor workplace behavior and detect insider attacks, and CounterCraft, which runs decoy computers to fool hackers. These companies will have access to GCHQ's expertise and network of international partners, as well as a £5,000 grant each and access to government tenders.

The partnership is seen as a significant step forward in the UK's efforts to boost its £22bn cybersecurity sector. According to Prof Alan Woodward, a cybersecurity expert at the University of Surrey, the government recognizes that innovative ideas on cybersecurity are no longer limited to big companies. The accelerator program aims to attract new businesses to Cheltenham and provide a platform for start-ups to develop and test their products.

However, the partnership also raises concerns about security risks. Prof Anthony Glees, the director of the Buckingham University Centre for Security and Intelligence Studies, warned that working with the private sector could be a "twin-edged sword" for GCHQ. While it brings in new ideas, it also increases the risk of sensitive information being compromised. GCHQ has assured that all companies have undergone rigorous background checks and have been selected through a competitive process.

The launch of the GCHQ Cyber Accelerator is part of a broader effort to establish Cheltenham as a hub for cybersecurity innovation.
