The city is already home to a number of defence contractors working with GCHQ, and the new National Cyber Security Centre is also located there. With the support of the government and telecoms firm Telefonica, the accelerator program is set to play a key role in boosting the UK's cybersecurity sector and protecting the country from increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.

A recent report has revealed that the £465m of EU convergence money invested in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly between 2007 and 2013 has been deemed "poor value" by independent consultants. The investment, which was intended to boost the local economy, failed to deliver the expected results, with private sector investment coming in at £440m lower than anticipated.

Despite creating 3,557 jobs, the project has been widely criticized, with Kim Conchie, chief executive of the Cornwall Chamber of Commerce, describing the findings as "pretty damning". The report highlights that the cost per job in the research and development fund was a staggering £160,000 per person, raising serious questions about the effectiveness of the funding.

The region received €654m from the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) and European Social Fund due to its economic performance being below 75% of the European Union average. The funding was used to support various projects, including the construction of a link road at Camborne and the development of the Wave Hub at Hayle.

The ERDF convergence team has acknowledged that the targets set for the program were developed prior to the 2008 financial crisis, but argues that they were retained in order to aim high and achieve the best possible return on investment. However, the report's findings suggest that the uncertain economic climate had a significant impact on the project's performance, leading to "significant under-performance" in achieving its target results regarding jobs, Gross Value Added, and private sector investment. The lessons learned from this program will be carried forward into the next European Funding Programme.

Tottenham Hotspur have rejected a world-record £86m bid from Spanish giants Real Madrid for star player Gareth Bale. Despite the substantial offer, Spurs insist that no deal has been agreed, and they are in no rush to sell their prized asset. The north London club is aware that the sale of Bale could trigger a series of transfers that may ultimately benefit their rivals, including Arsenal, who have been linked with Real Madrid players Karim Benzema and Angel Di Maria.

The transfer window is set to close on September 2, and Tottenham is happy to wait and see how the situation unfolds. The club has already missed out on signing Brazilian midfielder Willian, who joined Chelsea for £30m after completing a medical at Tottenham. Spurs have been linked with Roma's Erik Lamela and Chelsea's Juan Mata, although Jose Mourinho has stated that the Spanish playmaker is not for sale.

Meanwhile, Bale failed to report for training on Tuesday, following a club-authorised break in Marbella. The reason for his absence is unknown, but it is believed that he is eager to secure a move to Real Madrid. The Spanish club has made two separate bids for the Welshman and is waiting to see if Tottenham will accept either offer. A special stage, nicknamed the "Bale Box," has been erected at the Bernabeu ground, reportedly to unveil Bale to the club's fans.

Real Madrid has already spent over £50m this summer, signing Spanish midfielders Asier Illarramendi and Isco from Real Sociedad and Malaga, respectively. The club's next home game is on Sunday against Athletic Bilbao, just a day before the transfer window closes. Bale, who joined Spurs in 2007, was named player of the year by both the Professional Footballers' Association and Football Writers last season after scoring 26 goals for the club. As the transfer saga continues, Tottenham remains firm in its stance, and it remains to be seen what the future holds for the talented Welshman.

Manchester City midfielder Yaya Toure has expressed his discontent with the criticism he has been receiving, stating that it has left him unhappy. In an interview with French sports magazine L'Equipe, the Ivorian captain revealed that winning trophies and earning a substantial amount of money has not brought him the happiness he desired. Toure feels that his name has been tarnished by "lots of bitter people" and is hurt by the lack of recognition for his performances. City manager Manuel Pellegrini has come to Toure's defense, citing his impressive performances over the last four years as proof of his importance to the team. Pellegrini acknowledged that Toure may have concerns about the criticism, but emphasized that it is separate from his overall happiness at the club. Toure has scored just one goal in 11 appearances this season, sparking criticism from some quarters.

Federal Charges Filed Against Suspect in New York and New Jersey Bombings

Ahmad Khan Rahami, the 28-year-old suspect in the recent bombings in New York and New Jersey, has been charged with federal offenses, including the use of a weapon of mass destruction, bombing, and use of a destructive device. The Afghan-born US citizen remains in hospital, recovering from gunshot wounds sustained during a police shootout on Monday.

The FBI complaint, unsealed on Tuesday in a Manhattan federal court, reveals that 31 people were injured in the Chelsea neighborhood of Manhattan on Saturday, including an unnamed Briton. The victims suffered severe injuries, with one woman requiring the removal of multiple ball bearings from her body, as well as metal fragmentation from her ear and wood shards from her neck.

According to the complaint, Rahami was found with a notebook containing writings that suggest a radical ideology. The journal includes passages that praise Osama Bin Laden, Anwar al-Awlaki, and Nidal Hasan, and references jihad and the mujahideen. The writings also express anger towards the US government, stating, "You [USA Government] continue your [unintelligible] slaught[er]" against holy warriors in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and Palestine.

The investigation has revealed that Rahami had been preparing for the attack for months, purchasing bomb-making equipment on eBay, including citric acid, a circuit board, and electric igniters for fireworks. The FBI also recovered video footage from a mobile phone belonging to one of Rahami's relatives, which shows the suspect igniting incendiary material in a cylindrical container two days before the blasts.

Rahami, who worked at a family-owned fried chicken shop in Elizabeth, New Jersey, is also accused of planting two bombs in Chelsea, one of which failed to detonate. Another bomb exploded in a New Jersey seaside town earlier on the same day, but no one was hurt. He is also accused of leaving explosives in a discarded rucksack in a rubbish bin in Elizabeth, New Jersey.

The suspect's wife, a Pakistani national, is being questioned in the United Arab Emirates, according to US media reports. The FBI had previously investigated Rahami for terrorism in 2014, following a complaint from his father, but found no link despite alleged acts of violence.

The series of bombings has sparked a heated debate about national security between the two presidential candidates, just days before their first televised debate. The attacks have raised questions about the effectiveness of the US government's counter-terrorism strategies and the need for increased vigilance in the face of growing threats from radical ideologies.

Rahami is also facing state charges in New Jersey, including attempted murder of police, stemming from his arrest on Monday outside a bar in Linden, New Jersey. As the investigation continues, authorities are working to piece together the events leading up to the bombings and to determine whether Rahami had any accomplices or connections to larger terrorist networks.

Thieves broke into The Owl and Falconry Centre in Shipley, Wolverhampton, stealing seven birds overnight on September 24. The stolen birds include Gyr Saker Falcons, Barn Owls, and Burrowing Owls. The Gyr Saker Falcons are valued at £7,000 each. Despite the damage to aviaries, the centre will remain open. The falconry, run by volunteers, visits nursing homes and schools for educational tours. The incident is under investigation, with CCTV footage yielding no suspects. The centre, home to about 50 birds and mammals, is seeking support to recover from the loss.

The stage is set for the Irn-Bru Cup Final, with Dundee United set to face St Mirren at Fir Park. The match, scheduled for a 12:30 GMT kick-off, will be broadcast live on BBC Alba. Both teams secured their spots in the final with impressive semi-final wins, with Dundee United edging out Queen of the South 3-2 and St Mirren coming from behind to defeat The New Saints 4-1.

This year's competition featured teams from Wales and Northern Ireland, and next season will see the addition of League of Ireland sides Sligo Rovers and Bray Wanderers. Dundee United is seeking their first Challenge Cup title, while St Mirren aims to repeat their 2005 victory. SPFL chief executive Neil Doncaster expressed his delight at hosting the final at Fir Park, where tickets will be available for as little as £5. With excitement building, fans can look forward to a thrilling match between two Championship sides.

A 45-year-old man, Craig Whyte, appeared in the High Court in Glasgow to face two charges related to his involvement with Rangers football club. The charges include one count of fraud and a second allegation under the Companies Act. The alleged fraud occurred between May 2010 and May 2011, during which time Whyte obtained a majority stake in the club. It is claimed that he and his representatives misled then-owner Sir David Murray and others about the availability of funds to make payments.

The second charge relates to an £18m payment made in connection with the takeover. Whyte entered no plea and his bail was continued. A provisional trial date has been set for April 2017, with a two-day hearing scheduled for December. Donald Findlay QC represented Whyte, while Alex Prentice QC has taken over as the lead prosecutor in the case. Prentice stated that he would step in as requested by the Lord Advocate. The case will continue to unfold in the coming months.

Crystal Palace midfielder Joe Ledley has been released by the club. The 30-year-old joined Palace in 2014 after stints with Cardiff City and Celtic. The news was announced as Ledley prepares for Wales' World Cup qualifier against Serbia. He is currently with the Wales squad in Belgrade. Meanwhile, Southampton's Lloyd Isgrove is also seeking a new club after being released. Swansea City has confirmed the departures of several players, including Jonathan Dyson, Marvin Emnes, and Gerhard Tremmel. These moves come as the soccer world prepares for upcoming matches and transfers. Ledley's future is now uncertain.

Manx2 has announced flight services between two islands for three months until early September. The company credits last year's short season for boosting tourism. Following a recent Welsh Government contract win, Manx2.com chairman Noel Hayes expressed delight in offering passengers a unique opportunity to visit Anglesey by air, building on positive feedback from last year's trial. The extended season aims to further enhance tourism at both destinations, with services running through the summer.

US and Russia Agree to Ceasefire in Syria

A ceasefire has been announced in Syria, following a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the G20 talks in Hamburg, Germany. The truce, which is also backed by Jordan, is currently in force along a line agreed by Syrian government forces and rebels. This move is a significant development in the six-year conflict, which has resulted in the deaths of approximately 300,000 people and displaced 11 million more.

The US and Russia have been supporting opposing sides in the conflict, with Russia backing the Syrian government and the US calling for the removal of President Bashar al-Assad. Despite their differences, US Secretary of State Rex Tillerson stated that the two countries' ultimate goals for Syria are "exactly the same." The ceasefire, which covers the regions of Deraa, Quneitra, and Sweida, is the result of months of secret talks between Russian and US officials. This agreement marks a crucial step towards ending the violence in Syria and working towards a peaceful resolution.

Worcestershire Take Control Against Northants in Championship Clash

Worcestershire continued their impressive form in the Championship, taking control of their match against Northants on the first day at Northampton. Skipper Joe Leach led from the front, taking 3-36 as the home side were bowled out for a modest total. Jack Shantry, Ed Barnard, and Josh Tongue shared the other wickets, with Shantry finishing with 3-54.

In response, Worcestershire's openers made a solid start, with Brett D'Oliveira and Daryl Mitchell putting on 75 before D'Oliveira fell for 35. Mitchell remained unbeaten on 52, guiding the visitors to 108-2 at the close of play. The partnership between D'Oliveira and Mitchell has been a key factor in Worcestershire's success, with the pair having shared a 243-run stand in their previous match against Derbyshire.

Northants captain Alex Wakely expressed his disappointment with the day's events, praising Worcestershire's bowling effort. "They bowled really well this morning, in partnerships and dried the scoreboard," he said. "We were probably going to bat anyway because it looked like a bat first pitch." Wakely acknowledged that his team's bowling had been poor at times, but was hopeful that they could recover on the second day.

Worcestershire assistant coach Matt Mason was delighted with his team's performance, citing the bravery of their decision to bowl first. "The pitch had a lot of dead grass, but we took the brave decision to bowl first," he said. "The ball seemed to go through periods of doing something. The key was just sticking to our plans and we got our rewards." With Leach now having taken 25 wickets for the season, Mason will be hoping that his team can continue their winning streak, which currently stands at five matches.

The Bank of Scotland has released its Affordable Cities Review, which reveals that city living in Scotland is more affordable than the UK city average. The average price for a city home in Scotland stands at £175,962, which is 5.24 times the gross annual average earnings. Although this represents a 7% increase on last year, it is still significantly below the peak of 6.12 in 2008.

The report suggests that affordability has improved since 2008 due to a combination of a 6% decline in average house prices and a 10% increase in average annual earnings. Stirling remains the UK's most affordable city for the second year running, with an average property price of £158,645, which is 3.85 times the gross average annual earnings. Glasgow and Dundee follow closely as Scotland's most affordable cities.

In contrast, Edinburgh is Scotland's least affordable city, with an average house price of £216,424, or 6.11 times the gross annual average earnings. Aberdeen has recorded the biggest price rise of any UK city over the past decade, with an 88% gain, largely due to the strong performance of the oil and gas sector. The report also notes that London has recorded the highest house price growth in recent years, with a 40% rise over the past five years. Overall, the review indicates that city living in Scotland is becoming more affordable, although there are still significant variations between cities.

Intensive Manhunt Continues for Accused Cop Killer Eric Frein in Pennsylvania

A massive search operation is underway in the dense north-east woodlands of Pennsylvania for 31-year-old Eric Frein, accused of fatally shooting one police officer and critically wounding another. Over 200 officers are scouring the area, focusing on the vicinity of Frein's parents' home in the Pocono mountains. The search has been hindered by the rugged terrain and heavy forest canopy, which has blocked police helicopters' view of the ground in some areas.

According to Lt Col George Bivens of the state police, "I do believe we are close to him at this point." The police have found an AK-47 rifle, ammunition, and other items believed to have been left behind by Frein, a self-described survivalist. Frein has been added to the FBI's 10 Most Wanted List, and a $175,000 reward is being offered for information leading to his capture.

The shooting occurred on September 12 outside the Blooming Grove state police barracks during an evening shift change, resulting in the death of Capt Bryon Dickson and injuring State Trooper Alex Douglass. Frein allegedly has a history of making statements about killing law enforcement officers and has received survivalist training. He was also part of a re-enactment group that portrayed soldiers from eastern Europe.

Thousands of law enforcement officers recently gathered to pay their respects to Capt Dickson, who was remembered as a devoted and impeccable officer. Fellow officer Derek Felsman praised Dickson's commitment to his work and family, saying he "held himself to the highest standards in every aspect of his life." The search for Frein continues, with police determined to bring him to justice for the tragic attack on their colleagues.

Local Heroes Honoured with Prestigious Awards

The New Year's Honours list has recognized the outstanding achievements of several local individuals, including Olympic gold medallist Nick Skelton and football referee Sian Massey-Ellis. Skelton, 58, from Bedworth, Warwickshire, has been honoured for his remarkable career, which includes winning individual gold at his seventh Olympic Games. Despite initially retiring 16 years ago after a serious neck injury, Skelton made a remarkable comeback to become Britain's second-oldest Olympic gold medallist at Rio 2016.

Sian Massey-Ellis, 31, from Coventry, has been awarded an MBE for her services to football. The referee has overcome sexism and misogyny in the sport, including a high-profile incident in 2011. Massey-Ellis hopes to inspire the next generation of female officials and footballers, saying, "I love football and it's a privilege to officiate in Premier League and EFL matches." 

Additionally, football coach Annie Zaidi from Nuneaton has received a British Empire Medal. The 32-year-old has faced racism, sexism, and Islamophobia in her career but has persevered to become a successful coach and role model for young women in the sport. These honours recognize the dedication and perseverance of these local heroes, who continue to inspire and make a positive impact in their respective fields.

Northern Ireland's Aileen Reid has made a remarkable comeback in the triathlon event, finishing 21st overall. Despite a challenging start, placing 32nd in the swim and 36th in the bike stage, Reid gained 15 places in the 10k run. Her strong finish came after a tumultuous training period, hindered by illness. Reid's determination paid off, as she crossed the line just under five minutes behind winner Gwen Jorgensen. The American took gold with a time of 1:56.16, followed by Nicola Sprig of Switzerland. Britain's Vicky Holland secured bronze, outsprinting teammate Non Stanford in a thrilling finish. Reid's result is a significant improvement from her 43rd place finish four years ago, where a cycling crash derailed her Olympic dreams.

Millwall striker Alfie Pavey joins Aldershot Town. The 20-year-old had a spell at Barnet and made six substitute appearances for Millwall. Shots manager Barry Smith praised Pavey's pedigree and coaching. He is eligible to debut against Chester on Saturday, following interest from other National League clubs.

The FIFA awards ceremony is set to take place in Zurich, where the best players and coaches in men's and women's football will be honored. Real Madrid forward Cristiano Ronaldo is fresh from his fourth Ballon d'Or win, having beaten rival Lionel Messi to the award last month. Messi, along with Antoine Griezmann, has also been nominated for the men's prize. The best women's player, as well as the top coaches in men's and women's football, will also be announced.

Claudio Ranieri, who led Leicester City to a historic Premier League title, is among the nominees for best coach, alongside Portugal's Fernando Santos and Zinedine Zidane. The winners will be determined by a combination of votes from national team captains and coaches, selected journalists, and an online poll of fans, with each category accounting for 25% of the points.

Additionally, the Puskas award for best goal will be presented, and a prize for best fans will be awarded to one of the nominated teams, including Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund, ADO Den Haag, or the Iceland fans who impressed with their clapping salute at Euro 2016. The ceremony promises to be an exciting celebration of the best in football.

Patients and Visitors Share Mixed Views on Addenbrooke's Hospital

Following the news that Addenbrooke's hospital has been placed in special measures, the BBC reached out to those who have used the hospital's services to gather their opinions. The responses were varied, with some praising the hospital's care and others expressing concerns and disappointment.

Many patients and visitors spoke highly of the hospital, citing the dedication and hard work of the staff. Sue Munro, who has been cared for by the hospital her entire life, said, "Addenbrooke's have cared for me in a timely and efficient way. Without them, I wouldn't be alive. They're great!" Eric and Ern Col also shared their positive experience, stating that their mother received "SECOND TO NONE! Brilliant staff!" care after a hip replacement.

However, not all experiences were positive. David Harding expressed his frustration, stating that the hospital has had problems for years and has worked to cover them up. Paul Bernal shared his disappointing experience, where an appointment was delayed by three months due to computer problems. Carole, who worked in the NHS for 14 years, was horrified by the care her late husband received, saying it was "appalling."

Some patients acknowledged that the hospital may have its flaws, but overall, they felt that the staff did a brilliant job. Sonya Louise-Bubbles Pledger praised the staff, saying they do a "wonderful job considering their low wages and cutbacks." Phil, on the other hand, felt that the hospital had become "too big and too arrogant," with some consultants being "untouchable and unanswerable."

Despite the mixed views, one thing is clear: the patients and visitors of Addenbrooke's hospital are passionate about the care they receive. As Sue said, "Perhaps we should look at the bigger picture here, they do a brilliant job, and waiting a while tells me they have time to spend with each person, to me this feels good." The hospital's placement in special measures may be an opportunity for improvement, and it remains to be seen how the hospital will address the concerns and praises of its patients and visitors.

David Burdett, inspired by Strictly and Billy Elliot, began dancing 18 months ago. He found it "hard, but fun" and plans to continue. The Gorleston, Norfolk resident will star at Gorleston Pavilion Theatre, a notable achievement after just a year and a half of lessons, showcasing his dedication and passion for dance.

Giant panda numbers have seen a significant increase, with the latest count revealing 1,864 individuals in the wild, up from 1,596 in 2003. Nearly 75% of these pandas reside in China's Sichuan province. The population in captivity has also grown, with almost 200 more pandas than in 2003. According to Ginette Hemley of the World Wildlife Fund, this rise is a "victory for conservation" and a cause for celebration. However, the main threat to panda numbers remains the construction of roads and power stations, with over 300 hydropower stations and 800 miles of roads built in panda habitats, posing a significant risk to their survival.

Comedian Matt Lucas Returns to University Roots, Receives Honorary Degree

In a humorous and lighthearted ceremony, comedian Matt Lucas was awarded an honorary degree from Bristol University, where he briefly studied Theatre, Film, and Television in 1993. Lucas, known for his work on the hit comedy sketch show Little Britain, which he co-created with fellow university alumnus David Walliams, poked fun at his own university experience.

After high-fiving university chancellor Sir Paul Nurse, Lucas jokingly referred to himself as a "charlatan" who left university a year early to pursue a career in comedy. He reminisced about his time at Bristol, saying he quickly realized he was on a "serious course" but struggled to find his place, often spending his days walking up and down nearby Whiteladies Road. Lucas also joked about being "generally useless" at university life, with few friends and a tendency to stay in his room.

Despite his humorous take on his university days, Lucas's career has been marked by significant success, including his work on Little Britain and various other TV shows and films. His honorary degree is a testament to his achievements in the entertainment industry, and he was clearly thrilled to return to his university roots, even if it was just to tease his alma mater about bringing the "entire university honours system into question" by celebrating his accomplishments.
Over 15,000 youths competed in singing and dancing at the Urdd in Nelson, Wales' largest youth festival, promoting Welsh language and culture since 1922.

Fidel Castro, the 88-year-old Cuban revolutionary icon, made a rare public appearance on Tuesday, meeting with a delegation of Venezuelan officials on a solidarity mission to the island. According to local press, Castro was "full of vitality" during the encounter, which took place at a local school. The meeting marked one of Castro's few public appearances in recent years, with his last being in January 2014 at a Havana cultural centre opening.

Official media released images of Castro, seated in a vehicle, shaking hands with the Venezuelan visitors through the window. He was pictured wearing a baseball cap and windbreaker. The visit highlights the strong alliance between Cuba and Venezuela, which has been in place since the fall of the Soviet Union. Castro has maintained a low public profile since stepping down as president in 2008, handing over to his brother Raul. Despite this, he remains a significant figure in Cuban politics.

Exeter Chiefs' newest recruit, 28-year-old Australian international Joe Turner, has expressed his excitement about joining the club, despite facing stiff competition for a starting spot. Turner, who has won 15 caps for Australia and can play at centre, wing, or full-back, made the move to Sandy Park this week. However, he is aware that he will have to fight for a place in the team, given the impressive form of the club's existing backs, including Jack Nowell, Henry Slade, and Sam Hill.

Rather than seeing this as a challenge, Turner views it as an opportunity to improve his game. "I wouldn't want to go somewhere I was guaranteed a position, because you become lazy and complacent," he said. "The growth that you get as a rugby player doesn't happen on Saturdays and Sundays, it happens through the week." Turner is looking forward to learning from and being challenged by his new teammates, while also pushing them to raise their game.

Having previously helped the Waratahs reach the Super Rugby final and semi-finals, Turner believes that Exeter have the talent and potential to achieve great things. "They're a very talented group of players and by the end of the season, a lot of people are looking at them now wondering where they're going to be," he said. With Exeter currently sitting in second place, Turner is eager to contribute to the team's success and see where they finish the season.

A bomb disposal team from RAF Wittering safely detonated a World War-era Mills grenade on Gunton Cliff beach in Lowestoft, Suffolk. The device, also known as a "pineapple bomb," was discovered by a metal detectorist at 05:30 BST. The beach was sealed off, but reopened after the controlled explosion at 11:00 BST. Experts confirmed no other explosives were found. The RAF team left the scene just before midday. According to authorities, ordnance washing up on the beach is not uncommon. The successful disposal ensured public safety, and the area has been cleared for normal activities to resume.

London Marathon 2016 Sees Millionth Finisher and New Course Record

The 2016 London Marathon has come to a close, with the millionth finisher in the event's history crossing the line on The Mall. The annual race, which was first held in 1981, has become a staple of the British sporting calendar, attracting thousands of runners and spectators each year. This year's event was marked by a number of notable achievements, including a new course record set by men's elite winner Eliud Kipchoge.

Kipchoge, from Kenya, completed the 26.2-mile course in a time of two hours, three minutes, and four seconds, just seven seconds outside the world record. The women's elite race was won by Jemima Sumgong, also from Kenya, who pulled clear of Ethiopia's Tigist Tufa despite falling at a drink station earlier in the race.

The men's and women's wheelchair races were won by Marcel Hug from Switzerland and Tatyana McFadden from the US, respectively. Britain's David Weir came third in the men's wheelchair race. The winners were presented with their prizes by Prince Harry, patron of the London Marathon Charitable Trust.

One of the most unique aspects of this year's event was the participation of astronaut Maj Tim Peake, who completed a marathon distance on a treadmill aboard the International Space Station. Peake recorded a message wishing the competitors good luck, which was shown to the runners on a big screen, and completed his own marathon in a time of three hours and 35 minutes.

The event was not without its challenges, however. One runner collapsed at mile 23 near Southwark Bridge and was taken to St Thomas' Hospital after suffering a cardiac arrest. Fortunately, the runner is receiving treatment and is expected to recover.

The London Marathon is known for its lively and eclectic atmosphere, with many runners dressing up in costume to raise money for charity. This year was no exception, with runners dressed as Shakespeare, hot dogs, dinosaurs, and Disney princesses taking to the streets. The event also saw a number of celebrity participants, including double Olympic champion Dame Kelly Holmes, former rugby union international Shane Williams, and Games of Thrones actress Natalie Dormer.

In a romantic moment, one runner proposed to his girlfriend at Tower Bridge, while another couple got engaged at the finish line. The oldest competitor in this year's race was 88-year-old Bedford grandmother Iva Barr, who has been running marathons for over 30 years and took part in the first London Marathon in 1981. Although she was unable to complete the course, Barr made it past halfway before stopping near Canary Wharf.

The London Marathon is a major event in the capital, with road closures in place from 7am to 7pm in some areas. Despite the disruptions, the event is a significant fundraiser for charity, with many runners taking part to raise money for good causes. The event was broadcast live on the BBC, with coverage available to watch again on iPlayer.

A heartwarming memorial has been unveiled for five-year-old April Jones, who was tragically abducted and killed in 2012. The memorial features a teddy bear looking over the top and a poignant verse in Welsh about a small, pink star. April's love for teddies, butterflies, and shooting stars is beautifully captured in the design.

April's mother, Coral Jones, and father, Paul Jones, recently visited the grave, where they expressed their relief and gratitude for the memorial. "It's April down to a tee," said Coral, fighting back tears. "We've been waiting two years for this day, and it's lovely that the headstone will be in place for Christmas." The family plans to visit April's grave on Christmas Day, bringing some sense of comfort and closure.

April's father, Paul, acknowledged the difficulty of seeing their daughter's name on a headstone but praised the tribute as "really lovely." The family has endured an unimaginable ordeal, with April's body never found despite an extensive search. Her killer, Mark Bridger, was jailed for life in 2013. The memorial brings a sense of peace, and the family can now visit their daughter's grave with a more personal and meaningful tribute.

A British man and his American wife, who were jailed in China last year for their role in the GlaxoSmithKline corruption scandal, are finally returning to the UK. Peter Humphrey and Yu Yingzeng boarded a flight from Shanghai to London, marking the end of a long and tumultuous ordeal for the couple. 

Peter Humphrey, who was released early on health grounds on June 9, still had seven months left on his two-and-a-half-year sentence. His wife, Yu Yingzeng, a Chinese-born US citizen, was freed two days later with just a month left on her two-year term. The couple's son, Harvey, who resides in the UK, received a call from his parents just before they boarded the flight. According to Harvey, his father was eager to see him, while his mother was overcome with emotion.

The couple's troubles began when they helped GSK investigate a secretly filmed sex tape of its top manager in China. They were subsequently found guilty of illegally obtaining Chinese citizens' data and selling it to firms, including GSK China. Although they admitted to buying background information, they claimed they were unaware that this was against the law. The couple's return to the UK brings an end to their ordeal, which has been a long and difficult journey for them and their family.

The FTSE 100 index fell 0.45% to 6,600.54 by lunchtime, with Anglo American down 1.3%. Royal Bank of Scotland dropped 1.5% amid reports of a potential $13bn settlement. The pound declined 0.3% against the euro to â‚¬1.4035 and 0.22% against the dollar to $1.5575. Mining stocks rebounded, leaving only Anglo American in the red.

Bristow Helicopters' revenue fell 19% to $356m in the quarter ending June, down from $440m last year. Offshore earnings dropped 27% due to challenging oil and gas industry conditions. The decline was partially offset by the UK search and rescue contract, the company reported.

A Thai-based company's liquidation has resulted in 2,200 job losses at the Redcar site. To mitigate the impact, over 30 employers are offering new opportunities in various sectors. According to Sue Soroczan, the affected workers possess excellent, transferable skills, attracting interest from local and external companies. A job fair is showcasing vacancies in heavy industry, administration, and logistics, providing hope for those affected by the redundancies.

Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir has arrived in South Africa to attend the African Union summit, despite being wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) for war crimes. The ICC has called on South Africa to detain Bashir, who is accused of war crimes in the Darfur region, but instead, he was welcomed by South African officials upon his arrival in Johannesburg.

The ICC issued a statement saying that South Africa should "spare no effort" in detaining Bashir and respecting their obligations to cooperate with the court. However, it is unlikely that South Africa will take action, given the country's history of refusing to arrest Bashir during previous visits. Human rights organizations and South Africa's main opposition party have also called for his arrest, but their pleas are likely to fall on deaf ears.

Bashir's visit to South Africa is a contentious issue, given the tensions between the ICC and the African Union (AU). The AU has previously urged the ICC to stop proceedings against sitting leaders, accusing the court of unfairly targeting Africans. Bashir has denied the allegations against him and has restricted his overseas travel to friendly states in Africa and the Middle East.

The AU summit, which is being held in South Africa, is expected to focus on a range of issues, including the crisis in Burundi, the conflict in South Sudan, and the fight against terrorism. However, analysts say that discussions will be held, but the outcome will be vague. The summit's official theme is the "Year of Women's Empowerment and Development," but it is likely to be overshadowed by the presence of Bashir and the controversy surrounding his visit.

South Africa's hosting of the summit has also been marred by the recent xenophobic violence in Johannesburg and Durban, which has left the country embarrassed. Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and Nigeria have lashed out at President Jacob Zuma's government for the attacks, which have put a damper on the summit. Despite the challenges, the AU is expected to press on with the summit, but the presence of Bashir is likely to remain a contentious issue throughout the proceedings.

Tom Daley has taken a significant step towards realizing his Olympic dreams by emerging victorious at the British diving championships. The 22-year-old diver accumulated an impressive 507.95 points from his six routines, surpassing his competitors Matty Lee and Noah Williams, who scored 428.00 and 389.05 points respectively.

Daley's outstanding performance has bolstered his chances of being selected for the Team GB lineup at the Rio Olympics this summer. Having made his Olympic debut at the tender age of 14 in Beijing and winning a bronze medal at the London 2012 Games, Daley is now more confident than ever of securing his first Olympic gold medal. He attributes his improved consistency over the past 12 months to his newfound confidence in executing big scores.

Meanwhile, Scotland's Grace Reid has also boosted her chances of being named in the Team GB lineup after winning the 3m springboard title. The 20-year-old diver has enjoyed a remarkable year, having secured Britain a place in the women's individual 3m event at the Rio Olympic test event and becoming the first Scottish diver to win an individual European medal in 62 years.

Reid's impressive performance has left her hopeful of being selected for the Rio Olympics, which would be a dream come true for the young diver. "It's just amazing, and I'm really pleased not only with the result today but also the new consistency that I've found," she exclaimed. The British diving team will learn later this week whether they have been selected to represent Team GB at the Rio Olympics. With their impressive performances, Daley and Reid are certainly strong contenders for a spot on the team.

South Korean Prosecutors Investigate Samsung's Alleged Ties to President's Friend

Prosecutors in South Korea are investigating allegations that Samsung, the country's largest conglomerate, provided millions of euros to a company co-owned by Choi Soon-sil, a close friend of President Park Geun-hye, and her daughter. The funds allegedly bankrolled the daughter's equestrian training in Germany. Samsung confirmed that its offices were raided by prosecutors but declined to comment further.

The investigation is the latest twist in a scandal that has been rocking South Korea for weeks. President Park has apologized for her ties to Ms. Choi, who is accused of using their friendship to interfere in politics and solicit business donations. However, the apology has done little to quell the growing calls for the president's resignation.

Ms. Choi was arrested on November 3 and charged with fraud and abuse of power. She is alleged to have pushed businesses to donate millions of dollars to foundations she controlled and even helped choose the president's clothes. President Park has admitted that she allowed Ms. Choi to edit her speeches, sparking widespread outrage and protests.

Tens of thousands of South Koreans have taken to the streets in recent days, demanding the president's resignation. The scandal has left President Park with a record-low approval rating of just 5%. Opposition leaders have called for her impeachment, and there are growing demands for her to accept a new prime minister recommended by parliament.

The raids on Samsung's offices and those of the Korea Equestrian Federation and the Korea Horse Affairs Association mark a significant escalation of the investigation. If the allegations are proven, it could have far-reaching implications for Samsung and the president's administration. As the scandal continues to unfold, it remains to be seen whether President Park will be able to weather the storm and maintain her grip on power. With her popularity at an all-time low, it seems increasingly unlikely that she will be able to survive the crisis.

Linfield FC has announced the resignation of Jim Kerr as chairman and board director. The club expressed deep regret over his departure, midway through the season, but did not disclose the reason. Linfield praised Kerr's immense contribution and hard work, stating the board is unanimous in their appreciation. The club plans to formally recognize Kerr's long service at a later date, paying tribute to his dedication to Linfield over many years. Kerr's resignation has come as a surprise, and the club will likely feel his absence in the remaining season.

The Ebola outbreak continues to ravage Guinea, with clinics struggling to cope. According to the WHO, there have been 15,935 reported cases and 5,689 deaths. The epidemic, which began eight months ago, shows no signs of slowing, with the remote area still in dire need of support and resources to combat the crisis.

Gamba Osaka has been fined 2 million yen (£13,500) by the J-League after a flag bearing a Nazi-style symbol was displayed at a match against Cerezo Osaka. The flag, featuring a double 'S' logo, was seen on April 16. In response, Gamba has banned the responsible supporter group and prohibited flags and banners at games. The J-League criticized the club's monitoring efforts, stating they are not sufficient to prevent discriminatory actions. Despite the incident, Gamba remains third in the league with 19 points from 10 games, and will face Hokkaido Consadole Sapporo on Sunday. The club has taken swift action to address the issue.

Usain Bolt blamed a "bad race" for his modest 10.09 seconds finish in the 100m. Despite carrying a hamstring problem, the triple Olympic champion claimed it wasn't a factor. Training partner Kemar Bailey-Cole also finished in 10.09 seconds. Bolt plans to review the race with his coach to identify what went wrong. Meanwhile, Antigua's Daniel Bailey took third with 10.23 seconds. In the women's 100m, America's Carmelita Jeter secured a world-leading time of 10.95 seconds, outpacing her competitors in the Cayman Islands event. Bolt's subpar performance has raised questions about his upcoming races.

Violent Protests Erupt in Srinagar After Eid Prayers, 12 Injured

At least 12 people were injured in clashes between protesters and riot police in the capital city of Srinagar and other parts of the state after Eid prayers turned violent. The unrest was sparked by the arrest of four prominent religious and separatist leaders, as well as a 40-hour ban on internet services. The ban was imposed after local Muslim leaders urged people to upload pictures of cows being slaughtered for Eid, defying a 1932 law that prohibits the slaughter of cows, considered sacred in Hinduism.

Eyewitnesses reported that protesters marched with posters of armed militants, leading to clashes with riot police who fired plastic bullets and tear gas. Tensions have been running high in the mostly Muslim region of India-administered Kashmir, where some religious leaders and separatist groups called for the slaughter of cows instead of traditional sheep and goats. The authorities' decision to block internet access to prevent the uploading of images of cow slaughter further fuelled the anger.

The arrests of high-profile separatist leaders, including Mirwais Omar Farooq, Syed Ali Gilani, and Yasin Malik, have also contributed to the unrest. The Indian authorities' decision to enforce the long-dormant law has been seen as an attempt to impose Hindu values on the Muslim-majority region, leading to widespread resentment and protests. The situation remains volatile, with many fearing further escalation of violence in the coming days.

A prison officer at Maghaberry Prison in County Antrim has spoken out about the dire conditions and staffing shortages within the facility, following a damning report that described the jail as being in a "state of crisis". The officer, who wished to remain anonymous, expressed concerns over the safety and stability of both prisoners and staff, citing inadequate staffing levels as a major contributor to the problems.

The report, which was published after inspectors visited the prison in May, highlighted significant failures in leadership and raised concerns about the welfare of those held within the prison. The officer's comments corroborate these findings, painting a picture of a prison struggling to cope with the demands placed upon it. "Landings are running with two officers for 50 prisoners and posts are being stood down all over the prison," the officer told the BBC's Evening Extra.

The officer described the situation in the prison's pods, where a single staff member is often responsible for overseeing the movement of prisoners, issuing passes, and monitoring cameras. This, they claimed, is a situation that is "crazy" and unsustainable. The recommended staffing level for these areas is at least two people, but the officer said that this is often not the case.

The staffing shortages are also having a significant impact on the prison's ability to safely restrain prisoners. The officer explained that the recommended control and restraint techniques require three people, but often only two officers are available. This, they said, means that the techniques are not being used effectively, putting both staff and prisoners at risk. The officer recounted a disturbing incident in which they had to rely on another prisoner to press the alarm while they were restraining a prisoner, highlighting the desperation of the situation.

In response to the report and the officer's comments, Stormont Justice Minister David Ford has said that steps have been taken to improve standards within the jail. However, the officer's testimony suggests that much work still needs to be done to address the deep-seated problems within Maghaberry Prison. The situation is a cause for concern, and it remains to be seen whether the measures being taken will be enough to bring the prison out of its "state of crisis" and ensure the safety and well-being of both prisoners and staff.

A trial date has been set for three medical staff accused of manslaughter by gross negligence. Aisha Chithira, 32, died after an abortion at a Marie Stopes clinic in 2012. Dr Adedayo Adedeji, Margaret Miller, and Gemma Pullen denied the charge at the Old Bailey. They will stand trial on March 7. The trio, from various UK locations, were granted bail. The case alleges negligence led to Chithira's death, sparking a lengthy investigation and impending trial, set to commence in early March, with the defendants maintaining their innocence.

Sheffield United signs highly-rated 18-year-old winger Chapman. He played 14 games on loan at Barnsley, helping them earn League One promotion. Manager Chris Wilder praises Chapman's ability as a wide player. The youngster previously played for Boro's under-19 team in the Uefa Youth League.

Celtic Winger James Forrest Rejects Contract Offer, Sparks Debate on Future

James Forrest, the 24-year-old Celtic winger, has turned down a four-year contract offer from the club, sparking speculation about his future. The Scotland midfielder's current deal is set to expire at the end of 2016, and his decision has left many wondering what's next for the talented player.

According to former Celtic goalkeeper Pat Bonner, Forrest should remain at Celtic Park, where he has the opportunity to prove himself as a regular starter. "He should be a regular fixture in the starting line-up every single week," Bonner told BBC Scotland. "I would love him to stay at Celtic because there is no better place if you are playing really well."

Forrest, who has made 13 Scotland appearances, has been linked to English clubs Norwich and Queens Park Rangers. However, Bonner believes that the player's inconsistent form is a mental issue, rather than a lack of ability. "James is a wonderful talent, he has great ability on the ball," Bonner said. "The problem with James is inconsistency. He's had his injuries, but for me, it looks like a mental thing."

Despite his inconsistency, Forrest has shown glimpses of brilliance, scoring twice in 32 appearances this season. Bonner believes that the player has the potential to be a fan favorite, saying, "When he is effective, there's nobody better at getting the fans up out of their seats."

As Forrest weighs his options, Bonner has warned him that leaving Celtic for more money may not be the right decision. "Sometimes, going away for more money might not be the right decision," he said. "Maybe he feels a wee bit stagnated and thinks he needs a change of scenery just to kick on. That can happen, of course." With his international career also to consider, Forrest must carefully think about his next move, and whether staying at Celtic is the best decision for his future.

Miriam Santiago, the "Iron Lady of Filipino politics," passed away on Thursday morning after a long battle with lung cancer. The former judge and senator died peacefully in a hospital in Manila, according to her husband. Santiago's death has sent shockwaves throughout the Philippines, with many taking to social media to pay tribute to her legacy.

Santiago was a prominent figure in Filipino politics, known for her fearless and frank style. She ran for president in May's elections, but ultimately lost to Rodrigo Duterte. Despite her ill health, which plagued her campaign, Santiago insisted that she was fit to hold office. This was not her first attempt at the presidency, having also sought the position in 1992 and 1998.

Born in Iloilo city, Santiago announced in 2014 that she was suffering from stage four lung cancer. She turned down a judicial position at the International Criminal Court due to her illness, but continued to be a vocal presence in politics. Her weakening health was a concern during the presidential election, where she was often seen sitting down and resting during televised debates.

Santiago was a feisty senator who took bold stands on major issues like corruption and defense agreements. She was known for her quick wit and sharp tongue, which earned her both admiration and fear. Many remember her as being accommodating and jovial, often joking with the media.

Filipinos have flooded social media with tributes to the late senator, with many describing her as the "best president the Philippines never had." A Facebook post from the GMA News agency drew over 300,000 reactions and close to 50,000 comments, with many expressing their sadness and gratitude for her legacy. "We just lost a great woman, a great Filipino and a great public servant," said one user. "You could have been one of our greatest presidents. This is a very sad day for the Philippines. We lost a gem," said another. As the nation mourns her passing, Santiago's legacy will undoubtedly be remembered for years to come.

A high-profile trial involving a journalist and two others has been delayed amid a review of prosecutions related to the Metropolitan Police's Operation Elveden. Journalist Greig Box Turnbull, prison officer Grant Pizzey, and his partner Desra Reilly were set to stand trial this week on charges of conspiracy to commit misconduct in public office. However, the trial has been put on hold as the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) re-examines its cases in light of a recent Court of Appeal ruling.

The ruling, which overturned the conviction of another journalist, raised questions about the direction given by the trial judge and the impact of the offence on the public interest. The journalist, who cannot be named, had been convicted of illegally paying a prison officer for stories. The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge's direction did not fully consider the seriousness of the offence and its potential harm to the public interest.

The delay in Mr. Box Turnbull's trial is the second to result from the Court of Appeal's decision, with nine more trials and re-trials related to Operation Elveden scheduled to take place over the summer. A further hearing in the case of Mr. Box Turnbull, Mr. Pizzey, and Ms. Reilly is set for April 27. The development has thrown Operation Elveden, which investigates payments by journalists to public officials, into disarray, according to home affairs correspondent Daniel Sandford.

Mass Grave Uncovered in Syria, Revealing Horrors of IS Brutality

A disturbing discovery has been made in eastern Syria, where a mass grave containing the bodies of 230 people has been uncovered. According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, the victims are believed to be members of the Sheitat tribe, who were brutally killed by the Islamic State (IS) group in the summer.

The mass grave was discovered near the village of Kashkiya, in Deir al-Zour province, after IS leaders allowed the tribe to return to their homes. The Syrian Observatory reported that the "vast majority" of the victims were civilians, and many had been executed in cold blood. The discovery brings the total number of Sheitat tribespeople killed during the summer to over 900, with hundreds more still missing.

The killings are thought to have taken place after negotiations between the tribe and IS broke down, with the tribe's elders refusing to pledge allegiance to the extremist group. IS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi had issued a statement in early November, granting the tribe permission to return home on the condition that they surrendered their weapons and informed on any "apostates".

The brutal massacre is just one example of the atrocities committed by IS in their struggle for control of oil resources in the region. Video footage published online appears to show IS fighters conducting mass beheadings of Sheitat tribesmen, with some victims reportedly being forced out of hospital before being decapitated. The UN had previously received reports of a massacre in the area, and the latest discovery confirms the worst fears of human rights groups.

The international community has condemned the atrocities committed by IS, and the discovery of the mass grave serves as a stark reminder of the horrors faced by civilians in Syria. The Syrian Observatory has called for further investigation into the massacre, and for those responsible to be held accountable for their crimes.

A car drove down beach steps at 15:00 BST, prompting emergency services to respond. Gardaí and firefighters removed the lodged vehicle. Onlookers expressed relief, calling it "very lucky" and an "absolute miracle" that no one was seriously hurt. The cause of the incident is unknown and police are investigating. Witnesses described the scene as fortunate, with no major injuries reported despite the shocking accident.

Maidstone United signs a 25-year-old after two years with the Fleet. The team has also added Ben Greenhalgh, Kevin Lokko, and Tom Murphy, while Callum Driver, Dumebi Dumaka, and Bobby-Joe Taylor renewed contracts, bolstering their roster after promotion to the top non-league flight.

A former senior police officer has expressed her outrage and disappointment over the decision to pay a convicted child rapist £10,300 for his role in helping to convict 17 men and one woman of abusing girls in Newcastle. Sue Sim, who retired in 2015, said she was "appalled" and "horrified" by the move, which she claimed she would never have agreed to.

The controversy surrounds the use of a man known as XY, who provided information that led to the convictions as part of Operation Sanctuary. The current chief constable of Northumbria Police, Steve Ashman, has defended the decision, saying it was "morally" right and that it had helped to put "dangerous men behind bars" and protect vulnerable women and girls.

However, Ms Sim, who created the operation, has called for a public inquiry into the matter. She said that while she was delighted with the success of the operation, she was shocked and dismayed by the use of XY as an informant. "I would never have agreed to the payment of a convicted child rapist," she said. "I keep hearing it was a very difficult decision - clearly it was so difficult that they didn't tell me. Probably because they knew I would totally and utterly disagree."

Ms Sim also questioned the effectiveness of the evidence provided by XY, saying that she had not seen or heard anything that suggested what evidence he had actually produced. "Two wrongs don't make a right - he was a convicted child rapist and you can never put sufficient safeguards in place," she said.

Northumbria Police has responded to the criticism, saying that it had been "open and transparent" in its response to Operation Sanctuary and the use of XY. However, the force said it would not comment on individuals' opinions. The chief constable, Steve Ashman, has maintained that the decision to use XY was "inside the law and inside accepted policy and practice".

The controversy has sparked a heated debate about the use of informants in policing and the moral implications of paying a convicted child rapist for his help. Ms Sim has apologized to any rape victims who may feel let down by the decision, saying that the success of the operation should not be tarnished by this, but it does need further serious investigation. The incident has raised questions about the tactics used by police and the need for greater transparency and accountability in such cases.

EU's New Migrant Rescue Operation Raises Concerns Over Future Rescues

The European Union's new migrant rescue operation, Triton, is set to replace Italy's Mare Nostrum operation, which has been rescuing migrants off the Libyan coast for the past year. However, concerns have been raised over the reduced budget and changed focus of the new operation, which may put the lives of thousands of migrants at risk.

Mare Nostrum was launched in response to the tragic deaths of hundreds of migrants who drowned off the island of Lampedusa. Since then, the operation has rescued over 150,000 migrants, mostly fleeing violence in the Horn of Africa and Middle East. However, this year has seen a surge in migrant boats heading for Europe, with at least 3,000 migrants drowning in the Mediterranean.

The new Triton operation will have only a third of Mare Nostrum's budget and will focus on border control, such as vetting asylum seekers and coastal patrols, rather than search and rescue in international waters. Italian Admiral Filippo Foffi has expressed concerns over the reduced scope of the new operation, stating that EU-Italian naval cooperation must continue in international waters to prevent further tragedies.

While there has been no official order to stop Mare Nostrum, Italian officials have indicated that they intend to scale down the operation as Triton takes over. The EU's Frontex border agency will lead the new operation, with six ships, two planes, and one helicopter pledged by EU countries so far. However, many operational details, including the amount of time spent in international waters, are still to be determined.

Admiral Foffi warned that if the operation is limited to territorial waters, "we won't see people in danger and if they die we won't see it." He emphasized that Frontex relies on member states to provide personnel and equipment, and that the success of the operation depends on the resources offered by EU partners.

The UK has announced that it will not support future search and rescue operations, citing concerns that they may encourage more people to attempt the dangerous sea crossing. However, critics argue that this approach is misguided and will only lead to more deaths at sea. As the migrant crisis continues to escalate, the EU must ensure that its new operation prioritizes the safety and dignity of those fleeing persecution and violence.

New Research Reveals Complex Role of "Good" Cholesterol in Heart Health

For years, it has been widely accepted that high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, also known as "good" cholesterol, plays a crucial role in maintaining a healthy heart. HDL cholesterol helps to keep arteries clear by shipping excess cholesterol to the liver, reducing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. However, a recent study by researchers at the Cleveland Clinic has shed new light on the complex role of HDL cholesterol in heart health.

The study, published in the journal Nature Medicine, reveals that HDL cholesterol can become abnormal and contribute to the development of heart disease. According to Dr. Stanley Hazen, one of the lead researchers, HDL cholesterol can become modified in the walls of the artery, leading to the formation of dysfunctional HDL. This abnormal HDL can then seep back into the bloodstream, where it can be detected and used to predict the risk of cardiovascular disease.

The researchers analyzed blood samples from 627 patients and found that levels of abnormal HDL in the blood could be used to predict the risk of heart disease. This discovery challenges the traditional view of HDL cholesterol as simply "good" cholesterol and highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of its role in heart health.

Despite these findings, experts emphasize that a healthy diet and lifestyle remain essential for maintaining good heart health. "This data does not change the message of eat healthily," said Dr. Hazen. Instead, the research will be used to develop new tests for abnormal HDL cholesterol and to investigate the development of drugs that can help block its formation.

The British Heart Foundation has welcomed the research, noting that it highlights the complexity of HDL cholesterol's role in heart health. "Although traditionally we think of HDL as 'good' cholesterol, the reality is much more complex," said Dr. Shannon Amoils, a senior research adviser for the organization. "This interesting research pins down the exact chemical change that causes the 'good' HDL cholesterol to become bad, and could allow scientists to monitor coronary artery disease more closely or even target the 'bad' HDL with drugs."

England's Rokoduguni Sent Back to Club Despite Impressive Return

Roko Rokoduguni's return to Test rugby was short-lived, as the Bath winger was sent back to his club on Tuesday, just days after scoring twice against Fiji. Despite his impressive performance, Rokoduguni will not feature in England's upcoming match against Argentina on Saturday. 

According to England's defense coach, Paul Gustard, Rokoduguni's exclusion is not a reflection on his abilities, but rather a tactical decision to field the best possible team against the Pumas. "Roko acquitted himself pretty well, and this is one game he is not chosen for," Gustard said. "It is not a reflection of anything that will come after that."

Gustard emphasized that the team's priority is to secure a win, and they believe the selected squad is the right one to achieve that goal. Rokoduguni's confidence is not expected to be affected by his exclusion, as he has had a positive conversation with coach Eddie Jones and is aware of the areas he needs to improve.

In Rokoduguni's place, Jonny May is expected to return to the right wing, while Elliot Daly and Mike Brown are likely to retain their positions on the left wing and full-back, respectively. Meanwhile, George Kruis has made a speedy recovery from ankle surgery and is expected to start in the second row. Kruis, who has been sidelined for the past month, worked hard to meet his goal of returning to the squad within four to five weeks. England will announce their starting XV and replacements on Thursday morning.

Arsenal has claimed the Emirates Cup trophy despite losing 2-1 to Sevilla in their final match. The Gunners' Alexandre Lacazette scored his first competitive goal for the club, tapping home a cross from Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain. However, Sevilla's Joaquin Correa and Steven N'Zonzi secured the win for the La Liga side. Arsenal won the tournament on goals scored, having beaten Benfica 5-2 earlier. Lacazette was substituted shortly after scoring, but manager Arsene Wenger attributed the change to tactical reasons, not the apparent leg injury. The Emirates Cup win is a confidence boost for Arsenal ahead of their Community Shield match against Chelsea on August 6 and their Premier League opener against Leicester City on August 11.

A stunning collection of miniature houses has found a new home at Newby Hall near Ripon. The "historically accurate" houses, created by collectors and miniaturists Caroline Hamilton and Jane Fiddick, are now on display in the former potting sheds at the historic estate. The collection includes a miniature Adam house featuring a replica of Newby Hall's tapestry room, showcasing the miniaturist's exceptional skills.

The houses are made with intricate details, including hallmarked silver, hand-blown glass, real china, and hand-carved wood. The collection was donated to Newby Hall after it became too large for the collectors to house themselves. Newby Hall, built by Sir Christopher Wren in the 1690s and later adapted by Robert Adam, is considered one of Britain's finest examples of Adam-style architecture.

The potting sheds were converted at a cost of £150,000, with £97,000 contributed by the Heritage Lottery Fund. The dolls' house collection will be open to the public from June 30 to September 27 and will be a permanent exhibit from April to September each year. According to Ms Fiddick, the hall's Adam rooms are a "miniaturist's dream," making it the perfect setting for the collection.

UK Communities Encouraged to Hold Vigils for Somme Centenary

The government and the Royal British Legion are calling on villages, towns, and cities across the UK to organize their own remembrance events to mark the centenary of the Battle of the Somme. The devastating battle, which began on July 1, 1916, resulted in over 600,000 British and French casualties, leaving a profound impact on communities throughout the UK and Commonwealth.

To commemorate this significant event, evening vigils are being planned for June 30 or July 1, allowing people to come together and reflect on the sacrifices made by those who fought in the battle. The Right Reverend Nigel McCulloch, head of remembrance at the Royal British Legion, emphasized the importance of remembering the tragic scale and futility of modern industrialized warfare, which the Battle of the Somme has come to symbolize.

The vigils are designed to recreate the apprehension felt by soldiers as they waited in the trenches for "zero hour" at 7:30 am, when they would go "over the top" into battle. To support local events, the Royal British Legion has created a toolkit with ideas for organizing vigils, while the government has launched an online guide on remembrance events. Suggestions include gathering at meaningful places, lighting candles, reading poems, listening to music, and sharing photographs of relatives who fought in the battle.

Culture Secretary John Whittingdale stressed the importance of honoring the memory and bravery of those who fought in the Battle of the Somme, saying, "It is important that we never forget what happened on the battlefields and honour their memory and bravery for generations to come." National events, including a national vigil at Westminster Abbey and commemorative services in Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Manchester, will also take place to mark the centenary. As the UK prepares to remember the sacrifices of the past, communities are encouraged to come together to pay their respects and ensure that the legacy of the Battle of the Somme is never forgotten.

Nicholas Rhea, a renowned author and former policeman, has passed away at his home in Ampleforth, North Yorkshire. Rhea, whose real name was Peter Walker, died on Friday surrounded by his family after his cancer returned two weeks ago. His daughter, Tricia, described him as a "Yorkshireman to the end." Rhea is best known for his Constable series of books, which inspired the popular Yorkshire Television production that aired from 1992 to 2010. The show followed a young police officer's life in the North York Moors. Rhea's funeral will be held at Our Lady's & St Benedict's Church, Ampleforth, on Friday, a fitting tribute to a man who lived in the village for 50 years. He will be deeply missed by his family and fans alike.

Tories' £12bn Welfare Cut Plan Sparks Fury from Opposition

The Conservative Party's plan to cut the welfare bill by £12bn if they win the next election has sparked outrage from opposition parties. While the Tories have not explicitly stated where the cuts will come from, concerns have been raised that child benefit and child tax credits may be targeted. Dolores Kelly MLA slammed the proposal, calling it a "further attack on struggling families."

The controversy began when Lib Dem Danny Alexander claimed that the Tories had previously proposed limiting child benefit and tax credits to two children during their coalition government. However, George Osborne denied the claims, stating that they were three years old and never official policy.

Kelly criticized the Tories' "slash and burn ideology" and accused local parties of not doing enough to oppose the cuts. She argued that the best way to prevent the cuts is to vote for a strong Labour government, which would be held accountable by social democrats in the SDLP, SNP, and Plaid Cymru.

Kelly also took aim at Sinn Féin, accusing them of hypocrisy for claiming to oppose Tory cuts while failing to take action. She alleged that Sinn Féin would "stand idly by" and support the cuts when they come before the assembly. The row highlights the deep divisions between parties on welfare reform and the impact of austerity measures on vulnerable families. As the election approaches, the debate is likely to intensify, with opposition parties pushing for greater transparency on the Tories' plans.

A 37-year-old woman, Nicola Cross, was tragically stabbed to death at her home in Dunlin Road, Hemel Hempstead, on Monday night. Marcin Porczynski, 23, of Claymore Avenue, has been charged with her murder, as well as two counts of kidnap and trespass with intent to inflict grievous bodily harm.

Porczynski appeared at Hatfield Remand Court, where he was remanded in custody to appear at St Albans Crown Court on Friday. Using a Polish interpreter, he confirmed his name, age, and address, but did not enter a plea. The police investigation into Mrs. Cross's death is ongoing, and the incident has been referred to the Independent Police Complaints Commission.

In a heartfelt tribute, Mrs. Cross's family described her as "kind, generous, and brave." They said she was the "heart and soul" of their family and a "perfect wife and amazing mummy." Her family praised her talent and core values, which she instilled in her children. The community is in shock following the tragic event, and an investigation is underway to determine the circumstances surrounding Mrs. Cross's death.

Police were initially called to the scene after reports of a suspicious individual, but they released him without incident. However, they were called back to the area an hour later, responding to a report of a burglary at a neighboring home, where they discovered Mrs. Cross's body. A 19-year-old man arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to burgle has been released on police bail until September 24. The investigation is ongoing, and the community is awaiting further updates on the case.

A private funeral service was held for Courtney Boyle and Philip Tron, victims of the Manchester Arena attack. The pair, from Gateshead, were killed on May 22 while picking up Courtney's sister after the Ariana Grande concert. Family and friends wore yellow to the service at Saltwell Crematorium. A minute's silence was observed at the start of the inquests into the 22 deaths. Meanwhile, a joint funeral for Chloe Rutherford, 17, and Liam Curry, 19, will be held on June 15 at St Hilda's Church in South Shields, followed by private cremations. The community comes together to mourn the loss of these young lives.

A vital mental health support line in Norfolk is set to close at the end of the month after the local NHS clinical commissioning groups (CCGs) decided not to continue funding it. The support line, run by staff from charity Mind, has received over 6,000 calls in its first six months of operation, providing a lifeline for patients in need of mental health support.

The pilot project was launched in January by former health minister Norman Lamb, with the aim of providing support for patients over 18 under the care of Norfolk and Suffolk NHS Foundation Trust (NSFT) or those who have been seen by the trust's services within the last 12 months. Despite its success, the CCGs have stated that they are unable to commit sufficient new funds to keep the service running.

Amanda Hedley, chief executive of Norwich and Central Norfolk Mind, expressed her disappointment at the decision, stating that the service had been a lifeline for many patients. "We have been able to answer 6,111 calls between January and May, and I am very shocked and extremely disappointed that the funding will not be continued," she said.

Service users and advocates have also spoken out against the decision, citing the importance of the support line in meeting the needs of mental health patients. Kevin James, service user governor for the NSFT in Norfolk, said that the support line had filled a gap in services and that he was "beyond concerned" for the welfare of patients who would no longer have access to it.

The CCGs have stated that they are exploring alternative models for crisis response, including a new mental health pathway in partnership with the NSFT team. However, for now, the future of mental health support in Norfolk remains uncertain, leaving many patients and advocates worried about the consequences of the support line's closure.

Emma announced a new live-action Beauty and the Beast film, directed by Bill Condon. The 1991 animated classic was a "big part" of her childhood. She'll dance to "Be Our Guest" and sing "Something There". Emma expressed excitement, saying her "six-year-old self is on the ceiling" and her "heart is bursting". A release date has not been set for the highly anticipated film.

Police Officers' Fitness Test Results Revealed: Overall Pass Rate of 98%

A recent report released by the College of Policing has revealed the results of the compulsory fitness test taken by police officers in England and Wales. The test, which was taken 93,956 times from September 2014 to August 2015, showed an overall pass rate of 98%. However, 1,863 officers failed to meet the required standard.

The results varied across the 43 territorial police forces, with South Yorkshire Police having the lowest pass rate at 95%. This meant that 5% of its officers failed the test. On the other hand, the City of London Police achieved a perfect pass rate, with all 120 of its officers passing the test.

The test, which was introduced in 2014, is designed to ensure that police officers are physically fit enough to perform their duties effectively. It involves a 15-metre shuttle run, which requires officers to run 525 metres in three minutes 40 seconds or less. The College of Policing recommends that officers who fail the test be given the opportunity to retake it twice.

According to the report, female officers had a lower pass rate than their male counterparts. Of the 23,154 times a female officer took the test, 95.4% passed, compared to 98.9% of male officers. However, the College of Policing has emphasized that it is committed to supporting officers who struggle with the test, particularly female officers. National lead for fitness testing, Assistant Chief Constable Jo Shiner, noted that the College's guidance on fitness tests includes advice on positive action measures such as specialized training and mentoring programs.

Despite the few failures, the overall results suggest that the vast majority of police officers are fit and able to protect the public. As Assistant Chief Constable Shiner pointed out, "The public want their officers to be fit and able to protect them in the face of danger, and these results show they are able to do just that." The College of Policing will continue to monitor the results and provide support to officers who need it, ensuring that police forces across England and Wales maintain the highest standards of physical fitness.

Conlan Advances to Finals with Unanimous Decision. Belfast bantamweight Michael Conlan secured a spot in the finals with a unanimous decision win, earning scorecards of 30-27, 29-28, and 29-28. The 23-year-old European champion has already qualified for the 2016 Rio Olympics. Conlan's victory sets him up for a strong finish, while teammates Michael O'Reilly and Joe Ward prepare for their semi-final matches.

The Pirate Bay, one of the internet's most-visited websites, is set to make a comeback this Sunday, February 1, according to a countdown on thepiratebay.se. The website, which provided links to pirated content, was taken offline in December following a raid by Swedish police. The raid, which was prompted by a complaint from the Rights Alliance, resulted in the seizure of servers in Stockholm.

Despite previous attempts to shut down the site, including a 2006 raid, The Pirate Bay has consistently managed to reappear online. The site's resilience has been a thorn in the side of the film, music, and software industries, which blame it for billions of pounds in losses. In 2012, UK internet service providers were ordered to block access to the site, but it continues to be accessible through various means.

The site's co-founders have also faced legal troubles, with Gottfrid Warg sentenced to three-and-a-half years in prison for hacking and copyright violations, and Peter Sunde sentenced to eight months in prison for violating copyright laws. Another co-founder, Hans Fredrik Lennart Neij, was arrested in November while trying to cross into Thailand from Laos. The Pirate Bay's return is likely to be met with both excitement and concern, as the site's impact on the entertainment industry and internet freedom continues to be debated.

A Bosnian court has sentenced Mevlid Jasarevic to 18 years in prison for committing a "terrorist act" by firing over 100 bullets at the US embassy in Sarajevo. The attack, which occurred in 2011, resulted in the injury of one policeman before Jasarevic was shot and arrested by a police sniper. 

Jasarevic, a member of a fundamentalist Wahhabi group, was found to have acted alone in the attack, with two alleged accomplices, Emrah Fojnica and Munib Ahmetspahic, being acquitted. The three men were residents of Gornja Maoca, a village known for its Islamist community, which has been the subject of several police raids in recent years.
