The US embassy was locked down during the attack, and fortunately, no one inside was injured. Judge Branko Peric described the sentence as the harshest ever given for terrorism, intending it to serve as a warning. He also expressed concern over the Islamist community in Gornja Maoca, which refuses to recognize the authority of the Bosnian state. 

Jasarevic's motivations for the attack are believed to have stemmed from opposition to US policy towards Muslims worldwide. The attack was widely condemned, including by Bakir Izetbegovic, the Bosniak member of the Bosnian presidency, who labeled it a terrorist attack. The incident has raised concerns about the potential for extremist activity in the region, which is still recovering from the bitter 1992-95 conflict.

A fire broke out at a property in the Tiger Court area early Friday morning. Luckily, two brave police officers helped rescue residents from the burning building, and no one was injured. Councillor Neil Kelly praised the officers' actions, saying they put their lives at risk to protect the public. He expressed relief that the incident didn't result in a tragedy, especially during Christmas time. Kelly condemned the arson attack, stating that those responsible have no regard for human life and must be caught by the police. The councillor wished the officers a swift recovery, acknowledging their selfless bravery in the face of danger.

Castleford Tigers' star player Greg Eden's season is likely over due to an injury sustained during Friday's 38-14 win against Salford. Eden, 26, scored his 33rd and 34th tries of the season but suffered the injury while diving over for his second. Tigers coach Powell confirmed the injury would "probably" end Eden's season. Teammate Michael Shenton expressed his disappointment, saying, "I'm absolutely gutted, he's had a superb year... He's been a massive part of what we've been doing." Eden's impressive form has been crucial to the Tigers' success, and his absence will be felt. Despite the setback, the Tigers remain top of Super League, eight points clear heading into the Super 8s competition. Eden's injury is a significant blow, as he was just six tries short of breaking the record for most tries in a single season, held by former Castleford winger Denny Solomona.

Diageo, the UK-based manufacturer of renowned spirits such as Johnnie Walker whisky and Smirnoff vodka, has reported a 9% decline in net sales to £10.3 billion for the year ending June 30. The company experienced a 5% decrease in sales volume across its Asia Pacific, Africa, Eastern Europe, and Turkey divisions, while sales in North America and Latin America were slightly down, and Western Europe remained flat.

The weak performance in certain regions was largely attributed to economic challenges and regulatory changes. In China and South East Asia, sales plummeted by 20% and 25%, respectively, due to anti-extravagance measures and tax increases. Venezuela also posed a significant challenge, with a 47% decline in Scotch whisky sales resulting from currency devaluation and inflation.

Despite these setbacks, Diageo's North American operations delivered top-line growth, driven by a 5% increase in US spirits and wines sales. The company remains optimistic about its long-term prospects, particularly in emerging markets. According to John Kennedy, President of Diageo Europe, the growing number of high net worth individuals and increasing consumer wealth will drive demand for premium brands. Notably, sales of single malts surged by 18% compared to the previous year, indicating a strong potential for growth in the high-end Scotch whisky category. Despite the mixed results, Diageo is confident in its ability to capitalize on emerging market opportunities and achieve long-term growth.

Wales international Rhodri Jones has announced that he will be leaving the Scarlets to join the Ospreys on a new contract. The 24-year-old tight-head prop has played 13 internationals for Wales and signed a national contract in December 2014. However, his new deal is solely with the Ospreys and not an extension of his national contract, which was jointly funded by the Welsh Rugby Union.

Jones made his 100th appearance for the Scarlets in their recent win over Edinburgh, and despite his loyalty to the region, he has decided to make the move to the Ospreys. The Scarlets' general manager, Jon Daniels, expressed disappointment at Jones' departure but respected his decision. Jones stated that he is excited about the new opportunity and is looking forward to contributing to the Ospreys' success.

Jones' opportunities at the Scarlets and with the national team have been limited by the emergence of Samson Lee and Exeter's Tomas Francis. However, the Ospreys' rugby manager, Andrew Millward, believes that Jones has huge potential to become a quality player. Millward welcomes the signing, stating that Jones fits the Ospreys' requirements in terms of ability and character. The Ospreys are confident that they can help Jones improve his set piece work and reach his full potential. Jones will remain with the Scarlets until the end of the season, where he will continue to give his all to help the region secure a Pro12 play-off position.

India has seen a significant number of elephant deaths, with many caused by accidental electrocution. According to Bijayshree Routray, over a third of the elephant deaths were due to electric shock from hanging wires. The country is home to around 26,000 wild elephants, a heritage animal. To address the issue, the government has formed a joint committee to monitor elephant deaths. The committee will comprise members from the forest, environment, and energy departments. Other causes of elephant deaths include poaching, poisoning by farmers, and being hit by trains. As elephants' habitats shrink, conflicts with humans have increased, leading to the deaths of these protected animals. The government's efforts aim to reduce elephant fatalities and preserve the species.

Bloomberg Considers Presidential Bid, Citing "Banal" Debate

In a recent interview with the Financial Times, Michael Bloomberg revealed that he is "looking at all the options" regarding a potential presidential bid. This marks the first time the former New York City mayor has publicly acknowledged the possibility of running. Bloomberg's aides had previously hinted at a potential bid, citing his concern over the increasingly polarized nature of the race.

Bloomberg expressed his disappointment with the current state of the debate, stating that US voters "deserve a lot better" than the "distressingly banal" discussions currently taking place. He criticized the level of discourse, calling it "an outrage and an insult to the voters." As a former Democrat, Republican, and current independent, Bloomberg's pro-business views and liberal stance on issues like gun control and abortion could make him a wild card in the election.

If Bloomberg were to run as an independent, his candidacy could potentially damage the Democratic party's chances. According to BBC North America reporter Anthony Zurcher, Bloomberg's liberal views would likely draw support away from the Democrats, rather than the Republicans. With Donald Trump leading the Republican pack and Bernie Sanders challenging Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination, the 2016 presidential election is already shaping up to be a highly contested and unpredictable race. Bloomberg's potential entry could further shake up the landscape, offering voters an alternative to the traditional party candidates.

A dramatic incident occurred at a Spanish airport when a passenger, who had missed his flight to Gran Canaria, attempted to reach the plane by jumping onto the airbridge. The man, reportedly from Bolivia, had cleared security but missed boarding. In a desperate bid to catch his flight, he jumped 10ft into the air, shouldered his two bags, and ran towards the tunnel. He broke through fire escape doors to access the airbridge, sparking concerns over airport security.

The incident was captured on video and posted on Facebook, showing the man's daring attempt to reach the plane. The footage has raised questions about the effectiveness of the airport's security measures, which are currently at level 4, the second-highest alert level. The man could face a fine of up to €45,000 for breaching airport security laws. Ryanair, the airline involved, has stated that the incident is a matter for airport security to handle. The identity of the man has not been officially confirmed, but local media reports suggest he panicked when he saw the plane start to move. An investigation into the incident is likely to follow.

The Introduction of Video Technology in Football: A Step Closer to Reality

The debate over the introduction of video technology in football has been ongoing for several years, with many arguing that it is long overdue. Recently, the International Football Association Board pushed back trials in competitive matches by a year, but according to Gijs de Jong, operations director at the Dutch FA (KNVB), the technology will be used in the not-too-distant future. De Jong predicts that it will take no more than five years for video technology to be implemented in the sport.

The need for video technology has been highlighted by a number of high-profile errors made by referees in recent matches. In the English top-flight, referees have come under intense scrutiny, with mistakes affecting the outcome of games. For example, West Brom's Gareth McAuley was initially sent off against Manchester City, only for the red card to be transferred to teammate Craig Dawson after the referee admitted his mistake. Similarly, Sunderland's Wes Brown was sent off for a foul that was actually committed by his teammate John O'Shea.

Managers such as Tony Pulis and Nigel Pearson have called for the introduction of video technology to help referees make accurate decisions. Pulis suggested a 30-second call-back option, twice a game, to review contentious decisions, while Pearson argued that technology would have prevented a mistaken yellow card being shown to Leicester City's Wes Morgan.

De Jong believes that every mistake made by referees strengthens the case for video technology and can help bring forward its introduction. He points to recent examples in the Premier League and Champions League as evidence that the sport is ready for the implementation of video technology. With the support of managers, players, and fans, it is likely that video technology will become a reality in football sooner rather than later. As De Jong said, "When we get some good examples... then hopefully it'll speed up and we do reach the five year period."

Breakthrough Study Reveals Snakes' Deadly Secret: Constriction Causes Circulatory Arrest, Not Suffocation

For decades, it was believed that snakes, specifically constrictors, suffocated their victims to death. However, a groundbreaking study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology has debunked this myth, revealing that the snakes' lethal grip actually restricts blood flow, causing a rapid and efficient circulatory arrest. This innovative research, led by Professor Scott Boback from Dickinson College in Pennsylvania, has shed new light on the unique killing method of these fascinating creatures.

To conduct the study, researchers took measurements from anaesthetised rats that were gripped by boa constrictors. The team recorded blood pressure, heart activity, and other vital signs, providing a detailed understanding of the physiological effects of constriction on the prey. The results showed that the snake's grip severely restricted blood flow, effectively cutting off the oxygen supply to the vital organs. This circulatory arrest, the scientists explained, is a much more efficient and rapid way of killing prey than previously thought.

According to Professor Boback, restricting blood flow to the brain would cause a rodent to "pass out within seconds." The researchers believe that their findings could have implications beyond the realm of herpetology, as recording during a constriction could reveal useful details about how crush injuries cause complex tissue damage in humans. However, the primary focus of the study remains on understanding the fundamental question of how and why these snakes evolved their unique killing method.

As Professor Boback noted, "The thing I find fascinating is that all snakes have is their mouth to engage with prey. A constrictor has to hold a potentially dangerous animal right next to it, and that animal's fighting for its life, so it will absolutely take chunks out of the snake if it can." To measure this life-or-death battle, the researchers presented anaesthetised lab rats to boa constrictors and recorded from the rats' arteries and heart as they were squeezed. The team also took blood samples before and after, revealing how the blood chemistry of a constricted victim changed.

The study's findings have significant implications for our understanding of constrictor snakes and their behavior. As Professor Brad Moon from the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, who has studied snake movements for two decades, explained, "It shows that constriction is stronger, faster, and more effective than expected." The research also highlights the remarkable adaptability of these snakes, which have evolved to use their bodies to lethal effect.

In a previous study, the same Dickinson College team discovered that the snakes were able to sense their victim's heartbeat and stopped squeezing only when it stopped. This latest research builds on that finding, providing a more detailed understanding of the physiological mechanisms underlying the snakes' killing method. As the scientific community continues to unravel the secrets of these fascinating creatures, one thing is clear: constrictor snakes are more efficient and deadly predators than previously thought.

Swansea's Ashley Williams is set to join Everton in a £12m deal after undergoing a medical. The 31-year-old centre-half will bolster the Toffees' defence following John Stones' £47.5m move to Manchester City. Everton have already signed Idrissa Gueye and Maarten Stekelenburg this summer, strengthening their squad ahead of the new season.

Wasps have announced new contract deals for three young players. Full-back Miller, who has scored seven tries in 35 appearances, has committed to the team, along with wing Bassett, who has scored 27 points in 21 appearances. Centre Macken, yet to make his debut, has also signed on. The announcements come as the team prepares for the departure of fly-half Alex Lozowski to Saracens. This news follows recent contract deals for captain James Haskell and Nathan Hughes. Haskell is one of four Wasps players named to England's 33-man squad for the Six Nations, alongside Joe Launchbury, Matt Mullan, and Elliot Daly. These signings demonstrate Wasps' investment in their young talent and veteran players alike.

EastEnders Fans Prepare for Emotional Farewell as Peggy Mitchell Says Goodbye

In a highly anticipated and emotional storyline, Dame Barbara Windsor's iconic character Peggy Mitchell will be making her final appearance on the BBC soap EastEnders. The actress, who has been battling terminal cancer, will be joined by her on-screen sons Phil and Grant as the Mitchell family reunites to bid their final goodbyes. 

Peggy's return to Albert Square, set to air on May 9, promises to be a dramatic and flamboyant one, as she is greeted by her extended family, including grandchildren Ben and Louise, Billy Mitchell, and niece Ronnie Mitchell. Notably, Grant Mitchell, played by Ross Kemp, will be making a comeback to the show after a 10-year absence. Kemp has expressed his gratitude to the show, stating that his time on EastEnders was a significant springboard for his career.

Dame Barbara, 78, has played the beloved character since 1994 and has made sporadic appearances since her full-time departure in 2010. Her last appearance was earlier this year, when she revealed to her son Phil that her cancer had returned. The show's executive producer, Dominic Treadwell-Collins, has promised that Peggy's exit will be "one of the most heartbreaking, uplifting, and epic exits an EastEnders character has ever had." Fans are bracing themselves for an emotional farewell as they say goodbye to a true EastEnders legend.

The women's grass court event at Devonshire Park has been a staple of the tennis calendar since 1974. This prestigious tournament traditionally draws top female players ahead of Wimbledon. The 2023 final saw Karolina Pliskova defeat Caroline Wozniacki. Past winners include legends Martina Navratilova and Chris Evert. The Lawn Tennis Association has announced that free coverage will continue on TV, radio, and online. According to Oliver Scadgell, the LTA's director of major events, the BBC's support helps to promote tennis and increase participation, building on the success of players like Andy Murray and Johanna Konta. The event's popularity is set to endure.

Liverpool FC and Liverpool City Council have announced a joint plan to redevelop the iconic Anfield stadium, increasing its capacity to 60,000 and transforming the surrounding area. The £150m project is part of the council's £175m regeneration scheme for the L4 area, which aims to create employment and business opportunities for the local community.

The redevelopment will see a number of streets demolished, while hundreds of homes in the area will be refurbished. The project is expected to bring significant benefits to the local community, including the creation of new jobs, improved housing, and enhanced amenities. A public consultation will be held to ensure that residents are kept informed and involved in the planning process.

Alan Blundell, chair of the Walton Breck Road Residents' Association, has welcomed the proposals, stating that he is "very pleased" with the plans. However, he emphasized the importance of keeping residents informed and consulted throughout the process, particularly those who may be affected by Compulsory Purchase Orders (CPOs). "We have got a new school, medical centre, housing; the main thing is we have got to involve the community at all stages," he said.

The plans have also been cautiously welcomed by fans' union Spirit of Shankly, who have long advocated for the club to remain at Anfield. Paul Martin, a representative of the group, stated that while the proposals are promising, there are still many details to be ironed out. "We will only really believe it when the team is running onto the pitch," he said. The group has also suggested the creation of a "football quarter" around the refurbished ground, featuring bars and restaurants.

Liverpool Mayor Joe Anderson has expressed his support for the project, stating that he wants to create a "regenerated Anfield" that will bring employment and business opportunities to the area. Ian Ayre, Liverpool FC's managing director, has emphasized the importance of gaining the support of local homeowners, stating that "any final decision depends on home owners being supportive of the proposed stadium extension."

The redevelopment of Anfield is expected to begin in 2014, with a planning application to be submitted next summer. The project is likely to see extensions to the Main Stand and the Anfield Road end, as well as the construction of a new hotel. While there have been false starts in the past, the club and council are hopeful that this project will finally come to fruition, bringing benefits to both the football club and the local community. As Ian Ayre noted, "there's a lot of wounds to heal" in terms of the club's relationship with local residents, but the proposed redevelopment is a significant step towards healing those wounds and creating a brighter future for Anfield.

England is set to face Wales at Twickenham without injured centre Jonathan Joseph, who suffered a chest injury during the team's 35-11 win over Fiji on Friday. Rugby league convert Sam Burgess, 26, will start alongside Brad Barritt, earning only his third England cap. Meanwhile, number eight Ben Morgan will miss the match due to a minor knee injury, with Billy Vunipola taking his place.

Joseph's injury is not considered serious, but he is a significant doubt for the upcoming match against Australia on October 3. The 24-year-old centre scored four tries in England's Six Nations campaign earlier this year and is a key player in the team's backline. England attack coach Andy Farrell stated that Joseph's injury would likely keep him out for "not more than a week."

The team will face Wales, followed by Australia and Uruguay, with the top two teams from the group progressing to the quarter-finals. Head coach Stuart Lancaster will announce the team on Thursday morning. James Haskell will step up to the bench to face Wales, providing additional support to the team. England will look to build on their strong start to the tournament, and fans can follow the latest rugby union news on Twitter @bbcrugbyunion.

A Bittersweet Reunion: Argentine Grandmother's Hopes Dashed in Search for Abducted Granddaughter

In a heart-wrenching turn of events, Maria Isabel Mariani, a 92-year-old Argentine grandmother, was left devastated when DNA tests revealed that the woman she had recently met was not her long-lost granddaughter, Clara Anahi Mariani Teruggi. The young girl was abducted by the military in 1976, at just three months old, and Ms. Mariani had been searching for her for nearly four decades.

The announcement of their supposed reunion on Thursday had been hailed as a triumph for the campaign group Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo, which was formed to reunite families with their missing children. Even President Mauricio Macri had taken to Twitter to celebrate the news. However, two days later, the prosecutor working on the case, Pablo Parenti, revealed that DNA tests had shown no genetic match between Ms. Mariani and the woman she had met.

The woman, identified as Maria Elena Wehrli, had arrived at Ms. Mariani's house on Christmas Eve with the results of a private DNA test, but these were deemed inconclusive by the authorities. The National Genetic Database, the only body authorized to determine identity in such cases, had found no match. According to Juan Martin Ramos Padilla, a spokesman for the Anahi Foundation, which Ms. Mariani founded, the news was a "hard blow" for the elderly grandmother, who is nearly blind. Nevertheless, Ms. Mariani remains determined to continue her search for her granddaughter.

Clara Anahi's parents, Daniel Mariani and Diana Teruggi, were members of the left-wing group Montoneros, and their daughter was taken from their home during a military operation in which Diana Teruggi was killed. Ms. Mariani's son, Daniel, escaped but went into hiding and was killed a few months later. The Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo estimate that some 500 children were abducted from their mothers in captivity during the military rule in Argentina, which lasted from 1976 to 1983. Many of these children were given for adoption to non-communist families, while others were handed over to orphanages.

Despite the setback, Ms. Mariani's resolve remains unbroken. "She is 92 and will continue searching for her granddaughter," said Mr. Ramos Padilla. "We just hope to be able to find her." The Anahi Foundation, which includes one of Clara Anahi's names, will continue to work towards reuniting families with their missing children. The Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo have already reunited 119 children with their families, with the most recent reunion taking place just last month.

As the search for Clara Anahi continues, the case serves as a poignant reminder of the atrocities committed during Argentina's military rule, during which an estimated 30,000 people were killed. The Grandmothers' campaign is a testament to the power of perseverance and the human spirit, and their work will undoubtedly continue to bring hope to families who have been torn apart by the brutal regime. For Ms. Mariani, the search for her granddaughter will go on, driven by a mother's unwavering love and a grandmother's unrelenting determination.

Liberia's Senate has voted to jail Finance Minister Amara Konneh for proposing a $1.2m budget cut without proper authority. The move has sparked controversy, particularly given Konneh's reputation as a skilled financial manager, having been named African Finance Minister of the Year in 2014 by Banker Magazine. The Supreme Court has since intervened, halting Konneh's imprisonment "until further notice". The Senate's decision was unanimous, with leader Armah Jallah citing Konneh's lack of power to reduce their budget as the reason. The issue has highlighted the sensitive topic of politicians' salaries, with Liberia's 103 lawmakers earning $13,000 per month. As the country faces economic pressure due to declining foreign-exchange earnings from rubber and iron ore, all government sectors are being forced to cut budgets, leading to increased scrutiny of politicians' pay.

Tragedy Strikes Rare Sea Bird Colony in Hartlepool

A devastating incident has occurred at the Crimdon coastal site near Hartlepool, where a colony of little terns, one of the UK's rarest sea birds, has been severely impacted. According to wardens, only 29 nests remain, with evidence suggesting that dogs were deliberately let loose on the site over the weekend, destroying approximately 50 nests.

Durham Heritage Coast (DHC), which manages the site, has described the incident as "heartbreaking". The little tern is a protected species, and the site, one of only 20 in the UK, is typically safeguarded by fences and monitored by wardens during the day. Despite these measures, it appears that someone intentionally entered the site with dogs, causing widespread destruction to the nests.

The DHC has expressed disappointment and dismay at the incident, citing the significant time and effort invested by staff and volunteers in the Little Tern Recovery Project. Unfortunately, this is not the first time the site has been targeted by vandals and egg thieves. In 2013, 50 eggs were stolen from 65 nesting pairs, and it is believed that some eggs were also taken during the recent incident, while others were likely destroyed or eaten by dogs.

The remaining 29 nests are now at risk, and the DHC is holding out hope that they will survive. The colony had previously experienced a difficult year in 2015, and conservationists had been optimistic about this year's prospects due to favorable weather conditions. The DHC will be reviewing its security measures, but funding limitations may hinder its ability to implement more robust protections. The incident is currently under investigation by the police.

Newcastle Falcons bounced back from last week's defeat in France with a convincing 59-14 win over Lyon. The hosts dominated the first half, with Juan Pablo Socino scoring two tries and Sonatane Takulua and Charlie Hodgson also crossing the line. Hodgson kicked seven from seven as the Falcons took a 34-10 lead into the break. Zach Kibirige and Callum Chick added further tries after the interval, securing a strong victory. Lyon earned a try bonus-point with Paul Bonnefond's late score, but the Falcons' win lifts them to third in their group, just a point behind the French side. The result marks a significant turnaround for Newcastle after their 42-12 loss in Lyon last week.

Court of Appeal Upholds Compensation Scheme for Jimmy Savile Victims

The Court of Appeal has dismissed a challenge to the compensation scheme set up for victims of disgraced BBC presenter Jimmy Savile, paving the way for hundreds of claimants to receive payments. The scheme, which was established by the Savile estate, the BBC, the NHS, and charity Barnardo's, aims to provide compensation to those who were abused by Savile during his lifetime.

The Jimmy Savile Charitable Trust, which is a beneficiary of the estate, had argued that the scheme would not effectively weed out fake claims and that too much money would go to lawyers. However, appeal judges rejected this challenge, ruling that the scheme should proceed as planned.

The court also rejected the trust's application to remove NatWest as the executor of Savile's estate. The ruling brings relief to the many victims of Savile who have been waiting for justice. According to lawyers, over 200 people have come forward to make compensation claims, with payments capped at £60,000.

Liz Dux, a lawyer representing many of the victims, welcomed the ruling, saying it would bring "great relief" to those who have been living with uncertainty. "They just want some recognition of what they have been through so they can then be able to move on with their lives," she said.

The compensation scheme was established after a documentary broadcast in 2012 alleged that Savile was a "serial child abuser and sex offender." The former BBC presenter was accused of abusing people in hospitals and other institutions, and a large number of people came forward to make claims after the programme.

In a separate development, abuse survivors who met with Home Secretary Theresa May on Monday announced that the government would be creating a £2m fund to support groups helping people who will give evidence to the forthcoming public inquiry into abuse. A further £1.5m fund will be established to support charities that help abuse survivors. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood said it was represented at the meeting, although the Home Office has not yet announced any details.

The ruling and the government's announcement are seen as significant steps towards providing justice and support to the victims of Jimmy Savile and other abuse survivors. As the public inquiry into abuse prepares to get underway, it is hoped that these developments will help to bring closure and recognition to those who have suffered at the hands of abusers.

A young musician from Carnoustie has brought together an impressive array of celebrities to feature on his latest song, "The Highland Road". Craig Weir, 23, has enlisted the help of Hollywood actor Alan Cumming, Queen guitarist Brian May, and The Libertines' Peter Doherty, among others, to contribute to the track.

The song begins and ends with a poem written by Craig and his friend Chris Brown, which was inspired by a trip they took along the Highland Road in Canada last year. The poem is bookended by 21 guest voices, including former AC/DC bassist Mark Evans, television presenter Lorraine Kelly, and Kyle Falconer from Dundee band The View.

Craig, who has previously performed for Arnold Schwarzenegger in Edinburgh, said the idea for the song had been in the back of his mind for a while. He got in touch with his core contributors, including Brian May and Alan Cumming, and was thrilled when they agreed to take part. Peter Doherty was also a key contributor, recording his line in Buenos Aires while on tour.

The contributions were largely recorded on the celebrities' phones and emailed or texted to Craig, who then pieced them together in the studio. Despite initial doubts about how the song would sound, Craig is delighted with the final result. "Now I've got this fantastic piece together with a whole range of voices representing entertainment around the world," he said.

The celebrities involved have been similarly impressed with the song, with Alan Cumming describing it as "beautiful" and "really moving". Brian May said he was "happy to pour a little of my Scottish blood into this epic", while Lorraine Kelly said she was "delighted" to contribute and that hearing the final product gave her "goose bumps".

Craig, who performs with his band The Cabalistic Cavalry, has had a number of high-profile encounters in the past, including six dates with the Bay City Rollers and a performance of "We Will Rock You" with Queen at the SSE Hydro. Despite his musical success, Craig still teaches music and said his pupils take a "great interest" in his other career. "It's like a Jekyll and Hyde character," he joked. "The bell goes on Friday afternoon and that's me away playing around the world."

"The Highland Road" is a unique and exciting collaboration that brings together some of the biggest names in entertainment. With its inspiring poem and array of talented contributors, it's a song that is sure to leave a lasting impression on listeners.

Labour Leader Jeremy Corbyn to Raise Human Rights Concerns with Chinese President Xi

The upcoming state visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to the United Kingdom has sparked a flurry of diplomatic activity, with Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn announcing his intention to raise concerns about human rights issues with the Chinese leader. Mr. Corbyn's spokesman confirmed that the Labour leader would be "using the opportunity" of President Xi's four-day visit to discuss his concerns, citing Mr. Corbyn's long-standing commitment to human rights causes.

The visit, which begins next week, will be President Xi's first to the UK as Chinese leader and will include a state banquet at Buckingham Palace, where Mr. Corbyn will be in attendance. The Labour leader's spokesman stated that discussions are underway to arrange private meetings with Chinese officials during the visit, but did not rule out the possibility of Mr. Corbyn raising human rights issues during the royal function if necessary.

Mr. Corbyn's decision to raise human rights concerns comes after Chancellor George Osborne's visit to China last month, where he addressed the issue privately with Chinese officials. However, campaigners had urged Mr. Osborne to be more vocal about the treatment of the Muslim Uighur minority in the restive Xinjiang province, which the Chancellor visited during his trip.

The UK government has faced criticism for its approach to human rights issues in China, with some accusing ministers of prioritizing trade and economic ties over human rights concerns. Mr. Osborne has stated that the UK and China have different political systems and traditions, but that this does not preclude cooperation in areas such as commerce and culture.

Mr. Corbyn, who has a long history of campaigning on human rights cases, has been critical of the government's approach to human rights issues in the past. As a backbench MP, he urged the release of political prisoners and called on the UK to stop selling arms to "repressive" regimes. In his conference speech last month, he highlighted the case of Ali Mohammed Baqir al-Nimr, a Saudi man who faces beheading after being convicted of crimes including breaking allegiance to the country's king.

The government's decision to withdraw from talks about a £5.9m contract to provide services to Saudi jails has been seen as a response to criticism of the country's criminal justice system. However, ministers have denied that the decision was related to any individual case.

As for Mr. Corbyn's attendance at the state banquet, his spokesman was unable to confirm whether he would wear the traditional white tie attire, or if he even owned such clothing. However, the spokesman did confirm that Mr. Corbyn would "take full part" in the event, including singing the national anthem, after being criticized for not doing so at a Battle of Britain memorial service last month.

During the visit, President Xi is expected to address Parliament and hold talks with Prime Minister David Cameron. The visit marks a significant improvement in relations between the two countries, which were strained in 2012 following a diplomatic row over David Cameron's meeting with the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama. As the visit gets underway, all eyes will be on Mr. Corbyn and his efforts to raise human rights concerns with the Chinese leader, and whether his actions will have any impact on the UK's relationship with China.

Tata Steel's Decision to Cut Jobs Sends Shockwaves Through Welsh Economy

The Welsh economy has been dealt a devastating blow as Tata Steel announced plans to cut hundreds of jobs, leaving many to wonder about the future of the steel industry in the region. This news comes at a particularly sensitive time, with an assembly election and a possible EU referendum looming on the horizon. The response from the government is expected to be far more tailored to the steel industry this time around, compared to the more general approach taken during the recession seven years ago.

The timing of Tata's announcement is also significant, coming less than a fortnight after Chancellor George Osborne warned about the dangers facing the British economy. Many saw Osborne's warning as a cautionary tale about the risks of leaving the EU, but the counter view is that the steel industry's woes will only serve to fuel anger towards Brussels for failing to tackle cheap Chinese steel imports. This could potentially sway voters to reconsider their stance on EU membership.

The losses will undoubtedly dominate the economic debate in the lead-up to the assembly elections. First Minister Carwyn Jones has already come out swinging, suggesting that the UK government's lack of urgency in addressing Chinese imports and energy costs contributed to the job losses. Jones stopped short of declaring all-out war with Westminster, but it's clear that he will be seeking to capitalize on criticism of the UK government's handling of the steel crisis.

The UK government has defended its response, citing efforts to address concerns over energy and imports, while also acknowledging that the problem is largely caused by over-capacity in the global steel supply. However, this explanation is unlikely to provide much comfort to the hundreds of workers facing redundancy. In the short term, the Welsh government will focus on providing re-training programs for those affected, but in the longer term, a broader debate will need to take place about the level of financial support that should be committed to the steel industry.

Plaid Cymru has already suggested that some form of state-ownership should be considered, but any proposals will ultimately come down to the question of whether it's worth risking resources on an industry that is largely beyond the government's control. As one senior Tata manager noted last year, the steel industry is facing a "new reality" that will require significant adjustments in order to survive.

The difference between the current situation and the recession of 2009 is stark. While the previous downturn was seen as a cyclical phenomenon, the current crisis is viewed as a more permanent shift in the global steel landscape. As the Welsh government grapples with the implications of Tata's decision, one thing is clear: the steel industry will never be the same again, and the region will need to adapt quickly in order to mitigate the damage. The coming weeks and months will be crucial in determining the future of the steel industry in Wales, and the impact that it will have on the wider economy.

A British Army major is on trial for causing the death of a 24-year-old man by careless driving. Maj Richard Scott, 40, is accused of driving his Audi A6 at speeds of up to 95mph on a B-road in Wiltshire despite bad weather conditions. On October 6, 2014, Gareth Hicks, a passenger in a Ford Transit van, suffered fatal injuries when the vehicle was hit head-on by Maj Scott's car.

Prosecutor Charles Gabb told the court that Maj Scott had crossed the carriageway of the 60mph-limit B390 in Shrewton, near Amesbury, before colliding with the van. The weather at the time was described as "awful" with strong winds and heavy rain. Mr Gabb alleged that Maj Scott's car was "twitching" and may have been aquaplaning before striking a BMW driven by Craig Reed, and then crossing the carriageway again to collide with the van.

Maj Scott denies the charge, suggesting that it was actually Mr Reed who had crossed the carriageway, causing the collision. The defendant suffered substantial injuries in the crash and claims to have no memory of the incident. The trial continues, with the jury considering the evidence presented. Gareth Hicks, from Bath, Somerset, was on his way to a construction site in Salisbury when the accident occurred. His family and friends are awaiting the outcome of the trial, seeking justice for his tragic death.

Former Labour Prime Minister Gordon Brown has launched a scathing attack on both Scottish and Brexit nationalism, stating that voters are caught between the "extremes" of these two ideologies. In a campaign speech delivered in Fife, Brown emphasized the need for social justice to be the defining issue of the upcoming general election on June 8.

Brown's speech, which made no mention of current UK Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, centered on the forecasted rise in child poverty in Scotland. According to the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), 320,000 children living in Scotland will be in poverty by 2022. Brown argued that nationalism offers no solutions to this pressing issue and that it is imperative to address poverty through a commitment to social justice.

The former Prime Minister also warned against giving Theresa May a "free hand" or "blank cheque" in the election, stressing the importance of sending Labour MPs to parliament to "fight a war against poverty." However, his remarks were quickly countered by SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon, who claimed that Labour is "incapable" of defeating the Conservatives.

Sturgeon argued that only the SNP can protect Scotland from the "full force" of policies implemented by a future Conservative government. She criticized Brown's speech as being overly familiar, stating that he has been making the same arguments for years. The SNP leader also highlighted the chaos at the heart of the Labour Party, which she believes has contributed to the Tories' significant lead in England.

Scottish Conservative leader Ruth Davidson also responded to Brown's speech, accusing him of taking Scotland back to the 1990s. Davidson called on the SNP to remove the threat of a second independence referendum from the table, emphasizing the importance of the union between Scotland and the rest of the United Kingdom. She positioned the Scottish Conservatives as a forward-thinking party, focused on the future and the well-being of young people.

Meanwhile, Scottish Liberal Democrat leader Willie Rennie echoed Sturgeon's sentiments, stating that Labour is incapable of providing a competent opposition to the Conservatives. Rennie argued that his party is the main challenger to the SNP in many marginal seats and that the Liberal Democrats can offer a fairer and more competent voice for the country.

As the general election campaign gains momentum, it is clear that the debate in Scotland will be shaped by the interplay between nationalist and unionist sentiments. With the SNP, Labour, and the Conservatives all vying for dominance, the outcome of the election remains uncertain. One thing is certain, however: the issue of social justice and the need to address poverty will be a key battleground in the campaign ahead. As Brown's speech highlighted, the fate of thousands of children living in poverty in Scotland hangs in the balance, and it is up to voters to decide which party is best equipped to tackle this pressing issue.

Wales Forward Robson-Kanu Declares Fitness for Euro 2016 Opener

After a string of leg and ankle injuries that kept him out of Wales' last four friendly matches, forward Hal Robson-Kanu has announced that he is ready to play a full 90 minutes in the team's Euro 2016 opener against Slovakia. The 27-year-old, who is currently unattached after leaving Reading in May, has resumed full training with the Wales squad in France and is confident in his ability to participate in the upcoming match.

"I've trained, I'm feeling good, feeling fresh. Come Saturday, I'll be 100%," Robson-Kanu said, dispelling concerns about his fitness. Wales is set to face a demanding schedule, with three group games in 10 days against Slovakia, England, and Russia. Despite his recent injuries, Robson-Kanu believes he can cope with the physical demands of the tournament, citing his high levels of fitness and recent training sessions.

Wales manager Chris Coleman has also expressed optimism about the availability of other injured players, including midfielders Joe Ledley and Joe Allen. However, midfielder David Vaughan missed training on Thursday, casting some uncertainty over his participation in the upcoming match. With the team's journey to Bordeaux set to begin on Friday, Robson-Kanu's declaration of fitness is a welcome boost to Wales' chances in their first major tournament appearance since the 1958 World Cup.

A crash on the A329 Oxford Road occurred at 05:30 GMT, involving a red Peugeot 206. Two of three occupants are being treated in hospital, while a fourth person is being sought by police. The road is closed as a structural engineer assesses two damaged buildings. Thames Valley Police are investigating, with no arrests made. Motorists are advised to find alternative routes due to lengthy delays, with a diversion in place. Inquiries are ongoing to establish the circumstances of the crash.

Christina Rees has been appointed as the Labour party's new spokesperson on Wales in Westminster, becoming the fifth person to hold the position since 2015. Speaking to BBC Wales for the first time since her appointment, Ms Rees expressed her hope that she will be the last to hold the role before the 2020 general election. Her predecessor, Jo Stevens, resigned over the party's stance on Brexit, specifically the vote to trigger Article 50.

Ms Rees has pledged her support to Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, stating that he is the democratically elected leader and deserves the party's backing. She emphasized the importance of unity within the party and ruled out any involvement in attempts to unseat Mr. Corbyn. With a focus on unity, Ms Rees aims to bring stability to the role and serve out the remainder of the term until 2020. She hopes to be the last shadow Welsh secretary before the next election.

A Filipino national has been convicted of attempted murder and voyeurism after a brutal attack on his former partner in Cardiff. Arnel Martinez Raymundo, 48, was found guilty at Cardiff Crown Court on Thursday of stabbing Anna Caladiao, 43, in the back at their former home on June 12.

The court heard that Miss Caladiao suffered life-threatening injuries, including stomach and lung wounds, and was forced to spend six days in intensive care on a ventilator. She would have died if not for the timely intervention of workmen who came to her aid when she stumbled into the street.

Raymundo fled the scene and made his way to London, where he was arrested 13 days later in Croydon. During his trial, he denied the charges, claiming that Miss Caladiao had fed him crystal meth and that he had started stabbing randomly during a dream. However, the jury rejected his claims and found him guilty of both attempted murder and voyeurism.

In a victim impact statement, Miss Caladiao described the devastating effects of the attack, saying she was left "badly scarred" and in need of a wheelchair for weeks. She also revealed that she was suffering from nightmares, stress, and panic attacks, and that she could still feel the knife going into her body.

Judge Eleri Rees condemned Raymundo's actions, saying that he had shown "not the slightest remorse" for his crimes. She described the attack as "ferocious" and said that Raymundo's behavior had demonstrated a disregard for Miss Caladiao's life. Raymundo was jailed for his crimes, bringing an end to a traumatic ordeal for Miss Caladiao and her family.

Foxconn, the world's largest contract electronics manufacturer, has announced a historic deal to acquire a 66% stake in Sharp, a Japanese electronics firm, for approximately $3.5 billion. The deal, set to be signed on April 2, marks the first foreign takeover of a major Japanese electronics company. Foxconn, which assembles the majority of the world's iPhones, had initially attempted to invest in Sharp in 2012, but talks collapsed. Sharp, founded in 1912, has struggled with heavy debts and has undergone two major bailouts in the last four years. Despite its financial woes, the company remains a leader in liquid display technology, a key asset for Foxconn. The acquisition will form a "historic strategic alliance" between the two companies, with Foxconn seeking to leverage Sharp's innovative technologies. Japanese officials had previously been hesitant to allow Sharp to fall under foreign ownership due to its distinctive display panel technology. The deal surpasses a rival offer from a government-backed consortium of Japanese investors, securing Foxconn's position as a major player in the global electronics industry.

Cardiff council's new penalty scheme has seen a significant impact in its first month. A total of 3,544 penalty notices were handed out in December 2014, with 370 offenders already paying the £35 charge, totaling £12,950. The scheme, which currently focuses on bus lanes, will expand to yellow box junctions and illegal parking around schools. Drivers are warned that unpaid fines can double to £70 if not paid within 21 days. A council spokesman emphasized that the goal is to encourage drivers to follow the Highway Code, stating "if you don't want to be fined, don't breach it." The revenue generated will fund the project and other traffic-related initiatives. The council's message is clear: comply with the rules to avoid penalties.

Oculus Rift has made a significant reversal in its policy regarding the use of its games on rival headsets. A recent software update has removed the checks that prevented Oculus games from being played on the HTC Vive using the Revive software. The move comes as a surprise, given the company's previous efforts to lock down its content and prevent it from being used on other devices.

The Revive software, released in April, allowed users to play Oculus games on the HTC Vive, much to the dismay of Oculus. The company had updated its software to include a headset check, ensuring that only Oculus Rift headsets could play the games. However, the developers behind Revive found ways to work around this check, allowing users to continue playing Oculus games on the Vive.

The removal of the headset check has been confirmed by Oculus, which stated that it would not use such checks in the future. The company emphasized the importance of protecting developer content, citing it as crucial to the long-term success of the VR industry. The move has been met with surprise and relief from the VR community, with many criticizing Oculus's initial decision to lock down its content.

The Revive developers expressed their surprise and disbelief at the change, posting a message on their Github page. The decision is seen as a significant shift in Oculus's approach to content protection and compatibility. By removing the headset check, Oculus is effectively allowing its games to be played on other devices, including the HTC Vive. The move is likely to be welcomed by VR enthusiasts, who value the ability to play a wide range of games across different platforms.

MPs Demand Action in 31-Year-Old Disappearance Case of Katrice Lee

A debate was held in the House of Commons to discuss the handling of the investigation into the disappearance of Katrice Lee, who vanished 31 years ago from a shop at a German military base. Katrice's family, including her mother Sharon Lee, sister Natasha, and father Richard Lee, have been waiting for answers for far too long. The family believes that Katrice, who disappeared on her second birthday, is still alive and was abducted.

Hartlepool Labour MP Iain Wright expressed his frustration, stating that the family has waited "far too long" and "action must be taken." Conservative MP Caroline Dinenage also criticized former Prime Minister David Cameron for refusing to meet with the family. Defence Minister Mark Francois assured the family that he would try to meet with them before Christmas and that the Royal Military Police are using modern investigative techniques to get to the bottom of the case.

Katrice's disappearance occurred when her mother left her at the checkout with her aunt for a moment to get crisps. When she returned, Katrice was gone. The family is still holding out hope that Katrice will be found, and they are seeking justice and closure. The debate has brought renewed attention to the case, and the family is hoping that it will lead to a breakthrough in the investigation.

Ireland Names 14-Man Panel for Round-Robin Competition

The Irish cricket team has announced a 14-man squad for the upcoming round-robin competition, featuring eight associate countries. The team will face off against Afghanistan, Scotland, Hong Kong, Oman, Namibia, and the UAE in the tournament. Notably, the squad includes the return of several key players who missed most of Ireland's 2016 campaign due to injury or personal issues.

Boyd Rankin, Andrew Balbirnie, and Greg Thompson are all back in the fold, bringing valuable experience and skills to the team. Rankin's height and pace are expected to add an extra dimension to Ireland's attack, while Balbirnie and Thompson will provide stability and depth to the batting lineup. Head coach John Bracewell expressed his delight at having the trio back in the squad, citing the benefits of their experience and expertise.

The selectors have opted to take Gary Wilson as the sole wicket-keeper, omitting Niall O'Brien from the squad. Middlesex seamer Tim Murtagh has also been left out. Meanwhile, young players Jacob Mulder and Josh Little have retained their places in the T20 squad, following impressive debuts against Hong Kong. The Ireland squad will be led by captain William Porterfield, and will look to make a strong impression in the round-robin competition.

A devastating attack occurred in el-Arish as a bomber rammed a lorry filled with explosives into a building. Militants then opened fire on the station, causing chaos. Although no group has claimed responsibility, the area is frequently targeted by Islamists linked to the Islamic State group. The North Sinai region has seen over 400 attacks between 2012 and 2015, with the Sinai Province jihadist group being the most active insurgents. This group, formerly known as Ansar Beit al-Maqdis, has around 1,000 to 1,500 members and swore loyalty to IS in 2014, posing a significant threat to the region.

A damning report has revealed the shocking conditions faced by thousands of migrants who arrived in the UK over the summer, with many being held in squalid and inhumane facilities. The prisons watchdog, led by chief inspector Peter Clarke, investigated conditions at Channel facilities in Folkestone and Dover, and found that officials were unable to cope with the influx of arrivals.

The report found that over 3,500 people, including 370 children who had arrived without adults, were held in facilities that lacked basic decency. Many were forced to sleep on concrete floors in unhygienic conditions, with no access to clean or dry clothes, food, or hot drinks. Inspectors found that many migrants had not eaten for long periods and were dehydrated, while others suffered from scabies, headaches, and diarrhoea.

The Longport Freight Shed in Folkestone, which was used as a temporary holding facility, was found to be particularly unsuitable. Inspectors described the conditions as "fundamentally lacking in decency", with migrants forced to endure cramped and unsanitary conditions. Another facility, Frontier House in Folkestone, had nowhere suitable for migrants to sleep, while a third facility at Dover Seaport was "crowded, poorly ventilated, and smelled badly".

Mr Clarke said that it was "unacceptable" that officials did not work out more quickly how to manage the crisis, and that arrangements were still not in place to process detainees quickly and efficiently. He welcomed plans to refurbish the Dover Seaport holding room and praised a project that helped charities and other organisations support detained migrants.

Immigration minister James Brokenshire acknowledged that the conditions were "not acceptable" and said that the Home Office had already accepted most of Mr Clarke's recommendations. He confirmed that the Longport Freight Shed would not be used again as a holding facility, saying that it was only used temporarily to ease exceptional pressures on existing screening centres.

The report highlights the need for urgent action to address the crisis in migrant detention facilities. The number of detentions in the first nine months of 2015 more than doubled to 4,785, compared to 2,118 in the same period the previous year. Many of the arrivals were from Eritrea, Sudan, and Syria, and were fleeing conflict and persecution in their home countries.

The government has faced criticism for its handling of the migrant crisis, with many arguing that more needs to be done to provide safe and humane accommodation for those seeking to enter the UK. The report's findings are a stark reminder of the need for a more compassionate and effective approach to managing migration, and for ensuring that the basic human rights of all individuals are respected and protected.

A romantic gesture by a Southampton university student has gone viral on social media, earning him admiration and date offers from around the world. Alfonso, a 25-year-old student from Mexico City, mustered up the courage to ask his crush, Naomi Lucking, out on a coffee date in a rather unconventional way. While studying in the university library, he penned a creative note that read: "Sorry to disturb your studies, but I really need to ask.... would you like to have a coffee with me someday?" The note even provided two possible replies, including a humorous option that mentioned a 7ft tall boyfriend.

Although Naomi politely declined the offer, she was impressed by Alfonso's inventiveness and took to Twitter to share a photo of the note. Her tweet, which has been shared over 30,000 times, described the encounter as the "most awkward experience of my life," but also gave Alfonso "10/10 for creativity." In a follow-up tweet, Naomi revealed that she had told Alfonso that her boyfriend was actually 6ft 3", leaving him "crushed."

The reaction to Alfonso's note has been overwhelming, with people from all over the world reaching out to him with date offers. Despite being turned down by Naomi, who is already in a relationship, Alfonso has described the experience as "really great." He explained that he wanted to approach Naomi in a unique way, as they were in a quiet room and he didn't want to disturb her. Alfonso's creative effort has not only earned him admiration but also taught him a valuable lesson about the power of social media.

Naomi, on the other hand, has been left "completely bewildered" by the response to her tweet, saying she had no idea it would garner so much attention. While she appreciated Alfonso's effort, she has no plans to reconsider his offer, citing her existing relationship. Nevertheless, Alfonso's romantic gesture has clearly made an impact, and he can take comfort in knowing that his creativity has been recognized and appreciated by thousands of people around the world.

The Royal Regiment has been bestowed with the prestigious Freedom of the Borough award, recognizing its strong ties to the East Midlands region. A ceremony was held on Saturday to grant the honour, with Commanding Officer Lt Col Richard Slack expressing his gratitude. "It's a great honour," he said, acknowledging the support of the borough council and local community.

The regiment, currently based in Germany, has a long history of recruiting from Northamptonshire and has seen action in various conflict zones, including Bosnia, Iraq, and Afghanistan. Council leader David Mackintosh praised the regiment's vital role in defending the country, noting the sacrifices made by its members. The council has invited the regiment to parade through Northampton's streets upon its return from deployment, a tradition that drew over 1,000 spectators last year. The regiment is set to be redeployed to Afghanistan in 2013.

Ronnie O'Sullivan Edges Out Liang Wenbo in Thrilling Masters Opener

The 2023 Masters tournament got off to a thrilling start as England's Ronnie O'Sullivan battled back from the brink of defeat to overcome China's Liang Wenbo in a nail-biting 6-5 victory. O'Sullivan, seeking a record seventh Masters title, was pushed to the limit by the Chinese world number 11, who fought from 4-2 down to lead 5-4 before missing a crucial black in the 10th frame.

Despite struggling with illness and fatigue, O'Sullivan showed his trademark resilience to hang in the match and eventually seal the win with a stunning 121 break in the deciding frame. The 41-year-old, who has been ranked as high as world number one, was relieved to have advanced to the quarterfinals, where he will face either Neil Robertson or Ali Carter.

In the post-match interview, O'Sullivan admitted that he didn't deserve to win and felt for his opponent, Liang, who had come so close to pulling off a major upset. "I didn't feel well today, and I was tired," O'Sullivan said. "I've had it for about a month, but I just tried to stay professional and hang in there." The five-time world champion also expressed his admiration for Liang's skill and dedication, acknowledging that the Chinese player had given him a run for his money.

Meanwhile, 2011 winner Ding Junhui made a successful return to the Masters, defeating English world number 16 Kyren Wilson 6-3 in the day's other first-round match. The Chinese world number six, who had not won a Masters match in five years, produced a break of 50 in the ninth frame to seal the win. Ding will now face either former world champion Stuart Bingham or Joe Perry in the quarterfinals.

O'Sullivan's victory sets up an intriguing quarterfinal match against either Robertson or Carter, and the Englishman will be looking to build on his momentum as he bids to break the record for the most Masters titles. However, the 41-year-old seems unconcerned about the pressure to win, stating that he can play until he's 50 and that he doesn't see much grassroots talent emerging to challenge him. With his experience and skill, O'Sullivan remains a force to be reckoned with in the world of snooker, and his fans will be eagerly anticipating his next match at Alexandra Palace in London.

A Southeastern train travelling from Victoria to Dartford was evacuated at Denmark Hill Station in south London after flames were spotted underneath the train. The incident occurred at approximately 18:45 GMT, and the station was shut down as a precautionary measure. Passengers on board filmed sparks visible above the track, and one witness, Cosmin Suttu, described seeing "big flames" from the train window.

The London Fire Brigade reported that the fire affected eight carriages and damaged one electrical box, but fortunately, there were no reports of injuries. The station has since reopened, and an investigation into the cause of the fire is underway. This is the second fire involving a Southeastern train in just 10 days, following a track fire at Charing Cross Station on November 23 that closed the station for about two hours. A spokesman for Southeastern confirmed that the driver took the decision to evacuate the train and the station, and the company is working to determine the cause of the incident.

Wales manager Chris Coleman has expressed optimism over the recovery of star player Gareth Bale, who underwent surgery in November after suffering an injury while playing for Real Madrid in the Champions League. With Wales' next 2018 World Cup qualifier against Republic of Ireland in Dublin on March 24, Coleman believes Bale is on track to regain full fitness. "So far, so good," Coleman told BBC Wales Sport. "There are no problems, no alarm bells ringing."

Coleman plans to visit Bale in Madrid, a trip that was already scheduled, to check on his progress. The manager is confident that the changes to the World Cup format, which will expand from 32 to 48 teams, will benefit smaller nations like Wales. "It gives us a better chance to compete," Coleman said. Bale played a crucial role in Wales' run to the semi-finals of the 2016 European Championship, and his return to fitness will be a significant boost to the team's World Cup qualifying campaign.

Ofsted Inspections Deemed "Ineffective" in Detecting Child Abuse in Rotherham

A scathing report by the Communities and Local Government Committee has deemed Ofsted inspections "ineffective" in detecting the widespread abuse of children in Rotherham. The committee's investigation into the abuse of over 1,400 children in the town between 1997 and 2013 found that Ofsted's inspections failed to expose the extent of the problem and the council's inability to combat it.

According to the report, Ofsted's inquiries relied too heavily on what council staff said, rather than verifying that policies were being implemented and were effective. The inspections were also criticized for being "too short and narrowly focused," failing to probe beyond the information provided by council officials. This led to a failure to detect the "professional jealousy and incompetence" that hindered the operation of Children's Social Care in Rotherham.

The committee's chair, Labour MP Clive Betts, stated that while the perpetrators of the abuse bear ultimate responsibility, Ofsted's ineffectiveness contributed to the failure to expose the problem. He expressed concerns that similar shortcomings in inspection arrangements may have allowed child sexual exploitation to go undetected in other areas.

The report highlighted the need for Ofsted to re-inspect all local authorities in England as soon as possible to ensure that councils are identifying and tackling child sexual exploitation in their communities. Betts emphasized that Ofsted needs to "get under the skin of what is happening in local authorities" and not just focus on paperwork and procedures.

Ofsted has welcomed the report and acknowledged that its inspection methods have changed since 2012. A spokesman apologized for the agency's historical mistakes in Rotherham, stating that the changes made since then strengthen its ability to uncover where children are at risk. The report's findings serve as a stark reminder of the need for effective inspection and oversight to protect vulnerable children and prevent such atrocities from happening again.

Stephen Board, 66, of Bognor, is charged with multiple sexual assaults at two hospitals. The incidents allegedly occurred at St Richard's Hospital and Worthing Hospital between 2006 and 2015. He will appear at Worthing Magistrates' Court on November 29. The charges include assaults on women aged 19, 34, and 78 at the time of the incidents, according to Sussex Police.

Melania Trump Marks World Reading Day with Hospital Visit

In celebration of World Reading Day, US First Lady Melania Trump made a solo appearance at the Manhattan paediatrics ward of New York Presbyterian Hospital. The visit was a rare public outing for the first lady, who has kept a relatively low profile since her husband's inauguration. Accompanied by a small entourage, including two cameramen, Mrs Trump brought a special gift for the young patients - a collection of Dr Seuss books, including one of her personal favorites, "Oh, The Places You'll Go!"

As she sat down to read to the children, Mrs Trump encouraged them to develop a love for reading and to think about their aspirations in life. "We will read some books today," she said with a smile. "So do you know what is today? It's a reading day." The children listened intently as she read from the iconic book, holding up the colorful illustrations and emphasizing the inspiring words.

The first lady's visit was a heartwarming gesture, and the children seemed to enjoy her company. As she read, she wore a elegant outfit, complete with black stilettos and a large diamond ring. The Dr Seuss books she brought were beautifully presented in a white box, tied with a golden ribbon. After the reading, Mrs Trump was asked about her visit, but was briefly pulled away to pose for photos before she could respond.

Despite her reserved nature, Mrs Trump's hospital visit suggested that she may be ready to take on a more public role. As she told the children, "You'll be as famous as famous can be, with the whole wide world watching you win on TV." Her message of encouragement and empowerment was a positive note, and it will be interesting to see how she chooses to use her platform as first lady in the future.

Researchers at the University of Warwick have utilized advanced scanning technology to create a 3D image of the Megalosaurus, a dinosaur discovered in Stonesfield, Oxfordshire, and named in 1824. The team, led by Professor Mark Williams, took over 3,000 X-ray images of the dinosaur's jawbone, revealing previously unseen teeth and allowing for a detailed examination of the fossil. The scans showed the roots of teeth, the extent of repairs, and even tiny newly-growing teeth that were hidden deep within the jaw.

This groundbreaking research will aid in future restoration work on the specimen, which is owned by the Oxford University Museum of Natural History. The university plans to use the scans to make informed decisions about any upcoming restoration projects. Professor Williams expressed his excitement about the opportunity to use state-of-the-art technology on such an iconic specimen. The discovery of the hidden teeth has provided new insights into the life and biology of the Megalosaurus, shedding more light on this ancient creature. The scans have opened up new possibilities for the study and preservation of this historic fossil.

West Brom striker Saido Berahino has taken a step towards regaining his fitness after playing for the club's U-23 team against Brighton on Monday. The 23-year-old was sent to a conditioning camp in France to help him lose weight and improve his overall fitness. Berahino's last appearance for the first team was on September 10, and he has not scored since February 27 against Chelsea.

With his contract set to expire at the end of the season, Berahino's future at the club remains uncertain. He is eligible to sign a pre-contract agreement with an overseas club from January 1, which would allow him to leave for free. If he chooses to join another English club, his transfer fee would be determined by a tribunal, similar to the situation with Danny Ings when he left Burnley for Liverpool in 2015. Despite interest from Stoke and Crystal Palace, who both made £20m offers last summer, Berahino's future remains up in the air. His return to fitness is a positive step, but it remains to be seen what the future holds for the Burundi-born player.

Tensions in the South China Sea have escalated after a US warship sailed near the disputed Fiery Cross Reef, which is controlled by China. The move was deemed "illegal" by Chinese authorities, who claim it has "damaged regional peace". The reef, which has been transformed into an artificial island through a massive dredging operation, is at the center of a longstanding territorial dispute between China and several of its neighbors, including Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, and Brunei.

According to US Defense Department spokesman Bill Urban, the naval operation was designed to "challenge excessive maritime claims" in the region and ensure access to key shipping and air routes. The US has maintained a policy of not taking sides in the territorial disputes, but has conducted regular "freedom of navigation" patrols to assert its presence in the area.

China, however, has strongly objected to the US move, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Lu Kang stating that the warship had "threatened China's sovereignty and security interests" and endangered the staff and facilities on the reef. The incident has raised concerns among neighboring countries, who are wary of China's military ambitions in the region. The latest tensions come as the Philippines, a US ally, has elected a new president, Rodrigo Duterte, who has vowed to take a tough stance on the country's territorial dispute with China.

Nicky Hayden, the 2006 MotoGP World Champion, has passed away at the age of 35, following a tragic accident on the Rimini coastline in Italy. The American motorcycle racer suffered "serious cerebral damage" after colliding with a car on Wednesday, May 17, and had been in the intensive care unit of Cesena's Maurizio Bufalini Hospital.

Hayden's family released a statement, saying, "We would like everyone to remember Nicky at his happiest - riding a motorcycle." His brother, Tommy, a former motorcycle racer himself, fondly remembered Nicky's passion for the sport, saying, "He dreamed as a kid of being a pro-rider and not only achieved that but also managed to reach the pinnacle of his chosen sport. We are all so proud of that. We will all miss him terribly."

Nicky's sister, Kathleen, added, "Today I not only lost my big brother, but I lost a best friend." The outpouring of tributes from the racing community has been immense, with Red Bull Honda World Superbike saying, "The racing world has said goodbye to one of its dearest sons. The 'Kentucky Kid' will be sorely missed by all that ever had the pleasure of meeting him or the privilege to see him race a motorcycle around a track, be it dirt or asphalt."

Born in Kentucky, Hayden began competing in MotoGP in 2003 and quickly made a name for himself in the sport. He finished third in the standings in 2005 and went on to win the championship in 2006, ending Valentino Rossi's five-year winning streak in a dramatic final race in Valencia. Hayden's third-place finish allowed him to take the title by five points, and he remains the last American to win the premier class of motorcycle road racing.

Hayden's achievement was hailed as one of the greatest moments in MotoGP history, with BBC commentator Steve Parrish describing the 2006 season as "the most entertaining I have ever seen." Nicky's family was instrumental in his success, with his parents and siblings all involved in the sport. His Twitter handle, "bikes and family," reflected the importance of his loved ones in his life.

BBC's Azi Farni remembered Nicky as "a real gentleman" who came from a "wonderful family, a big racing family." He added, "His family were such a huge part of who he was. This is going to be such a great loss for them." The motorcycle racing community will deeply miss Nicky Hayden, a talented and beloved rider who left an indelible mark on the sport. His legacy will live on, inspiring future generations of riders and fans alike.

A recent study published in the journal Thorax has suggested a potential link between consuming large amounts of processed meat and worsening asthma symptoms. The research, which involved nearly 1,000 French people, found that those who ate more than four portions of processed meat per week experienced a significant deterioration in their lung symptoms. 

The study, which spanned a decade from 2003 to 2013, looked specifically at the intake of cured meat, such as sausages, salami, and ham, and its impact on asthma symptoms like breathlessness, wheeze, and chest tightness. The participants, around half of whom were asthma patients, were asked to report their consumption of processed meat, with a single portion defined as two slices of ham, one sausage, or two slices of salami.

The results showed that among the people with asthma, higher meat consumption was linked with a worsening of their lung symptoms. Those who consumed more than four portions a week, equivalent to eight slices of ham or four sausages, experienced the biggest deterioration of their asthma by the end of the study. The researchers believe that a preservative called nitrite, used in meats like sausages and ham, may be to blame for aggravating the airways.

However, experts are cautioning that the link between processed meat and worsening asthma has not been proven and more investigations are needed. Dr. Erika Kennington, Head of Research at Asthma UK, noted that while certain foods can trigger allergies in some people, there is no specific dietary advice for managing asthma symptoms. Instead, she recommended that people with asthma follow the same healthy eating advice as everyone else, which includes a balanced diet with plenty of fresh and unprocessed food, low in sugar, salt, and saturated fat.

Catherine Collins of the British Dietetic Association also emphasized the importance of a varied and Mediterranean-style diet, rich in fresh produce, for overall health, whether or not one has asthma. The experts agree that rather than focusing on a single type of food, people should prioritize eating a healthy and varied diet. This is particularly important given the existing link between processed meat and cancer, with experts advising that people consume no more than 70g of red and processed meat per day, equivalent to one sausage plus a rasher of bacon. By adopting a balanced and healthy diet, individuals can reduce their risk of chronic diseases and promote overall well-being.

Guernsey's Environment Department has requested a delay in the debate on the proposed 'width tax' and related charges until January. The discussion was initially scheduled for the December States sitting, but Environment Minister Yvonne Burford has indicated that the proposals may undergo changes. This decision comes after a massive 2,000-strong protest last month, organized by the campaign group Enough is Enough, which opposed the 'width tax' as well as other plans, including a goods and services tax, increased parking charges, and a refuse tax.

The Guernsey Motor Trades Association has also voiced its criticism, arguing that the charges would be too costly and pose a threat to jobs in the motor industry. K'han Holden, one of the protest organizers, expressed pride in the impact of the demonstration, stating that it has prompted the department to re-examine the proposals. Holden emphasized the need for the department to "throw it out and start afresh." The proposed charges are part of an island transport strategy introduced in March, and Deputy Burford has assured that the States remain committed to introducing this key element, but wants to address "various concerns" raised by the community. Deputy Al Brouard, who opposed the strategy, has called for a new transport strategy that is "fit for purpose."

Sinn Féin's Corporation Tax Stance Under Scrutiny After Conflicting Comments

The devolution of corporation tax to Northern Ireland has sparked controversy, with Sinn Féin's comments on the issue coming under fire. Under the Fresh Start Agreement, the executive committed to introducing a new corporation tax rate from April 2018. However, the cost of implementing this change remains unclear. On the Nolan Show, Sinn Féin's Conor Murphy failed to clarify whether the cost would be £150m per year or £150m over four years.

Murphy stated that the cost would "incrementally drop over the course of the years," but admitted that a final figure had not been determined. The SDLP has criticized Sinn Féin for their lack of clarity on the issue, with finance spokesperson Claire Hanna accusing the party of "muddling numbers." Later, Sinn Féin clarified that the £150m figure referred to a one-year cost. The proposed reduction in corporation tax to 12.5% would bring Northern Ireland in line with the Republic of Ireland, but the parties remain at odds over the issue.
