The SDLP is calling on Sinn Féin to "come clean" on their stance on corporation tax devolution.

Waste management workers in the city have voted overwhelmingly in favor of taking industrial action, with over 90% of GMB members employed at five sites backing the move. The first strike is set to take place on October 1, with a further five days of action planned for later in the month. The dispute centers around issues such as reduced hours and lack of extra pay for weekend work.

According to Pete Davies from the GMB union, staff are frustrated with the current situation and are calling on decision-makers to resolve the issue. "I wish that we didn't have to do this," he said. "I wish that the decision-makers in this city would get round the table and resolve this." The union has been seeking a resolution to the dispute, but so far, no agreement has been reached.

Veolia, the French firm contracted to run the city's waste services, has stated that it wants to "sort any issues out speedily." The company has assured that discussions between the union and the Green Company, which employs the workforce, are still ongoing. If the strike action goes ahead, Veolia has pledged to minimize disruption and keep as many sites open as possible. The Green Company has referred all comments to Veolia's statement. The industrial action is set to continue on October 6, with a further four days starting on October 10.

Tragedy on the Slopes: Trial Looms for Ski Resort and Supervisor

A trial is set to take place this year for a French ski resort and its supervisor, following the death of a 14-year-old British boy in 2011. Kieran Brookes, from Devon, died after his backpack became entangled in a ski lift in Chatel, France. The incident occurred when Kieran attempted to climb off the six-seat lift at the top of the slope, causing him to become suspended by his clothing for approximately four minutes.

Lawyers for SAEM Sports et Tourisme a Chatel have confirmed that the company, along with supervisor Richard Cettour, 50, will face trial for their alleged role in Kieran's death. The prosecution accuses SAEM of failing to enforce safety rules, including a ban on skiers wearing backpacks on the lift, and not conducting daily equipment checks. Mr. Cettour is also accused of several failings, including not being present at his post during the accident and failing to respond to emergency calls from other skiers.

Kieran's family, including his father Nick, are still seeking answers about the circumstances surrounding his death. "Not knowing the events that led to his death holds back the healing process," said Nick Brookes. The trial is expected to shed light on the tragic events and provide some closure for the Brookes family. SAEM and Mr. Cettour will face trial later this year, with the outcome potentially bringing justice to Kieran's loved ones.

Northern Ireland's Power-Sharing Government Teeters on the Brink as Parties Engage in Procedural Game-Playing

The power-sharing government in Northern Ireland is facing an uncertain future as the parties engage in a complex game of procedural maneuvering. The crisis deepened after the arrest and release of Sinn Féin's northern chair, who was being investigated in connection with the murder of Kevin McGuigan Sr. The incident sparked a chain reaction of events, with the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) ministerial team resigning or standing aside, except for Finance Minister Arlene Foster, who has taken on the role of Acting First Minister.

According to the Northern Ireland Act, Foster can only occupy the acting role for a continuous period of six weeks. However, a senior DUP source has suggested that this period can be interrupted if the party's leader, Peter Robinson, were to return to office for a brief period, allowing Foster to step back into the breach. This "cunning plan" has raised concerns that the parties may engage in a series of tactical maneuvers to maintain control and influence.

Meanwhile, Robinson has stated that he has no intention of allowing Sinn Féin and Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) ministers to take over the health, enterprise, and social development departments vacated by his colleagues. Instead, he may nominate DUP politicians to fill the vacant positions, only to have them step down again almost immediately. This game of musical chairs is likely to continue in parallel with renewed Stormont House talks, which aim to address the underlying issues threatening the power-sharing agreement.

The public may view these procedural games as "too clever by half," and the parties are aware that they will eventually have to face the voters. With the next election scheduled to take place within the next eight months, the parties are under pressure to resolve their differences and find a way forward. However, the issues on the table, including welfare reform, the budget, corporation tax, paramilitary activity, parades, the past, and the weakness of the current Stormont system, are complex and deeply entrenched.

The absence of a regional development minister has already begun to have practical negative impacts, with common sense measures such as speed restrictions near rural primary schools being delayed. If the current impasse continues, it is likely that similar problems will arise in the health and housing sectors, highlighting the need for a swift resolution to the crisis. As the parties engage in their procedural game-playing, they must also be mindful of the need to find a lasting solution to the challenges facing Northern Ireland, lest they face the wrath of the voters in the upcoming election.

The town of Beverley is set to host the start of a major cycling event, bringing a significant boost to the local economy. The announcement has been welcomed by Stephen Parnaby, Conservative leader of East Riding of Yorkshire Council, who described it as "great news for the town and the wider East Riding". The council is investing around £100,000 to host the event, which is expected to attract thousands of spectators.

Last year's inaugural race brought in an estimated £50m to the region's economy, and organizers are hoping to replicate this success. The three-day event was launched by Welcome to Yorkshire after the county hosted the Tour de France Grand Depart in 2014, which drew in over 1.2m spectators. Local residents and business owners are excited about the opportunity, with amateur cyclist Ed Neilson hoping it will encourage more cyclists to visit the town.

Garry Payne, owner of a cycling cafe, described the news as "fantastic" for fans, who will have the chance to get up close to the riders and get autographs. The event is expected to provide a significant boost to local traders, with the council believing the investment will be "money well spent". With the start of the race taking place in Beverley, the town is likely to receive increased recognition and attention, making it a great opportunity for the local community to showcase its charm and hospitality.

The north coast of Northern Ireland is set to host a star-studded field of golfers as the Dubai Duty Free Irish Open gets underway from July 6 to 9. The tournament, which boasts a prize pot of £5.3 million, will feature ten of the world's top 40 golfers, including defending champion Rory McIlroy and world number two Hideki Matsuyama.

BBC Northern Ireland will provide extensive coverage of the event, with Stephen Watson presenting hour-long highlights on BBC One NI every night from Thursday to Sunday. A special 30-minute preview programme will air on Wednesday, July 5, at 22:40, featuring contributions from Major champions Rory McIlroy, Graeme McDowell, and Darren Clarke.

BBC Radio Ulster will also have live coverage, starting with a preview from the course on Wednesday at 18:30 BST, followed by half-hour programmes on Thursday and Friday. The Summer Club will air on Saturday, with a final day round-up on Sunday at 18:00. Joel Taggart will present the Radio Ulster programmes, joined by Michael McNamee for The Summer Club live from Portstewart on Saturday.

Notable entries in the tournament include Jon Rahm, Justin Rose, Lee Westwood, Ian Poulter, and Danny Willett. The event forms part of a new Rolex Series, and fans can keep up with all the action on the BBC Sport NI website, BBC iPlayer, and social media outlets. Grant Cameron will provide updates on the action throughout the week on BBC Radio Ulster, while the BBC Sport NI website will feature leaderboard, reports, and interviews. With its strong field and extensive coverage, the Dubai Duty Free Irish Open is set to be an exciting event for golf fans.

Local Authority Under Fire for Insufficient Housing Plans

The Cheshire East Council has come under scrutiny for its inadequate plans to build new homes, with a government inspector deeming their target of 27,000 new homes by 2030 to be insufficient. The inspector has suggested that the figure needs to be closer to 40,000 to meet the area's growing housing needs. This criticism has sparked concerns among local leaders, with Council leader Michael Jones expressing his worry about the findings.

Jones attributed the council's shortcomings to outdated policies and guidelines, stating that the starting point for the plan was based on 2009 data. He acknowledged that the council had failed to adapt to changing circumstances and pledged to re-examine their analysis and methodology to ensure accuracy. Meanwhile, Cheadle MP Mark Hunter has been vocal in his criticism of the council's plans, describing them as a demonstration of "ineptitude".

Hunter's comments come after he spoke out against the council's proposal to build 2,000 new homes at Handforth, near Wilmslow. The independent inspector's report highlighted significant flaws in the council's process, particularly with regards to the release of land from the green belt. The report's findings have been seen as a victory for objectors, with Hunter claiming it as "round one" in their favor. The council must now revisit its plans and strive to meet the inspector's recommended target to address the area's housing needs.

A bizarre incident involving bagels brought a train to a halt in Hertfordshire on Sunday. The train, operated by Great Northern, was stopped at Potters Bar station at 01:00 GMT after a disturbance broke out on board. A video posted on Twitter showed a group of women placing bagels on a man's head, before he threw them out of the window. The footage also captured brawls in the carriage and on the platform, although it is unclear if these were related to the bagel incident.

The train was held for 18 minutes while police took statements from passengers. British Transport Police (BTP) responded to the incident, tweeting about "BagelGate" and condemning the intimidating behaviour. The video of the incident has gone viral, with over 17,000 likes and 10,000 retweets. Despite the commotion, no arrests have been made. Great Northern has encouraged passengers to report any incidents of intimidating behaviour to the BTP, taking all such incidents seriously. The unusual incident has left many puzzled, with the BTP reminding passengers that "no bagel should be treated so cruelly" and that everyone deserves to feel safe on public transport.

Gabon Unveils 23-Man Squad for Africa Cup of Nations

The Gabonese Football Federation has announced its final 23-man squad for the upcoming Africa Cup of Nations, which kicks off on January 14 in Libreville. The hosts, led by team captain and Borussia Dortmund star Pierre Emerick Aubameyang, will face debutants Guinea-Bissau in the opening game of the tournament.

Aubameyang, who is also the team's star player, will lead the Panthers out onto the pitch, and fans are expecting great things from the talented striker. Joining him in the squad is Sunderland midfielder Didier Ndong, who was surprisingly included despite being left out of November's World Cup qualifier in Mali. Ndong had failed to turn up for international duty ahead of the Mali game, but after holding clear-the-air talks with the Gabonese Football Federation, he has been given a second chance.

Other notable names in the squad include Juventus midfielder Mario Lemina, Cardiff City defender Bruno Ecuélé Manga, and China-based striker Malick Evouna. Gabon coach José Antonio Camacho has also included three domestic-based stars in the squad, as well as three players on standby.

Gabon is hosting the continental tournament for the second time, having previously co-organized the competition with Equatorial Guinea in 2012. The Panthers will face a tough challenge in Group A, where they will also face four-time winners Cameroon and Burkina Faso, runners-up in 2013.

The squad announcement makes Gabon the first of the 16 participants to unveil its final squad for the tournament. Fans are eagerly awaiting the start of the competition, which runs from January 14 to February 5. With a strong squad and home advantage, Gabon will be looking to make a deep run in the tournament and bring glory to their country.

The full Gabon squad is as follows: Goalkeepers: Didier Ovono, Yves Stéphane Bitséki Moto, and Anthony Mfa Mezui. Defenders: Lloyd Palun, André Biyogho Poko, Aaron Appindangoye, Franck Perrin Obambou, Bruno Ecuélé Manga, Yoann Wachter, Johann Serge Obiang, and Benjamin Zé Ondo. Midfielders: Mario René Junior Lemina, Junior Serge Martinsson Ngouali, Levy Clément Madinda, Guélor Kanga Kaku, Merlin Tandjigora, Didier Ibrahim Ndong, and Samson Mbingui. Forwards: Pierre Emerick Aubameyang, Malick Evouna, Denis Athanase Bouanga, Serge Kevyn Aboue Angoue, and Cedric Ondo Biyoghe. The three players on standby are Axel Meyé, Johan Lengoualama, and Donald Nzé.

England's Early World Cup Exit Sparks Review and Debate

The English rugby team's disappointing performance in the World Cup has led to a comprehensive review, with a five-man panel tasked with examining the factors that contributed to their early exit from the tournament. The review, which will include input from players, coaches, and management staff, is being led by RFU chief executive Ian Ritchie and will also feature former Football Association chief executive Ian Watmore and Professional Game Board chairman Ian Metcalfe.

England's elimination at the group stage, following losses to Wales and Australia, marks the first time a World Cup host nation has failed to progress to the knockout stages. The RFU has emphasized that the review will be thorough and that all feedback will remain confidential, with recommendations to be made to the RFU board at a later date.

The performance of head coach Stuart Lancaster and his assistants, Andy Farrell, Graham Rowntree, and Mike Catt, will be under scrutiny as part of the review. Lancaster, who has a contract until 2020, has stated that he would find it "hard to walk away" from the job, despite the team's disappointing performance.

The review panel does not include RFU professional rugby director Rob Andrew or 2003 World Cup-winning coach Sir Clive Woodward, a decision that has been questioned by some. Former England player Will Greenwood, who was part of Woodward's squad in 2003, believes that his former coach should have been involved in the review, saying "he's a giant spectre that gets thrown into the pot the whole time."

Others, including BBC Sport pundit Jeremy Guscott, have argued that players and coaches should not be involved in the review, as their feedback may not be impartial. Sir Clive Woodward has also expressed concerns that player input could be "very divisive."

In contrast, former Scotland coach Ian McGeechan has defended Lancaster and his coaching team, saying that he "cannot see anything better" than the current set-up. McGeechan, who was part of the group that approved Lancaster's appointment in 2012, has urged the RFU not to make "any rash decisions," pointing out that England would have qualified from any other pool and that defeat to two strong teams was "no disgrace."

The review is expected to take some time, with no date set for its completion. The next RFU board meeting will take place on November 17, and it is likely that the review will be discussed further at that time. As the English rugby team looks to rebuild and move forward, the outcome of the review will be eagerly anticipated by fans and pundits alike.

US President Barack Obama has criticized the National Rifle Association (NRA) for misrepresenting his proposed gun control legislation, sparking a heated debate on the highly contentious issue. In a speech at George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, Mr. Obama accused the NRA of spreading false information, claiming that his administration was seeking to seize all firearms. He emphasized that his goal was to strengthen background checks, not take away guns from law-abiding citizens.

The NRA declined to participate in the discussion, labeling it a "public relations spectacle" orchestrated by the White House. In a statement, NRA spokesman Andrew Arulanandam said the group saw "no reason to participate" in the event. This move has been seen as a reflection of the deep divide between the NRA and the Obama administration on the issue of gun control.

Meanwhile, US Republican presidential hopeful Donald Trump weighed in on the issue, promising to eliminate gun-free zones in schools on his first day in office, if elected. Speaking at a rally in Vermont, Trump described gun-free zones as "bait" for potential shooters, echoing a long-held NRA stance. His comments have sparked controversy, with many arguing that such a move would put more lives at risk.

The debate comes as Mr. Obama unveiled a package of executive actions aimed at keeping guns from people who should not have access to them. The measures, which bypass Congress, have been met with fierce resistance from leading Republicans, including House of Representatives Speaker Paul Ryan. Ryan denounced the move, saying it "undermined liberty" and would be challenged in court.

In an article published in the New York Times, Mr. Obama called gun violence a national crisis, urging gun owners and manufacturers to play their part in ending it. He also announced that he would not campaign for Democrats who do not back gun reforms, saying he wanted leaders brave enough to stand up to the gun lobby's lies.

The NRA, founded in 1871, has become one of the most powerful special interest groups in the US, with a budget of around $250 million per year. The group boasts of nearly 5 million members, although analysts estimate the figure is likely closer to 3 million. Famous members have included Charlton Heston, Whoopi Goldberg, and former president George Bush Snr.

The NRA has been widely criticized for its statements on mass shootings, including a claim that a lack of armed guards at schools was to blame for the Sandy Hook massacre. The group's stance on gun control has been seen as a major obstacle to reform, with many arguing that its influence has prevented meaningful action from being taken.

As the debate continues, it remains to be seen whether Mr. Obama's efforts will lead to meaningful change. With the NRA and other gun rights groups firmly opposed to reform, it is likely that the issue will remain a contentious one for years to come. Nevertheless, the president's efforts have sparked a national conversation on the issue, and it is clear that something needs to be done to address the scourge of gun violence in the US.

A 42-year-old man was found with significant injuries in Greenend Avenue, Johnstone, on Saturday at approximately 10:45. Police believe the victim, identified as Mr. Quail, was killed following a disturbance at his home in the early hours of the morning. Detectives are urging anyone with information or who may have witnessed something suspicious to come forward.

According to Detective Chief Inspector Raymond Brown, the disturbance occurred around 00:50 on Saturday. He emphasized that the key to solving the murder inquiry lies within the local community. Brown appealed to residents, stating that even seemingly insignificant information could be vital to the investigation.

The area where the incident occurred is a busy residential neighborhood, increasing the likelihood that someone may have seen or heard something suspicious. The police are encouraging anyone with information to contact the inquiry team at Helen Street Police Office through 101. By working together, the community can help bring justice to the victim and his family. The investigation is ongoing, with extensive inquiries underway to establish the circumstances surrounding Mr. Quail's death.

Nottingham's Tram Extension Nears Completion, Despite Delays

The long-awaited tram extension to Chilwell and Clifton is nearing completion, according to Phil Hewitt, executive chair of Tramlink Nottingham. The project, which began in 2012, was initially scheduled to open in December 2014. However, due to unforeseen problems, the opening has been delayed. Hewitt attributed the delays to a lack of "risk time" factored into the construction timeline, which has resulted in a significant extension to the planned completion date.

Despite the setbacks, Hewitt remains optimistic, stating that the opening is "tantalisingly close." Further driver training and timetable testing are currently underway to ensure a smooth launch. The extension will significantly expand Nottingham's tram network, adding approximately 10 miles of new track and 28 tram stops. This will more than double the size of the existing network.

Hewitt also addressed rumors surrounding the delays, dismissing claims that the wrong type of concrete was used and that tram lines were incorrectly installed. He explained that some localized concrete cracking issues have arisen, but these are being addressed. With the completion of the project imminent, residents and commuters can look forward to improved transportation links and a more efficient tram network. Although a specific opening date has not been confirmed, it is expected to be announced soon.

Yorkshire spinner Adil Rashid has announced that he will not be playing in the crucial match against Middlesex at Lord's, citing mental and physical exhaustion. The 28-year-old initially stated that he needed rest, but has since revealed that he is not in the right mental frame of mind to perform at his best. Rashid expressed his concerns on social media, stating that he would be letting his teammates down if he played.

This news comes as a blow to Yorkshire, who are currently second in Division One and trailing Middlesex by nine points. The team is also missing Jonny Bairstow, as the ECB has refused their request to field the wicketkeeper-batsman. Despite his absence, Rashid has expressed his support for the team and is hoping they can secure their third consecutive Championship title.

Rashid has had a busy schedule recently, playing for both Yorkshire and England, and has been included in the squad for England's tour of Bangladesh in October. He emphasized the importance of family and his upcoming England duties, wishing his teammates the best of luck for the match. Yorkshire will now have to rely on their remaining players to secure a win and keep their title hopes alive.

Gillingham Manager Andy Hessenthaler has announced that two of the club's players, a 37-year-old and striker Dennis Oli, 28, are free to leave the team. The 37-year-old, who has made 73 appearances for the Gills since joining in 2010, and Oli, who has started only one game this season, have been informed that their contracts will not be renewed.

Hessenthaler stated that the decision is part of his plan to reduce the wage bill, which will give him more flexibility to sign new players, including former Charlton defender Jonathan Fortune and ex-Wolves midfielder Rohan Ricketts, who have both been training with the club. The manager is keen to bring in fresh talent, but this may require him to loan out some of his current players.

Despite the team's recent struggles, including six consecutive defeats, Hessenthaler has received a vote of confidence from chairman Paul Scally. In a text message, Scally expressed his support for the manager, stating that he will back him until the end of the season as long as the team continues to show desire, commitment, and effort. Hessenthaler remains focused on turning the team's fortunes around and is not dwelling on the possibility of being sacked. With the chairman's backing, he is looking to make the necessary changes to get the team back on track.

A recent report compiled by the Higher Education Funding Council for Wales (Hefcw) has shed light on the significant disparities in pay among university staff in Wales. The research, which was released to BBC Wales under the Freedom of Information Act, reveals that senior staff at Welsh universities are earning substantial salaries, with some vice-chancellors taking home over £200,000 per year, including pension contributions.

According to the report, Cardiff University has the largest number of higher-paid staff in Wales, with 136 employees receiving more than £100,000 between 2014-15. The university's Vice Chancellor, Colin Riordan, is the highest-paid head of a Welsh university, earning £288,000 after pension contributions. The report also notes that seven of Wales' eight vice-chancellors were paid more than £200,000 last year.

While the report acknowledges that pay in Welsh universities is comparable to other institutions of the same size and stature in the UK, the University and College Union (UCU) has expressed concerns about the pay gaps at universities. The union argues that the high pay of senior staff is in stark contrast to the average salaries of other university teaching staff, many of whom are on insecure contracts and struggle to make ends meet.

The UCU spokesman stated, "Our main concern is the inequality between the average salary of VCs in Wales, compared to the average salary of other staff in our universities, particularly when taking into account that undergraduates are likely to be taught by a member of staff on an insecure, fixed-term contract." The union believes that staff on insecure contracts are underpaid, vulnerable, and constantly facing the prospect of unemployment, which can negatively impact their ability to deliver high-quality teaching and services.

The Higher Education Funding Council for Wales argues that Welsh universities need to compete to attract the best staff, and that pay needs to be comparable to other UK universities in order to recruit top talent. However, the UCU counters that this argument does not justify the significant pay disparities between senior staff and other university employees.

In response to the report, a Cardiff University spokesman pointed out that the university is distinct from other Welsh universities in having large medical and dental schools, as well as the Postgraduate Deanery for Wales. The spokesman noted that clinical staff salaries are set by the NHS, and that the university offers competitive salaries to attract and retain the best staff.

The issue of university pay has sparked a wider debate about the funding and management of higher education in Wales. The previous Welsh education minister, Huw Lewis, warned that higher education could not expect to avoid cuts forever, and the current report highlights the need for a more nuanced discussion about university funding and resource allocation.

As the debate continues, it is clear that the pay disparities at Welsh universities are a complex issue that requires careful consideration. While the Higher Education Funding Council for Wales argues that competitive pay is necessary to attract top talent, the UCU believes that the current pay gaps are unsustainable and unfair. Ultimately, finding a solution that balances the need to recruit and retain top staff with the need to address pay inequality and support all university employees will be crucial to ensuring the long-term sustainability and success of Welsh universities.

A French court has fined Robert Menard, the mayor of the southern town of Beziers, 2,000 euros for inciting hatred and discrimination against Muslims. Menard, an ally of the anti-immigrant National Front party, sparked controversy with his comments on the first day of school in 2016, tweeting about the "great replacement" of France's white Christian population by migrants.

In a subsequent television interview, Menard claimed that 91% of children in a class in his town's city center were Muslims, calling it a "problem" that exceeded the limits of tolerance. French law prohibits collecting data based on people's religious beliefs or ethnicity, and Menard's comments were widely criticized.

The court ruled that Menard's statements were a "clear infringement" of the law and awarded 1,000 euros in court costs to anti-racist groups that brought the case. The fine was higher than the 1,800 euros requested by the public prosecutor, who argued that Menard had unfairly targeted children. Menard has defended his comments, saying they were simply a description of the situation in his town, but has announced plans to appeal the ruling. The case has drawn attention to the divisive rhetoric surrounding immigration in France, ahead of the presidential election on May 7.

Mohammad Amir, the 22-year-old left-arm bowler, has been given a second chance in cricket after being cleared to play domestic cricket in Pakistan. Amir was jailed for six months and banned from all cricket for his role in a spot-fixing scam during Pakistan's tour of England in 2010. However, with the approval of the International Cricket Council (ICC), the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB), and Sir Ronnie Flanagan, the head of the ICC's Anti-Corruption and Security Unit, Amir's ban has been lifted early.

Amir expressed his gratitude and stated, "It's a new life for me and you will see not only Mohammad Amir as a better cricketer but also a better human being." The ICC stated that Sir Ronnie Flanagan was satisfied that Amir had shown remorse and cooperated with the authorities, which led to the decision to allow him to return to domestic cricket.

Before his suspension, Amir had taken 51 wickets in 14 Test matches and 25 wickets in 15 one-day internationals, showcasing his talent and potential. Unlike his co-conspirators, Mohammad Asif and Salman Butt, Amir admitted his guilt and showed remorse, which likely contributed to his early return to the sport. Asif and Butt were also jailed and banned from cricket, with Asif receiving a seven-year ban and Butt a 10-year ban. Amir's return to domestic cricket is seen as a fresh start for the young bowler, and fans will be eager to see him back in action.

A fire broke out at the Mill O'Mains Community Pavilion on Sunday evening. Firefighters responded quickly, bringing the blaze under control by 23:00. A joint investigation is underway to determine the cause. The pavilion, which provided meals for deprived children, suffered significant damage in the fire that was finally extinguished by 01:00.

A 34-year-old man has been arrested in connection with the brutal murder of David Clarke, a 26-year-old with learning difficulties, in 2001. Clarke's body was found in his flat on Forthriver Road in north Belfast after friends raised concerns for his welfare. The killing was described by police as one of the most savage and brutal they had ever dealt with.

The arrested man was detained in north Belfast on Monday morning and has been bailed pending further inquiries. The arrest comes after police re-opened the murder investigation following new information. It has emerged that Clarke was bullied in the weeks leading up to his murder. Former Assistant Chief Constable Allan McQuillan, who was involved in the original inquiry, described Clarke's death as a "mystery" and said it was not related to the Troubles.

Detective Chief Inspector Alan Dickson paid tribute to Clarke, describing him as an "inoffensive and vulnerable" man who died after an "increasingly frenzied" assault. The case has been re-examined, and police are hopeful that justice may finally be served for Clarke and his family. The investigation is ongoing, and police are urging anyone with information to come forward.

Borussia Dortmund defender Mats Hummels is facing a crucial decision regarding his future. The 27-year-old has one year left on his contract, but has been linked to several top clubs, including Bayern Munich, Barcelona, Manchester United, and Liverpool. Hummels has admitted that the uncertainty is affecting his sleep, taking him an extra 30 minutes to fall asleep each night. His father and agent, Hermann Hummels, says a return to Bayern Munich is a possibility, citing the club as one of the few top-tier teams his son would consider joining. With two Bundesliga titles and a World Cup win under his belt, Hummels' next move will be closely watched. As he weighs his options, Hummels must consider what's best for his career and life, with his father guiding him through the decision-making process. A decision is expected soon, with several clubs eagerly awaiting his choice.

A cannabis factory with approximately 200 plants was discovered in a Smethwick flat after a fire broke out. The fire service was alerted by a nearby resident who saw smoke billowing from a fourth-floor window of the five-story block on Beakes Road. Upon arrival, crews made a forced entry into the empty flat and found a fire in the back bedroom. 

According to West Midlands Fire Service, the fire is believed to have been caused by an electrical fault, possibly due to overloaded equipment used for the cannabis grow. West Midlands Police are working to locate the owner of the property, with enquiries still ongoing. The discovery was made at around 9:10 am, and police are investigating the incident. The flat was unoccupied at the time of the fire, and no injuries were reported. An investigation into the cannabis factory is underway.

A dramatic incident occurred at Cleghorn level crossing in Lanark on Saturday evening, when a car was struck by a Virgin train traveling from Preston to Glasgow. Fortunately, the occupants of the vehicle managed to escape before the collision, which happened just before 19:00. The train, carrying around 60 passengers, was able to continue on its journey without reported injuries.

British Transport Police (BTP) and Police Scotland are currently investigating the incident, with support from the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service. The BTP stated that their priority is to ensure the safety of everyone involved and to understand how the car came to be on the tracks. The Rail Accident Investigation Branch and Office of Rail and Road have also been notified.

The incident caused significant disruption to train services, with routes being re-routed as a result of the collision. An investigation is ongoing to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. The fact that the occupants of the vehicle were able to escape unharmed is a relief, and authorities are now focused on preventing such incidents in the future.

Bouygues Telecom has made a bid to acquire Vivendi-owned SFR, a move that would create the largest mobile phone service provider in France. If successful, the merger would leave only three mobile phone companies in the country, with Bouygues and SFR overtaking current leader Orange. The combined entity would be a significant player in the French market, with Bouygues Telecom and SFR currently ranking as the second and third largest mobile phone companies.

However, the deal is not without competition, as rival firm Altice, owner of French cable TV operator Numericable, has also made an offer for SFR. Although the details of Altice's offer have not been disclosed, industry analysts believe that Bouygues' bid is likely to be viewed as the most appealing by Vivendi. According to Dario Talmesia, principal analyst at Informa Telecomes and Media, "Vivendi would view the offer from Bouygues as the most appealing one."

The proposed merger is part of a broader trend of consolidation among mobile phone operators in Europe, where there are currently 150 companies, compared to just four in the United States. If approved, the deal would require significant investment in infrastructure, which Bouygues claims would help protect jobs and boost the ailing French economy. Kester Mann, an analyst at CCS Insight, noted that Bouygues is positioning the deal as a way to bring economic benefits and job security.

However, market analysts have warned that the merger could lead to an end to price cuts, which have benefited French mobile phone customers since the arrival of Free Mobile seven years ago. This could prompt the government to reconsider allowing the deal to go through. Before the merger can proceed, it must be approved by competition regulators in both France and the European Union. The European Union's response to a similar deal in Germany, where Telefonica is seeking to acquire E-Plus, may provide an indication of how the Bouygues-SFR merger will be received. As Talmesia noted, "What's happening in Germany can be a good indicator of what can be happening in France and the rest of Europe."

Great Britain's Cycling Team Gears Up for World Championships

The Great Britain cycling team has announced its 20-rider squad for the upcoming World Championships, featuring a mix of experienced Olympians and debutants. Olympic champions Katie Archibald, Elinor Barker, Steven Burke, and Callum Skinner are among the notable names on the roster, which includes 10 riders making their World Championship debut.

The team will be looking to replicate its success from last year's event in London, where they topped the medal table with five gold medals. However, they will be without several star names, including six-time Olympic champion Jason Kenny and his wife Laura, who are expecting their first child. Bradley Wiggins has retired, and Mark Cavendish is focusing on road racing.

The women's endurance team features a strong lineup, with Archibald and Barker joined by Ellie Dickinson, Neah Evans, Emily Kay, Manon Lloyd, and Emily Nelson. The men's endurance team includes Matt Bostock, Steven Burke, Kian Emadi, Chris Latham, Mark Stewart, Andy Tennant, and Oliver Wood.

The sprint team is led by Jack Carlin, Katy Marchant, Lewis Oliva, Ryan Owens, Callum Skinner, and Joe Truman. The team will be competing in a range of events, including the team pursuit, individual pursuit, sprint, and keirin.

The World Championships will be broadcast on the BBC, with coverage starting on Wednesday, April 12, and running through to Sunday, April 16. Fans can watch live on BBC Two and Connected TV, with repeat broadcasts available on the Red Button. The BBC Sport website and app will also provide live streams, text commentaries, news, and reports.

With a strong squad and a packed schedule of events, Great Britain's cycling team will be looking to make a big impact at the World Championships. Can they match their success from last year and bring home a haul of medals? Tune in to the BBC's coverage to find out.

Bristol Rovers have contacted the EFL's legal department amid claims that Bristol City knew about a confidential release clause in striker Matthew Taylor's contract. The clause's details are supposed to remain private under EFL rules. Bristol City confirmed making an offer for Taylor, which was accepted, but declined further comment. Taylor, 26, scored 61 goals in 118 league appearances for Rovers. His transfer to City marks the first time a player has moved directly from Rovers to City since Trevor Morgan in 1987. The situation has sparked controversy, with Rovers seeking clarification from the EFL.

Disney Parks Introduce Blanket Ban on Selfie Sticks

In a move to enhance safety for its visitors, Disney has announced a complete ban on selfie sticks in its theme parks. The ban, which comes into effect in the US on Tuesday and in Paris and Hong Kong on Wednesday, prohibits guests from bringing the handheld extension poles into the parks altogether. previously, they were only banned on rides.

According to a Disney spokeswoman, the decision was made due to growing safety concerns for both guests and staff. The long arms of selfie sticks pose a risk of injury if accidentally used to strike someone, and they can also interfere with ride mechanisms. Visitors will now be required to leave their selfie sticks in lockers at the park entrances and collect them later.

Disney is not the first institution to ban selfie sticks. Several football clubs, the National Gallery, and the All England Lawn Tennis & Croquet Club have already implemented similar bans due to concerns over safety and nuisance. Apple also prohibited the use of selfie sticks at its recent WWDC developers conference in the US.

While St John Ambulance has not reported a significant increase in selfie stick-related injuries, the charity has offered advice on how to treat head injuries caused by the devices. If someone is hit on the head with a selfie stick, they should sit down, apply a cold compress, and seek medical help if symptoms such as dizziness, nausea, or confusion occur. With the ban in place, Disney hopes to create a safer and more enjoyable experience for its visitors.

An art exhibit, "Suspended Forest," features discarded Christmas trees from Brooklyn. Artist Michael Neff created the display, hanging trees in a grid formation. The pine-scented installation took a day and a half to set up and will be on show for a month, showcasing a unique reuse of festive foliage.

A devastating arson attack on a family home in Meadow Drive has left a mother and her two young children "distraught" and shaken the local community. The incident, which occurred at approximately 06:20 GMT on Friday, is being treated as a hate crime by police.

Subi Philip, a cardiac nurse, was at home with her ten and eight-year-old daughters when the attack happened. Her husband was not present, having returned to India for his father's funeral. The family, originally from India, has been living in the area for several years and is well-integrated into the local community.

According to Mrs. Philip, the family was alerted to the attack by a loud noise outside. She described the scene as "chaotic" and said she was initially unsure of what was happening. "I just heard a big bang and got out of my bed and saw a big fire. When I came downstairs and saw it, I started screaming. My girls didn't know why I was screaming and they were screaming too. I was really panicking," she told the BBC.

Neighbours, who had rushed to the scene to offer assistance, urged Mrs. Philip to evacuate the house. However, she was initially hesitant, fearing that they might be the perpetrators of the attack. It was only when she realized they were trying to help that she opened the door and fled with her children. "I got out and I ran," she said. "It was so scary."

The attack has been widely condemned by local politicians and community leaders. UUP MLA for South Antrim, Adrian Cochrane-Watson, praised Mrs. Philip's bravery and quick thinking in getting her children to safety. "This is a young mother who has been living in this country for a number of years, set up home. This is a lady, a professional who is saving lives every day of the week and rehabilitating people who are suffering from heart disease or heart attacks," he said.

The local Indian community has rallied around the family, offering support and condemnation of the attack. Siba Thomas, a friend of Mrs. Philip, said he was shocked and saddened by the incident. "We have around 60 Indian families here, most of us work in the Antrim Area Hospital as either nurses or doctors. We work along with the community. Most of our children were born here and go to the local school. The community here is very welcoming, the people are so nice. So it's very unfortunate to see things happening like this, that someone would have that mindset," he said.

Police have appealed for information and are treating the attack as a deliberate act of arson. Chief Inspector John Allen said, "We believe that the attack was motivated by racial hatred. Any attack on property is unacceptable, however I totally condemn the racial hate crime element of this attack, which makes it particularly repugnant." The Fire and Rescue Service is also investigating the incident.

The community is coming together to support the Philip family, and a fundraising campaign has been launched to help them rebuild their lives. The attack has sent shockwaves through the local community, and many are left wondering how such a horrific incident could occur in their neighborhood. As the investigation continues, one thing is clear: the Philip family will not be alone in their time of need, and the community will rally around them to provide support and comfort.

A 29-year-old father, Kevin Toye, has been sentenced to six years in prison for killing his infant son, Baylee Varley. The sentencing took place at Norwich Crown Court, where it was revealed that Baylee suffered severe brain and retinal injuries in 2008, consistent with shaking. The injuries ultimately led to Baylee's death in 2014. Judge Mr Justice Spencer emphasized that Toye's refusal to acknowledge his role in Baylee's death was a significant aggravating factor. Despite acknowledging that Toye loved his son, the judge stated that his culpability remained high due to the victim being a "tiny, defenceless baby." Detective Constable Mike Proctor expressed that the investigation, which spanned several years, aimed to give Baylee a voice and seek justice for his tragic and avoidable death. The sentence reflects the severity of the crime, bringing closure to a heartbreaking case. Toye's actions have been condemned, and the court's decision serves as a reminder of the importance of protecting vulnerable children.

A recent survey by the CAF has revealed the world's most charitable countries. Thailand took the top spot, with 85% of its population making regular charitable contributions. The UK followed closely, with 79% of its citizens regularly giving to charity. The Irish Republic, Australia, and New Zealand also ranked highly. Despite a slight fall in charitable donations due to the global economic crisis, the survey found that more people are likely to perform charitable acts this year compared to 2010. Interestingly, the richest countries are not necessarily the most charitable, with only five of the top 20 economies by GDP appearing in the CAF's top 20 giving index. The survey highlights the generosity of nations and their people.

Actor Dan Haggerty, best known for his role as Grizzly Adams, has passed away after a battle with cancer. His manager, Terry Bomar, confirmed the news to ABC News. Haggerty's career in Hollywood began as a stuntman and animal handler, with guest appearances on popular TV shows like "CHiPs," "Charlie's Angels," and "The Love Boat." He starred in the 1974 film "The Life and Times of Grizzly Adams," which became a huge success, and later in the NBC TV series of the same name from 1977 to 1978. The film and series were inspired by the true story of James Capen Adams, a 19th-century bear trainer. Haggerty's iconic portrayal of the nature-loving mountain man has left a lasting impression on fans. His legacy will be remembered through his notable work in the entertainment industry.

Aberdeen Takes Down "No Ball Games" Signs to Encourage Outdoor Play

Aberdeen has begun removing "no ball games" signs from public areas, with the help of former Manchester United star, Denis Law. The football legend, born in Aberdeen, was on hand to take down the first of hundreds of signs, citing the importance of outdoor play for young people. "You need to get young people out playing - the streets were where we learned our trade," he said.

The city's plan to remove the signs was announced in August, with a report deeming them unenforceable and a deterrent to outdoor activity. Law expressed his support for the initiative, stating that parents would be happy for their children to engage in outdoor play, rather than being confined to computer games.

The campaign is being assisted by local charity Aberdeen Greenspace, with the goal of improving the health and skills of the city's children. To mark the occasion, hundreds of sports balls will be given to underprivileged children. Law reflected on his own childhood, playing football in the streets without the presence of such signs, and welcomed the change, saying "it's nice to have this come round, taking the signs down."
Northern Ireland's election is underway, with 276 candidates vying for 108 seats. Polling stations were open from 07:00 to 22:00 BST, with counting to begin Friday.

UK Government Unveils New Powers for Welsh Assembly

In a significant move towards devolution, the UK Government has announced plans to grant the Welsh Assembly more powers over income tax rates, energy, transport, and its own elections. The Wales Bill, which received an unopposed third reading in the Commons on Monday, marks a major milestone in the devolution settlement for Wales. According to Secretary of State for Wales, Alun Cairns, the new powers will transform the assembly into a "fully-fledged Welsh legislature" and make it a permanent part of the UK's constitutional fabric.

The proposed laws will give the assembly the power to make decisions on policies such as setting speed limits and whether fracking should be permitted. Additionally, the assembly will have more control over taxes, making it responsible not only for how money is spent in Wales but also for how it is raised. This move is expected to usher in a new era of devolution, one that will bring clarity and accountability to the people of Wales.

However, the Bill has faced criticism from other parties, who feel that it does not go far enough. Shadow Welsh secretary Paul Flynn expressed his disappointment, stating that the Bill is "just a stage" and not the end of devolution. He called for a separate Welsh government with powers similar to those of Scotland. Hywel Williams, Plaid Cymru's Westminster leader, and Welsh Liberal Democrat leader Mark Williams also echoed similar sentiments, saying that the new Bill does not grant enough powers to the Welsh Assembly.

One notable omission from the Bill is the establishment of a separate justice system for Wales. Despite this, Mr. Cairns insisted that the move marks a significant step forward in the devolution settlement for Wales, one that is "clearer, fairer and stronger." The Bill will now undergo further scrutiny in the House of Lords, where it is expected to face more debate and potential amendments.

As the Bill progresses, it is clear that the UK Government's decision to grant more powers to the Welsh Assembly is a significant step towards greater autonomy for Wales. While some parties may feel that the Bill does not go far enough, it is undeniable that this move marks a new era in the devolution settlement for Wales, one that will bring greater clarity, accountability, and powers to the Welsh people.

Stirling Castle has won a prestigious award, beating Edinburgh Zoo and Dynamic Earth. The castle attracts 460,000 visitors annually. Executive manager Liz Grant called the win a "wonderful achievement", noting it recognizes Scotland's heritage attractions. The award was voted on by the public, making it a special accolade for the castle and its contribution to Scotland's tourism and leisure offerings.

A 30-year-old motorcyclist is being treated for a serious head injury after crashing into a wall on the B743 near Dungavel. The incident occurred at 19:25 on Wednesday, with the man losing control of his Suzuki motorcycle. He was airlifted to Queen Elizabeth University Hospital in Glasgow. Two friends, who were travelling on the same road, were nearby at the time of the crash. Police are urging witnesses to come forward, asking anyone with information to contact them on 101. Inquiries into the crash are ongoing, led by PC Dougie Bryson. Witnesses are encouraged to share any information.

President Trump's Advisory Commission on Election Integrity held its first meeting on Wednesday, sparking controversy and concerns over voter suppression. The commission, established by the president in May, aims to investigate voter fraud and election integrity. However, Democrats suspect that the commission's true intention is to disenfranchise left-leaning voters.

During the meeting, President Trump pledged his strong support for the commission, emphasizing the importance of ensuring the integrity of the electoral process. "Every time voter fraud occurs, it cancels out the vote of a lawful citizen, and undermines democracy," he said. "Can't let that happen." The president has repeatedly claimed that he would have won the popular vote in the 2016 presidential election if not for millions of illegal votes cast, despite lacking evidence to support this assertion.

The commission's chairman, Kris Kobach, echoed the president's sentiments, stating that it is impossible to know the true outcome of the election due to the presence of ineligible voters. "I think the President-elect is absolutely correct when he says the number of illegal votes cast exceeds the popular vote margin between him and Hillary Clinton," Kobach said. However, he acknowledged that even if the commission were to identify ineligible votes, it would be impossible to determine which candidate they voted for.

Kobach, who is also the secretary of state of Kansas, has been a vocal advocate for stricter voter ID laws and immigration policies. His involvement in the commission has raised concerns among voting rights advocates, who have dubbed him the "king of voter suppression." The American Civil Liberties Union's voting rights project has criticized Kobach's efforts to restrict voting access, particularly among minority and low-income communities.

The commission's request for voter data, including names, addresses, and voting history, has been met with resistance from at least 20 states. Kentucky Secretary of State Alison Lundergan Grimes has refused to submit voter records to the commission, calling it a "waste of taxpayer money" and an attempt to "legitimize voter suppression efforts." Other states have expressed similar concerns, citing the potential for the commission's findings to be used to justify restrictive voting laws.

The controversy surrounding the commission has highlighted the deepening partisan divide over voting rights and election integrity. While the president and his allies claim that the commission is necessary to prevent voter fraud, opponents argue that it is a thinly veiled attempt to suppress Democratic votes. As the commission continues its work, it remains to be seen whether it will be able to achieve its stated goals or if it will become a tool for partisan manipulation. One thing is certain, however: the debate over voting rights and election integrity will continue to be a contentious issue in American politics.

Renowned Author Margaret Forster Passes Away at 77

Margaret Forster, the award-winning author of novels such as "Georgy Girl" and "Diary of an Ordinary Woman", has passed away at the age of 77. Forster, who had been suffering from cancer in her back, died on Monday morning at the Marie Curie Hospice in north London. The news was confirmed by her daughter, Caitlin Davies, who took to Twitter to pay tribute to her mother, saying "Her books will live on."

Forster's writing career spanned over five decades, during which she published more than 25 novels, as well as several biographies of notable figures such as Dame Daphne du Maurier and William Makepeace Thackeray. Her most famous novel, "Georgy Girl", was published in 1965 and was later adapted into a film starring Lynn Redgrave and Charlotte Rampling. The book told the story of a young woman in 1960s London, navigating a complex web of relationships and identity.

Fellow novelist Elizabeth Day paid tribute to Forster, describing her as "an under-appreciated wonder of a writer" who was "once very nice to me as a debut novelist". Forster's husband, writer Hunter Davies, also spoke fondly of his wife, describing her as "the cleverest woman I ever met". He praised her emotional intelligence, saying she had a unique ability to understand people and predict their actions and feelings.

Forster's life was marked by her bravery and resilience in the face of adversity. She underwent a double mastectomy 40 years ago, and yet continued to write and publish books until recent years. Her most recent book, "My Life In Houses", was published in 2014 and offered a poignant and introspective look at her life through the places she had lived.

Despite her literary success, Forster rarely sought to draw attention to herself, and gave few interviews throughout her career. However, she did appear on Radio 4's Desert Island Discs in 1994, offering a rare glimpse into her life and personality. Her legacy will live on through her books, which continue to captivate readers with their insightful and nuanced portrayals of human experience.

Tragedy Strikes Deganwy as Beloved Business Owners Perish in House Fire

A devastating house fire in Deganwy, Conwy, has claimed the lives of Ted and Lucy Hocknell, a well-respected and beloved couple in the community. The blaze, which occurred at their home in Gannock Park West at approximately 07:40 BST on Tuesday, is thought to have been caused by an electrical fault. Despite being brought out of the house, the couple sadly passed away afterwards.

Ted Hocknell, 93, was a decorated war veteran who received the Ushakov medal from the Russian government in 2014 for his bravery in keeping Arctic supply lines open during World War Two. A former policeman, he was also known for his heroic actions in the community, including saving two children from the tide on Llandudno's West Shore and apprehending a handbag thief. His friend, Ian Turner, remembered him as a "really nice guy" who would never seek to draw attention to himself.

Lucy Hocknell, 88, was a former hairdresser and a "real lady" who was always seen walking arm in arm with her sister in town. The couple owned the popular Bryant and Hocknell furniture shop on Gloddaeth Street, and their presence will be deeply missed in the community. Aberconwy AM Janet Finch-Saunders expressed her shock and sadness at the news, stating that the town will "miss them tremendously."

Thousands of Swansea City fans are set to descend upon Wembley Stadium this weekend as the team prepares to face off against Bradford City in the Capital One Cup final. The club's allocation of 33,000 tickets sold out weeks ago, demonstrating the immense excitement and dedication of the Swansea City faithful.

As the big day approaches, the BBC will be providing comprehensive coverage of the event. Fans are encouraged to share their experiences and photos from Wembley, Swansea, or anywhere else in the world where they will be cheering on their team. Photos can be emailed to newsonline.wales@bbc.co.uk, and a selection will be published online.

The BBC invites fans to share their stories and comments, which may be published along with their name and location. Fans can also include their phone number if they are willing to be contacted by a BBC journalist. As always, safety is paramount, and fans are reminded to avoid taking unnecessary risks or infringing on laws when sharing their content. A full gallery of fan photos is already available online, and more will be added throughout the weekend.

Indian President Pranab Mukherjee has introduced reforms to the protocols surrounding his office. According to his press secretary, Venu Rajamony, the president felt that certain practices needed to be reformed. As a result, Mr. Mukherjee will now be referred to as "Mr. President" instead of "His Excellency" in domestic contexts. The title "Excellency" will only be used when interacting with foreign leaders, following international customs. This change aims to promote equality, as enshrined in the Indian constitution. Additionally, the president has instructed his office to organize functions within the Rashtrapati Bhavan to minimize public inconvenience and reduce the burden on law enforcement. This move is part of a broader review of protocols undertaken by the new president, who was elected in July. The reforms reflect Mr. Mukherjee's commitment to simplicity and equality.

An incident occurred at HM Naval Base Clyde, home to the UK's Trident nuclear submarines, when a routine fire exercise on a surface ship triggered a fire suppression system. The incident happened at around 05:30, prompting emergency services to be called to the base. Six personnel inhaled a gas and were taken to the Royal Alexandria Hospital as a precaution. Their families have been informed and an investigation has been launched. A Royal Navy spokesman confirmed the incident, stating that all other personnel were declared fit after being checked at the base's sick bay. The cause of the incident is currently under investigation.

Belgian Cisse expressed excitement about his new opportunity, stating, "I am looking forward to showing my qualities." The 23-year-old made 27 appearances for Standard last season and is eager to contribute to his new team. He previously played for KVV Mechelen before returning to his hometown club.

Australian Election Results Remain Uncertain as Counting Continues

The Australian federal election results remain too close to call, with counting continuing on Wednesday in several key electorates. According to the Australian Broadcasting Corp. (ABC), the government has secured 71 seats in the lower house, with a possibility of reaching an absolute majority of 76. However, the outcome is still uncertain, and the possibility of a "hung parliament" looms.

Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has accepted responsibility for the government's mediocre performance, citing disillusionment with mainstream parties as a contributing factor. The coalition has lost over 20 seats, with many analysts surprised by the close result. Turnbull stated, "I want to make it quite clear that as Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal party, I take full responsibility for our campaign."

The ABC's election analyst, Antony Green, predicts that the government will win at least 73 seats, surpassing the opposition Labor Party's tally. Postal votes have favored the government, with results in several electorates hanging in the balance. In the Queensland seat of Forde, the Liberal candidate leads by a mere 94 votes, highlighting the intense competition.

If the coalition fails to secure 76 seats, it will face a "hung parliament," requiring them to negotiate with independent crossbenchers to form a government. The coalition is likely to seek support from Queensland rural MP Bob Katter and the Nick Xenophon Team's newly elected MP Rebekha Sharkie. Labor, on the other hand, is unlikely to have the numbers to form a minority government.

The poor showing during the coalition's re-election campaign has sparked speculation about Turnbull's position as prime minister. Opposition leader Bill Shorten has repeatedly called on Turnbull to step down, while some MPs have criticized the prime minister's campaign strategy. Turnbull, however, remains committed to his role, stating, "It's too early for definitive judgments... it will take time to absorb the learnings from the campaign."

As Australia waits for the final results, the country's history of frequent leadership changes looms large. With five prime ministers in the past six years, the political landscape remains uncertain. The outcome of the election will have significant implications for the country's future, and all eyes are on the ongoing counting process to determine the ultimate winner.

Pop stars Pixie Lott, Geri Halliwell, and Professor Green attended the Starlight charity party. EastEnders' Jake Wood and McBusted also joined. Starlight grants wishes and provides hospital entertainment for ill children, aiming to distract them from pain and isolation, bringing joy to those in need. The event supported the charity's mission to improve young lives.

Two Saudi women, Loujain al-Hathloul and Maysa al-Amoudi, have been released from detention after being arrested for campaigning against the country's ban on female drivers. Al-Hathloul, 25, was taken into custody on December 1 after attempting to drive into Saudi Arabia from the United Arab Emirates, while al-Amoudi, 33, a Saudi journalist, was detained when she arrived at the border to support her friend.

The women's arrest sparked widespread concern, particularly after reports emerged that their case was being transferred to a terrorism court. The move was reportedly due to comments they had made on social media, rather than their actions behind the wheel. Saudi Arabia is the only country in the world where women are forbidden from driving, and those who do risk being fined and arrested.

The women's release comes just days after Britain's Prince Charles met with Saudi Arabia's new monarch, Prince Salman. During the visit, Prince Charles raised the case of Raif Badawi, a blogger who has been sentenced to 1,000 lashes and 10 years in prison. The case of the women drivers has highlighted the restrictions faced by women in Saudi Arabia and has put pressure on the new monarch to address human rights concerns.

The release of al-Hathloul and al-Amoudi has been welcomed by activists, who believe that the British prince's visit may have played a role in securing their freedom. The women's large following on Twitter had helped to draw attention to their case, with many using social media to campaign for their release. The incident has shone a spotlight on Saudi Arabia's human rights record, and many are now calling for greater reforms to address the country's restrictive laws and practices.

Rentokil has announced the sale of its struggling delivery firm City Link to restructuring specialist Better Capital. City Link has incurred significant losses since 2007, including a £26m deficit in 2012, due to weakening demand from small businesses. Better Capital is expected to invest £40m into the business, which will continue to be run by its existing management team. Rentokil's decision to offload City Link is part of its strategy to focus on its core pest control and hygiene operations. Despite chief executive Alan Brown's optimism that City Link has "turned the corner," Rentokil's shares closed 0.6% down following the announcement. Better Capital has recently invested in Jaeger and Everest, and its investment in City Link is hoped to revitalize the struggling business. The sale marks a significant shift for Rentokil, which acquired City Link in 2006.

French conservatives are heading to the polls today to choose their candidate for next spring's presidential election, with former Prime Minister François Fillon emerging as the favorite to win. Fillon, 62, secured 44.1% of the votes in the first round of the primary election last week, leaving his rival, Alain Juppe, 71, trailing behind with 28.5%. The winner of today's run-off is expected to face off against far-right National Front leader Marine Le Pen in the general election.

The primary election, modeled on the US system, has been marked by a heated debate between the two candidates over their economic reform plans. Fillon has campaigned on a promise of radical change, pledging to slash 500,000 public jobs and implement sweeping economic reforms. Juppe, on the other hand, has proposed a more moderate approach, focusing on harmony and diversity, and planning to cut just over half the number of public jobs proposed by Fillon.

The debate between the two candidates has become increasingly personal, with Juppe attempting to mobilize centrist and left-wing voters by highlighting Fillon's conservative views on abortion and gay marriage. Juppe has also accused Fillon of being close to Russian President Vladimir Putin, amid growing tensions between the West and Moscow over the crises in Syria and Ukraine.

Fillon has hit back, arguing that the EU and the US "provoked" Russia by expanding in Eastern Europe, and calling for an alliance with Russia to fight Islamic State militants in Syria. He has also complained of being portrayed as a "medieval conservative", describing Juppe as a "man of the system" with no real plans for change.

The endorsement of former President Nicolas Sarkozy, who was knocked out of the race in the first round, has given Fillon a significant boost. Polls suggest that Fillon is now the favorite to win, with 71% of conservative respondents finding him more convincing in a recent TV debate.

Polls across France are due to open at 07:00 GMT and close at 18:00 GMT, with the results expected to be announced later today. The winner of the primary election will go on to represent the Republican party in the general election, where they are expected to face off against Marine Le Pen in a battle for the presidency. With the French economy struggling and the country facing a range of challenges, from terrorism to immigration, the outcome of today's election is being closely watched by politicians and voters across the country.

Actor Tom Chambers has sparked controversy after suggesting that men's salaries should be higher than women's because they often have families to support. The Casualty star, who plays Sam Strachan on the show and its sister program Holby City, made the comments at a book launch, where he also expressed his opinion that his co-star Derek Thompson deserved to be the BBC's highest-paid actor due to his 31 years of service.

Chambers, a former winner of Strictly Come Dancing, stated that as the sole breadwinner in his family, his salary was not just for himself, but also for his wife and children. However, his remarks were met with a social media backlash, with many criticizing him for perpetuating the gender pay gap.

In response to the backlash, Chambers has since apologized, claiming that his comments were "taken out of context" and that he does not advocate for the gender pay gap. He expressed his mortification at the stories that had run about his comments and emphasized his belief that change is needed to address the issue of gender pay disparity.

The controversy surrounding Chambers' comments comes amid ongoing debate about the BBC's pay disclosures, which have highlighted a significant disparity between the salaries of the corporation's male and female celebrities. The issue of gender pay disparity remains a contentious topic, with many calling for greater equality and transparency in pay practices. Chambers' comments have added fuel to the fire, sparking a renewed conversation about the need for change.

Andy Murray has made a strong return to the court, defeating Borna Coric 6-1 6-2 in the Paris Masters. The second-seeded Murray, who was playing for the first time since losing to Novak Djokovic in Shanghai 19 days ago, wasted little time in seeing off the 18-year-old Coric. The young Croatian, ranked 46 in the world, was unable to fashion a single break point as Murray broke serve twice in each set to secure the win in under an hour.

Murray's victory sets up a meeting with Belgian David Goffin, which will serve as a warm-up for their likely encounter in the Davis Cup final later this month. The Scot is looking to gain valuable information from their match on the Paris hard courts, which he can take to the indoor clay courts in Ghent. "Any time you spend time on court with opponents you can learn about their game," Murray said. "It's good to play against him but I will obviously, before the tie, watch matches of him playing on clay to learn and understand his game better on that surface."

Meanwhile, British number two Aljaz Bedene's run in the tournament came to an end with a 6-3 7-6 (7-3) loss to American 13th seed John Isner. Bedene, who could yet feature in the Davis Cup final pending an ITF ruling on his eligibility to represent Great Britain, had come through two rounds of qualifying and beaten Spain's Marcel Granollers in the main draw. His ranking is set to reach a new high of 46 next week.

Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer also progressed in the tournament, with Nadal beating Lukas Rosol 6-2 6-2 and Federer cruising past Italian Andreas Seppi 6-1 6-1. Murray will face Goffin at 09:30 GMT on Thursday, as he looks to build momentum ahead of the ATP Finals in London and the Davis Cup final. With a busy schedule over the next few weeks, Murray will be looking to make the most of his time on court and gain valuable experience that he can take into the upcoming tournaments.

London Launches Dedicated Hub to Combat Online Hate Crime

A new hub is being set up in London to tackle online hate crime, with a team of five officers dedicated to supporting victims and identifying abuse. The two-year pilot project, which will cost £1.7m, has received £452,000 in funding from the Home Office. The London Mayor's office has stated that there will be a "zero tolerance" approach to online abuse, with a spokesman emphasizing that there is "no place for hate" in the city.

The team will work to identify the location of online crimes and allocate them to the relevant police force. They will also be assisted by a team of volunteers. The Mayor's Office for Policing And Crime (Mopac) has highlighted the challenges posed by social media, which can provide perpetrators with anonymity and make it harder to bring them to justice. Victims of online hate crime can become isolated and fearful, with the potential for online abuse to spill into the real world.

The new hub will not only support victims but also provide training for police officers and community groups on how to identify, report, and challenge online abuse. This is the first time a dedicated police team has been set up to detect and respond to hate crimes, and it is seen as a significant step forward in tackling this growing issue. Community groups in London have welcomed the initiative, citing online hate crime as a major concern that has previously received an inconsistent police response.

North West Ambulance Service (NWAS) is facing scrutiny after two separate incidents where patients died after experiencing significant delays in receiving medical attention. The family of 71-year-old Jack Skelly from Burnley has lodged a complaint after he passed away following a 55-minute wait for an ambulance crew. In a separate incident, 65-year-old Richard Hansbury from Wigan bled to death after a staggering 150-minute delay.

According to NWAS, patient handovers are causing "significant delays" in their response times. The trust is currently facing its most challenging operating environment on record, with a 7% increase in 999 calls this year. Nurse Jo Needham, the niece of Mr. Skelly, expressed her concerns about the delay in response time, stating that her uncle "would've had a better chance" of survival if the ambulance had arrived earlier.

Mr. Skelly had complained of feeling unwell and collapsed in his bathroom on December 19. Despite multiple phone calls made by his family for an ambulance, the crew took 55 minutes to arrive. By the time they arrived, Nurse Needham was attempting to resuscitate her uncle. She believes that if he had collapsed in a public place with access to a defibrillator, his chances of survival would have been higher.

In the case of Mr. Hansbury, an ambulance crew had to wait nearly three hours for a second available crew to help them lift the 19-stone patient into an ambulance. His inquest is scheduled for Friday. NWAS has stated that it is fully investigating both incidents and has offered its condolences to the families. The trust attributed the delays to high demand for services and resources being tied up at nearby hospitals.

The incidents have raised concerns about the trust's ability to meet national targets for response times. In September, NWAS admitted that it was struggling to hit targets for reaching "red one" and "red two" calls within eight minutes. The trust must also reach non-life-threatening "green" calls within 20 minutes. As the investigation into these incidents continues, the families of the victims and the community at large are left to wonder about the adequacy of the emergency services in the region.

A British student, Hannah Bladon, was tragically killed in a stabbing attack on a tram in Jerusalem on Good Friday. The 20-year-old, from Burton-upon-Trent in Staffordshire, was studying at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem at the time of her death. She had been participating in an archaeological dig that morning and was on her way back when the attack occurred.

The incident took place on a tram travelling near the Old City, which was crowded with Christians marking Good Friday and Jews celebrating Passover. A 57-year-old Palestinian man, who had recently been released from a psychiatric hospital, pulled a knife from his bag and repeatedly stabbed Ms. Bladon in the chest. She died shortly after arrival at the hospital.

The attacker was detained at the scene by an off-duty policeman who was travelling on the tram with his family. The policeman, who wished to remain anonymous, told the AFP news agency that he heard the cries of "attack, attack" and immediately sounded the alarm. With the help of another passenger, he overpowered the attacker and prevented further harm.

Two other people, a 30-year-old pregnant woman and a 50-year-old man, were also injured in the attack. According to BBC Middle East correspondent Tom Bateman, they were either hurt when the tram came to a sudden stop or in the panic to get away from the scene.

Ms. Bladon was a student at the University of Birmingham, where she was studying bible studies, archaeology, and Hebrew. Her personal tutor, Dr. Andrew Davies, described her as a "rare treasure" and praised her enthusiasm and dedication to her studies. "She was always the first to be there for lectures, bright-eyed, bushy-tailed, even in the early hours of the morning," he said.

The Hebrew University of Jerusalem expressed "deep sorrow" over Ms. Bladon's death, and her family released a statement paying tribute to her memory. "Hannah was the most caring, sensitive, and compassionate daughter you could ever wish for," they said. "She was a talented musician, part of a serving team at her local church, and a member of her local archaeological group. She was an enthusiastic rugby player and a keen Derby County supporter. Her death leaves so much promise unfulfilled."

Israel's President Reuven Rivlin said he was "filled with sadness" about the attack and offered his thoughts and prayers to Ms. Bladon's family. The incident has sparked widespread condemnation, and Israeli police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the attack. The suspect, who has been named as a resident of Ras al-Amud in east Jerusalem, is being held in custody and is expected to face charges in the coming days.

The TweedLove Bike Festival has kicked off in the Borders, attracting thousands of visitors. The first week's events included a trail run, mountain bike marathon, and family day in Peebles. Hundreds of children participated in riding events. Now in its eighth year, the festival boasts over 40 events across three weeks. A "mega bike demo" is upcoming, featuring bikes worth up to £10,000 for the public to try, during the second "big weekend" from June 9-11. The festival is the UK's largest cycling celebration.
