Hayward expressed his excitement about the team's potential, despite acknowledging defensive improvements are needed. General manager Jon Daniels welcomed the news, citing the coaching staff's commitment to developing the current squad. The Scarlets are currently second in the Pro12 table, just two points behind leaders Connacht after eight matches. This contract extension is a boost to the team as they continue their push for the top spot.

Tiger Woods' Golf Career Hangs in Balance as He Faces Uncertain Recovery

In a candid and somber interview, 14-time major winner Tiger Woods has expressed his uncertainty and frustration regarding his return to professional golf. The 39-year-old golf legend has been sidelined since undergoing two operations in September and October to alleviate pain from a pinched nerve. With no clear timetable for his rehabilitation, Woods is facing an uncertain future, leaving fans and the golfing world wondering if he will ever regain his former glory.

Woods, who will turn 40 on December 30, revealed that he has not swung a golf club since his operations and has been limited to walking as his only form of physical activity. He has spent most of his time playing video games, a stark contrast to his usual rigorous training regimen. The American golfer admitted that he has not done any rehabilitation work on his back, leaving him without a clear goal or timeline to work towards.

This is not the first time Woods has faced a lengthy layoff due to injury. In 2014, he underwent surgery on a pinched nerve in his back and missed three months of the season, playing in only seven tournaments. However, this current setback seems to be the most challenging, with Woods himself describing it as "different from the other surgeries I've had in the past." The lack of a clear recovery timeline has left him feeling uncertain and demotivated, with no "light at the end of the tunnel" to look forward to.

Despite his uncertain future, Woods remains hopeful that he can still compete at the highest level. He has been named as one of United States captain Davis Love III's assistants for the 2016 Ryder Cup, but he still harbors ambitions of making the team as a player. Woods has played in seven Ryder Cups, with his most recent appearance in 2012 under Love's captaincy.

World number three Rory McIlroy has offered his support to Woods, posting on social media: "Wishing my idol and friend a speedy recovery. Golf without him doesn't bear thinking about. Hope to see you back on the course soon @tigerwoods." However, with no clear indication of when Woods will return to golf, it is difficult to predict if he will be able to regain his former form.

Woods' last major victory was at the US Open in 2008, and he has struggled to replicate that success in recent years. He missed the cut at three of the four majors this year and played in only 11 events, leaving him stuck on 79 PGA Tour victories. While he acknowledges that he has achieved a great deal in his 20-year career, Woods is clearly not ready to hang up his clubs just yet. The question on everyone's mind is: will he be able to overcome this latest setback and return to the top of the golfing world? Only time will tell.

A rare solar storm has brought a spectacular display of the Aurora Australis to New Zealand, with the phenomenon visible much further north than usual. The aurora, also known as the southern lights, occurs when cosmic rays or solar wind interact with the earth's upper atmosphere. This week, many New Zealanders braved the cold to capture images of the breathtaking display.

Aurora enthusiasts, known as "aurora chasers," were thrilled to witness the spectacle. Photographer Blair Pattinson from Queenstown described it as a "treat" to see such a strong aurora. "It's quite special," he said. "Many people wait years before they see them." The aurora is forecast to be active again on Thursday night, giving enthusiasts another chance to witness its beauty.

Despite the cold temperatures, with the South Island dropping to sub-zero temperatures overnight, many were undeterred. Medical practitioner Stephen Voss, who has been chasing aurorae for 15 years, summed up the experience: "There is one word to describe it...freezing." Nevertheless, the opportunity to see the Aurora Australis was too good to miss.

A 64-year-old South Korean monk, Venerable Jung-won, has died after setting himself on fire during a rally against President Park Geun-hye in Seoul. The monk's tragic death has sparked widespread outrage and reignited tensions between South Korea and Japan over the issue of "comfort women" - women who were forced to work in Japanese military brothels during World War Two.

Venerable Jung-won staged the protest on Saturday, and his condition deteriorated rapidly before he succumbed to multiple organ failures caused by his burns on Monday night. In a suicide note, the monk called President Park a "traitor", reportedly due to her handling of the comfort women issue. The social justice committee of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism released a statement saying that Venerable Jung-won had "sacrificed his life to convey people's sentiment" and demanded President Park's resignation.

The comfort women issue has been a long-standing point of contention between South Korea and Japan. In 2015, President Park reached a deal with Japan, which included a promise to pay into a fund for South Korean women who were forced to work in Japanese military brothels. However, critics argue that the deal does not go far enough in holding Japan responsible for wartime abuses and does not directly compensate the women.

Tensions between the two countries escalated last week after Tokyo withdrew its ambassador to South Korea in a row over a statue representing sex slaves. Japan claimed that the statue, which depicts a young, barefoot woman sitting in a chair, was a violation of the 2015 agreement. Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe has demanded the removal of the statue, saying that the South Korean side should show its sincerity and implement the agreement as a "matter of credibility".

The comfort women issue is just one of several controversies surrounding President Park, who has been embroiled in a scandal involving a close friend charged with corruption. She has been suspended from duties since December, when parliament voted to impeach her. The regular rallies against President Park in Seoul have drawn large crowds, with protesters calling for her resignation and demanding justice for the comfort women. Venerable Jung-won's tragic death has added to the sense of urgency and outrage, with many hoping that his sacrifice will not be in vain.

Tragedy Strikes in Penistone as Father and Son Lose Their Lives in Deliberate House Fire

A devastating house fire in Penistone, near Barnsley, has claimed the lives of a father and son, leaving a community in shock. Darren Sykes, 44, and his son Paul were found dead in the property on Tennyson Close on Wednesday evening. A second boy, 12-year-old Jack Sykes, was rescued from the house and remains critically ill in hospital.

According to South Yorkshire Police, the fire was started deliberately, and they are not seeking anyone else in connection with the incident. Ch Insp Debbie Mahmood expressed her condolences to the family, stating that a full investigation will be conducted. Emergency services responded to the call at around 18:30 BST, and the three victims were taken to hospital, where Mr. Sykes and his son were pronounced dead.

The head teacher of Springvale Primary School, Andy Platt, paid tribute to Paul, describing him as an outgoing and popular boy who will be greatly missed. Jack's mother is currently keeping a bedside vigil, and the house remains cordoned off. The police have declined to comment on whether any substances were used to accelerate the fire. A post-mortem examination is scheduled to take place on Friday. The incident has sent shockwaves through the community, and an investigation is underway to determine the circumstances surrounding the tragic event.

A former lottery winner has been handed a community service order and disqualified from driving for five years after pleading guilty to driving while disqualified and without insurance. Ryan Magee, 34, from Eglinton, appeared before Londonderry Magistrates Court, where he admitted to driving a Ford Focus along the city's Foyle Bridge last December.

Magee, who won a staggering £6.4m in the EuroMillions lottery seven years ago, was ordered to complete 200 hours of community service and fined £250. His legally aided barrister described his client's life as a series of unfortunate events, saying "every silver lining has a dark cloud." The barrister added that Magee had been traumatised by recent events and had only recently come to appreciate his responsibilities, particularly when it came to driving.

The court heard that police officers on mobile patrol had spotted Magee driving the Ford Focus at 20:40 GMT on December 4 last year. When stopped, Magee admitted to driving while disqualified, replying "yep, that's right" to the officers. This offence occurred just five months into an 18-month disqualification period for failing to provide a specimen.

The judge described Magee's criminal record, which includes 17 previous convictions, 12 of them for road traffic offences, as "appalling." He told Magee that he was a "menace" to himself and other road users, and that his actions had caused him "huge concern." The judge warned Magee that if he failed to comply with the community service order, he would face six months in jail.

Magee's lottery win had initially brought him a life of luxury, with him spending £170,000 on a Ferrari sports car and purchasing a house equipped with a champagne bar. However, the house is now up for auction, a testament to the tumultuous turn his life has taken. The case serves as a cautionary tale of the importance of responsible behaviour, particularly when it comes to driving, and the consequences of failing to do so.

Alcohol Consumption in the UK: A Growing Concern

A recent review by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has found that the average annual consumption of pure alcohol in the UK has risen to 10.6 litres per person, equivalent to 115 bottles of wine. This represents a significant increase from the early 1990s, when consumption was under 10 litres per person. The trend is particularly concerning, as it contrasts with falls in other nations, such as Germany and Italy, which have seen big reductions in drinking rates.

The OECD report highlights the UK as one of the heaviest drinking countries among the 34 wealthiest nations, with the average person consuming more than the current OECD average of 9.5 litres. In fact, the UK's drinking rates were below the current OECD average in the early 1990s, but have since surpassed it. The report suggests that the UK should consider implementing measures such as minimum pricing and tougher regulation to reduce consumption.

One notable trend highlighted by the report is the high rate of problem drinking among educated women. Nearly one in five women from the highest educated groups drinks to hazardous levels, compared to one in 10 among the least educated group. According to OECD economist Mark Pearson, this trend is "pretty unique" to the UK and appears to be related to the increasing employment opportunities women are getting in traditionally male-dominated sectors, such as the finance industry.

The report also notes that the UK has one of the heaviest concentrations of drinking among its population, with the heaviest-drinking one-fifth of the population accounting for nearly two-thirds of all alcohol consumed. Furthermore, there has been a rise in youth drinking, with the proportion of 15-year-olds who have experienced alcohol increasing from 71% to 75% between 2002 and 2010. Although there are signs that this trend may be starting to reverse in recent years, it remains a concern.

To address the issue of problem drinking, Mr. Pearson recommends that the UK consider taking tougher steps, including minimum pricing, banning sports sponsorship, and enforcing clear labelling, as well as improving access to treatment. He emphasizes that such measures present "opportunities" to reduce drinking rates, while also acknowledging the need to strike a balance between tackling harmful drinking and penalizing those who drink within recommended levels.

Sir Ian Gilmore, chairman of the Alcohol Health Alliance, agrees with Mr. Pearson's assessment, noting that the research shows there is "no silver bullet" and that a range of policies on "pricing, marketing, and availability" are needed to address the issue. He adds that drinking has been seen as a personal choice for too long, rather than a population-wide public health issue.

In response to the report, a Department of Health spokeswoman acknowledged that drinking too much too often can have devastating consequences for health and stated that local authorities have been given public health funding to help tackle problems like drinking. The spokeswoman emphasized that more needs to be done to prevent people from getting into dangerous drinking habits.

The OECD report serves as a wake-up call for the UK to take a closer look at its drinking culture and to consider implementing policies to reduce consumption and mitigate the negative consequences of excessive drinking. As Mr. Pearson notes, drinking costs a significant amount of money in terms of lost productivity, health spending, and accidents and ill health, making it an issue that any country serious about its economic performance cannot afford to ignore.

Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy has confirmed that he will remain the party's candidate for the East Renfrewshire Westminster seat in the upcoming general election. Despite previously announcing his intention to stand for the Scottish Parliament in 2016 and become the party's candidate for first minister, Murphy's team has clarified that he will retain his current position as MP for East Renfrewshire.

Murphy, who was elected leader of the Scottish Labour Party last month, had faced calls to clarify his position on the Westminster seat, which he has held since 1997. A spokesman for Murphy stated that his constituents would be the first to know if there were any changes to his candidacy.

It is worth noting that there is no rule preventing Murphy from holding seats in both the Scottish and UK parliaments simultaneously. In fact, former First Minister Alex Salmond previously served as both an MSP and an MP at the same time. However, Murphy has previously expressed his reluctance to pursue this option, stating that it is "not something I'm attracted to".

Murphy has given a "cast-iron guarantee" that he will be a candidate in the 2016 Scottish Parliament elections and will stand for the position of first minister. He has also hinted that he may attempt to enter the Scottish Parliament sooner, but has assured his constituents that they will be informed first of any changes to his plans.

The confirmation of Murphy's candidacy for the East Renfrewshire seat provides clarity on his immediate political future, but the longer-term question of whether he will attempt to hold seats in both parliaments remains uncertain. For now, Murphy's focus will be on the general election on May 7th, where he will seek to retain his Westminster seat.

Tory Recriminations Begin After Election Setback in Wales

The Conservative Party in Wales is left reeling after a disappointing election result, with many questioning the campaign strategy. Despite Theresa May's high-profile visits to Labour-held target seats in Bridgend, Wrexham, and Clwyd South, the party failed to make significant gains. In hindsight, it appears that shoring up support in marginal seats like Cardiff North, Gower, and Vale of Clwyd may have been a more effective approach.

The campaign has been criticized for its lack of a Welsh dimension, with sources suggesting that the party's message failed to resonate with local voters. The absence of a clear leader, with three different men representing the party in debates, may have also contributed to the confusion. In contrast, the Scottish Conservatives, led by Ruth Davidson, were able to make significant gains.

The election result has sparked a debate about what went wrong for the Tories in Wales. While some argue that the campaign was poorly run, others believe that the country's desire for a softer Brexit may have been a decisive factor. As the party begins to reflect on its performance, it is clear that there are lessons to be learned from the experience. The question now is whether the Welsh Tories can regroup and regain momentum in the face of a resurgent Labour party.

Northern Ireland's First Minister, Peter Robinson, 66, was hospitalized after feeling unwell. A party spokesman confirmed he underwent tests for a heart-related condition. Robinson, in office since 2008, was taken to the hospital by ambulance on Monday morning. His condition remains unclear, with no further details released.

Vin Diesel Reveals Newborn Daughter's Name as Tribute to Late Friend Paul Walker

In an emotional announcement on America's Today show, actor Vin Diesel revealed that he has named his newborn daughter Pauline, in honor of his late friend and co-star Paul Walker. Walker, who passed away in a car crash in 2013 at the age of 40, had a profound impact on Diesel's life, and the actor credits him with inspiring him to be more involved in the birth of his children.

Diesel recalled the advice Walker gave him seven years ago, before the birth of his first child, Hania. "Paul told me to go into the delivery room and own it, be present, and don't shy away from it," Diesel said. He took Walker's advice to heart and was present for the birth of his daughter, even cutting the umbilical cord. As he did so, he couldn't help but think of his late friend and the impact he had on his life.

Pauline is Diesel's third child with his partner, Paloma Jimenez. The couple also has a son, Vincent, aged four. Diesel's tribute to Walker is a testament to the strong bond the two actors shared, both on and off screen. Walker's death was a tragic loss for the film industry, and his brothers stepped in to complete his scenes in the seventh installment of the Fast and Furious franchise. Furious 7, which is dedicated to Walker's memory, is set to be released on April 10.

A Spanish air force pilot, Captain Fernando Lluna Carrascosa, was killed in a Eurofighter jet crash at the Moron air base near Seville. The incident occurred during a routine training flight at around 14:00 local time. Captain Carrascosa, from Madrid, had over 600 hours of experience flying Eurofighter jets. He leaves behind a wife and daughter. The crash is the second fatal Eurofighter incident at the base, following a 2010 accident that claimed the life of a Saudi national. Images on social media showed black smoke rising from the area. The Spanish ministry of defence confirmed the crash and is investigating the circumstances. Captain Carrascosa's death is a tragic loss for the Spanish air force and his family. An investigation into the cause of the crash is underway.

A large fire broke out at a property in Great Haseley on Sunday, engulfing nearly half of the roof. Smoke was spotted at 17:30 BST, prompting a response from up to 50 firefighters. A specialist team used chainsaws to cut fire breaks, protecting the rest of the home. Crews in breathing apparatus tackled the flames from inside. The cause of the fire is unknown. Oxfordshire fire service employed a new technique, using ladders and chainsaws to limit fire spread, allowing for the salvage of personal possessions. This innovative method was praised for its effectiveness in tackling thatch fires.

Scotland's retail sector has shown signs of growth, with the latest retail sales index revealing a 0.8% increase in value and a 1.7% rise in volume in the fourth quarter of 2014. Although these figures are lower than the country-wide averages of 1.5% and 2.3% respectively, they indicate a positive trend for the industry north of the border.

On an annual basis, however, Scotland lagged behind Great Britain in both volume and value terms. The volume of sales in Scotland increased by 1.6% year-on-year, compared to a 5% rise for the whole of Britain. This suggests that while the Scottish retail sector is recovering, it still has some ground to make up.

The large shops with at least 250 employees, which account for around 70% of retail industry sales, saw a 0.9% increase in sales volumes compared to the previous quarter. Small and medium-sized stores, on the other hand, experienced a more significant growth of 3%. This disparity highlights the ongoing challenges faced by smaller retailers in competing with their larger counterparts.

Euan Murray of Barclays Corporate Banking attributed the boost in sales to the "extravaganza of planned promotions" in November and the last-minute Christmas shopping rush. He also noted that non-food products, such as clothing, performed particularly well towards the end of 2014. With the new spring ranges now in stores, fashion retailers will be hoping for milder weather to encourage shoppers to update their wardrobes.

Scottish Retail Consortium director David Lonsdale welcomed the resumption of growth in retail sales, citing falling prices at shop checkouts and petrol pumps as contributing factors. However, he cautioned that the recovery in consumer confidence remains fragile and that upcoming public policy decisions, such as the proposed replacement of council tax and the setting of the Scottish rate of income tax, could impact disposable incomes and take-home pay.

Deputy First Minister John Swinney highlighted the positive trends in the wider Scottish economy, including record jobs figures, low unemployment, and high employment and economic activity. Scotland Office Minister David Mundell also emphasized the benefits of being part of a strong and diverse UK economy, citing the country's status as the fastest-growing economy in the western world.

While there are still challenges to be addressed, the latest retail sales index suggests that Scotland's retail sector is on the path to recovery. As the industry looks to the future, it will be crucial for policymakers to create an environment that supports consumer spending and economic growth. With the right conditions in place, Scottish retailers can continue to thrive and contribute to the country's ongoing prosperity.

UK Retail Sales Disappoint in November Ahead of Christmas Season

According to the latest BRC/KPMG survey, sales at UK stores open for more than a year fell 0.4% in November compared to the same month in 2014. The decline is attributed to shoppers holding back on purchases in anticipation of deep discounts on Black Friday, which took place on November 28. However, many retailers failed to deliver the expected discounts, resulting in a relatively flat sales performance.

Total sales across all stores increased by a mere 0.7%, significantly lower than the 2.2% rise seen last year. Despite the hype surrounding Black Friday, the event failed to spark a significant surge in sales, with trading up only 25% compared to the beginning of the month. Online sales of non-food items were a bright spot, rising 11.8% year-on-year.

The survey also found that sales of furniture and electrical appliances were higher than last year. Nevertheless, the rise of "omni-channel" shopping, where consumers use a mix of online and in-store purchases, has made it challenging for retailers to predict spending patterns during the crucial Christmas shopping period. BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson warned that the conversion of higher disposable income into retail sales should not be taken for granted. As the retail sector heads into the festive season, retailers will be closely watching consumer behavior to gauge the impact of changing shopping habits on sales.

Home Office Delays Police Funding Reform Due to Statistical Error

The Home Office has announced a delay in the proposed changes to the police funding formula for 2016/17 due to a statistical error. Minister Mike Penning apologized to the Commons for the mistake, which has caused significant concern among police forces in England and Wales. The error was discovered in a new formula that assesses population size, social and economic factors, and crime rates to calculate funding for each of the 43 police forces.

The government had launched a consultation on the proposed changes, but six police and crime commissioners threatened legal action, arguing that the plans were "unjustified and deeply flawed." The Home Office has since revealed that the new formula was based on flawed calculations. As a result, the government will now seek the views of police and crime commissioners and the National Police Chiefs Council before proceeding with the changes.

Penning expressed regret over the mistake and apologized to MPs and police forces. The delay is expected to give the government time to re-evaluate the funding formula and ensure that it is fair and accurate. The exact duration of the delay has not been specified, but it is seen as a positive step towards addressing the concerns of police forces and ensuring that they receive the necessary funding to effectively serve their communities.

Tragedy Strikes as Irish Nun Killed in Ecuador Earthquake

A devastating 7.8-magnitude earthquake struck Ecuador, leaving a trail of destruction and claiming the lives of at least 480 people. Among the victims was Sister Clare Theresa Crockett, a 33-year-old Irish nun from the Long Tower area of Derry. Sister Clare was one of six people killed when a school collapsed in Playa Prieta, including five young women who were entering the religious order.

Sister Clare and another Irish nun, Sister Thérèse Ryan from County Limerick, were part of the Home of the Mother order and had been teaching guitar and singing to the postulants when the earthquake struck. It is believed that they were attempting to evacuate the building when they became trapped on a stairway.

The Kevin Bell Repatriation Trust has been working tirelessly with the authorities in Ecuador to bring Sister Clare's body back to her family. Colin Bell, founder of the trust, stated that they are making progress, but the process is being hindered by the country's turmoil. "We have been working with a repatriation company and we know that Sister Clare is now with the undertakers. It's only now a matter of getting the paperwork done and getting a flight as soon as possible," he said.

Sister Clare's family is anxiously waiting for her body to be brought home, and Mr. Bell is hopeful that this will happen within a week. Before joining the religious order, Sister Clare was a fan of karaoke and had dreams of stardom. Her tragic death has sent shockwaves through the community, and she will be deeply missed. The Kevin Bell Repatriation Trust was set up by Mr. Bell after the death of his son in 2013, and has since helped numerous families bring their loved ones home.

Australian Duo Faces Imminent Execution in Indonesia Amid Bribery Allegations

The fate of two Australian men, Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran, hangs in the balance as they face imminent execution in Indonesia for their roles in a 2005 heroin smuggling operation. The pair, who were sentenced to death in 2006, could be put to death within days, despite a last-ditch effort by their lawyers to have their cases reviewed.

In a shocking twist, the men's lawyers have alleged that the judges who presided over their trial in Bali had asked for bribes in exchange for lighter sentences. The claim, which was reported by Australian media outlets on Monday, has sparked outrage and raised questions about the integrity of the Indonesian judiciary.

According to the Sydney Morning Herald and Herald Sun newspapers, the lawyers' letter alleges that the six judges who heard the case had offered to reduce the sentences in exchange for money. The letter also claims that the judges were pressured by "certain parts" to hand down the death penalty, which breached ethical standards.

The allegations have been met with silence from Indonesian judicial officials, who have not publicly commented on the claim. However, the Australian government has continued to campaign for clemency for the two men, with Prime Minister Tony Abbott and Foreign Minister Julie Bishop urging Indonesia to spare their lives.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Mr. Abbott declined to comment directly on the allegations but said that the Australian government was still making representations to Indonesia about the planned executions. "What we understand is that there are still legal options open to these two Australians and their legal teams," he said. "Until those options are exhausted, Indonesia should not execute these two men."

Ms. Bishop also refused to comment on the letter, but said that there were "very serious allegations" and that the lawyers for Mr. Sukumaran and Mr. Chan would continue to raise these matters. She urged the Indonesians to follow all appeals processes, but said that she had to respect its legal systems.

The case has sparked widespread outrage in Australia, with a recent poll conducted by the Lowy Institute finding that 62% of Australians opposed the executions of Chan and Sukumaran. The poll of 1,211 randomly selected respondents also found that 69% thought the death penalty should not be applied to drug traffickers.

The Indonesian government has been unmoved by the opposition, with President Joko Widodo supporting capital punishment for drug crimes. The country has some of the toughest drug laws in the world and ended a four-year moratorium on executions in 2013.

Last month, Indonesia executed convicts from several countries, including Malawi, Nigeria, Vietnam, Brazil, and the Netherlands, as well as one from Indonesia. The move prompted Brazil and the Netherlands to recall their ambassadors in protest, and Australian authorities have threatened to do the same if Chan and Sukumaran are put to death.

As the clock ticks down for the two Australian men, their lawyers and supporters are holding out hope that the Indonesian government will grant them a last-minute reprieve. However, with the country's tough stance on drug crimes and the lack of comment from judicial officials, it remains to be seen whether their efforts will be successful.

Work and Pensions Committee Chairman Urges New Rules to Protect Pensions

The chairman of the Work and Pensions Committee, Frank Field, has written to Chancellor George Osborne, calling for new rules to be introduced in the Queen's Speech to protect pensions. The committee is currently conducting inquiries into pensions automatic enrolment and pensions regulation, using the collapse of High Street retailer BHS as a case study.

BHS's pension scheme has a significant deficit of £571m, highlighting the need for stronger regulations. Mr. Field expressed concern over "gaps in the regulatory framework" that have allowed "potentially unstable master trusts onto the market," putting the retirement savings of thousands of people at risk. Master trusts are defined-contribution workplace schemes overseen by a board of trustees.

The committee's inquiry into the Pension Protection Fund and pensions regulation has also raised concerns over the effectiveness of powers available to the regulator and fund trustees. The Pensions Regulator, which oversees work-based pension schemes, and the Pension Protection Fund, which pays compensation when an employer goes out of business, may not have sufficient powers to protect pension funds.

The issue has become increasingly pressing following the collapse of BHS, which has put 11,000 jobs at risk. Former BHS owner Sir Philip Green has faced criticism over his role in the company's demise and has been called upon to repay the £571m deficit to the pension fund. Mr. Field has suggested that Sir Philip's knighthood should be removed if he fails to do so. Sir Philip has agreed to appear before the committee to answer questions about the collapse, but has denied any wrongdoing. The committee's inquiry is ongoing, and Mr. Field's letter to the Chancellor highlights the need for urgent action to protect pensions and prevent similar collapses in the future.

Ballymena United midfielder Allan Jenkins has announced his decision to leave the club after eight years of service. The 35-year-old Scotsman, who made 254 appearances for the Braidmen, turned down a new one-year contract due to family and work commitments. Jenkins, who is head of youth development at Stranraer, has been commuting from his home in Scotland to play for the club since 2011.

Jenkins stated that he has chosen to prioritize his life outside of football, citing the need to spend more time with his eight-year-old daughter. He described the decision as the "hardest of his life," highlighting his love for the club and the sport. Ballymena boss David Jeffrey paid tribute to Jenkins' service, saying that he was wanted to stay at the club but ultimately understood his decision.

Jenkins' departure comes on the heels of a successful season, which saw him score Ballymena's first goal in the League Cup final win over Carrick Rangers. He also helped the team secure a Europa League place by defeating Glenavon in a play-off. The club has already begun to rebuild, releasing six players, including striker Darren Henderson, and signing several new players, including Michael Gault, Stephen McAlorum, and Emmet Friars, as well as defenders Andrew Burns and Steven McCullough. Jenkins will be remembered for his dedication and contributions to the club, and his legacy will be felt for years to come.

A long-lost train rumored to be carrying gold, gems, and guns from World War II has sparked a frenzy of treasure hunting in the south-western Polish city of Walbrzych. The train, which allegedly disappeared in 1945 as Soviet forces approached, is believed to be hidden in the area. Recently, a Polish and German duo claimed to have located the armoured train, and through their lawyers, they are seeking a 10% reward of the value of any findings.

However, Polish officials are urging the public to exercise caution and refrain from searching for the train until official procedures are in place to secure the site. According to Piotr Zuchowski, a senior official at the Polish culture ministry, the train may contain hazardous substances and is likely to be booby-trapped. Zuchowski confirmed that he is certain of the train's existence, despite decades of unsuccessful searching.

The exact location of the train and the identities of the two men who claim to have found it are being kept secret. Walbrzych's deputy mayor, Zygmunt Nowaczyk, revealed that the train is within the city's administrative boundaries but refused to disclose the exact location. Local folklore suggests that the train went missing near Ksiaz castle, just 3km from Walbrzych. As the search for the train continues, officials are working to ensure that the site is secured and any potential hazards are mitigated.

Peel Ports Medway has been granted approval by Swale Borough Council to build a factory at the Port of Sheerness on the Isle of Sheppey. The move comes after Danish wind turbine firm Vestas cancelled its plans for a manufacturing facility on the island in June, which would have created approximately 1,600 jobs. Despite the setback, Peel Ports Medway remains optimistic about attracting manufacturers to the area.

According to Gary Parkinson, managing director of Peel Ports Medway, the company has been in confidential discussions with several manufacturers and believes the Port of Sheerness is an ideal location for wind turbine production and related activities. Parkinson emphasized that the Vestas decision was not a reflection on the site's suitability, but rather a separate issue. With the green light from the council, Peel Ports Medway is poised to invest in the area's infrastructure, reinforcing its commitment to bringing new business and job opportunities to the island. The approval has been welcomed as a positive step towards revitalizing the local economy and exploring renewable energy possibilities.

An appeal has been lodged with the Planning Appeals Commission by sand companies and the Earl of Shaftesbury, who owns the bed of the lough, against an enforcement notice to stop sand extraction. The notice was issued by Environment Minister Mark H Durkan in May, requiring the companies to submit a planning application before resuming operations. Despite a deadline to comply, the appeal allows extraction to continue pending the outcome. Approximately 1.7m tonnes of sand are extracted annually, meeting a quarter of Northern Ireland's construction needs. However, environmentalists argue that the extraction is taking place without permission in a protected bird habitat. The Environment Minister has declined to comment, with his department citing the case as a "live enforcement issue." The appeal will be reviewed, and a decision will be made in due course, determining the fate of sand extraction in the area.

Two Luton men, Ibrahim Anderson, 38, and Shah Jahan Khan, 62, have been accused of supporting a banned organisation. They were arrested by Met Police counter-terror officers and bailed to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on April 21. Anderson also faces a charge of possessing terrorist information. The alleged offences occurred in August and December 2014. Both men are set to appear in court to face the charges.

A heartwarming reunion took place in Sheffield after two young siblings stumbled upon stolen items belonging to 93-year-old Doris Wilcock. Tyler, 10, and Amelia Exelby, 9, discovered the treasures under a blue tarpaulin in woodland, initially thinking they had found lost riches. However, upon taking the items home, their father contacted South Yorkshire Police, who successfully traced the owner.

Mrs. Wilcock was overjoyed to be reunited with some of her stolen belongings, describing the children as her "heroes." Although the items held little monetary value, they were sentimental to her. Unfortunately, a pendant given by her late husband was not among the recovered items. The children's selfless act was praised by PCSO Michelle Tatterton, who described the experience as "an emotional and very rewarding end to a busy shift." The reunion highlighted the importance of community kindness and the positive impact it can have on people's lives. Mrs. Wilcock's gratitude was evident as she thanked the young duo for their honesty and kindness.

Scotland's Rugby Team Faces Injury Concerns Ahead of Six Nations Tournament

As the Six Nations tournament approaches, Scotland's rugby team is facing injury concerns that may impact their performance in the early rounds. Mark Bennett, a 22-year-old centre, suffered an injury while playing for Glasgow earlier this month, and it was initially feared that he would miss the tournament's early matches. However, head coach Vern Cotter has provided a positive update on Bennett's progress, stating that he is recovering well and that a decision on his availability will be made next week.

Cotter described Bennett's chances of playing as "50-50," which highlights the uncertainty surrounding his injury. The team is already dealing with other injury concerns, including a thigh strain sustained by Alex Dunbar during Glasgow's win over Racing 92 on Saturday. Peter Horne is also struggling with a foot problem, while Richie Vernon is a long-term injury absentee. This leaves Matt Scott and Duncan Taylor as the only currently fit centres in Cotter's squad.

Cotter has acknowledged that Scotland lacks strength in depth, which could be a significant challenge for the team during the tournament. "We've got some good character and we've got some good individuals, but if we get banged up, we know what that means," he said. Despite these concerns, Cotter believes that his team can be competitive, and he is focusing on building momentum from the start of the tournament.

The team is still reeling from their 35-34 defeat by Australia in the quarter-final of the World Cup, which was marked by a controversial penalty decision. However, Cotter wants his players to move on from that loss and focus on improving their performance. "The memory of the World Cup will stay with the players for a long time, but it's part of history now," he said. "I feel for them, but I don't think I need to use it as motivation. The desire in the team is to improve, and that's the energy generated within the team."

Cotter has not been set a win ratio target for the tournament, which suggests that the focus is on performance rather than results. The team's goal is to win every game, but Cotter wants to avoid adding stress and weight on the shoulders of his players. Instead, he is emphasizing the importance of starting well and building momentum throughout the tournament. With a "no excuse" mentality, the team is determined to improve and make a strong showing in the Six Nations.

A non-denominational service will be held on November 6 at Aberdeen's Mither Kirk. The event honors infants cremated in the city, whose ashes were secretly mixed with adults' and given to wrong families. Parents were wrongly told no ashes existed. The service addresses the 2013 revelation, which echoed Edinburgh's Mortonhall crematorium scandal.

Trinity College's library has received a remarkable bequest of over 7,000 books from the late Mary, Duchess of Roxburghe. The duchess, who passed away in 2014 at the age of 99, left behind a treasure trove of rare and undiscovered works, including first editions by famous authors such as Wordsworth, Shelley, and Byron. The collection, which had been stored in part in an old blue suitcase, includes previously unknown manuscripts by notable historical figures like Napoleon Bonaparte, George Washington, Florence Nightingale, and Charles Dickens.

According to Bamber Gascoigne, the former University Challenge presenter who inherited the duchess's former home, the collection contains "treasures and rarities unknown to anyone" since the death of his aunt's father in 1945. Gascoigne expressed his delight at seeing the books in their new home, stating that it is "thrilling" that they will now be available to everyone. Trinity College's librarian, Dr. Nicolas Bell, described the find as "an extraordinary library - one of the most important private collections in Britain, which offers untold discoveries." The college is eager to make the collection accessible to scholars and the public, uncovering the secrets and stories hidden within its pages.

A rare painting from Claude Monet's famous Nympheas series is set to be auctioned on May 5, with an estimated value of $30-45m. The piece, unseen in public since 1945, will be sold alongside five other Monet works, including Le Palais Ducal and La Seine a Vetheuil. The six paintings, held in private collections, are expected to raise over $78m. The impressionist masterpieces will be on display in London until April 14, before moving to New York from May 1. This rare opportunity to view Monet's works is highly anticipated, with art enthusiasts eager to catch a glimpse of these stunning pieces.

Tragedy Strikes Taiwan Water Park as Fire Claims First Fatality

A 20-year-old woman, Lee Pei-yu, has become the first fatality of the devastating fire that swept through a water park in Taiwan on Saturday. Doctors, with the support of her family, made the difficult decision to turn off her life support ventilator on Monday. Lee suffered second-degree burns over 90% of her body and had been fighting for her life since the incident.

The fire, which broke out at around 20:30 local time, injured over 500 people, with at least 200 still in hospital in a critical condition. Among those injured is Lee's 12-year-old brother, who remains in hospital. Eight patients are reported to have life-threatening injuries. The incident occurred when colored powder, sprayed from the stage onto the audience, suddenly ignited, engulfing the crowd in a deadly inferno.

The cause of the fire is still under investigation, but officials believe that the flammable powder may have been set alight by cigarette embers, a lighter, or electrical sparks. The powder, which was used to create a party atmosphere, was sprayed into the crowd of over 1,000 people near the stage. Amateur video footage shows the moment the powder burst into flames, sending the crowd into a state of panic as they ran for their lives.

The organizers of the event have been questioned by authorities, and the use of colored powder at events has been banned while its safety is assessed. The water park itself remains closed. The seller who provided the powder has stated that the buyer was warned about the risk of fire.

Three people, including party organizer Lu Chung-chi, have been arrested and released on bail in connection with the incident. They have been ordered not to leave the island and are likely to face charges of professional neglect and public endangerment. Lu has apologized for the incident and pledged to take responsibility for it.

The incident has sent shockwaves through Taiwan, with many calling for greater safety measures to be put in place at public events. The BBC's Cindy Sui, reporting from Taipei, described the scene as "like hell," with many people suffering serious burns. The investigation into the incident is ongoing, and it is likely that more information will come to light in the coming days. For now, the people of Taiwan are left to mourn the loss of Lee Pei-yu and pray for the recovery of those still in hospital.

Reading FC manager Jaap Stam is preparing his team for a crucial play-off meeting with Fulham, while also acknowledging the challenges that lie ahead in the Championship next season. After leading the Royals to a third-place finish in his first season in charge, Stam believes the division will become even more competitive with several big-spending clubs vying for promotion.

Stam emphasized the importance of retaining key players, stating, "If you want to make steps yourself as a club, you don't want to sell your best players." He also cautioned that rapid progress can be a double-edged sword, saying, "Sometimes you can have things too quick, but if the opportunity's there to do things well, you need to enjoy it and that's what we're doing."

The Royals face Fulham in the first leg of their semi-final at Craven Cottage on Saturday, followed by the return leg at the Madejski Stadium on Tuesday. Stam's initial target of a top-10 finish has been surpassed, and the team is now just three games away from a potential return to the Premier League. The manager admitted that he is worried about losing key players, but is focused on the task at hand. With several clubs investing heavily in their squads, Stam warned that the top six will be increasingly difficult to reach for teams with limited budgets. Despite this, he remains optimistic about Reading's chances and is determined to make the most of their play-off opportunity.

A dramatic incident unfolded in western Sydney's Riverstone suburb on Tuesday morning. Police responded to reports of a man attempting to cut down a power pole. The 51-year-old allegedly threw petrol at officers, and his clothes caught fire when they used a Taser and pepper spray. After extinguishing the flames, the man barricaded himself inside his house. He surrendered an hour later and was treated for minor burns. A police officer, whose eyes were splashed with petrol, was also hospitalized. Charges are expected to be laid against the man. The situation was brought under control without major injuries.

Great Britain's men's hockey team has secured top spot in Pool A despite being held to a draw by Belgium. The British team took the lead three times through Phil Roper, Alastair Brogdon, and Alan Forsyth, but were pegged back on each occasion. Although they didn't play to their full potential, the team achieved their goal of topping the group, thanks to previous wins against Canada and world champions Australia.

Captain Dan Fox expressed disappointment with the team's performance but remains optimistic about their chances. On Thursday, they will face hosts India, who finished bottom of Pool B. Fox acknowledged that India has a skilled team and a passionate crowd, but plans to take the game to them. With a much-changed squad, Great Britain aims to reach the semi-finals, and a win against India would bring them closer to achieving this goal.

Morrissey Considered for London Mayoral Candidacy by Animal Welfare Party

The Animal Welfare Party has approached renowned singer Morrissey to represent them in the upcoming London mayoral election. A statement on his semi-official website revealed that Morrissey has been asked to stand for the party, citing his long-standing advocacy for animal rights and vegetarianism. 

Morrissey expressed his desire to "speak out against the hellish and archaic social injustice allotted to animals" and emphasized the need for immediate action to address animal welfare concerns. The party's leader, Vanessa Hudson, stated that they aim to bring attention to animal welfare issues in the mayoral contest, seeking a candidate who will champion London as a leading city for both people and animals.

To be eligible, Morrissey would need to meet certain requirements, including being registered to vote in London or having lived, worked, or owned property there for 12 months. He would also require the signatures of 10 registered electors from each London borough and a £10,000 deposit. Nominations for London mayoral candidates close at the end of March, leaving a short window for Morrissey to decide on his candidacy. If he chooses to run, his involvement could bring significant attention to animal welfare issues in the city.

Invest Northern Ireland (Invest NI) has unveiled a new strategy aimed at securing up to £1.2bn in new export orders for local companies. The plan, approved by the Department for the Economy, also promotes the commitment to reduce corporation tax to 12.5%. However, the implementation of this tax cut, initially planned for 2018, remains uncertain due to the need for a functioning executive and assembly.

Despite the challenges, Invest NI chief executive Alastair Hamilton reported that Northern Ireland continues to attract significant inward investment, with 22 new companies setting up operations in the region over the past year. The organization promoted 5,600 new jobs in the last financial year, similar to the previous year. Although only 1,300 of these jobs have been publicly announced, Invest NI attributes the delay to "purdah" rules surrounding recent elections and the EU referendum. Hamilton remains optimistic about the region's economic prospects, citing strong investment and job creation.

The British Embassy in Belgrade has partnered with Serbia Post to launch a new set of stamps honoring the bravery and selflessness of six British women who played a crucial role in Serbia during World War I. The stamps feature five Scottish women who worked as doctors, nurses, and drivers, as well as Captain Flora Sandes, the only British female to bear arms during the war. Captain Sandes, who initially went to Serbia as a nurse, enlisted in the Serbian Army and remained in Belgrade after the war, even volunteering to fight against the Nazis in 1941. She was awarded the highest Serbian military medal for her contributions. The stamps are part of a wider campaign by the British Embassy to recognize the efforts of over 600 British women who contributed to the war effort in Serbia, highlighting their roles in promoting universal suffrage, solidarity, and gender equality.

A veteran musician of the Bolshoi Theatre's orchestra has tragically died after an incident at the theatre. Viktor Sedov, 65, who played in the second violins for four decades, passed away in hospital on Wednesday from his injuries. The exact circumstances of the incident, which occurred on Tuesday, remain unclear. Sedov was beloved by his colleagues for his sense of humour and vast knowledge. The Bolshoi Theatre has been plagued by scandals, including an acid attack on ballet director Sergei Filin. The theatre's former head, Anatoly Iksanov, was recently removed from his post. New general director Vladimir Urin has been tasked with leading the theatre out of its crisis. The death of Sedov is the latest blow to the esteemed institution, considered one of the world's greatest theatres. An investigation into Sedov's death is likely to be launched, shedding more light on the incident.

UK Sees Thousands of Children Holding Firearms Certificates, Sparking Debate on Gun Control

According to recent Home Office figures, a total of 3,602 children under the age of 18 held firearms certificates in 2016/17, with 327 of them being 13 or younger. These certificates, which allow the holders to possess firearms and/or shotguns, were issued by local police forces after a series of checks, including interviews, visits, and references.

The police force with the largest number of children holding firearms certificates was Devon and Cornwall, with 206 certificates issued. This trend is reflected in the overall number of firearms certificates held in the region, with Devon and Cornwall having the highest number of certificates at 11,144, followed by Sussex and North Yorkshire.

While the number of children holding firearms certificates may seem alarming, it is worth noting that there are strict controls in place to ensure their safe use. Children under the age of 15 are required to be supervised by an adult aged at least 21 when using shotguns, and those under 18 are prohibited from purchasing or hiring firearms or ammunition.

The British Association for Shooting and Conservation has argued that teaching children to use firearms safely and responsibly can have numerous benefits, including promoting self-control and responsibility towards others. Chairman Peter Glenser stated that shooting has many aspects, from pest control to competitive sports, and that an early start in life is essential for those who wish to compete at top levels.

However, the fact that children as young as seven have been known to hold firearms certificates has raised concerns about the effectiveness of the current system. The Home Office has emphasized that there are "very strict controls" in place, but some may argue that more needs to be done to ensure that firearms are kept out of the wrong hands.

The UK is widely regarded as having some of the toughest gun control laws in the world, and the Policing and Crime Act 2017 has further strengthened firearms legislation by closing legal loopholes exploited by criminals. The number of firearms certificates revoked in 2016/17 fell by 10% compared to the previous year, with 358 firearms certificates and 1,216 shotgun certificates being revoked.

Overall, the issue of children holding firearms certificates highlights the need for ongoing debate and discussion about gun control in the UK. While the current system has its strengths, it is essential that lawmakers and regulators continue to monitor and adapt the rules to ensure that firearms are used safely and responsibly by all holders, regardless of age.

Karl Dickson, 32, has made 124 appearances for Quins, scoring 16 tries. Director of rugby Conor O'Shea praised Dickson, calling him "one of the most competitive and best people" he's met. A qualified referee, Dickson also represented England in 2012. O'Shea expects him to continue pushing himself and the team to improve.

Ulster Unionist Party Leader Vindicated by Security Report

The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has been vindicated in its decision to withdraw from the Northern Ireland Executive, according to party leader Mike Nesbitt. This comes after a security report revealed that the IRA's ruling army council still exists and has influence over Sinn Féin. The report's findings have sparked widespread criticism of Sinn Féin, with many questioning the party's denials of ongoing IRA activity.

The UUP withdrew from government last month amidst allegations that IRA members were involved in the murder of Kevin McGuigan Sr, a former IRA member. The party's decision to pull out of the executive was seen as a bold move, but one that has now been justified by the security report. "I took a principled stand, I took an unambiguous stand that everybody understands," said Mr. Nesbitt.

The report's findings have also been welcomed by former UUP leader Sir Reg Empey, who spoke at the party's annual conference on Saturday. Sir Reg criticized First Minister Peter Robinson for returning to "business as usual" despite the report's damning findings. "How awful," he said, "that [Mr. Robinson] goes back to business as usual, sending the clear signal to Sinn Féin that they can get away with it again."

Sir Reg also attacked Sinn Féin's denials of ongoing IRA activity, saying that they were "sapping credibility out of politics" and must be reversed if effective devolution is to be achieved at Stormont. He criticized the current administration, saying that it was "the worst so far" and was "failing on nearly all fronts."

The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) had also withdrawn its ministers from the executive last month, but returned to government after the security report's release. The report's findings have raised questions about the future of the power-sharing government at Stormont, with many calling for greater transparency and accountability from Sinn Féin.

Mr. Nesbitt will address the UUP's annual conference later today, where he is expected to reiterate his party's commitment to principled politics and its determination to hold Sinn Féin to account. The party's decision to withdraw from government has been seen as a significant moment in Northern Irish politics, and one that has sparked a wider debate about the future of the power-sharing executive. As Mr. Nesbitt said, "I set out to do the right thing" by removing the UUP from the executive, and the report has shown that his decision was justified.

Maharashtra Farmers Suspend Protests After Government Agrees to Loan Waiver

In a significant development, farmers in the western state of Maharashtra have temporarily called off their protests after the state government agreed to a loan waiver for all sections of farmers. The decision comes after a week-long agitation, which began on June 1, demanding better prices for their produce and relief from debts. Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced on Sunday that a committee would be formed to decide on the specific terms of the loan waiver.

The farmers, however, have warned that they will restart their protests if a satisfactory decision is not taken by July 25. "We have decided to temporarily call off our agitation, but if no concrete decision is taken, we will restart our stir," said farmer leader Raju Shetti. The loan waiver is expected to put pressure on the state's fiscal health, according to experts.

Meanwhile, a similar standoff continues in the central state of Madhya Pradesh, where five farmers died in police shooting last week. The state government has promised to consider a complete reversal of loans, but farmers are demanding a more comprehensive change in agricultural policy to prevent them from becoming indebted. The issue of loan waivers has also been raised by farmers in other states, with Uttar Pradesh and Telangana already announcing similar measures. The situation remains tense, with farmers across the country seeking better support and relief from their debts.

Emergency services launched a major search operation in Dumfries after a man fell into the River Nith on Sunday evening. The incident occurred near the rowing club in the Greensands area at around 21:00, prompting a large-scale response from multiple agencies. Police Scotland, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, and the Maritime and Coastguard Agency were among those involved in the search.

The man has been identified as 41-year-old Brian Cowie from Queensberry Street in Dumfries. He is described as being around 6ft tall and was last seen wearing a dark jacket, grey hooded top, light-colored jeans, and grey/black shoes. Extensive searches were carried out along the River Nith, downstream to the Solway Estuary, on Sunday night and resumed at first light on Monday morning.

A helicopter from the Maritime and Coastguard Agency at Prestwick was also deployed to assist in the operation. Inspector Rory Caldow urged anyone with information to come forward, as searches continue with the help of volunteers from the Moffat Mountain Rescue Team. The public's assistance is crucial in locating Brian Cowie, and police are appealing for anyone who may have witnessed the incident to contact them immediately.

England's rugby hopes have been dealt a blow with the news that promising young flanker Sam Underhill will undergo surgery for a shoulder injury. The 20-year-old Ospreys player suffered a high-grade AC joint injury in training and is expected to be sidelined for around four months. This puts his participation in the autumn internationals in jeopardy, despite England coach Eddie Jones previously tipping him for a role.

Underhill had broken into Ospreys' first team last season, making 16 appearances and impressing with his performances. Born in the US, he has pledged his allegiance to England, although he could also qualify for Wales in the future under residency rules. Underhill will have surgery later this week, followed by a rehabilitation program. Ospreys' medical performance manager Chris Towers confirmed the injury and prognosis, saying Underhill's rehabilitation will commence after surgery. This injury is a significant setback for the young player's promising career.

The infamous "Essex Boys" murder case has once again resurfaced, with the family of one of the convicted men, Jack Whomes, continuing to fight for his freedom. On December 6, 1995, three drug dealers, Craig Rolfe, Tony Tucker, and Pat Tate, were shot dead in a Range Rover in Rettendon, Essex. The brutal ambush was reportedly over an unsellable consignment of cannabis. Whomes and his co-defendant, Michael Steele, were jailed for life in 1998 for their murders, following a high-profile trial at the Old Bailey.

Despite their convictions, both Whomes and Steele have always maintained their innocence. Whomes' mother, Pam, 77, remains resolute in her belief that her son is innocent and is now pinning her hopes on fresh evidence to overturn his conviction. "He wouldn't put us through this if he had done it," she said. "He would have been out 10 years ago if he admitted it, but he won't confess to something he didn't do." Mrs. Whomes' determination is unwavering, and she hopes to see her son walk out of prison before she passes away.

However, not everyone shares Mrs. Whomes' doubts about the conviction. Former Detective Superintendent David Bright, who played a key role in the original investigation, is adamant that justice was served. "I have no doubts whatsoever about the conviction," he said. "It was a long and very thorough trial, and the decision was unanimous by the jury. They were very satisfied with the evidence." Bright also pointed out that the defendants have exhausted almost every avenue for appeal, only to have their claims rejected.

The case against Whomes and Steele was built largely on the testimony of a police informant, which was corroborated by mobile phone records. However, these records have since been called into question, casting a shadow of doubt over the conviction. Despite this, two appeals have already been turned down, and Whomes' third bid for freedom was recently rejected before reaching the appeal stage. His legal team is now working to overturn this decision, although the nature of the fresh evidence they claim to have is being kept under wraps.

Meanwhile, Michael Steele is also pursuing a separate attempt to overturn his conviction. Whomes, a father of two, is currently detained in HMP Whitemoor in Cambridgeshire, where he has been teaching and has gained an impressive 27 City and Guilds qualifications. His mother remains hopeful that one day he will be exonerated and released from prison. "I think we've got a hell of a struggle the way the legal system is, but I really believe that he will eventually walk out," she said. The "Essex Boys" case continues to be a source of fascination and debate, with the 2000 film starring Sean Bean cementing its place in popular culture. As the fight for justice continues, one thing is certain – the case will remain a topic of discussion for years to come.

Breakthrough in Ultrasound Technology: Dundee University Researchers Create "Sonic Screwdriver"

In a groundbreaking achievement, researchers at Dundee University have successfully created a machine that utilizes ultrasound to lift and rotate a rubber disc floating in a cylinder of water. This innovative technology has the potential to revolutionize the field of surgery, enabling more precise and non-invasive treatments. The study, led by Dr. Mike MacDonald of the Institute for Medical Science and Technology (IMSAT), has demonstrated the ability to steer ultrasound waves to specific locations, allowing for more effective treatments.

The machine, dubbed the "sonic screwdriver," uses energy from an ultrasound array to form a beam that can both push and rotate objects. By shaping the beam into a helix or vortex, the researchers were able to cause the rubber disc to rotate, a feat that was previously thought to be impossible with ultrasound waves. This breakthrough has significant implications for the medical field, where ultrasound is already used to treat a range of conditions without requiring invasive surgery.

The ability to precisely control ultrasound waves could enable surgeons to target specific areas of the body, making treatments more effective and reducing the risk of complications. Additionally, the technology could be used to guide drug capsules through the body, activating them at precise locations, such as inside tumors. The possibilities for this technology are vast, and the researchers are eager to explore its potential applications.

The "sonic screwdriver" is part of the EU-funded nanoporation project, which aims to develop new techniques for targeted drug delivery and cellular surgery. The research is also connected to the UK-wide Sonotweezers project, which seeks to bring dexterity and flexibility to ultrasonic manipulation, with applications in regenerative medicine, tissue engineering, and physics.

Dr. MacDonald noted that the experiment not only confirms a fundamental physics theory but also demonstrates a new level of control over ultrasound beams. "Like Doctor Who's own device, our sonic screwdriver is capable of much more than just spinning things around," he said. The results of the study will be published in the American Physical Society's journal Physical Review Letters, and the researchers are excited to continue exploring the potential of this innovative technology. With its potential to revolutionize the field of surgery and beyond, the "sonic screwdriver" is an exciting development that could have a significant impact on the medical field and beyond.

Heavyweight Champion Wladimir Klitschko has been cleared to fight after a calf injury forced him to withdraw from his title defense against Tyson Fury. The 39-year-old Ukrainian was set to face Fury on October 24, but the bout was postponed due to the injury. However, it has now been revealed that Klitschko has been declared fit to fight on November 28. The news was announced by Fury himself on Twitter, and the two fighters are now awaiting confirmation from broadcaster Sky Sports to proceed with the new date.

Fury, 27, has been vocal about his opponent, previously calling him "boring." The Bolton fighter has been unbeaten in 24 fights and successfully defended his European title in March. Klitschko, who has been unbeaten for 11 years, will be putting his WBA, IBF, and WBO titles on the line in what will be his record-breaking 28th heavyweight title bout. The highly anticipated fight is expected to be a thrilling matchup between two of the sport's top heavyweights.

A double-decker bus destined for Ivory Coast was completely destroyed by a fire on the A11 near Cambridge yesterday. The bus, which was purchased for approximately £6,000, had just been collected from a garage in Croydon and was being driven to Norfolk to be fitted out before its journey to Africa. 

Fortunately, the three people on board, including the owner Eunice Jokrasset, escaped without injury. The driver managed to steer the bus into a layby on the busy dual carriageway, near Worsted Lodge, after the fire broke out at around 13:30 BST. 

Ms Jokrasset, who runs the Crown Inn in Smallburgh, north Norfolk, had been fundraising for the bus since February, collecting books and school equipment to fill the vehicle. The community had planned to hold an opening ceremony later this month before the bus was shipped to Ivory Coast in September. 

The fire service reported that the blaze started in the engine compartment. Ms Jokrasset expressed her devastation, saying "I cannot explain how I'm feeling. It's dreadful." The incident is a significant setback for the community's charitable efforts, and it remains to be seen how they will recover from the loss of the bus.

Wanda Campbell, 43, has lost her appeal against a jail sentence for embezzling £110,000. Campbell, from Auchenmalg, was found guilty at Dumfries Sheriff Court of taking money from James Haugh between 2012 and 2013. She was ordered to pay £110,000 in compensation. The High Court in Edinburgh heard her appeal, which was denied by Lord Brodie and Lord Drummond Young. Campbell had been entrusted with the money for business cash flow, but instead used it for personal expenses, leading to the business's liquidation in 2016. Her conviction and sentence remain in place.

A Heartwarming Reunion: Shamsher Sherin Finds Safety in the UK

In a touching turn of events, 13-year-old Shamsher Sherin, a young refugee from Afghanistan, has been reunited with his father in Birmingham, UK. The boy's story gained international attention after he was interviewed by a pop star at a Calais refugee camp, where he had been living for two months. Shamsher's tale of resilience and determination moved the singer to apologize "on behalf of my country for what we've put you through."

Shamsher's journey to the UK was not an easy one. He fled his home in Afghanistan and traveled to the Calais refugee camp, where he attempted to cross the border into the UK on several occasions. During one failed attempt, he was kicked and slapped by police. However, he persevered, driven by the hope of reuniting with his father, Hazrat Gul Sherin, who has lived in Birmingham since fleeing Afghanistan in 2005.

Thanks to the efforts of the Home Office, Shamsher was among dozens of child migrants brought to the UK on Wednesday to join their families. His father, who had been anxiously waiting for news of his son's safe arrival, was overjoyed to be reunited with Shamsher. According to translator Mohammad Ishaq, Mr. Sherin was "very happy" and "emotional" when he received the news, saying "my dream is completed now."

The pop star who interviewed Shamsher took to Twitter to express her relief and happiness at the news of his safe arrival, saying "So happy to see that Sham Sher made it to the UK safely and won't be risking his life jumping on to moving vehicles." Shamsher is now looking forward to starting a new life in England, where he hopes to attend school and build a brighter future. His story serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of compassion and support for refugees and migrants seeking a safer and more stable life.

Bordeaux's Jeremy Menez underwent surgery after a collision with Lorient's Didier Ndong. The 29-year-old was accidentally hit on the head, injuring his ear. Menez had joined Bordeaux just three days prior. He was operated on under local anesthesia and the team wishes him a speedy recovery. Ndong apologized, calling the incident "completely involuntary" with unfortunate consequences. Both teams hope to see Menez back in Ligue 1 action soon.

A fire broke out at the iconic Trellick Tower in Kensal Town, prompting the evacuation of up to 200 people. The blaze, which is believed to have been caused by a discarded cigarette, engulfed a flat in the Grade II listed building just before 9:30pm. Eight fire crews responded to the scene, bringing the fire under control. Fortunately, no injuries were reported. Trellick Tower, designed by Ernő Goldfinger in the brutalist style, has been featured in numerous films and TV shows, and was the inspiration for JG Ballard's novel "High Rise". The incident highlights the importance of fire safety and responsible disposal of smoking materials.

Long-time Labour Party member John Ferrett has announced his resignation from the party after 27 years, citing the party's shift under Jeremy Corbyn's leadership as the reason. Ferrett, who stood in general elections in 2010 and 2015, stated that the party has become a "protest movement that has no interest in winning power". This decision comes after Corbyn's re-election as Labour leader, where he secured 61.8% of the vote, defeating challenger Owen Smith.

Ferrett expressed his disappointment with the party's direction, saying it has become "almost impossible to win" in places like Portsmouth, where Labour traditionally had a strong base. He called on members of the Parliamentary Labour Party to create a new political party as a "reasoned social democratic alternative" to the Conservative government. Ferrett will continue to serve as an independent councillor in the Paulsgrove Ward and plans to consult with residents.

The Portsmouth Labour Party has expressed disappointment at Ferrett's resignation, with co-chair Sion Reynolds calling on him to resign his council seat to allow residents to "have their say" in a by-election. Meanwhile, Shadow Foreign Secretary Emily Thornberry has urged party unity, stating that opponents of Corbyn need to work for the "greater good" by providing a strong opposition. Ferrett's resignation highlights the ongoing divisions within the Labour Party, with some members calling for a new direction and others urging unity under Corbyn's leadership.

New rules set to take effect in 2016 will revolutionize the way La Liga sells its broadcasting rights. In a bid to modernize and bring the league in line with the Premier League, the rights to show La Liga will be pooled and sold collectively. This change is expected to increase revenue for broadcasters, with the bigger clubs still benefiting, albeit to a lesser extent.

The new ruling will regulate the transmission rights for the Spanish first and second divisions, as well as the Copa del Rey and Super Cup competitions. Under the new system, 90% of the total revenue will be distributed among La Liga clubs, with 50% shared equally and the remaining 50% divided based on performance and size. The remaining 10% will go to second division clubs, with 70% of that amount divided equally.

According to Sport Ministry spokesman Miguel Cardenal, this change is necessary for Spain to "adapt to modern times." He cited the significant revenue disparity between the Premier League and La Liga, noting that the last-placed Premier League team earned more than current Spanish champions Atletico Madrid. The move aims to bridge this gap, with the Premier League recently selling its television rights for a record £5.136bn.

It's been 20 years since the hit Channel 4 comedy "Father Ted" first aired, and its legacy continues to captivate audiences across the UK and Ireland. The show, which follows the misadventures of three priests and their housekeeper on remote Craggy Island, has become a cult classic with its unique brand of humor. Pauline McLynn, who played the lovable and eccentric housekeeper Mrs. Doyle, recalls the show's humble beginnings. "We didn't think anybody would watch it, or notice it was on," she said in an interview with BBC NI's Good Morning Ulster. "Although we found it funny, that doesn't necessarily mean everybody else would."

Despite initial doubts, "Father Ted" went on to become a massive success, attracting a wide range of fans with its simple yet hilarious storylines. McLynn attributes the show's enduring appeal to its innocence and absurdity. "It's about these four people who are stuck with one another, and every week we start at the same place, which is hell," she explained. "It's so simple and so stupid that everybody can enjoy it. By stupid, I mean desperately funny." The show's catchphrases, including Mrs. Doyle's iconic "You will, you will, you will" as she presses tea upon newcomers, have become ingrained in popular culture.

McLynn has gone on to appear in other notable roles, including her current stint as Yvonne, Charlie Cotton's mother, in the BBC's "Eastenders." However, she confessed that it took her years to be able to offer someone tea on screen without being reminded of her "Father Ted" days. The show's impact extends beyond its original run, with new generations of fans discovering its humor. McLynn noted that her friend's children, aged five and seven, are "totally devoted" to the show, demonstrating its timeless appeal.

The anniversary of "Father Ted" is also a bittersweet reminder of the passing of Dermot Morgan, who played the lovable rogue Fr. Ted. Morgan died suddenly in 1998 at the age of 45, leaving behind a legacy that continues to inspire and entertain. McLynn fondly remembered her co-star, saying, "The best thing would be if he was here. He'd be dining out on Father Ted. But he will never grow old, and he will always be gorgeous." As "Father Ted" celebrates its 20th anniversary, its influence on British comedy and its enduring popularity are a testament to the show's genius and the talents of its cast.

Renowned Artist David Hockney Intervenes to Protect Beloved Country Lane

David Hockney, one of the most celebrated artists of our time, has taken it upon himself to ensure that a roadwork project in East Yorkshire does not cause lasting damage to a picturesque country lane that has inspired many of his works. Woldgate, a tranquil and unspoiled lane, has been the subject of Hockney's paintings, drawings, photographs, and films for several years, and the artist is determined to preserve its natural beauty.

Hockney has been working closely with roadwork managers, inviting them to his studio to showcase his latest paintings of Woldgate and stressing the importance of minimizing the impact of the construction project on the surrounding environment. The project involves laying a new gas pipe for the town, which requires digging up the road. However, Hockney has provided the workers with a list of specific spots to avoid damaging, including a tree stump and a bluebell wood.

According to John O'Grady, communications manager for Northern Gas Networks, Hockney's concerns were taken seriously, and the company has made a concerted effort to avoid disrupting the environment. "His concern was that, because we are putting in this massive new gas pipeline, the environment could have been affected detrimentally," O'Grady said.
