"We're happy to work with Mr. Hockney and the other local people to ensure that the construction project is carried out with minimal disruption to the natural beauty of the area."

Hockney's love affair with Woldgate is evident in the numerous works he has created inspired by the lane. A photographic piece, comprising three 27-foot images of the Bridlington end of the road, taken at different times of the year, has recently gone on display at Salts Mill in Saltaire, West Yorkshire. The exhibition also features pictures created by Hockney on his iPad and iPhone, as well as portraits of his family, friends, and acquaintances drawn on a computer.

Next year, the Royal Academy in London will host a major exhibition of Hockney's works, including his Woldgate series. The show will feature a film made by Hockney using 18 cameras, which will be displayed on multiple screens. The artist has described Woldgate as "a lovely little bit of England that is not spoiled," and his efforts to protect it demonstrate his deep appreciation for the natural world and his commitment to preserving its beauty for future generations.

As O'Grady noted, Hockney's involvement in the roadwork project has been constructive, and the company is grateful for his input. "He has been down several times and kept a very close eye on what we've been doing," O'Grady said. "We're happy to work with Mr. Hockney and the other local people to ensure that the construction project is carried out with minimal disruption to the natural beauty of the area." Hockney's dedication to protecting Woldgate is a testament to the power of art to inspire and motivate people to take action in preserving the world around us.

Concerns over the availability of Mothers Pride Scottish Plain bread were sparked after a post on Facebook suggested that only one factory was now producing it due to falling sales. The post, which was shared over 13,000 times, prompted an outpouring of support from loyal consumers. However, Hovis, the firm behind the Mothers Pride brand, has reassured fans that it has no plans to stop producing the bread.

A spokeswoman for Hovis expressed appreciation for the strong response from Scottish consumers, acknowledging the brand's loyal following. Mothers Pride has been a staple in Scotland for 80 years, with its unique batch baking process setting it apart from other breads. The bread is made in a large baking tray, resulting in a crust only on the top and bottom, unlike pan loaves which are baked in individual trays.

The brand's rich history and cultural significance were even immortalized in the classic Scots folk song "Jeely Piece" in the 1960s. Despite a decline in sales, Mothers Pride remains a beloved favorite, and its production will continue at the only batch plant left in the UK, located in Glasgow. Fans of the bread can rest assured that it will remain available, thanks to the dedication of its loyal consumer base.

A talented border collie from Glemsford, Suffolk, has made headlines for retrieving over 20 balls from the open space behind her home. Maggie, the skilled canine, belongs to Meg Brace and has been featured in the East Anglian Daily Times for her impressive ability. The mystery of the missing balls was solved after a public appeal, revealing they had been taken from the Epic Youth Club's kickabouts at the nearby village hall.

Youth club manager Stuart Ayling praised Maggie, calling her "one remarkable pet." Maggie's owner, Meg Brace, noted that while her pet can be challenging at times, her talent for retrieving balls is undeniable. Interestingly, Ms Brace's other border collie, Gizmo, has a unique talent of its own - picking up litter from the playing field and bringing it to her to dispose of properly. The incident has highlighted the issue of missing footballs, which Mr Ayling attributed to older teenagers taking them without permission.

Armed police are at Meteor Street in Adamsdown, with a cordon in place. A man in his late teens to early 20s was stabbed, suffering serious but non-life-threatening injuries. He was taken to the University Hospital of Wales, as officers actively search for the offender.

American Couple Sentenced for Murder in Bali

A US couple has been sentenced for the brutal murder of the woman's mother, whose body was found stuffed inside a suitcase in Bali last August. Tommy Schaefer, 21, was sentenced to 18 years in prison for the killing of Sheila von Wiese-Mack, 62, a wealthy American academic. His partner, 19-year-old Heather Mack, received a 10-year sentence for her role in the crime.

The presiding judge described the killing as "sadistic" and stated that Schaefer's actions had disturbed the public. However, the judge took into account Schaefer's remorse and politeness during the trial, which prevented him from receiving a harsher sentence. Mack's sentence was also influenced by the fact that she had recently given birth to a baby.

The couple's troubles began when von Wiese-Mack discovered that her daughter was pregnant, leading to a heated argument at a five-star resort. Schaefer claimed he was defending himself after von Wiese-Mack became angry, and hit her with a fruit bowl. The couple then hid her body in a suitcase and left it in a taxi, which was later discovered by the driver. The police found the couple at another hotel in Bali, leading to their arrest and subsequent conviction.

Lance Bombardier Ben Parkinson Honoured at Buckingham Palace

Lance Bombardier Ben Parkinson, a paratrooper who suffered severe injuries in a bomb attack in Afghanistan in 2006, has received a special honour from the Prince of Wales at Buckingham Palace. The ceremony, which took place recently, saw Parkinson recognised for his bravery and determination in the face of adversity.

Parkinson, who carried the Olympic flame through his hometown last year on his prosthetic legs, was praised by Prince Charles as an "inspiration". The paratrooper, who broke his pelvis, back, and arm, and lost both legs in the attack, was visibly moved by the Prince's words. "I was surprised at how much Prince Charles knew about me," he said. "He said I was an inspiration. It made me feel so proud."

In addition to carrying the Olympic flame, Parkinson has also taken part in a charity trek in Norway, where he and a group of injured veterans travelled 65 miles across the Hardangervidda mountain in challenging conditions. The expedition, organised by the charity Pilgrim Bandits, marked the 70th anniversary of a World War II mission. Parkinson's courage and resilience have made him a role model for many, and his honour at Buckingham Palace is a testament to his inspiring story.

US Deploys Additional Armored Brigade to Europe in Response to Russian Aggression

The United States has announced plans to deploy an additional armored brigade to Europe, bringing the total number of brigades to three. This significant reinforcement is seen as a response to increasing tensions with Russia, particularly in the wake of its annexation of Crimea in 2014. The move is the most substantial US reinforcement of NATO since the conflict in Ukraine began.

According to General Philip Breedlove, the senior US commander in Europe, the additional presence demonstrates a "strong and balanced approach" to reassuring NATO allies and partners in the face of Russian aggression. Each brigade, comprising approximately 4,200 soldiers, will rotate through the region for nine months, bringing with them modernized equipment and military vehicles.

The deployment is part of a broader effort to bolster European defense, with the Pentagon announcing plans to quadruple its budget for European defense in 2017. The increased military presence will enable the US to conduct more frequent and extensive military exercises in the region, enhancing its ability to respond to potential threats.

The move has been welcomed by NATO allies, who have expressed concerns about Russian intentions in Eastern Europe. British Foreign Secretary Philip Hammond noted that the situation in Ukraine has "gone backwards" in recent months, with increased ceasefire violations. Russia, however, has accused NATO of using the situation in Ukraine as a pretext to move closer to its borders.

The deployment has also sparked speculation about the US military's plans for the post-Obama era, particularly given the views of Republican presidential frontrunner Donald Trump, who has criticized the economic cost of US foreign policy. With 62,000 US service personnel already permanently based in Europe, the additional brigade will further strengthen the US military presence on the continent. The US has 21 bases across Europe, with 25,000 army soldiers currently stationed there. The new deployment will add 4,200 more soldiers to this number, demonstrating the US commitment to European security and defense.

Northern Ireland's unemployment rate has dropped to 5.2%, its lowest level since 2008. Official figures show 300 people came off the jobless register in March, bringing the total to 31,500. Although this decrease is a positive sign, the region still lags behind the UK average of 4.7%. The employment rate also trails the rest of the UK, with 69% of the workforce in employment compared to 75% nationwide. Economist Dr Esmond Birnie notes that the data reveals "a lost decade" with little improvement in employment figures over the past 10 years. The labour market has also seen a shift towards more self-employed and part-time workers. Despite the progress, there is still work to be done to bridge the employment gap with the rest of the UK.

Conservative Party Strategist Lynton Crosby has assured Tory MPs that Labour's lead in the opinion polls is fragile and vulnerable to attack. At a private meeting of the 1922 committee on Tuesday, Crosby presented private polling data indicating that Labour is weak on key issues such as welfare, deficit reduction, and Europe. The meeting, attended by Prime Minister David Cameron and Chancellor George Osborne, aimed to sharpen the party's campaigning strategy ahead of the 2015 general election.

Crosby, who successfully ran the 2005 Tory election campaign and Boris Johnson's London mayoral campaign, advised MPs to target Labour leader Ed Miliband and shadow chancellor Ed Balls, who are perceived as weak by some floating voters. He argued that the pair should be held accountable for the country's economic problems. The Conservatives believe Labour has made a significant mistake by suggesting pensioners should lose their winter fuel allowance, and plan to capitalize on this in their upcoming campaigns. With Crosby's guidance, the Tories are gearing up to launch a strong attack on Labour's policies, which they claim will lead to more spending, borrowing, and debt.

President Obama has formally requested that Congress raise the nation's debt ceiling to $16.4 trillion, citing the need for further borrowing to meet existing spending commitments. The proposal, which must be voted on within 15 days, aims to avoid a repeat of last year's near-default crisis. In a letter, Mr. Obama emphasized the necessity of increasing the debt limit to ensure the government can pay its bills.

The move is expected to pass, but it will likely provide Republicans with ammunition to criticize the president's handling of deficit reduction. The issue has been a point of contention between the administration and Congress, with an uneasy truce reached last year over long-term deficit reduction plans. To avoid a default, the administration has had to tap into the Exchange Stabilization Fund, and may need to take additional measures, such as suspending pension fund reinvestments, until the debt limit increase is secured.

Wales ended their friendly tournament with a 1-1 draw against Hungary. Henrietta Csiszar scored early for Hungary, but 17-year-old substitute Charlie Estcourt leveled the score on 75 minutes. The result marked Wales' second draw and second defeat in the tournament, with a total of four goals scored. Hungary, ranked 42nd in Fifa's rankings, finished third in Group A after beating the Republic of Ireland 1-0 earlier. Wales finished third in Group B following a 1-0 loss to the Czech Republic. The tournament's final match will feature Group winners Austria and Poland in Larnaca.

A trial is underway at Nottingham Crown Court for Sukhraj Singh Atwal, a 29-year-old man accused of brutally murdering 74-year-old Satnam Singh in Derby. The prosecution alleges that Atwal repeatedly stamped and jumped on Mr. Singh, causing severe injuries that ultimately led to his death. The incident occurred on July 23, 2015, as Mr. Singh was walking to a temple where he volunteered in the early hours of the morning.

According to evidence presented in court, Mr. Singh suffered 41 fractures to his ribs, lacerations to his heart, and blunt force injuries to his head and face. The prosecution claims that Atwal's car was seen on local CCTV footage near the scene of the crime, entering the area immediately before the attack and leaving four minutes later. Although the beating itself was not caught on camera, footage from a nearby garage forecourt appears to show Atwal inspecting his light-colored trousers.

The prosecution also alleges that Atwal returned to the scene several times, wearing different trousers, to observe the aftermath of the attack. Atwal was initially arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving, but was later arrested on suspicion of murder in April 2016 after forensic tests determined that Mr. Singh had not been hit by a car. Examination of Atwal's phone revealed that he had traveled to a remote location near Carsington Water, where the prosecution believes he disposed of his trousers. The trial is ongoing, with Atwal denying the murder charge. The court will continue to hear evidence in the coming days to determine Atwal's fate.

Team Sky principal Dave Brailsford has expressed his pride and patriotism ahead of the Tour de France, despite facing intense scrutiny over the team's use of banned substances. Brailsford, who has been at the helm of the team since its inception, has been under fire for the team's handling of Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs) and the contents of a medical package sent to Sir Bradley Wiggins in 2011.

However, Brailsford remains defiant, stating that he has always conducted himself and the team with the utmost integrity. "I've been involved in this sport a long time, and I've tried to do it absolutely in the way that I've always thought it should be done," he said. "I wouldn't want to be doing anything else. I'm proud of cycling in Britain, I'm proud of everything that's been achieved, I'm proud of these guys, proud of Team Sky. I love it, I'm going nowhere."

Brailsford's comments come as Team Sky prepares to defend its title at the Tour de France, which begins on Saturday. The team is seeking its fifth win in six years, with Chris Froome aiming for his fourth Tour de France title. Froome, who has been the subject of doping allegations in the past, expressed his full support for Brailsford and the team. "I don't have any trust issues, I can't make it any more plain," he said.

Froome, who is close to signing a new contract with Team Sky that would extend his stay until 2021, acknowledged that the team's reputation has been tarnished by the controversy surrounding TUEs and the medical package sent to Wiggins. However, he believes that the team has done nothing wrong and that the criticism is unfair. "Certainly I've learned to grow a thicker skin over the years and I understand where it's coming from given cycling's history," he said.

Despite the challenges facing the team, Brailsford remains committed to his "zero tolerance" policy on doping. He has faced intense questioning from the media and lawmakers, including a grilling from the Culture, Media and Sport Committee in December. However, he remains steadfast in his denial of any wrongdoing and is confident that the team will emerge from the controversy with its reputation intact. As the Tour de France gets underway, Team Sky will be looking to put the controversy behind them and focus on winning another title. With Froome leading the charge, they will be a force to be reckoned with, and Brailsford will be hoping that his team can prove their doubters wrong once again.

UK Furniture Market Sees Mixed Results as Consumers Play Catch-Up

The UK furniture market has seen a mixed bag of results, with upmarket sofa retailer DFS experiencing a significant boost in sales, while home furnishings retailer Dunelm saw a decline in sales. According to retail analyst Richard Hyman, the market is cyclical, and consumers are playing catch-up after delaying big-ticket purchases during the financial crisis.

DFS, which sponsored Team GB at the Rio Olympics, reported a 7.1% increase in annual sales to £756m, driven by a surge in demand for its high-end sofas, including brands like French Connection. Online sales also saw a significant increase, rising 15.6% over the year. The company's chairman, Richard Baker, expressed confidence in the company's ability to weather the uncertainty surrounding Brexit, citing its 47-year history of navigating economic turbulence.

In contrast, Dunelm, known for its duvets and curtains, saw a 3.8% decline in same-store sales in the first quarter, attributed to the unusually warm weather that kept consumers outdoors and away from its stores. However, online sales continued to grow, with home delivery sales up 17.9%. The company is looking forward to the second quarter, which includes the Christmas and New Year period, when it plans to invest in extra seasonal space.

The mixed results reflect the ongoing recovery of the furniture market, which has not yet returned to its pre-crisis peak in 2007. According to DFS, the market remains 20% smaller in value than its peak, but has recovered from the low point reached in 2011. Retail analyst Patrick O'Brien warned that 2017 may be a tough year for retailers due to the sharp fall in the value of the pound following the UK's vote to leave the EU, which may force companies to pass on higher costs to consumers.

Despite the challenges, DFS remains optimistic about its prospects, with Baker stating that the company has "weathered many forms of political and economic turbulence" and is well-positioned to navigate the uncertainty surrounding Brexit. As consumers continue to play catch-up on big-ticket purchases, it remains to be seen how the furniture market will fare in the coming year. One thing is certain, however: the market will be closely watched as retailers navigate the challenges and opportunities presented by the UK's decision to leave the EU.

A man in his 40s, who was acquitted of rape charges last year, is now facing a new challenge as North Yorkshire Police seeks to impose a permanent sexual risk order on him. The order, which was initially imposed in December and extended in January, requires the man to disclose any planned sexual activity to the police at least 24 hours in advance, as well as provide details of his partners, including their name, address, and date of birth.

The man, who claims the complainant in his rape trial had consented to sex, has been charged with breaching the terms of the order after refusing to give police the PIN to his phone. He has accused North Yorkshire Police of "sour grapes" in applying for the order, which he believes has devastated his personal life and contravened his human rights.

"I had more freedom in prison," the man said, speaking after an adjourned hearing at York Magistrates' Court on Wednesday. "I'm in a state of shock, I cannot believe this is how the justice system works." He claimed that the order has made it impossible for him to form relationships, saying "Can you imagine, 24 hours before sex? Come on." He gave the example of trying to ask a woman out on a date, only to have to inform her that the police would need to be notified beforehand.

The man's trial heard that he had an interest in sado-masochistic sex, which he claims was misunderstood by a doctor he had spoken to. He believes that this misunderstanding was seized upon by police and used as evidence against him. He credits the popularity of the book "50 Shades of Grey" with helping to normalize his interests and aid his defense.

Sexual risk orders were introduced in England and Wales last year and can be applied to anyone who the police believe poses a risk of sexual harm, regardless of whether they have been convicted of a crime. The orders are civil and can be imposed by magistrates at the request of police. In this case, the police believe that the man poses a risk of sexual harm, despite his acquittal on rape charges.

The case is due back in court on July 14, ahead of a hearing on August 19, which will decide whether to grant the police's application to make the interim order permanent. If the order is made permanent, the man could face up to five years in prison if he fails to comply with its terms. The man's lawyers will argue that the order is an infringement of his human rights and that it is not proportionate to the risk he poses.

North Yorkshire Police has declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing legal proceedings. However, the man's case has raised questions about the use of sexual risk orders and the balance between public safety and individual freedom. As the case continues to make its way through the courts, it is likely to spark further debate about the role of these orders in preventing sexual harm.

Professor John Beetlestone, founder of the science discovery centre Techniquest in Cardiff, has passed away at the age of 84. The centre announced his death on Friday, following a short illness. Beetlestone dedicated his life to making science and technology accessible and enjoyable for all. Techniquest's chief executive, Lesley Kirkpatrick, praised his contribution to scientific education, saying it will "benefit children across Wales for generations to come." Beetlestone founded Techniquest in 1985 in a gas showroom opposite Cardiff Castle. The centre has since moved to Cardiff Bay and expanded to include a location at Glyndwr University's campus in Wrexham. His legacy will continue to educate and inspire future generations of scientists. Beetlestone's impact on scientific education in Wales will be remembered and celebrated for years to come.

Petra Kvitova's recovery from a stabbing incident is progressing as planned. The 27-year-old tennis champion was attacked by an intruder in the Czech Republic. Initially, doctors estimated a six-month hiatus from competition. However, Kvitova's spokesman, Karel Tejkal, reports her psychological recovery is "very encouraging." She has been fitness training in the Canary Islands and can use her hand for daily activities without issue, despite some weakness. A return date remains uncertain, with Tejkal stating "no-one can give a concrete date" for her comeback to tennis. Kvitova's determination and progress offer hope for her eventual return.

Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust has been granted foundation trust status, giving it the autonomy to set its own financial and operational priorities. This change applies to John Radcliffe, Churchill, Horton, and the Nuffield Orthopaedic Centre hospitals. As a result, local residents can now become members and serve as governors, allowing them to have a greater say in the decision-making process.

According to Chief Executive Sir Jonathan Michael, the trust's finances are currently in good shape, but he acknowledges that this is no guarantee of success. "You've still got to run the business effectively and deliver operational performance," he said. The new status, granted by Monitor, the regulator of NHS services in England, is a recognition of the trust's quality services and efficiency.

The GMB union, which represents some of the trust's staff, has welcomed the change but highlighted concerns about low pay and job insecurity within the organization. The union's steward, Mark Ladbrooke, urged the trust to address these issues, as well as invest in staff accommodation and resolve long-standing problems with car parking for patients and staff. With its new status, the trust can now manage its services to better meet the needs of the local community.

Government Relaxes Bird Flu Restrictions in England, Allowing Free-Range Birds to Roam

The UK government has announced a relaxation of bird flu restrictions in England, allowing poultry farmers to let their birds roam freely outdoors once again. The decision, made by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), brings the rules for poultry in higher-risk areas in line with the rest of England. As of Thursday, normally free-range eggs will no longer require stickers indicating that the birds have been kept indoors for their welfare.

The move affects flocks that have been housed or placed under netting to protect them from wild birds, which can carry the highly pathogenic avian flu H5N8 virus. According to Chief Veterinary Officer Nigel Gibbens, the latest evidence suggests that the risk of infection from wild birds has decreased, making it safe for kept birds to be let outside.

However, poultry and bird keepers in England are still required to comply with strict biosecurity measures to prevent the spread of bird flu. A ban on poultry fairs and gatherings remains in place, and keepers must take steps to reduce the risk of contamination from the environment, where the virus can survive for several weeks in bird droppings.

The restrictions were first put in place in December, as the H5N8 virus was circulating in Europe. Since then, there have been several outbreaks of the virus in poultry and wild birds in the UK. While the Scottish government has chosen to maintain restrictions until the end of April, measures in Wales had previously been relaxed. The relaxation of restrictions in England is a welcome move for poultry farmers, who can now resume normal operations and label their eggs as free-range once again.

A wave of vandalism has swept through Orange Halls in County Tyrone, with three separate incidents reported over the weekend. The attacks began on Friday when windows were smashed at Strawletterdallon Orange Hall outside Newtownstewart. The hall was targeted again on Sunday when an oil drum was placed against a door and set alight, causing damage to the door and wall.

Meanwhile, Dergina Orange Hall outside Aughnacloy was also vandalized, with windows smashed and paint thrown over the door. The hall, which was built in 2009, was targeted early on Saturday. Nearby, Mullnahunch Orange Hall was defaced with graffiti.

Drew Nelson, secretary of the Grand Orange Lodge of Ireland, expressed relief that the Strawletterdallon hall was not destroyed, thanks to the quick thinking of a passing motorist who raised the alarm. "A tyre was placed at the emergency exit and set on fire, with oil poured over it to accelerate the flames," he said. "We are fortunate the hall was not destroyed."

The Orange Order has expressed concern over the apparent upsurge in attacks, with Nelson calling for increased police resources to detect those responsible. Ulster Unionist leader Tom Elliott condemned the attacks, blaming "mindless thugs intent on creating community division." The incidents have raised concerns about community tensions in the region.

Breakthrough in Fight Against Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria: Scientists Discover Key to Disrupting Defensive Barrier

In a significant breakthrough, researchers have made a major discovery in the fight against antibiotic-resistant bacteria, identifying a key protein complex that plays a crucial role in the construction of a defensive barrier that makes these bacteria so difficult to kill. The study, published in the journal Nature, reveals that the protein complex LptDE is responsible for building the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria, which are responsible for a wide range of infections, including salmonella and meningitis.

Using the intense X-rays of the Diamond Light Source in Oxfordshire, the researchers were able to map the structure of LptDE, revealing a complex process that involves a "path" and a "gate" that allows the protein to pull up lipopolysaccharide "bricks" from inside the bacterium and insert them into the cell wall. By understanding how this process works, the researchers believe that they can develop new drugs that can interfere with LptDE, effectively disrupting the defensive barrier and killing the bacteria.

According to Prof Changjiang Dong, from the University of East Anglia's Norwich Medical School, "We identified how LptDE builds up the outer membrane, and we have shown that if we block the path or the gate, the bacteria will die." The researchers believe that by targeting LptDE, they can develop new antibiotics that do not need to get inside the bacteria to be effective, which is a major advantage over existing treatments.

The rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria is a major public health concern, with many infections becoming increasingly difficult to treat. Gram-negative bacteria, in particular, are notorious for their ability to resist antibiotic treatments, thanks to the impermeability of their lipid-based outer coating. However, by targeting LptDE, researchers believe that they can develop new antibiotics that can effectively kill these bacteria, without the need for the drugs to penetrate the cell wall.

The study has been welcomed by experts in the field, who believe that it offers a promising new avenue for the development of antibiotics. Prof Mark Fielder, from the Society for Applied Microbiology, commented, "The work reported is at a very early stage but does offer some potentially useful information in the fight against bacterial resistance." Prof Brendan Wren, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, added, "New antibiotics against gram-negative bacteria, including many hospital superbugs, are notoriously difficult to develop, and the problem is exacerbated as many of these bacteria are increasingly resistant to currently used antibiotics."

While the study is still in its early stages, the researchers believe that their discovery has the potential to lead to the development of new antibiotics that can effectively target gram-negative bacteria. As Prof Dong explained, "If the bacteria do not have the outer membrane, they cannot withstand environmental changes, and it also makes it easier for the human immune system to kill them." With the rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria posing a major threat to public health, this breakthrough offers a glimmer of hope in the fight against these deadly infections.

Tragedy Strikes Nice: Social Media Unites to Offer Help and Support

In the wake of the devastating attack in Nice, France, where a lorry plowed into a crowd of people celebrating Bastille Day, social media has become a powerful tool for people to express their grief, offer help, and show solidarity with the victims. The attack, which has left many dead and injured, has sent shockwaves around the world, and social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook have been flooded with messages of condolence, support, and offers of assistance.

One of the most heartwarming aspects of the social media response has been the use of the hashtag #PorteOuverte, or "Open Door," which has been used by Twitter users in Nice to offer their homes to those in need of shelter. Many have also offered to provide free transportation, with taxi drivers giving free rides to those in the area. This outpouring of kindness and generosity is a testament to the resilience and compassion of the people of Nice and beyond.

As the search for missing loved ones continues, social media has also become a vital tool for people to connect with each other and share information. The hashtag #RechercheNice, or "search Nice," has been used by thousands to post pictures and descriptions of those who are missing, in the hope of finding them. An account called @NiceFindPeople was quickly set up, which has been circulating a list of names of those reported lost, and has been retweeted almost 500 times.

One story that has captured the hearts of many is that of Tiava Banner, a Facebook user who lost her 8-month-old baby in the chaos. She posted a desperate plea for help, asking if anyone had seen her baby, and was later able to update her post to say that the baby had been found, thanks to the help of a woman named Joy Ruez. While the BBC has not been able to independently verify this story, its spread shows the power of social media to bring people together and offer hope in times of tragedy.

The #JeSuisNice hashtag, which emerged quickly after the attack, has become a symbol of solidarity with the people of Nice, and has been used by celebrities and political figures around the world to express their condolences and support. However, not everyone has been supportive of the hashtag, with some expressing cynicism and frustration at the use of social media to respond to tragedy.

Facebook has also played a crucial role in responding to the attack, activating its safety check feature, which allows users in the affected area to let their friends and family know that they are safe. This feature has been widely used, and has helped to alleviate some of the uncertainty and worry that has followed the attack.

As France comes to terms with this latest tragedy, social media will continue to play a vital role in bringing people together, offering support, and providing a platform for people to express their grief and outrage. The state of emergency, which was due to end on July 26, will now be extended, and the people of France will need all the support and solidarity they can get in the days and weeks ahead.

British tennis player Kyle Edmund has advanced to the second round of the Delray Beach Open after his opponent, Adrian Mannarino, was penalized a game for unsportsmanlike conduct. Edmund, 22, was leading 6-3 5-0 with a 15-0 advantage when Mannarino smashed a ball out of the court, resulting in the penalty. The Frenchman had earlier kicked a chair and hit a ball towards a ball boy, displaying his frustration. Edmund will face either American Bjorn Fratangelo or Taiwan's Yen-Hsun Lu in the next round. The world number 49 could potentially meet top seed Milos Raonic in the quarter-finals. Meanwhile, Argentina's Juan Martin del Potro is making his 2017 debut at the tournament after a prolonged off-season following his Davis Cup win in November. Edmund's victory comes after a dramatic previous match, where his opponent was defaulted for hitting an umpire with a ball.

English rugby players are set to receive a significant pay boost, with new terms offering over £20,000 per Test match, excluding bonuses. According to RFU chief executive Ian Ritchie, "these are exciting times for English Rugby" with the deal marking a major uplift from the previous agreement. The RFU posted record profits of over £100m last year, following England's World Cup hosting. Despite a disappointing World Cup, England has since achieved success under coach Eddie Jones, winning the Six Nations Grand Slam and a 3-0 series in Australia. The new deal, negotiated by the Rugby Players Association, covers training fees, image rights, and squad performance bonuses.

Aberdeen Hosts Classes to Educate Seniors on Avoiding Online Frauds

In an effort to combat cyber scamming, Police Scotland and the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS) have launched a series of classes in Aberdeen aimed at educating seniors on how to avoid online frauds. The sessions, specifically designed for individuals over 60, are being held at the city's Stratosphere and are led by Silver City Surfers, an organization that promotes computer literacy among older adults.

The classes focus on raising awareness about various types of cyber scams, including those that use email, websites, chatrooms, and message boards. According to David Bernard, COPFS equality ambassador for age, the goal is to empower seniors with the knowledge and confidence to protect themselves from online threats. "Criminals who prey on the vulnerable are particularly detestable," he said. "Through education, we hope to prevent our older generation from falling victim to these scams and inspire confidence in the criminal justice system."

Police Scotland's Det Insp Eamonn Keane emphasized the importance of educating all communities about online safety. "We recognize the internet as a vital part of people's lives, and we welcome this opportunity to improve awareness and prevent crime," he said. By working together, the organizations aim to reduce the risk of cyber exploitation and create a safer online environment for everyone.

JBS plans to sell Moy Park as part of a $6bn fundraising effort. The Brazilian firm acquired Moy Park in 2015 for $1.5bn. Headquartered in Northern Ireland, Moy Park employs over 9,000 people, making it one of the region's largest companies. CEO Janet McCollum stated that the company's priority remains "business as usual," focusing on quality and innovation. Despite the potential sale, McCollum expressed confidence in Moy Park's success, citing its strong financial standing and exceptional workforce. The company will continue to operate normally, delivering high-quality products to customers and consumers. Moy Park's future remains uncertain.

Tragedy Strikes on Lake: Boat Capsizes, Killing Over 100 Refugees

A devastating boat accident on Lake Albert has resulted in the loss of over 100 lives, with many more feared dead. The boat, which was carrying refugees from the Democratic Republic of Congo back to their home country, capsized due to overloading. With a capacity of only 80 passengers, the vessel was grossly overcrowded, carrying up to 250 people.

According to Uganda's Refugees Minister Hillary Onek, rescue operations are underway, involving the police, military, and civilian fishing boats. So far, 107 bodies have been recovered, including 57 children. The exact number of passengers on board remains unknown. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Antonio Guterres, has expressed his shock and condolences, praising the government's rescue efforts.

The boat was one of two that departed from Uganda's Hoima district on Saturday, carrying refugees who had chosen to return to eastern DR Congo from a camp in Uganda. The incident highlights the poor safety standards and frequent accidents on Uganda's lakes, often caused by overloading and lack of life jackets. As the rescue operation continues, the international community is left to mourn the loss of life and support the survivors.

Olympic swimmer Adam Peaty returned to his hometown of Uttoxeter to open a redeveloped sports centre. The facility, named after Peaty, features a 25m pool, gym, and sports hall. It's designed to host competitions, with seating for 140 spectators. Peaty, a Commonwealth Games medalist, unveiled the centre on Saturday, bringing new recreational opportunities to the community.

A 43-year-old man was seriously injured when his car crashed on the B6355 Chirnside to Ayton road on Monday. The silver Seat Alhambra struck a tree and came to rest down an embankment at 16:30. The man was taken to Edinburgh Royal Infirmary, where he is now stable. The road was closed for four hours near Peelwalls Farm. Police are investigating and appeal for witnesses to come forward. PC Davy Johnson urges anyone with information to contact them to help establish the circumstances surrounding the accident. The driver's condition is being closely monitored.

A 21-year-old man from Wolverhampton is facing an uncertain future after his application for British citizenship was rejected, leaving him at risk of being returned to his birth country of Botswana. Brian White, who was adopted by a British family at the age of six, has lived in the UK for most of his life, but a technicality has thrown his future into doubt.

Mr. White's family moved to the UK from Botswana when he was 15, and he was granted limited leave to remain, rather than indefinite leave, which is required for naturalization. Despite appealing the decision, his application was rejected in 2014. He is now awaiting the outcome of a new application, but the delay has already had significant consequences. Mr. White was forced to turn down a place to study chemistry at Oxford University in 2016 because he was ineligible for student finance.

The situation has sparked widespread concern, with a petition set up by Mr. White's friend, Luke Wilcox, gaining over 4,000 signatures and attracting support from celebrities such as journalist Caitlin Moran and writer Philip Pullman. Mr. Wilcox described the situation as "disgusting" and said it would be "terrifying" for Mr. White to be returned to a country where he has no links, family, or friends.

The Home Office has acknowledged the urgency of Mr. White's case and has reassured him that it is working to resolve his application as soon as possible. However, the delay has already taken a significant toll on Mr. White, who is trying to stay focused on his future despite the uncertainty. "I don't think I've ever had time to sit down and think about it," he said. "I'm trying my best to get it out of my mind." With the support of his community and high-profile backers, Mr. White is hoping for a positive outcome and the chance to build a secure future in the country he calls home.

A unique art exhibition has opened at the Old Low Lights Heritage Centre in North Shields, aiming to raise funds for the restoration of Tynemouth Pool. The outdoor pool, which was once a popular visitor attraction, has lain derelict since the 1990s. The exhibition features specially commissioned artworks, including a previously unseen print by renowned photographer Sirkka-Liisa Konttinen. The artworks will be auctioned on November 26 to support the refurbishment efforts.

The Friends of Tynemouth Outdoor Pool, formed in 2012, has submitted detailed proposals to North Tyneside Council. The exhibition showcases a variety of mediums and artistic approaches, all sharing the common goal of returning the pool to its former glory. A highlight of the exhibition is an illuminated model of the restoration, created in Lego by architectural photographer Steve Mayes. After the exhibition, the model will be displayed at various locations around North Tyneside, raising awareness and support for the pool's restoration. The event is a significant step towards reviving the iconic pool and restoring it to its former beauty.

Tottenham Hotspur's pursuit of West Brom forward Saido Berahino has hit a roadblock after the Baggies rejected two offers for the 22-year-old. West Brom chairman Jeremy Peace has reiterated that Berahino will not be sold during this transfer window, despite Tottenham's interest. 

According to Peace, the offers made by Tottenham were not only too low but also based on stage-payments and add-ons over a long period, which do not reflect Berahino's ability and potential. Peace emphasized that selling their top goalscorer was never on the agenda this summer, and the club would have needed to find a suitable replacement if Berahino were to leave.

Tottenham manager Mauricio Pochettino expressed his admiration for Berahino, likening his desire to sign the player to being in love. "It's like when you are in love with some lady," Pochettino said. "There are a lot of women around the world, but you want only one. Sometimes it is impossible. It's about love. And in football, it is the same."

Meanwhile, Tottenham are in talks to sign Bayer Leverkusen and South Korea forward Son Heung-min in a proposed transfer worth 30m euros (£22m). However, their priority remains signing Berahino, who scored 20 goals last season. Berahino was dropped from West Brom's squad last weekend, with manager Tony Pulis citing that the player was not in the right frame of mind to play. With the transfer window still open, it remains to be seen whether Tottenham will make another bid for Berahino or pursue other targets.

Everton Manager Ronald Koeman Pledges Commitment to Club Amid Barcelona Speculation

Ronald Koeman, the manager of Everton Football Club, has reaffirmed his commitment to the team despite recent speculation linking him to a return to his former club, Barcelona. In an interview with Catalan newspaper Sport, Koeman expressed his dream of coaching Barcelona, where he spent six years as a player from 1989 to 1995. However, the 54-year-old Dutchman was quick to dismiss any rumors of an imminent departure from Goodison Park.

Speaking on Thursday, Koeman stated, "There's no chance that I will leave Everton before the end of my contract." He also downplayed the possibility of becoming the next manager of Barcelona, saying, "I don't see me being the next manager." Koeman's comments come after current Barcelona manager Luis Enrique announced his decision to step down at the end of the season.

Koeman, who is in the first season of his contract with Everton, emphasized his ambition to lead the team to Champions League qualification. "We have a very powerful and exciting project and we're going to strengthen as best as possible to try and reach the Champions League next season," he said. The Toffees currently sit seventh in the Premier League with three games remaining and are unlikely to secure a Champions League spot this year.

When asked about the possibility of Barcelona approaching him, Koeman replied, "That's a hypothesis we cannot go into too much. In football, like in life, like in business, you can talk and discuss everything." The Everton manager also announced that striker Arouna Kone will be leaving the club at the end of the season. The 33-year-old Ivory Coast striker has been with the Toffees since 2013, joining from Wigan Athletic for £6m.

Despite the speculation surrounding his future, Koeman appears focused on the task at hand, guiding Everton to a strong finish in the Premier League and building a team capable of competing at the highest level next season. With his contract commitment and stated ambition to lead the team to Champions League qualification, Koeman's future at Goodison Park seems secure for now.

Violent Protests Erupt in Andhra Pradesh as Kapu Community Demands Job Reservations

Protests turned violent in Andhra Pradesh on Sunday as members of the Kapu community took to the streets, demanding that the government fulfill its promise of reserving government jobs for them. The community, which makes up nearly 26% of the state's population, had organized a public meeting that escalated into chaos. Protesters set fire to railway carriages, a police station, and dozens of vehicles, causing widespread destruction.

The violence disrupted railway and highway services, with protesters blocking tracks and stopping trains. The Ratnachal Express train was targeted, with four coaches set ablaze after passengers were ordered to disembark. At least 15 policemen were injured in clashes with protesters, who attacked them with stones near the town of Tuni. The local railway station was also ransacked, and 25 cars and other vehicles were torched.

The protests were reportedly called off late on Sunday, but not before causing significant damage. Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu condemned the violence, citing the government's commitment to social justice. Despite laws against caste-based discrimination, the influence of the caste system remains strong in India, leading to ongoing demands for job and education quotas. The Kapu community's demands highlight the ongoing struggle for social equality in the region.

Former Maldivian President Mohamed Nasheed's lawyers have accused the government of reneging on a deal to commute his 13-year prison sentence to house arrest. Nasheed was sentenced in March under anti-terror laws, which his lawyers claim is a politically motivated case. The government, however, denies any agreement to commute the sentence, stating that house arrest was only temporarily granted on medical grounds.

According to Nasheed's lawyers, they possess a document dated July 19, which proves that his sentence was commuted to house arrest for the remainder of its duration. Nevertheless, presidential spokesperson Ibrahim Muaz Ali has dismissed the document as fake, asserting that the Maldives Correctional Service has not issued any such document altering the Criminal Court's ruling.

Amal Clooney, one of Nasheed's lawyers, has condemned the government's actions, stating that they demonstrate "a complete disregard for the rule of law." Nasheed, a former human rights campaigner, was the Maldives' first democratically elected leader, serving from 2008 until his resignation in 2012. His current imprisonment has sparked concerns over the country's democratic trajectory, particularly under the leadership of President Abdulla Yameen, who is the half-brother of former President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom. The situation has raised questions about the independence of the judiciary and the government's commitment to upholding the rule of law in the Maldives.

Flooding Concerns Persist in Clady as Funding Delays Repair Work

Residents of Clady are still reeling from the devastating floods that hit their community last December. The storm caused significant damage to homes and businesses, with many still recovering from the aftermath. An initial study has been conducted to replace a damaged floodwall and flood-banks, but progress is now hindered by funding constraints. According to David Porter of the Rivers Agency, the project's viability is being assessed, taking into account affordability and the availability of funds.

With many competing priorities for funding, Mr. Porter emphasized the need for residents in at-risk areas to take proactive measures to protect themselves from flooding. This warning comes as a couple in their 60s, Eugene and Mary McShane, continue to live in a caravan after their home on Urney Road was severely damaged by 5ft of water last year. As winter approaches, concerns about repeat flooding are growing, highlighting the urgent need for a long-term solution to Clady's flooding woes.

Linus Torvalds, the creator of the Linux operating system, has been awarded the prestigious Millennium Technology Prize, sharing the honor with Dr. Shinya Yamanaka, a renowned stem cell scientist. The award, presented by Technology Academy Finland, recognizes Mr. Torvalds's significant contributions to the development of shared software, networking, and the openness of the web.

Mr. Torvalds, who developed the first version of Linux in 1991 while studying at the University of Helsinki, Finland, has had a profound impact on the technology industry. The Linux kernel, which he created, has undergone numerous revisions and is now used in a wide range of applications, including computer servers, digital video recorders, stock exchange equipment, and Google's Android smartphone platform.

The Millennium Technology Prize, awarded every two years, is considered one of the most prestigious awards in the field of technology. This year, the award is being split for the first time, with each winner receiving 600,000 euros ($752,000; £483,000). Dr. Ainomaija Haarla, president of Technology Academy Finland, praised Mr. Torvalds's work, stating that it has "kept the web open for the pursuit of knowledge and the benefit of humanity - not simply for financial interests."

Mr. Torvalds, who now works from his home office in Oregon, acknowledged his roots in accepting the award, expressing gratitude to the Technology Academy of Finland and to the thousands of software engineers who have contributed to the Linux project over the years. The Linux kernel has been developed through the contributions of thousands of volunteers, with an estimated 73,000 man-years spent working on the code.

The award is a testament to Mr. Torvalds's dedication to the open-source movement and his commitment to keeping the web open and accessible to all. Despite receiving job offers from top companies, including Apple's founder Steve Jobs, Mr. Torvalds has chosen to remain neutral and independent, working with the Linux Foundation, a non-profit organization that promotes and supports the development of the Linux kernel.

In a recent interview with the BBC, Mr. Torvalds revealed that he had no intention of leaving the Linux Foundation, citing the importance of his neutral status and the preference of companies involved with Linux for his independence. "I seriously believe that even though the Linux kernel has become a big thing for a number of large companies, people really do appreciate how nice it is that I don't work for any of them," he said.

The Millennium Technology Prize is a well-deserved recognition of Mr. Torvalds's contributions to the technology industry, and his commitment to the principles of openness and collaboration. As the Linux operating system continues to play a vital role in shaping the digital landscape, Mr. Torvalds's work will remain an essential part of the internet's infrastructure, promoting innovation and accessibility for generations to come.

Tom Lawrence, the 23-year-old Wales international, is set to leave Leicester after limited appearances. Since joining from Manchester United in 2014, he has featured just four times. Lawrence spent the past two seasons on loan in the Championship with Blackburn, Cardiff, and Ipswich. He impressed with Ipswich, scoring 11 goals in 36 appearances. Derby and Premier League newcomers Brighton are reportedly interested in signing him. Ipswich boss Mick McCarthy had previously stated the club had "no chance" of signing Lawrence permanently due to high demand for the player. A move is expected soon.

A Staffordshire coroner has suggested that there may be a rising trend in suicides linked to concerns over state benefits. Andrew Haigh made the comment after recently presiding over an inquest into the death of Kim Burns, a 51-year-old woman from Codsall, near Wolverhampton. Ms Burns, who suffered from multiple sclerosis, took her own life on January 17, leaving behind a note criticizing the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

According to her friend, Christine Hammonds, Ms Burns had been struggling with depression and was worried about losing her benefits, including her mobility allowance. She had been receiving personal independence payments, but was concerned that she would lose £1,000 a year in benefits from April. Ms Hammonds described Ms Burns as a proud and independent woman who feared losing her independence and becoming reliant on others.

The DWP has disputed the claim that Ms Burns' death was linked to the loss of benefits, stating that she was still receiving the higher rate of mobility allowance and that personal independence payments were not a factor in her death. However, Coroner Haigh believes that the issue is worth exploring, and has noted that he has dealt with similar cases in the past where individuals have taken their own lives due to perceived problems with state benefits.

Another case, that of 73-year-old Valerie Grant from Great Bridgeford, is also being investigated. Her son had been told that he would lose his disability allowance on May 3, and her inquest is yet to be heard. While the DWP has declined to comment on Mrs Grant's case, Coroner Haigh has expressed concern that these types of cases may be on the rise. He has called for further exploration of the issue, highlighting the need for greater support and understanding for individuals struggling with the complexities of the benefits system.

Former New Zealand cricket star Chris Cairns is facing prosecution for perjury and perverting the course of justice in a high-profile trial. The charges stem from a libel case in 2012, where Cairns successfully sued Indian Premier League chairman Lalit Modi over a tweet accusing him of match-fixing. During the trial, Cairns testified under oath that he had never cheated at cricket, a claim the prosecution now alleges is untrue.

Cairns, who was once considered the "golden boy" of cricket, won damages of $130,000 in the libel case. However, his reputation was tarnished after Modi's tweet in 2010, which accused him of match-fixing while playing for the Chandigarh Lions in the Indian Cricket League. The prosecution claims that Cairns's testimony in the libel case was false and that he had indeed engaged in match-fixing.

The trial is expected to hear evidence from current New Zealand cricket captain Brendon McCullum and former teammate Lou Vincent, who were both allegedly targeted by Cairns to help him fix matches. McCullum reportedly refused to participate, while Vincent was "corrupted" by Cairns. The prosecution also alleges that Cairns and his co-defendant, Andrew Fitch Holland, a barrister friend, attempted to induce Vincent to give false evidence in order to help Cairns's case.

A recorded Skype conversation between Fitch Holland and Vincent, who has admitted to being involved in match-fixing, was played in court. The prosecution claims that the conversation was an attempt to persuade Vincent to lie to the court and support Cairns's claims of innocence. Cairns and Fitch Holland deny all charges, but the prosecution argues that the evidence will show that Cairns was indeed guilty of match-fixing. The trial is ongoing, with the jury set to hear further evidence in the coming days.

A historic Torah scroll has been returned to a Jewish community in Cornwall after being restored and housed at the Royal Cornwall Museum. The scroll, one of the holiest objects in the Jewish faith, was given back to Kehillat Kernow, a local Jewish group, by the Duke of Gloucester on behalf of the museum. This is believed to be the first Kosher scroll in the country to be returned by a museum. The Torah scroll is considered precious and is typically read using a pointer, or "yad". It will now be used in festivals and ceremonies, including Bar and Bat Mitzvahs and baby blessings. Kehillat Kernow chairman Harvey Kurzfield welcomed the return, saying it provides a "great link with the past" and will be used in a "living, vibrant Jewish community" 350 years after its initial use. The scroll's return is a significant moment for the local Jewish community.

Celtic's Nadir Ciftci has left Scotland on loan for the third consecutive season. The 25-year-old Turkish player joined Celtic in 2015 for £1.5m but made just 11 starts. He last played for Celtic in February and hasn't scored since 2015. Ciftci has had loan spells at Eskisehirspor and Pogon Szczecin, and previously played for Portsmouth in England. Check our football transfers page for the latest updates.

Derry City manager Kenny Shiels has made a shocking allegation against a member of Cork City's backroom staff, claiming he was called a "sectarian name" following Friday night's 2-1 loss at Turner's Cross. The incident occurred after Cork City scored two late goals to secure their first victory over Derry this season, with Kenny Browne netting the winner in stoppage time.

Shiels expressed his outrage and disappointment at the alleged abuse, stating that he will "not tolerate" such behavior and is determined to pursue the matter further. However, Cork City chairman Pat Lyons has denied any knowledge of the incident, while manager John Caulfield expressed surprise at Shiels' allegation, attributing it to "excitement" and disappointment.

Shiels had taken issue with the home team's reaction after the final whistle, describing their lack of hospitality as "outrageous." He vowed to "fight his own corner" and take action to address the alleged abuse. The incident has sparked controversy, with Shiels insisting that he will not be "walked over" and that Cork City staff will be held accountable for their actions. The matter is likely to be investigated further, with Shiels seeking a resolution to the alleged incident.

A unique weight loss program has proven to be a winning formula for overweight soccer fans in Glasgow. The 12-week program, which involved training sessions at local football clubs, resulted in an average weight loss of 11lb (5kg) per participant, with nearly 40% of men maintaining a weight loss of at least 5% of their original body weight a year later.

The program, which was conducted by researchers at Glasgow University, involved 748 overweight men, with half participating in the training sessions and the other half placed on a waiting list. All participants received healthy-eating advice and weight management tips, but only those who attended the training sessions at the football clubs achieved significant and sustained weight loss.

Thirteen football clubs took part in the program, including Aberdeen, Celtic, and Rangers, providing a male-friendly environment that encouraged participants to take control of their health. According to Prof Kate Hunt, co-author of the study, the program's success lies in its ability to tap into men's interests and provide a supportive community. "Participants really enjoyed being with other men like them, with a shared interest in football and similar health issues to address," she said. The program's success has significant implications for the development of weight loss programs tailored to men's needs, and its potential for future applications is substantial.

Zambian Referee Janny Sikazwe Invited to Officiate at Under-20 World Cup

The FIFA Under-20 World Cup, set to kick off in South Korea on May 20, will feature 22 top referees from around the globe, including Zambia's Janny Sikazwe. The 37-year-old school teacher from Kapiri Mposhi is one of three African referees selected for the tournament, alongside Egypt's Grisha Ghead and Cameroon's Alioum Alioum.

Sikazwe's rise to the top has been nothing short of remarkable. Despite hailing from a small town with limited resources, he has consistently demonstrated his skills and dedication to the sport. In Kapiri Mposhi, referees are forced to train on a subpar pitch at a local school, and the town lacks a single stadium. However, Sikazwe remains undaunted, drawing on his experiences to stay focused under pressure.

His career has been on an upward trajectory since officiating at the 2015 FIFA Under-17 World Cup in Chile. He went on to referee the 2016 FIFA Club World Cup final between Real Madrid and Kashima Antlers, and most recently, handled the Africa Cup of Nations final between Cameroon and Egypt. Sikazwe's sights are now set on the 2018 World Cup in Russia, where he hopes to represent Africa. With his ambition and determination, he is certainly one to watch in the world of refereeing.

General Motors (GM), the largest US carmaker, has reported a net income of $1.4 billion, a 7.6% decrease from the same period last year. Despite a 9.2% increase in North American car sales, with 794,000 vehicles sold, profits were impacted by a $900 million settlement for faulty ignition recalls and $600 million in civil settlements. However, GM's underlying performance was strong, with North American pre-tax earnings reaching a record $3.3 billion, up 34%. The company also saw improved results in Europe, with losses decreasing to $231 million. GM's shares rose 4% in New York, reflecting the company's overall resilience. Additionally, September saw the strongest US car sales in a decade, with GM selling 814,000 cars in China, albeit at a lower volume than the previous year, but with slightly higher profit margins.

South Korea's Response to MERS Outbreak Criticized as Cases Rise

The South Korean government is facing criticism over its handling of the Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) outbreak, which has now infected 35 people and resulted in one death. The latest victim, who contracted the virus from another patient in the same hospital room, died in hospital on Thursday. The outbreak, which is the largest outside of the Middle East, has prompted the quarantine of over 1,600 people, with 160 being isolated in state medical facilities and the remainder instructed to stay at home.

The criticism stems from the fact that one infected person was allowed to play golf, while another flew to China, potentially putting hundreds of people at risk of infection. The government has been accused of being slow to respond to the outbreak, which was first detected in a 68-year-old man who had recently returned from a trip to Saudi Arabia.

As the number of cases continues to rise, public anxiety is growing. Many people in Seoul are now wearing face masks on public transport and in crowded places, and the Korea Tourism Organisation has reported that around 7,000 tourists, mostly from China and Taiwan, have cancelled planned group trips to South Korea. This is a significant blow to the country's tourism industry, with many travellers citing the MERS outbreak as the main reason for their cancellation.

Experts say that MERS is not highly contagious and can only spread through close contact in a confined space. However, the virus has a death rate of 27%, according to the World Health Organization, and has resulted in 479 deaths worldwide out of 1,167 reported cases.

The South Korean health ministry has confirmed that all of the cases so far are linked to the initial sufferer, and authorities are working to contain the outbreak. However, the government's response has been criticized as inadequate, and there are concerns that the outbreak could spread further if not properly contained. As the situation continues to unfold, the government is under pressure to take more decisive action to prevent the spread of the virus and reassure the public.

St Johnstone Ease Past Stirling Albion in League Cup Clash

St Johnstone secured a comfortable 4-0 victory over Stirling Albion in their League Cup match, with the Perth team dominating from start to finish. The Saints took an early lead in the fourth minute, as Steven Anderson headed in a Liam Craig corner at the back post. This set the tone for the rest of the match, with St Johnstone creating numerous scoring opportunities.

The home team doubled their lead 12 minutes before half-time, as another Craig corner was flicked on and Steven Maclean netted with an unmarked header. Stirling Albion struggled to create any meaningful chances, with their best effort coming from Bryan Hodge's 25-yard shot that sailed just over the bar.

St Johnstone wrapped up their victory with a third goal in the 43rd minute, as Maclean's cross was glanced in by Craig for his first goal of the match. The second half saw a lengthy delay due to an injury to Stirling Albion keeper Chris Smith, who was stretchered off after falling awkwardly while catching a cross.

Despite Maclean missing several glaring opportunities to add to the scoreline, he laid on the fourth goal for David Wotherspoon to lash home in stoppage time. The win sees St Johnstone progress comfortably in the League Cup, while Stirling Albion will look to regroup and bounce back from the defeat.

Outrage has erupted in the cycling world after a podium presentation at the Flanders Diamond Tour was marred by controversy. Following Wiggle-Honda's Jolien d'Hoore's win in the Antwerp to Nijlen stage, a picture of the podium was posted on Twitter, showing the winner standing alongside two models in revealing outfits. The image sparked widespread criticism, with Dutch racing cyclist and journalist Marijn de Vries describing the scene as "an utter disgrace".

The Lotto Cycling Cup organisers were quick to apologise for the incident, stating that they were not responsible for the podium presentation and found the models "inappropriate". According to the organisers, the local event planners had hired the models from Hostessen Service No Limit, a company that also offers striptease acts. The manager of the company, Gerrid, seemed unfazed by the backlash, stating that he didn't understand what the problem was and that he wouldn't be apologising.

However, Johan Molineaux, the local organiser of the event, took a different stance, saying that he would not be using Hostessen Service No Limit again and planned to personally apologise to the competitors. Molineaux explained that the women were supposed to wear cycling shirts but took them off, and he was not present during the presentation. The UCI, world cycling's governing body, has also looked into the incident and contacted the organisers, who apologised.

The controversy has sparked a wider debate about the use of podium girls in cycling. British cyclist Helen Wyman, speaking at the launch of the Women's Tour of Britain, said that she thinks podium girls should be a thing of the past. "It's 2015. I'd much prefer to see the race sponsors on the podium, as it's their money that allow us to do what we do, and we'd prefer to see them rewarded," she told BBC Sport. The incident has highlighted the need for greater respect and professionalism in the sport, and it remains to be seen how the cycling world will respond to the controversy in the future.

A 26-year-old man from Edinburgh has been sentenced to 16 months in prison for embezzling over £134,000 from his employer, RS McColl's. Daryl Louden pleaded guilty to the crime, which took place between January and September 2016, and had been deferred for background reports.

At Edinburgh Sheriff Court, Sheriff Frank Crowe expressed his disappointment and frustration with Louden's actions, stating that his breach of trust had been "enormous" and devastating for his colleagues. Louden had been a trusted employee and was even in line for promotion to area manager before his addiction took over.

The court heard that Louden's gambling habit had spiralled out of control, with him taking out loans and trying to repay them by betting on football and horse racing. When he lost money, he would bet more in an attempt to recoup his losses, eventually leading to the embezzlement of £134,177.46 from the Ferry Road branch.

Defence solicitor Jennifer McEvinney argued that Louden's actions were "extremely out of character" and that he had since sought help and turned his life around. She presented a letter from Louden's superior, David Richardson, which expressed concern for Louden's mental health and suggested that he was capable of making amends through community service.

However, Sheriff Crowe was unsympathetic, stating that only a prison sentence was suitable for the crime. He emphasized that Louden had wasted public money and disappointed those who trusted him, including his area manager, colleagues, and friends. While reducing the initial sentence of two years to 16 months, Sheriff Crowe also ensured that Louden would receive proper support and help in prison to address his addiction and get his life back on track.

Samsung Sells Shares in Four Companies Amid Galaxy Note 7 Recall

Samsung has sold its shares in four companies, including US chipmaker Rambus and hard drive producer Seagate, in a move to efficiently manage its assets. The sales, which raised over 1 trillion won ($888.9m), come as the company faces a major recall of its flagship Galaxy Note 7 phone due to reports of fires caused by faulty batteries. The recall, which affects 2.5 million devices globally, is expected to cost Samsung over $1bn.

The shares sold include a 4.2% stake in Seagate, 4.5% of Rambus, and 0.7% of Sharp, as well as half of a 3% stake in Dutch semiconductor firm ASML. Samsung stated that the sale was for "efficient management of assets." The move is seen as an effort to mitigate the financial impact of the Galaxy Note 7 recall, which has already led to a formal recall order from US regulators. With reports of fires in China, despite initial claims that phones in the country were safe, Samsung's woes are far from over. The company has already recalled a small batch of phones in China and is investigating the latest incidents. The recall is a major blow to Samsung's reputation and finances, and the company will be closely watched as it navigates this crisis.

Animal Cruelty Cases on the Rise in England and Wales

The RSPCA has released disturbing statistics showing a significant increase in animal cruelty cases in England and Wales. In 2014, a total of 159,831 incidents were investigated, up from 153,770 in 2013. Shocking cases include a rabbit being microwaved to death in Gloucestershire and incidents in Barrow and Peterborough. Despite the rise in cases, the number of people convicted of animal cruelty fell to 1,029, down from 1,371 in 2013.

Greater London had the highest number of complaints at 12,202, followed by West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester. The RSPCA reported that 20,258 cases involved deliberate and violent cruelty. Chief veterinary officer James Yeates expressed concern over the inventive and disturbing ways people are being cruel to animals. The charity also highlighted the "Neknomination" online craze, which led to five prosecutions involving the swallowing of live animals. West Yorkshire saw the highest number of convictions at 93, with County Durham and the West Midlands also having high numbers. The RSPCA urges the public to report any cases of animal cruelty and offers welfare advice to prevent neglect and abuse.

Crystal Palace has secured the signing of left-back Patrick van Aanholt from Sunderland. The 26-year-old will be reunited with Eagles boss Sam Allardyce, who he played under last season. Allardyce praised Van Aanholt, stating he brings "great energy" and will increase the speed and energy levels of the squad. Van Aanholt started his career at Chelsea before joining Sunderland in 2014, making 95 appearances for the Black Cats. Allardyce confirmed that Palace has not received bids for any of their players and is hopeful of signing further targets. However, he denied that Norwich's Robbie Brady and Lille's Ibrahim Amadou are among them, citing the high cost of doing business in the current market. The signing is a positive move for Palace, and Allardyce is looking forward to working with Van Aanholt again.

Queen Silvia of Sweden has revealed that she shares her 17th-century Drottningholm Palace with some unexpected "small friends" - ghosts. In a documentary airing on Swedish public broadcaster SVT, the queen expressed her excitement about the paranormal presence, but assured that they are "all very friendly" and don't scare her. The palace, located near Stockholm, has been the permanent residence of the queen and her husband, King Carl XVI Gustaf, for decades.

Princess Christina, the king's sister, corroborated the queen's claims, stating that the palace has a lot of energy, which could manifest as ghostly apparitions. The queen's comments have sparked amusement, with Swedish website The Local joking that brave amateur ghost hunters could visit the palace to test the rumors. However, some areas of the palace, including the southern wing, are reserved for the royal family and their alleged ghostly companions.

Queen Silvia, who has been Sweden's longest-serving queen for 40 years, has been open about her experiences in the palace. In a 2015 book, she spoke about feeling lonely in her first year as queen, despite the support of her husband and staff. Recently, the queen was hospitalized briefly before Christmas due to dizziness but was released two days later. The documentary, Drottningholm Palace: A Royal Home, offers a glimpse into the queen's life and her unique relationship with the historic palace and its inhabitants, both living and dead.

Emmerdale's rape scene deemed suitable by media watchdog. A controversial scene from the soap opera, in which Rhona Goskirk was raped by her husband Pierce Harris, has been defended by Ofcom. The scene, broadcast at 7pm on April 24, was the culmination of a long-running storyline involving Rhona and her abusive partner. Some viewers felt it was not suitable for broadcast before 9pm, but Ofcom ruled it was "likely to have been in line with what most viewers were expecting." The watchdog noted that a warning had been issued and the scene was limited. Emmerdale producer Iain MacLeod also defended the scene, stating that the show has a responsibility to cover hard-hitting subjects. He added that Emmerdale has always tackled challenging social issues, and this scene was no exception. The ruling has sparked debate about what is suitable for broadcast during early evening time slots.

AFC Telford United, a non-league football club based in Shropshire, has parted ways with manager Rob Smith and his assistant Larry Chambers. This sudden change in management is part of a larger plan to secure new investment and ensure the club's future. According to BBC Radio Shropshire, the club's decision to let go of Smith and Chambers is a result of an offer that was too good to turn down.

Director Andy Pryce expressed his gratitude towards the departing management duo, stating that it was tough to part with them. However, he is excited about the future of the club under the guidance of new manager Rob Edwards. Edwards, a 34-year-old Shropshire-born former player, has had a successful career and has made a promising start to his coaching career. He was heavily linked with the manager's job at Shrewsbury Town earlier this year and has now returned to football just four weeks after leaving his role at Wolverhampton Wanderers.

Edwards has expressed his commitment to his hometown club, stating that he will work hard to achieve great things and raise the club's profile to a new level. This is a significant development for AFC Telford, who were formed by fans in 2004 following the liquidation of the old Telford United. The club has experienced a mix of promotions and relegations over the years, currently playing in the sixth tier of English football.

The new investment is expected to bring about significant changes to the club, including the potential arrival of Football League players on loan. Additionally, the club will receive extra financial support from Wolverhampton Wanderers, who currently use AFC Telford's Bucks Head home to stage their Under-23 games. This support will be on top of their existing agreement and is a major boost to the club's finances.

The club's chairman, Ian Dosser, will also be leaving his position, with Andy Pryce taking over as interim chairman. Despite the changes, the club's share structure and name will remain unchanged. The new investment is seen as a game-changer for AFC Telford, and fans are eagerly awaiting the impact it will have on the club's performance and reputation.

In a statement, BBC Radio Shropshire's Nick Southall said, "This is a pretty major development for the club. We're talking about pretty major investment, and the prospect of some Football League players joining on loan." The arrival of Rob Edwards as manager and the new investment are expected to bring about a new era of success and stability to AFC Telford United. With the club's future looking brighter than ever, fans are excited to see what the upcoming season holds for their team.

Researchers at King's College London have made a breakthrough in the quest to identify the earliest signs of Alzheimer's disease. By analyzing the levels of 1,129 proteins in the blood of over 200 twins, they discovered a potential link between a protein called MAPKAPK5 and cognitive decline. The study, published in Translational Psychiatry, compared the protein levels with data from cognitive-function tests over a decade and found that individuals with lower levels of MAPKAPK5 were more likely to experience brain decline.

The discovery of this protein marker could be a crucial step in the development of early diagnosis and treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
