Currently, dementia cases are expected to treble globally by 2050, with no cure or treatment available. The disease can take over a decade to progress from the first changes in the brain to the onset of symptoms such as memory loss, confusion, and personality change.

According to Dr. Steven Kiddle, a Medical Research Council scientist at King's College London, identifying people at risk of Alzheimer's disease years before symptoms appear could be key to developing effective treatments. "People think it may be hard to reverse 20 years of potential damage to your brain," he said. "But if you could start much earlier in that process, then you might be able to find something that works."

While the study's findings are promising, Dr. Kiddle cautions that a blood test for Alzheimer's disease is still a long way off. The twins in the study will need to be followed for many more years to determine whether levels of MAPKAPK5 can predict dementia. Dr. Eric Karran from Alzheimer's Research UK agrees, stating that more research is needed to understand the mechanism linking MAPKAPK5 to cognitive decline. Nevertheless, the study brings hope for the development of new treatments and earlier diagnosis, which is essential for combating this devastating disease.

Scotland's "Living it Up" Initiative Fails to Meet User Targets

A Scottish health initiative aimed at helping people over 50 manage their health and wellbeing online has fallen short of its user targets. The "Living it Up" (LiU) programme, launched in 2013, had hoped to attract 55,000 users across Scotland by May 2015, but so far, it has only managed to sign up 15,000 people.

Despite the disappointing uptake, NHS 24, which manages the project, remains optimistic about its potential. The organisation pointed out that the website receives an average of 50,000 hits per month, suggesting that there is still significant interest in the service. The LiU website offers a range of tools and resources, including a quiz to help users identify their strengths and interests, a search function to find local community projects, and guides to social media platforms like Twitter and Instagram.

The initiative was designed to use technology to match individuals with professional information, local services, and beneficial activities in their community. It was announced by then-Scottish health secretary Alex Neil in November 2013, with the aim of providing accessible health services via familiar technology such as televisions, computers, and smartphones.

The project has received £10.375m in funding over three years from the Scottish government, the Technology Strategy Board, Scottish Enterprise, and local health boards and authorities. Despite the significant investment, the cost per patient has worked out at £690, raising questions about the value for money of the initiative.

NHS 24 acknowledged that recruitment had been "challenging" but claimed that uptake was now picking up, with a 55% growth in users over the past six months. The organisation described LiU as a "pioneering and ambitious project" that aimed to embed digital tools within health and care service pathways. The project is currently available to patients in several regions, including Forth Valley, Lothian, and the Highlands. While the initiative may not have met its original targets, it remains to be seen whether it can still make a positive impact on the health and wellbeing of Scotland's over-50s.

Northern Ireland's Rail Upgrade Project to Commence in May 2015

The long-awaited rail upgrade project in Northern Ireland is set to begin in May 2015, according to David Strahan, Chief Executive of Translink. Strahan confirmed the start date while giving evidence to a Northern Ireland Assembly inquiry into the rail project. The inquiry was established last year to investigate the significant cost overrun of the upgrade, which has nearly doubled from its initial estimate of £20m to £40m.

As part of the inquiry, members of the Regional Development Committee traveled to Derry by train, speaking with passengers about issues on the rail line. The second stage of the upgrade will involve major re-signalling between Derry and Coleraine, as well as the introduction of a passing loop. The work is expected to be completed by 2016.

Committee member John Dallat expressed his enthusiasm for the project, stating that Derry needs a proper inter-city service. "I hope that the city of Derry and all the towns in-between will have a new rail service by 2016," he said. "It's not a dream, it's a reality, and I'm absolutely confident because I know that no other city in the world doesn't have a decent inter-city service."

Translink has confirmed that an hourly service on the route is a priority, and senior representatives of the company were questioned alongside government officials at the Derry hearing. A Translink spokesperson stated that the work on phase 2 of the project is expected to commence in May 2015, subject to the successful completion of a tender process. With four contractors expressing interest in the project, compared to only one last time, there is optimism that the upgrade will be completed on time and within budget. The new rail service is expected to bring a "new era" to the north west, providing a much-needed boost to the region's transportation infrastructure.

Sweden's Economy Thrives with Unique Public-Private Partnership Model

Sweden's economy is experiencing a period of unprecedented strength, with low unemployment rates and a thriving mixed economy. At the heart of this success is the "Swedish model," a public-private partnership developed by the Social Democrats, who governed the country for most of the last 70 years. This model features centralized wage negotiations and a heavily tax-subsidized social security network, providing citizens with a high standard of living and life expectancy.

The country's advanced welfare system and strong economy have made it a popular destination for refugees and asylum seekers, with immigrants making up over 10% of the population. Sweden is also known for its commitment to environmental sustainability, having initially phased out nuclear power in the 1990s. However, in 2009, the government reversed this decision, citing concerns over climate change and energy security.

Sweden's neutral foreign policy has led to its politicians taking on key international roles, often mediating between conflicting groups. The country joined the European Union in 1995 but declined to join NATO and the single European currency, with voters rejecting euro membership in a 2003 referendum. Today, Sweden continues to thrive, with its unique economic model and commitment to social welfare and sustainability serving as a model for other countries to follow.

A petition is to be delivered to Prime Minister David Cameron and Home Secretary Theresa May, calling for a reversal of a decision to deny visas to the grandparents and aunt of a five-year-old girl who died after being hit by a car in Eastbourne. Andrea Gada's mother, Charity Gada, will be joined by family and friends as she presents the petition, which argues that the family poses no risk to the country and simply wishes to support her and grieve the loss of her child.

The case was raised in Parliament by local MP Stephen Lloyd, who urged the Prime Minister to intervene. Although David Cameron agreed to look into the matter, the Home Office has upheld its decision to deny the visas, citing immigration rules. The family's application was reviewed for a second time, with the Home Office considering "compelling and compassionate circumstances," but ultimately deciding against granting the visas.

Andrea's mother has expressed her devastation at being separated from her family during this difficult time. She claims that the Home Office denied the visas because her family is "too poor," assuming they would attempt to stay in the UK illegally. The local community has rallied around Mrs. Gada, raising money to help her family attend the funeral. In a heartfelt plea, Mrs. Gada said, "At the heart of it, all I really want is to have my mother at my side whilst I grieve the loss of my child." The petition highlights the human cost of strict immigration policies and the need for compassion in exceptional circumstances.

Charlie Hebdo Releases New Edition with Defiant Cover

The French satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo has released a new edition, just one week after a devastating terrorist attack on its offices. The cover features a caricature of the Prophet Muhammad holding a sign that reads "I am Charlie" under the headline "all is forgiven". This move is seen as a defiant statement against extremism, with the magazine's lawyer Richard Malka stating that staff will "cede nothing" to terrorists.

The attack on Charlie Hebdo last Wednesday resulted in the deaths of 12 people, including five of the magazine's top cartoonists. The gunmen responsible claimed to have "avenged the Prophet Muhammad" after the magazine had previously published cartoons depicting him. Despite the tragedy, Charlie Hebdo is refusing to back down, with three million copies of the new edition being printed, a significant increase from the usual 60,000.

The magazine's staff, who have been working from the offices of another French title, Liberation, have created the new edition without contributions from other cartoonists. The edition is a powerful statement of the magazine's commitment to freedom of speech and its refusal to be intimidated by extremism. As the magazine's financial director, Eric Portheault, stated, the new edition will be created "only by people from Charlie Hebdo", a testament to the magazine's resilience and determination.

Plans for a major shake-up of health services in Herefordshire and Worcestershire have been unveiled, with a focus on merging certain departments and investing more in GP services. The proposed changes aim to keep patients out of hospital and address the significant funding gap facing the local health and social care system. According to the draft NHS plan, despite increased funding, the current projections indicate that it will not be enough to meet future demands.

The Herefordshire and Worcestershire Sustainability and Transformation Plan identifies potential savings of £5.4m on planned operations and suggests reducing spending on low-priority treatments. Community hospitals may be transformed into local hubs providing outpatient and support services, allowing patients to receive care closer to home. Sarah Dugan from Worcestershire Health and Care NHS Trust emphasized the need for collective action to address the challenges facing the health and care system.

The proposed changes have been welcomed by Dr. Mike Smith, chair of the Patients Association, who stressed the importance of consulting with the community. He noted that treating patients at home is often preferable, provided they can access the necessary social care. The Wye Valley NHS Trust and Worcestershire Acute Hospital are facing significant financial pressures, with required savings of £18m and £24.9m respectively for the 2017-18 period. The plans aim to ensure the long-term sustainability of health services in the region.

Plymouth City Council has taken a significant step towards transforming its waterfront by exchanging contracts to purchase the Quality Inn hotel. The 10-storey building, deemed an "eyesore" by the authority, has been a magnet for anti-social behaviour since its closure two years ago. Council leader Tudor Evans stated that the site would make an "amazing location" for a new hotel, and discussions are already underway with interested parties. The council plans to demolish the building, which was constructed in the late 1960s, to make way for a new development. Although the purchase price remains undisclosed due to "commercially sensitive discussions," a report on the acquisition will be presented to the Cabinet for discussion. This move is expected to revitalize the area and enhance the city's stunning waterfront.

A victim of the 2005 London Tube bombings is still waiting for compensation over a decade after the devastating attack. Stefano Poborko, 52, suffered severe burns and was left using a wheelchair after a suicide bomber detonated a device on a train between King's Cross and Aldgate. The attack, which was one of four explosions targeting three Tube trains and a bus, claimed the lives of 52 people and injured over 770 others.

Mr. Poborko, who now lives in Newbridge, Caerphilly county, was running late for a work meeting on the day of the attack. He suffered burns to his back, head, and ear in the blast and witnessed a fellow passenger die in his arms before emergency services arrived. The traumatic experience has had a lasting impact on his life, and he now relies on his fiancée, Louise Britt, as his primary carer.

In March 2015, Mr. Poborko applied to the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (CICA) for compensation, but he is still awaiting a decision. The CICA is a government body responsible for compensating people who suffer physical or mental injuries arising from violent crime. Despite the authority's claim that it deals with all applications "as quickly and sensitively as possible," Mr. Poborko's case has been plagued by delays, including issues with his medical records being misnamed on the CICA's system.

Recent figures show that the CICA took an average of over 11 months to reach a first decision on cases in 2015-2016, which is slightly longer than the previous year. The authority attributes the increase to the "changing nature of our caseload." However, for Mr. Poborko, the wait has been frustrating and debilitating. He hopes to gain compensation as some "recognition" of what he has been through and to improve his quality of life by enabling him to buy his home instead of renting.

Mr. Poborko's solicitor, Glyn Maddocks, believes that his client is entitled to compensation despite the claim being outside the two-year limit stipulated. "He was a victim of a crime which was the terrorist outrage on 7 July," Mr. Maddocks said. "He witnessed it, the experiences that he had and what he saw on that day are horrific and life-changing, and he's entitled to receive compensation from the public body because of that."

A CICA spokesperson expressed sympathy to all victims of crime and stated that the authority is committed to resolving applications as quickly and sensitively as possible. However, for Mr. Poborko, the wait continues. "I want it sorted – it's ridiculous," he said. "All I was doing was running late for work, and I got blown up. I just want to get on with my life, with Louise, in our home." As he waits for a decision, Mr. Poborko's condition, which includes multiple sclerosis, continues to affect his daily life. He hopes that the compensation will bring some sense of closure and enable him to move forward with his life.

Cardiff City has signed Canadian winger Junior Hoilett after his departure from QPR. The 26-year-old expressed his excitement, stating he's "ready to go" and aims to bring creativity and goals to the team. Meanwhile, striker Marouane Chamakh and centre-back Sol Bamba underwent medicals ahead of their free transfers. Chamakh, a 32-year-old Moroccan, was released by Crystal Palace, while Bamba, 31, left Leeds United due to personal reasons. The additions are expected to bolster Cardiff's squad, with Hoilett eager to get started and make an impact under the team's manager. The new signings are a positive move for the club.

The FTSE 100 experienced a significant surge, rising 45.41 points to 6,873.52, with Tullow Oil leading the charge. The oil company's shares soared 5.1% as the price of Brent crude surpassed $60 a barrel, boosting investor confidence. The upward trend was also evident in mining shares, with BHP Billiton and Glencore increasing by 5% and 3.7%, respectively. Despite reporting a 25% drop in underlying annual operating profit, Anglo American's shares rose 3.3%, demonstrating the sector's resilience.

The positive sentiment was further fueled by news of stronger-than-expected growth in Germany, with the economy expanding by 0.7% in the fourth quarter. This growth lifted the German stock index, the Dax, to a record high, and had a ripple effect on the UK market. Rolls-Royce, despite cutting its profit forecast for 2015, saw its shares rise by over 4%. The company's diversified business and cost-cutting measures are expected to help it withstand potential declines in demand.

In contrast, BT Group's shares fell 2.4% after Virgin Media announced plans to invest £3bn in its fibre optic broadband network. The move is set to increase competition in the sector, putting pressure on BT to respond. On the currency markets, the pound remained stable against the dollar at $1.5388, while slipping 0.03% against the euro to €1.3486. Overall, the market's positive performance was driven by rising commodity prices and encouraging economic data from Germany, with investors remaining cautious amid ongoing market uncertainties.

Raspberry Pi Foundation Releases Pixel Desktop for PCs and Macs

The Raspberry Pi Foundation has announced that its Pixel desktop environment, previously exclusive to Raspberry Pi devices, is now available for PCs and Apple Mac machines. This move aims to provide a consistent user experience across different platforms, making it easier for users to work on projects regardless of the device they are using.

According to Eben Upton, co-creator of the Raspberry Pi, the new release is particularly beneficial for schoolchildren who use the Raspberry Pi in class or for personal projects, but often have to continue their work on PCs or Macs. With the Pixel desktop now available on these machines, users can enjoy the same productivity software and programming tools in the same desktop environment, eliminating the need to adapt to different operating systems.

The foundation believes that this release will also help to improve the overall quality of the Pixel desktop, as it will highlight areas of the user interface that require attention. Upton noted that the core software underlying Pixel is based on a relatively old computer architecture, making it compatible with "vintage" machines. However, he cautioned that the software is still experimental and may have minor issues or bugs that could affect its performance on some devices.

The Pixel desktop was first introduced in September and is based on the open-source Linux software, Debian. The desktop version for PCs and Macs lacks two programs, Minecraft and Mathematica, which are only licensed for use on Raspberry Pi devices. With over 10 million Raspberry Pi devices sold, the foundation is committed to providing the best possible desktop computing experience for its users. The release of Pixel for PCs and Macs is a significant step towards achieving this goal, and the foundation is eager to receive feedback from users to further improve the software.

Met Police Close Lord Sewel Investigation Due to Lack of Evidence

The Metropolitan Police have closed their investigation into Lord Sewel, the peer who resigned from the House of Lords in July after being filmed allegedly taking drugs with prostitutes. The decision comes after a thorough inquiry, which included a raid on a property in central London and a forensic examination of the address. According to Scotland Yard, there was "insufficient evidence to proceed" with the case.

The incident led to widespread calls for reform of the House of Lords and prompted Lord Sewel, 69, to quit as deputy speaker and chairman of the Lords Privileges and Conduct Committee. He later resigned from Parliament altogether, apologizing for the "pain and embarrassment" caused and stating that his exit would help repair the damage to the reputation of the Lords.

The BBC's home affairs correspondent, Danny Shaw, said the decision to close the investigation seemingly draws a line under the episode. The Met Police launched the inquiry on July 27, following a complaint about Lord Sewel's conduct. With the case now closed, attention is likely to turn back to the broader issue of reforming the House of Lords. Lord Sewel's resignation had highlighted concerns about the accountability and conduct of members of the upper house.

Australia's cricket match was abandoned due to rain, leaving their semi-final hopes uncertain. Chasing a target of 183, Australia were 83-1 after 16 overs when the rain arrived, falling short of the minimum required overs for a game. This is Australia's second abandonment, and they now face a must-win situation against England to reach the semi-finals.

Captain Steve Smith expressed understanding for the umpires' decision, stating that the groundsmen did their best despite a lack of urgency. Smith was willing to continue playing through the rain but acknowledged the umpires' authority. The abandonment has added pressure to Australia's campaign, and they must now secure a win against England to advance. Australia's previous match against New Zealand was also abandoned, but Smith admitted they "got away with one" on that occasion. The team's fate now hangs in the balance as they prepare for their crucial match against England.

A fire broke out in a downstairs flat on Railway Road, Leigh, at 03:20 GMT Wednesday. Two people were rescued from a bedroom using a nine-metre ladder. They were "shook up but OK". The fire is suspected to have been started deliberately, according to Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service.

Scotland's Parliament Debates Trident Renewal Ahead of Vote

The Scottish Parliament has engaged in a heated debate on the issue of Trident renewal, with ministers and MSPs from various parties presenting their arguments for and against the proposed £167bn replacement of the UK's nuclear weapons programme. The debate, which was opened by Minister Keith Brown, highlighted the deep divisions within the Labour party on the issue, as well as the strong opposition from the Scottish National Party (SNP).

Minister Brown criticized the massive budget allocated for the Trident replacement, questioning why the funds could not be redirected to offset welfare cuts. He argued that the UK government's prioritization of nuclear weapons over social welfare was misguided, particularly in light of the "massive cuts" being introduced. Brown emphasized that the UK government's enthusiasm for nuclear weapons was misplaced, and that the renewal of Trident would have significant implications for conventional defense forces and public spending.

The debate also saw Dumbarton MSP Jackie Baillie, the only Labour member to vote against the call to reject renewal, defend her position. Baillie, whose constituency includes the Faslane naval base, which houses Trident, argued that the base was the largest employer in the area, providing "good-quality, well-paid jobs" to over a quarter of West Dunbartonshire's full-time workforce. She accused the SNP of engaging in "gesture politics" and ignoring the concerns of workers who would be affected by the cancellation of Trident.

However, Labour MSP Claire Baker countered that opposition to Trident renewal was her party's "clear position," citing the strong case presented against the programme at the Scottish Labour conference in Perth. Baker acknowledged that cancelling Trident would have significant consequences for the workforce and communities relying on the jobs, but emphasized that the fundamental argument against nuclear weapons was a strong one.

Conservative MSP John Lamont criticized Labour's stance on the issue, describing it as "muddled." He pointed out that UK Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and Scottish leader Kezia Dugdale held different views on Trident, with Corbyn opposing renewal and Dugdale supporting multilateral disarmament. Lamont argued that unilateral disarmament would severely damage the UK's national security and potentially encourage other states to acquire nuclear weapons.

The debate reflects the complex and divisive nature of the Trident renewal issue, with different parties and politicians holding strongly opposing views. As the UK government prepares to make a decision on the programme, the arguments presented in the Scottish Parliament highlight the need for careful consideration of the implications of renewal, including the impact on jobs, national security, and public spending. The outcome of the vote will be closely watched, as it may have significant consequences for the future of the UK's nuclear weapons programme.

UK Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson has called for a more balanced distribution of defense spending within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato), stating that it is unjustified for the United States to account for approximately 70% of the alliance's defense spending. In a speech to the Royal Institute of International Affairs at Chatham House, Johnson emphasized the need for all Nato member countries to meet the agreed target of spending 2% of their gross domestic product (GDP) on defense, as well as allocating 20% of their defense budget to new equipment.

Johnson's remarks come amidst concerns over the future of Nato, particularly after US President-elect Donald Trump described the Western military alliance as "obsolete" during his election campaign. Trump suggested that the US would think twice about coming to the aid of any Nato ally under attack if it had not paid its "fair share" of defense spending. The UK, which meets the commitment to spend 2% of GDP on defense, has also been urging other countries to increase their contributions.

In his speech, Johnson reaffirmed the UK's commitment to collective Nato defense, citing the security guarantee contained in the North Atlantic Treaty Article 5, which states that an attack on any one member shall be considered an attack against them all. He emphasized the importance of this institution, describing Nato as "the most durable and successful defense alliance in history." Johnson also acknowledged that the world is facing significant challenges, including the "cult of the strong man," democracy in retreat, and an "arc of instability" across the Middle East.

Despite these challenges, Johnson expressed his confidence in the ability of the UK and its allies to defend and preserve the rules-based international order. He stated that the UK must "redouble our resolve" to prevent a return to "an older and more brutal system where the strong are free to devour the weak." Johnson also committed Britain to working with its allies to address these challenges, including the ongoing tensions with Russia over Crimea and the bombing campaign in Syria.

In a notable departure from previous UK policy, Johnson stated that Britain would not oppose attempts by the European Union to form a common defense policy. He emphasized that the UK would not seek to block or impede further steps towards EU integration, provided that EU member states meet their defense spending commitments. This shift in policy reflects the UK's desire to maintain a strong and cooperative relationship with its European allies, even as it navigates its exit from the EU.

Johnson also addressed the issue of Russia, stating that strong defense did not preclude negotiations. He believed that pressure could be brought to bear on Russia to halt its bombing campaign in Syria, deliver Assad to peace talks, and abide by the letter of the Minsk agreements in Ukraine. Johnson emphasized that the UK could not "normalize" relations with Russia or return to "business as usual" until these conditions were met.

In conclusion, Johnson's speech highlights the UK's commitment to Nato and its desire for a more balanced distribution of defense spending within the alliance. The UK's willingness to support EU efforts to form a common defense policy also reflects its desire to maintain a strong and cooperative relationship with its European allies. As the international community faces significant challenges, the UK's resolve to defend and preserve the rules-based international order remains unwavering.

England cricket star Sarah Taylor has taken a significant step towards returning to the sport after joining the team's training camp in preparation for the World Cup. The 27-year-old wicketkeeper-batter had been on an indefinite break to address anxiety issues. Despite being initially left out of the squad, Taylor has now linked up with the 24-member team. The squad will play two intra-squad games and three matches against Ireland as part of their preparations.

Taylor's central contract was renewed in December with the aim of having her fit for the World Cup. Her return to training is being gradually managed, with regular reviews to ensure she reaches full fitness. Coach Mark Robinson confirmed that Taylor is "going really well" and her goal remains to participate in the World Cup. The team has also been bolstered by the addition of former Lancashire all-rounder Tom Smith to the coaching staff. Smith was forced to retire in January due to injury. With Taylor's return and the new coaching appointment, England's prospects for the World Cup are looking increasingly positive.

Tragedy at Chelmsford Care Centre: Inquest Reveals Multiple Failings

An inquest into the death of Matthew Leahy, who was found hanged in his room at the Linden Centre in Chelmsford, has exposed a series of shocking failures in his care. The Chelmsford Coroner's Court heard that Mr. Leahy's paperwork was incomplete, and he had not been assigned a key worker. Coroner Caroline Beasley Murray delivered an open narrative verdict, calling for the health trust to consider an inquiry into the circumstances surrounding Mr. Leahy's death.

The court was told that Mr. Leahy had been subjected to "multiple failings and missed opportunities" during his time at the centre. Despite his history of drug-induced psychosis and previous threats of self-harm, he did not have a care plan in place. In a disturbing twist, it was revealed that staff had falsified a care plan after his death and back-dated it. One member of staff has been sacked and will face a disciplinary hearing, along with two others. The North Essex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust has insisted that these actions did not affect the quality of care Mr. Leahy received. The inquest highlighted the need for urgent action to prevent similar tragedies from occurring in the future.

Nigerian President Muhammadu Buhari has provided an update on his health, stating that he has made significant progress but will remain in the UK for further medical treatment. The 74-year-old leader has spent more time in the UK than in Nigeria since the start of 2017, sparking concerns about his ability to govern the country.

In a statement, President Buhari acknowledged that he is eager to return home but is being held back by his doctors. "I feel I could go home, but the doctors are in charge," he said. "I've now learnt to obey orders, rather than be obeyed." The president also expressed gratitude for the support he has received, citing a "tremendous improvement" in his health.

The nature of President Buhari's illness remains undisclosed, fueling speculation and demands for transparency from protesters in the capital city of Abuja. Some have called for his resignation, while others have urged the government to be more open about his condition. Deputy President Yemi Osinbajo has been appointed to carry out the president's duties in his absence.

President Buhari's health challenges have raised questions about his potential candidacy for the 2019 presidential election. If he is unable to seek re-election, it could lead to tensions between different factions in the country. The health of Nigerian leaders has been a sensitive topic since the death of President Umaru Musa Yar'Adua in 2010, who passed away in office after months of treatment overseas. For now, President Buhari remains in the UK, with his return to Nigeria uncertain.

Arsenal and Everton have discovered their opponents for the upcoming Europa League group stage. The Gunners, who finished fifth in the Premier League last season, will be competing in Europe's second-tier competition for the first time in 20 years. They have been drawn into Group H alongside BATE Borisov, Cologne, and Red Star Belgrade.

Everton, who secured their spot in the competition with a play-off victory over Hajduk Split, will face a challenging group. They have been drawn into Group E alongside Lyon, who will host the final on May 16, 2018, as well as Italian Serie A side Atalanta and Apollon Limassol of Cyprus.

The Toffees are returning to European competition for the first time since the 2014-15 season. The group stage is set to begin on September 14, with 48 teams competing across 12 groups. Other notable teams in the competition include AC Milan, who will face Austria Vienna, Rijeka, and AEK Athens in Group D, and Athletic Bilbao, who will take on Hertha Berlin, Zorya Luhansk, and Ostersund in Group J. The competition promises to be exciting, with a range of talented teams vying for the top prize.

Young People Share Body Image Struggles in #BodyPositive Campaign

An 18-year-old university student, Nikki, has bravely shared her story of struggling with body image issues. Despite pursuing a career as a mental health nurse, Nikki has faced her own demons, including self-harm and suicidal thoughts. With the support of her school and GP, she sought treatment for anxiety and depression. Nikki's story highlights the importance of addressing body image concerns, particularly among young people. According to the charity Young Minds, poor body image can affect many teenagers, exacerbated by media portrayals of the "perfect" body. Those with pre-existing mental health issues may find it even harder to cope. By sharing her story, Nikki hopes to inspire others to open up about their own struggles, promoting a culture of acceptance and support. The #BodyPositive campaign aims to encourage honest and heartwarming accounts from young people.

A 28-year-old man from Edinburgh has been found guilty of attempting to murder an infant in his care. Ross Dunn was left in charge of the baby and her older sister when the child's mother went out on November 17, 2013. However, instead of providing proper care, Dunn shook the little girl and struck her against a surface, leaving her with severe and lifelong disabilities.

The child's mother testified in court, describing the devastating impact of the attack on her daughter's life. "She is not mobile," she said. "She is very floppy like a small baby. She will likely never stand, walk, or even sit by herself." The court heard that Dunn had claimed the injuries were the result of an accident, but prosecutors argued that the pattern of multiple injuries was consistent with shaking.

The advocate depute, Bruce Erroch, described the consequences of Dunn's actions as "the most appalling combination of disability for a baby to live with for the rest of her life." He also noted that Dunn had admitted to having problems with his temper, which likely contributed to the violent outburst. The sentence has been deferred pending background reports, but it is clear that Dunn's actions will have a lasting impact on the young victim and her family.

A campaign to give on-duty blue light workers priority service at cafes in Ripon has gained momentum after a chance encounter between a paramedic and a local resident. Gail Carpenter was inspired to take action when she saw a paramedic waiting in line at a cafe, only to be called away to an emergency before she could purchase her lunch. Moved by the paramedic's situation, Carpenter wrote a post on Facebook, which was shared hundreds of times and sparked a wave of support for the idea.

The post struck a chord with many people, including those who have relied on emergency services in the past. Comments poured in, with individuals expressing their appreciation for the selfless work of paramedics and other blue light workers. Kathy Myers, a commenter, shared her own experience of frequently being called away from food queues, while Jacqui Morrell expressed her respect for emergency services workers, having needed their help herself two years ago.

The campaign caught the attention of Liz Guest, owner of Big Bites cafe in Ripon, who has since implemented a priority service policy for on-duty blue light workers. Guest explained that she understood the importance of providing a quick and efficient service to these workers, who often have to sacrifice their breaks to respond to emergencies. By offering priority service, Guest hopes to make a small but meaningful contribution to supporting the local emergency services community.

Paramedic Jacqui Pound, who inadvertently sparked the campaign, expressed her gratitude for the outpouring of support. She emphasized the importance of being able to take quick breaks, which can make a significant difference in the ability of paramedics to respond to emergencies effectively. Richard Bentley, a paramedic and Unison member, also welcomed the initiative, acknowledging that while he initially felt hesitant about jumping the queue, he now fully supports the idea. As the campaign continues to gain traction, it is clear that the people of Ripon are eager to show their appreciation for the hardworking men and women who serve their community.

A stunning exhibition of insect photographs, titled Microsculpture, has opened at Oxford's Museum of Natural History. The show features 24 large-format images, some measuring three metres wide, taken by British photographer Levon Biss. Biss's passion for insect photography was sparked by his son's fascination with a ground beetle found in their garden. Using a microscope, Biss was amazed by the beetle's beauty and decided to capture its details through photography.

To create the intricate images, Biss photographs each insect in approximately 30 sections, using strobe lights to highlight the micro-sculptural beauty of each section. The individual shots are then merged to form a detailed, large-format picture. The result is a breathtaking display of the tiny creatures' intricate details. The Microsculpture exhibition will be on display at the museum until October, offering visitors a unique glimpse into the tiny world of insects. Biss's work is a testament to the beauty and complexity of these tiny creatures.

Nottinghamshire Police Face Budget Cuts and Potential Referendum

Nottinghamshire Police are facing significant budget cuts, resulting in a 25% reduction in community support officer numbers. The force needs to save £2.4m from its budget due to government cuts, which will also lead to the closure of four police stations and five front counters. Unison, the union representing police staff, believes that an above 2% rise in council tax could help mitigate these cuts and is calling for a public referendum on the issue.

However, Police and Crime Commissioner Paddy Tipping is skeptical about the success of such a referendum, citing the example of a recent vote in Bedfordshire where a proposed increase in the police precept was rejected by 70% of the population. Tipping stated that he is willing to discuss the issue but does not think that people will vote for an increase.

Despite the challenges, a recent report from HMIC found that the force is making good progress towards achieving the required savings while maintaining an effective service to the public. Unison's Dave Ratchford pointed to a consultation conducted by the commissioner last year, which showed that 67% of respondents were willing to pay additional money to protect police services, and 82% were against further cuts. The debate highlights the difficult decisions facing police forces across the country as they struggle to balance budgets and maintain public services.

A 24-year-old man has been jailed for a vicious and unprovoked attack on a stranger in Bellshill. Kieran Kiely, who had absconded from Castle Huntly prison just four days earlier, targeted 37-year-old Christopher Smith on July 17. The High Court in Glasgow heard that Kiely approached Mr Smith as he worked on his Renault Clio 172 sport car and began talking to him about the vehicle.

However, the conversation quickly turned violent as Kiely announced his intention to steal the car, punching Mr Smith and smashing a half brick into his face. The attack continued as Kiely kicked and hit Mr Smith with the brick, stealing his car keys, house keys, and mobile phone in the process. Despite being severely injured, Mr Smith managed to immobilize the car by pulling out leads from under the bonnet.

As Kiely tried to escape, Mr Smith ran for help, but was chased and continued to be attacked. The ordeal only ended when police arrived, prompting Kiely to flee and discard the stolen keys. Kiely was later arrested and found to be wearing clothes with Mr Smith's blood on them. The victim suffered severe bruising and three head wounds, which will leave permanent scarring.

Kiely, who has a history of convictions including car theft and assault, admitted charges of assault, theft, and attempted theft. Judge Lord Boyd condemned the attack as "vicious and unprovoked," stating that it must have been a "terrifying ordeal" for the victim. Kiely was subsequently jailed for his crimes. The court's decision reflects the severity of the attack and the need to protect the public from individuals with a history of violent behavior.

A Devon doctor who came to the aid of an elderly woman on a flight from Gatwick to Thessaloniki, Greece, has been offered a free flight by Easyjet after initially being rewarded with just a free hot drink. Dr Ed Southall, from Totnes, was on the flight in January when he was asked to assist the woman. Despite his good deed, he was only offered a complimentary coffee, and was even told he would have to pay for a Kit Kat.

Dr Southall made several requests to Easyjet to inquire about their policy on rewarding passengers who provide medical assistance, but was met with a lackluster response. He was offered free baggage handling, but it wasn't until he wrote to travel reporter Simon Calder that the airline took notice. Easyjet has since apologized and offered Dr Southall a free flight as a gesture of goodwill.

The airline stated that they are "grateful for the assistance Dr Southall provided" and acknowledged that they "didn't get this right" on the occasion. Dr Southall expressed that all he wanted was an apology, saying "you would think an airline would encourage people to help." The incident highlights the importance of recognizing and rewarding passengers who provide crucial assistance during flights.

Sir Bob Geldof Brings Together Music Stars for Band Aid 30

In a remarkable display of musical unity, Sir Bob Geldof has gathered some of the biggest names in the industry to record the fourth version of the iconic charity single, "Do They Know It's Christmas?" The star-studded lineup includes One Direction, Rita Ora, Olly Murs, Chris Martin, Sam Smith, Bono, and Ellie Goulding, among others. As the musicians came together to lend their voices to the cause, Sir Bob's witty one-liners kept everyone entertained throughout the day.

The recording session was filled with memorable moments, including One Direction's soulful rendition of the song's opening lines. Sir Bob was impressed, saying, "It's beautiful. I mean seriously. I never expected that from them. It's very moody the start, and they just come sort of whispering in. It's great." He also noted that many of the younger artists, such as Ellie Goulding, Sam Smith, and the One Direction guys, grew up singing this song at their nativity plays.

The new version of the song features changed lyrics that reflect the current Ebola outbreak in West Africa. When asked about the revised lyrics, Sir Bob was tight-lipped, jokingly swearing and saying it was meant to be a surprise. However, he did reveal that there would be a fight over Bono's re-vamped line, which has become a notable aspect of the song. Chris Martin was initially hesitant to sing the line, saying it belonged to Bono, but Sir Bob eventually convinced him to give it a try. After Bono recorded the line, Sir Bob described it as "mega."

The song will make its debut on The X Factor results show, but fans won't be able to download it until Monday morning. Sir Bob explained that this is due to technical reasons, and the version played on The X Factor will be a rough edit. He also revealed that Simon Cowell, not many people know, always joins in on these charity efforts and offered him five minutes on The X Factor to promote the single.

Other notable artists who were involved in the project include Bastille, who gave up two stadium shows in America to fly back and participate. Sir Bob praised their dedication, saying they didn't receive any compensation for their time or expenses. Unfortunately, not all artists were able to join in, including Adele, who is currently taking a break from music, and Jake Bugg, who had a prior gig commitment in Rio.

Sir Bob emphasized that the true spirit of Band Aid 30 is about being part of an event and turning it into a phenomenon. He encouraged fans to support the cause by purchasing the single, rather than streaming it for free. "Don't do any of the free stuff, it's nonsense. Pay for it," he said. With the song's release on Monday, Sir Bob is confident it will reach number one by 8am. As the music world comes together to support this worthy cause, one thing is certain – Band Aid 30 is an event not to be missed.

Co-ordinated Protests Bring UK Cities to a Standstill as Activists Demand Action Against Racial Injustice

A wave of protests swept across the UK on Friday, with campaigners blocking major roads and transport links in London, Nottingham, and Birmingham. The co-ordinated action, which saw 19 people arrested, was timed to coincide with the fifth anniversary of the death of Mark Duggan, who was shot by police in 2011.

The protests, organized by a national network of anti-racists, brought severe disruption to holidaymakers driving to Heathrow airport, as well as commuters in Nottingham city centre. In London, activists barricaded the junction leading to Heathrow, causing tailbacks and delays for those trying to reach the airport. A spokesman for the airport confirmed that while there were significant delays, no one missed their flight as a result of the action.

In Nottingham, protesters lay across tram tracks outside the Theatre Royal, bringing the city's transport network to a standstill during rush hour. The city centre was described as "gridlocked" as traffic struggled to navigate the blocked roads. Meanwhile, in Birmingham, campaigners blocked a road near the city's airport, causing further disruption to traffic.

The protests were met with a significant police response, with officers using specialist cutting machinery to remove the activists, who had linked arms and sealed themselves in tubes filled with concrete. In total, 19 people were arrested in connection with the protests, with four people charged with wilful obstruction of a highway by Nottinghamshire Police.

The activists behind the protests say they are demanding action against racial injustice and police brutality. Wail Qasim, who helped organize the Heathrow protest, said: "There's a constant disruption of black people's lives in the everyday. We face everyday forms of racism, from stop and search to increased levels of unemployment and over-representation in the prison system." Cara Thompson, part of the Nottingham movement, added: "We need people to listen, to really stop and listen to what is happening to black people - not just in the USA, but here in the UK."

The national organization behind the protests says it is seeking to create a movement similar to the Black Lives Matter campaign in the US. In a statement, they said: "We have shutdown roads in London, Birmingham, Manchester, and Nottingham to mourn those who have died in custody and to protest the ongoing racist violence of the police, border enforcement, structural inequalities, and the everyday indignity of street racism."

The protests are expected to continue throughout the day, with further demonstrations planned in cities across the UK. As the activists continue to demand action against racial injustice, it remains to be seen what impact their efforts will have on the government and law enforcement agencies. One thing is certain, however: the protests have brought the issue of racial inequality to the forefront of the national conversation, and it will be difficult to ignore the voices of those demanding change.

A former ice hockey player who represented Great Britain has been jailed for sexually exploiting young girls. Tom Squires, 26, pleaded guilty to one count of sexual activity with a child and four counts of inciting sexual activity with a child. The offences took place between 2011 and 2016, against five girls under the age of 16, in the Sheffield area.

Squires, who played for the Sheffield Steelers and Hull Stingrays, used social media to approach his victims and request sexual images. He also used his position as an ice hockey coach to groom and exploit the girls, some of whom recognized him as a local hockey star. Squires was sentenced to five years and four months in prison, and will spend an additional three years on extended licence after his release. He has also been barred from working with children. Detective Sergeant Aneela Khalil-Khan praised the bravery of the victims in coming forward, and warned that Squires' actions were a clear abuse of his position of power and trust.

Tragedy Strikes: Cyclist Killed in Accident Involving Beer Delivery Truck

A devastating incident occurred on July 3, 2014, in Nottingham city centre, resulting in the loss of a young life. Louise Wright, a 29-year-old cyclist, was fatally dragged under a beer delivery truck driven by Adam Haywood, 31, from Whitwell in Derbyshire. The tragic event has left the community in shock and highlighted the importance of road safety.

According to prosecutors, Haywood failed to check his mirrors before turning left at traffic lights, leading to the fatal accident. The trial at Derby Crown Court revealed that Wright had cycled down the left side of the lorry and waited near the front of the vehicle, a practice not recommended by the Highway Code, but not illegal. The prosecution argued that Wright would not have been aware of Haywood's intention to turn left, as he did not have his indicators on.

Haywood claimed he had checked his mirrors before turning left but did not see Wright, attributing her presence to his blind spot. However, he could not recall whether he had put on his indicators, which he stated was his usual practice. The Highway Code advises drivers to indicate their intentions, although it is not a legal requirement.

The jury delivered a majority verdict, finding Haywood guilty of causing death by careless driving. Judge Jonathan Bennett sentenced Haywood to an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, and banned him from driving for two years. Additionally, Haywood was ordered to perform 150 hours of unpaid work and pay £1,500 in costs.

Speaking after the verdict, Wright's mother, Sharon Brown, expressed her emotions, stating, "Nobody is a winner in this. It is just tragic what has happened." She acknowledged the verdict and sentence, saying, "I do feel the right verdict has been reached and the sentence was fair." Brown poignantly reflected on the what-ifs, highlighting the fleeting nature of life and the devastating consequences of a momentary lapse in concentration.

Judge Bennett echoed Brown's sentiments, stating, "There are no winners in this particular case." He emphasized the need to "balance justice and mercy" in such tragic circumstances. The incident serves as a stark reminder of the importance of vigilance and responsible behavior on the roads, and the need for drivers and cyclists to be aware of their surroundings and follow safety guidelines. The community mourns the loss of a young life, and the case will undoubtedly have a lasting impact on all those involved.

Mike Phillips, the 33-year-old Welsh scrum-half, is set to join Aviva Premiership club Sale in the summer on a one-year contract from French side Racing 92. When asked if Sale could be his last club before retirement, Phillips remained uncertain, stating that he will assess his body and performance over the next few months. The five-cap British and Irish Lions player has had a storied career, playing for Bayonne, Ospreys, Cardiff Blues, and Scarlets. After five years in France, Phillips is eager to return to the UK and finish his career on a high note. He expressed enthusiasm for Sale, citing positive conversations with former players and coaching staff, and believes the club is "moving in the right direction." Phillips, who retired from international rugby in 2015, is looking forward to this new chapter in his career.

A rare bird species, the White's thrush, has been spotted in Scotland for the first time using a camera trap. The Wildlife Conservation Research Unit (WildCRU) at Oxford University's Zoology Department set up the camera trap in the Woodland Trust Scotland's Ledmore and Migdale Woods, near Bonar Bridge. The primary goal of the camera trap was to monitor for wildcats, but it captured an unexpected surprise.

The camera trap, triggered by changes in heat and motion, took a photograph of the White's thrush, which breeds mainly in Siberia and Asia. Project manager Kerry Kilshaw expressed her delight at the discovery, crediting her field assistant Ruiradh Campbell for spotting the bird in one of the camera trap photos. WildCRU director Prof David Macdonald praised the technology, saying it has revolutionized field research, providing "eyes in the backs of our heads" and enabling breakthroughs in monitoring endangered species.

The Ledmore and Migdale Woods site manager, Eleanor Garty, highlighted the area's diverse wildlife, including scarce summer visitors such as wood warblers and tree pipits. The discovery of the White's thrush is a significant bonus, demonstrating the woods' importance as a habitat for rare migrants. The camera trap's success underscores the value of innovative technology in conservation efforts, allowing researchers to gather valuable insights into the lives of elusive and endangered species.

BBC England Launches Festive Photo and Video Submission Campaign

To celebrate the festive season, BBC England is inviting the public to submit their photographs and videos inspired by the classic "12 Days of Christmas" song. The campaign, titled England's Big Picture, encourages individuals to share their creative and festive captures via email, social media, or Instagram using the hashtag #englandsbigpicture.

Those wishing to participate can email their submissions to england@bbc.co.uk or post them on Facebook and Twitter using the handle @BBCEngland. The BBC also has a dedicated Pinterest board, England's Big Picture, where a recent archive of pictures can be viewed.

When submitting images, participants are asked to include relevant information and ensure that their photos were taken within the past week. By submitting content, individuals agree to grant the BBC a royalty-free, non-exclusive license to publish and use the material. However, contributors retain the copyright to their work, and their names will be published alongside their accepted images.

The BBC reminds participants to prioritize their safety and the safety of others while collecting media and to respect all laws and regulations. While not all submissions are guaranteed to be used, the BBC looks forward to receiving a wide range of creative and festive submissions to showcase on their platforms.

In a surprising move, the British Horseracing Authority (BHA) has ruled that Diore Lia, a 1,000-1 outsider, will not be allowed to compete in the upcoming Derby at Epsom. The decision was made due to concerns over the inexperience of the horse's jockey, Kayleigh Mangan, who has only ridden one winner in her career, back in 2009 at Roscommon. 

The news has sparked controversy, particularly as the prize money from the race was set to be donated to Great Ormond Street's children's hospital. Owner Richard Aylward expressed his disappointment, stating that he would now refuse to run the horse. Aylward claimed that the BHA had "been got to" and had changed their mind, potentially due to pressure from other stakeholders.

The BHA defended their decision, citing the need to prioritize the welfare of both human and equine participants. In a statement, they noted that while Mangan holds a license, her lack of experience, with only 69 rides and one winner, made it a risk to allow her to compete in a high-stakes event like the Derby. The authority emphasized that the unique challenges of the Derby, including its scale and stage, made it an unsuitable platform for an inexperienced jockey.

The total purse for the Derby is a record £1.625m, with the winner set to receive £920,913. Despite the charitable intentions of Diore Lia's owners, the BHA's decision has been supported by some in the racing community, who argue that the risk of an incident occurring with an inexperienced jockey is too high. BBC Sport horse racing correspondent Cornelius Lysaght noted that while the story has a "romantic, David against Goliath" quality to it, the authority's decision is likely correct, given the potential consequences of an accident. The incident has sparked debate about the balance between charitable intentions and the need to prioritize safety in high-stakes sporting events.

Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink has parted ways with Queens Park Rangers (QPR) after a disappointing run of results. The 44-year-old Dutchman, who was appointed in December last year, won only 14 of his 47 matches in charge. His departure comes after a 1-1 draw with Nottingham Forest on Saturday, leaving QPR 17th in the table and six points above the relegation zone. Despite their poor form, the team is still within six points of sixth-placed Leeds in a tightly packed league table. Hasselbaink had been under pressure following a run of just two wins since August. The club has stated that an announcement regarding the managerial situation will be made in due course. Former Tottenham and Aston Villa boss Tim Sherwood has been linked to the job. Hasselbaink's tenure was also marred by controversy, including a Daily Telegraph investigation alleging corruption in football.

Gloucester's 22-year-old player, Evans, suffered a serious injury during last Saturday's 18-17 loss to Bath. The injury occurred in the first half after a tackle by Matt Garvey, who received a yellow card. According to Gloucester boss Nigel Davies, the injury appears to be a ligament issue and is "pretty serious." Davies expressed disappointment, stating that Evans had been playing exceptionally well and was close to international honors. Evans, who came through the club's academy, had made significant progress this season, earning his first Premiership and Heineken Cup starts. His injury is a significant blow to the team.

A "data protection issue" has been raised at the annual general meeting of DG Unlimited, a regional arts organization. The meeting, chaired by Cathy Agnew, was attended by members from across Dumfries and Galloway. Agnew confirmed that two members had raised concerns about the handling of private details. The issue is understood to center on the sharing of members' personal information without proper consent. Dumfries and Galloway Council has been made aware of the potential breach and is providing advice and assistance to investigate the matter. Although the council considers it an independent organization's issue, it is offering support to help resolve the problem. DG Unlimited operates four arts hubs across the region, covering Annandale and Eskdale, Nithsdale, the Stewartry, and Wigtownshire. The organization was established after the previous region-wide arts group, dgArts, ceased trading. An investigation is currently underway.

Joe Henson, founder of the Rare Breeds Survival Trust, has been made an MBE for his conservation services. He received the honor at Windsor Castle, accompanied by his wife Gill and children Louise and Adam, a farmer and TV presenter. The Henson family has run the Cotswold Farm Park since 1971. Henson expressed delight at the recognition, citing the park's ongoing work in saving rare breeds. He was particularly pleased to receive the award from Princess Anne, a rare breeds advocate. The honor acknowledges Henson's dedication to conservation and his lasting impact on the field.

A key witness in the trial of Ronnie Coulter, accused of murdering Surjit Singh Chhokar in 1998, has testified that the defendant and his nephew Andrew Coulter made disturbing comments about the victim on the day of the fatal stabbing. Donna Campbell, 33, took the stand at the High Court in Glasgow, recounting a conversation she overheard at Ronnie Coulter's flat in Overtown, North Lanarkshire, on the evening of November 4, 1998.

At the time, Ms. Campbell was just 15 years old and had been dating Andrew Coulter for a couple of weeks. She was in the flat with her friend Corrine Chambers, as well as Ronnie and Andrew Coulter. According to her testimony, the men were discussing a plan to meet Mr. Chhokar later that night regarding a £100 Giro cheque. Ms. Campbell initially seemed hesitant to recall the specifics of the conversation, but when pressed by prosecutor Alex Prentice QC, she revealed that Ronnie and Andrew Coulter had been "laughing and joking" about Mr. Chhokar.

Ms. Campbell stated that one of the men had mentioned hitting Mr. Chhokar on the knees with a bat, and when asked to elaborate, she referenced a statement she had given to police in 2012. In that statement, she had said that Ronnie and Andrew Coulter were "laughing and joking about going to see Chhokar" and that one of them had said they were going to "batter him." When asked to confirm the accuracy of this statement, Ms. Campbell replied, "Yes."

Under cross-examination by defence QC Donald Findlay, Ms. Campbell acknowledged that the conversation had been "not particularly nice" but seemed to downplay its significance. She agreed that the tone had been "joking or light-hearted" and suggested that the men may have been "talking big" to impress her and her friend. However, the jury has already heard that Ronnie and Andrew Coulter, along with David Montgomery, did indeed meet Mr. Chhokar in Garrion Street later that night, and that the encounter ended in tragedy.

Mr. Chhokar, 32, was fatally stabbed and left dying in the street. Ronnie Coulter, 48, denies murder and has lodged a special defence blaming his nephew Andrew Coulter and David Montgomery for the crime. The trial, which is now in its third week, continues before Judge Lord Matthews. As the prosecution presents its case, the jury must weigh the evidence and consider the events of that fateful night in 1998. The testimony of Donna Campbell has provided a glimpse into the events leading up to the tragic death of Surjit Singh Chhokar, and the trial will continue to unfold in the coming days.

A young Dublin boy's heartfelt message to boxer Michael Conlan has led to a special gift. Finn McManus, who had written to Conlan after his controversial loss at the Rio Olympics, was presented with custom-made boxing gloves on RTÉ's The Late Late Show. The gloves bear both Finn's and Conlan's names, fulfilling a promise the boxer made after receiving the youngster's message of support.

Finn had offered Conlan his school medal and words of comfort after the boxer's quarter-final bantamweight bout against Russia's Vladimir Nikitin. The message, written by Finn's sister Lily, was sent to Conlan via Facebook and later shared on Twitter, where it sparked a "social media storm." Conlan, who won bronze at the London 2012 Olympics, described the message as "very warming" and vowed to send a gift to his young fan.

Conlan, who recently confirmed he is turning professional, made headlines at Rio 2016 with his outspoken criticism of the judges who decided against him. Despite the controversy, he remains a beloved figure in Irish boxing, and his gesture to Finn has only added to his popularity. The custom-made gloves are a touching tribute to the young boy's kindness and a reminder of the power of sport to inspire and connect people. Conlan is currently in negotiations with promoters as he prepares to embark on his professional career.

British Cycling Faces Funding Uncertainty Amid Governance Concerns

Sport England, the organization responsible for funding grassroots sports, has warned British Cycling that it must meet the highest standards of governance before receiving its allocated £17m in funding. This comes after a draft report into the culture of British Cycling's elite program was leaked, revealing concerns about decision-making within the governing body. The report, which is due to be released imminently, follows accusations of bullying and sexism against elite cyclists.

British Cycling's chairman, Jonathan Browning, has already apologized for "failings" within the organization, and the body has begun working on an action plan to address the issues. However, Sport England's chair, Nick Bitel, has stated that more work is required on this plan before funding can be released. Bitel emphasized the importance of ensuring that all sports organizations receiving public funding meet the highest standards of governance.

The funding in question is intended for grassroots cycling programs, and Sport England is keen to ensure that it is being used effectively. The organization's board will review the final report of the Cycling Independent Review and a revised version of British Cycling's action plan before making a decision on any additional requirements. This decision is expected to be made within the next month.

The warning from Sport England has significant implications for British Cycling, with the potential for the organization's leadership to be called into question. Unless substantial reforms are implemented, there is a possibility that Sport England may demand the replacement of Jonathan Browning as chairman. The fate of the £17m in funding hangs in the balance, and British Cycling must take immediate action to address the concerns surrounding its governance and culture.

A 27-year-old cold case has taken a significant step forward with the arrest of a woman in connection with the death of a newborn baby. The infant's body was discovered at Windmill Pit in Weasenham St Peter, Norfolk, on June 5, 1988. The woman, who has since been released on bail, claimed the baby was stillborn and that she had concealed her pregnancy from family and friends. Norfolk Police exhumed the baby's body last April to conduct tests. While the woman was initially arrested on suspicion of infanticide, the Crown Prosecution Service is considering all options, including charges related to failing to register the birth and preventing a lawful burial. Detective Inspector Andy Guy expressed sympathy for the woman, who has carried the secret for nearly three decades, and confirmed that police do not believe anyone else was involved in the incident.

Trefeglwys Community Council to Dissolve Amid Ongoing Dispute

The Trefeglwys Community Council will cease to function after the upcoming polls on May 4, with its responsibilities being absorbed by Powys Council. This decision comes after a three-year dispute that has taken a significant toll on the community council's ability to serve its residents. The row, initially sparked by plans to build pylons in the area, has led to investigations by the Information Commissioner, One Voice Wales, and the police.

According to a letter sent to Powys Council, the ongoing dispute has caused "disruption and distress" for the community council, resulting in the resignation of two clerks. The councillors have stated that they are no longer able to effectively serve the community due to the time-consuming and disruptive nature of the issue. The community council has also incurred significant costs, including solicitors' fees and extra hours paid to clerks.

Powys Council has announced that temporary councillors may be appointed as an interim measure to ensure a smooth transition. A meeting to discuss the future of the community council will be held on May 18, after the elections. The dissolution of the Trefeglwys Community Council marks the end of a tumultuous period for the community, and residents will be looking to Powys Council to provide stability and effective governance moving forward.

A recent survey by uSwitch has revealed that a significant portion of Britons will be carrying credit card debt into the new year. Approximately 85% of respondents stated that they will still be paying off their credit cards in 2017, with an average debt of £636. Furthermore, over half of those surveyed believe they will still be settling their Christmas expenses by the time next year's festive season arrives.

The survey, which questioned 1,261 adults, found that 65% are concerned about their level of debt. This concern is echoed by Bank of England Governor Mark Carney, who has warned about the high debt levels within British households. The survey also revealed that 19% of respondents spent beyond their means over the festive period, with a quarter doing so to capture the "magic of Christmas". The main reasons cited for overspending were the increased expense of Christmas this year and the pressure to keep up with others.

Lena Dunham Takes a Stand Against Unrealistic Beauty Standards with Unretouched Magazine Cover

Actress and writer Lena Dunham is making a bold statement against unrealistic beauty standards by appearing on the cover of Glamour magazine's February issue with her cellulite on full display. The issue, which is 100% produced by women, features Dunham alongside her Girls co-stars Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, and Jemima Kirke. Dunham took to Instagram to express her pride and gratitude to the magazine for allowing her to showcase her natural beauty, imperfections and all.

In her post, Dunham reflected on her past struggles with body image, revealing that she was often told she was "funny looking" as a teenager. She recalled being self-conscious about her "potbelly, rabbit teeth, knock knees," and feeling haunted by careless comments and hostility. However, Dunham emphasized that she never hated her own appearance, but rather the culture that perpetuated negative body image.

Dunham's decision to appear unretouched on the cover of Glamour is a significant statement, particularly given her history of speaking out against the use of Photoshop in the media. Earlier this year, she complained about a Spanish magazine that allegedly used "mad Photoshop" on a photo of her, only to later retract her statement after the magazine claimed it had not altered the image.

The actress has long been known for her confidence and willingness to bare her skin on television, but she has also faced criticism and scrutiny over her body. Dunham noted that when her career began, people would often comment on her appearance, framing it as a "bold move" to show her body on TV. However, she argued that this kind of commentary only serves to perpetuate the idea that women's bodies need to be perfected or hidden.

By appearing on the cover of Glamour without retouching, Dunham is taking a powerful stand against the unrealistic beauty standards that plague the media. Cellulite, which affects people of all sizes, is a natural and inevitable part of the aging process, and Dunham's decision to showcase it proudly is a refreshing change from the airbrushed and Photoshopped images that typically dominate magazine covers. As Dunham herself said, "I never want to be retouched again," and her commitment to promoting body positivity and self-acceptance is an inspiration to women everywhere.

World Champion Shi Dominates 3m Springboard Event

At the recent Olympic games, 24-year-old world champion Shi took home the top prize in the 3m springboard event with a score of 406.05. This impressive score left her nearly 20 points ahead of her nearest rival, compatriot He Zi. Italian athlete Tania Cagnotto secured the bronze medal in her final Olympic appearance.

Meanwhile, British diver Grace Reid made history by becoming the first British woman to reach the final of the 3m springboard event since 1972. The 20-year-old finished in eighth place with a final dive score of 67.50. Reid expressed her excitement and satisfaction with her performance, stating that she "loved every second" of the experience. She also joked about her mother, who used to be anxious about her diving, finally being able to watch her compete without worry. Reid's impressive debut has sparked excitement for the future of British diving.

Diego Maradona, the legendary Argentine footballer, has undergone a new gastric bypass surgery in Venezuela. The procedure took place in the city of Maracaibo, 10 years after his initial surgery. Despite the first operation, Maradona had gained weight and developed complications. According to Dr. Carlos Felipe Chaux, Maradona is recovering well and feeling fine with no pain. He will remain in Maracaibo for at least eight days before traveling to Caracas to complete his recovery. Maradona's health issues are well-documented, including struggles with obesity and alcohol addiction. The football icon led Argentina to World Cup victory in 1986 and has been in the spotlight recently, supporting the Argentine rugby team in the Rugby World Cup in England. Fans around the world are wishing Maradona a speedy recovery and hoping he will regain his health and well-being. His legacy as a football great continues to inspire fans globally.

Former lord mayor Nichola Mallon has been selected as the SDLP's candidate for North Belfast, replacing retiring MLA Alban Maginness. Mallon was chosen by party members at a convention in Belfast on Thursday. She expressed her gratitude, calling it a "great honour" to defend the seat and a "privilege" to take over from Maginness. Mallon praised Maginness' dedication to justice and human rights, saying his voice will be "sorely missed" from politics. SDLP leader Colum Eastwood endorsed Mallon, citing her compassion and dedication to the city's people, which made her a successful lord mayor. With her selection, Mallon is poised to bring her unique perspective and experience to the role, building on Maginness' legacy in North Belfast. Her candidacy is expected to be a strong contender in the upcoming election.

A mysterious blast that shook properties and sparked widespread speculation has been linked to activity at a Ministry of Defence (MoD) live firing test site in the Hebrides. The loud bang was heard across the islands, with residents in South Uist, Benbecula, and Barra reporting the incident. Sheila MacCormick, owner of the Borrodale Hotel in South Uist, described the moment the blast occurred, saying the building shook and people were left standing in the road, looking around in confusion.

Aviation authorities have ruled out the possibility of an aircraft's sonic boom, while initial speculation about an earthquake has also been dismissed. Instead, it is believed that the blast may have been related to a controlled explosion of out-of-date explosives at the MoD's Hebrides Range. Some residents reported receiving letters alerting them to activity at the rocket range, adding weight to this theory. The incident has caused concern among local residents, who were left wondering what had caused the loud noise. Despite the initial confusion, it appears that the blast was likely a planned event, although the MoD has yet to confirm the details.

Linfield have secured a vital away goal in their first round qualifying tie against Cork, thanks to a strike from Maguire. The goal sets up an exciting second leg at Turner's Cross next week. Northern Ireland goalkeeper Roy Carroll, making his debut for Linfield, played a crucial role in denying Cork a second goal with several fine saves.

The match saw both teams create scoring opportunities, with Paul Smyth missing a chance to score from six yards in the first half. Linfield, who finished as runners-up in the Irish Premiership and lost in the Irish Cup final, were without injured defender Sean Ward and Jimmy Callacher, who is on honeymoon.

Cork, currently second in the Irish Premier Division, came into the tie with confidence, but were unable to capitalize on their chances. Visiting goalkeeper Mark McNulty made several key saves, including tipping Ross Gaynor's free-kick over the bar and denying Kirk Millar and Karl Sheppard.

Maguire's goal broke the deadlock, and he continued to cause problems for the Cork defense, forcing Carroll into a point-blank save and flashing a shot narrowly wide. The second leg is set to be an intense encounter, with Linfield looking to build on their away goal and Cork seeking to overturn the deficit. With both teams creating scoring opportunities, the tie is far from over, and next week's match promises to be an exciting conclusion to the qualifying tie.

England Manager Roy Hodgson's contract is set to expire after Euro 2016, but FA chief Martin Glenn remains confident in his position. Despite a disappointing 2014 World Cup, where England failed to win a game, the team has shown significant improvement under Hodgson, winning all eight qualifying games for the upcoming tournament in France. Glenn stated that Hodgson is "very comfortable" with his situation and would not push for a contract extension if he doesn't perform well. This approach is a departure from the past, as seen with former manager Fabio Capello, who signed a new contract before the 2010 World Cup, only to be eliminated by Germany. Glenn also addressed England's image in the global game, acknowledging that the FA is often perceived as arrogant, but disagrees with this assessment.

A recent video sparked controversy when it appeared to show US President Trump refusing to shake hands with a young boy in a wheelchair at the White House. Renowned author J.K. Rowling was among those who expressed outrage, calling the president's behavior "stunning" and "horrible." However, the boy's mother, Marjorie Kelly Weer, has come forward to set the record straight.

According to Weer, the video clip did not accurately represent the interaction between her son, Monty, and President Trump. In fact, Trump had shaken Monty's hand as he entered the room. Weer took to Facebook to clarify the situation, stating that her son wasn't even trying to shake the president's hand and isn't particularly fond of shaking hands in general.

Rowling has since apologized for her misunderstanding, tweeting that she had "projected her own sensitivities" onto the situation. While she apologized to the boy and his family, she did not extend the apology to President Trump. The author has deleted her initial tweets on the subject, and the controversy appears to have been resolved. The incident serves as a reminder to be cautious when interpreting video footage and to verify information before jumping to conclusions.

Nottingham Man Admits to Human Trafficking and Forced Labour Charges
