A 43-year-old man from Nottingham has pleaded guilty to human trafficking and forced labour charges after exploiting a Polish worker. Sajmon Brzezinski, of Overdale Road, Old Basford, admitted to bringing the man to the UK in 2011 and forcing him to work for minimal pay.

According to police, Brzezinski paid the worker just £20 to £30 per week, despite earning £480. He also took control of the worker's passport and set up bank accounts in his name, but kept the bank card, preventing the worker from accessing his wages. The worker was told he owed £2,000, which he was forced to pay off through his labour.

The exploitation came to light when the worker confided in a colleague at a Christmas party. Brzezinski's arrest followed an investigation by the Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority (GLAA) and Nottinghamshire Police. The GLAA's head of operations, Ian Waterfield, said Brzezinski controlled the worker through threats of violence.

Brzezinski, who owned multiple cars and properties, including a "palace" with 50 windows in Poland, also admitted to a charge of fraud against another victim. His sentencing is scheduled for June 15. The case has highlighted the issue of modern-day slavery and the need for vigilance in detecting exploitation. Jon Hammond, who employed the worker on a farm near Arnold, Nottingham, described the situation as "shocking" and "abhorrent", saying it was "happening under our nose" without being detected.

Zambian Government Expels South African Opposition Leader Mmusi Maimane

In a shocking turn of events, South African opposition leader Mmusi Maimane was expelled from Zambia on Friday, just hours before he was set to attend a court appearance of Zambian opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema. The Zambian government cited concerns that Maimane's presence would put "undue pressure" on the judiciary, but Maimane and his party, the Democratic Alliance (DA), have condemned the move as a clear sign of Zambia's descent into dictatorship.

Maimane had planned to show solidarity with Hichilema, who was arrested in April and charged with treason after his convoy allegedly refused to give way to President Edgar Lungu's motorcade. The charges have been widely criticized as "trumped up" and an attempt to silence Hichilema, who narrowly lost to Lungu in last year's disputed presidential elections.

According to the DA, Maimane was "aggressively confronted" by police when his plane landed in Lusaka, and was "forcefully" prevented from entering the country. The party has called the Zambian government's behavior "shameful" and has urged the South African government to lodge a diplomatic protest.

Maimane has been vocal about his support for Hichilema, using social media to call for solidarity and awareness about the Zambian opposition leader's plight. He has argued that as a fellow African, he has a responsibility to speak out against oppression and stand in solidarity with those fighting for the rule of law.

The Zambian government, however, has defended its decision to expel Maimane, saying that his presence in court would have undermined the independence of the judiciary. Zambia's top diplomat in South Africa, Emmanuel Mwamba, said that it was imperative that the due process of the law was respected without undue pressure or interference.

The case against Hichilema is set to continue, with the magistrate's court ruling that his lawyers can seek a judicial review of the charges. If convicted, Hichilema faces a minimum jail term of 15 years and a maximum sentence of death. The international community is watching the case closely, with many calling for Hichilema's release and an end to the persecution of opposition leaders in Zambia.
Cyprus enjoys a free media landscape, with state-run and private operators competing, and unrestricted internet access for over 656,000 users, according to Freedom House.

A recent inspection at Queen's House, a private care home in Kelso, has highlighted concerns over staffing after a nurse was found to be working without suitable qualifications. The Care Inspectorate, which carried out the inspection, graded the facility's staffing as "weak", despite awarding excellent ratings in three other categories.

The incident, which was described as an "isolated incident" by Queen's House chairman Alastair Turnbull, involved a member of staff who was appointed to a position without being suitably qualified. An investigation was launched, involving the police and Scottish Borders Council's social work department, and the staff member was subsequently dismissed.

According to the Care Inspectorate, the issue was identified by the care service itself, which "acted swiftly and took the appropriate action". A spokesman for the inspectorate said that the safety, welfare, and dignity of service users were the top priority, and that they were satisfied that the well-being of residents was not affected.

However, relatives of residents have expressed concerns over the fact that the woman was not a registered nurse. Inspector Lesley Smith, who carried out the inspection in January, noted that Queen's House had a recruitment policy in place, but that it had not been "strenuously followed" in this instance.

Chairman Alastair Turnbull acknowledged that there had been an incident, but emphasized that it had been dealt with and that there was "no issue with care". He pointed out that the home had received excellent ratings in all other areas, and that the incident was an isolated one.

Queen's House is a not-for-profit home that cares for 32 older people, and is run by a voluntary management committee. The Care Inspectorate has emphasized the importance of robust recruitment practices in care services, particularly when working with vulnerable individuals. The incident highlights the need for care homes to ensure that staff are properly qualified and vetted to provide the highest level of care.

High Court Hears Shocking Alleged Confession in Murder Trial

A dramatic turn of events unfolded at the High Court in Glasgow as a key witness testified against Ronnie Coulter, the 48-year-old accused of murdering Surjit Singh Chhokar in 1998. Noreen McPolland, 54, took the stand and revealed a shocking alleged confession made by Coulter during a prison visit in 1998 or 1999.

According to McPolland, Coulter made the startling admission while she and his sister, Margaret Chisholm, visited him at Barlinnie Prison. When asked by prosecutor Alex Prentice QC if Coulter had ever spoken about Chhokar's death, McPolland replied, "He said 'I stabbed him'." She further testified that Coulter's sister had urged him to own up to his actions, prompting him to make the incriminating statement.

McPolland, who was married to Coulter's brother Andrew for 15 years, described her reaction to the alleged confession as one of shock and disengagement. She claimed to have gotten up and gone to the canteen, not wanting to be involved in the conversation. However, she did recall another instance where Coulter allegedly spoke about the murder, this time during a visit to his brother's home just days after Chhokar's death.

On that occasion, McPolland testified that her husband had asked Coulter if he had stabbed Chhokar, to which Coulter allegedly replied that he had. Coulter also reportedly mentioned that Chhokar was shouting for his partner, Liz Bryce, after being stabbed. The prosecution has alleged that Coulter, along with his nephew Andrew Coulter and David Montgomery, had gone to see Chhokar on the day of the murder over a dispute regarding a £100 Giro cheque.

The trial has heard that Andrew Coulter admitted to hitting Chhokar with a homemade lead-filled bat but denied stabbing him. Montgomery has also denied any involvement in the stabbing. Pathologist Dr. Marjorie Turner previously testified that Chhokar suffered three stab wounds to the chest and died from massive blood loss.

Notably, Ronnie Coulter was tried and acquitted of Chhokar's murder in 1999. However, the case was reopened, and Coulter now faces trial again, with a special defense blaming his nephew Andrew Coulter and David Montgomery for the crime. The trial, presided over by Judge Lord Matthews, continues, with the jury carefully considering the evidence presented. As the proceedings unfold, the court awaits further testimony and evidence that will ultimately determine Coulter's fate.

Bristol's homeless population is receiving support from two new initiatives. Keep Bristol Warm is collecting rucksacks filled with essential items at the city's Bearpit. Meanwhile, Pending Coffee has launched, allowing customers to buy extra cups for homeless individuals to claim. Organiser Gavyn Emery was inspired by a similar project in Edinburgh after seeing a man in need with his dog. With 74 people recorded as sleeping rough in Bristol, these projects aim to provide vital assistance. Emery's father described Pending Coffee as "people giving to people," highlighting the simple yet effective nature of the initiative.

A 27-year-old man from Kent is recovering after a lucky escape on Helvellyn. He fractured his ankle falling from Striding Edge, near Red Tarn, in "full-on winter conditions" on Thursday. The Patterdale Mountain Rescue Team responded, airlifting him to hospital in Carlisle with coastguard assistance. The four-hour rescue involved support from Penrith Mountain Rescue Team. Team leader Mike Blakey warned that Helvellyn is in full winter conditions, stressing the need for proper equipment, including ice axes and crampons, and knowledge of how to use them to enjoy the mountains safely.

A theme park playground incident has sparked a police appeal after two six-year-old girls were inappropriately touched by a man. The incident occurred on August 11 at Legoland in Windsor, Berkshire, in the pirate-themed Castaway Camp play area. One parent expressed surprise that an adult was inside the playground, stating she had not expected it and was more concerned about her child getting lost.

The assaults happened between 12:15 and 12:30 BST, when approximately 14,200 people attended the theme park. Thames Valley Police have released an e-fit of the suspect and will air a reconstruction on BBC One's Crimewatch, followed by a police appeal. The mothers of the girls shared their concerns, with one saying the incident was a shock, as Legoland was a highlight of their summer holiday plans. A man in his 20s from Bracknell was arrested but released without charge on August 31. The police are now seeking the public's help to identify the suspect and bring him to justice. The incident has raised concerns about safety at the theme park.

Hershey, North America's largest chocolate maker, has revised its sales forecast downward due to macroeconomic challenges in China. The company now expects net sales to increase by 2.5%-3.5% this year, a significant decrease from its previous prediction of 4.5%-5.5%. To adapt to changing consumer behavior, Hershey plans to cut 300 jobs and shift its focus to smaller format stores. The company will also prioritize brands with high returns. While sales in China have been slow, Hershey's North America confectionery business is thriving, driven by solid gross margin expansion. The company is on track to meet its 2015 financial objectives at home. Shares in Hershey fell over 2.5% in New York trading following the announcement. Despite this, the company remains a major player in the industry, producing iconic brands like Hershey chocolate bars and Reese's Peanut Butter Cups.

US Regulators Demand Improved "Living Will" Plans from Major Banks

The US Federal Reserve and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp (FDIC) have issued a stern warning to three major banks, including HSBC, Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS), and French bank BNP Paribas. The regulators have deemed the banks' "living wills" - plans outlining how they would be wound up in the event of a catastrophic shock - as inadequate and in need of significant improvement.

The plans, which were submitted as part of the 2010 Dodd Frank Act, failed to meet the required standards, with the FDIC describing them as "not credible". The regulators have called for the banks to make considerable changes, including improving derivative contracts to allow for quick termination in the event of bankruptcy. Additionally, the banks must ensure that critical functions can continue to operate during a crisis and that they can produce reliable information rapidly.

The warning comes as part of a broader effort to prevent a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis, where taxpayer funds were used to bail out struggling banks. The Dodd Frank Act requires banks to draw up living wills to demonstrate how they can navigate ordinary bankruptcy without relying on government assistance. The US Fed and FDIC have the power to shut down or split up the operations of a US bank or subsidiary of a foreign bank if their plans are deemed insufficient. This is not the first time regulators have criticized banks for their living wills, with 11 banks, including JP Morgan Chase and Deutsche Bank, being censured last year.

A 19-year-old man has been jailed for six months for religiously aggravated harassment of four Orthodox Jews, including a 13-year-old boy. Patrick Delaney, from Twin Oaks Caravan Park in Essex, admitted to the offense, which occurred on January 6, 2016, at Tottenham Hale retail park. Delaney, who was under the influence of nitrous oxide, yelled "Hitler" at the victims and threw gas canisters. One victim and her son took shelter in a nearby supermarket. Judge John Dodd QC condemned Delaney's actions as unacceptable in "any civilised society". The sentencing comes amid rising anti-Semitic hate incidents in the UK, with recent figures reaching record levels. Delaney's actions were widely condemned, highlighting the need for greater tolerance and respect for all communities.
An inventor has created a road-making method using recycled plastic to replace bitumen, combining it with rocks and sand for a sustainable alternative.

A 26-year-old man has been fined and ordered to pay court costs after stealing a pink beret from comedian Eddie Izzard during a Brexit march in London. David Czerwonko, of Clitherow Road, Brentford, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court where he pleaded guilty to the offense. The court heard that Izzard was leading the march down Whitehall when a group of masked men blocked the path with a large Brexit campaign banner. Izzard responded by condemning the group, calling them "the face of Brexit, masked and dangerous."

Czerwonko, who did not recognize the comedian, then snatched Izzard's beret, which had sentimental value due to its UK and EU badges. However, Izzard quickly chased after him and reclaimed the hat with the help of police. Czerwonko's defense argued that the act was an "instinctive and silly reaction" and not a premeditated attempt to cause trouble. The court acknowledged that the incident was spontaneous and that the beret was recovered.

Czerwonko was fined £185 and ordered to pay £85 in court costs, as well as a £30 victim surcharge. The incident has raised questions about the police's response to the incident, with Green Party peer Jenny Jones suggesting that Izzard's fame may have influenced the swift reaction and sentencing. Jones stated that it would be "fantastic" if all small crimes were treated with the same level of seriousness. The march was one of several rallies held across the country on the anniversary of the outbreak of World War II, calling for a pause in the Brexit process.

Gocompare Founder Hayley Parsons to Step Down in £190m Deal

In a significant development, Gocompare's founder and chief executive, Hayley Parsons, will be standing down from her position as part of a £190m deal. The company, which was started by Ms Parsons eight years ago, will continue to operate from its current headquarters in Newport. The deal, which requires regulatory approval, values Ms Parsons' remaining 23% stake at almost £44m.

Esure, which already owns 50% of Gocompare after investing in the company in 2010, will now take full control. Ms Parsons expressed her pride in the company's achievements, stating that it has become a leading price comparison business in the UK. She attributed this success to the hard work of her team in Newport.

Gocompare gained widespread recognition for its advertising campaigns featuring the fictional Italian tenor, Gio Compario. Ms Parsons, 41, has had a distinguished career in the insurance industry, having spent 14 years at Admiral insurance in Cardiff before setting up Gocompare in 2006. She has won several awards for her entrepreneurial achievements, including an OBE for services to the economy in 2012.

The deal marks a significant milestone for Gocompare, which has grown rapidly since its inception. Ms Parsons' decision to step down will likely have a significant impact on the company's future direction. However, with Esure at the helm, Gocompare is expected to continue its growth trajectory and remain a major player in the UK's price comparison market. The regulatory approval process is expected to be completed in the coming months, paving the way for a new era at Gocompare.

A Dundee University student is shedding light on the potential knee injuries faced by curlers, particularly those using the toe-sliding technique. Iona Robertson, who is studying applied orthopaedic technology, has been collecting data from members of the men's British curling team that competed in the 2014 Winter Olympics. The research sessions, held at The Peak sports village in Stirling, involved Olympians David Murdoch, Scott Andrews, and Michael Goodfellow.

As part of the study, the team members delivered 12 stones, with six from a flat foot slide position and six from a toe slide, while wearing in-shoe pressure measurement insoles. Robertson also recorded video footage of the deliveries to measure the knee angles of the players. Her preliminary findings suggest that toe-sliding may indeed be more likely to cause knee injuries, with significantly higher joint forces in the knee compared to flat-footed slides. Although the final results are not yet complete, Robertson is optimistic about the promising data collected so far. The study aims to understand and establish the differences in knee force between the two delivery techniques, providing valuable insights for curlers and coaches to minimize the risk of injury.

Share Your Photos with England's Big Picture

The BBC is inviting readers to share their favorite photos with England's Big Picture. Whether you've captured a stunning sunset, a bustling city scene, or a peaceful landscape, we want to see it. However, you still retain the copyright to your work, and we will publish your name alongside your photo if it's selected for use. Remember to always follow safety guidelines and respect the law when taking photos. We look forward to seeing your contributions to England's Big Picture.

Former Thai Monk Arrives in Bangkok to Face Charges

Wirapol Sukphol, a former Thai monk, has arrived in Bangkok to face charges of child molestation, child abduction, money laundering, and fraud. Sukphol, who was once known as Nen Kham, gained notoriety in 2013 after a YouTube video showed him on a private jet with luxury items. He was later accused of having sex with an underage girl and fled to the US, where he resisted extradition efforts.

Sukphol, who was expelled from the monkhood, arrived in Bangkok on Wednesday wearing clerical garments. He is expected to strongly contest the charges against him. The case has drawn attention to the scandals plaguing the Thai monkhood, which is a cornerstone of Thai society. The military, which has been in power since 2014, is under pressure to address the alleged excesses of the monkhood.

The charges against Sukphol include the discovery of millions of dollars in assets in his name. His case is one of several high-profile scandals involving the monkhood, including that of influential abbot Phra Dhammajayo, who is wanted on money laundering charges. The arrival of Sukphol in Bangkok marks a significant development in the case, and his trial is expected to be closely watched. The outcome may have implications for the reputation of the Thai monkhood and the military's efforts to reform it.

Turing Pharmaceuticals to Lower Price of Daraprim After Public Outcry

Following widespread criticism and outrage, Martin Shkreli, the CEO of Turing Pharmaceuticals, has announced that the company will lower the price of Daraprim, a life-saving medication used to treat a parasitic infection. The decision comes after Turing Pharmaceuticals raised the cost of the drug from $13.50 to $750 in August, sparking accusations of price-gouging.

Shkreli initially defended the price hike, stating that the increased revenue would be used to fund research and development of new treatments. However, the move was met with fierce criticism from medical groups, with one organization describing the price increase as "unjustifiable." The pharmaceutical industry's main lobbying group, PhRMA, also distanced itself from Turing, tweeting that the company "does not represent the values of PhRMA member companies."

In an interview with ABC News, Shkreli announced that the company would reduce the price of Daraprim to a more affordable level, allowing the company to make a "very small profit." While the exact price reduction has not been disclosed, the move is seen as a significant concession in the face of public pressure.

The controversy surrounding Daraprim highlights the complex and often contentious issue of drug pricing. In the US, prices are determined by a market-driven system, where private insurance companies and government programs such as Medicare and Medicaid negotiate with pharmaceutical companies. This can lead to significant price fluctuations, with some medications becoming prohibitively expensive for patients. The debate over fair pricing for life-saving medications is likely to continue, with many arguing that profits should not come at the expense of patient access to essential treatments.

Small Energy Providers Fear CMA Rule Change Will Stifle Competition

A group of six smaller energy providers has expressed deep concern over proposed new rules by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), which they believe will favor the "Big Six" energy companies and discourage competition in the market. The CMA's proposals, which follow its energy market review earlier this year, suggest that price comparison websites will no longer be required to show all available energy deals, but rather only those from companies that have paid them a commission or fee.

The smaller providers, including GB Energy Supply, COOP Energy, Go Effortless Energy, Bulb, So Energy, and Zog Energy, have written to Energy Secretary Amber Rudd, warning that this move will lead to a lack of transparency and create an unfair market. They argue that consumers use price comparison websites believing they will be shown the cheapest prices available, but under the new rules, these websites will only show deals from the Big Six suppliers who have paid for advertising.

"This will mean that millions of people will be misled into thinking they are getting the best deal, when in fact they are only being shown a limited selection of options," the providers said in their letter. "We are deeply worried about the serious ramifications of this proposal and urge the Government to think again."

The CMA's investigation into the energy market found that price comparison websites often allowed consumers to switch energy suppliers immediately, but it was not always clear that they only showed options from firms that had paid a commission or fee. The watchdog believes that allowing price comparison websites to prioritize certain deals will lead to increased competition and lower prices, as sites will be incentivized to compete for exclusive deals with suppliers.

However, the smaller providers disagree, arguing that this will only serve to strengthen the dominance of the Big Six energy companies. They point out that these companies already have a significant market share and will be able to pay more for advertising, making it even harder for smaller providers to compete.

Uswitch, the UK's third-largest price comparison website, has disagreed with the smaller providers' analysis. A spokesperson for the site said that price comparison websites offer a cost-effective way for energy suppliers to advertise their products and acquire customers. "The CMA's package of proposals will incentivise sites to compete for exclusive deals with suppliers, boost competition and lower energy prices for consumers," they said.

The Government has said that it wants a "competitive and effective energy market" that works for consumers. A spokesperson for the Department for Energy said that the number of energy suppliers has increased significantly since 2010, with over 40 providers now operating in the market, and smaller firms making up 15% of the dual fuel market.

The CMA is set to publish its final recommendations on remedies for the energy sector before the end of June. The smaller providers will be hoping that their concerns are taken into account and that the Government will reconsider the proposed rule change. If not, they fear that the energy market will become even more dominated by the Big Six, and consumers will lose out as a result.

Former Tory Chief Whip Andrew Mitchell has spoken out about the media storm that led to his resignation, claiming that his treatment by the press was "completely wrong". In an interview with Channel 4's Dispatches programme, Mr Mitchell denied allegations that he called Downing Street police officers "plebs" and insisted that he did not lose his temper during the incident on September 19 last year.

The altercation, which took place when a police officer refused to let Mr Mitchell exit through the main Downing Street gate with his bicycle, sparked a wave of media criticism and demands for his resignation. However, Mr Mitchell claims that the coverage was unfair and that he was "caught between the pincers of the police on the one hand and the media on the other".

CCTV footage of the incident has cast doubt on the original police accounts, and four people have been arrested in an investigation into their handling and reporting of the episode. Mr Mitchell's denial of the allegations has been supported by some, including Steve White, vice-chairman of the Police Federation, who attempted to distance the national organisation from the criticism of Mr Mitchell.

Despite this, Prime Minister David Cameron has repeated his desire for a "thorough" inquiry into the incident, and a Downing Street spokesman has said that the prime minister takes full responsibility for the way the case was handled. Mr Mitchell has also criticised Number 10's handling of the situation, claiming that they did not do enough to support him in the days following the incident.

The incident has raised questions about the relationship between the police and the media, and the impact of media pressure on public figures. Mr Mitchell's comments come as the Leveson Inquiry into media standards has highlighted the need for greater accountability and transparency in the way that the media reports on public figures.

In the interview, Mr Mitchell expressed his frustration with the way that the incident was handled, saying that it was "completely wrong" and that it led to his demise. He also argued that the media coverage made it appear that the Leveson Inquiry had never taken place, and that the principles of fairness and accuracy that it established had been ignored.

The Dispatches programme, which is due to be broadcast on Monday night, will provide a detailed examination of the incident and the surrounding controversy. It is likely to add to the ongoing debate about the relationship between the police, the media, and public figures, and the need for greater accountability and transparency in the way that the media reports on those in power.

England Rugby Coach Excited About Sam Burgess's Code-Switching Move

In a move that has sent shockwaves through the rugby world, Sam Burgess, the 25-year-old Australian rugby league star, has completed his highly-anticipated switch to rugby union. The former South Sydney Rabbitohs player has joined Bath Rugby Club, and England coach Stuart Lancaster has expressed his excitement about the prospect of Burgess representing England in the 2015 World Cup.

Lancaster praised Burgess's leadership qualities, mental strength, and ability as a player, saying, "He's got the ability as a player, but also as a leader. I think he's got great mental strength." The England coach cited Burgess's man-of-the-match performance in the NRL grand final, where he played on despite breaking a cheekbone in the opening minute, as evidence of his ability to adapt to the 15-a-side game.

Bath head coach Mike Ford echoed Lancaster's comments, saying that Burgess's mentality can take him "all the way to the top, to international rugby." However, Ford noted that it is still unclear which position Burgess will play in for the Aviva Premiership side, with options including the centres and back row. "He's gone out to Australia and actually been the best player in the competition, and that takes some mental strength to do that," Ford said.

Despite the excitement surrounding Burgess's move, not everyone is convinced that he can make a seamless transition to rugby union. Former England captain Martin Corry expressed his doubts about Burgess's credentials as a potential World Cup star, saying, "Sam has to come out and prove himself. The timeframe does scare me - can someone be fast-tracked so quickly?" Corry urged caution, saying that he doesn't want to get "caught up in the hype" surrounding Burgess's code-switching move.

Burgess, who is still recovering from the injury he suffered in October's grand final, is unsure when he will make his Bath debut. However, with Lancaster and Ford backing him to succeed, the young player is likely to be given every opportunity to prove himself in the rugby union arena. As Lancaster noted, "He's in a competitive position and he'll have to earn the right to get into our [England] team. But if he gets in our squad I'm sure he'll make an impact." Only time will tell if Burgess can live up to the hype and become a star player for England in the 2015 World Cup.

BBC Launches Digital Store with Over 60 Years of Content

The BBC has launched a new digital service, allowing the public to purchase and download over 60 years of its iconic shows. The BBC Store, available through bbcstore.com and the iPlayer, offers a vast library of content, including cult comedies, popular dramas, and even some previously banned programs.

The store boasts an impressive collection of BBC programmes, with prices starting at £1.89 per episode. Series can be purchased for £6.99, with prices clearly marked on the site. According to Marcus Arthur of BBC Worldwide, the prices are "broadly competitive" and offer a convenient way for fans to own their favorite shows.

Among the notable titles available are the 1976 Dennis Potter drama Brimstone and Treacle and the 1965 documentary The War Game, which depicts the impact of a nuclear war in Britain. Classic comedies such as Morecambe & Wise and Dad's Army can also be purchased digitally for the first time, along with legendary interviews conducted by David Frost.

In addition to its extensive archive, the BBC Store will offer exclusive content, including a series of Top Gear clips fronted by Matt LeBlanc. The store will also feature a "Best Of" collection from the popular car show. Furthermore, popular dramas like EastEnders and Holby City can be bought just a day after transmission.

The BBC plans to expand its service over time, offering "value added material" to shows, such as behind-the-scenes footage or cast interviews. The store's initial focus is on drama, comedy, and factual entertainment, including a collection of Sir David Attenborough's most memorable documentaries. However, the BBC hopes to include more content for children and music programming in the future.

The launch of the BBC Store marks a significant shift in the way the corporation makes its content available to the public. While consumers can still access BBC shows through subscription services like Netflix, the BBC Store provides a unique opportunity for fans to own and download their favorite programmes. The BBC iPlayer will continue to offer a free catch-up service for 30 days after shows have aired. With its vast library and competitive pricing, the BBC Store is set to revolutionize the way we consume and engage with BBC content.

Colombian Rebel Group Farc Urges Dissenters to Abandon Violent Path

The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) has issued a statement urging a group of rebel commanders to abandon their plans to continue the armed struggle. The call comes as the country prepares to implement a historic peace accord, which will see the Farc transform into a political party and lay down their arms.

The statement, released by the Farc, condemned the actions of five commanders who have allegedly refused to adhere to the peace agreement. The commanders, identified as Gentil Duarte, Euclides Mora, John Cuarenta, Giovanny Chuspas, and Julian Chollo, were based in a jungle area in south-east Colombia and had been part of the Farc's command structure until recently.

According to reports, the commanders may have left their base with a group of fighters, money, and arms, and are no longer following orders from the Farc central command. The Farc has warned that their actions could jeopardize the peace process, which has been years in the making.

The peace accord, signed last month by Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and Farc leader Timoleon Jimenez, aims to bring an end to the country's 52-year conflict, which has claimed the lives of at least 220,000 people. The agreement has been the result of four years of negotiations in Havana, and its implementation is seen as a crucial step towards lasting peace in Colombia.

However, there are concerns that some Farc members may be reluctant to give up their involvement in the lucrative cocaine smuggling business, which has been a key source of funding for the rebel group. The Farc has urged its members to abandon this "futureless path" and to work towards a peaceful and democratic future.

As the country moves forward with the implementation of the peace accord, there are still challenges to be overcome. Opponents of the deal, led by former President Alvaro Uribe, have expressed concerns that the agreement is too lenient on Farc leaders, and that it does not do enough to address the issue of impunity for those who have committed crimes during the conflict. Despite these challenges, the Farc's call for its members to abandon violence and work towards peace is a significant step towards a more peaceful and stable future for Colombia.

Spanish authorities have rescued two migrants from Guinea who were found hidden in a car during a customs check near the Moroccan border. The incident occurred late on Sunday at El Tarajal, a border crossing in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. The two men, identified as TD and AB from Guinea Conakry, were discovered suffering from a lack of oxygen and were given first aid by Spain's Guardia Civil police.

The migrants were found in a Mercedes 300 with false number plates, and two Moroccan men who were in the car at the time were detained by police. One of the migrants was hiding in the engine compartment, where he had been inhaling noxious fumes. The length of time he was exposed to the fumes is unclear. The migrants, who did not have any papers, are now under official investigation. This incident highlights the desperate measures some migrants take to enter the EU through Ceuta and Melilla, tiny Spanish enclaves on the North African coast.

Bali Nine Leaders Set to be Executed in Indonesia, Lawyers to File Constitutional Court Challenge

The leaders of the "Bali Nine" group of heroin smugglers, Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran, are one step closer to being executed in Indonesia after a court ruled that they cannot challenge the president's decision to refuse them clemency. However, their lawyers have vowed to take the case to the constitutional court, arguing that the president has an obligation to properly consider their exceptional rehabilitation.

Chan and Sukumaran, both Australians, were arrested in Bali in 2005 while attempting to smuggle heroin to Australia. They were found to be the organizers of a nine-member smuggling operation and have been on death row ever since. Despite their initial sentences, the two men have undergone significant rehabilitation, with many arguing that they have reformed and should be shown mercy.

The Indonesian President, Joko Widodo, has a policy of denying clemency to drug offenders, citing the huge damage that the drug trade has caused to Indonesia. Earlier this year, he rejected the clemency appeals of Chan and Sukumaran, paving the way for their potential execution. In January, he authorized the executions of six drug offenders, including five foreigners, and the two Australians are part of a second group of 10 foreign nationals who are set to be put to death.

However, their lawyers argue that the president's decision to reject their clemency appeals was not properly considered, and that their rehabilitation was not taken into account. "We believe that these men over the last 10 years have rehabilitated themselves and we are very concerned that that fact has not been properly and genuinely considered by the Indonesian authorities and the Indonesian legal system," said Michael O'Connell, one of the lawyers representing the men.

The case will now go to the constitutional court, where Chan and Sukumaran's lawyers will argue that the president has an obligation to properly consider their clemency appeals. The application is expected to be filed this week, with a preliminary hearing to follow in the coming weeks.

The news has sparked a passionate response from the Australian government, with Foreign Minister Julie Bishop stating that it is "important that all legal processes are allowed to run their course." The Australian government has mounted a diplomatic campaign on behalf of the two men, arguing that they have reformed and should be shown mercy.

Indonesia has faced criticism from other countries whose nationals are facing execution, including Brazil, France, Nigeria, and the Philippines. The executions have sparked a debate about the use of the death penalty, with many arguing that it is an inhumane and ineffective deterrent.

As the case continues to unfold, the fate of Chan and Sukumaran remains uncertain. While the Indonesian authorities have stated that they are waiting for all legal avenues to be exhausted before carrying out the executions, the two men's lawyers remain hopeful that their clients will be given a chance to have their clemency appeals properly heard. The world waits with bated breath as the story of the Bali Nine continues to unfold, a stark reminder of the complexities and challenges of the international justice system.

A revolutionary new treatment for heart attacks is being trialled at the Essex Cardiothoracic Centre, with a 50-year-old man becoming one of the first to benefit from the innovative procedure. Steve Jaggers, a maintenance worker at a care home, was rushed to Basildon Hospital in Essex last month after suffering a heart attack. In a bid to minimise damage to his heart, doctors used a pioneering technique known as "therapeutic hypothermia" to cool his body temperature from the inside.

The procedure involves inserting a catheter with a balloon into the main vein, which is then filled with a cool liquid to bring the body's temperature down. According to Dr Thomas Keeble, a consultant cardiologist, the goal is to cool the patient quickly while keeping their outside warm, much like a "baked Alaska". This helps to protect the heart muscle from further damage when the blocked artery is opened.

Mr Jaggers was fully conscious during the procedure, which he described as a "strange sensation". To prevent shivering, a common side effect of cooling, doctors used blankets to keep him warm. A stent was also inserted into his heart to keep the artery open. After the procedure, Mr Jaggers' body was slowly warmed up in recovery, a feeling he likened to being abroad in the sun. Remarkably, he now feels "completely fine", with no lingering effects from the heart attack. The Essex Cardiothoracic Centre is the only site in the UK currently trialling this groundbreaking technology, which has the potential to significantly reduce heart damage in patients suffering from heart attacks.

Crystal Palace manager Alan Pardew has confirmed that Yannick Bolasie is close to joining Premier League rivals Everton. The 27-year-old winger, who came on as a substitute in Palace's 1-0 home loss to West Brom, is expected to complete a move to Goodison Park. Pardew revealed that a "big offer" has been made for Bolasie and the deal is nearing completion. Although no medical has taken place, Pardew has given his blessing for the transfer to go ahead. Bolasie, a DR Congo international, has been with Palace since 2012 and was warmly applauded by the home crowd when he came on during Saturday's match. Pardew praised Bolasie's commitment, saying it showed his love for the club. The manager acknowledged that Palace will miss Bolasie if he leaves, but wishes him well. The transfer is expected to be finalized soon.

A Southampton school has reversed its decision to let pupils finish early to watch the England v Wales football match, following accusations of "hypocrisy" from term-time holiday campaigners. Oasis Academy Lord's Hill had initially planned to finish at lunchtime on June 16, allowing students to watch the Euro 2016 game. However, principal Ian Golding has since stated that it is "more appropriate" for pupils to stay in class, with the game being screened during school time instead.

The initial decision had been met with criticism from campaigners, including Jon Platt, who recently won a High Court ruling after refusing to pay a fine for taking his daughter on an unauthorised term-time holiday. Platt argued that the school's decision was hypocritical, given that they have fined parents in the past for taking their children out of school for holidays. "I understand that there is a little bit of hypocrisy here," he said. "This school has fined parents in the past for taking their kids out of school for holidays, so they are going to come in for a bit of stick."

In a statement, principal Golding said that the school takes attendance "extremely seriously" and that sporting events like the Euro 2016 match are "a cause for celebration and enjoyment" that can be experienced by pupils during school time. He announced that the game would be shown during the last hour of school time for those who wish to watch it, allowing students to enjoy the event together. The reversal of the decision has been seen as a victory for campaigners, who argue that schools should be consistent in their approach to attendance and term-time holidays.

A landmark ruling has been made in the High Court, deeming Westminster City Council's decision to ban a mother-of-three from re-applying for social housing in the borough for 12 months as unlawful. The woman, known as "Ms A", lost her home in March 2014 when her housing benefit was cut, leaving her unable to afford the rent. The council temporarily relocated her to north London and offered her temporary accommodation in Enfield, but also imposed a 12-month ban on applying for social housing in Westminster.

The family's lawyers argued that this ban breached the 1996 Housing Act, which requires councils to give homeless families "reasonable preference" for social housing. Judge Peter Blair QC agreed, stating that the ban was unlawful. Jayesh Kunwardia, the family's solicitor, welcomed the ruling, saying it makes clear that homeless people have the right to bid for social housing from the time they secure a full housing duty from a local authority.

The ruling highlights the significant challenges faced by those in need of social housing in Westminster, where demand far outstrips supply. Judge Blair noted that the waiting lists are "so vast" that applicants can expect a seven to 10-year wait before being allocated a permanent council home. The case has significant implications for local authorities and their treatment of homeless families, and is likely to have far-reaching consequences for social housing policy.

Yemen's Humanitarian Crisis Worsens as Two Million People Face Emergency Food Aid Shortage

The humanitarian situation in Yemen has reached catastrophic levels, with two million people in dire need of emergency food aid to survive, according to the United Nations. The warning comes as child malnutrition has risen by a staggering 63% in just one year, with a child under the age of five dying every 10 minutes from preventable causes.

The crisis is attributed to a combination of factors, including severe poverty, war damage, and a naval embargo imposed by the Saudi-led coalition. The blockade has had a devastating impact on food security, with approximately 14 million people currently facing food insecurity, including 2.2 million children who are acutely malnourished and nearly 500,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition.

Stephen O'Brien, the UN's emergency relief coordinator, has urged the Saudi-led coalition to lift its no-fly zone and reopen Sanaa airport, citing the "disproportionate impact" of the blockade on civilians. The closure of the airport has prevented life-saving medication from being flown in and has denied 20,000 Yemenis access to specialist medical treatment abroad.

The situation on the ground is dire, with Jamie McGoldrick, the UN's humanitarian coordinator in Yemen, describing the desperation of the population. "Everywhere you go, you see people begging in the streets in bigger numbers, you see people rummaging through rubbish to survive," he said. "You hear catastrophic stories of children dying because they can't get to health centers. People dying of malnutrition, people dying of preventable diseases."

The economic situation in Yemen is also in shambles, with the banking sector barely functioning and 1.25 million civil servants not receiving regular salaries. Widows, orphans, the disabled, and elderly are no longer receiving a monthly allowance from the government, leaving them without a safety net.

The conflict in Yemen, which has been raging for nearly two years, has destroyed half of the country's medical facilities, with some being bombed by the Saudi-led coalition and others struggling with funding shortages. The naval embargo has also crippled the country's ability to import food, with Yemen previously reliant on imports for 90% of its staple food.

Despite the gravity of the situation, Yemen's humanitarian crisis remains overlooked by donors and the international community, with the conflict attracting less attention than those in Syria and Iraq. The lack of media coverage has been attributed to the difficulty of accessing the country, with only UN flights allowed to land at Sanaa airport and Saudi Arabia restricting journalist access.

As the situation continues to deteriorate, the international community is being urged to take action to address the crisis. The UN is calling for an immediate lifting of the blockade and for increased funding to support humanitarian efforts. With wheat supplies expected to last only an estimated three more months, the clock is ticking for the people of Yemen, and urgent action is needed to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe.

A fatal car crash occurred in Irlam on Tuesday. A Daewoo Matiz collided with a Volkswagen Tiguan at the junction of Cadishead Way and Fairhills Road. The driver, a woman, and her 15-year-old passenger were trapped. They were freed by emergency services. The woman was airlifted to Wythenshawe hospital, where she died. The teenager was taken to Manchester Royal Children's Hospital. The Volkswagen driver, 52, is being treated for injuries at Salford Royal Hospital. Police are appealing for witnesses to come forward and contact Greater Manchester Police.

Kettering General Hospital has been criticized by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) for failing to provide adequate care and support to its patients. The CQC visited the hospital in June and found that "people did not always experience care, treatment and support that met their needs". This is the second damning report in just a few months, with the hospital being told to raise its quality and safety standards in May.

Despite making some significant improvements in areas such as cleanliness and infection control, the hospital was found to be lacking in its care and welfare of patients. Inspectors discovered that daily care plans were often brief and lacked important patient information, and in some cases, there were no instructions for staff to follow. The hospital was also found to have staffing issues, particularly at weekends, and was not providing enough specialist attention to children in Accident & Emergency.

The CQC has taken enforcement action against the hospital trust and has outlined a number of improvements that need to be made. The hospital's director of nursing, Clare Culpin, has stated that the hospital is "absolutely committed" to improving safety and the patient experience, and that action plans are in place to tackle the problems. The trust is acting on all issues raised by inspectors and is working to implement systematic changes to address the concerns.

Residents of Orchard Village in Rainham are at their wit's end as they continue to deal with a plethora of problems, including raw sewage, mice infestations, and gas leaks. The estate, which was opened in 2014, was built using £31m of public money as part of an £80m project to replace the notorious Mardyke housing estate. Despite its promising beginnings, the estate has been plagued by issues, leaving residents to suffer.

One resident, Colin Nickless, has had to endure a nightmare situation. He moved into the estate in 2015 to be near a special school for his daughter, who has cystic fibrosis. However, his family has been beset by problems, including wastewater leaks, roof leaks, and mould growth. His daughter has been hospitalized with a bacterial infection, while his son has been admitted with breathing difficulties. Nickless has dubbed the situation the "Orchard Village Sickness" or "Orchard Village Flu," highlighting the widespread nature of the issues.

The association managing the estate, Clarion Housing, has acknowledged the situation is "unacceptable" and has offered to buy back 58 of the 387 homes. However, some residents and local officials are calling for more drastic action. Havering UKIP councillor Phil Martin has suggested that the entire estate be demolished, citing the severity of the problems and the plummeting property values. "We've had residents living on sewer-soaked carpets for days before anything was done about it," he said. "The only solution is to start again from scratch."

Clarion Housing has stated that it is taking concerns seriously and has instructed specialists to conduct rigorous scientific tests to address the build defects. The organization's dedicated project team has already made significant progress, according to a spokesperson. Nevertheless, residents remain frustrated and concerned about their living conditions, and it remains to be seen whether Clarion's efforts will be enough to resolve the issues plaguing Orchard Village.

The Great British Bake Off returned to BBC One on Wednesday, attracting a massive audience of 10 million viewers at its peak. The popular baking competition, hosted by Sue Perkins and Mel Giedroyc, saw 12 amateur bakers embark on their journey to be crowned the latest winner. The show's premiere did not disappoint, with musician Stuart Henshall becoming the first contestant to leave after his bakes failed to impress judges Mary Berry and Paul Hollywood.

The episode was filled with drama, including a signature bake that completely collapsed after the contestant's chocolate mousse did not set. Dorret Conway's sunken gateau brought on the first tears of the series, setting the tone for what promises to be an exciting competition. The judges were tough but fair, providing constructive feedback to the contestants as they navigated the challenges of the first episode.

Sue Perkins made a triumphant return to Twitter ahead of the premiere, joking about a fictional "Swimwear Round" replacing the Showstopper Challenge. Her return to social media came after a four-month sabbatical, during which she faced a barrage of hateful tweets. Perkins and Giedroyc are a major part of the show's appeal, bringing their unique blend of humor and warmth to the hosting duties.

The show's massive audience and popularity have also sparked controversy, with Ladbrokes suspending betting on the show due to a flurry of suspicious wagers. The bookmaker reported a "run of bets" placed on one contestant, many of which were made in shops in the Ipswich area, leading to fears that the winner's name may have been leaked. Despite the controversy, The Great British Bake Off remains one of the most popular shows on British television, with its unique blend of baking, humor, and competition continuing to captivate audiences.

Hillary Clinton Set to Announce Presidential Bid, Eyes Democratic Nomination

In a move that has been widely anticipated, Hillary Clinton is expected to announce her candidacy for the 2016 presidential election on social media. The 67-year-old former First Lady and Secretary of State will then embark on a trip to Iowa and New Hampshire, two crucial early primary contests in the Democratic nomination process. This will mark Clinton's second attempt at the presidency, having previously run in 2008.

Clinton's decision to announce her candidacy on social media, rather than with a large, formal speech, is seen as a strategic move to connect with a wider audience and build momentum for her campaign. She is expected to release a video outlining her campaign themes, which will provide insight into her vision for the country and the issues she intends to prioritize.

As one of the most recognizable and experienced candidates in the Democratic field, Clinton is already considered a strong contender for the nomination. Her previous bid for the presidency in 2008 ultimately fell short, as she was defeated by then-Senator Barack Obama in the Democratic primaries. However, she has since gained valuable experience as Secretary of State under Obama, serving from 2009 to 2013.

Despite her impressive resume, Clinton's campaign is not without its challenges. She has recently faced criticism over her use of a private email address to conduct official business as Secretary of State, as well as her handling of public records. These controversies have raised questions about her transparency and accountability, which she will need to address in order to win over skeptical voters.

The Democratic field is currently relatively narrow, with Clinton as the clear frontrunner. However, she may still face challenges from other candidates, including former Maryland Governor Martin O'Malley and possibly Vice-President Joe Biden. Some on the left-wing of the party are also urging Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren to enter the race, although she has repeatedly stated that she is not running.

On the Republican side, two major candidates, Ted Cruz and Rand Paul, have already formally announced their campaigns. Several other high-profile Republicans, including former Florida Governor Jeb Bush, are also expected to enter the race. A Clinton-Bush matchup would revive the debate about powerful political dynasties in the US, with the Bush and Clinton families having produced three presidents between them.

As Clinton embarks on her campaign, she will need to demonstrate what she has learned from her past mistakes and how she plans to connect with voters. With a long and grueling campaign season ahead, Clinton will need to prove that she is ready to lead the country and that voters are ready for her. Only time will tell if she has what it takes to succeed where she fell short in 2008.

The search for a new bishop of Southwell and Nottingham is underway, with candidates being interviewed on Tuesday and Wednesday. For the first time, applications from women are being considered for the vacancy, following the Church of England's decision to allow women to become bishops. The move, which was formally adopted in November, marks a significant shift for the Church, which has previously restricted women from taking on senior roles.

After the interviews, a preferred candidate and a second preference will be put forward. However, no announcements will be made until 2015, as the appointment needs to be approved by the Queen on the recommendation of the prime minister. The vacancy arose after Bishop Paul Butler left to become the Bishop of Durham in January. The appointment is being closely watched, as it could potentially see one of the first women bishops in the Church of England.

Former Peterborough United player, Joe Gormley, has parted ways with the club due to a serious knee injury. Gormley, who joined Posh in 2015, became "disillusioned with football" after struggling to recover. He has returned to Northern Ireland and is seeking to return to part-time football. Director of football, Barry Fry, confirmed that all parties have written to Fifa for special dispensation to cancel his contract by mutual consent outside the January window. Gormley had previously broken records for goals scored at Cliftonville, but failed to score after turning full-time.

Catherine Coulson, the beloved actress best known for her iconic role as the Log Lady in the cult TV series Twin Peaks, has passed away. Her agent and friend, Mary Dangerfield, confirmed the news to The Hollywood Reporter, stating that the family has not yet disclosed the cause of death. Dangerfield expressed the profound sadness felt by all who knew Coulson, saying, "We are all deeply sad - she meant so much to so many."

Director David Lynch, who created Twin Peaks with Mark Frost, released a heartfelt statement mourning the loss of his dear friend. He praised Coulson's unwavering dedication to her work, her great sense of humor, and her spiritual nature. Lynch fondly remembered Coulson as "solid gold" and "a long-time meditator" who was always there for her friends and family.

Coulson's collaboration with Lynch began in the 1970s, when she appeared in his short film The Amputee and worked as an assistant director on his debut feature film Eraserhead. The idea for the Log Lady character was born on the set of Eraserhead, and Coulson brought the character to life in Twin Peaks, as well as in the prequel film Twin Peaks: Fire Walk With Me. Despite describing her character as the "only normal person on the show," Coulson noted that the Log Lady had experienced trauma and formed a deep bond with her iconic log.

Twin Peaks, which premiered in the early 1990s, was a groundbreaking series that won three Golden Globe awards in 1991. The show's influence can still be seen in modern TV dramas, and its legacy continues to endure. A sequel series, directed by Lynch, is set to air on Showtime next year. Coulson's passing is a significant loss for the Twin Peaks community, and she will be deeply missed by her friends, family, and fans around the world.

Valtteri Bottas edged out fellow Finn Kimi Raikkonen to top the timesheets in the final practice session for the Grand Prix, with Mercedes teammate Lewis Hamilton finishing third. Bottas' fastest lap was 0.095 seconds quicker than Raikkonen, while Hamilton was 0.416 seconds off the pace.

The session was a mixed bag for the championship contenders, with Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel struggling with a suspected water leak that limited him to just one quick lap. As a result, he finished 12th fastest, which will be a concern given his 12-point lead over Hamilton in the standings.

Hamilton, on the other hand, will be encouraged by his performance after a difficult Friday. He had struggled with tyre temperature and traffic, but was able to record a more representative lap in the final session. However, the margin to Bottas will still be a concern, and some of the deficit may be attributed to the fact that Bottas secured a slipstream from Red Bull's Max Verstappen on both his best laps.

Verstappen was looking strong before his engine cut out about 10 minutes before the end of the session, and he ended up sixth. His teammate Daniel Ricciardo finished fourth, 0.545 seconds off the pace, while the impressive Esteban Ocon in the Force India was fifth.

Williams' Felipe Massa finished seventh, ahead of rookie teammate Lance Stroll, who continues to show improved confidence after scoring his first points in Canada two weeks ago. Stroll's session ended with a trip into the escape road at Turn Two after overshooting his braking.

McLaren's Fernando Alonso finished 14th, but will start from the back of the grid due to a total of 40 places of grid penalties for using too many engine parts. Renault's Jolyon Palmer had another difficult session, pulling off early with flames and smoke pouring from the back of his car after crashing on Friday. Overall, the final practice session set the stage for an intriguing qualifying session, with the championship contenders looking to gain an edge ahead of the Grand Prix.

A 42-year-old man, Mohammed Khalil, was found seriously injured at his Sheffield home and later died in hospital. South Yorkshire Police have made four arrests in connection with the killing. Two 20-year-old men are in custody on suspicion of murder. A 26-year-old man, also detained on suspicion of murder, remains in custody. A 46-year-old man, arrested on suspicion of murder and possession of a weapon, has been released on bail as the investigation continues.

The Independent Monitoring Board (IMB) for the city centre jail is seeking to expand its membership from eight to 15 volunteers. The board ensures fairness and decency for all prisoners, and members are responsible for checking on inmates in solitary confinement and evaluating cell conditions. New members will receive training to prepare them for their duties.

According to Steve Cocks, chairman of the Cardiff IMB, the board is looking to diversify its membership, particularly seeking ethnic minority representation and younger individuals. Currently, the board consists of mostly white British members. Cocks described the role as "challenging but rewarding," with members having complete access to the prison as official representatives of the justice minister.

As part of their duties, members sample food, visit education facilities, and monitor the admission of new prisoners. They also attend disciplinary hearings and investigate serious incidents within the prison. The IMB plays a crucial role in ensuring the well-being of prisoners and bringing any concerns to the attention of those responsible.

A former hospital worker has been jailed for 16 months for stealing from semi-conscious patients at Morriston Hospital in Swansea. Jacqueline Perry, 49, from Morriston, pleaded guilty to nine counts of theft and was sentenced at Swansea Crown Court on Friday.

Perry's colleagues became suspicious about items disappearing and reported their concerns to the authorities, leading to a sting operation being set up by police. Marked bank notes were placed around Ward G, and when one disappeared, officers searched staff and found it in Perry's possession.

It was revealed that Perry had stolen a total of £2,739, including three gold rings worth £1,800 from an 89-year-old patient. The court heard that the thefts had a major impact on Perry's colleagues, with lead nurse Tina Smith stating that morale was affected as staff were all under suspicion. The patients targeted by Perry were described as "quite sick and quite vulnerable".

Perry's defense team claimed that the offenses were motivated by financial hardship, rather than greed, and that she had stolen the money to pay for alcohol for her husband. However, Recorder Christopher Clee QC described her actions as "a despicable offense" and said he had no good reason to suspend the sentence.

Perry will serve half of her sentence in prison and half on licence. Abertawe Bro Morgannwg University Health Board has apologized to the victims and stated that the sentence should "act as a deterrent" to others. The board emphasized that theft from patients or staff is a serious criminal offense and a severe breach of trust that will not be tolerated. Perry's actions have caused significant distress to her victims and former colleagues, and a disciplinary hearing will follow the court proceedings, which is expected to result in her losing her job.

Principals from 15 schools in Comber and Newtownards have joined forces to warn parents about the devastating impact of spending cuts on education. In a joint letter, the principals urged parents to contact local authorities, including MLAs, the Department of Education, and the Education Authority, to express their concerns about the issue. The letter stated that the cuts would result in fewer teachers and resources, larger classes, and ultimately, worse education outcomes for students.

The principals emphasized that every school in the area is facing a financial crisis, regardless of its size or enrollment numbers. They pointed out that over the past five years, the funding per child has only increased by 0.9%, while costs have risen by approximately 14.5%. This significant shortfall is having a "real, urgent, and disastrous" impact on schools.

In response to the letter, a spokesperson for the Department of Education claimed that providing financial assistance to schools has been a priority for Education Minister Peter Weir. The spokesperson highlighted that Mr. Weir had reallocated over £7m of new funding to the 2016-17 schools budget. However, the principals' letter suggests that this measure is insufficient to address the scale of the problem. In fact, Mr. Weir himself has stated that schools need an extra £240m over the next three years just to maintain spending at 2015/16 levels. The principals are calling on parents to take action and make their voices heard to prevent further damage to the education system.

A year-long project aimed at reducing patient frustration and aggression in NHS accident and emergency departments has yielded promising results. The initiative, commissioned by the Department of Health, sought to identify simple and cost-effective solutions to ease tensions in A&E units. With the help of psychologists, designers identified key factors that contribute to patient violence, including inhospitable environments and lack of communication.

The project's findings come at a time when attacks on NHS staff are on the rise. According to recent figures, there were 57,830 physical assaults on NHS staff in England in 2010-11, resulting in significant costs to the healthcare system. It is estimated that these attacks cost at least £69m a year, primarily due to staff taking time off work and legal costs associated with pursuing cases.

To address this issue, the Design Council worked with experts to develop practical solutions that can be easily implemented in A&E departments. One key strategy involves improving communication with patients, including a new approach to greeting them upon arrival and providing clear answers to their questions. Additionally, the use of clearer signs and maps can help patients understand the different stages of treatment, reducing confusion and frustration.

Other suggestions include the use of screens to provide live updates on the number of cases being handled by staff, as well as guidance on lighting, decor, and seating for hospital managers planning refurbishments. These solutions can be implemented at a relatively low cost, with estimates suggesting that hospitals can install the system for around £60,000.

Three hospitals in Chesterfield, Southampton, and London are set to test these ideas, with the goal of reducing patient aggression and creating a calmer environment. According to David Kester, head of the Design Council, "This is design at its best - solving a long-standing, high-cost problem through creativity, simplicity, and collaboration." Health Minister Simon Burns echoed this sentiment, stating that "difficult situations can be diffused by simply giving patients more information."

Dr. John Heyworth, a consultant in the emergency department at Southampton General Hospital, emphasized the importance of addressing this issue. "Violence and aggression towards staff and other patients in the emergency department is a major nationwide issue," he said. "While there will always be a small minority intent on causing trouble, there are others who can resort to aggressive behavior because they don't feel they have been communicated with effectively and they don't know what to expect."

By implementing these simple yet effective solutions, hospitals can take a significant step towards reducing patient aggression and creating a more positive experience for both patients and staff. As the project moves forward, it is hoped that these innovations will be adopted by hospitals across the country, ultimately leading to a safer and more compassionate healthcare system.

Microsoft's Focus on Cloud Computing Pays Off, While eBay's Profits Take a Hit

Microsoft has reported a significant increase in revenue and profits, thanks to its focus on cloud computing. The tech giant's revenue rose to $23.3 billion in the quarter, up from $20.6 billion in the prior year, while profits jumped to $5.3 billion, up from $3 billion the year before. The company's emphasis on cloud-based software, storage, and services has paid off, with executives citing strong sales and renewals.

Chief Executive Satya Nadella said, "Overall, the approach we have taken for multiple years now is to transform everything that we do. We've now got very good customer momentum." The company's share price climbed more than 3% in after-market trading, beating analyst expectations.

In contrast, eBay's profits took a hit, dropping 94% in the three months that ended in June. The e-commerce firm recorded an income tax provision of more than $400 million, which included a $311 million tax charge related to a reorganization since it split from PayPal in 2015. eBay's stock dropped almost 4% in after-hours trade, as its profit forecast largely fell below estimates.

Despite the drop in profits, eBay's quarterly revenue increased 4% year-on-year to $2.3 billion, with two million new buyers turning to its platforms. However, the company's US StubHub business suffered without major events such as Hamilton and the Copa America football tournament to drive buyers. eBay has been working to move beyond its identity as an auction site, spending on marketing and updating its websites. The company is looking to reinvent itself and become more competitive in the e-commerce market.

Brazil's volleyball team secured their seventh gold medal in Rio, defeating their opponents 3-0. The win came in a lively atmosphere at Maracanazinho arena, where Neymar was in attendance. The victory made up for their 2012 loss to Russia, and the USA took bronze with a comeback win over Russia.

Chelsea captain John Terry has praised the return of Didier Drogba to Stamford Bridge, stating that the Ivory Coast striker is still a "nightmare" to play against in training. Drogba, 36, signed a one-year deal with the club last month, marking his second spell with the Blues. The striker scored 157 goals in 342 games during his initial eight-year stint with the team.

Terry, 33, expressed his admiration for Drogba's enduring skills, saying, "He's still strong, sharp, and hungry." The Chelsea captain believes that Drogba's presence will have a positive impact on the team's younger players, such as Kurt Zouma, by instilling a winning mentality.

This summer, Chelsea has made several high-profile signings, including Diego Costa, Cesc Fabregas, and Filipe Luis, at a combined cost of £75m. Terry is impressed with the new additions, saying, "If I was a Chelsea fan, I'd be impressed from what I have seen so far." However, he admits it feels strange to see former teammates Frank Lampard and Ashley Cole playing for other clubs, with Lampard joining Manchester City and Cole signing with Roma. Terry noted, "It just doesn't seem right to see them in different shirts." With Drogba's return and the influx of new talent, Chelsea is poised for a successful season.

Serbia's Capital Belgrade Sees Daily Protests Against Vucic's Victory

For the past several weeks, the streets of Belgrade have been filled with the sounds of whistling, chanting, and drum-beating protesters, as thousands of people gather daily to express their discontent with the outcome of the presidential election. The vote, which took place on April 2, saw Prime Minister Aleksandar Vucic win an overwhelming majority, securing over 50% of the vote and avoiding a second-round runoff.

However, rather than accepting the results, many of Vucic's detractors have taken to the streets to voice their concerns about the direction of the country. The protests, which have been largely peaceful, have become a daily routine, with demonstrators gathering in front of key landmarks such as the National Assembly, Republic Square, and the headquarters of state broadcaster RTS.

The protesters, many of whom are university students, have been vocal about their opposition to Vucic's government, which they claim is becoming increasingly authoritarian. They have also expressed frustration with the lack of media freedom in the country, with many outlets being heavily biased towards the ruling Progressive Party (SNS).

According to an analysis, over half of the pre-election media coverage focused on Vucic, with that figure rising to over 90% when reporting on his activities as prime minister was included. This has raised concerns about self-censorship and government interference, with many protesters accusing the media of being too cozy with the government.

In response, protesters have taken to buying and carrying copies of Danas, a newspaper critical of the government, which has been struggling to attract advertisers. "The people voted like this because nobody had access to the media," said Stefan, a protester. "We want to show that there are alternative voices in this country, and that we will not be silenced."

Despite the protests, Vucic has remained unperturbed, stating that everyone has the right to be unhappy with the election results as long as the demonstrations remain peaceful. So far, the police have shown a light touch, and the protesters have also been restrained, with some even displaying a sense of humor, carrying placards that read "Wenger Out" and "No to Salty Plazma," a reference to a controversial savory variant of a popular Yugoslav biscuit.

As the protests continue, it remains to be seen how long they will last and what impact they will have on the government. However, for now, the demonstrators show no signs of letting up, with their daily chants of "see you tomorrow" becoming a familiar refrain in the streets of Belgrade. With a sense of humor and determination, the protesters are determined to make their voices heard and bring about change in Serbia.

Scotland's transportation landscape has undergone significant changes over the past decade, with mixed results. According to the updated National Transport Strategy, the overall use of public transportation has declined by 6% since 2006. This decline is attributed to a 12% decrease in bus passengers and a 7% decrease in ferry passengers. However, ScotRail has bucked this trend, with a remarkable 29% increase in passengers.

Despite the decline in public transportation use, the Scottish government has invested heavily in the sector. Transport Minister Derek Mackay noted that progress has been made in key areas, including a significant reduction in road deaths. The number of fatalities on Scotland's roads has decreased by 36%, from 314 in 2006 to 200 in 2014.

However, not everyone is pleased with the progress made. Colin Howden, Director of Transform Scotland, described the lack of progress in moving people from cars to public transportation as "tragic." He pointed out that while public transportation use has declined, traffic on the country's roads has increased by 2% over the same period.

On the other hand, Mr. Mackay highlighted the successes in the rail sector, citing the newly opened Borders Railway as a major factor in the 29% increase in ScotRail passengers. The Scottish government has committed £5 billion to transforming Scotland's rail network, including a £475 million train improvement program. This investment is expected to result in a 10% increase in trains for the ScotRail fleet, providing 23% extra seats for passengers.

Transport Scotland acknowledged that more work needs to be done, particularly in improving bus patronage figures. A review is planned for the next parliament to explore these issues in more depth. Despite the challenges, the updated National Transport Strategy provides a roadmap for future investment and development in Scotland's transportation sector. As the country continues to grow and evolve, it is likely that transportation will remain a key priority for the Scottish government.

A leap second will be added to clocks worldwide at the end of June. This adjustment is made to keep pace with the Earth's rotation, which can vary in speed. Atomic clocks, which measure atomic vibrations for precise timekeeping, are used to determine when a leap second is needed. Since their introduction in 1972, 25 leap seconds have been added, including one in 2012. While not everyone agrees with the practice, scientists argue that it prevents significant inaccuracies over time. Without leap seconds, clocks could drift away from actual time, causing problems in navigation and other fields that rely on precise timing.

UK MPs Reveal Lavish Freebies in Latest Register Update

The latest update to the UK Parliament's register of members' financial interests has revealed a slew of lavish freebies received by MPs. Speaker John Bercow, a self-proclaimed tennis enthusiast, topped the list with two Royal Box tickets to Wimbledon, valued at a staggering £8,590. Labour deputy leader Tom Watson also received two Wimbledon tickets, although at a significantly lower price point.

Meanwhile, Conservative MPs Damian Collins and Nigel Adams declared tickets to the iconic Glastonbury music festival. Collins, chairman of the Commons Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee, and Adams, a committee member, did not disclose the value of their tickets. Labour Leader Jeremy Corbyn, who addressed the crowds at Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage, had previously declared two tickets worth £476, which he claimed were given to a family member.

Other notable freebies included two tickets to the England v South Africa test match at Lords for Defence Secretary Sir Michael Fallon, and two tickets to the Grand Prix at Silverstone for Labour's Richard Burden.
