Conservative Mims Davies received a ticket to Royal Ascot, while Labour's Stephen Doughty and Tory John Howell got tickets to the Royal International Air Tattoo.

In addition to event tickets, several MPs declared significant payments for various endeavors. Former Labour leader Ed Miliband is set to receive £2,500 for hosting Jeremy Vine's BBC Radio 2 show for a week, while Conservative backbencher Nadine Dorries declared a £50,000 signing fee for a new book deal.

Under parliamentary rules, MPs are required to declare any financial interest that could be seen as influencing their actions or words within 28 days. The register update provides a glimpse into the perks and privileges enjoyed by UK lawmakers, with Prime Minister Theresa May also registering a discount card from luxury shoe retailer Russell & Bromley. The value of the discount card, valid from January 2017 to January 2018, was not disclosed.

A Scottish family is growing increasingly concerned that their loved one, Kausar Uddin, is being left to languish in a Saudi Arabian prison despite serving his 35-day sentence. The 47-year-old taxi driver from Sighthill was arrested during a pilgrimage to Mecca in February after allegedly assaulting a policeman. However, his family claims that the incident was a misunderstanding, and that Uddin was only trying to steady himself in a crowded area.

According to his 17-year-old daughter, Kaulsom Uddin, her father lost his balance and grabbed onto the nearest person, who happened to be a police officer. The officer allegedly misinterpreted the situation and began punching Uddin, who attempted to leave the scene to avoid further conflict. Despite his sentence being completed, Uddin remains in prison, awaiting a decision from a Saudi court on his future.

The family is now fearing that Uddin's case is in danger of being forgotten. Kaulsom Uddin expressed her frustration with the Foreign Office, stating that she does not feel they are doing enough to secure her father's release. "We were hoping ideally that he would be out before his sentence finishes, but even after his sentence has finished, they still haven't got him out," she said. The Foreign Office has confirmed that they are providing assistance to Uddin and his family, and will remain in contact with local authorities. However, for the Uddin family, time is of the essence, and they are urging the authorities to take swift action to bring Kausar Uddin home.

Share Your England: Join the Big Picture Project

The BBC is inviting the public to share their stunning images and videos of England as part of the England's Big Picture project. Whether you're a professional photographer or an amateur snapper, we want to see your best shots of the country's landscapes, cities, and landmarks.

To submit your pictures, simply email them to england@bbc.co.uk, post them on our Facebook page, or tweet them to @BBCEngland. You can also share your images on Instagram using the hashtag #englandsbigpicture. A selection of the best photos will be featured on our Pinterest board and may even be used on the BBC website or social media channels.

When submitting your photos, please include your name and any relevant details about the image. Please note that we prioritize photos taken in the past week, and by submitting your image, you agree to grant the BBC a royalty-free licence to use it. Don't worry, you'll still own the copyright, and we'll make sure to credit your name if your photo is used. So, grab your camera or phone and start snapping – we can't wait to see your England!

Wolverhampton Wanderers secured a thrilling 3-1 comeback victory over local rivals Birmingham City, earning their second league win of the season. Despite trailing to Che Adams' opener, Wolves' manager Walter Zenga's side rallied in the second half, with Iceland striker Jon Dadi Bodvarsson scoring one of three goals to seal the win.

Zenga attributed the success to his experienced starting XI, which featured 10 players from last season's squad. "They're good players and they only need a warm up," he said. "They understood what is the spirit of Wolves and what they have to do to create enthusiasm." The Italian manager emphasized the importance of dedication and focus in training, stating that his team's style is to "give 100% all the time" and concentrate on daily tasks. With this win, Wolves continue to build momentum, but Zenga remains calm and focused, choosing not to dwell on the team's current standing in the table.

Cambridge University Hospitals has faced significant challenges with its new online patient record system. The system, designed by US firm Epic, was launched in October and allows staff to access and update records on hand-held devices and 7,000 computers. However, the system has failed in key areas, prompting Epic to send in expert staff and doctors from California to provide assistance. 

Local GPs have raised concerns about the system, citing issues such as complex patient reporting and the inability of computers to communicate with other devices like printers. Medical director Dr Jag Ahluwalia has acknowledged these concerns and announced an urgent meeting to address "communication" issues. The problems have had significant consequences, including ambulances being rerouted away from Addenbrooke's accident and emergency department in early November. According to Cambridgeshire Clinical Commissioning Group, the department's performance has fallen by 20% since the system's launch. Hospital staff are working to resolve these issues to ensure patient safety and efficient care.

BBC Disputes Rwanda's Claim of Biased Documentary

The BBC has expressed extreme disappointment over the findings of an inquiry led by Martin Ngoga, which claims that a documentary about the 1994 Rwandan genocide failed to meet the broadcaster's own editorial standards. The documentary, titled "Rwanda, The Untold Story," was aired in October 2014 and included interviews with researchers and former aides of President Paul Kagame, who accused him of plotting to shoot down the presidential plane that triggered the genocide.

The Rwandan government has been critical of the documentary, claiming that it attempts to revise the history and facts of the genocide and disrespects the memory of those who died. In response, the BBC has strongly rejected any suggestion that the documentary constitutes genocide denial. The broadcaster argued that it has a duty to investigate difficult and challenging subjects and believes that the program was a valuable contribution to the understanding of the tragic history of the country and the region.

The inquiry's findings have led to Rwanda suspending broadcasts by the BBC's Kinyarwanda language service. The BBC has stated that it stands by its right to produce independent journalism, which has made it the world's most trusted news source. The broadcaster's editorial complaints process is still ongoing, but provisional findings suggest that the documentary does not breach the BBC's editorial standards.

The genocide, which occurred over a 100-day period in 1994, resulted in the deaths of at least 800,000 people, mostly from the minority ethnic Tutsi group and Hutus opposed to the mass slaughter. The documentary's claims that most of those killed may have been Hutus, killed by members of the then-rebel Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), have been met with criticism from the Rwandan government and some survivors of the genocide.

The BBC has attempted to get the Rwandan government to respond to the allegations made in the documentary, but these attempts have been unsuccessful. Despite the controversy surrounding the documentary, the BBC remains committed to independent journalism and will continue to investigate challenging subjects, including the complex and tragic history of the Rwandan genocide. The broadcaster's commitment to editorial standards and independence has made it a trusted source of news and information around the world.

Rangers Search for New Manager After Warburton's Departure

The Scottish football world is abuzz with speculation as Rangers Football Club searches for a new manager following the departure of Mark Warburton. The 53-year-old Englishman left the club on Friday, along with his assistant David Weir and head of recruitment Frank McParland. As the club navigates this transition period, former players and coaches are weighing in on potential candidates to take the reins.

One name that has been mentioned is Billy Davies, a 52-year-old veteran coach with a proven track record in the English Championship. Davies has been out of coaching for nearly three years since his second stint at Nottingham Forest came to an end. However, his impressive resume and ability to drive results have caught the attention of many, including former Rangers striker Kris Boyd.

Boyd, who spent time on loan at Nottingham Forest during Davies' first stint, sang the praises of his former coach. "He'll do anything to win," Boyd told BBC Scotland. "It's a results-driven world, and for me, there's not a better man." Boyd, who had a prolific spell at Rangers from 2006 to 2010, credited Davies with helping him regain his scoring form during a difficult period at Middlesbrough. "He got me back scoring goals inside a week," Boyd recalled. "That didn't happen by coincidence."

Davies' ability to motivate players and drive results is well-documented. During his time at Motherwell, he took the club from relegation candidates to European contenders. His tenure at Derby and Preston also yielded impressive results, with Boyd noting that "a lot of the good work he's done in England has gone unnoticed up here."

Another name in the running is Alex McLeish, a former Rangers manager and player. McLeish, 58, has expressed interest in returning to the club, and former Rangers captain Barry Ferguson believes he would be an excellent choice. "He knows what the club is all about, he knows the traditions and what is expected," Ferguson said. "He assembled a good team at Rangers, and we had a real togetherness. He wanted us to work hard and play attacking football."

Ferguson, who played under McLeish for Scotland, Rangers, and Birmingham, believes that McLeish's experience and knowledge of the club make him an ideal candidate for the short-term solution that Rangers are seeking. "He has more experience now, and if they are looking for someone to take over until the end of the season, he's a serious contender," Ferguson said.

As Rangers continues their search for a new manager, one thing is certain – the club needs a leader who can drive results and restore the team's former glory. With the Scottish Cup win over Morton on Sunday, the team has shown glimpses of their potential, but it will be up to the new manager to harness that energy and propel the team forward. Whether it's Billy Davies, Alex McLeish, or another candidate, the Rangers faithful will be watching with bated breath as the club navigates this critical period in their history.

Colombia's Historic Step Towards Peace: Farc Rebels Decommission 60% of Registered Weapons

In a significant milestone towards achieving lasting peace, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) have decommissioned 60% of their registered weapons, marking a crucial step in the implementation of the peace agreement signed with the government. The gesture has been welcomed by President Juan Manuel Santos, who described it as a "historic day" in the country's journey towards peace.

The decommissioning ceremony took place in the south-western Cauca region, where Farc leaders and UN officials gathered at La Elvira, one of several transition zones designated for the rebels to gather before reintegrating into civilian life. Although President Santos was unable to attend the ceremony due to bad weather, he expressed his commitment to the peace process, stating that "peace will be built little by little, like a cathedral, which you build brick by brick."

The Farc has agreed to give up more than five decades of armed struggle under the terms of the accord, which was signed after four years of negotiations in Cuba. The peace deal was initially rejected in a referendum last October but was reworked and approved by Congress a month later. As part of the agreement, the rebels have until June 20 to hand over the remaining weapons, a deadline that was extended from the original date of May 30.

The decommissioned weapons, including rifles, RPGs, and pistols, are being stored at 26 locations around the country under the supervision of UN observers. The images of the weapons being checked and stored have been released, providing visual evidence of the Farc's commitment to the peace process. While some may have expected more dramatic images of fighters handing over their rifles, the Farc insists that such a display would be perceived as a sign of defeat, rather than a voluntary decision to lay down arms.

Farc leader Pablo Catatumbo emphasized the group's commitment to peace, stating, "We are totally committed to peace and will do all we can to help build this country we dream of." The decommissioning of weapons is a critical step towards the Farc's transformation into a political party, a process that is expected to be completed once all registered weapons have been handed over.

President Santos's efforts to reach a peace agreement with the Farc earned him the Nobel Peace Prize last year. The successful implementation of the peace deal is seen as a major achievement for the country, which has been plagued by conflict for over five decades. As Colombia continues on its path towards peace, the international community remains hopeful that the country will finally be able to put its troubled past behind it and build a brighter future for its citizens.

In a surprising turn of events, Malik Obama, the half-brother of President Barack Obama, has expressed his support for Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump. In an interview with the BBC, Malik Obama, a Muslim with both Kenyan and US citizenship, stated that Trump's proposal for a temporary ban on Muslims entering the US was "common sense". This statement comes despite the widespread condemnation of Trump's plan, which has been touted as a security measure.

Malik Obama also criticized his half-brother, President Obama, for allegedly turning his back on their family. He noted that it was "disappointing" and "hypocritical" that no representatives from the Obama family in Kenya were attending the Democratic convention in Philadelphia. The president has often spoken proudly of his heritage, but Malik Obama feels that he has not been supportive of their family.

As an aspiring politician in Kenya, Malik Obama has decided to vote for Trump in the upcoming election, marking a shift in his allegiance from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party. This unexpected endorsement has sparked interest in the presidential race, with Trump facing off against Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton in November.

Geert Wilders, the leader of the Freedom Party in the Netherlands, has once again sparked controversy with his latest comments on Moroccan immigrants. Speaking to his supporters in the ethnically diverse area of Spijkenisse, near Rotterdam, Wilders vowed to crack down on what he termed "Moroccan scum" who make the streets of Holland unsafe. This comes just two months after he was convicted in a hate speech trial over his promise to reduce the number of Moroccans in the country.

Wilders, who is currently topping opinion polls ahead of the 15 March parliamentary vote, addressed his supporters on Saturday amid tight security. He emphasized that not all Moroccans are a problem, but his words were met with concern and outrage from many. According to the 2011 census, there are over 167,000 Moroccan-born residents of the Netherlands, making up the third-largest group of non-EU residents. This figure does not take into account second or third-generation Moroccans, who are also likely to be affected by Wilders' policies.

The Freedom Party leader has vowed to ban Muslim immigration and shut mosques if he wins the election. His comments have been met with widespread criticism, with many accusing him of promoting hate speech and discrimination. A small group of demonstrators turned up to protest against Wilders' comments, with one protester, Emma Smeets, telling the Associated Press that she was "very, very scared" of what Wilders might do if he comes to power.

Despite his lead in the polls, Wilders' support appears to be waning in recent weeks. His nearest rival, right-wing Prime Minister Mark Rutte, has narrowed the gap, and many Dutch voters are increasingly concerned about the impact of Wilders' policies on the country's stability and reputation. The BBC's Anna Holligan, reporting from The Hague, notes that Wilders' championing of US President Donald Trump's policies appears to be backfiring, with many voters believing that Trump is bad for global stability.

Wilders' three-week trial last year was triggered by his comments during a municipal election campaign in The Hague, in which he asked supporters whether they wanted "fewer or more Moroccans in your city and in the Netherlands". The crowd's response of "Fewer! Fewer!" was met with a smiling Wilders, who said "We're going to take care of that". At the trial, prosecutors took testimony from Dutch-Moroccans who said Wilders' comments made them feel like "third-rate citizens". He was ultimately convicted of insulting a group and inciting discrimination.

Even if Wilders wins the election, he may struggle to put together a coalition, as leading parties have said they would not work with him. The Freedom Party currently holds 12 of the 150 seats in the lower house of Parliament, and it remains to be seen whether Wilders will be able to translate his popularity into a workable government. As the election approaches, Dutch voters will be closely watching Wilders' next moves, and weighing the potential consequences of his policies on the country's future.

Researchers at the University of Dundee have made a groundbreaking discovery that could potentially lead to new treatments for fertility issues in women. A study analyzing medical records from over half a million British women found that those who had their tonsils and appendix removed were more likely to become pregnant. The findings, published in Fertility and Sterility, suggest that the removal of these organs may have a direct impact on fertility or be linked to behavioral factors.

According to the study, for every 100 pregnancies in women who had no surgical procedures, there were significantly more pregnancies in women who had undergone tonsillectomy or appendectomy. Dr. Sami Shimi, one of the researchers, noted that the findings dispel the common myth that having an appendix removed damages fertility. In fact, the study found that removing inflamed or potentially inflamed organs, such as the appendix and tonsils, may actually improve a woman's chances of becoming pregnant.

The exact explanation for these findings is still unclear, and more research is needed to determine the underlying causes. One possibility is that chronic inflammation in the body, caused by infected tonsils or appendixes, may affect the ovaries and womb, making it more difficult to conceive. Alternatively, the researchers suggest that behavioral factors, such as increased sexual activity, may be at play. Women who are more likely to engage in liberal sexual activity may also be more likely to have pelvic inflammatory disease, which could lead to the removal of the appendix.

While the study's findings are promising, experts caution against drawing premature conclusions. Prof. Allan Pacey, from the University of Sheffield, noted that the study is "interesting" but more research is needed to fully understand the relationship between organ removal and fertility. He advised against suggesting that infertile women undergo unnecessary surgery, such as tonsillectomy or appendectomy, as a means of improving their fertility. Instead, the study may ultimately lead to the development of new treatments or therapies that can enhance women's fertility. As the research continues to unfold, one thing is clear: this study has opened up new avenues for exploration and may potentially lead to breakthroughs in the field of fertility medicine.

Bombardier has secured a significant deal with Malaysian airline Flymojo, worth approximately $3 billion. The airline has signed a letter of intent to purchase 20 CS100 aircraft, with the option to buy 20 more. The wings of the CSeries will be manufactured by Bombardier in Belfast. Despite years of delays and cost overruns, the CSeries is set to enter service later this year. Michael Ryan, VP and GM of Bombardier Belfast, expressed his pleasure with the deal, citing it as an endorsement of the aircraft's credentials. This brings Bombardier's total orders and commitments for the CSeries to 603 aircraft, marking a major milestone for the company.

Leicestershire police have introduced a unique initiative to prevent gold necklace thefts in the Belgrave area. Scarves have been designed to cover up valuable gold chains, particularly popular among Asian women. The garments were made by individuals on the Community Payback scheme using donated fabric from local businesses. Following a spike in thefts in previous summers, officers have been visiting community centres and temples to distribute the scarves and raise awareness about the issue. In 2014, 72 chain snatches were reported in the area, prompting police to take proactive measures to combat the problem. So far, this year has seen no incidents, thanks to the efforts of the police and community.

A groundbreaking investigation is set to take place in a Moray cave where human remains from the Late Bronze Age were previously discovered. Michelle Walker, a graduate of the University of the Highlands and Islands (UHI), will lead the research, which aims to explore the acoustic properties of Sculptors Cave. The cave is believed to have been used by prehistoric people for burial rituals, which involved beating a drum.

As part of the study, Ms Walker plans to beat a drum in the cave, replicating the ancient rituals. Volunteers will be asked to complete a questionnaire, recording their thoughts and feelings during the two-minute drumming session. The research, known as archaeoacoustics, has previously shed light on the behavior of sound in Neolithic temples in England and Ireland.

The UHI has been at the forefront of uncovering clues to life in prehistoric Scotland. Recently, archaeologists from the university discovered a significant complex of Bronze Age buildings at Tresness in Sanday, which were buried by sand dunes over 3,000 years ago. Additionally, the remains of 8,000-year-old hazelnut shells were found at a dig on the island of Skye, providing insight into the lives of Mesolithic hunter-gatherers. The new investigation in Sculptors Cave is expected to further our understanding of the lives and rituals of Scotland's ancient inhabitants.

US Missile Mistakenly Sent to Cuba, Sparking Diplomatic Efforts

A highly sensitive US missile was inadvertently shipped to Cuba, sparking a diplomatic effort to retrieve the advanced weaponry. The AGM 114 Hellfire missile, which did not contain explosives, was originally sent to Spain for a NATO training exercise before being routed to Germany and eventually to Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris. However, instead of being sent to its intended destination in Florida, the missile was loaded onto an Air France flight to Havana.

The incident has been deemed a serious mistake, with US officials expressing concern that Cuba could share the missile's advanced technology with countries such as North Korea, China, or Russia. The Cuban government has stated that the missile arrived in the country "by mistake or mishandling in the country of origin" and has cooperated with US efforts to retrieve the missile. The US and Cuba, which restored diplomatic relations last year after more than 50 years, are working to resolve the issue. The incident is an embarrassment for the US, which has had to request the return of its own military technology. Despite the setback, the two countries are expected to announce the reinstatement of commercial flights between US cities and Havana on Tuesday, marking a significant step forward in their efforts to rebuild economic and trade ties.

Cardiff Blues prop Anton Peikrishvili has been handed a five-week ban for biting an opponent. The 29-year-old Georgian was sent off during a game against Ospreys after biting back-rower Rob McCusker. Peikrishvili's ban has been back-dated to November 22, making him eligible to play again from January 2, 2017. He joined the Blues on a short-term contract and featured in two games, including a debut against Exeter Chiefs. The Rugby Football Union oversaw the case, as the competition falls under their jurisdiction. Meanwhile, Scarlets' Jack Condy was also banned for punching in a separate match. Peikrishvili previously played for Ulster on a short-term contract but did not make an appearance for the province. His suspension will keep him sidelined until the new year.

Concerns have been raised by the Northern Ireland Police Federation regarding the potential impact of physical border posts on officer safety and community relations. Mark Lindsay, chair of the federation, expressed his concerns that enforcing border controls would put officers at risk and have a negative effect on PSNI resources. The government has repeatedly stated its desire to avoid recreating the "borders of the past," instead suggesting the use of technological solutions to manage the border.

However, Mr. Lindsay believes that regardless of the type of border implemented, the police will be required to enforce new post-Brexit regulations. This, he argues, would create a security threat and necessitate police protection for customs agencies, putting officers in the line of fire. The predictable patterns of police patrols would make them an easy target for terrorist attacks.

The comments come as Prime Minister Theresa May announced plans for the UK to leave the European Customs Union, a move that Sinn Féin claims would result in a "hard border" on the island of Ireland and undermine the Good Friday Agreement. Mr. Lindsay warned that enforcing a hard border would be a "step backwards" for community policing, as it would require significant additional resources and potentially disrupt communities that straddle the border. The PSNI currently lacks the resources to effectively manage a hard border, highlighting the need for alternative solutions to be explored.

A major breakthrough has been made in the 35-year-old murder case of Lorraine McCausland, with police preparing a file for the Public Prosecution Service. The 23-year-old's body was found beside a stream in Forthriver in 1987. She was last seen alive in a loyalist club at Tyndale, where police believe she was raped and "savagely beaten" before her body was dumped.

Recently, several arrests were made in connection with the case, including a 54-year-old and a 56-year-old in Belfast, and two men aged 53 and 59 in Antrim. Additional arrests were made in Scotland and England, bringing the total number of suspects to seven. The original investigation in 1987 resulted in 14 arrests, but no charges were filed. Lorraine's son, Craig, who was just two when she was killed, was tragically murdered 18 years later in a separate incident. The case has sent shockwaves through the community, and police are hopeful that justice will finally be served for Lorraine and her family. Detectives have conducted extensive searches and gathered over 100 witness statements, bringing them closer to resolving the case.

In a significant victory for multinational corporations operating in India, the Bombay High Court has ruled in favor of Shell's Indian unit in a long-standing tax dispute. The court dismissed allegations that the company had under-priced shares transferred to its parent firm by $2.5 billion in 2013, which would have resulted in a substantial tax bill.

The Indian tax authorities had claimed that the company should pay tax on the interest that would have been earned if the shares had been transferred at a higher price. However, the court ruled that the stock transfers were exempt from taxation under the country's share transfer provisions. Shell's India lawyer, Mukesh Butani, welcomed the decision, stating that the tax department had "clearly exceeded its jurisdiction".

This ruling is a major boost for Shell and other international companies operating in India, which have been targeted in a series of high-profile tax disputes in recent years. Companies such as IBM, Nokia, HSBC, and AT&T have all been embroiled in tax battles with Indian authorities, which has damaged the country's reputation as a destination for foreign investment.

The Indian government, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has pledged to end the "tax terrorism" that has been scaring companies away. The court's decision in the Shell case, combined with a similar ruling in favor of Vodafone in October, will be closely watched by other multinationals involved in similar disputes. The outcome is seen as a positive step towards improving India's investment climate and attracting much-needed overseas investment.

The ruling is also expected to provide a boost to India's efforts to attract foreign investment, which is crucial for the country's economic growth. With the government's initiatives to improve the business environment and reduce bureaucratic hurdles, this decision is likely to send a positive signal to international companies considering investing in India. As the country continues to navigate its complex tax landscape, this victory for Shell is a significant step in the right direction.

In the city of El Alto, Bolivia, a burst of color has emerged in the form of vibrant, ostentatious mansions designed by local architect Freddy Mamani. Dubbed "cholets," a combination of the words "chalet" and "chola," meaning indigenous woman, these structures are a stark contrast to the city's predominantly unpainted brick houses, many of which remain unfinished. Mamani's creations have not only transformed the cityscape but have also become a status symbol for the wealthy Aymara indigenous community.

Mamani's inspiration stems from indigenous Andean iconography, drawing from the geometric patterns found in the pre-Incan ruins of Tiwanaku, located near Lake Titicaca. By incorporating these traditional designs into his buildings, Mamani aims to celebrate the cultural heritage of Bolivia's indigenous people. The result is a unique blend of modern architecture and ancient cultural influences.

The cholets, which can cost anywhere from $150,000 to $300,000, feature elaborate designs, including penthouses, shops, and party halls. These spaces can be rented out, providing a lucrative source of income for the owners. The party halls, in particular, have become a popular venue for weddings and other celebrations within the Aymara community.

Mamani's work has gained widespread recognition, with 70 of his cholets already constructed in El Alto and many more orders pouring in daily. His designs have also inspired a new generation of architects and builders, some of whom have attempted to replicate his style. However, according to Mamani, what sets his work apart is the essence and language that underlies his creations. "Mine have an identity, a language that can be described," he explains.

As one drives through El Alto with Mamani, it becomes apparent that his influence extends beyond his own designs. The city is dotted with colorful buildings, many of which bear a resemblance to Mamani's signature style. While some may be copies, Mamani remains unfazed, acknowledging that his work has inspired a new wave of creativity in the city. With his cholets continuing to leave a lasting impression on El Alto's landscape, Mamani's contribution to the city's cultural and architectural heritage is undeniable.

A shocking discovery was made at Hull Royal Infirmary when a mouse was spotted sticking its head out from under a door. Julie Saunders, a visitor to the hospital, alerted staff after her son made the unsettling observation. "It was a bit of a shock really, you don't expect mice in a hospital," she expressed. In response, staff took immediate action, placing blankets along the bottom of the door to prevent the rodents from entering. Saunders and her son reported seeing two mice, while other patients claimed to have seen four. The Hull and East Yorkshire Hospitals NHS Trust quickly called in a pest control team to address the issue. The team is currently working to minimize disruption and reopen the affected unit as soon as possible. The incident has raised concerns about the hospital's pest control measures.

Tragedy Strikes in Dalgety Bay: Twin Toddlers Found Dead in Garden Tank

A devastating incident occurred in Dalgety Bay on Saturday, leaving a family and community in shock. Two-year-old twins, Rhys and Shaun Scott, were discovered in a garden tank at their rented home at approximately 08:20. Despite being rushed to the hospital by ambulance, the twins were pronounced dead upon arrival.

The rented property, formerly used as a business selling ornamental koi carp, had been granted planning permission by Fife Council in 2012 for the installation of a fish tank and enclosure, valued at £25,000. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is currently liaising with the police to investigate the circumstances surrounding the twins' deaths.

The twins' parents, Mervyn Scott and Sarah Aitken, have released a heart-wrenching statement, describing their children as "miracle babies" who were "full of love, happiness, fun, and cheek." They expressed their devastation and shock at the loss, stating that the twins had touched the lives of everyone they met and would be "forever missed and loved."

Police Scotland is continuing to investigate the incident, with a specialist family liaison officer providing support to the grieving family. The HSE may compile reports for prosecutors if it is found that the landlords had put tenants in danger. The community is left to mourn the tragic loss of two young lives, taken far too soon in a freak accident.

The National Trust property in Enniskillen, Castle Coole, is set to host the prestigious Last Night of the Proms event on September 9. Approximately 6,000 people are expected to attend the classical music show, which will feature internationally acclaimed musicians performing alongside the Ulster Orchestra, led by conductor David Brophy.

This year's event marks the 16th year of the Northern Ireland Proms, with previous years seeing major outside broadcasts in Hillsborough, Carrickfergus, and Bangor. The BBC Proms is the world's largest classical music festival, boasting over 90 concerts and events across the UK over eight weeks.

According to BBC Northern Ireland director Peter Johnston, audiences can expect "a very special evening" with "the very best in music-making" from the Castle Coole show. The concert will be hosted by Claire McCollum and Noel Thompson, with key moments broadcast live on BBC television and a highlights programme shown at a later date. The show will also be live on BBC Radio Ulster. Robert Gibson of Fermanagh and Omagh District Council praised Castle Coole as an "inspired choice" to mark the Last Night of the Proms, promising an unforgettable experience for attendees.

Papua New Guinea Toughens Penalties for Violence, Repeals Sorcery Act

In a move aimed at addressing the country's high levels of violence, Papua New Guinea's parliament has passed legislation that repeals the 1971 Sorcery Act and introduces tougher penalties for various crimes. The new laws make killings linked to allegations of witchcraft punishable as murder, with the death penalty applicable in such cases. The decision has been met with mixed reactions, with human rights groups condemning the introduction of stricter penalties.

The repeal of the Sorcery Act is seen as a significant step forward in protecting women from violence, as accusations of sorcery are often used to justify brutal attacks on women. In recent years, several high-profile cases of sorcery-related killings have made headlines, including the burning alive of a 20-year-old mother in a village market and the beheading of a woman accused of black magic. Under the new laws, such killings will be treated as murder, and perpetrators will face the death penalty.

However, the introduction of stricter penalties for other crimes, including rape and armed robbery, has been criticized by human rights groups. Amnesty International has condemned the move, stating that Papua New Guinea has "taken one step forward in protecting women from violence, but several giant steps back by moving closer to executions." The organization's deputy director for the Asia-Pacific, Isabelle Arradon, accused the government of "attempting to end one form of violence by perpetrating state-sanctioned violence."

The new laws also prescribe longer jail terms for kidnapping, theft, and white-collar crime, and introduce several methods of execution, including hanging, lethal injection, firing squad, and electrocution. Justice and Attorney General Kerenga Kua defended the tough new laws, stating that they reflect the country's high crime levels and community demands. Prime Minister Peter O'Neil has announced plans to begin implementing the death penalty and increasing prison sentences for violent crimes, citing the need for "draconian" measures to address the country's crime problem.

Despite the introduction of the death penalty for murder in 1991, Papua New Guinea has not carried out an execution since 1954. At least 10 people are currently on death row, according to Amnesty International. The introduction of stricter penalties has sparked concerns about the country's human rights record and the potential for miscarriages of justice. As Papua New Guinea continues to grapple with high levels of violence, the effectiveness of the new laws in addressing the root causes of crime remains to be seen.

A young entrepreneur, Ms Kgatlhanye, has won $50,000 to launch her innovative business. She creates bags with built-in solar lights, allowing school children without electricity to study after dark. With her prize money, she invested in machinery and staff, employing 20 people. The company plans to expand production, introducing new lines. Her success story is part of the BBC's "Women of Africa" series, highlighting inspiring female entrepreneurs across the continent. Kgatlhanye's initiative is making a difference in her community, providing a sustainable solution for children to continue their education after dark.

New Evidence Emerges in Hillsborough Disaster Inquests

The ongoing inquests into the 1989 Hillsborough disaster have heard new evidence regarding the final moments of two of the 96 fans who lost their lives in the tragic event. The court, sitting in Warrington, Cheshire, was presented with witness statements and video footage detailing the desperate attempts to save Ian Glover, 20, and Christopher Edwards, 29, who were both fatally injured in the crush on the Leppings Lane terrace during the Liverpool versus Nottingham Forest FA Cup semi-final.

Ian Glover, from Walton in Liverpool, had attended the match with his brother Joseph and two friends. According to a witness statement given by Joseph in 1989, the brothers were thrown forward by a crowd surge, and while Joseph managed to escape through a gate in the perimeter fence, Ian was left trapped. Joseph described how he watched in horror as his brother's face turned blue, and his voice grew quieter as he shouted for help. Despite attempting to give his brother mouth-to-mouth resuscitation when his body was brought onto the pitch, Ian sadly did not survive.

The court heard that Ian Edwards, a Liverpool supporter who had been in the North Stand, helped to carry Ian Glover on a makeshift stretcher to a nearby gymnasium where casualties had been taken. Along with a police officer, Edwards performed CPR on Glover, and at one point, he believed he saw a "flicker of the eyes," suggesting that Glover may have shown signs of life. However, despite their best efforts, there were no further signs of life, and Edwards realized that Glover had sadly passed away.

The inquests also heard about the final movements of Christopher Edwards, who had traveled to the game with a friend and his son. Video footage shown to the court depicted fans and police attempting to carry Edwards out of pen three on the Leppings Lane terrace, over 20 minutes after the game had been stopped. Former police sergeant Martin Hemingway, who was treating another victim in the central pens, stated that he believed Edwards was still breathing when he was first alerted to his condition. However, upon reaching the pitch, there were no signs of life, and Edwards was later pronounced dead by a doctor in the gymnasium.

The difficulties in accessing medical assistance at the time of the disaster were also highlighted during the inquests. The court heard that the lack of adequate medical care and the chaos on the pitch made it challenging for those attempting to save the lives of the injured fans. The inquests, which are expected to resume on Wednesday, continue to shed new light on the tragic events of that day and the devastating consequences for the families of the 96 victims.

As the inquests progress, the families of those who lost their lives in the Hillsborough disaster remain hopeful that the truth will finally be revealed, and justice will be served. The tragedy, which occurred on April 15, 1989, remains one of the darkest days in British sporting history, and the ongoing inquests serve as a poignant reminder of the importance of ensuring that such a disaster never happens again.

UK leaders weigh in on the upcoming election, each making their case for why they should hold the balance of power. Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg stated that his party, along with UKIP's Nigel Farage or the SNP's Alex Salmond, could be the deciding factor on May 8. Farage emphasized UKIP's plan to improve the lives of working people through a "low tax revolution." Meanwhile, Labour leader Ed Miliband remained unfazed by media scrutiny, saying he would be overwhelmed if he reacted to every story. As the campaign heats up, the BBC Election 2015 newsletter offers a daily round-up of the latest news, available in your inbox every weekday afternoon. With just days to go, the UK's political landscape is poised for a significant shift, and each leader is making a strong pitch to voters. The election's outcome remains uncertain.

Swansea's Kingsway road is set to undergo significant changes as part of a plan to improve safety and reduce accidents. The road will be converted into a full one-way system, following a series of tragic incidents, including the deaths of two people. In recent months, the road has been the scene of numerous accidents, prompting concerns over its safety.

The current traffic system, which allows two lanes of traffic to travel west on one side and two lanes of public transport to travel in both directions on the other, has been criticized for its "serious design issues". A coroner's investigation into the death of Daniel Foss, 37, who was hit by a bus, called for urgent action to address these issues. In response, Swansea council installed barriers along the carriageway to prevent pedestrians from crossing.

However, council leader Rob Stewart has stated that any further changes, including the possibility of introducing a two-way traffic system, will depend on the outcome of plans to regenerate the Kingsway into a business district. Work on this project is set to begin in October, with the demolition of the former Oceana building. The site is being considered as a potential new home for the council. Mr Stewart has promised that necessary changes will be made to the road, but a final decision on its layout will be made once the master plan for the Kingsway is finalized.

A collection of belongings from the late actress Lauren Bacall has been sold at auction, exceeding expectations. A hand-coloured etching of an American white pelican by John James Audubon sold for $173,000, three times its predicted value. Additionally, a granite games table from her Los Angeles home, which she shared with Humphrey Bogart, fetched $26,250. The auction, held by Bonhams, featured other unique items, including a Tiffany necklace, a brass Japanese tea set, and sculptures by Henry Moore. The proceeds will benefit Bacall's three children. The sale showcases Bacall's eclectic taste and collecting sense, according to Bonhams' vice president Jon King. The actress passed away in August at 89, and her New York home is currently on the market for $26m. The auction highlights the enduring legacy of the Hollywood star and her distinctive style.

Scotland Sees Significant Reduction in Single-Use Bag Usage

A recent report has revealed that Scotland has witnessed a substantial decrease in the use of single-use bags, with a reduction of 129 million bags in the final quarter of 2014. This decline came after the introduction of a 5p levy on single-use bags, which was implemented for the last 11 weeks of the year. The statistics, released by the Scottish government, demonstrate the effectiveness of the charge in reducing the number of bags used by shoppers.

Environment Secretary Richard Lochhead described the figures as "astounding" and highlighted the country's commitment to tackling litter and reducing waste. He expressed his hope that the public will continue to reuse their bags and that more retailers will donate money to good causes when bags are necessary. Lochhead emphasized that small changes can make a significant difference, and the reduction in single-use bag usage is a testament to this.

In contrast, England saw an increase of 200 million single-use bags in 2014, with supermarkets distributing over 7.6 billion bags, according to research by waste reduction body Wrap. However, from October, large retailers in England will be required to charge a minimum of 5p for single-use bags, bringing the country in line with Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.

Northern Ireland has seen a significant reduction in single-use bag usage, with a 42.6% decrease in 2014, following a 71% drop after the introduction of a carrier bag charge in 2013. Wales, on the other hand, experienced a 5.2% increase in single-use bag usage last year, although the number of bags handed out has fallen by 78.2% since 2010.

The Scottish government aims to reduce the use of single-use bags by 80% in the first full year of the charge, a target that has been achieved by Wales and Northern Ireland in their respective campaigns. The reduction in single-use bag usage is a step towards minimizing litter and waste, and the Scottish government's efforts are expected to have a positive impact on the environment. As the rest of the UK follows suit, it is likely that the country will see a significant decrease in single-use bag usage, contributing to a more sustainable future.

Rangers' Under-20s coach Graeme Murty has been handed a significant boost after his side secured a thrilling 3-2 victory over St Johnstone at Ibrox. The win, which marked Murty's first Premiership triumph in charge, has been hailed by the players as a testament to his exceptional leadership and coaching skills.

Midfielder Emerson Hyndman, who scored the late winner against the Saints, praised Murty's ability to establish a clear vision for the team despite the challenges he faced as an interim manager. "He's been brilliant," Hyndman said. "It's always a tough position, but he's come in and established what he wants us to do, and the boys have gotten behind him."

Hyndman's sentiments were echoed by fellow loan player Jon Toral, who joined Rangers from Arsenal in January. "It was massive for Graeme on Wednesday," Toral said. "He has put a lot of effort into the other games as well, and for us to give him that first league win was crucial."

The victory has reignited hope for Rangers, who are now just six points behind second-placed Aberdeen in the Premiership table. With a Scottish Cup quarter-final against Hamilton Academical on the horizon, Hyndman believes there is still plenty to play for this season. "Of course, there is," he said. "We need to get ourselves right, and I think we took our first step against Saints. It was about the three points, not about how we got it."

Despite the expected appointment of a new head coach next week, the players are focused on the task at hand. "At the minute, we are just thinking about the cup tie on Saturday, and then whatever happens, happens," Toral said. With Murty's interim tenure potentially coming to an end, the players are eager to give him a strong finish to his spell in charge. As Hyndman noted, "It was nice to give him that positive feeling on Wednesday night."

Tobacco Giants Take EU to Court Over New Packaging Rules

In a significant move, major tobacco companies, including Philip Morris, British American Tobacco (BAT), and Imperial Tobacco, have joined forces to challenge the European Union's (EU) new tobacco regulations. The case, which was heard in London's High Court on Monday, has been referred to the EU's Court of Justice. The tobacco companies are contesting the EU's Tobacco Products Directive, which requires health warnings to cover 65% of the front and back of cigarette packaging.

The EU's highest court will now be tasked with determining whether the EU has overstepped its authority in introducing the new rules and whether they are proportionate. The court must also decide if the directive complies with European guarantees on fundamental rights and the principle of subsidiarity, which dictates that decisions should be made at the national or regional level whenever possible.

The tobacco companies argue that the new rules disrupt the balance between the EU and its member states, and raise concerns about the free movement of goods and competition within the EU. Philip Morris senior vice president Marc Firestone stated that while the company agrees that tobacco products should be strictly regulated, "measures must honour the EU treaties." The review by the Court of Justice is expected to take up to two years, and its ruling will have significant implications for the tobacco industry and public health policies in the EU.

Pakistan Heatwave Claims Hundreds of Lives in Karachi

A severe heatwave has gripped the city of Karachi, Pakistan, resulting in the deaths of hundreds of people, mostly elderly individuals, over the past few days. The city has been experiencing temperatures as high as 45C (113F), with power cuts exacerbating the situation due to increased demand for electricity. The power outages have been particularly problematic during the holy month of Ramadan, when Muslims fast during daylight hours and rely on air conditioning to cope with the heat.

According to provincial health secretary Saeed Mangnejo, hundreds of patients are being treated at government hospitals for heat-related illnesses, including fever, dehydration, and gastric problems. The Edhi morgue in Sohrab Goth has reported a significant increase in the number of bodies received, with over 150 bodies taken in since Saturday, compared to the usual daily average of 20.

The heatwave has sparked angry protests in parts of the city, with some residents blaming the government and the city's main power utility, K-Electric, for failing to prevent the deaths. "In our area, there is no electricity since morning. We have complained several times, but there is no response from K-Electric," said Karachi resident Iqbal, who added that his family has been unable to go outside to work due to the extreme heat.

The prolonged power outages have made it difficult for people to access basic necessities like cool water and air conditioning, which are essential for survival in such extreme temperatures. The human body is not equipped to handle temperatures above 40C, and prolonged exposure can lead to heat exhaustion, heatstroke, and even multiple organ failure.

Experts warn that heatstroke can occur at any temperature over 40C and requires immediate medical attention. In extreme heat, the body's normal cooling mechanisms, such as sweating, can fail, leading to a rapid deterioration in health. To mitigate the effects of the heatwave, residents are advised to stay indoors, stay hydrated, and avoid strenuous activities during the hottest part of the day.

The Pakistan Meteorological Office has forecast that the hot and humid weather is likely to continue on Monday, but cooler temperatures are expected from Tuesday. The all-time record temperature in Karachi is 47C (117F), recorded in 1979. The current heatwave has drawn comparisons to a similar heatwave in neighboring India last month, which claimed the lives of nearly 1,700 people.

As the city struggles to cope with the heatwave, authorities are under pressure to provide relief to affected residents and prevent further deaths. The government has been criticized for its handling of the situation, and there are growing calls for increased investment in the city's infrastructure, including its power grid, to prevent such disasters in the future.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has issued a mixed assessment of Japan's economic outlook, citing a "modest recovery" but warning that bold structural reforms are needed to sustain growth and achieve financial consolidation. The IMF's latest annual report comes as Tokyo's reform package, known as Abenomics, marks its tenth year since its introduction in 2012.

According to the IMF, Japan's growth is expected to stabilize at around 0.7% over the medium term, with inflation projected to reach 1.5%, still below the Bank of Japan's target of 2%. While the decline of the yen has been beneficial for Japan's exports sector, the outlook remains negative due to weak domestic demand and incomplete policies, particularly with regards to fiscal consolidation and structural reforms.

The IMF has cautioned against relying too heavily on yen depreciation and has called for Abenomics to be "reloaded" to address policy shortcomings. The next round of reforms should focus on increasing labor supply and reducing labor market flexibility, as well as continuing deregulation of the agricultural and services sectors. The financial sector should also be leveraged as a driver of reforms.

Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's reform package has achieved short-term growth, but the government has struggled to deregulate the job market and open up protected industry sectors. The IMF's report serves as a reminder that more needs to be done to ensure Japan's long-term economic prosperity. With the right reforms in place, Japan can unlock its growth potential and achieve sustainable economic recovery.

Welsh Government Introduces New Measures to Hold Health Boards Accountable

The Welsh government has announced new arrangements to strengthen the inspection and regulation of health boards in Wales, following a damning report into the mismanagement of the Betsi Cadwaladr Health Board in north Wales. The new measures, which come into effect next month, are designed to provide clarity on the roles and responsibilities of the Welsh government, Healthcare Inspectorate Wales (HIW), and the Auditor General Wales in dealing with potential problems.

Under the new arrangements, the Welsh government will have the power to suspend a health board's board or ask another body to run the service in cases of severe mismanagement. Less drastic options, such as "enhanced monitoring" and "targeted intervention", will also be available. These measures are intended to ensure that health boards are held accountable for poor performance and that patients receive the best possible care.

The need for a stronger inspection and regulation regime emerged from last year's joint HIW and Wales Audit Office (WAO) report into governance arrangements at Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board. The report found that the board had delayed operations and allowed waiting lists to grow to avoid financial problems, and that "significant management failings" had risked patient safety by under-reporting infections.

Health Minister Mark Drakeford said that the new arrangements would provide a clear set of processes for dealing with issues that give rise to concern. "I am confident that, where issues do emerge which give rise to concern, we now have a clear set of arrangements for all to understand how such matters will be systematically dealt with, to ensure proportionate and timely action," he said.

The Conservatives have welcomed the changes, saying that the situation at Betsi Cadwaladr health board had been "allowed to fester for far too long" and that the previous processes were "far too murky and needed to change". Shadow Health Minister Darren Millar said that patients and their families need to have confidence that health boards will be held to account for poor performance, and that these changes should go some way to ensuring that this is the case.

The new arrangements are expected to provide greater transparency and accountability in the Welsh healthcare system, and to ensure that patients receive the best possible care. With Wales already having one of the most closely inspected healthcare systems in the UK, these changes are intended to build on this foundation and provide a robust quality assurance system.

Daily flights from the Isle of Man to Glasgow will resume on May 2, operated by Eastern Airways. The route was previously cancelled when Citywing went into liquidation in March. Eastern Airways has already taken over services to Belfast and Newcastle. The renewed link is "very important" according to Isle of Man Airport's Director of Ports, Ann Reynolds. The airline prioritized protecting vital routes before reinstating the Glasgow service. The new daily flights will operate from Ronaldsway to Glasgow, reestablishing a crucial connection between the island and the UK city.

Welsh First Minister Criticizes UK Government's "Laggardly" Response to Refugee Crisis

During the first First Minister's Questions session after the summer recess, Welsh First Minister Carwyn Jones slammed UK Prime Minister David Cameron's response to the ongoing refugee crisis as "laggardly". The criticism came as opposition parties called for a full debate on the crisis in the Welsh Assembly. Jones' comments were in response to a question from Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood, in which he expressed his support for a quota system for each nation to handle the influx of refugees.

The Welsh Tory leader, Andrew RT Davies, had earlier emphasized the need for a "substantial package of integration" for migrants, rather than just "tokenism". Meanwhile, Deputy Plaid leader Elin Jones expressed disappointment and surprise at the lack of a Welsh government response to an urgent question on the crisis. Despite no scheduled statement on the refugee crisis, several Assembly Members raised the issue during the session.

Jones announced that he would be calling a summit on the crisis for Thursday, inviting charities and local councils to send representatives to coordinate the Welsh response. The summit aims to develop a coordinated Wales-wide response to the crisis, which will be the start of a government-led action that will continue throughout the autumn.

The UK government has pledged to accept up to 20,000 refugees from camps surrounding Syria, with priority given to vulnerable children. The Welsh Refugee Council estimates that Wales could provide sanctuary to around 1,600 Syrians. However, local councils have expressed concerns about meeting the costs, highlighting the need for support from the government.

The First Minister's criticism of the UK government's response reflects the growing concern among Welsh politicians and charities about the need for a more effective and coordinated approach to addressing the refugee crisis. As the situation continues to unfold, the Welsh government's summit on Thursday is expected to play a crucial role in shaping the country's response to this humanitarian crisis.

Rare 'Floating Gold' Worth £40,000 Found by Young Boy on Beach

A young boy from Christchurch has stumbled upon a rare and valuable treasure while exploring the shores of Hengistbury Head in Bournemouth. Charlie Naysmith, with the help of his father Alex, discovered a 600g lump of ambergris, a natural substance produced by sperm whales, hidden among a patch of seaweed. Initially, Charlie thought he had found a "normal stone," but after researching online, they realized the significance of their discovery.

Ambergris, often referred to as "floating gold," is a rare and highly sought-after material used in perfumes and some medicines. It is produced by sperm whales as a digestion aid and can float on the ocean for years before washing ashore. The lump found by Charlie is estimated to be around 20 years old and could be worth up to £40,000.

Charlie's father, Alex Naysmith, expressed his excitement and surprise at the discovery, stating, "It's very rare. You don't hear of it coming around very often, and it's only found in small amounts usually." He added that while the value of ambergris may have decreased over time, the family is hopeful that they can sell it for a significant amount.

Charlie has already made plans for what he will do with the money if they are able to sell the ambergris. The young boy wants to use the funds to create a nature reserve for animals in the UK, showcasing his passion for wildlife conservation.

Ambergris has been mythologized for thousands of years, with its unique properties and rarity making it a highly prized material. However, its association with whaling and the vulnerable status of sperm whales have led many perfume makers to opt for synthetic alternatives. Despite this, the discovery of ambergris remains a significant find, and Charlie's luck has sparked excitement among scientists and treasure hunters alike. As the family waits to determine the authenticity and value of their discovery, Charlie's find has already made waves in the scientific community and beyond.

Canberra Ranked as Best City to Live in the World, Australia Tops Country Rankings

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has released its latest survey, ranking 362 regions across its 34 member nations based on nine measures of well-being. The results show that Canberra, the capital city of Australia, is the best place to live in the world, with Australia also leading the country rankings. Norway follows closely behind in the country rankings.

The OECD's survey takes into account various factors such as income, education, jobs, safety, health, and environment to determine the quality of life in each region. The top 10 regional rankings feature five Australian cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, and Perth, in addition to Canberra. Other high-scoring regions include the states of New Hampshire and Minnesota in the US.

On the other hand, Mexican states occupy all 10 of the bottom regional rankings, with Mexico, Turkey, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia being ranked as the hardest places to live at a country level. The OECD's findings have been met with a mix of pride and surprise in Australian media outlets. While some have hailed Canberra as the best city in the world, others have expressed skepticism, with one headline reading "Is Canberra really the world's best city? More like capital punishment".

Despite its reputation for being dull and devoid of soul, Canberra has been defended by its residents and some media outlets. The Canberra Times has said that the rankings "yet again confirmed what many Canberrans have long known; that our city is the best place to live in the world". An opinion piece on news.com.au has also come to the city's defense, describing it as a great place to live and work.

The OECD study highlights the importance of considering a range of factors beyond economic statistics when evaluating the quality of life in different regions. As the OECD notes, "recent years have seen an increasing awareness that macroeconomic statistics, such as GDP, do not provide policy-makers with a sufficiently detailed picture of the living conditions that ordinary people experience". The organization's survey is one of the few to analyze the quality of life in countries, making it a valuable resource for policymakers and individuals alike.

Overall, the OECD's rankings provide a unique insight into the quality of life in different regions around the world. While there may be some debate about the merits of Canberra as the best city to live in, the fact that Australia tops the country rankings is a testament to the country's high standard of living and strong economy. As the world continues to urbanize and populations grow, understanding what makes a city or region a great place to live will become increasingly important.

Sun European Partners, a subsidiary of Sun Capital, has acquired O&S Holdings, a business established in 1988 by Peter O'Donnell. The company employs over 360 people and has shown significant financial growth, with a pre-tax profit of £6m on a turnover of £32m in 2014. Chris Carney, vice president at Sun European Partners, praised O&S for its exceptional customer service and product quality. The acquisition is expected to increase market share and build upon valuable customer relationships. Peter O'Donnell believes the deal will help develop the company and strengthen its offerings. O&S was advised by PwC Corporate Finance during the acquisition process. With Sun European Partners' support, O&S is poised for further growth and expansion, leveraging its strong reputation and financial foundation. The acquisition marks a new chapter for the company, with exciting opportunities ahead.

Surrey County Council Leader David Hodge has issued a stark warning that the authority may be unable to guarantee school places for children from 2015 unless it receives additional funding from the government. The council is facing a significant shortfall in its budget, which would require it to borrow £200m over the next five years to meet the rising demand for school places.

According to Hodge, the council has been forced to borrow tens of millions of pounds to fund the expansion of schools, but this cannot continue. The borrowing would leave the council with a significant debt that would take 40 years to pay off, placing a substantial burden on Surrey taxpayers. Hodge expressed his frustration, stating that despite repeated requests, the government has failed to guarantee the necessary funding to meet the growing need for school places.

The issue of school places in Surrey has been a longstanding concern, with the council struggling to keep up with the rising demand due to an unanticipated increase in the birth rate over the past decade. In October, Hodge warned that the council had only managed to find places for every child "by the skin of our teeth." The council has been working to provide additional spaces, including 4,100 extra places in September 2014, but the problem persists.

The Conservative-controlled council has been critical of the government's funding allocation, arguing that Surrey contributes more in tax than any region outside the City of London but receives less money than the average county council. The Department for Education (DoE) has responded by stating that Surrey will have received £104m for new school places between 2011-2015, compared to £24m allocated by the previous government over an equivalent period.

Additionally, the government has announced that Surrey County Council will receive a further £60m to spend on new school places in 2015-17. The DoE has also pointed to the opening of two free schools in the county, with another due to open in September, which will provide over 1,800 extra places. However, Hodge and the council remain unconvinced, arguing that the funding is insufficient to meet the growing demand for school places.

The opposition councillors have criticized the council's "failures" in forecasting and planning for schools, but Hodge's warning has highlighted the urgent need for a solution to the school places crisis in Surrey. As the council awaits the government's response to its funding request, parents and children in the county remain anxious about the future of their education. The situation is a stark reminder of the challenges facing local authorities in providing essential services, and the need for a fair and sustainable funding settlement to ensure that every child has access to a quality education.

Everton is on the verge of signing Malaga's Sandro, a 21-year-old striker who had a remarkable season in La Liga, scoring 14 goals. The young player has a £5.2m buy-out clause, which has caught the attention of several top-tier clubs, including Atletico Madrid. However, due to Atletico's transfer ban, Everton manager Ronald Koeman has seized the opportunity to bring Sandro to Goodison Park.

Sandro's potential signing is seen as an addition to Everton's striking resources, rather than a replacement for Romelu Lukaku, who has been linked with a return to Chelsea. Koeman is also keen on signing Ajax captain Davy Klaassen, a 24-year-old midfielder who played against Manchester United in the Europa League Final. The Netherlands international has attracted interest from other clubs, including Inter Milan and Napoli, but Everton is reportedly in talks with Ajax to secure his signature.

Meanwhile, Everton remains in pursuit of Burnley defender Michael Keane and Sunderland goalkeeper Jordan Pickford. However, the future of midfielder Ross Barkley remains uncertain, as he continues to refuse a new contract. With several key signings on the horizon, Koeman is shaping up his squad for a strong season ahead.

Aurimas Butkys, 25, escaped Boston Police Station in Lincolnshire on Thursday. He was detained on an extradition warrant for a Lithuanian assault. Lincolnshire Police called the incident "embarrassing" and are investigating. Butkys had just entered the station before fleeing, prompting a search effort.

A charity auction of 64 snowdog sculptures has raised a significant amount for St Oswald's Hospice. The public art trail featured colourful designs, including some with North East themes. According to Jane Hogan, the response was "beyond anything we imagined". The event's success has led to plans for a similar initiative in autumn 2019. St Oswald's provides care for those with incurable conditions and relies on £7m in annual donations. The auction and subsequent donations will help support the charity's vital work in the North East, caring for adults, young people, and children.

Scotstown Edges Trillick to Reach Provincial Final

In a thrilling match at Brewster Park, Scotstown secured a spot in the provincial final with a 1-9 to 2-6 victory over Trillick. Darren Hughes stole the show, scoring two goals and adding two points to lead the Monaghan team to their first provincial final since 1989. 

Trillick's Daniel McDonnell opened the scoring, but Hughes' first goal helped Scotstown take a 1-5 to 1-4 lead at halftime. Hughes completed his double, and Niall Gormley's goal brought Trillick within a point. However, points from Orin Heaphy and Rory Beggan sealed the win for Scotstown.

Trillick, led by All Star Mattie Donnelly, squandered several opportunities in the second half, ultimately costing them the game. Scotstown will face Crossmaglen, who defeated Kilcoo by four points, on November 29. Joint-manager Mattie McGleenan praised his team's performance, saying they were "outstanding" in difficult conditions. McGleenan expressed pride in his team and vowed to give Crossmaglen a good game, despite acknowledging their opponents' strength.

A Damning Report: Health Board Failed to Protect Patient from Avoidable Stroke

A scathing report by the Public Services Ombudsman has revealed that Cwm Taf health board failed to properly protect Margaret Harries, a patient from Porth, Rhondda Cynon Taff, from an avoidable stroke in 2012. The report, which upheld the family's complaint, found that the health board failed to assess and treat Mrs. Harries' symptoms promptly and effectively, leading to a devastating second stroke.

Mrs. Harries was admitted to the Royal Glamorgan Hospital in Llantrisant on March 24, 2012, with symptoms of diarrhea and vomiting. However, despite her family's repeated requests for medical attention, she was not seen by a doctor for over six hours after suffering her first stroke on April 4, 2012. Tragically, she suffered a further significant stroke overnight while sleeping.

The ombudsman's report identified several failings in Mrs. Harries' care, including a delay in her being seen by a suitably trained clinician and in transferring her to an acute stroke unit. The report's findings have left Mrs. Harries' family feeling angry and upset. Her son, Ceri Harries, expressed his dissatisfaction with the way the complaint was handled by the health board, stating, "I still feel angry about it. Just reading the report now is quite upsetting."

In response to the report, Cwm Taf University Health Board has apologized for the failings and agreed to pay £5,500 in compensation. Allison Williams, the chief executive of the health board, said, "We reiterate our sincere apologies to Mrs. M's family following her treatment in April 2012, and apologize for the distress caused as a result of the failings identified within the report." The health board has also committed to implementing the report's recommendations to prevent similar incidents in the future.

Mrs. Harries was transferred to another hospital for rehabilitation a week after her stroke and was later discharged to a nursing home in February 2013. Sadly, she passed away in November 2014. The report's findings serve as a stark reminder of the importance of prompt and effective medical care, and the devastating consequences that can occur when this standard is not met. The Harries family hopes that their mother's case will lead to improvements in patient care and prevent similar tragedies from occurring in the future.

Egyptian Military Strikes Down Top Jihadist Leader in Sinai

The Egyptian military has announced the death of Abu Duaa al-Ansari, a key leader of the Sinai Province jihadist group, in a series of air strikes near the town of El-Arish. The raids, which targeted strongholds of the group, also known as Ansar Beit al-Maqdis, resulted in the deaths of over 45 terrorists and injured dozens more. Several arms caches were also destroyed in the operation.

According to Brig-Gen Mohammed Samir, the military operation was guided by "accurate intelligence" and led to the killing of Ansari. The air strikes were carried out in southern and south-western areas of El-Arish, the largest town in northern Sinai. The Sinai Province group has been active in the region since 2011 and has been linked to numerous deadly attacks in Sinai and Cairo.

The group's activities have increased since the army deposed President Mohammed Morsi in 2013, with a recent survey showing that they carried out over 31 attacks in a two-week period in March 2016. The Egyptian military has been actively targeting the group, and this latest operation is a significant blow to their leadership. The Sinai Province group has not commented on Ansari's death, but a recent video from the group issued a rare direct threat to Israel, warning that they would soon "pay a high price".

Cracks Discovered in Windsor Park Stadium, But Euro 2016 Qualifier to Proceed as Planned

Despite the recent discovery of cracks in the East Stand of Windsor Park stadium, the Irish Football Association (IFA) has confirmed that the crucial Euro 2016 qualifier against Romania will go ahead as scheduled on June 13. The decision was announced by Patrick Nelson, who addressed Stormont's Culture, Arts and Leisure committee, reassuring fans that the necessary repairs will be made to ensure the stadium's safety.

The cracks were first discovered last month, after a match between Northern Ireland and Finland, which drew a crowd of 4,000 spectators to the stand. Following a structural engineer's report, the IFA board has decided to demolish the stand, with work set to begin immediately. According to Nelson, the demolition is necessary to make the stand safe, and investigations into the cause of the damage are ongoing.

In the meantime, the IFA has accelerated work on the East Stand, South East Quadrant, and South Stand to ensure that the stadium's 10,000 capacity is met for the upcoming match against Romania. The Irish Cup Final, which was originally scheduled to take place at Windsor Park, has been relocated to the Oval in east Belfast, with the IFA working closely with Belfast City Council, the clubs, and the ground to accommodate as many fans as possible.

Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill has expressed his confidence in the plan, stating that he was impressed by the attention to detail and is looking forward to the match against Romania. Martin Lennon, of the construction firm O'Hare & McGovern, which is redeveloping Windsor Park, has assured that the company is committed to carrying out the IFA's instructions and has plans in place for the controlled demolition of the stand.

Gary McAllister, of the Amalgamation of Northern Ireland Supporters Clubs, has welcomed the IFA's statement, believing that fans will be reassured by the plans for the stadium and the upcoming match. With the Euro 2016 qualifier just weeks away, the IFA and its partners are working tirelessly to ensure that the stadium is safe and ready for the big match. As the football community comes together to support the team, fans can rest assured that everything is being done to make the event a success.

Defending Masters Champion Danny Willett Returns to Augusta with High Hopes

It's been a year since Danny Willett shocked the golf world with his maiden major win at the Augusta Masters. The Englishman's impressive five-under-par 67 in the final round, combined with Jordan Spieth's dramatic collapse, earned him the coveted Green Jacket and a career-high ninth spot in the world rankings. However, since his historic victory, Willett has struggled to replicate his form, dropping to 17th in the world rankings.

As Willett returns to Augusta as the defending champion, he admits that the experience has given him a newfound spring in his step. Nevertheless, he acknowledges that his game remains unchanged, and the pressure to perform has mounted. "You do have a spring in your step coming back as champion, but you can't change your game like that," he said.

Despite his inconsistent form, Willett remains optimistic about his chances at this year's Masters. He has had some notable performances, including a third-place finish at the PGA Championship and a second-place finish at the Italian Open, following his Masters win. However, a dip in form ahead of his Ryder Cup debut in October, where he failed to win a single point, raised concerns about his ability to perform under pressure.

Willett attributes the pressure to his own high expectations, rather than external factors. "The pressure has been more from myself.
