It's not a nice feeling to not hit good golf shots when you know what you can do," he said. The 29-year-old Yorkshireman has only managed one top-10 finish so far in 2017, blowing a three-shot lead to finish fifth at the Maybank Championship in February.

As part of his defending champion duties, Willett has chosen the menu for the annual Masters champions' dinner on Tuesday. The 34 former winners in attendance will be treated to a traditional British feast, featuring cottage pie, roast beef with Yorkshire pudding, and apple crumble. Willett is eager to share a taste of his hometown, Sheffield, with his fellow champions, and has warned Augusta's chef to get the Yorkshire puddings just right.

With the Masters tournament just around the corner, Willett is focused on rediscovering his winning form. Despite the challenges he has faced over the past year, he remains confident in his abilities and is determined to make a strong defense of his title. As he prepares to tee off at Augusta, Willett will be drawing on the experience and knowledge he gained from his historic win last year, hoping to once again don the Green Jacket and prove himself as a major champion.

Liberal Democrat MP Mr George has expressed concerns over the upcoming axing of the helicopter service to the Isles of Scilly. Following a meeting with Transport Minister Norman Baker, Mr George stated that he is in discussions with various companies to find a replacement service to commence next year. The current service, operated by British International Helicopters (BIH), will cease on October 31 due to financial difficulties.

Mr Baker announced plans to invest millions of pounds in improving St Mary's Airport, as well as the harbours on the islands and in Penzance. However, locals are calling for a reliable and affordable transport link, particularly during the winter months when the Scillonian ferry is not in operation and the Skybus service is weather-dependent.

Marion Bennett, from Friends of Isles of Scilly Transport (FRIST), highlighted the significant costs involved in establishing a new helicopter service from scratch. She is scheduled to meet with Mr Baker later this month to reiterate the need for a transport service that meets the criteria of being affordable, all year round, and reliable. Mr George has been advocating for improved transport links to the Isles of Scilly for over 15 years, drawing comparisons with the subsidized ferry and air services in the Scottish islands.

At 109 years old, John McLarnon has witnessed a multitude of significant historical events, including two world wars and the creation of the Irish Free State. Born in 1914, he has lived in the same house in Largy, near Portglenone, his entire life. John's childhood was marked by simplicity, with he and his peers often going to school barefoot. However, the invention of the bicycle brought about a significant improvement in his life, providing a means of transportation and freedom.

John's secret to longevity is a life of moderation. He neither smokes nor drinks, but does have a weakness for sweets, despite having all his own teeth. He gave up driving at the age of 100, citing the increasing speed of cars as a concern. John credits his good health as the greatest gift of all and is thankful for his ability to remain active.

As part of a BBC NI appeal for Age NI, John is sharing his wisdom on living a long and healthy life. His advice is simple yet profound: "Take care of your health, because if you lose your health it never comes back," and "Don't put off tomorrow what you can do today." John's experiences and insights are invaluable, and his participation in the "Playing Our Part" appeal highlights the significant contributions older people make to society. Through his story, John serves as an inspiration to people of all ages, demonstrating the importance of living a balanced and active life.

The south of Scotland is gearing up for a spectacular 10-day celebration, running from January 20 to 29 next year. The event promises "something for everybody" with a diverse lineup of acts, including Peatbog Faeries, Skerryvore, and Dervish. Previously announced performers include The Ukulele Orchestra of Great Britain, Charlie Landsborough, Seth Lakeman, and Hackney Colliery Band.

One of the highlights of the event is a carnival on January 22, themed around Tam O' Shanter, which will feature over 2,000 participants. The popular Le Haggis cabaret show will also return for its fourth edition. A special Burns Night Live event on January 25 will be hosted by local folk artist Emily Smith.

This year's event will also feature a new community development project, Transform Dumfries, which aims to encourage local participation. Eight neighbourhood "hubs" will present 35 different events across various locations, including Lochside, Lincluden, and the town centre. According to Executive Producer Graham Main, the project is about putting audiences at the centre of the celebration and inviting more people to join in. The event is expected to re-energise Dumfries as a cultural winter destination, with parties and events happening throughout the town.

Wales' Rugby Team Prepares for Summer Tour with Young Squad

Wales' national rugby team is gearing up for their summer tour, which kicks off on June 17 against Tonga, followed by a match against Samoa on June 24. The team, led by coach Robin McBryde, features 12 uncapped players, making for a exciting and unpredictable series of matches.

According to McBryde, the team is well aware of the challenges that lie ahead. "It's going to be a huge test for us," he said. "The boys are pretty switched on and have been exceptional in their preparation." The team warmed up for the tour with an impressive 88-14 win over Welsh Premiership side RGC 1404 in Colwyn Bay.

The summer tour will be a significant step up in intensity for the young squad, with the first match against Tonga at Eden Park in Auckland promising to be a thrilling encounter. The team will then face Samoa on their home turf, just a week after the Samoans take on the All Blacks. McBryde acknowledges that this will be a tough test, but is confident that the more experienced members of the squad will help guide the younger players.

Injury setbacks have forced Exeter full-back Phil Dollman and Scarlets prop Samson Lee to pull out of the tour, but they have been replaced by Scarlets fly-half Rhys Patchell and Ospreys prop Rhodri Jones. With a mix of youth and experience, Wales' rugby team is ready to take on the challenges of the summer tour.

The Welsh Government has revised its proposal to rename the National Assembly for Wales, following a postponement of the original vote. The motion, which was due to be voted on by Assembly Members (AMs) on Tuesday, has been re-tabled for next week with significant changes. The term "Welsh Parliament" has been dropped, and instead, the motion calls for the assembly to change its name to reflect its constitutional status as a national parliament.

The revised motion, tabled by Labour's chief whip Jane Hutt, invites the Presiding Officer, Elin Jones, and the Assembly Commission to consider the implications of the name change and how to implement it. This move has been seen as a compromise, with the Welsh Government working closely with the Presiding Officer to agree on the new motion.

The proposal to rename the assembly has been debated for several years, with many arguing that the current name does not accurately reflect the institution's powers and responsibilities. Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies has previously stated that the assembly is a parliament "in all but name." However, the Welsh Tories have criticized the government for "overestimating its influence" in the matter, suggesting that the original motion was too prescriptive.

Plaid Cymru AM Bethan Jenkins plans to amend the motion to propose that the Welsh language word "Senedd" be used to refer to the institution itself, rather than just the building that houses the assembly chamber. The word "Senedd" is currently used to refer to the UK Parliament in Welsh.

The Welsh Government and the assembly have stated that they are happy to work together on the wording of the motion, with the Presiding Officer playing a key role in defending the autonomy of the assembly. The proposal will require a majority vote from AMs to proceed. The Welsh Conservatives have welcomed the revised motion and the involvement of the Presiding Officer, stating that they look forward to the proposal being taken forward if it secures the necessary support. The vote is now scheduled to take place next Tuesday.

A wild tiger that wandered into the Nandankanan Zoological Park in Orissa, India, has sparked debate among wildlife officials and zookeepers. The big cat, estimated to be around seven years old, entered the zoo on Monday night and has been roaming around the enclosure of a female tigress named Sara, indicating its desire to mate. The tiger had been causing panic in the adjacent safari park for several months, prompting officials to open the emergency gates and allow it to enter the zoo.

The tiger's movement is being closely monitored with high-resolution cameras, and officials are now discussing whether to release it back into the wild or keep it in the zoo. Orissa's chief wildlife warden, JD Sharma, suggests that putting a radio collar on the tiger would enable them to track its movement and monitor its activity if it is released. However, senior zoo officials and wildlife activists argue that keeping the tiger in the zoo would be beneficial for the conservation and breeding program.

The zoo currently has 24 tigers, all of which are descendants of a single male tiger brought to the park in 1965. Keeping the new tiger would introduce new genes and infuse fresh blood into the program, according to wildlife activist Subhendu Mallick. India's tiger population has been declining alarmingly due to poaching, with numbers shrinking from an estimated 100,000 a century ago to just 1,700 in the wild, according to a 2011 census. The decision on the tiger's fate is still pending, with officials weighing the pros and cons of releasing it back into the wild or keeping it in the zoo.

UK Minister Tobias Ellwood has warned that air drops of food and medical supplies to Aleppo could be "hugely complicated" and put British forces "in harm's way". The statement came in response to an urgent question in the Commons, where over 120 MPs have urged the government to authorize aid drops to the besieged city. Labour's Alison McGovern reiterated the demands, reading out a statement from the Syrian Civil Defence, which described Aleppo as being "in a state of emergency" with 279,000 people under siege for 94 days.

Ellwood cautioned that aid drops could land in the wrong place or fall into the wrong hands, and emphasized that negotiating safe passage for land vehicles was a more viable option. He also highlighted the enormous scale of aid required, stating that the number of aid drops needed would be staggering. When challenged by shadow foreign secretary Emily Thornberry, Ellwood warned that British aircraft carrying out aid drops could be shot down, putting air personnel at risk.

Thornberry argued that despite the complexity and risks involved, air drops were a necessary measure to prevent thousands of deaths. She emphasized that with no alternative solutions, the government must be prepared to take these risks. Ellwood, however, maintained that any such action would require the full support of Parliament. The debate comes as the humanitarian crisis in Aleppo continues to worsen, with the international community facing mounting pressure to take action. The UK government is under increasing scrutiny to explore all possible options to alleviate the suffering of civilians trapped in the city. As the situation remains dire, the government must weigh the risks and complexities of air drops against the urgent need for humanitarian aid.

Scottish club Edinburgh is set to lose one of its key players, Sam Beard, as the 25-year-old has announced that he will be joining Welsh region Dragons at the end of the season. Beard's contract with Edinburgh expires in the summer, and he has opted to make the move to Wales, where he also holds qualification.

Beard, who has played 41 times for Edinburgh, including 24 starts, has expressed his gratitude to the Scottish club for the opportunities he has had. "My time at Edinburgh has been really good," he said. "We've been heading in the right direction and it's good to have been a part of it." Despite only making five appearances this season, Beard is hopeful of getting some decent game-time before the end of the season to finish his time at the club on a high.

Dragons director of rugby Lyn Jones is thrilled to have secured Beard's services, saying: "Sam has played exceptionally well for Edinburgh and starred against us. He's a talented individual and we look forward to him joining the region." Edinburgh head coach Alan Solomons has also praised Beard, wishing him all the best in his new challenge and describing him as a "first-class bloke and a good team man." Beard's move to Dragons is seen as a significant boost to the Welsh region, and he is expected to make a big impact when he joins the team.

Wales Air Ambulance Unveils New State-of-the-Art Helicopter

The Wales Air Ambulance (WAA) has taken a significant step towards providing 24-hour emergency services with the launch of its new H145 aircraft. The custom-built helicopter, based in Llanelli, will serve south Wales and is the first of three new aircraft to be introduced by the charity this year. The new helicopter is equipped with night vision technology, weather radar, and additional lighting, enabling it to operate effectively in the dark.

According to WAA chief executive Angela Hughes, the new aircraft brings the charity closer to its goal of providing round-the-clock services. "With continued fundraising, this new aircraft will support our aim to progress to a 24-hour operation, so we can help anyone in their most difficult hour," she said. The H145 replaces the older EC135 model and boasts a top speed of 150mph, extra room for treatments, and a longer flying range without refuelling.

The new helicopter also features a high-speed internet connection, allowing crews to transmit vital medical information directly to hospitals while en route. Operations manager Mark Winter praised the new aircraft, saying it is "a significantly more advanced machine" that will enable the team to provide better care to those in need. The WAA hopes to utilize the new helicopter to respond to time-critical missions more efficiently, staying within the crucial "golden hour" that can mean the difference between life and death.

A goalless draw was the outcome as Woking hosted Guiseley, with both teams creating scoring opportunities but failing to capitalize. Guiseley's Jordan Preston had an early chance, but his header sailed over the bar. Jake Cassidy came close to breaking the deadlock just before half-time, hitting the post with a well-struck shot. After the restart, Guiseley continued to dominate, with Michael Rankine's shot saved by Woking's busy goalkeeper, Brandon Hall. Hall's best save came in the 68th minute, when he repelled Cassidy's long-range effort. Despite multiple substitutions and yellow cards issued to Simon Walton, Connor Brown, and Fabio Saraiva, neither team could find the back of the net. The match ended 0-0, with Woking and Guiseley sharing the points. The draw highlights the closely contested nature of the match, with both teams demonstrating strong defensive performances.

Herefordshire Voters Express Diverse Views Ahead of General Election

As the general election approaches, voters in Herefordshire are making their voices heard, expressing a wide range of opinions and concerns. The county, which shifted from Liberal Democrat to Conservative control in 2010, is now seeing a rise in independent candidates, with many residents skeptical of national political parties.

At a recent market stall, residents shared their thoughts on the upcoming election, with many citing the National Health Service (NHS) as a top priority. The NHS has been a consistent concern among voters in the area, with many expressing worries about its future. Other issues, such as the potential impact of a European Union exit on farmers and the need to encourage tourism in the area, were also raised.

Some residents, like Dorian from Hereford, advocated for a reduction in government spending and taxation, suggesting that the focus should be on essential services like the police, military, and court systems. Others, like Sue, emphasized the importance of increasing the number of women in government, believing that they would do a better job running the country.

Young people, like Joe from north Herefordshire, are concerned about the lack of opportunities and affordable housing. Joe suggested that building more houses should be a priority, citing the struggles of young people facing high house prices and the prospect of renting until they are 50 or older.

The diverse views expressed by Herefordshire voters reflect the county's independent streak, with many residents looking beyond traditional party lines for solutions. As the election approaches, it remains to be seen how these concerns will be addressed by the candidates. Voters will have a choice between the Conservative, Liberal Democrat, Labour, UKIP, and Green parties, but the presence of independent candidates on the local ballot paper may indicate a desire for alternative voices to be heard.

For a comprehensive guide to the general election in Herefordshire and Worcestershire, including videos and interviews with candidates, visit our website. The election takes place on May 7, and residents are encouraged to make their voices heard by casting their ballots.

A trial is underway for a man accused of murdering a book dealer in his Oxford home. Michael Danaher, 50, denies stabbing Adrian Greenwood, 42, to death in April. The court has heard testimony from several individuals who knew the victim and the defendant, painting a picture of two men with troubled pasts.

Evelyn Altemeyer, Mr. Greenwood's ex-girlfriend, described him as "often in fights" and "could be really aggressive." She stated that he had been blacklisted by a post office after attacking a postman and had a history of heavy drinking. Despite this, she said he was never physically violent towards her. Ms. Altemeyer also revealed that Mr. Greenwood had been taking anti-depressants in 2011 and had held a man hostage during a dispute over a washing machine installation.

A friend of Mr. Greenwood's, Martha Stewart, who attended Christ Church College with him, described him as "defensive and aggressive, like a cross little boy." On the other hand, Mr. Danaher's estranged wife, Elaine Danaher, testified that her husband had admitted to having a temper when he was younger. The couple was married for 12 years before splitting in 2012 and have two sons together.

The prosecution alleges that Mr. Danaher's motive for the stabbing was to steal a valuable first edition of Wind in the Willows, worth £50,000, which Mr. Greenwood had listed on eBay for £2,000. A spreadsheet found on Mr. Danaher's computer contained a list of "people of means" he intended to steal from or kidnap, including high-profile individuals like Kate Moss and Jeffrey Archer.

A witness, Michael Gillnagh, who has known Mr. Danaher since childhood, visited him in prison after his arrest. According to Mr. Gillnagh, Mr. Danaher claimed that Mr. Greenwood had come at him with a knife, and he had acted in self-defense. Mr. Danaher reportedly became tearful during their conversation. The trial is ongoing, with the jury continuing to hear evidence in the case.

A march and rally were held in west London to demonstrate unity and condemn the rise of racist incidents in the area. The event was organized by the local council in response to the discovery of "racist" graffiti scrawled on a Polish Cultural centre in Hammersmith, which occurred in the aftermath of the European referendum. The centre, a beloved local institution for 50 years, was vandalized with hateful messages, prompting widespread outrage and concern.

Hammersmith MP Andy Slaughter expressed his support for the protest, stating that it was a necessary response to the "terrible racist attack" on the Polish centre. He noted that the incident reflects a broader concern that the EU referendum and Brexit have emboldened a small minority of people to express offensive and racist opinions. Slaughter emphasized that the protest and rally were a testament to the community's commitment to unity and inclusivity.

Residents from the area attended the march, including Michael Roach, who felt it was his "duty" to participate. Roach stressed the importance of coming together as a community, stating that "we need to come together as just one family, one world family." He also highlighted the need for solidarity with other marginalized groups, saying "black lives matter" and expressing his concern for the future of his children and grandchildren.

The Metropolitan Police reported a significant increase in racial and religious hate crimes, with 771 incidents reported between June 24 and July 5. While exact statistics for the period before the referendum are not available, reports of hate crimes had risen 13% in the 12 months leading up to May. The community's response to the incident serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of standing together against hate and promoting a culture of inclusivity and respect.

Fresh from her Strictly Come Dancing win, Joanne Clifton is set to take the stage as a lead dancer in the musical 'Thoroughly Modern Millie'. Over 13 million viewers watched her lift the glitterball trophy with partner Ore Oduba just before Christmas. Rather than taking a break, Joanne has been busy in rehearsals, preparing for her new role as a New York dancer. This has been a childhood dream for Joanne, who will need to adapt to acting and singing in addition to dancing. She draws parallels between herself and the character Millie, who moves to New York to pursue her dreams, much like Joanne's own move to Italy at 16 to join a dance school. Cast in the musical last summer, Joanne's Strictly commitments delayed her start in rehearsals. She hopes to return to the show later this year to defend her title.

Plans for the North East's first directly elected mayor have been abandoned after four out of seven local councils voted to halt the proposal. The decision was made due to concerns over funding from the government following the UK's decision to leave the European Union. Sunderland, Durham, Gateshead, and South Tyneside councils expressed dissatisfaction with the reassurances provided, prompting them to reject the devolution deal.

The Communities Secretary, Sajid Javid, expressed his disappointment at the decision, stating that the region would miss out on over £1 billion in investment as a result. The deal would have brought significant powers and funding to the area, including £30 million annually for 30 years, as well as control over transport, skills, and training.

Newcastle, North Tyneside, and Northumberland councils, however, remain committed to the plan. Mr. Javid has announced that the government will now focus on securing a new agreement with these councils to progress with devolution. The North East Combined Authority chairman, Paul Watson, described the government's decision to end discussions as "very disappointing," emphasizing that all council leaders were committed to devolution, but a majority agreement could not be reached.

The scrapped plans were part of the government's Northern Powerhouse program, which aims to decentralize power and promote economic growth in the north of England. Elections for directly elected mayors are still scheduled to take place in other areas of England in May 2017. Meanwhile, the Department for Communities and Local Government has confirmed that work is ongoing to secure a devolution deal for the Tees Valley.

Liam Laverick, 25, appeared at Hull Crown Court regarding the death of Tommy Lee Laverick-Whitworth. The charge will be altered to murder at his next appearance in September. Laverick was remanded in custody and is due back in court on September 11. The victim died in hospital on September 25 after an ambulance call to Anlaby Road, Hull, two days prior.

Renowned Bhutanese filmmaker Tshering Wangyel has passed away, leaving the nation's movie industry in shock. The Bhutan Film Association announced his death, stating that he was hospitalized last month with pneumonia while shooting his latest movie. With a career spanning over two decades, Wangyel made 40 films that uniquely blended Bollywood with Buddhist themes. He played a pivotal role in developing Bhutan's film industry, providing opportunities for countless actors and actresses. According to Yeshi Dorji, executive director of the Bhutan Film Association, Wangyel's contributions were immense, creating jobs and launching careers. His first film, "Rawa," was released in 1999, and he went on to transport screens and projectors to villages, bringing cinema to the people. Wangyel's legacy will be deeply felt in the Bhutanese film community. His death is a huge loss, and he will be remembered for his dedication to Bhutanese cinema.

New Study Reveals Nine Key Risk Factors for Dementia, Emphasizes Importance of Lifestyle Changes

A groundbreaking study presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference in London has identified nine key risk factors for dementia, including lack of education, hearing loss, smoking, and physical inactivity. The research, which combines the work of 24 international experts, suggests that lifestyle factors can play a significant role in increasing or reducing an individual's dementia risk, with modifiable risk factors accounting for 35% of the total risk.

The study, led by Professor Gill Livingston from University College London, emphasizes the importance of acting now to reduce the risk of dementia, which is projected to affect 131 million people globally by 2050. Currently, there are an estimated 47 million people living with the condition. "Although dementia is diagnosed in later life, the brain changes usually begin to develop years before," said Prof Livingston. "Acting now will vastly improve life for people with dementia and their families and, in doing so, will transform the future of society."

The report highlights the benefits of building a "cognitive reserve," which involves strengthening the brain's networks to enable it to function effectively in later life despite damage. Failure to complete secondary education is identified as a major risk factor, while continuing to learn throughout life can help build additional brain reserves. Hearing loss in middle age is also a significant risk factor, as it can lead to social isolation and depression, which are among other modifiable risk factors for dementia.

The study also emphasizes the importance of maintaining a healthy lifestyle, with factors such as not smoking, exercising regularly, and keeping a healthy weight all contributing to a reduced risk of dementia. Treating high blood pressure and diabetes is also crucial, as these conditions can increase the risk of dementia, as well as cardiovascular disease and cancer.

While the researchers did not have enough data to include dietary factors or alcohol in their calculations, they believe that these could also be important factors in reducing the risk of dementia. Dr Doug Brown, director of research at Alzheimer's Society, said: "Though it's not inevitable, dementia is currently set to be the 21st Century's biggest killer. We all need to be aware of the risks and start making positive lifestyle changes." Dr David Reynolds, chief scientific officer at Alzheimer's Research UK, added: "Alongside prevention research, we must continue to invest in research to find a life-changing treatment for people with this devastating condition." By making informed lifestyle choices and taking steps to reduce our risk of dementia, we can help create a healthier and more supportive society for all.

A new record high temperature for November has been set in the UK, with the mercury reaching 22.4C (72.3F) in Trawsgoed, Ceredigion, on Sunday afternoon. This surpasses the previous record of 21.7C (71.1F) set in Prestatyn, Wales, in 1946. According to BBC Weather's Helen Willetts, the record-breaking temperature is due to mild southerly winds and humid air. However, fog in many areas brought temperatures down, with some flights cancelled at Heathrow.

Despite the fog, areas without it experienced temperatures in the high teens. The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for fog, effective from Sunday evening to Monday midday, covering much of England and parts of eastern Wales. The warning advises of potential travel disruptions due to poor visibility. More warm air is forecast for Monday, but showers are expected on Wednesday and Thursday. Willetts noted that the record could potentially be broken again on Monday, highlighting the unusual warmth for this time of year. The average UK temperature for November is typically around 10-15C (50-59F), making this warm spell a notable exception.

Body Image Concerns Plaguing UK Teenagers, Says New Report

A shocking new report has revealed that almost a third of UK teenagers are avoiding activities such as physical education due to fears about their appearance. The Be Real Campaign, which conducted a survey of 2,000 UK teenagers, found that 52% of 11 to 16-year-olds regularly worry about their looks, with 60% of girls and 43% of boys affected.

One teenager, Josh from Renfrew near Glasgow, has spoken out about his own struggles with body image. The teenager, who has already had to leave one school due to bullying related to his weight, says he feels pressure to conform to a certain physical ideal. "I genuinely don't know one big male model," he said, highlighting the lack of diversity in the fashion industry. Josh also admitted to photoshopping all of his online profile pictures, spending up to 25 minutes editing out imperfections such as spots and double chins.

The report warns that fears about appearance are having a "profoundly negative effect" on young people, with many suffering in silence due to fear of sharing their insecurities. The Be Real Campaign is calling on schools to play a key role in combating body anxiety, and has launched a toolkit to help teachers promote positive body image in the classroom.

Denise Hatton, YMCA chief executive for England and Wales, said: "Evidence shows that schools are uniquely placed to support young people to hold positive discussions around body image with their peers and help reduce the negative impact low body confidence can have." Julie Hunter, assistant head teacher at Bradon Forest School in Wiltshire, welcomed the toolkit, saying it would help teachers to use "accurate language" when discussing body image and make students more aware of the issue.

The report's findings are a stark reminder of the need for greater support and education around body image in UK schools. By working together, teachers, parents, and young people can help to promote positive body confidence and reduce the negative impact of low self-esteem. As Josh's story highlights, the pressure to conform to unrealistic beauty standards can have serious consequences for young people's mental health and wellbeing. It is time for schools and society as a whole to take action and promote a more inclusive and accepting definition of beauty.

BNP Launches Campaign, Vows to Outdo UKIP on Immigration and EU Withdrawal

The British National Party (BNP) has officially launched its campaign for the upcoming European and local elections, with leader Nick Griffin asserting that his party's policies on immigration and EU withdrawal are more robust than those of its rival, UKIP. Speaking to the BBC, Griffin claimed that the BNP has been instrumental in bringing the debates on cutting immigration and leaving the EU to the forefront of public discourse.

Despite the party's declining opinion poll ratings and internal feuding, which has led to the loss of members, including one of its MEPs, Andrew Brons, Griffin remains confident that the BNP's stance on immigration and EU withdrawal will resonate with voters. The party won almost a million votes in the 2009 European elections, securing two seats in the European Parliament, including Griffin's own seat in North West England.

Griffin took aim at UKIP, accusing the party of being soft on immigration. While UKIP advocates for tighter border controls, the BNP is calling for a total halt to immigration, citing Britain's already strained resources. "We are the only party that, when we say 'Stop immigration,' we actually mean it," Griffin said. "UKIP is saying 50,000 net, but that would actually mean 300,000 Africans and Asians coming in every year under their plans. Our position is very simple: Britain's full, and we should shut the doors."

The BNP leader also reiterated his party's commitment to British withdrawal from the EU, dismissing the idea of a referendum as a potential "rigged" process. Instead, Griffin argues that Britain should withdraw from the EU immediately, without hesitation or further debate. This stance is in contrast to UKIP, which has called for a referendum on EU membership.

Griffin's comments come as the BNP faces increased competition from UKIP, which has gained significant traction in recent years. However, Griffin remains undeterred, citing his party's unique approach to politics and his own reputation as a known quantity among voters. "A lot of people are going to be fooled into voting for UKIP, but we really don't need that many voters to get me back in the North West," he said. "A lot of people want to have an MEP where they actually know who he is. The others are all faceless. I'm a character."

The European and local elections are scheduled to take place on May 22, with the BNP fielding a full slate of 70 candidates. Despite the party's current low opinion poll ratings, Griffin is confident that his party can make a significant impact, particularly in the North West region, where he has a strong base of support. As the campaign heats up, it remains to be seen whether the BNP's uncompromising stance on immigration and EU withdrawal will resonate with voters, or if the party will continue to struggle in the face of increased competition from UKIP.

Motorists who slowed down to gawk at a three-lorry collision in Thurrock on Thursday are being issued court summonses by Essex Police. The incident, which occurred at 04:40 BST, resulted in one lorry driver being trapped in his cabin, although his injuries were not serious. However, the real concern for authorities was the behavior of other drivers on the scene.

As police and emergency services worked to free the trapped driver and clear the damaged vehicles, many motorists on the opposite carriageway were caught "rubber-necking," or slowing down to look at the crash scene. Some were even using their mobile phones to film the incident, putting themselves and others at risk of further accidents. Charges will include careless driving and using a mobile phone while driving.

The anti-clockwise carriageway was closed until 14:00, resulting in tailbacks of up to 12 miles. Adam Pipe, casualty reduction manager for Essex Police, expressed his disappointment at the behavior of these drivers, stating that it showed a lack of respect for the casualties and emergency services. He also warned that sharing crash footage on social media can lead to families of victims finding out about the incident before being officially notified by police.

Belfast Airport Targets New European Routes with Government Aid

Belfast Airport is in talks with the government to explore potential aid for establishing new routes to major European cities. Brian Ambrose, the airport's representative, has identified Frankfurt, Munich, and Brussels as key targets for expansion. Although a timeline for these new services is uncertain, Ambrose expressed optimism about the prospects. 

The news comes as Vueling announces its entry into the Northern Irish market with flights from George Best Belfast City airport to Barcelona. Meanwhile, Belfast International has unveiled ten new routes, including a service to Iceland. A report on air connectivity is forthcoming from Stormont, which may pave the way for a new air development fund. This initiative would be similar to a previous £4m fund that successfully attracted routes such as New York in 2003. Ambrose confirmed that the government is open to supporting route development, provided a state-aid compliant solution can be found.

In a groundbreaking move, Scotland and Iceland have signed a historic agreement that brings together all snowsports areas in both countries. The deal, announced at the North Atlantic Ski Areas' Association conference, is believed to be a world first. Five Scottish ski centres, including CairnGorm Mountain, Glencoe Mountain, Glenshee, Nevis Range, and The Lecht, have joined forces with all nine of Iceland's snowsports centres.

This innovative partnership aims to share information, advice, and best practices on quality development, sustainability, and other key areas. The agreement is an extension of the memorandum of understanding signed earlier this month between VisitScotland and the Icelandic Tourist Board. According to Heather Negus, chairwoman of Ski-Scotland, this deal is unique in that it includes every lift at every resort in both countries, making it a comprehensive and exciting collaboration.

With daily flights connecting Glasgow, Aberdeen, and Edinburgh to Reykjavik, skiers and snowboarders from both countries can now explore new terrain and experience the culture of a new country. Malcolm Roughead, chief executive of VisitScotland, highlighted the strong relationship between the two countries, saying that both Scotland and Iceland "punch well above their weight on the global tourism stage." This partnership is expected to boost tourism and promote the sharing of expertise, ultimately enhancing the snowsports experience for visitors to both countries. The collaboration is a significant step forward for the snowsports industry and is set to bring numerous benefits to both Scotland and Iceland.

A 33-year-old man who reversed his car at speed and struck his mother, causing her serious injury, has had his prison sentence reduced on appeal. Abdul Abbasi, of Thorndale, Hull, was initially jailed for two years and four months for causing serious injury by dangerous driving. However, at a Court of Appeal hearing, his sentence was reduced to 16 months.

The incident occurred in October on Redmire Close, Hull, where Abbasi reversed into his 65-year-old mother, Rehana Abassi, after a disagreement. He then crashed into a parked car and drove off with his mother still under the vehicle. Mrs Abassi suffered serious injuries, including broken ribs, and spent two weeks in hospital.

Despite the severity of the incident, the court heard that Mrs Abassi has forgiven her son. The jury at Abbasi's trial had cleared him of attempted murder and causing grievous bodily harm, as they were "not satisfied" that he knew his mother was behind the car when he reversed into her.

The Court of Appeal judges, Sir Andrew Smith and Geoffrey Marson QC, took into account Abbasi's previously good character and mental wellbeing when reducing his sentence. Abbasi, a taxi driver with no previous convictions, was described as "mentally fragile" and a "decent man who lost control under pressure". His six-year driving ban was also cut to two years.

Austrian police have seized medical equipment, products, and mobile phones from the Kazakhstan biathlon team's accommodation. The raid was conducted in collaboration with Austria's anti-doping authority, which also collected blood and urine samples. The International Biathlon Union (IBU) has stated that Kazakhstan can still participate in Thursday's mixed relay event in Hochfilzen.

According to Manas Ussenov of the Kazak biathlon federation, the seized medical equipment was found in the team doctor's room, but they have all necessary documentation for the medicines. The raid was prompted by the discovery of a cardboard box containing used medical equipment and notes suggesting doping activity at a nearby petrol station last month.

Meanwhile, French biathlete Martin Fourcade protested against Russian athletes by walking off the podium during the medal ceremony. Fourcade, a two-time Olympic champion, has been vocal about the need for the IBU to take a stronger stance against doping. The incident occurred during the mixed relay event, which was the first competition since Russian athlete Alexander Loginov's return from a doping ban. The Russian team refused to shake hands with Fourcade, who eventually rejoined his team on stage.

A major fire at Bakers Quay in Gloucester has been brought under control by the Gloucestershire Fire and Rescue Service. The blaze was reported at 18:47 BST, and two 19-year-old men have been arrested on suspicion of arson. The historic 19th Century building is now structurally unsafe, with a section having collapsed. Fortunately, nearby rugby fans watching the England v Australia match were not at risk and did not need to be evacuated. The fire service will remain on site, and engineers will assess the building's safety. The cause of the fire is being investigated, with the two suspects currently in police custody.

A Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) worker had a harrowing experience when he was confronted by a swarm of angry honey bees while checking a meter box at a house in Belleeks. The bees had built a nest around the meter, and the worker was stung up to 10 times on his face and neck before he managed to escape to safety.

Fortunately, the worker did not have a bee sting allergy, which could have made the incident much more serious. According to NIE's meter reading manager, Cormac McCamphill, the company's priority was the safety of their staff member, but they also wanted to avoid destroying the bees. Instead, they called in an expert from the Ulster Beekeepers' Association, Darren Nugent, to safely relocate the bees.

Nugent used a homemade suction device to remove the bees from the meter box and transferred them to a hive at his home in Kilkeel, County Down. The operation was a success, and the bees have settled into their new home. Nugent even managed to harvest half a dozen jars of honey from the nest, which he shared with the farmer who owned the house.

The incident was a first for NIE staff, who sometimes encounter animal hazards like livestock and dogs, but never bees in a meter box. The bees are believed to have been in the box for around eight weeks and were thriving in their unusual location. As Nugent noted, "They were doing well in there. In fact, they were doing better than some of the bees in the hives outside my house." The successful relocation of the bees is a testament to the importance of preserving these vital pollinators and finding humane solutions to unexpected problems.

Broughty Ferry lifeboat station responded to the same number of calls in 2016 as 2015, launching 92 times. The crew rescued 29 people, a 45% increase from 2015, making it the UK's 11th busiest station.

A former council leader has referred himself to the standards committee for investigation, following reports that council officers failed to act quickly enough on claims made against a councillor before the 2015 elections. The councillor in question, Simon Carter, later admitted to 16 charges of making indecent images of children.

The move comes after an independent review found that former chief executive Mike Owen and head of children's services Mark Carriline had "inexplicably" and "deliberately" delayed implementing safeguarding procedures when allegations about Carter first came to light in 2015. The review suggested that the pair had done so to help the council's ruling Labour group before the 2015 election and protect the then-leader, Mr. Connolly, from public scrutiny.

Mr. Connolly, who quit as leader last year, has apologized for giving Carter a written reference on council-headed notepaper ahead of his sentencing, describing him as "trustworthy, honest and reliable". He has stated that he wants to be "open and transparent" and has cooperated fully with the independent review. He will also cooperate fully with the standards committee investigation.

The disciplinary reports have been published, and the council has agreed to carry out a further investigation into councillors' conduct. Current council leader Rishi Shori has said that Mr. Connolly has apologized for writing the reference and accepts that it was a "terrible error of judgement". Any necessary action will be taken once the investigation is complete.

The leader of the Conservative group, James Daly, has expressed his sadness and disappointment at the events, stating that the political fortunes of a party should never trump the responsibility to look after vulnerable children. Mr. Shori has also emphasized that no child was put at risk in relation to these proceedings and that he acted decisively when he received information from a member of the public.

The council's decision to publish the reports and carry out a further investigation is a step towards transparency and accountability. The investigation will aim to determine the extent of the failures and whether any further action is needed to prevent similar incidents in the future. The people of Bury deserve to know that their council is committed to protecting the most vulnerable members of their community.

Dilwyn Williams of Caerphilly died in a collision on the A4058 Trehafod bypass. His family remembered him as a "loveable local character." Kim Jong-nam, the Half-Brother of North Korea's Leader, Killed in Malaysia Airport

In a shocking turn of events, Kim Jong-nam, the half-brother of North Korea's leader Kim Jong-un, was killed at Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Malaysia on Monday. The 45-year-old was waiting to board a flight to Macau when he was allegedly poisoned by two women, who were later arrested along with a man. The incident has sparked widespread speculation and concern, with many questions still unanswered.

According to Indonesian national police chief Tito Karnavian, one of the women, Siti Aisyah, claimed to have been paid to perform what she thought was a prank. She allegedly told authorities that she and another woman had previously performed the prank on other men, convincing them to close their eyes before spraying them with water. However, on this occasion, the sprayer allegedly contained a poisonous substance that was sprayed into Kim Jong-nam's face.

Karnavian said that Aisyah had been given a few dollars for each prank and was unaware that the latest incident was an assassination attempt by alleged foreign agents. A grainy image broadcast in South Korea and Malaysia showed a woman, believed to be Aisyah, running in the airport wearing a white T-shirt with the letters "LOL" written on the front.

Aisyah's family and former neighbors in Indonesia have expressed shock and surprise at her arrest. Her former father-in-law, Tjia Liang Kiong, told the Associated Press that she had moved to Malaysia in 2011 with her then-husband to find work after their garment-making business went bust. Hundreds of thousands of Indonesian migrants work in Malaysia, where incomes are much higher.

Meanwhile, North Korea has demanded that Malaysia immediately release the body of Kim Jong-nam. The North Korean ambassador to Malaysia, Kang Chol, said that his country had not consented to the post-mortem already carried out and would categorically reject its findings. He urged Malaysia not to be "entangled with the political plot" by forces hostile to North Korea and to release the body without condition.

However, Malaysia has refused to release the body until it receives a DNA sample from Kim Jong-nam's next-of-kin. The Malaysian authorities are still investigating the incident and have arrested several individuals in connection with the murder.

South Korea's intelligence agency has accused North Korea of assassinating Kim Jong-nam, saying that Pyongyang had wanted to kill him for years but that he was being protected by China. Kim Jong-nam was largely estranged from his family after being passed over for the North Korean leadership in favor of his younger half-brother. He spent most of his time overseas in Macau, mainland China, and Singapore, and had spoken out in the past against his family's dynastic control of North Korea.

The incident has sparked widespread concern and speculation, with many questions still unanswered. The investigation is ongoing, and it remains to be seen what further developments will emerge in the coming days. One thing is certain, however: the death of Kim Jong-nam has sent shockwaves around the world and has raised concerns about the safety and security of individuals who are seen as threats to the North Korean regime.

A charity football match is set to take place on Thursday, with the current Glenavon squad facing off against a Derry team comprised mainly of former teammates of Mark Farren, a former Derry City player. The match aims to raise funds for Farren, who is battling a brain tumour. Farren, 33, recently underwent his third operation to remove the tumour, with surgeons successfully removing over 80% of it. However, the tumour has been found to be highly aggressive, and Farren's speech and mobility have been affected.

The football community has rallied around Farren, with his former teammate James McClean pledging £1,000 to the fund. Farren's family has appealed for financial help to raise around £25,000, which will enable him to undergo treatment at a specialist cancer centre in Germany. Glenavon manager Gary Hamilton has urged fans to support the match, saying, "I'm sure all the good people around the club will come out and support Mark in this very serious situation in his life."

Farren, a Greencastle native, had a successful career with Derry City, becoming the club's record goal-scorer in 2012. He was initially diagnosed with a benign brain tumour in 2008 but continued to play until 2009. After undergoing surgery, he returned to the pitch in 2011 and broke the club's scoring record a year later. Farren joined Glenavon in 2013 and was named the Irish League's player of the month in April of that year. The charity match on Thursday is expected to feature former Derry City players such as Barry Molloy, Ciaran Martyn, and Ruaidhri Higgins, all of whom will be playing in support of their former teammate.

A lesbian student in China has spoken out against the Guangdong University of Foreign Studies after she was initially refused her diploma following a public proposal from her girlfriend at their graduation ceremony. Xiaoyu Wang, a 23-year-old translation student, said that the university told the couple that their act had "violated regulations" and that they should "keep our homosexuality to ourselves."

The proposal, which took place on campus, was a romantic gesture that aimed to express the couple's feelings and raise awareness about LGBT issues. However, it was met with backlash from university officials, who reportedly told the couple that they would "face punishment" after pictures of them kissing went viral on social media. One official even accused Ms. Wang of spreading vulgar content and misbehaving in public, despite previous warnings from the university.

Ms. Wang said that the university's actions caused her significant emotional harm, and that the experience turned what was supposed to be a joyful day into a "nightmare." She took to social media to express her feelings, writing, "I'm devastated and humiliated, but I'm fighting back and need your help." The university has since given Ms. Wang her diploma, but the incident has sparked widespread outrage and calls for greater support and protection for LGBT students on campus.

The incident has also drawn attention to the broader issue of discrimination against LGBT individuals in China. A 2012 poll by the Aibai Centre, an LGBT organization, found that 77% of gay students reported being subjected to bullying on campus because of their sexual orientation or gender identity. Ms. Wang's case is not an isolated one, and she hopes that by speaking out, she can help spark change and bring an end to discrimination against LGBT individuals.

The LGBT group All Out has called on the university to apologize publicly to the two students and to take comprehensive measures to prevent discrimination and homophobic harassment on campus. Supporters have delivered a statement to the university headmaster, who said he would look into the matter. Ms. Wang's girlfriend, Jean Ouyang, who proposed to her at the graduation ceremony, told Chinese media that the "mental and emotional harm" caused by the university's actions could not be erased.

Ms. Wang's experience has also had a personal cost, as university officials reportedly outed her to her parents by asking them to come and collect her diploma together. An official even sent a video of the marriage proposal to Ms. Wang's mother, causing tension and stress for the family. Ms. Wang said that her biggest headache now is mending her relationship with her parents, who were hurt by the incident.

As Ms. Wang fights for justice and equality, she remains determined to speak out against discrimination and to advocate for the rights of LGBT individuals. "I'm sick of staying silent," she wrote. "No school should intimidate students for who they are or who they love. My case is just one in many, but it could spark a change." Her courage and resilience have inspired many, and her story serves as a reminder of the importance of promoting inclusivity, acceptance, and support for all individuals, regardless of their sexual orientation or gender identity.

Brazilian Judge Orders Immediate Reinstatement of WhatsApp Service

In a dramatic turn of events, a Brazilian judge has ordered the immediate reinstatement of the WhatsApp messaging service, which was suspended for 48 hours on Thursday. The suspension, which was imposed due to the company's failure to comply with a court order, had sparked widespread outrage and frustration among the app's millions of users in Brazil.

Judge Xavier de Souza ruled that the suspension was unreasonable and that it was not fair to punish millions of users for the company's inertia. The court had ordered WhatsApp to provide investigators with information related to a criminal court case, but the company failed to comply, leading to the suspension.

The suspension of WhatsApp had a significant impact on Brazilians, who rely heavily on the app to communicate with family, friends, and colleagues both inside and outside the country. According to the TechCrunch website, a staggering 93% of Brazil's internet population uses WhatsApp, making it an essential tool for communication.

Many Brazilians took to social media to express their frustration and disappointment, with the hashtag #Nessas48HorasEuVou (#Inthese48hoursIwill) trending on Twitter. The hashtag was used to joke about all the things people would do during the suspension, from reading books to taking long walks.

The suspension also had significant implications for expats living in Brazil, who rely on WhatsApp to keep in touch with loved ones back home. With mobile providers charging high rates for monthly plans and international calls, WhatsApp's free text message and internet telephone service is a lifeline for many.

Facebook, which owns WhatsApp, also weighed in on the issue, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg expressing his shock and disappointment at the suspension. "I am stunned that our efforts to protect people's data would result in such an extreme decision by a single judge to punish every person in Brazil who uses WhatsApp," he wrote in a post on Facebook.

The suspension was ordered after WhatsApp failed to comply with a court order related to a criminal case. According to Brazilian media, the company was asked to provide details of communication by a suspected gang member who allegedly used WhatsApp to organize illegal activity.

The incident has also highlighted the ongoing tensions between WhatsApp and Brazilian phone companies, which have urged the government to restrict the use of free voice-over-internet services offered through the app. The phone companies argue that the rise of WhatsApp has damaged their businesses, and have been seeking to limit its use.

Meanwhile, other messaging services have reported a surge in new users since the suspension was imposed. Telegram, a rival messaging app, reported that over 1.5 million Brazilian users had joined its platform since the court order was handed down.

With the reinstatement of WhatsApp, Brazilians can once again communicate freely with each other and with the rest of the world. The incident has highlighted the importance of WhatsApp in Brazilian life and the need for the company to comply with court orders to avoid similar disruptions in the future.
A body was found near a Haddington plant in East Lothian on Monday at 06:00. Police are treating the death as unexplained, with forensic officers investigating the scene.

Australian Police Rescue Stranded Sailors in Treacherous Seas

In a daring rescue operation, Australian police saved two stranded sailors, Irishman Nick Dwyer, 55, and Frenchwoman Barbara Heftman, 44, who were battling turbulent seas 210 nautical miles off Sydney. The couple, on a 10-year circumnavigation of the globe, had activated an emergency beacon on Tuesday after their rudder broke three days earlier.

The sailors described the conditions as "enormous seas, waves the size of buildings" and gale-force winds that made it impossible to stand up. Their 40ft yacht "rolled" on Tuesday, prompting them to issue a distress call. "We weren't sure whether we were going to be rolled again, and each time a wave hit, we thought, 'is this the one that's going to take us?'" Mr. Dwyer said.

The Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) responded to the distress call by sending a jet to the remote location, followed by a request for police assistance. The New South Wales Police rescue boat took over 13 hours to reach the pair amid "treacherous conditions." Mr. Dwyer expressed his gratitude, saying, "It was truly amazing, to think that somebody had to come that far to save us... I owe them my life. We owe them our lives."

The couple will remain in Sydney while deciding their next move. Despite losing their yacht, they are relieved to be alive. "Our home's gone, we're alive, I expect to live a little bit longer, and that'll be okay," Mr. Dwyer said. The rescue operation is a testament to the bravery and dedication of the Australian police and maritime authorities, who risked their lives to save the stranded sailors in the treacherous seas.

SNP Calls for Abolition of House of Lords Amid Reform Resistance

The Scottish National Party (SNP) has renewed its calls for the abolition of the House of Lords, citing the chamber's lack of democratic legitimacy and recent scandals. The comments come after Lord Sewel resigned from the House of Lords following allegations of taking drugs with prostitutes. Pete Wishart, MP for Perth and North Perthshire, argued that the unelected chamber has no place in modern society, and that its reputation has been further tarnished by the recent scandal.

Wishart criticized the House of Lords as a "repository for the cronies and donors of the UK parties," and expressed concern over the increasing costs of maintaining the parliament. He also highlighted the hypocrisy of the government considering reducing the number of elected members while planning to appoint more Conservative peers to the Lords. The SNP has long refused to take seats in the House of Lords on principle, and Wishart reiterated the party's commitment to democratic reform.

Despite growing calls for wider reforms, Prime Minister David Cameron is resisting pressure from other parties to address the issue. A recent report suggested that Cameron intends to press ahead with plans to appoint more Conservative peers, which would further entrench the party's dominance in the chamber. The current composition of the House of Lords stands at 226 Tory peers, 212 Labour, 101 Liberal Democrats, and 179 crossbenchers.

In response to the criticism, Lord Hill defended the House of Lords, arguing that the actions of a few individuals should not tarnish the reputation of the entire chamber. He claimed that the House of Lords remains an effective revising chamber, despite its flaws. However, Wishart remained unconvinced, stating that the current House of Lords is "beyond reform" and must be abolished and reconstituted on democratic principles. The debate is set to continue, with the SNP and other parties pushing for meaningful reform and the government resisting calls for change.

Gillingham Avoid Points Deduction Despite Fielding Ineligible Player

Gillingham Football Club has escaped a points deduction after midfielder Emmanuel Osadebe played in their 4-0 win over Sheffield United on August 8 without proper clearance. The 19-year-old, who joined the club from Tottenham's youth development program last August, was found to have been registered with the Football League but not the Football Association due to an error in his documentation.

Osadebe's previous registration was with Irish side Dundalk, and he required international clearance to play for Gillingham. However, the Football Association failed to process his registration ahead of the 2015-16 season. A football disciplinary commission has fined the club, but the penalty will only be enforced if Gillingham fields another ineligible player within the next 12 months.

The Football League acknowledged that Gillingham had admitted to the mistake, but also noted that the FA should have identified the issue earlier. As a result, the commission ruled that a points deduction would be unfair, given the exceptional circumstances of the case. Gillingham currently sits third in the League One table, just one point off the automatic promotion places. The decision is a welcome relief for the club, which can now focus on maintaining its strong start to the season.

Tranmere Rovers striker Andy Mangan has made a surprise return to Shrewsbury Town, just six months after leaving the club. The 29-year-old joined Rovers on a one-year deal in July, but has struggled to regain his starting place after an injury. Mangan expressed his desire to play regular 90-minute matches, which Tranmere manager Gary Brabin could not guarantee.

Shrewsbury, currently 20th in League One, offered Mangan an 18-month contract, and he has opted to rejoin his former club. Mangan's return is seen as a significant boost to the team, and fans will be eager to see him back in action.

Essex County Cricket Club has announced the signing of Pakistani left-arm bowler Mohammad Amir. The 24-year-old will join the team following his international commitments and will be available for all formats of the game. Amir's signing is a significant coup for Essex, who won the Division Two title this summer and will play in Division One of the County Championship in 2017.

Amir has played 20 Tests for Pakistan, including four against England this summer. His career was put on hold in 2010 when he was banned from cricket for five years after being convicted of spot-fixing in a Lord's Test. He served three months in prison and was cleared to play domestic cricket in Pakistan in January last year.

Essex head coach Chris Silverwood expressed his delight at the signing, stating that Amir showed a "real desire" to join the club. Silverwood praised Amir's talent, noting that he has already proven himself at international level despite being only 24 years old. Amir's addition to the team is expected to strengthen Essex's chances in the upcoming season.

Golf Action Resumes After Thunderstorm Delay

The Golf Club of Houston in Humble, Texas, played host to a busy Saturday morning as 27 players, including Ryder Cup player Jamie Donaldson, returned to complete their second rounds. Friday's play was delayed by 90 minutes due to thunderstorms, and bad light eventually curtailed the action. Donaldson, 40, had three holes to finish and returned a 68, but dropped a shot in the process.

Charley Hoffman currently leads the pack at 10 under, closely followed by Jamie Lovemark at 9 under. Donaldson's impressive seven birdies in 15 holes on Friday propelled him up the leaderboard by 29 places. However, a dropped shot on Saturday saw him slip back slightly. Scotland's Martin Laird also dropped a shot to finish at 5 under, while world number two Jordan Spieth trails behind at 6 shots back. The cut was made at level par, resulting in the elimination of players such as Englishman Greg Owen and three-time major winner Padraig Harrington.

A pedestrian was fatally struck in Hilton, Derbyshire, on Tuesday at approximately 16:50 BST. The incident occurred on Main Street after a police pursuit was initiated. A Vauxhall Astra, signaled to stop by a marked Derbyshire Police vehicle near the A38, failed to comply, prompting a chase. Although the pursuit was eventually abandoned, the Astra later collided with two vehicles and a pedestrian. Matthew Luke Hogg, 24, has been remanded in custody and is set to appear at Derby Crown Court next month. The Independent Police Complaints Commission is investigating the "tragic incident" to determine if police policies and procedures were followed. The incident has raised questions about the events leading up to the crash, and the IPCC's findings will be crucial in providing answers. The community is awaiting the outcome of the investigation.

A widow's tragic death from asbestos-related cancer has sparked a legal investigation into the safety protocols of a former Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) site. Jayne Eustace, 48, passed away in March after a battle with pericardial mesothelioma, an aggressive form of cancer caused by exposure to asbestos dust. Her husband, Andy, has instructed lawyers to pursue whether GCHQ provided adequate protection against asbestos dust during her time at the ex-Oakley base in Cheltenham.

Mrs. Eustace worked at the Oakley site from 1983 to 1990, where demolition work was carried out, releasing asbestos fibers into the air. According to her recollection, a wrecking ball was used to demolish buildings near her workspace, and her car was often dusty from the demolition work. Despite this, she and her colleagues were not provided with protective clothing or equipment.

A post-mortem examination revealed alarming levels of asbestos fibers in Mrs. Eustace's lungs, with 4,200 fibers per gram of dried tissue. Her husband is concerned that other workers may have been similarly affected. A GCHQ spokesman stated that they cannot comment on individual staff members but will "deal appropriately with any legal correspondence received." The case highlights the importance of proper safety measures in workplaces where asbestos is present, and an investigation is ongoing to determine whether GCHQ failed to provide adequate protection for its employees.

A Newport man faces charges including vehicle theft and drunk driving after a fatal crash on Usk Way. Xana Doyle, 19, died when a Toyota Avensis overturned. A 15-year-old girl was injured. The man will appear in court Monday. A 21-year-old arrested in connection with the incident was released without further action, according to Gwent Police.

Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau is facing a formal investigation by the federal ethics commissioner over his recent winter vacation to the Bahamas. The trip, which took place over the New Year's holiday, has raised questions about potential conflicts of interest due to Trudeau's acceptance of hospitality from the Aga Khan, a wealthy businessman and spiritual leader.

Trudeau, his family, and several Liberal Party officials, including MP Seamus O'Reagan and Party President Anna Gainey, were guests at the Aga Khan's private island home. The Aga Khan Foundation has received significant funding from the Canadian government over the years, totaling hundreds of millions of dollars. This has led to concerns that Trudeau's trip may have violated Canadian conflict of interest laws, which prohibit ministers from accepting gifts, including free travel.

The ethics commissioner, Mary Dawson, launched a preliminary inquiry into the matter last week and has since announced that she will conduct a formal investigation. Trudeau has stated that he is "more than happy" to answer any questions and is working with the commissioner's office to set up a meeting. He has characterized the trip as a "personal family vacation" and noted that the Aga Khan is a close family friend.

The Aga Khan, also known as Prince Karim Aga Khan, is a prominent figure in the Ismaili Muslim community and has a long history of philanthropic work. He is also one of the wealthiest royals in the world, with an estimated net worth of $1 billion. Trudeau's father, Pierre, had a close relationship with the Aga Khan, who served as an honorary pallbearer at his funeral.

If the ethics commissioner finds that Trudeau breached conflict of interest rules, he could face a fine of up to $500 per penalty. While no Canadian prime minister has been found in breach of a federal statute to date, the fallout from this investigation could potentially damage Trudeau's reputation and popularity. Analysts suggest that the scandal could hurt Trudeau's image as an accessible and transparent leader, which has been a key factor in his popularity with the voting public. As the investigation continues, Trudeau will likely face ongoing questions and scrutiny over his decision to accept the Aga Khan's hospitality.

HSBC Reports 5% Rise in Pre-Tax Profit, Announces $2bn Share Buyback

Europe's largest bank, HSBC, has reported a 5% increase in pre-tax profit to $10.2 billion (£7.8 billion) for the first six months of 2017, exceeding expectations by approximately $500 million. The bank has also announced plans to buy back up to $2 billion worth of shares, which it expects to complete by the end of the year. This news sent HSBC shares soaring by 3% initially, although they later fell back. However, the bank's share price has rallied over the past year, largely due to the weak pound, which has made profits earned abroad more valuable when repatriated to the UK.

The share buyback is part of HSBC's ongoing efforts to return value to shareholders. Since the 2008 financial crisis, the bank has been streamlining its operations, cutting jobs, and selling assets to boost profitability while maintaining dividend payments to shareholders. According to HSBC's chief executive, Stuart Gulliver, the bank has paid out more in dividends than any other European or American bank over the past 12 months and has returned $3.5 billion to shareholders through share buybacks. The latest announcement brings the total value of HSBC's share buybacks since the second half of 2016 to $5.5 billion.

While HSBC's headline numbers were encouraging, the bank's results also highlighted the ongoing challenges it faces in the aftermath of the financial crisis. The bank is still grappling with pending litigation from investors, ongoing investigations by US and UK authorities, and the significant costs associated with meeting new financial regulations. In the UK, one of the major regulatory requirements is the "ring-fence," which aims to separate retail and investment banking operations by 2019. HSBC has already spent nearly £400 million on this project, which involves setting up a new Birmingham headquarters for its retail arm.

The ring-fencing process has been a complex and costly exercise, employing up to 2,000 people at its peak, according to HSBC chairman Douglas Flint. The bank has spent around $500 million on splitting its retail and investment banking arms, describing it as "one of the largest projects ever undertaken by the group." The new Birmingham headquarters for HSBC's UK retail business is expected to begin operating in July 2018.

Experts believe that the ring-fencing requirement is a significant expense that is creating uncertainty for banks. "The ring-fence is a big expense creating lots of uncertainty," said Peter Hahn of the London Institute of Banking and Finance. "It's not just the headquarters, it's separating lots of the systems in the bank." HSBC also took a charge of £228 million ($300 million) during the reporting period for PPI claims, primarily due to a recent increase in complaint volumes. The bank has set aside £3.3 billion to date to deal with claims related to mis-sold mortgage payment protection, a issue that continues to cast a long shadow over the balance sheets of UK banks.

Overall, HSBC's results demonstrate the bank's progress in recovering from the financial crisis, but also highlight the ongoing challenges it faces in navigating the complex regulatory landscape. As the bank continues to streamline its operations and return value to shareholders, it must also contend with the significant costs and uncertainties associated with meeting new regulatory requirements.

Manchester United midfielder Juan Mata is confident that the club will return to winning major trophies in the near future. Despite not claiming any significant silverware since Sir Alex Ferguson's retirement in 2013, Mata believes that the Red Devils have the mentality and talent to compete for titles.

The Spanish international's comments come ahead of the FA Cup final against Crystal Palace on Saturday, where United have the opportunity to end the season with a trophy. Mata acknowledged that failing to qualify for the Champions League next season was a disappointment, but highlighted the emergence of young players such as Marcus Rashford and the form of Anthony Martial as positives from the current campaign.

Rashford, who has scored eight goals in 17 appearances, and Martial, who has impressed since his £36m signing, have been standout performers for United. Mata praised the pair, stating that they are "exciting players" who have shown their talent to the world. The 28-year-old also emphasized the importance of Rashford's Manchester roots, saying that he has "known the club since he was a kid."

As United prepare to face Crystal Palace, Mata is hopeful that the team can bring home the FA Cup and end the season on a high note. With the club's rich history of success, Mata is convinced that they will be "fighting for titles" again soon. Fans can also have their say on who should start the FA Cup final by using the team selector tool to pick their ideal XI.

Hanna Sabic, missing since Monday, has been found in Edinburgh. Police had expressed concern for her welfare after she failed to arrive at work. She was last seen at Falkirk Grahamston Station. Police Scotland thanked the public and media for their help in tracing her, located at 13:45 on Tuesday.

Australian snooker player Neil Robertson has vowed to change his approach to the game after a disappointing loss in the World Championship second round. The 35-year-old was beaten 13-11 by Marco Fu on Tuesday, and he was scathing in his assessment of his own performance, labeling it "garbage".

Robertson's loss was marked by a dramatic turn of events, as he celebrated going 11-10 up by shouting and punching the table, only to lose the next three frames. The Cambridgeshire-based player acknowledged that his emotions got the better of him, but he believes that playing with passion is essential to his success.

"I've tried to play within myself, but I need adrenaline and need to be pumped up to play well," Robertson said. "Otherwise, you'll see snoring snooker like that." He added that he will not be holding back his emotions in the future, saying "I won't be giving it a fist pump every frame, but I will be showing my emotion when I feel like it."

Robertson's struggles this season have been well-documented, with his only major success coming in the Riga Open. He was knocked out in the first round of the UK Championship and lost in the quarterfinals of the Masters. The 12-time ranking event winner believes that a change in tactics will benefit not only himself but also the sport as a whole.

"At the moment, there are probably only three or four players in the world worth watching, and I am not one of them," Robertson said. "I need to play a lot more aggressively and with a lot more freedom. I will not be running around the table taking 15 seconds a shot, but I will be playing with a lot more passion and emotion."

Robertson cited players like Ronnie O'Sullivan and Judd Trump as examples of the kind of exciting, attacking snooker that he wants to play. He believes that this style of play is essential to bringing more fans to the sport, saying "as soon as Ronnie goes out, a large interest from the general public goes from a tournament - Judd as well." With a renewed focus on playing with passion and aggression, Robertson will be looking to bounce back from his disappointing loss and make a stronger impact in the world of snooker.

The 2015 Rugby World Cup is expected to bring a significant economic boost to England and Wales, according to a report by accountancy firm EY. The tournament, which will be hosted in 11 cities across the two countries, is predicted to attract 466,000 visitors who will spend up to £869m. US Researchers Discover Hidden Fat in Bones of Overweight Individuals

A groundbreaking study conducted by researchers at Harvard Medical School in Boston has revealed that some overweight individuals may be harboring hidden fat inside their bones, making them more susceptible to weakness and fractures. The study, published in the journal Radiology, involved body scans of 106 obese but healthy men and women.

The scans showed that some participants carried fat in unexpected areas, including their liver, muscles, and bone marrow, in addition to their belly, hips, or thighs. Dr. Miriam Bredella, who led the research, notes that individuals with an apple-shaped body, who tend to carry weight around their waist, may be at greatest risk.

The discovery is significant, as bone marrow is responsible for producing osteoblast cells, which are essential for new bone formation. When fat cells take over the marrow, it can weaken the bones, making them more prone to fractures. Dr. Bredella warns that having a spine filled with fat can compromise its strength. The findings challenge the long-held assumption that obesity is protective against bone loss. With almost three million people in the UK estimated to have osteoporosis, the researchers emphasize the importance of maintaining a healthy weight to prevent bone-related issues.

In a groundbreaking effort to preserve the native species of South Georgia, a team of conservationists has embarked on a three-month mission to eradicate brown rats from the island. The rodents, which have been a menace to the island's ecosystem since the 18th century, will be targeted with 100 million poisonous pellets dropped from three former air ambulance helicopters.
