The project, led by Prof Tony Martin from the University of Dundee, aims to clear more than half of the remaining area of brown rats, building on the success of the first phase in 2011, which saw the extermination of the rodents from a smaller portion of the island. The brown rats, with no natural predators on the island, have thrived since their arrival as stowaways on sealing ships, posing a significant threat to ground-nesting birds such as the South Georgia pipit and pintail.

The helicopters will employ mathematical precision to distribute the bait pellets, covering every square meter of the island. According to Prof Martin, the mission's success hinges on eradicating every single rat, as "killing 99.999% is a failure." The team's goal is to eradicate, not control, the invasive species, and the unique terrain of South Georgia, with its glaciers separating rat colonies into isolated pockets, makes this ambitious project feasible.

Despite facing challenging weather conditions, including gale-force winds and blizzards, the team is poised to resume the largest-ever species eradication project. Time is of the essence, as the retreating glaciers threaten to allow the separate colonies to mingle, making eradication much more difficult. With the weather improving, the team is ready to tackle this critical phase of the four-year project, ultimately aiming to safeguard the future of South Georgia's native species.

Hull FC Snatch Victory Over St Helens with Sneyd's Stunning Kick

In a game marred by bad weather, Hull FC managed to secure a hard-fought win over St Helens, thanks to a brilliant 50-meter penalty kick from Marc Sneyd. The match, which saw few clear-cut chances, was decided by Sneyd's solo effort, which sailed over the bar to give Hull FC a narrow victory.

The game got off to a flying start, with Saints winger Regan Grace opening the scoring inside four minutes with an acrobatic finish. However, Sneyd leveled the scores just before the half-time break, converting his own solo effort. Despite having few openings, Sneyd's kick proved to be the difference-maker, securing a crucial win for Hull FC.

Grace will rue the chances he had to extend his team's lead, having knocked on 20 meters out and later dropping a pass from Theo Fages in open space. The win keeps Hull FC in third place in the Super 8s table, while St Helens remain in fifth, one point behind fourth-placed Wakefield Trinity.

Hull FC head coach Lee Radford hailed the win as one of the team's most significant of the season, saying, "We had to win ugly and I was pleased when the heavens opened up because then I knew they were going to play with a bar of soap." St Helens head coach Justin Holbrook, on the other hand, described the game as "one of the worst games of rugby league I have been involved in," citing the poor weather conditions and numerous errors from both teams. Despite the disappointing performance, Holbrook acknowledged that the game was closely contested, with Sneyd's penalty kick ultimately proving to be the decisive factor.

Legendary Actress Julie Harris Passes Away at 87

The theater world is mourning the loss of Julie Harris, a renowned actress who jointly holds the record for the most Tony Award wins. Harris passed away at her home in Massachusetts due to congestive heart failure, according to family friend and actress Francesca James. She was 87 years old.

Harris' illustrious career spanned over six decades, with her breakthrough role coming in 1950 with the hit play "The Member of the Wedding." Her portrayal of the lonely 12-year-old Frankie earned her critical acclaim and paved the way for her future success. She went on to win her first Tony Award in 1952 for her role as Sally Bowles in "I Am a Camera," which was later adapted into the iconic musical "Cabaret."

Throughout her career, Harris won a total of five competitive Tony Awards, with her final win coming in 1977 for her one-woman show "The Belle of Amherst." She also received a special lifetime achievement Tony in 2002 and holds the record for the most nominated performer in the awards' history. Harris is joined by Angela Lansbury and Audra McDonald as the only performers to have won five competitive Tonys.

In addition to her theater work, Harris appeared in over 30 films, including the 1955 classic "East of Eden" alongside James Dean. She also had a successful television career, winning three Emmy Awards and starring in the popular soap opera "Knot's Landing" in the 1980s.

Harris' health had been declining in recent years, with her suffering two strokes in 2001 and 2010. Despite her health issues, she remained a beloved figure in the entertainment industry, and her passing has sent shockwaves throughout the theater and film communities. She will be deeply missed by her fans and fellow performers, who remember her as a talented and dedicated actress who left an indelible mark on the world of entertainment.

A major infrastructure project is underway in Glasgow with the construction of the Shieldhall Tunnel, a 3.1-mile sewer tunnel that will run from Craigton to Queen's Park. The tunnel, which will be capable of handling sewage and excess rainfall, is set to be one of the largest in Scotland and will play a crucial role in protecting the environment and reducing the risk of flooding.

Scottish Water is investing over £100m in the project, which is part of a larger £250m, five-year programme to improve the waste water network in the Glasgow area. The tunnel will be big enough to fit a double-decker bus inside and will stretch for over five times the length of the Clyde Tunnel.

A 1,000 tonne, 180 metre-long tunnel boring machine is set to arrive on site in the coming weeks, marking a major milestone in the project. The machine will be used to construct the tunnel, which will follow a route from Craigton industrial estate to Queen's Park, passing under several parks and roads along the way.

According to Scottish Water chief executive Douglas Millican, the project is the biggest investment in waste water infrastructure in Glasgow for over a century. "The modernisation of the system and construction of new underground assets, such as the Shieldhall Tunnel, will protect the natural environment, reduce the risk of flooding and meet the needs of growth, economic development and regeneration," he said. The tunnel is expected to be completed by 2018.

Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos has expressed his enthusiasm for a potential free trade agreement with the UK, suggesting it could surpass the country's current deal with the EU. In an interview with the BBC's Andrew Marr Show, Santos emphasized the opportunities for increased trade between the UK and emerging markets, particularly with the Pacific Alliance bloc comprising Colombia, Chile, Peru, and Mexico.

During his recent state visit to the UK, Santos held talks with Prime Minister Theresa May at Downing Street, where he highlighted the "huge opportunity for British business" in the region. He proposed a free trade agreement with the UK, offering "the same conditions or even improved" terms as the current EU deal. However, Santos clarified that negotiations would only commence once the UK's economic relationship with the EU is finalized.

The UK and Colombia's trading relationship is already valued at £1 billion, with a new oil and gas partnership announced during Santos' visit. Prime Minister May has also encouraged Colombian businesses to view the UK as a leading hub for finance, innovation, and research. With the UK's departure from the EU looming, Santos' comments suggest a potential boost to trade relations between the two nations.

Blades defender McGahey to join Rochdale on July 1, after his contract expires. The 20-year-old made 34 appearances over two seasons, but started only nine games last season, leading to his release under new manager Chris Wilder.

Carers Scotland Sounds Alarm on Financial Burden of Unpaid Caregivers

A shocking new report from Carers Scotland has highlighted the devastating financial impact of unpaid caregiving on families across the UK. The charity's year-long investigation, known as the Caring & Family Finances Inquiry, reveals that vast numbers of carers are struggling with unmanageable debt, with one in six owing more than £10,000. The findings have prompted Carers Scotland to call for urgent reform of the financial help available to carers and a commitment from the UK and Scottish governments to ensure that future policy does not leave carers worse off.

The research paints a stark picture of the challenges faced by those caring for loved ones who may be old, disabled, or seriously ill. Almost half (47%) of carers are in debt as a result of their caregiving responsibilities, with a fifth relying on overdrafts or credit cards to make ends meet. A staggering third of carers are said to be more than £20,000 worse off as a result of caring, while 44% have been forced to cut back on essentials like food. Furthermore, 59% of carers are living in fuel poverty, highlighting the desperate need for support.

Simon Hodgson, director of Carers Scotland, emphasized the importance of recognizing the vital role that carers play in society. "Those caring, unpaid, for loved ones save society vast sums, but at huge personal cost – a cost this inquiry shows is pushing families to the brink," he said. Hodgson argued that the current system is unsustainable and that government cuts to support are leaving carers across the UK facing a £1bn cut.

In response to the report, the UK government claimed that it is spending around £2bn this year on carer's allowance, with even more allocated for future years. A Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) spokeswoman acknowledged the invaluable service provided by carers and highlighted the government's commitment to supporting them. However, Carers Scotland argues that this funding is insufficient to address the scale of the problem.

The Scottish government has announced an additional £9.2m for the Scottish Welfare Fund, which it claims will help alleviate the burden of poverty on carers. A Scottish government spokesman acknowledged the difficulties faced by full-time carers and emphasized the need to ensure they receive the support they deserve. However, the charity argues that more needs to be done to address the root causes of the financial struggles faced by carers.

Carers Scotland is urging the UK and Scottish governments to implement a "carer test" for future benefits and social care proposals, ensuring that carers are not left worse off by policy changes. The charity's director, Simon Hodgson, warned that the current situation is unacceptable and unsustainable, with the ageing population set to increase the number of people caring for loved ones. As the charity's report makes clear, it is time for urgent action to support the unsung heroes of unpaid caregiving.

UK Government to Match Donations to Aid Gaza Crisis as Ceasefire Enters Final Day

The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) has issued a dire warning that hundreds of thousands of people in Gaza are in desperate need of food, water, shelter, and medical care following four weeks of intense conflict between Israeli forces and Hamas militants. In response, the UK government has pledged to match donations to the DEC, effectively doubling the impact of public generosity.

International Development Secretary Justine Greening emphasized the urgency of the situation, stating that the British people have consistently shown immense kindness in times of crisis. "The UK government will help that generosity go twice as far," she said. "For people wanting to help civilians in Gaza caught up in this crisis, giving now means every pound they donate will buy twice as many food parcels, provide twice as many blankets, and help twice as many people to get through this crisis."

The UK government has committed £2 million to the DEC appeal, bringing its total support for the people of Gaza since the start of the crisis to £17 million. Saleh Saeed, chief executive of the DEC, described this as a "vital moment" for Gaza, where hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced and are struggling to access basic necessities like food and water. The healthcare system, he warned, is on the verge of collapse.

As a three-day ceasefire in Gaza enters its final day, indirect talks are ongoing in Cairo to negotiate a long-term truce. While Israeli officials have expressed willingness to extend the ceasefire, Hamas has stated that there is no agreement and significant gaps remain between the two sides' positions. The conflict has claimed over 1,900 lives, including at least 1,875 Palestinians and 64 Israeli soldiers.

The DEC, an umbrella organization representing 13 UK aid charities, is scaling up its relief efforts as the ceasefire continues to hold. However, the organization urgently needs funds to support its work. With the UK government's matching commitment, donations to the DEC will have twice the impact, providing vital assistance to those affected by the crisis in Gaza.

A 2nd Century sculpture depicting Buddha's footprints has been returned to Pakistan after being smuggled into the US. The piece, which features religious symbols, was taken from the Swat Valley and eventually made its way to New York, where it was expected to sell for $1 million at auction. However, the sale was intercepted by authorities, and a Japanese antiques dealer, Tatsuzo Kaku, pleaded guilty to possessing stolen property in April.

At a ceremony on Wednesday, New York prosecutors returned the sculpture to Pakistan's Deputy Chief of Mission, Rizwan Saeed Sheikh. Sheikh described the piece as "an important element of the cultural history of Pakistan" and said it would likely be kept in New York for the short term, possibly going on display. Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus R Vance Jr emphasized the significance of the sculpture, stating it was "so much more than a piece of property" and a vital part of Pakistan's cultural heritage. Kaku was fined $5,000 and left the country voluntarily after serving his sentence. Experts have dismissed Kaku's claim that he was motivated by a desire to protect Pakistan's artefacts, citing the country's existing structures for preservation.

The Football Association of Malawi (FAM) has announced that it will continue its search for a foreign coach, despite appointing former international striker, Phiri, as the new head coach of the national team. Phiri's first task will be to lead the team in the Africa Nations Championship (CHAN) qualifier against Madagascar in April. 

Phiri, who will be assisted by Deklerk Msakakuona, has acknowledged the challenge ahead, stating that the team needs to come up with a winning system. FAM General Secretary, Alfred Gunda, clarified that Phiri and his assistant will sign one-year contracts, but the association is still looking for an expatriate coach to join the team. 

Phiri, who will turn 49 next month, previously led the team as a caretaker in a friendly match against Guangzhou FC in January. He replaces Ernest Mtawali, who was fired in June 2016, following a poor performance at the Cosafa Cup. The team will begin a training camp on April 2, ahead of their CHAN game in Madagascar on April 22. A friendly match against Kenya is also scheduled for April 18. FAM is expected to announce the appointment of a foreign coach once the selection process is complete.

A fire broke out at a disused building in Leicester, causing significant structural damage. The blaze started at 03:00 GMT on the corner of Littleton Street and Bradgate Street. Firefighters arrived to find the building "well alight" but managed to contain the fire. An attached chimney remained stable. Nearby units suffered minor damage, and surrounding roads were closed. The fire service is working with police to trace the owners of the affected units. Firefighters will remain on site throughout Thursday to dampen down the area, ensuring the fire is fully extinguished. An investigation into the cause is ongoing.

A 32-year-old pregnant woman, Sarah Keegan, has been sentenced to prison for her role in supplying heroin in a Scottish caravan park. Keegan, who is due to give birth in June, pleaded guilty to the offense, which took place in April last year at the Moffat Manor Country Park in Beattock. Despite her defense counsel's plea for a non-custodial sentence, Judge Lord Boyd deemed the crime too serious and sentenced her to prison.

The court heard that Keegan had been arrested alongside her co-accused, Jason Jolley, 45, following a police operation codenamed Operation Boswell. The operation uncovered a significant heroin supply ring, with Jolley and Keegan believed to be flooding the Dumfries area with the drug. Police recovered heroin and cutting agent worth a potential £65,000 from the caravan, as well as drugs paraphernalia, including scales and knotted bags of heroin.

Keegan's defense counsel, Susan Duff, argued that her client had been a heroin addict at the time of the offense but had since overcome her addiction and was determined to be a "role model" for her unborn child. Duff pleaded with the court to consider a non-custodial sentence, citing Keegan's pregnancy and her desire to be with her baby when it is born. However, Lord Boyd was unmoved, stating that Keegan's involvement in the crime, although lesser than Jolley's, was still significant.

The court was told that Keegan's DNA and fingerprints were found on various items in the caravan, and a small amount of heroin was discovered in her underwear during a strip search. While Lord Boyd acknowledged that Jolley was the "moving force" behind the operation, he emphasized that Keegan's involvement was still a serious offense. "You have yourself been an addict," he said. "You should know the misery that drugs bring to people and the communities blighted by it."

Jolley, who was jailed for five years, was found to be directly supplying others and had local dealers working for him. The police operation that led to their arrest was the result of intelligence suggesting that Jolley and Keegan were organizing deliveries of heroin from the caravan park into Dumfries and the surrounding area. The recovery of the significant quantity of heroin and paraphernalia from the caravan highlighted the scale of the operation and the seriousness of the offense.

In sentencing Keegan, Lord Boyd made it clear that he could not ignore the severity of the crime, despite her pregnancy and desire to be with her baby. The case serves as a reminder of the devastating impact of drug supply and addiction on individuals and communities, and the need for robust law enforcement to combat these issues.

Students at Delhi's Ghandi Memorial Public School investigated air pollution's effects on children's health. They measured air quality, finding high pollution levels due to heavy traffic, posing health risks to young residents in the city.

A plane crash in Ecuador's eastern province of Pastaza has resulted in no survivors. The Israeli-built Arava plane carried 19 Ecuadoran soldiers, two pilots, and a mechanic. President Rafael Correa expressed solidarity with the families and armed forces, calling it a "tragedy." The cause of the crash, which occurred at 14:30 local time, is unknown. Defence Minister Ricardo Patino and rescue teams are en route to the area to investigate.

Barrow's loan spell for 24-year-old Parry has ended. The player, who can play in defense and midfield, had previously played for Altrincham. Bluebirds boss Paul Cox hopes to make another signing soon. Nearby, Luton's transfer activity is expected to be quiet, having already signed Alan Sheehan and Joe Pigott, with Luke Guttridge and Luke Wilkinson leaving for other clubs.

Former Tottenham defender Gary Mabbutt, 55, has been released from Kings College Hospital in London. He was admitted last Monday with chest pains and breathing issues. Mabbutt, who won the 1991 FA Cup, will recover at home. He thanked hospital staff, the cardiac team, and Spurs fans for their support and get-well messages. The Tottenham legend played over 600 games for the club.

Sri Lankan cricketer Kusal Perera faces a doping ban after failing an out-of-competition test. The sports minister is backing him, citing a possible "conspiracy" to keep him out of the T20 World Cup, and will provide legal representation to appeal the decision.

Yeovil Town has signed MK Dons striker Kabongo Tshimanga on loan. The 20-year-old impressed Glovers manager Darren Way, who noted his threat behind the back four and eye for goal. Tshimanga came through the Stadium MK academy and previously played for Nuneaton Town. He has played 12 games for MK Dons this season, including a Football League Trophy match against Yeovil. Tshimanga is Yeovil's fifth January signing, joining Shayon Harrison and Andre Wright on loan at the club.

A man has taken to living in a tree to protest a 225-bedroom hotel development in Edinburgh. The project, led by developer Andy Jansons, includes a bar, restaurant, and retail units, and involves historic buildings. The man, who wishes to remain anonymous, has been in the tree for a week. Jansons is seeking an eviction notice from Edinburgh Sheriff Court. Work on the site was set to begin on Monday, but the protester's actions have caused a delay, sparking a showdown over the redevelopment of the derelict site. A court decision is expected soon.

A teenager has been charged after an incident at a Blackheath supermarket. Armed officers responded on Saturday, closing several roads. The boy, now in custody, faces charges including making an explosive substance and possessing a bladed article. No one was hurt, and road closures have been lifted, according to West Midlands Police.

A fatal car accident occurred on Plodder Lane in Bolton early Thursday morning, claiming the life of Latham Schofield. He was one of four people in a silver Renault Megane when the incident happened. Schofield's family remembered him as "cheeky and silly sometimes," but loved him even more for it. Another 17-year-old boy was hospitalized and remains in serious but stable condition. An 18-year-old from Bolton has been charged with various offenses, including causing serious injury by dangerous driving. He is set to appear in Bolton Crown Court on March 11. A 19-year-old man who was also arrested has been released without charge, pending further investigation.
The 23-year-old midfielder rejoined Marseille on loan, scoring twice in 14 games, after making just 16 appearances for Newcastle following a £12m summer transfer.

A 40-year-old woman has been charged with the murder of her 82-year-old neighbour in Leven. Sandra Weir appeared at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court, facing five charges including murder, theft, and attempting to pervert the course of justice. Mary Logie, 82, was found dead in her Green Gates home on January 5. Weir made no plea and was fully committed for trial. Additional charges were added to the initial murder charge. Her solicitor, David Fitzpatrick, did not request bail, and she was remanded in custody. Weir will now await trial for the alleged crimes. The case has shocked the local community.

Blues have signed defender Ryan Shotton on a deal until 2019 for an undisclosed fee. The 27-year-old, who played for the team earlier this year, becomes their second summer signing. Shotton previously played for Stoke City, Wigan, and Barnsley, and scored one goal in nine appearances for Blues. He joins midfielder Robert Tesche as the club's new additions ahead of the upcoming season.

A search operation is underway for Josh Winsper, a man from Cornwall who went missing in Milford Haven. The captain of a vessel alerted authorities on Saturday morning after crew members realized he was missing. Police divers and HM Coastguard are involved in the search. Winsper was last seen at Astoria nightclub at 02:30 BST on Saturday. His family has posted a plea on social media, with his aunt saying they are "holding out for a miracle." The family has praised the support from the local community and the Welsh police, who are working to locate Winsper.

Local TV stations feature home-grown comedies and Spanish soaps, while cable TV offers multichannel options and radio plays popular formats like news and Spanish pop music, with 1.8 million internet users reported.

In Copenhagen, thousands created the world's largest chalk pavement painting, breaking the US record. Over a kilometre of pavement was covered in flags, flowers, and artwork within hours. The new record spans 18,598 square metres, exceeding the 2008 record of 8,361 square metres by over 10,000 square metres.

Nominations have closed for the May 4 by-election to replace late MP Sir Gerald Kaufman. The poll coincides with Greater Manchester's mayoral election, marking a significant day in local politics. Candidates are set to contest the seat left vacant by Sir Gerald's passing in February.

Glamorgan made a strong start on the first day of their match, despite losing Jacques Rudolph early on for 17 runs. James Kettleborough and Colin Ingram formed a solid partnership, adding 71 runs for the second wicket. Kettleborough went on to score 81, putting on a further 66 runs with Aneurin Donald before being caught off David Payne's bowling.

Donald, just 18 years old, continued to impress, scoring an unbeaten 91 and surpassing his previous best of 67. Chris Cooke also made a significant contribution, hitting a quickfire 65 as the team reached 315-4 before rain brought an early close to the day's play. A total of 19 overs were lost due to the bad weather, which could have seen Glamorgan's score even higher. Kettleborough expressed satisfaction with his performance, and praised Donald and Cooke for their impressive batting. He also voiced his support for Donald to become Glamorgan's youngest Championship centurion.

Australia's hopes of winning the mixed 4x100m relay were dashed after a disqualification due to a botched handover between Jack Hale and Fabrice Lapierre. The team's mistake in the change from the second to the third leg resulted in a score of -10, ultimately leading to their downfall. Usain Bolt's All-Stars took advantage of the error, winning the relay and securing a total of 930 points to Australia's 895.

Initially, a refereeing error awarded Australia the top ranking, but this was quickly corrected after Bolt threatened to protest. The eight-time Olympic champion, competing in his farewell season, has been selective with his events, only participating in the relays on the first two nights of the series. However, he may make an appearance in the 150m on Saturday, depending on the meeting's progression.

Bolt's All-Stars have now claimed their second victory in the three-event series, with England currently sitting in fourth place, ahead of New Zealand and Japan. The Nitro Athletics series has been praised by IAAF president Lord Coe, who believes it will "revolutionise" the sport. Despite the disappointment, Australia will look to bounce back in the remaining events, while Bolt's team will aim to continue their dominance.

Subah Amini, a member of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Youth Association, was among 350 volunteers who aided flood victims in Cumbria and Yorkshire. After a near-fatal fall in 2014, Amini spent 10 months in hospitals in London, Wakefield, and China. Grateful to be alive, he now dedicates his life to helping others. Volunteers assisted with transportation, sandbag organization, and emotional support. Amini noted that the efforts brought the community together, making them feel more connected to Christmas than ever before. The flooding, which hit parts of Yorkshire and Lancashire on December 26, was met with a strong response from volunteers like Amini.

Bath's new signing will debut on Thursday in the Premiership Rugby Sevens at Kingsholm. The 27-year-old back-rower expressed excitement to join Bath, eager to start his career. With experience playing sevens for Samoa and a nomination for IRB International Sevens Player of the Year, he's well-suited for the competition. He previously played for Toulouse and Bristol, bringing valuable experience to his new team.

A 43-year-old man, John Parker, was found injured in Hedderley Walk, St Ann's, on Sunday and later died in hospital. Jonathan Jones, 39, has been charged with murder and is set to appear before magistrates. Another 39-year-old man is being held for questioning in connection with the incident. A 14-year-old boy, arrested for suspected involvement, has been released without charge. A 35-year-old woman, arrested for GBH related to an earlier incident involving the victim, has been bailed. Police are seeking the occupants of a silver Ford Focus seen in the area, as they may have information about the incident. The occupants are not believed to be involved, but detectives hope they can provide valuable insights to aid the investigation. The community is urged to come forward with any information that may help the police.

A 17-year-old motorcyclist, Jack Mander, was killed in a collision with a heavy goods vehicle in Strood, Kent. The incident occurred on Anthony's Way, and Jack died at the scene. His family described him as a careful rider. The lorry driver, 44, was released on bail. Kent Police are investigating and appealing for witnesses to come forward. The collision happened on Thursday at 21:00 BST.

Ireland's bid to become a full member of the International Cricket Council (ICC) has taken a significant step forward. Following Wednesday's ICC meeting, Cricket Ireland's application will now be reviewed by a newly-created membership committee. The committee will assess whether Ireland meets the necessary criteria, including governance, finance, national team performance, and development programs.

Cricket Ireland chief executive Warren Deutrom expressed cautious optimism about the application, stating that while there are some uncertainties surrounding the financial criteria, Ireland appears to be in a strong position. Deutrom emphasized the importance of respecting the opinions of ICC members, whose decision is ultimate. The ICC's board agreed on the new membership process at a meeting in Dubai, marking a change from the previous system where teams required a proposal and seconding from full member nations. Ireland and Afghanistan are currently seeking to upgrade from associate member status to full membership, joining the current 10 full member countries. A decision on their applications is expected to be made after the membership committee's review.

A hot air balloon made an unexpected landing in Northampton on Friday evening. Matt Rate brought the balloon down in Hilldrop Road, citing a sudden wind drop. Resident Ian Callaghan captured the landing on film. The quick thinking ensured a safe landing, avoiding a potential descent over the town centre.

A record-breaking attempt in Yangzhou, east China, has ended in controversy. The city cooked 4,192kg of fried rice, surpassing Turkey's previous record. However, celebrations were short-lived as photos showed the rice being loaded into waste lorries. Guinness World Records has disqualified the attempt, stating that the food was not consumed by humans. Event organizers claimed the rice would be donated to local canteens, but the tourism bureau revealed that 150kg of "inedible" rice was sent to pig farms. Guinness World Records has clarified that it will not accept claims for large food items if they are inedible or unfit for consumption. Yangzhou's signature dish, fried rice, typically combines rice, eggs, chicken, and vegetables. The city's attempt to showcase its culinary pride has ultimately ended in disappointment. The incident highlights the importance of ensuring that record-breaking attempts are both impressive and responsible.

A fatal collision occurred on the highway between junctions 46 and 45 on Friday. A Peugeot Partner van passenger suffered fatal injuries, while the driver was taken to Morriston Hospital. The road has reopened, easing traffic queues that stretched up to six miles. South Wales Police have launched an investigation into the incident's cause. Motorists are advised to check for updates to avoid disruptions to their journey. The incident occurred after 06:10 GMT, causing significant morning traffic congestion.

An inquest has concluded that an 18-day-old baby, James Rawlings, died due to a lack of oxygen and sepsis. James was born at Ipswich Hospital and passed away at home in May last year. The hearing revealed that despite concerns from a midwife and James' mother, Jo Rawlings, a Caesarean delivery was delayed by Dr. Lovelina Das. The hospital trust admitted that an earlier delivery would have likely saved James' life. Dr. Das is no longer employed at the hospital and is believed to be working abroad. The coroner, Peter Dean, stated that the evidence shows James would not have died if delivered earlier. James' parents, who now have a new son, Joshua, praised the midwife for her support during a difficult time. The hospital trust has acknowledged its mistakes and is taking steps to prevent similar tragedies in the future.

Jersey's cricket team is gearing up to compete in the fourth tier of the global tournament for the third time, seeking to break their relegation curse. Having won Division Five in May, the island side is confident of making a strong showing in the 2016 event. Coach Neil MacRae expressed his team's optimism, stating that they have a young squad with a lot of experience and are eager to take on the challenge.

The team's previous appearances in the fourth tier, in 2008 and 2014, ended in relegation. However, they go into this tournament on a high note, having won the World League Five final in May. Their first opponents will be Oman, a team they defeated in the final earlier this summer. MacRae believes that his team's two-year gain in experience will make a significant difference in their performance.

Jersey has been an international cricket nation since 2005 and has made significant strides in recent years, including qualifying for the World Twenty20 global qualifiers in 2015. With their sights set on promotion to the highest level they've ever played at, the team is excited and motivated. MacRae is looking forward to the challenge, citing his team's exceptional performance in tough conditions during their previous tournament in Singapore. With their recent win and added experience, Jersey's cricket team is ready to take on the best in the world.

A police officer was struck by a silver Honda Estate in Evesham on Tuesday at 13:20 GMT. The officer suffered minor leg and head injuries. The vehicle was found unoccupied in Warwickshire and the driver is being sought. Witnesses are urged to come forward to aid the investigation into the incident at the junction of Chapel Street and Oat Street.

Michael Kightly joins Southend after leaving Burnley. The 31-year-old made 88 appearances for Burnley and had a loan stint at Burton Albion. Kightly previously played for Southend from 2003 to 2005, featuring in 19 games. He is the team's second summer signing, following Stephen Hendrie's arrival.

Nigerian Authorities Seize $43.4m in Cash from Lagos Flat

In a shocking discovery, Nigerian authorities have seized a massive stash of cash from a flat in Lagos's affluent Ikoyi area. The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) revealed that investigators found US notes worth $43.4m, along with nearly £27,800 and 23m naira ($75,000), in a four-bedroom flat on the seventh floor of a building. The cash was neatly arranged in sealed wrappers and stashed in wardrobes and cabinets.

The raid was carried out after a tip-off about a "haggard-looking" woman in "dirty clothes" taking bags in and out of the flat. Guards at the building reported that no one lived in the flat, but a source claimed that the woman would often appear with Ghana Must Go bags, sparking suspicion. The EFCC believes the money may be from unlawful activity, but no arrests have been made yet. This is the latest in a series of raids that have uncovered large amounts of cash in Nigeria, Africa's biggest economy.

A heartwarming reunion has taken place in Beijing after a blind man's beloved dog, Qiaoqiao, was abducted by a group of men on Monday. The seven-year-old Labrador was taken while being walked outside, leaving her owner Tian Fengbo in a state of distress. Mr. Tian, who relies on Qiaoqiao for companionship, said he was unable to eat or sleep after her disappearance.

The incident sparked widespread outrage among Chinese netizens, with many taking to social media to condemn the actions of the dog thieves. Residents in the area reported a series of recent dog thefts, fueling speculation that Qiaoqiao may have been targeted for sale to meat markets. Fortunately, Qiaoqiao was found on Tuesday with a letter attached to her collar, reading "We were wrong... we beg pardon."

The motive behind Qiaoqiao's abduction remains unclear, but the incident has highlighted the growing concern over dog theft in China. Many have called for harsher punishment for those involved in the trade, with some expressing frustration over the lack of protection for pets. As one netizen remarked, "Dogs are man's best friend, not food." The case has sparked a national conversation, with many celebrating the safe return of Qiaoqiao and calling for greater action to prevent similar incidents in the future. Mr. Tian has been reunited with his beloved dog, and the community is breathing a sigh of relief.

Proposals for a statue commemorating the birthplace of football on Parker's Piece are now on display at the Grand Arcade. The public is invited to view the four shortlisted designs, submitted by artists Neville Gabie, Alan Ward, Kenny Hunter, Nayan Kulkarni, and Mark Titchner, and provide their feedback until December 5. 

The statue aims to celebrate the city centre green as the spot where students developed the original rules of football in 1848. A plaque already exists at the park, acknowledging the "Cambridge Rules" as a defining influence on the 1863 Football Association rules. However, the Football Association notes that while elements of the Cambridge Rules were incorporated, there are significant differences between the two sets of rules.

City councillor Carina O'Reilly believes the statue could become a "significant landmark" for the city. The proposed designs include a granite slab with the rules inscribed in multiple languages, a mirror-like design with a bench, a life-size bronze of a female referee, and a word sculpture. The chosen design will be selected by city councillors on January 15, with the project costing up to £115,000, funded by public art money from developers. The public's opinions will play a crucial role in determining which sculpture will be brought to life.

A rare and historic book has been stolen from St Oswald's Church in Grasmere, Cumbria. The book, dated 1835, was on display in a glass cabinet and was taken between Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning. Church warden Sonia Rickman described the book as "irreplaceable" and believes the thieves knew what they were looking for. The book holds significant value due to its connection to William Wordsworth, who lived and prayed in Grasmere and is buried in the churchyard. The church was open at the time of the theft, and the discovery was made when a caller reported smashed glass. Cumbria Police is appealing for information and urging antique dealers to be vigilant for anyone attempting to sell the stolen book. The loss is felt deeply by the community, who come to visit Wordsworth's grave and the church where he worshiped.

RWE Npower has announced plans to demolish the remaining structure of the boiler house at the Didcot A plant, where a partial collapse in February resulted in the deaths of four men. Despite ongoing protests from the families of the three men whose bodies are yet to be recovered, the energy company has begun preparations for a controlled explosive demolition.

Residents living near the site have been informed of the plans through letters, which stated that the exact timing of the demolition would be made public 48 hours in advance. The letter warned that the explosion may be heard off-site and could generate airborne dust, although this is not expected to be harmful. To minimize noise and dust disturbance, residents are advised to keep their doors and windows closed.

The plans are currently being finalized and will be submitted to a multi-agency strategy team, including the Health and Safety Executive. The recovery of the men's bodies, including Christopher Huxtable, Ken Cresswell, and John Shaw, has been halted due to safety concerns, with contractors unable to access the area within the 50m exclusion zone. The delay has been criticized by family members and Labour MP Sarah Champion, who has branded it a "national scandal." The incident has also incurred significant costs, with Oxfordshire Fire and Rescue Service spending £300,000 on attendance and search operations.

Scotland's rugby team has been dealt a blow with the news that centre Duncan Taylor will miss the second Test against Japan due to a hamstring injury. The 26-year-old Saracens player picked up the injury in last weekend's 26-13 win over Japan in Toyota City and has failed to recover in time for the upcoming match.

Despite the loss, Scotland has ample cover in midfield, with Peter Horne, Matt Scott, and uncapped Huw Jones all available for selection. Additionally, winger Sean Lamont has experience playing Test rugby at centre, providing coach Vern Cotter with a range of options.

The team, which will be announced on Thursday, is expected to show several changes from the first Test. One player who will definitely start is 23-year-old Rory Sutherland, who will make his debut at loose-head prop in place of the injured Alasdair Dickinson. Sutherland will be joined by Gordon Reid, who was called up to the squad as a replacement for Dickinson and had his first full training session with the team on Tuesday.

Reid, who was enjoying a day on the beach with his family when he received the call-up, joked that he had brought the Scottish weather with him to Tokyo, as the team trained in persistent rain. The Glasgow Warriors forward is likely to feature in the upcoming match, along with back-row forward Josh Strauss, who was not in the squad for the first Test.

However, there are some injury concerns for Scotland, with flanker John Barclay carrying an injury and props WP Nel and Ryan Wilson also nursing slight injuries. Despite these concerns, Cotter is expected to give all of his players game time on tour, as he seeks to build depth and experience within the squad.

Former Nigerian President Goodluck Jonathan has expressed concerns that his allies may face corruption investigations under the new administration of General Muhammadu Buhari. In a church service held on Sunday, Mr. Jonathan stated that his friends and former ministers may be "persecuted" as a result of his decision to concede defeat in the March elections. This move was widely praised for preventing a potential crisis in the country.

General Buhari, who is set to be inaugurated on May 29, has pledged to tackle corruption in Nigeria, Africa's largest oil producer. Many Nigerians are eagerly awaiting his administration to investigate numerous corruption scandals that plagued Mr. Jonathan's government. Mr. Jonathan became president in 2010 after the death of President Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and made history by being the first Nigerian leader to relinquish power after losing an election.

The former president's comments suggest that he fears his allies may be targeted in corruption probes, and he has urged them to be prepared for potential persecution. Despite his concerns, Mr. Jonathan's decision to accept defeat has been hailed as a significant step towards consolidating democracy in Nigeria. As General Buhari prepares to take office, Nigerians are watching closely to see if he will deliver on his promise to tackle corruption and bring about positive change to the country.

Mysterious Skulls Discovered in Totnes, Devon

In a bizarre incident, two human skulls were discovered in Totnes, Devon, on Monday. The first skull was found by workmen behind an empty shop on Fore Street at 12:15 BST, while the second skull was later discovered on the banks of the River Dart, approximately half a mile away. According to Devon and Cornwall Police, the discoveries are not being treated as a criminal investigation at present.

The police revealed that the "owner" of the first skull came forward and informed them about the presence of another skull in the area, which is frequently visited by homeless people. Upon examination, it was determined that one skull belonged to a male and the other to a female, both of whom were over 21 years old at the time of death. Notably, the female skull was better preserved, with traces of hair still present, suggesting it had been kept in a crypt-like environment.

Specialist officers have dated the skulls to be over 100 years old, with further forensic analysis to be conducted to determine a more accurate date. The skulls will be sent to the Centre for Anatomy and Human Identification at the University of Dundee, where experts will attempt to calculate the time since death, potentially using radiocarbon dating. While the discoveries are not currently being treated as a criminal investigation, Totnes Police's Criminal Investigation Department is making further enquiries to uncover the origins of the mysterious skulls.

Brentford Crush Fulham 4-1 to Move Up to Fifth in the Table

Brentford secured a convincing 4-1 victory over Fulham at Griffin Park, moving up to fifth in the table and leaving their opponents seven points above the relegation zone. The win marked a significant boost for the Bees, who began the day in seventh place, and has kept their promotion hopes alive.

The game got off to a flying start, with Dallas scoring a fine low shot from 20 yards out in the 24th minute, beating Fulham keeper Marcus Bettinelli. The home side had earlier created a chance, with Alex Kacaniklic forcing a good save from Brentford keeper David Button. However, it was Brentford who took the lead, and they doubled their advantage in the second half through Dallas's stunning 25-yard strike into the top corner.

Fulham pushed hard for an equalizer, with Cauley Woodrow forcing a save from Button with a low 25-yard strike. However, their efforts were in vain, and Brentford should have wrapped up the game shortly after the hour mark when Andre Gray fired over from close range with the goal gaping.

The Cottagers were given a lifeline when Toumani Diagouraga was adjudged to have tripped James Husband in the box, and Ross McCormack scored from the spot in the 67th minute. Fulham pressed for the equalizer, with Kacaniklic's free-kick going off target, but it was Brentford who ultimately sealed the victory.

In the last minute of the game, Judge curled a stunning free-kick into the top corner via the underside of the crossbar, giving Brentford a 3-1 lead. And to add insult to injury, Jota converted a pass across the box on the half-volley from 12 yards out in injury time, securing a 4-1 win for the Bees.

Brentford manager Mark Warburton expressed his delight at the result, saying, "I'm really pleased. After that 15-minute spell, I thought we were very good. It keeps us going. We are in contention, be that for top or the play-offs, we are still in with a chance." Warburton also emphasized the importance of focusing on his own team's performance, rather than worrying about other teams.

Fulham manager Kit Symons, on the other hand, was left to rue his team's mistakes, saying, "Ultimately, people just look at the scoreline at the end of the game, and 4-1 looks like a hammering. But the actual fact of the matter is that it wasn't. We were well in the game, but obviously, we didn't get anything out of it. We shot ourselves in the foot for the first two goals."

The defeat leaves Fulham with just one win from their past six games, and Symons acknowledged that his team has work to do to avoid relegation trouble. "We are not out of it," he said. "We have work to do, especially with Millwall winning today." The Cottagers will need to regroup and refocus if they are to climb away from danger and secure their place in the league.

California has taken a significant step towards introducing driverless autonomous vehicles on its roadways. The state's Department of Motor Vehicles has proposed new rules to allow testing of autonomous vehicles without a human driver present. Currently, 27 manufacturers, including Google's Waymo, have permits to test autonomous vehicles, but a human must always be in the car. Waymo reported 124 human interventions in 636,000 miles driven in 2016, down from 341 in 2015. The proposed framework outlines testing procedures and requirements for manufacturers to make vehicles available outside of tests. The public can provide written feedback until April 24. According to Jean Shiomoto, director of the California DMV, this is a crucial step towards eventually allowing driverless vehicles on California roads.

Liverpool FC is set to announce the signing of Southampton midfielder Adam Lallana, 26, after the England international completes his medical and formalities this weekend. The Reds had initially seen two bids rejected for Lallana before the World Cup, but resumed talks upon his return from Brazil. 

Lallana will be joining former teammate Rickie Lambert at Anfield, following Lambert's move to the club earlier in the transfer window. The midfielder has spent 14 years at Southampton, joining the club at the age of 12 from Bournemouth, who will receive 25% of the transfer fee due to a sell-on clause.

The sale of Lallana will bring Southampton's summer transfer earnings to £56m, following the departures of Luke Shaw to Manchester United for £27m and Rickie Lambert to Liverpool for £4m. Executive director Les Reed has assured that new manager Ronald Koeman will be able to reinvest the revenues generated from the transfers into the team.

Liverpool has already secured the signing of Emre Can from Bayer Leverkusen, and is rumored to be targeting Sevilla left-back Alberto Moreno and Belgian forward Divock Origi. The arrival of Lallana is expected to strengthen the Reds' midfield, and his experience at the international level will be a valuable asset to the team.

Delhi Toddler Fighting for Life After Brutal Attack Raises Fresh Concerns Over Women's Safety

A horrific attack on a toddler in the Indian capital has sparked fresh concerns over women's safety in Delhi. The two-year-old girl, who was found unconscious near her home in a poor neighborhood in north Delhi on Friday night, is currently in intensive care after undergoing surgery for extensive injuries.

According to the family, the child was lured away by a group of men who offered her food or sweets. The deputy commissioner of police, Vijay Singh, told the BBC that no arrests have been made yet, and an investigation is underway. The Delhi commissioner for women, Swati Maliwal, who visited the child in hospital, described her injuries as "horrific" and called for swift action to bring the perpetrators to justice.

The incident has raised disturbing questions about the safety of women and children in Delhi, a city that was shocked by the brutal gang rape and murder of a student in 2012. The attack led to widespread protests and the introduction of new anti-rape laws, but despite these efforts, brutal sexual attacks against women and children continue to be reported across the country.

The family of the toddler lives in a small, cramped house near a railway track, where locals often relieve themselves due to a lack of proper toilets. Women in the area say they are afraid to let their children out of their sight, fearing they may be taken away by unknown men. The presence of liquor shops in the area is also a concern, as drunk men often tease and harass women who venture out to use the makeshift toilets.

The attack on the toddler is just one of many cases of rape and sexual assault that have been reported in Delhi this year. According to police records, over 1,500 cases of rape have been recorded so far, but many more are believed to go unreported. In July, a man was arrested for confessing to sexually assaulting and murdering 30 children in and around Delhi, highlighting the need for greater vigilance and action to protect women and children.

As the toddler fights for her life in hospital, her family and community are demanding justice and calling for greater efforts to ensure women's safety in Delhi. The incident is a stark reminder of the need for continued action to address the deep-seated social and cultural attitudes that perpetuate violence against women and children in India.

The Royal Air Force (RAF) has bid farewell to the Tornado, its key fast attack jet for nearly 40 years. A flypast and simulated ground attack marked the final formal sortie of 15 Squadron, the training unit for the Tornado. The squadron is the last of four to be disbanded as the aircraft is replaced by Eurofighter Typhoons. Based at Lossiemouth since the 1990s, the Tornado's distinctive noise will be missed in Moray's skies. The multi-role aircraft saw combat in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Libya. The Eurofighter Typhoons will now form the Quick Reaction Force, tasked with intercepting unidentified aircraft in British airspace. The Tornado's retirement marks the end of an era for the RAF, as it welcomes a new generation of fighter jets. The Typhoons will provide enhanced capabilities, ensuring the UK's airspace remains secure.

Violence Erupts on Turkish-Syrian Border as IS Militants Advance on Kobane

The Turkish-Syrian border has descended into chaos as Islamic State (IS) militants continue their relentless advance on the strategic town of Kobane. The situation has become increasingly volatile, with clashes between Turkish security forces and Kurdish activists, as well as refugees, escalating into violent confrontations. The latest incident involved a team of journalists who were fired upon by police with tear gas canisters, one of which smashed into their vehicle, filling it with gas and starting a fire.

The incident occurred near Kobane, where fierce fighting has been ongoing between IS militants and Syrian Kurds defending the town. The Kurdish community in Turkey is outraged at what they perceive as Turkish inaction in the face of the IS onslaught, and their anger boiled over into violent protests on the border. The Turkish authorities, attempting to maintain order, responded with a heavy-handed approach, using volleys of tear gas to disperse the crowds.

As the situation spiralled out of control, a rocket landed in a house on the Turkish side of the border, prompting the authorities to evacuate the area. However, their methods were widely criticized as excessive, with Kurdish activists being pursued across fields by white clouds of tear gas. The violence showed no signs of abating, with angry Kurdish youths in the nearby town of Suruc blocking roads and brandishing stones, spoiling for a fight.

Meanwhile, reports from the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights indicate that a female Kurdish fighter has carried out a suicide attack on IS positions in the east of Kobane, killing a number of jihadists. The US-led coalition has been conducting air strikes on IS positions in the area, which appear to have slowed the militants' advance. However, IS has captured part of a strategically important hill, which would give them a significant advantage in their bid to take the town.

The fate of Kobane hangs in the balance, with over 160,000 Syrians, mainly Kurds, having fled across the border since the IS offensive began nearly three weeks ago. Capturing the town would give IS unbroken control of a long stretch of the Syrian-Turkish border, a prospect that has sparked widespread concern. Turkey, which has pledged to prevent Kobane from falling to the militants, has come under intense criticism for its perceived inaction. Its parliament has authorized military operations against militants in Iraq and Syria, but so far, no action has been taken to prevent the fighting.

The reason for Turkey's reluctance to lend support to the Kurdish forces in Kobane is believed to be their alliance with the PKK, a banned terrorist organization in Turkey. The situation is complex and delicate, with Turkey walking a fine line between preventing the fall of Kobane and avoiding being drawn into a conflict with the IS militants. As the violence continues to escalate, it remains to be seen how the situation will unfold, but one thing is certain – the fate of Kobane and the stability of the region hang precariously in the balance.

A Scottish man named Steve Bannon has found himself at the center of a Twitter storm, as he's constantly being mistaken for Stephen Bannon, the former chief strategist to US President Donald Trump. To clear up the confusion, Steve, who lives in England, has updated his Twitter bio to "Nothing to do with US politics or running the White House" and changed his banner to "This is not the Steve Bannon you're looking for."

Despite his phone being "melted" by the sheer volume of tweets, Steve has been patiently responding to messages intended for his American namesake. He's been directing people to "go after the other guy" and "get the right guy," and has even seen the humor in the situation. Steve, originally from East Kilbride, told BBC Scotland News that his younger girls think the attention from social media has been hilarious.

This isn't the first time a Scot has been mistaken for someone involved in US politics. Last November, a Glasgow woman named Kellyanne Conway was confused with her US namesake, a Republican Party campaign manager who worked at Trump HQ. The Scottish Kellyanne received strange emails, including one thanking her for "boarding the Trump train!" and was forced to issue a disclaimer on her Facebook profile warning that she was the "wrong Kellyanne Conway!" Steve Bannon's experience serves as a reminder of the importance of verifying identities online, especially in the age of social media.

Myndtown Church in Shropshire has been awarded a significant grant from the Heritage Lottery Fund to undergo much-needed restoration work. The Grade II-listed building will receive £20,600 for the development phase, which is expected to last up to one year, and a further £202,500 for construction. This investment will enable the church to address essential repairs, including a new roof, stonework repairs, and re-rendering of interior and exterior walls, as well as the installation of underground drainage.

Reverend Norman Morris, rector of Myndtown, expressed his delight at the news, highlighting the church's rich history and potential as a hub for walkers and cyclists. Despite having a small population, the church holds significant value to the community and beyond. Local fundraisers had already raised £8,000 towards the restoration scheme, demonstrating the community's commitment to preserving the historic building.

John Burt, project organiser, thanked the Heritage Lottery Fund for their support, stating that without the grant, the church would likely have fallen into disrepair. He emphasized that the building's significance extends beyond its current usage, citing its largely untouched Victorian-era architecture as a unique feature. The restoration work will ensure the long-term preservation of this 800-year-old church, allowing future generations to appreciate its history and beauty.

Tragedy Strikes Swithens Farm as Young Boy Dies in Accident

A devastating incident occurred at Swithens Farm in Rothwell on Friday morning, resulting in the death of a young boy. Harry Whitlam, from Wakefield, was injured at approximately 09:20 BST and airlifted to Leeds General Infirmary, where he underwent head surgery. Unfortunately, he succumbed to his injuries and passed away on Friday night.

A 48-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of drinking and driving and causing death by dangerous driving. He has been bailed pending further investigations. The farm's owners have described the incident as a "tragic accident" that occurred on the working part of the farm.

The community is in shock, with local MP Alec Shelbrooke expressing his condolences to the boy's family. "The community in Rothwell is very close and friendly, and these tragic events will have sent a shockwave through the local community," he said. Jim Reid, father of the farm's co-owner, added that everyone on the site is "very, very upset" and that their thoughts are with Harry's parents and family.

West Yorkshire Police are continuing their investigation into the incident and appeal for anyone with information to come forward. Despite the tragedy, Swithens Farm remains open to visitors, with the owners confirming that the shop, open farm, cafe, and play barn are still operational.

G20 Summit Overshadowed by Paris Attacks, Syria Conflict

The G20 summit in Turkey has been dominated by discussions on the recent Paris attacks and the ongoing conflict in Syria. European Council President Donald Tusk urged Russia to focus its efforts on combating Islamic State (IS) militants, rather than targeting moderate Syrian opposition groups. Tusk's comments come as Russia continues to carry out air strikes in Syria, which it claims are aimed at IS, but many in the West suspect are intended to prop up Moscow's ally, Syrian President Bashar al-Assad.

The two-day summit in Antalya, primarily focused on economic matters, has been overshadowed by the deadly attacks in Paris, which left 129 people dead. IS has claimed responsibility for the assaults, and Tusk emphasized the need for cooperation between the US and Russia in their efforts to combat the militant group in Syria. "We need not only more cooperation, but also more good will, especially from Russian action on the ground in Syria," he said.

US President Barack Obama also addressed the summit, condemning the Paris attacks as an "attack on the civilized world" and pledging to "redouble" efforts to bring an end to Syria's civil war. Obama met with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the summit, despite their differences on how to resolve the conflict. The US and its allies insist that Assad must step down as part of a political solution to the crisis. The conflict in Syria has contributed to a massive refugee crisis, with millions fleeing the country and seeking safety in Europe. Tusk warned that Russian operations in Syria could lead to a new wave of refugees, and expressed concern that this process may have already begun.

Raith Rovers have extended their unbeaten run to six games with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Morton at Cappielow. The decisive goal came early in the second half, courtesy of James Craigen's seventh strike of the season. The win sees Raith move 13 points clear of their opponents, who sit fifth in the Scottish Championship table with just five games remaining.

The visitors started strongly, utilizing the long throw capabilities of Rory McKeown to cause problems for the Morton defence. Mark Stewart and Ross Callachan both had opportunities to open the scoring, but their efforts were thwarted by the home side's goalkeeping and defending. As the half progressed, Morton began to gain the upper hand, with Bobby Barr and Stefan McCluskey both having shots blocked by the Raith defence.

The second half began with a bang, as Craigen pounced on a through pass from Callachan to give Raith the lead. The midfielder's shot went through the legs of advancing goalkeeper Derek Gaston, leaving the home side reeling. Morton pushed hard for a leveller, with McCluskey and Declan McManus both having efforts saved or deflected wide. The home side also had a penalty appeal turned down, as Craig Barr was deemed not to have handled the ball inside the box.

Despite the pressure, Raith held firm to secure a valuable win. The result means that Rovers have beaten Morton in all four meetings this term, a impressive feat that will give them confidence heading into the final stretch of the season. With five games remaining, Raith will be looking to maintain their momentum and finish the season on a high note. For Morton, the defeat is a setback, but they will be determined to bounce back and secure a strong finish to the campaign.

Andy Murray's Struggles Continue as French Open Looms

World number one Andy Murray is facing a crisis of form as the French Open approaches. The 30-year-old suffered a disappointing defeat to Fabio Fognini in Rome, losing 6-2 6-4. This latest setback means Murray has won only one title from eight events in 2017, a far cry from his impressive run of five consecutive victories at the end of last year.

Murray's struggles on clay have been evident, with the Scot reaching only one semi-final in his last four events on the surface. His movement, which has been a key factor in his success in recent years, has been hindered, and he has found it difficult to create chances for himself. Against Fognini, ranked 29th in the world, Murray was unable to find his rhythm, suffering a fifth defeat in 10 matches.

Despite his difficulties, Murray insists that the pressure of being world number one is not a contributing factor. However, he acknowledges that his form has been a long way from where he would like it to be. "I'm just not playing good tennis and need to try to work out how to turn it around," he said. "I believe I will." Murray's last title came in Dubai in February, and he will be looking to regain his momentum as he heads to Roland Garros, where he was runner-up to Novak Djokovic last year.

Murray's coach, Ivan Lendl, will join the team later this week as they prepare for the grand slam event in Paris. The Scot will need to improve significantly if he is to mount a serious challenge for the title. With nearly 4000 points to defend at the French Open, The Queen's Club, and Wimbledon, Murray's ranking is under threat. His successful run at the end of last year means he has a significant number of points to defend, and a poor performance in the coming months could see him lose his position at the top of the rankings.

BBC Sport tennis correspondent Russell Fuller believes that Murray will need to play exceptionally well to remain at the top of the rankings come the autumn. With the tennis ranking system calculated on an annual basis, Murray's recent losses in Madrid and Rome have already seen him shed a significant number of points. As the French Open approaches, Murray will be looking to turn his form around and regain his position as one of the dominant forces in men's tennis. The question is, can he do it? Only time will tell.

A nationwide strike is underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo, as opposition parties pressure President Joseph Kabila to revive a collapsed political deal. The deal, brokered by the Catholic church, aimed to create a transitional government and pave the way for a general election. However, the agreement fell apart over disagreements on power-sharing, including the appointment of a prime minister.

President Kabila, whose term ended last November, has refused to step down, citing financial and logistical difficulties in organizing elections. The opposition coalition, Rassemblement, has called for the strike, blaming the government for the collapse of the deal. Security forces have been deployed to protect businesses that have chosen to remain open, despite the strike.

The Catholic church has urged President Kabila to intervene and salvage the political process. The DR Congo has a history of instability and has never experienced a smooth transfer of power since gaining independence in 1960. The strike is the latest attempt by opposition parties to push for democratic reforms and a peaceful transition of power. The situation remains tense, with the opposition demanding that President Kabila honor the original agreement and step down to allow for free and fair elections.

British sprinter Darren Campbell has come out in support of a radical proposal to reset European athletics records in an effort to restore trust in the sport following a series of high-profile doping scandals. The plan, put forward by European Athletics, would see existing records reassessed against strict criteria, potentially resulting in the erasure of records set by athletes who have been implicated in doping.

Campbell, who won Olympic silver in 2000 and gold in 2004, could potentially lose his 4x100m European record from 1999 if the proposal is implemented. However, he has stated that he is willing to "sacrifice whatever it takes" to save the sport and restore its credibility. "I've lost medals in the past due to team-mates being involved in doping scandals, and while it's tough to accept, I believe it's for the greater good," he told BBC Radio 5 live.

Not all British athletes share Campbell's views, however. Paula Radcliffe, who faces losing her 2003 marathon world record, has spoken out against the proposal, stating that clean athletes like herself are being unfairly penalized for the actions of cheats. Colin Jackson, the 60m indoor hurdles record holder, has also expressed his opposition, arguing that clean athletes are still in the majority and should not be caught up in the fallout.

Despite the controversy surrounding the proposal, Campbell believes that tough decisions need to be made to restore trust in the sport. "Records are there to be broken, and some of those records can't be broken unless you're taking drugs," he said. "The punishment has to fit the crime, and the level of pain these people have put us through - we have to do something."

The proposal will be put to the world governing body, the IAAF, when its council meets in August. Campbell has called for the governing bodies to provide more details on how the proposal will be implemented and how it will help to save the sport. "We need to know how it's going to save the sport," he said. "We don't want to end up right back here in 20 years. It's radical, it's a recommendation, but tell me how it's going to save the sport? That's the important thing."

One Direction's surprise release of their new single "Drag Me Down" has taken the music world by storm. The track, which debuted on Friday, has already surpassed its closest competitor, Little Mix's "Black Magic", with more than double the sales. According to the Official Charts Company, "Drag Me Down" is dominating the charts, with an average of 3.11 million daily plays on Spotify.

Industry experts estimate that the song is earning around $21,700 per day, which could translate to approximately $152,000 in its opening week. This impressive feat comes just two days after former band member Zayn Malik announced his solo record deal. The song's success is a significant milestone for the band, now a foursome, and showcases their enduring popularity.

Meanwhile, the midweek chart has seen a re-entry from the late Cilla Black, with her classic hit "Anyone Who Had A Heart" climbing to number 91. The song is expected to rise further as the week progresses. In the album charts, The Maccabees are currently leading Lianne La Havas by a narrow margin of just over 300 copies. Fans can tune in to BBC Radio 1's Official Chart Show to stay up-to-date on the latest music rankings.

Horizon Nuclear Power has reached a significant milestone in its plans to build a new nuclear power plant at Wylfa on Anglesey, as the Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) begins a 19-month assessment of the site. The £8bn project, owned by Hitachi Ltd, is a major step forward for the company, which hopes to have all necessary permissions in place by 2018.

The ONR's assessment will evaluate the suitability of the site, the organization, and the reactor designs, ensuring that the project meets the highest safety standards. Horizon Nuclear's safety and licensing director, Anthony Webb, stated that the company is focused on providing the ONR with "confidence in our ability to safely deliver this crucial project." He added that the company has a proven technology, experienced leadership, and is rapidly building the necessary capability and organization to ensure success.

The site licence application is one of several key consents required before the project can proceed. Horizon is also preparing for a final public consultation in the summer, followed by a Development Consent Order request to the UK Government's Planning Inspectorate. Additionally, the advance boiling water reactors planned for the new power plant are undergoing the final stage of a Generic Design Assessment, which is expected to be completed by the end of 2017.

The ONR's deputy chief inspector, Mike Finnerty, noted that this is the first licence application for a new nuclear power station since 2011, and that the organization has been working closely with Horizon to ensure that the company meets the robust requirements expected of a nuclear site licensee. If all planning and safety regulations are approved, construction on the new site could begin as early as 2020, with the potential to generate significant economic benefits for the region.

Arsenal midfielder Aaron Ramsey is set to miss the next three weeks of action due to a hamstring injury. The 25-year-old international was forced off in the second half of Arsenal's opening Premier League defeat against Liverpool. According to Gunners boss Arsene Wenger, Ramsey will be sidelined until after the international break, ruling him out of league matches against Leicester and Watford.

The injury is a blow to Wales manager Chris Coleman, who is already dealing with other fitness concerns ahead of the team's upcoming qualifiers. Crystal Palace midfielder Jonny Williams will miss the opening three qualifiers with an ankle injury, and is expected to be out for up to 10 weeks. Striker Hal Robson-Kanu, who scored twice in Euro 2016, is also a concern due to his current lack of match fitness, having been released by Reading and not played since the semi-final.

Ramsey was a standout performer for Wales during their successful Euro 2016 campaign, earning a spot in Uefa's official team of the tournament. His absence will be felt, but Coleman will be hoping he can return to full fitness after the international break and help Wales in their upcoming qualifiers. With several key players struggling with injuries, Coleman faces a challenging task in preparing his team for the upcoming matches.

Lewis Hamilton Dominates First Practice Session at Hungaroring Amidst Drama

The first practice session of the Hungarian Grand Prix got off to a dramatic start as Sergio Perez's car flipped and landed upside down after a rear suspension failure. The incident, which occurred at Turn 11 of the Hungaroring, sent shockwaves through the paddock, reminding everyone of the ever-present dangers involved in Formula 1. Thankfully, Perez emerged unscathed and was able to conduct media interviews just minutes after the crash.

The Mexican driver's car suffered a rear suspension failure, causing him to spin out of control and hit the wall. The impact was severe, and the car flipped over, coming to rest upside down. Perez was quick to reassure his team that he was unhurt, and an investigation into the cause of the failure is currently underway.

Despite the drama, the session continued, and it was Mercedes' Lewis Hamilton who dominated the proceedings. The world champion set a blistering pace, ending the 90-minute session 0.109 seconds ahead of his teammate Nico Rosberg. Hamilton's performance was impressive, and he was two seconds clear of the field after the first 20 minutes.

Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen finished third, 0.671 seconds slower than Hamilton, while Red Bull's Daniel Ricciardo was fourth. The second Red Bull of Daniil Kvyat was sixth, ahead of Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel. Toro Rosso's Carlos Sainz, despite Perez's crash, finished eighth, while Williams's Valtteri Bottas and Toro Rosso's Max Verstappen completed the top 10.

The session was not without its other incidents, as Raikkonen's front wing dropped off his car coming out of Turn 12, leaving debris on the track and puncturing the Ferrari's front tire. The incident brought out the red flag, but the session was restarted with just a few minutes to go, allowing some teams to sneak in a few extra laps.

Lotus, who had earlier solved a financial dispute with tyre supplier Pirelli, had a limited outing, with Pastor Maldonado finishing 17th and reserve driver Jolyon Palmer 20th. At Manor, reserve driver Fabio Leimer had his first outing on a grand prix weekend, finishing 19th, about a second slower than teammate Will Stevens.

The incident involving Perez was a stark reminder of the risks involved in F1, coming just three days after the funeral of Jules Bianchi, who died last week from injuries sustained in a crash at last October's Japanese Grand Prix. The teams and drivers are all carrying tributes to the Frenchman on their cars and helmets at this weekend's race.

As the teams head into the second practice session, they will be looking to fine-tune their cars and make the necessary adjustments to challenge Hamilton and Mercedes. With the pace of the session being so intense, it promises to be an exciting weekend of racing at the Hungaroring.

Tragic Death of a Young Woman with a Dream to Become a Midwife

On July 7, 2005, a devastating act of terrorism shook the city of London, claiming the lives of 52 innocent people. Among the victims was 24-year-old Emily Jenkins, a vibrant and caring young woman who had her whole life ahead of her. Emily's dream of becoming a midwife was tragically cut short when she boarded the southbound Piccadilly Line Tube at King's Cross station, heading towards Russell Square, where a bomb exploded.

Born in Hammersmith, west London, Emily was the youngest of four children. From a young age, she showed signs of the compassionate and nurturing person she would become. At school, she would often befriend the quietest or most vulnerable members of her class, demonstrating a natural ability to care for others. Her love of dance led her to take ballet classes, which she continued until she was 18, passing all her exams with high grades.

As she grew older, Emily's rebellious streak began to emerge, particularly during her A-levels. However, this spirit of adventure and independence also led her to take a gap year in South America, where she learned to speak Spanish and developed valuable life skills. Her travels took her to Salamanca in western Spain, where she spent a year, and later to Australia, where she lived with a group of self-sufficient individuals in Melbourne.

Despite her love of travel and adventure, Emily eventually returned to the UK, settling in London and finding work at a project management company, AYH. She quickly became a valued member of the team, rising to the position of PA to her boss. Emily's family and friends remember her as a kind, sociable, and popular person, who adored her role as an aunt to her two nieces. Her parents, Sarah and Nick Jenkins, recalled her enthusiasm and deep passion for her family and friends, saying, "She had a love of life and a great ability to bring out the best in people."

Emily's dream of becoming a midwife was a testament to her caring nature and desire to help others. Although she did not have the necessary qualifications, she was determined to pursue her goal.
