Her former classmate, Rachael Oliver-Redgate, remembered Emily as a lively and funny girl, always surrounded by friends, and extremely kind and caring. "She would have made a great midwife," Rachael said.

The inquest into Emily's death heard from her parents, who described their daughter as a young woman on a path of fulfillment when her life was tragically cut short. Emily's story is a poignant reminder of the devastating consequences of terrorism and the importance of cherishing the time we have with loved ones. Her memory will live on through her family and friends, who will always remember her enthusiasm, kindness, and deep passion for life.

A stage adaptation of The Hunger Games is set to launch in a purpose-built theatre next to Wembley Stadium in London. The innovative production will be created by Robin de Levita, known for his work on a Dutch stage show about Anne Frank. The Hunger Games film franchise has taken in over $1.5 billion at the worldwide box office, with the latest installment, Mockingjay - Part 1, releasing this month. The stage show will bring to life the dystopian tales of Suzanne Collins, following heroine Katniss Everdeen. While details are scarce, Tim Phelan of Lionsgate promises a "uniquely immersive experience" for fans. De Levita adds that the theatre is an ideal medium to explore the depth of Collins' writing. The new theatre will be constructed specifically for the production, although further details have not been disclosed. The adaptation is expected to provide a new and exciting way for fans to experience the beloved series.

Police Investigation Underway into Possible Poisoning of 18-Year-Old Tennis Player

An investigation is currently underway by Scotland Yard into the alleged poisoning of 18-year-old tennis player Gabriella Taylor, who spent four days in intensive care after being diagnosed with a rare strain of leptospirosis, known as Weil's disease. Taylor, from Southampton, was admitted to hospital after falling ill during her girls' quarter-final match at Wimbledon last month.

According to her mother, Milena Taylor, it is "impossible" for her daughter to have simply become ill, given that she was staying in a "completely healthy environment". The police are investigating an allegation of poisoning with the "intent to endanger life" or cause grievous bodily harm. However, medical experts have expressed skepticism about the possibility of deliberate poisoning, citing the rarity of the disease and the difficulty of intentionally cultivating the bacteria.

Dr. Anna Checkley, from the Hospital for Tropical Diseases, stated that she had "never heard of it being used as a poisoning agent". Leptospirosis is a bacteria that can be transmitted through rat urine, and people in the UK usually contract the infection after coming into contact with contaminated water. Dr. Checkley noted that the disease is "pretty unusual" in the UK, with only 50-100 cases reported per year, mostly among workers who come into contact with contaminated water or animals.

Professor Elizabeth Wellington, an environmental microbiologist at the University of Warwick, also expressed doubts about the possibility of intentional poisoning, stating that it would require a high level of expertise to intentionally grow the bacteria. She described claims that the disease could be used to deliberately poison someone as "a bit laughable", suggesting that Taylor's illness was likely a case of bad luck, contracted through contaminated water.

The police investigation is ongoing, with no arrests made yet. The incident is alleged to have taken place at an address in Wimbledon between July 1 and 10, and Taylor was taken ill on July 6. As the investigation continues, Taylor's mother has expressed concern about her daughter's health, stating that she is "still not 100%". The rare and serious nature of Weil's disease has raised concerns about the potential risks of contracting the disease, and the need for further awareness and education about the risks of leptospirosis.

Chancellor George Osborne is scrambling to find alternative ways to save £4 billion after the House of Lords rejected his plans to cut working tax credits. The move has sparked a heated debate within the government, with Treasury officials exploring options to increase penalties for claimants who take on extra work. However, Work and Pensions Secretary Iain Duncan Smith is said to be strongly opposed to such measures, which he believes would undermine the principles of Universal Credit.

Universal Credit is a new benefit system designed to support people on low incomes or out of work, replacing six existing benefits. At its core is the principle that those who take on extra work should not see their benefits reduced disproportionately. Currently, for every extra pound earned over a set threshold, Universal Credit claimants lose 65p in benefits. However, Treasury officials are considering increasing this "taper rate" to 75p in the pound, which could raise £1.5 billion to £2 billion.

But Work and Pensions officials argue that such an increase would have a devastating impact on the effectiveness of Universal Credit, which is intended to encourage people to take on work without fear of losing their benefits. They claim that increasing the taper rate would create a disincentive for people to work extra hours, undermining the very purpose of the benefit system.

Shadow Chancellor John McDonnell has slammed the proposal, saying that it would create another "work penalty" for low- and middle-income families. He called for a full reversal of the Chancellor's plans to cut working tax credits, which would take £1,350 a year from over three million working families. "The reality is that it would simply create yet another work penalty for low and middle-paid families, which is what caused this huge cross-party calamity in the first place," he said.

An ally of Mr. Duncan Smith, who did not want to be named, told the BBC that the Work and Pensions Secretary had made it clear that increasing the taper rate was not an acceptable solution. "Iain is clear that increasing the taper rate of Universal Credit from 65p to 75p for every pound earned over the limit is not where you should go to find the money that would have come from tax credit savings," the ally said.

Instead, Mr. Duncan Smith is said to have suggested alternative options for finding savings, including a proposal put forward by Baroness Philippa Stroud, a former aide to the Work and Pensions Secretary. In a paper published this week for the Centre for Social Justice, Baroness Stroud argued that the Chancellor should not touch the Universal Credit taper rate if he is looking for savings.

The Treasury has refused to comment on the proposals ahead of the Autumn Statement later this month. However, it is clear that the government is facing a major challenge in finding alternative ways to save £4 billion. With the House of Lords having rejected the original plans to cut working tax credits, the Chancellor must now find new ways to balance the books without undermining the principles of Universal Credit. The coming weeks will be crucial in determining the fate of the benefit system and the millions of families who rely on it.

Schapelle Corby, the Australian woman convicted of drug smuggling in 2005, has been granted parole after serving nine years of her 20-year prison sentence. The 36-year-old former beauty student was found with 4.1kg of marijuana in her bag at Denpasar airport in Bali in 2004, and has always maintained her innocence.

The news of Corby's parole was announced by Indonesian Justice and Human Rights Minister Amir Syamsuddin at a press conference, where he revealed that Corby's application was one of 1,291 approved for parole. Syamsuddin emphasized that Corby had not been given special treatment, stating that "parole is not a matter of policy and not a minister's generosity. It's the right of inmates. We're a dignified country and we uphold the laws."

Corby's case has generated intense interest in Australia, with many people debating her guilt or innocence and criticizing the length of her sentence. A poll in 2012 found that 43% of Australians believed she should be granted clemency, despite 60% agreeing that she was guilty as charged. The case has also led to criticism of Indonesia's tough stance on drug smuggling, with some arguing that Corby's sentence was too harsh.

Corby's mental health is said to have deteriorated during her time in jail, and she will be required to serve out her parole period in Bali. She is expected to live with her sister, Mercedes, on the Indonesian island. However, she will not be able to return to Australia until 2017, as she is required to stay in Indonesia for an extra year after her sentence ends in 2016 to comply with her parole conditions.

The news of Corby's parole has sparked a frenzy of media interest, with large numbers of Australian journalists gathered outside Kerobokan prison in Bali, where Corby has been held. There are reports that Australian media outlets are competing to pay for Corby's story following her release, with some offering significant sums of money for exclusive interviews.

Not everyone is happy about Corby's release, however. Some Indonesian MPs have spoken out against her early parole, arguing that it is inconsistent with Jakarta's attempts to crack down on the drug trade. The MPs claim that Corby's release sends the wrong message and undermines the country's efforts to combat drug smuggling.

Despite the controversy surrounding her case, Corby's release is seen as a significant development in a saga that has captivated Australia for over a decade. Since Lindy Chamberlain, who was jailed and eventually acquitted of killing her own daughter in 1980, there has not been a more divisive female Australian inmate, nor such a feast of lurid headlines and allegations.

As Corby prepares to begin her new life in Bali, she will undoubtedly face intense scrutiny from the media and the public. However, for now, she will be focused on rebuilding her life and adjusting to freedom after nearly a decade behind bars. The prison governor has said that Corby could be released as early as Monday afternoon, once the correct paperwork is received, marking the beginning of a new chapter in her life.

Wakefield Council has secured a significant grant from the Heritage Lottery Fund to unlock previously inaccessible areas of Pontefract Castle. The £3.5m project will restore historic paths and platforms, allowing visitors to explore the Sally Port and Swillington Tower areas for the first time since the mid-1600s. This major restoration work could ultimately lead to the castle's removal from English Heritage's 'at risk' register.

The castle, built in the 11th Century, is steeped in history, having been a Lancastrian stronghold during the Wars of the Roses and the site of King Richard II's imprisonment and murder. The grant will also be used to extend the arts and crafts area, incorporating a new shop and café. Wakefield Council and English Heritage will provide additional funding to support the project.

Councillor Peter Box, leader of the council, expressed his delight at the funding, stating that it will "put Pontefract on the map for tourists" and bring economic benefits to the town. The project aims to build on the castle's existing popularity, attracting more visitors and showcasing its rich history. With work underway, Pontefract Castle is set to become an even more compelling destination for history enthusiasts and tourists alike.

Lewis Hamilton has been forced to miss a tyre testing session due to a minor foot issue. The Mercedes driver was scheduled to test the 2017 Pirelli tyres on Wednesday, but team-mate Nico Rosberg took his place instead. Hamilton's reserve driver, Pascal Wehrlein, also replaced him for Thursday's test. 

According to Mercedes, Hamilton experienced discomfort in his foot after a training session on Tuesday. The team decided it was best for him to rest and undergo physiotherapy to ensure he is in top shape for the upcoming US Grand Prix in Austin on October 23. 

Hamilton is currently 33 points behind his team-mate Nico Rosberg in the world championship with four races remaining. Despite the setback, Mercedes has stated that there is "no concern" over Hamilton's availability for the Austin race. The three-time world champion will be looking to close the gap on Rosberg and get back on track after a tumultuous weekend in Japan.

FanDuel, the fantasy sports firm, has welcomed new legislation in New York that clarifies the legality of its activities. The company was forced to stop operating in the state in November after regulators deemed its operations to be illegal gambling. However, since January, eight US states have passed laws that recognize fantasy sports as a legitimate activity, paving the way for FanDuel's return to the New York market.

The legislation is a significant victory for FanDuel, which claims to have six million registered users across the US and Canada. New York is one of the company's biggest markets, and its technology platform allows sports fans to pick fantasy teams from real players and follow their performances. FanDuel's chief executive, Nigel Eccles, praised the move, saying that sports fans in the state had played a crucial role in lobbying lawmakers to support the company's case.

According to Eccles, over 110,000 letters and nearly 3,000 calls were made to lawmakers by fans backing FanDuel. The company's future had been uncertain due to legal hurdles in several states, with Eccles warning that it may not be able to continue as a going concern. However, the new legislation has provided a significant boost, and FanDuel is now poised to resume operations in New York. The company has also expanded its reach to the UK, launching a new one-day fantasy football platform focused on the English Premier League. With its headquarters in New York and offices in Edinburgh and Glasgow, FanDuel is well-positioned to capitalize on the growing demand for fantasy sports.

A devastating crash on the M1 in Leicestershire in 2014 has led to a stark warning about the dangers of using mobile phones while driving. Christy George, 38, from Hucknall, was jailed for five years and banned from driving for 10 years after her car crashed into a lorry, causing a horrific eight-vehicle pile-up. The collision resulted in the death of Murray Simpson, from London, and left Liese Bowers-Straw, from Nottinghamshire, with severe injuries, including a broken neck and brain damage.

The incident occurred when George became distracted while using her phone, and her car collided with a lorry, which then crashed through to the opposite carriageway. The lorry's load of beer barrels spilled onto the road, and it crashed into a BMW traveling in the opposite direction. Bowers-Straw, who was involved in the crash, has spoken out about the traumatic experience, saying it has completely changed her life. She is now a "prisoner in her own home" and struggles to leave due to the severity of her injuries.

The release of a warning film by Leicestershire Police, featuring the incident, comes as the government announces plans to double penalty points and fines for drivers caught using handheld mobile phones next year. Detective Constable Pete Davies, who investigated the collision, described it as the "largest collision site" he had ever seen, and emphasized the devastating consequences of George's actions, saying someone died and Bowers-Straw was left with "appalling injuries" due to her selfishness. The incident serves as a harrowing reminder of the dangers of using mobile phones while driving and the importance of staying focused on the road.

UK Sends Additional Aid to Nepal as Earthquake Death Toll Continues to Rise

The UK government has announced plans to send nearly 20,000 more shelter kits to Nepal as part of its ongoing aid efforts in response to the devastating earthquake that struck the country on April 25. The move comes as aid agencies work tirelessly to deliver emergency supplies to the thousands of people displaced by the disaster.

According to International Development Secretary Justine Greening, the majority of shelter kits were already in place before the earthquake hit, allowing for the rapid provision of temporary homes to thousands of people within 24 hours of the quake. Ms Greening praised the UK's search and rescue workers for their heroic efforts, saying they had "saved many lives" in the aftermath of the disaster.

The 7.8-magnitude earthquake has had a catastrophic impact on Nepal, triggering avalanches and mudslides, and reducing entire villages to rubble. The death toll has now surpassed 7,500 and continues to climb, with at least one Briton confirmed to have died in the tragedy. The UN estimates that a staggering eight million people have been affected by the earthquake, with 2.8 million people displaced from their homes.

Ms Greening emphasized the importance of providing shelter to those affected, particularly with the monsoon season approaching. "Our pre-positioned shelter kits meant that within 24 hours of the earthquake, British aid was reaching communities who had been hit hard and providing temporary homes to thousands of people across Nepal," she said. "Ahead of the monsoon season, we are delivering thousands more to help the Nepalese people cope as they recover from this tragic disaster."

The UK's 60-strong international search and rescue team, which has been working tirelessly to locate people trapped in the rubble, is now returning home as the Nepalese government has announced the end of the search and rescue effort. The focus has shifted to providing aid to those left homeless, with a emphasis on delivering shelter, clean water, and food before the monsoon season arrives.

The UK public has responded generously to the disaster, with a UK Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) public appeal raising over £33 million to date. The UK government has also committed £17.5 million in humanitarian aid. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) is working to establish whether any other British nationals were among the dead, and has provided practical assistance to over 350 British nationals in Nepal, arranging flights out of the country for around 150.

Among those still missing is 23-year-old architecture student Matt Carapiet, from Bearsted, Kent, who was trekking through Langtang Valley when the earthquake struck. His family and friends are enduring an agonizing wait for news, with family friend Rob Bailey describing the situation as "a horrible feeling." The only option now is to be patient and hope that Matt was not in the village at the time of the earthquake. The thoughts of the nation are with the people of Nepal and all those affected by this tragic disaster.

A unique exhibition showcasing the portraits of five prominent UK party leaders, created from tweets about them, is set to open in central London. Birmingham artist Annemarie Wright has drawn the portraits of David Cameron, Ed Miliband, Nick Clegg, Nigel Farage, and Natalie Bennett, using a collection of tweets that range from praise to criticism.

The exhibition, titled "What do you think of?", aims to capture the public's opinion on the recent general election. Wright collected the tweets by setting up a Twitter account for each leader and following relevant hashtags between November 2014 and February 2015. She then spent 30-40 hours on each portrait, drawing the leaders before overlaying the tweets on top of the images.

The result is a fascinating insight into the public's perception of each leader, with opinions ranging from "vaguely complimentary to absolute condemnation". The portraits will be on display at the Woolff Gallery from April 30 to May 15. Joining the party leaders will be life-sized portraits of the Queen, Baroness Thatcher, Winston Churchill, and Nelson Mandela, composed from their famous speeches. Wright's innovative approach to art has previously caught the attention of notable figures, including Sir Alex Ferguson and Adele, who have both commissioned portraits from her. The exhibition promises to be a thought-provoking commentary on the power of social media and public opinion.

Worcestershire's Tom Fell scored his fourth first-class century to help his team gain a strong foothold in their County Championship match against Middlesex. Resuming on 195-3, Fell's 228-ball knock of 114 not out took Worcestershire past the hosts' first innings total of 309. His mature display, which included 17 boundaries, was a crucial factor in the visitors' overall score of 385.

Fell's innings was a testament to his growing reputation as a talented young batsman. At just 21 years old, he showed remarkable composure and concentration, even as wickets fell around him. His partnership with Jack Shantry, who contributed an unbeaten 41, was particularly impressive, and the two batsmen added 53 runs to the total before Shantry was dismissed.

Middlesex's reply got off to a disastrous start, with Sam Robson edging Charlie Morris behind for his second duck of the game. Nick Compton, however, steadied the ship with a solid 47, and Paul Stirling and Joe Burns' unbroken stand of 67 took the hosts to 140-3 at stumps. Despite this, Worcestershire will be optimistic about their chances of securing a win, particularly if they can take early wickets on the final day.

Fell was understandably pleased with his performance, and credited a pre-game chat with director of cricket Steve Rhodes for helping him to refocus his approach. "I've felt like I've had quite a few starts this season without really going on to get a big score, so it was nice to do it today," he said. "Actually, I had a chat with Steve Rhodes before this game and we spoke about going back to the plans I had in the first match of the season when I got a hundred against Yorkshire."

The pitch, which is becoming increasingly worn, may yet play a significant role in the outcome of the match. With variable bounce and a hint of unevenness, it could prove challenging for Middlesex's batsmen to negotiate. As Fell noted, "it was never easy out there... there's a little bit of up-and-down bounce which is obviously good for us." With the visitors still in with a chance of securing a win, the final day of the match promises to be an intriguing one.

Australian Transport Minister Warren Truss has announced the implementation of the "rule of two" for all domestic and international passenger planes carrying 50 people or more. This move comes in response to the recent Germanwings crash, where investigators believe the co-pilot deliberately crashed the aircraft, killing all 150 on board. The new rules, which take effect immediately, require two authorized personnel to be present in the cockpit at all times.

The "rule of two" is already common in the US, where cabin crew members enter the cockpit when one of the pilots is absent. Recently, airlines in Canada and New Zealand have also adopted this rule. The European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) has also recommended its adoption. In Australia, carriers such as Qantas, Jetstar, and Virgin Australia will be affected by the new rules. Minister Truss expects the policy to be in place within hours on major airlines. The rules will be reviewed in 12 months. This change aims to enhance safety and prevent similar incidents in the future. The Germanwings crash has raised concerns about pilot mental health and cockpit security, and the "rule of two" is seen as a step towards addressing these issues.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has confirmed that the country will hold a snap election on November 1, after Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu failed to form a coalition government following the June polls. The election was announced by the head of the election board, Sadi Guven, and comes as a result of the AK Party's loss of its 12-year majority rule.

The June elections saw the pro-Kurdish HDP party make significant gains, which led to the AK Party's loss of power. The HDP's success has been seen as a major factor in the AK Party's failure to form a coalition government. President Erdogan has now asked Prime Minister Davutoglu to serve as interim PM and oversee the upcoming elections.

As part of his role, Davutoglu will be responsible for forming a cabinet within the next five days. However, the constitution states that all parties should be represented in the interim administration, which could prove to be a challenge. The leader of the Kurdish Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP), Selahattin Demirtas, has stated that his party would be willing to take part in the interim government, but the main opposition Republican People's Party (CHP) and Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) have refused to do so.

The CHP had initially asked for a mandate to form a new government, but President Erdogan opted for a re-run of the elections instead. This decision has raised concerns that Erdogan may be attempting to undermine the coalition talks in order to force a new vote. The June election results had appeared to block Erdogan's plans to boost the powers of the presidency in Turkey, and the AKP will need to secure 60% of seats in the new election to be able to call a referendum on presidential powers.

The political uncertainty in Turkey comes amid rising violence in the region, including the recent breakdown of a two-year ceasefire with the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK). Turkish forces have carried out attacks on militants from the so-called Islamic State in Syria and have bombed Kurdish PKK camps in northern Iraq. The army reported on Tuesday that it had carried out further strikes against PKK bases in northern Iraq, killing 34 PKK members. The situation is likely to remain volatile in the lead-up to the November elections.

New Study Reveals Fair-Skinned Individuals May Need Vitamin D Supplements

A recent study funded by Cancer Research UK has found that individuals with pale skin may not be able to produce enough vitamin D, even with extensive sun exposure. The research, conducted by a team at the University of Leeds, suggests that fair-skinned individuals may need to consider taking vitamin D supplements to maintain optimal levels of the essential vitamin.

Vitamin D is crucial for healthy bones and teeth, and deficiency can lead to a range of health problems. While most people can get enough vitamin D through short periods of sun exposure, the study found that those with fair skin may not be able to produce sufficient amounts, even with prolonged sun exposure. In fact, the researchers found that 730 out of 1,200 participants had lower than optimal vitamin D levels, with many of these individuals having very pale, freckled skin.

The study's lead author, Professor Julia Newton-Bishop, explained that people with fair skin may be less able to make and process vitamin D in the body, regardless of how much time they spend in the sun. Additionally, those who burn easily are more likely to cover up and avoid the sun, further reducing their vitamin D production.

The findings suggest that fair-skinned individuals should be added to the list of groups recommended to take vitamin D supplements, which currently includes people with dark skin, the elderly, young children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and those who avoid the sun. Hazel Nunn, of Cancer Research UK, emphasized the importance of striking a balance between the benefits and harms of sun exposure, particularly for people with fair skin who are at higher risk of developing skin cancer.

While it is too soon to start recommending supplements for all fair-skinned individuals, the study's findings suggest that taking 10 micrograms of vitamin D per day may be a safe and effective way to maintain optimal levels. Nunn advised that individuals concerned about their vitamin D levels should consult their doctor, who may recommend a vitamin D test.

The study's results highlight the complexities of vitamin D production and the need for personalized advice. As Professor Newton-Bishop noted, "It's very difficult to give easy advice that everyone can follow. There's no one-size-fits-all." However, by taking a targeted approach to vitamin D supplementation, fair-skinned individuals can help maintain optimal levels of this essential vitamin and reduce their risk of related health problems. As research continues to uncover the nuances of vitamin D production, it is clear that a comprehensive approach to sun exposure and supplementation will be crucial in promoting public health.

Delays in Iraq Inquiry Report Publication Spark Frustration and Calls for Action

The long-awaited report from the Iraq Inquiry, led by Sir John Chilcot, has been delayed once again, sparking frustration and anger among the families of soldiers who lost their lives in the conflict. The inquiry, which began in 2009, has been plagued by delays, with Sir John citing the "Maxwellisation" process as the primary reason for the hold-up. This process allows individuals facing criticism in the report to respond and provide their side of the story.

In a statement released on Wednesday, Sir John expressed his understanding of the "anguish" felt by the families of the bereaved and acknowledged the need for closure. However, he also revealed that some of the responses received during the Maxwellisation process had opened up new lines of inquiry, further complicating the already lengthy process.

Lawyers representing the families of soldiers who died in Iraq have responded to Sir John's statement by announcing that they will take "further legal steps" to push for the publication of the report. Matthew Jury, of McCue and Partners, stated that Sir John had refused to impose a deadline on the Maxwellisation process, making it impossible to set a date for the report's publication.

Reg Keys, whose son Tom died in Iraq in 2003, expressed his "bitter disappointment" at Sir John's explanation for the delay. Keys argued that witnesses should have been given a maximum of six months to respond to criticism and that the prolonged process had become a "farce." He emphasized the unbearable pain and suffering that the delay was causing for the families of the fallen.

The Iraq Inquiry has faced intense criticism in recent weeks, with Prime Minister David Cameron expressing his frustration at the delays. Sir John has maintained that the inquiry has remained in control of its deadlines throughout the process, but critics argue that the Maxwellisation process is not the sole reason for the hold-up.

Clare Short, a former international development secretary, has questioned the validity of Sir John's explanation, suggesting that the draft report may be poorly written and in need of significant revisions. Short, who is among those criticized in the report, believes that the inquiry team may be struggling to produce a coherent and comprehensive document.

The Chairman of the Foreign Affairs Select Committee, Crispin Blunt, has weighed in on the debate, stating that Parliament cannot impose a deadline for the publication of the report as it would "wreck the inquiry." Blunt has called on Sir John to "bring clarity" to the process as soon as possible and hopes that the inquiry will conclude within six months.

As the delay in the Iraq Inquiry report publication continues, the families of soldiers who lost their lives in the conflict remain in limbo, seeking answers and closure. The ongoing saga has sparked widespread frustration and calls for action, with many demanding that Sir John and his team provide a clear timeline for the report's publication. With the inquiry already spanning over a decade, it remains to be seen when the truth about the UK's involvement in the Iraq War will finally be revealed.

A significant proportion of women born in the 1970s may remain childless, according to a recent report by France's National Institute of Demographic Studies. The study reveals that more than a fifth of women from this generation may not have children, exceeding the average rates in northern and western Europe, which stand at 15% and 18%, respectively.

The report attributes this trend to a combination of factors, including a precarious labor market and a lack of family-friendly work policies. These challenges have led to an increase in involuntary childlessness, as women are forced to postpone parenthood due to economic uncertainty and demanding careers. The study notes that very few women intentionally choose not to have children; instead, many end up delaying parenthood until it is too late.

Interestingly, the report highlights that childlessness was also prevalent among women born in the early 20th century, with 17-25% remaining childless due to factors such as the loss of potential partners during World War I, emigration, and the Great Depression. Since then, the trend has formed a U-shape, with childlessness declining among women born in the 1930s and 1940s, who benefited from post-war prosperity and generous welfare systems.

However, childlessness began to rise again among women born in the 1940s in western Europe and the 1960s in eastern Europe, driven by a complex interplay of personal and external factors. The report cites reliable contraception, delayed union formation and childbearing, and greater family fragility as contributing factors. Additionally, high unemployment, inadequate family policies, and persistent gender inequalities in domestic work and childcare have also played a significant role.

The study concludes that childlessness is likely to continue rising in southern Europe, where up to a quarter of women born in the 1970s may remain childless. Similarly, central and eastern Europe are also expected to see an increase in childlessness. In contrast, western and northern Europe have seen a stabilization of childlessness rates. As the report notes, the economic and cultural trends of the last half-century have steered women and men away from having children, highlighting the need for policymakers to address these underlying factors and implement supportive family policies to mitigate the rise in involuntary childlessness.

Groundbreaking Research Raises Questions About Gray Whale Conservation Status

A recent study published in Biology Letters has shed new light on the migratory patterns of gray whales, sparking concerns about their conservation status. The research, conducted by US and Russian biologists, reveals that a female gray whale made an astonishing 22,500 km (14,000 miles) round trip from the east coast of Russia to breeding grounds off Mexico and back. This remarkable journey, undertaken by a whale named Varvara, has significant implications for our understanding of gray whale populations.

Until now, it was believed that there were two distinct groups of gray whales: the Eastern gray whale, found along the west coast of North America, and the critically-endangered Western gray whale, found along the coast of eastern Asia. However, the study suggests that these populations may be more closely linked than previously thought. In fact, three of seven whales tagged off Russia crossed the North Pacific to breeding grounds off Mexico, indicating that they may be part of the same population.

The lead researcher, Prof Bruce Mate of Oregon State University Marine Mammal Institute, notes that the tagged whales were likely born in Mexico, which raises questions about the existence of a separate Western gray whale population. "If this small sample size is typical, it would suggest that [the two populations are one]," Prof Mate said. However, he also acknowledges that there may be an alternative explanation, suggesting that "true" Western gray whales may still exist, but in significantly lower numbers than previously thought.

The gray whale was driven to the brink of extinction by whaling last century, but the Eastern population has since recovered to around 20,000 animals. In contrast, the Western gray whale population remains critically low, with only around 180 individuals left, according to the International Whaling Commission. The research, combined with genetic fingerprinting and photo-identification evidence, suggests that the two populations may be closely linked or even the same, which could mean that "true" Western gray whales are now extinct.

The International Whaling Commission is currently conducting further research to determine whether the historic Western population still exists. Meanwhile, scientists have raised concerns about the threat of oil exploration in eastern Russia to gray whales in the area. As the conservation status of these majestic creatures continues to unfold, one thing is certain – further research is needed to ensure the long-term protection of gray whales.

Government's Plan to Convert All Schools to Academies by 2022 Raises Concerns

The government's recent announcement to convert all schools in England to academies by 2022 has sparked concerns among educators and experts. The plan, outlined in the White Paper on schools, aims to empower teachers and leaders by giving them more autonomy to make decisions that benefit their students and communities. However, Fasna, a national forum for self-governing schools and academies, has questioned whether there is sufficient capacity to execute this policy effectively.

According to Fasna chairman Tom Clark, the timeline for converting over 16,000 non-academy schools to academies is overly ambitious. "Given that there are 16,000 schools that are not academies, to get them to switch to that new structure on this timescale and for that to be effective is really quite challenging," he said. While Fasna supports the concept of autonomous schools and system leadership, Clark expressed surprise at the speed and timeline of the government's plan.

The government's White Paper relies heavily on system leadership by schools, where successful schools support and assist underperforming ones. However, Clark pointed out that there is a "shallow pool" of schools capable of providing this kind of support, estimated to be around a third of the 24,000 schools in England. "System leadership needs time to mature to be effective," he explained. "It's a big ask of established system leaders – the ones who are most able to help and support schools – to provide that effectively."

Moreover, Clark warned that the rapid expansion of multi-academy trusts could lead to difficulties in building supportive relationships between teachers and heads in different schools. This, he argued, is essential for successful collaboration and improvement. The Department for Education, however, remains confident in its plan, stating that the academy system "empowers great teachers and leaders and gives them the autonomy to make the decisions that are right for their community and their pupils."

A spokesman for the department emphasized that full academisation will enable schools to address underperformance decisively and become part of a dynamic self-improving system. The government has given schools until 2020 to consider their options and until 2022 to convert to academies. Regional School Commissioners will play a key role in recruiting new sponsors to take on underperforming schools, and the government will invest in the necessary people and systems.

Despite the government's reassurances, concerns about the feasibility of the plan persist. Fasna's concerns highlight the potential risks of rapid change and the need for careful planning and support to ensure that the conversion to academies is successful. As the education sector prepares for this significant transformation, it remains to be seen whether the government's ambitious timeline can be met without compromising the quality of education in England's schools.

Renowned War Hero's Medals and Logbooks Find New Home at Fleet Air Arm Museum

The remarkable collection of medals and logbooks belonging to Captain Eric "Winkle" Brown, a legendary war hero and record-breaking pilot, has been acquired by The Fleet Air Arm Museum in Yeovilton, Somerset. The museum successfully purchased the items, which include Brown's Distinguished Service Cross and CBE, after they failed to sell at auction. The exact sum of the purchase remains undisclosed, but the medals were previously valued between £150,000 and £200,000.

Captain Brown, who was born in Edinburgh's Leith area in 1919, passed away earlier this year at the age of 97. He left behind an incredible legacy as a pilot, having flown an unprecedented 487 different types of aircraft – a world record that is unlikely to be matched. During his illustrious career, Brown achieved numerous milestones, including the most aircraft carrier landings, with 2,407, and the most catapult launches, with 2,721. He also conducted some of the world's first helicopter tests and survived 11 plane crashes.

The collection, which features Brown's Air Force Cross, awarded in 1947, and the Defence Medal with King's Commendation for Brave Conduct, was put up for auction at Bonhams in London by the pilot's family. However, thanks to the intervention of a generous donor, the museum was able to reach an agreement with the family and secure the items. The donor, who wishes to remain anonymous, played a crucial role in facilitating the purchase.

The Fleet Air Arm Museum is thrilled to have acquired Brown's medals and logbooks, which date from 1942 to his final flights in 1970. A spokesman for the museum expressed their delight, stating, "Capt Brown was by many measures the Fleet Air Arm's most significant pilot of the post-war period, and we are thrilled and honoured to be able to class this collection as one of our own." The museum plans to preserve the record of innovation contained within Brown's logbooks, which includes previously untapped information, and display them for the public to see.

John Millensted, Bonhams head of medals and coins, commented that Captain Brown's family had decided to sell the extraordinary archive "so that others might appreciate them." He added, "We are delighted that the medals are going to such an appropriate home where visitors will be able to learn about the achievements of this extraordinary man." Captain Brown's remarkable life and achievements will now be showcased at the museum, inspiring future generations of aviation enthusiasts and historians. His legacy continues to fascinate, with a career that included witnessing the liberation of the Bergen Belsen concentration camp and forming a close friendship with the first man to walk on the moon, Neil Armstrong.

Gambian President Yahya Jammeh has rejected the results of the country's recent election, citing "abnormalities" in the voting process. In a surprise move, Jammeh, who has been in power since 1994, appeared on state TV to announce his decision. He claimed that a thorough investigation had uncovered "serious and unacceptable abnormalities" and called for fresh elections to be held.

Jammeh's defeat to opposition candidate Adama Barrow, a property developer, was seen as a major upset. Barrow won over 45% of the vote, securing his place as the country's next leader. However, Jammeh's rejection of the results has thrown the transition into uncertainty. Barrow is due to take office in late January, but it remains to be seen how Jammeh's announcement will affect the handover of power.

Jammeh's 22-year rule has been marked by accusations of human rights abuses and suppression of opposition. Ahead of the election, Human Rights Watch accused him of using violence to silence critics, with reports of activists dying in custody and dozens being jailed without access to medical or legal help. The international community will be watching closely to see how the situation unfolds in the small West African nation.

Jose Mourinho has opened the door for Bastian Schweinsteiger to remain at Manchester United beyond the January transfer window. The 32-year-old midfielder made his first appearance of the season on Wednesday, coming on as a late substitute in the EFL Cup win over West Ham. Schweinsteiger had been training on his own earlier in the season, but has since worked his way back into contention.

Despite being linked with a move to Major League Soccer side Chicago Fire, Mourinho insists that the decision is ultimately Schweinsteiger's. "Of course he can stay," said the United manager. "If you have a contract, you are the powerful one that can decide your future. In January, he is the powerful one - and with better feelings than before." Mourinho praised Schweinsteiger's dedication and work ethic, saying that "everybody was happy" to see him back on the pitch.

Mourinho's comments come as he prepares his team to face Everton on Sunday. United are currently sixth in the Premier League table, and the manager has been told that funds are available to make signings in the January transfer window. One player who has been heavily linked with a move to Old Trafford is Benfica's Victor Lindelof, with Mourinho keen to strengthen his defence.

The United manager has a large squad at his disposal, having used 24 outfield players so far this season. However, he insists that he is comfortable with the size of his squad, and that no player deserves to be pushed out. "I am comfortable having them all, and it hurts me not to select them because of the way they work," he said.

Mourinho was speaking after serving a one-match ban for being sent off during the Premier League match against West Ham. He was fined £16,000 and banned from the dugout for kicking a water bottle in anger. The United manager accepted the punishment, but called for consistency in the way that managers are treated. "I kick a bottle of water. I cannot do it. I accept the suspension of one match, it's as simple as that. But it has to be the same for every manager," he said.

Trinity Mirror, the publisher of the Western Mail, Daily Post, and Wales Online, has announced a 24% rise in annual profit despite declining print circulation. CEO Simon Fox attributed the success to the company's growing online audience. In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Fox emphasized the importance of regional journalism, stating that local councils, schools, and police forces are no longer being adequately covered. As a result, Trinity Mirror's digital audiences in the regions are larger than ever. However, when asked about the closure of four local papers in England last October, Fox did not rule out further closures, suggesting that the company may shift its focus to online platforms. He noted that some titles, particularly free ones, may be closed, with more news being made available on mobile sites and websites. This shift reflects the changing media landscape.

A controversy is brewing at Llangennech school as some parents object to the council's plan to extend Welsh medium provision. A solicitor's letter has been sent to the council on behalf of a parent. The council aims to increase bilingualism, citing a decline in Welsh speakers. However, parents argue that replacing the current schools with a Welsh-medium primary would significantly impact children seeking an English-medium education, sparking a petition against the move. The council's decision has ignited a debate about language and education in the community. Parents are awaiting the council's response.

Fighting Erupts on Lebanon-Syria Border as Hezbollah Launches Offensive Against Militants

A military operation launched by Hezbollah and Syrian forces against militant groups on the Lebanon-Syria border has raised concerns for the safety of thousands of Syrian refugees in the area. Pro-Hezbollah media reported that the forces are attacking the Jroud Arsal area and Qalamoun mountains from two directions, targeting around 1,000 militants affiliated with the Islamic State (IS) group and al-Qaeda's former affiliate, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).

The operation began with Syrian forces and Hezbollah shelling the area, followed by an advance from Flita on the Syrian side of the border and from the south of Arsal, on the Lebanese side. Television footage showed columns of smoke rising as Hezbollah fired artillery towards hills where the militants are based. The Lebanese army has also announced plans to launch its own offensive against militants in the area, who have used Arsal's refugee camps as a safe haven.

The influx of refugees from the war in Syria has heightened sectarian tensions in Lebanon, and the area around Arsal is home to tens of thousands of refugees. According to a Lebanese security source, hundreds of refugees are fleeing towards Arsal as the fighting intensifies. The situation is precarious, with many fearing for the safety of civilians caught in the crossfire. The offensive is expected to continue indefinitely, according to Hezbollah-affiliated media, which described the operation as a campaign to flush out "armed terrorists".

Seychelles: A Tropical Paradise with a Thriving Economy

Located in the Indian Ocean, the archipelago of Seychelles is a haven of fine beaches, turquoise seas, and an array of wildlife, including giant tortoises and sea turtles. With a population of 87,400 and a land area of 455 square kilometers, this former British colony has transformed into a thriving economy, boasting a high per capita income, excellent healthcare, and education system.

The country's economy is heavily reliant on the fishing industry and upmarket tourism, which attracts visitors from around the world to its stunning natural beauty. Much of the land is protected as part of nature reserves, preserving the unique biodiversity of the islands. The government has taken significant steps to conserve the environment, ensuring that the country's natural resources are utilized sustainably.

In recent years, Seychelles has experienced a significant shift in its political landscape. In 2016, Danny Faure was sworn in as president, succeeding James Michel, who resigned after parliamentary elections saw the opposition coalition, Linyon Demokratik (LDS), take control of the legislature for the first time in the country's history. President Faure, a former finance minister and governor of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), has pledged to continue the country's economic growth and development.

The media landscape in Seychelles is characterized by a mix of government-controlled and private outlets. While the government operates radio and TV stations, as well as the sole daily newspaper, private publications have been robust in their reporting, despite tough libel laws. However, steep licensing fees have discouraged the growth of private broadcast media. The internet has become increasingly popular, with around 50,000 users by the end of 2015, providing citizens with access to a wide range of information and news sources.

Seychelles has a rich history, with French planters and their slaves settling in the islands in 1768. The country was later annexed by Britain in 1794 and became a separate British colony in 1903. Seychelles gained independence in 1976, with James Mancham as president and France Rene as prime minister. However, a coup in 1977 saw Rene become president, a position he held until 2004, when he was succeeded by James Michel.

In recent years, Seychelles has faced challenges from Somali piracy, which has affected the country's fishing industry and tourism sector. However, with the help of international partners, including the US and the European Union, the country has been able to combat piracy and ensure the safety of its citizens and visitors. The EU has signed an anti-piracy agreement with Seychelles, allowing EU troops to be deployed on the islands, while the US has provided drone spy-planes to help fight piracy.

Today, Seychelles is a thriving democracy, with a strong economy and a high standard of living. The country's stunning natural beauty, rich history, and vibrant culture make it a popular destination for tourists and a great place to live for its citizens. With its commitment to conservation, sustainable development, and good governance, Seychelles is well-placed to continue its growth and prosperity in the years to come.

Astronomers have captured a remarkable transformation in a young star's development, observing the formation of an elongated column of hot, ionized gas in just 18 years. The star, known as W75N(B)-VLA2, is located approximately 4,200 light-years from Earth and is surrounded by a doughnut-shaped cloud of dust. This cloud slows down the star's powerful wind, causing it to form a column perpendicular to the dusty ring.

Using the Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico, a team of researchers compared data from 1996 and 2014, providing a unique "before and after" glimpse of the star's development. The results, published in the journal Science, show a compact, rounded wind in 1996 transforming into a distinctly elongated outflow by 2014. According to Carlos Carrasco-Gonzalez, the first author of the study, "The comparison is remarkable."

W75N(B)-VLA2 is an infant star that is about 300 times brighter than the Sun. Its dramatic growing pains are being observed in real-time, providing scientists with a rare opportunity to study the formation of a massive star. Prof Huib van Langevelde from Leiden University in the Netherlands noted, "This object is providing us an exciting opportunity to watch the developments over the next few years, as this very young star develops the characteristic bipolar outflow morphology."

The study also sheds light on the role of magnetism in the star's formation. Earlier research had shown that the large-scale magnetic field in the region is neatly aligned with the field surrounding the young star. The newly formed elongated outflow is also aligned with this magnetic field, suggesting that magnetism plays a crucial role in the star's development.

The team hopes to continue monitoring W75N(B)-VLA2 as it undergoes further changes. Dr Gabriele Surcis, a co-author of the study, noted, "Our understanding of how massive young stars develop is much less complete than our understanding of how Sun-like stars develop." The opportunity to observe this protostar's turbulent development in real-time is expected to provide valuable insights into the formation of massive stars. As the star continues to evolve, scientists will be watching closely, eager to learn more about the complex processes that shape the early lives of these celestial bodies.

A shocking revelation has emerged in the ongoing Takata airbag saga, with five major carmakers admitting to temporarily replacing defective airbags with identical devices in Australia. Toyota, Mazda, Lexus, BMW, and Subaru have all confessed to using the same faulty airbags as a stopgap measure, sparking outrage from consumer advocacy group Choice.

The organisation has slammed the carmakers, saying that people are being left to "drive ticking time-bombs". The defective airbags, made by Japanese manufacturer Takata, have been linked to at least 18 deaths worldwide, including one in Australia earlier this month. The airbags' faulty inflators can explode with too much force, spraying metal shrapnel and putting drivers' lives at risk.

Choice's investigation found that around 70% of the 2.1 million cars recalled in Australia had not yet been refitted with safe airbags. Toyota has defended its actions, saying that the temporary replacements would be safe for several years, but ultimately need to be replaced again due to environmental exposure. The Australian government's consumer watchdog has announced that it will investigate the recall, following a recent road death in Sydney linked to a defective Takata airbag. The incident highlights the urgency of the situation, and the need for carmakers to take immediate action to ensure public safety.

UK Defence Budget Faces "Budget Black Hole" Due to Sterling's Fall

The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) has warned that the UK's defence budget is facing a "budget black hole" due to the fall in sterling, which has made military equipment purchases from the US more expensive. The pound's decline to its lowest level against the dollar in over 30 years has resulted in increased costs for the Ministry of Defence (MoD), which buys much of its military equipment in US dollars.

According to Prof Trevor Taylor, from the RUSI think tank, the extra costs could present a serious problem for the UK's defence stance. "The UK pays the US about $10 billion a year for defence products, and with the fall in sterling, this is going to become even more expensive," he said. The MoD has already committed to buying several high-profile defence products from the US, including nine P8 maritime patrol aircraft, 138 F-35B aircraft, and 50 Apache aircraft.

The MoD will also have to buy spares and support services for their existing aircraft and defence systems, such as Chinook helicopters, Trident missiles, and the AWACS surveillance system. The UK has committed to spending 2% of its GDP on defence, a minimum set by NATO. However, with the UK's GDP potentially shrinking due to Brexit, this could result in a reduced spending figure.

Lord West, the former head of the Royal Navy and a Labour peer, described the issue as a "perfect storm" for the MoD. "The government has delayed the purchase of frigates, which will push up their costs, and now we have the fall in sterling making our defence purchases more expensive," he said. A source with experience of the issue at a high level of government warned that the situation could push an already stretched budget "to breaking point".

However, not everyone is alarmed by the situation. Another former insider, who did not wish to be named, argued that sterling could well recover and the issue was merely a "headache" for the MoD. Major Tim Cross, a retired British Army officer who supported the Leave campaign, called for time to be spent assessing the situation post-Brexit, rather than "running around like headless chickens".

The chairman of the House of Commons defence select committee, Julian Lewis, a Brexit supporter, said defence had "fallen too far down the scale of national priorities". He argued that the 2% of GDP spent on defence was "nowhere near where we need to be spending" and that the figure should be more like 3%. The MoD has said it takes "appropriate financial precautions in all its procurement contracts" and "remains committed to the procurement set out in last year's defence review".

Despite these reassurances, the situation remains a cause for concern. With the UK's defence budget already stretched, the extra costs resulting from the fall in sterling could have serious consequences for the country's defence capabilities. As Prof Taylor warned, "The UK's defence budget is facing a budget black hole, and it's not clear how it's going to be filled."

A primary school in Leyton has sparked controversy by advising parents that children will not be allowed to fast during Ramadan. Barclay Primary School cited concerns over student health and wellbeing, stating that some children had previously fallen ill or fainted while fasting. However, critics, including Imam Ajmal Masroor, have labeled the move as an "overreaction" and "stupidly foolish". Masroor argued that children, especially primary school age, are not expected to fast and that the issue could have been resolved through dialogue with parents. The school's decision has been seen as unnecessary and has drawn negative attention to the Muslim community. The school suggested that older children who wish to fast do so on weekends, citing a busy time of year with sports days and field trips, as well as a recent hot spell.

Residents of Lynton Avenue in Hull are up in arms after the government's Valuation Office Agency (VOA) raised their council tax bands from A to B, resulting in a £160 annual increase. The move has been met with widespread criticism, with many residents feeling that the decision is unfair and has been made without proper justification.

The controversy began when one unidentified neighbour complained to the VOA that their rates were too high. Instead of reducing the complainant's tax, the VOA reviewed the tax banding of the entire street and decided to raise everyone else's tax. Residents are outraged, claiming that the decision is a classic case of penalizing the many for the perceived mistake of one.

"All the houses on the street are identical, so we should all be paying the same rate," said one resident, who wished to remain anonymous. "One person on the street was paying a higher rate than everyone else, so they questioned it with the government, and I think they've been a bit cynical. Instead of admitting that this person has been overpaying all these years and giving them a refund, they have decided to put everyone else up. It's just so typical, if you ask me."

The VOA sent letters to each house on the street, informing residents that their homes would be revalued. However, the increase in council tax was implemented without further notice, leaving many residents feeling blindsided. Council tax bands in England are calculated based on the value of the property in April 1991, with Band A being the cheapest and Band H being the most expensive.

Accounts manager Kerry Wilson, who has lived on Lynton Avenue for 16 years, is leading the charge against the decision. "We have been in Band A as long as we've lived here," she said. "The move to Band B means our houses would have been valued at more than £40,000 in 1991, but there is no way that can be true. My husband has found all the house prices from that time, and none of them were more than that. It's caused a right rumpus, and we're making sure everyone in the street will send their letter of appeal in."

The increase in council tax will have a significant impact on many residents, particularly pensioners like Pat Garrett, who has lived on the street for almost 40 years. "As a pensioner, my monthly income isn't going up anytime soon, and I'll definitely feel the pinch," she said. "The amount doesn't sound like much, but it makes a big difference when you consider everything else is going up in price too."

A spokesman for the VOA defended the decision, stating that bands can change as a result of one person expressing concerns about the amount they were paying. "If a taxpayer contacts us with concerns about their council tax banding, we will review it free of charge," he said. "We might need to review the bands of similar neighbouring properties to ensure they are correct, which can lead to other properties' bands being changed. We alter council tax bands only if evidence indicates they are incorrect, or there has been a physical change to a property or its locality."

Hull City Council has declined to comment on the row, stating that it acts on the instructions of the Valuation Office Agency. The decision has left residents feeling frustrated and angry, and many are determined to appeal against the increase. As the row continues to simmer, one thing is clear: the residents of Lynton Avenue will not go down without a fight.

British tennis star Johanna Konta is on the verge of making history as she prepares to face Russian opponent Ekaterina Makarova in the Australian Open. A win would see Konta match Jo Durie's feat of reaching the quarter-finals at a major, a milestone not achieved by a British female since 1984. Konta, 24, has a promising record against Makarova, having beaten her in their only previous meeting at Eastbourne in June.

That victory marked a significant turning point in Konta's career, as it was her first win over a top-10 player and sparked her rise into the world's top 40. Since then, Konta has been in impressive form, defeating former world number one Venus Williams in the first round and taking down five top-20 players. Her win over Czech Denisa Allertova in the previous round made her the first British woman to reach the fourth round of the Australian Open since Jo Durie and Anne Hobbs in 1987.

Despite the growing interest and pressure, Konta remains grounded and focused on her game. "It's as big as you make it, really, and it becomes as important as you want it to," she said. Konta, who moved to England with her family in 2005, is aware of the significance of her potential achievement but is determined to stay humble and prioritize her goals. A win against Makarova would be a major breakthrough for British tennis, and Konta is ready to seize the opportunity and make her mark on the sport.

Tributes have been pouring in for Dan Rooney, the former US Ambassador to Ireland and chairman of the Pittsburgh Steelers, who has left behind a legacy of peace, reconciliation, and philanthropy. Irish President Michael D Higgins led the tributes, praising Mr. Rooney's contributions to Ireland and the Irish people. "He was deeply committed to Ireland and the Irish people, and his contributions to peace and reconciliation have left a real and tangible legacy," said President Higgins.

Mr. Rooney, who was born in Pittsburgh in 1932, was instrumental in setting up the Ireland Funds charity in 1976, which has since raised over $550 million for thousands of Irish organizations around the world. He co-founded the charity with Irish businessman Sir Anthony O'Reilly, with the aim of supporting and promoting peace efforts and Irish culture. Today, the charity is known as the Ireland Funds, and its work is a testament to Mr. Rooney's selfless dedication to the Irish people.

John Fitzpatrick, chairman of the Ireland Funds, described Mr. Rooney as "an utter gentleman and utterly selfless." "The work of the Ireland Funds is his legacy, and Ireland is a better place because of him," said Mr. Fitzpatrick. "Thousands have benefited from his care and concern, and his impact will be felt for generations to come."

Mr. Rooney's connection to Ireland ran deep, with his grandfather emigrating from County Down to the US in the 19th century. His family went on to found the Pittsburgh Steelers, which has won more Super Bowl titles than any other NFL team. Mr. Rooney was also instrumental in introducing the NFL's "Rooney Rule," which requires teams to interview at least one black or ethnic minority candidate for a head coach vacancy.

In 2008, Mr. Rooney was awarded an honorary CBE for his contributions to peace and reconciliation in Northern Ireland. He served as the US Ambassador to Ireland from 2009 to 2012, appointed by then-US President Barack Obama, who described him as "an unwavering supporter of Irish peace, culture, and education." Mr. Rooney's legacy is a testament to his commitment to Ireland and its people, and he will be deeply missed by all who knew him.

The state of emergency in the Maldives has been lifted, according to Foreign Affairs Minister Dunya Maumoon. The emergency was declared on November 4 to aid security forces in investigating an alleged plot to assassinate President Abdulla Yameen. The president had narrowly escaped injury when a blast struck his boat last month. However, US investigators found no evidence to support the claim that the blast was an assassination attempt.

During the state of emergency, police and armed forces were given wider powers to arrest suspects and restrict freedom of assembly and movement. The military patrolled the streets, and a planned protest by the opposition Maldivian Democratic Party was potentially disrupted. The Maldives has experienced political unrest in recent months, including the impeachment of Vice President Ahmed Adeeb, who is accused of high treason. The lifting of the state of emergency is seen as a step towards returning the country to normalcy. Minister Maumoon expressed satisfaction with the swift resolution of the matter, stating that the country is looking forward to getting back on track. The Maldives, a popular tourist destination, aims to regain stability and reassure visitors of their safety.

It's been 10 years since the passing of football legend Jeff Astle, a prolific goal-scorer who played for West Bromwich Albion during the 1960s and 1970s. Astle's death at the age of 59 was a tragic reminder of the potential risks associated with heading heavy leather footballs. A coroner's report concluded that Astle had suffered brain damage as a result of repeatedly heading the ball, leading to his untimely death.

Despite the coroner's findings, the Football Association (FA) has been criticized for its response to Astle's death. His widow, Laraine Astle, claims that the FA has been reluctant to acknowledge the potential dangers of heading footballs, stating that "they don't want to hold their hands up and own up that the game that we loved proved to be a killer." Astle's family has been unsuccessful in their bid to win compensation from the FA, despite the coroner's report highlighting the link between heading footballs and brain damage.

The FA has responded by stating that "there remain conflicting opinions on the possible effects of frequent heading of a football over time." While the organization acknowledges Astle's contributions to the sport, it has stopped short of accepting responsibility for his death. The FA has implemented standards for the size, weight, and pressure of footballs, and continues to work with FIFA on medical issues related to the sport.

Jeff Astle's legacy extends far beyond his tragic death. He was a talented footballer who scored 137 goals in 292 league appearances for West Bromwich Albion, earning him a place as one of the club's greatest players. He also represented England in the 1970 World Cup and made memorable appearances on TV's Fantasy Football League in the 1990s. As the football community remembers Astle's achievements, his family continues to push for greater recognition of the potential risks associated with heading footballs, and for the FA to take greater responsibility for protecting the health and wellbeing of its players.

Jurors in the Hillsborough inquest visited the site of the 1989 disaster yesterday, walking through the tunnel where a crush led to the deaths of 96 Liverpool fans. The eleven jurors, accompanied by coroner Lord Justice Goldring, made their way down the tunnel of the Leppings Lane stand, where the fatal crush occurred. The visit was part of the inquest into the deaths of the fans, which was ordered after the accidental death verdicts were quashed.

As they walked towards the stadium, Lord Justice Goldring pointed out key features, including the former location of exit gates and other areas that have changed since the disaster. The jurors carried photographs of the stadium in 1989 to help them visualize the old layout. They were also shown the police control box, which is now much larger than its 1989 counterpart, and the site of the former gymnasium, which was used as a temporary mortuary on the day of the disaster.

The jury's visit to the stadium was part of a larger tour of locations relevant to the inquests. They also visited the White Horse Inn, a pub where some Liverpool fans went before the match, and Wadsley Bridge railway station, from which supporters were accompanied by police to the stadium. The coroner explained the significance of each location, highlighting the events that unfolded on the day of the disaster.

In addition to the stadium and surrounding areas, the jurors visited the Northern General and Royal Hallamshire Hospitals, which both took casualties on the day. Lord Justice Goldring told the jury that the Northern General accepted 88 casualties, many of whom died, while 71 went to the Royal Hallamshire, where not all died. The visit was an important part of the inquest, allowing the jurors to gain a better understanding of the events that led to the tragedy.

The inquests into the deaths of the 96 Liverpool fans have been ongoing, with the jury hearing a minute-by-minute countdown of how the disaster unfolded earlier this week. The hearing included rarely seen footage of the day, taken by police and BBC cameras, as well as stadium CCTV. The fresh inquests were ordered after a panel of three High Court judges quashed the accidental death verdicts, and are aimed at providing a more detailed understanding of the events surrounding the tragedy.

Scottish Economy Shows Signs of Slowing Down, Survey Reveals

A recent survey conducted by the Scottish Chambers of Commerce (SCC) has indicated that the Scottish economy is experiencing a slowdown, with key sectors such as construction, tourism, and manufacturing showing disappointing results. The survey, which covered the three months to June 30, found that construction activity had decreased, while tourism performed "markedly" worse than the same period last year. Additionally, there was little sign of improvement in manufacturing, retail, and financial and business services.

According to the SCC report, business performance across the Scottish economy was more consistent in the second quarter of 2016 compared to the first quarter, but both performance and optimism were lower than in the same period of 2015. The report's findings have raised concerns about the potential impact of the Brexit vote on Scotland's economy, with the SCC calling on the UK and Scottish governments to take measures to prevent a further slowdown.

Neil Amner, chairman of the SCC economic advisory group, emphasized the need for clarity on the future of talented individuals working in Scotland, stating that everyone must have confidence in their ability to fulfill their long-term ambitions in the country. He also called on the government to reconsider policies that impose burdens on businesses and to use their powers to boost growth, suggesting measures such as a cut in business rates and an accelerated reduction in Air Passenger Duty.

The SCC is urging the government to take proactive steps to support businesses and attract new investment and trading opportunities to Scotland. With the Brexit vote presenting both challenges and opportunities, the organization believes that it is essential for businesses to be at the forefront of driving growth and stability in the Scottish economy. As the UK and Scottish governments navigate the post-Brexit landscape, they will need to work closely with businesses to ensure that Scotland remains an attractive place to do business and invest.

The Royal British Legion is utilizing the social media platform Thunderclap to encourage Twitter and Facebook users to observe a two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday. At 09:00 GMT, thousands of users are expected to simultaneously send the message "I'll be remembering the fallen at 11 o'clock #2MinuteSilence #LestWeForget" to show their respect for those who have paid the ultimate sacrifice.

This campaign aims to create the largest online show of remembrance, harnessing the power of social media to reach millions of Britons. The Royal British Legion hopes that the estimated 10 million Twitter and 33 million Facebook users in the UK will participate in the Two Minute Silence Thunderclap. Helen Hill, head of remembrance at The Royal British Legion, emphasized the importance of honoring the men and women who have given their lives in wars and conflicts.

Thunderclap, a crowdspeaking platform, has been used by international charities and causes, including the UN to support World Humanitarian Day. The platform allows users to be heard by saying something together, amplifying their message and increasing its impact. By using Thunderclap, The Royal British Legion aims to remind the nation of the significance of the two-minute silence, which began in 1919 after the Armistice at the end of World War I. The Royal British Legion is the UK's leading armed forces charity, dedicated to ensuring that those who have made the ultimate sacrifice are remembered and honored.

A historic warship that sank off the Essex coast in 1665 has yielded a treasure trove of artefacts, including soles and insoles, during a series of dives. The London, a British warship, mysteriously exploded while en route to Gravesend, resulting in a significant loss of life. Recent excavations have uncovered evidence of cabins and hand-made glass windows, offering a glimpse into life on board during a pivotal period in British history.

English Heritage has likened the discovery to the Mary Rose warship, suggesting it could be of similar scope and significance. The artefacts are expected to provide valuable insights into the daily lives of those on board, shedding light on Britain's emergence as a sea power during the 16th and 17th centuries. Following a review of the operation, the artefacts will undergo conservation and eventually be put on permanent display at Southend-on-Sea Borough Council's Museums Service, with further dives scheduled for next year.

Gerry Mallon has left Danske Bank to become Ulster Bank's CEO in the Republic of Ireland. Mallon, who led Danske in Belfast since 2008, will start his new role in June. His banking knowledge in Ireland is deemed "invaluable" by Ulster Bank's owner, Royal Bank of Scotland. Kevin Kingston, former deputy CEO, has replaced Mallon at Danske Bank, bringing his own experience as former president of the Northern Ireland Chamber of Commerce.

Ukraine Reconnects Electricity to Crimea After Talks with Activists

One of the damaged power lines supplying electricity to Crimea has been reconnected, bringing some relief to the peninsula's two million residents who have been struggling with widespread blackouts. The Kakhovskyy-Titan power line was reestablished overnight after negotiations with activists who have been blocking energy supplies to the region. The Ukrainian authorities and Russian energy ministry confirmed the resumption of power supply.

The move comes after unknown attackers damaged four power pylons on November 22, leaving Crimea without electricity. Anti-Russian activists were blamed for the incident, which highlighted the peninsula's reliance on Ukraine for power. With the four lines being the only source of electricity for Crimea, their damage plunged the territory into darkness, prompting the closure of schools and a state of emergency.

The reconnection of one line is a positive development, but three lines remain down, and the situation remains fragile. Russia has begun constructing an undersea cable to bypass Ukraine and provide a more stable source of electricity to Crimea. The incident has also led to a reduction in coal supplies to Ukraine from Russia and rebel-held eastern Ukraine, exacerbating the energy crisis in the region.

Violence Continues to Plague Israeli-Palestinian Conflict

A wave of violence between Israelis and Palestinians shows no signs of slowing down, with multiple incidents reported over the weekend. On Sunday, four Palestinians were killed in separate incidents, while a teenage girl was critically wounded in an attempted assault. No Israelis were hurt in any of the incidents.

The first incident occurred near Jenin in the northern West Bank, where two 15-year-old boys were throwing rocks at passing cars. When an Israeli army patrol arrived, one of the boys opened fire with a rifle, prompting the soldiers to return fire and kill both teenagers. Later, at a checkpoint in Jerusalem, a 17-year-old Palestinian youth with a knife ran at officers and was shot and killed.

In another incident, two Palestinians were killed after they opened fire on Israeli police with automatic weapons outside Jerusalem's Old City. Meanwhile, in Hebron, a 17-year-old woman who attempted to stab a policeman was shot and taken to hospital in critical condition.
