However, Palestinian media reported conflicting accounts of the incident, with some sources claiming that the girl had not attempted an attack and was shot six times while walking away from a military checkpoint with her sister.

The violence is part of a larger wave of stabbing, shooting, and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians and Israeli Arabs that has resulted in the deaths of over 160 Palestinians and 26 Israelis since October 2015. The attacks have been sporadic but persistent, with correspondents noting that they show no sign of abating. The situation remains volatile, with tensions between Israelis and Palestinians continuing to run high. As the conflict drags on, concerns about the safety and well-being of civilians on both sides continue to grow.

Fairfield Energy has announced that production from all Dunlin cluster fields will be shut down in mid-June, marking the beginning of the decommissioning process. Despite the shutdown, Dunlin Alpha will remain fully manned and operational, continuing to export third-party oil into the Brent system pipeline. The decision to decommission the fields comes as a result of the depressed oil price and challenging operational conditions in the North Sea.

The Dunlin field, located 300 miles north-east of Aberdeen in the East Shetland basin, has been in production since August 1978. At its peak, the field produced approximately 120,000 barrels of oil per day in 1979. Originally operated by Shell, the field was acquired by Fairfield in 2008, along with the Dunlin SW, Merlin, and Osprey fields.

The decommissioning process, which is expected to cost around £400m, will require regulatory approvals and is anticipated to take several years to complete. Fairfield has stated that its subsidiaries, Fairfield Betula and Fairfield Fagus, along with joint venture partner MCX Dunlin, will lead the decommissioning program. The company has assured that high offshore activity levels will be maintained throughout the process.

According to Fairfield's chief executive, David Peattie, the decision to decommission the Dunlin field is the most appropriate action, given the asset's lifecycle and the current market conditions. Peattie emphasized the company's commitment to delivering a safe and transparent decommissioning process, working closely with staff and stakeholders to achieve this goal.

The decommissioning of the Dunlin field is part of a larger trend in the North Sea, where many oil and gas installations are nearing the end of their lifespan. The industry body Oil and Gas UK estimates that the decommissioning of oil and gas installations in the UK sector of the North Sea could cost up to £40bn over the next 35 years. There are currently 113 oil platforms and 189 gas platforms in the UK Continental Shelf, many of which will require decommissioning in the coming years.

Environmental groups have welcomed the announcement, emphasizing the importance of protecting the marine environment during the decommissioning process. Lang Banks, director of WWF Scotland, stated that the oil industry has a responsibility to clean up its mess, having made significant profits over the years. Banks urged Fairfield to take all necessary steps to ensure the protection of the marine environment during the decommissioning process.

As the North Sea oil and gas industry continues to evolve, the decommissioning of fields like Dunlin will become an increasingly important issue. With the potential cost of decommissioning reaching £40bn over the next 35 years, it is essential that companies like Fairfield prioritize safe and responsible decommissioning practices, minimizing the impact on the environment and ensuring a sustainable future for the industry.

UK Manufacturing Sector Sees Slowdown in Growth and Job Losses

The UK manufacturing sector has experienced a slowdown in growth, with the purchasing managers' index (PMI) falling to 51.5 in August, down from 51.9 in July. Although the score remains above 50, indicating expansion, it is significantly lower than the average over the past two-and-a-half years. The sector has also seen a reduction in headcount for the first time in 26 months, marking the end of a two-year period of continuous job creation.

According to Rob Dobson from Markit, the compiler of the PMI, the sector is currently in a "holding pattern" with production growth stagnating and marginal job losses reported. The main culprit behind this slowdown is the weakness in export orders, which has been impacted by the strong sterling exchange rate, weak sales growth to the eurozone, and the slowdown in China.

Analysts have highlighted the weakness in exports as a major problem for UK manufacturers, with Howard Archer from IHS Global Insight stating that the sector is being "held back" by weak foreign orders. The strength of the pound, in particular, is making UK exports more expensive and less competitive in the global market.

On a more positive note, the survey found a significant drop in input prices, which fell at one of the steepest rates seen in the past 16 years. This is due to lower oil and commodity prices, as well as the strong pound making imports cheaper. The news has had an immediate impact on the currency markets, with the pound slipping against the dollar and euro as investors bet that the weaker manufacturing figures will push back the timing of any interest rate rise by the Bank of England.

Tragedy at Leicester Royal Infirmary: Two Medical Professionals Found Guilty of Manslaughter by Gross Negligence

A devastating case of medical negligence has come to a close, with two medical professionals being found guilty of manslaughter by gross negligence in the death of six-year-old Jack Adcock. Doctor Hadiza Bawa-Garba, 39, and nurse Isabel Amaro, 47, were both given a two-year suspended sentence for their roles in the tragic events that unfolded at Leicester Royal Infirmary in February 2011.

Jack, who had Down's syndrome, was admitted to the hospital with vomiting and diarrhoea, but his condition rapidly deteriorated, and he died approximately 11 hours later due to cardiac arrest caused by sepsis. The court heard that both Bawa-Garba and Amaro failed to realize the severity of Jack's illness, with Bawa-Garba stopping CPR after incorrectly assuming that Jack had a do-not-resuscitate order in place. Amaro, on the other hand, was criticized for her inadequate monitoring of Jack's treatment and her failure to alert colleagues to his deteriorating condition.

In his sentencing, Mr. Justice Nichol emphasized that the pair's medical careers "will come to an end" and stated that Jack's life was "cut short prematurely" due to their negligence. The judge acknowledged that neither Bawa-Garba nor Amaro had acted out of laziness or selfishness, but rather had failed to prioritize Jack's care amidst their other responsibilities. Bawa-Garba's sentence was influenced by her role as the sole carer for her five-year-old son, who has autism and behavioral problems, while Amaro's sentence took into account her psychiatric problems, which would be exacerbated by imprisonment.

The case has had a profound impact on Jack's family, with his mother, Nicky, expressing her anger and grief in a powerful impact statement. "Jack was neglected from the moment he entered the Leicester Royal Infirmary Children's Assessment Unit," she said. "I will never forgive myself for taking him there. I could have cared and looked after him better than they ever did." Jack's father, Vic, also spoke out, saying, "I wish I could forgive them, but at the moment, I don't know if I ever can. To hear their excuses has been so hard to bear. I had to watch my little man laid to rest."

In their defense, Bawa-Garba cited her exhausting 12-hour shift with no break and the miscommunication that occurred in the ward, while Amaro acknowledged that she had breached her duty of care but denied that her actions significantly contributed to Jack's death. Theresa Taylor, another nurse involved in Jack's care, was cleared of the same charge.

The outcome of this case serves as a stark reminder of the importance of prioritizing patient care and the devastating consequences that can result from medical negligence. As the medical community reflects on this tragedy, it is essential that lessons are learned, and measures are taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future. For Jack's family, the sentence brings a measure of closure, but the pain of their loss will undoubtedly endure.

A 55-year-old man has been cleared of causing serious injury by dangerous driving after a collision with a lollipop lady in Kempston, near Bedford. Brian Wright was acquitted by a jury at Luton Crown Court, who accepted that he was blinded by the sun at the time of the incident. The collision occurred on December 19 last year, when Wright's VW Golf failed to stop at a pedestrian crossing outside Bedford Road Lower School.

Sylvia Blackburn, 72, was on crossing patrol duty when the incident happened. She suffered serious head injuries, including a blow to the head that caused her to hit the pillar of the windscreen of Wright's car. Blackburn is still undergoing treatment at a care facility in Northampton, after initially being treated at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge. Her family has described her injuries as life-changing.

The court heard that traffic coming from the opposite direction had stopped at the red light, and Blackburn was wearing a high-visibility coat at the time of the incident. Wright claimed he could not remember whether the traffic lights were green or red, but said he was "totally blinded by the sun" and only heard a bump. He expressed remorse for the incident, stating that he had thought of nothing else but Blackburn and her family since the collision. Despite his acquittal, Wright acknowledged that he had "turned their world upside down."

A South Korean man, identified by his surname Lee, has been arrested for allegedly posting a threat against the US Ambassador to South Korea, Mark Lippert, on the White House website. According to Yonhap, Lee was taken into custody on July 14 at the request of US authorities. A search of his laptop revealed draft copies of the threatening letter, as well as a screenshot of the post on the White House website.

Ambassador Lippert has been the target of violence before, having been injured in a knife attack in Seoul last year. The attacker, Kim Ki-jong, is currently on trial for the incident. Lee denies any wrongdoing, but police believe he was acting alone. The US embassy has stated that the threat has not affected Ambassador Lippert's activities, and has praised the quick action of Korean authorities in identifying a suspect. The US is cooperating with South Korea on the investigation, with law enforcement agencies working together to gather more information. The details of the threatening letter have not been made public.

Scotland's Iconic Red Phone Boxes Get a New Lease on Life

In 2003, Scotland was home to nearly 7,000 phone boxes, a ubiquitous sight on streets and in towns across the country. However, with the rise of mobile phones, the number of call boxes has been steadily declining. Today, there are fewer than 5,000 phone boxes in Scotland, with just over 1,000 of them being the iconic red phone boxes that were once a staple of British streets. As the demand for payphones continues to decrease, some communities are finding new and creative ways to repurpose these nostalgic structures.

In the village of Comrie, a old phone box has been transformed into a life-saving device. The community has converted the phone box into a community access defibrillator site, complete with a defibrillator that can be used in emergency situations. The project was funded by locals in memory of Irene McCartney, who died in 2012. Her widower, Gordon, hopes that the defibrillator will make a real difference to someone in the future. According to Alan Moffat, the manager of the first response team in Comrie, the defibrillator is a vital piece of equipment that can greatly increase a person's chances of recovering from a cardiac arrest.

In Portobello, another phone box has been given a new lease on life as an art exhibition space. The Porty Light Box, as it is known, is the brainchild of Steven Wheatley, who wanted to retain the phone box as a feature of the street scene. The small space is now home to a vibrant and constantly changing array of artwork, showcasing the talents of local artists.

While these examples demonstrate the creativity and resourcefulness of Scottish communities, the question remains as to whether phone boxes will eventually disappear altogether. According to Brendan Dick, director of BT Scotland, the demand for payphones is indeed decreasing, but there is still a future for them in some areas. "In some urban parts, some of them are used very extensively, so there is a future for payphones in the broader sense," he said.

BT currently operates 4,864 kiosks in Scotland, down from 6,962 in 2003. The company has also seen a significant decrease in the number of paid calls made from phone boxes, with 1,723 payphones, including 684 red boxes, receiving no paid calls in the last 12 months.

In Alyth, Perthshire, another phone box is set to be transformed into a unique community resource. The Story Box, as it is known, will be a "time machine" that allows users to hear stories and histories from the town, both past and present. The project, which is being coordinated by Marian Bruce, will also involve young people in thinking about the future of Alyth and what the town will be like when they are grown up.

As Scotland's phone boxes continue to decline in number, it is heartening to see communities finding new and innovative ways to breathe new life into these iconic structures. Whether as a life-saving device, an art exhibition space, or a community resource, the humble phone box is proving that it still has a vital role to play in Scottish life.

Israel's President Reuven Rivlin has called for urgent action to address the grievances of the country's Ethiopian minority, following violent clashes between police and protesters in Tel Aviv on Sunday night. The unrest was sparked by the emergence of a video showing an Ethiopian Israeli soldier, Damas Pakedeh, being beaten by two police officers in a suburb of Tel Aviv.

The video, which was widely shared on social media, has fueled tensions and sparked widespread outrage, with many in the Ethiopian community feeling that it is just the latest example of systemic racism and discrimination. On Sunday, thousands of protesters took to the streets, blocking a busy road and marching through the city, before the demonstration turned violent as night fell.

Police fired tear gas and stun grenades as protesters threw stones, bottles, and chairs, and tried to enter the municipality building. At least 46 police officers and seven protesters were injured, and dozens of protesters were arrested. President Rivlin condemned the violence, blaming a "handful of violent trouble-makers" for the unrest, but acknowledged that the protests had exposed "the pain of a community crying out over a sense of discrimination, racism, and of being unanswered."

The Israeli government has been quick to respond to the crisis, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meeting with Damas Pakedeh, the soldier who was beaten by police. Netanyahu praised Pakedeh and expressed his shock at the video, saying that it was "unacceptable" and that those responsible would be held accountable. One of the police officers involved has already been fired, and the other has been suspended, pending an investigation.

The protests have highlighted the long-standing grievances of the Ethiopian community in Israel, who have struggled to integrate into Israeli society despite being airlifted to the country in secret operations in the 1980s and 1990s. Many have faced discrimination in jobs and education, and have lower incomes and limited opportunities compared to the general population. According to The Ethiopian National Project, a non-governmental organization that assists Ethiopian Jews in Israel, Ethiopian Jews are much more likely to face limited educational opportunities and to end up in prison.

The Israeli government has acknowledged that more needs to be done to address these issues, and has pledged to take action to address the community's grievances. President Rivlin has called for a national conversation about racism and discrimination, and has urged Israelis to "look directly at this open wound" and to work towards a more inclusive and equal society.

The crisis has also highlighted the complex and often fraught history of the Ethiopian community in Israel. The airlifts that brought tens of thousands of Ethiopian Jews to Israel were seen as a triumphant moment for Zionism, but the community has struggled to adjust to life in Israel. Many have felt that their treatment has not matched the generosity and imagination of the impulse that brought them to the country.

As the investigation into the beating of Damas Pakedeh continues, and the government works to address the grievances of the Ethiopian community, it is clear that this is a critical moment for Israel. The country must confront its own racism and discrimination, and work towards a more inclusive and equal society for all its citizens. The Ethiopian community has been crying out for justice and equality for too long, and it is time for Israel to listen.

Momentum, the Labour-supporting group formed from Jeremy Corbyn's 2015 leadership campaign, has launched a new initiative to provide childcare services and engage children in politics. The program, called Momentum Kids, aims to facilitate "political engagement" for single parents and offer "fun, engaging and child-friendly" activities for youngsters. This move is part of the group's efforts to create a "mass movement for real transformative change" and secure general election success for Labour.

Momentum Kids will provide a creche at the group's upcoming four-day festival, The World Transformed, in Liverpool, where Labour is holding its annual conference. The event will feature storytelling and workshops on campaigning, specifically designed for young people. Organisers hope to expand the program across Momentum's 150 local branches, creating a space for children to question, learn, and express themselves.

The initiative also seeks to address the issue of women being "shut out of many political spaces" due to their disproportionate caring responsibilities. Jeremy Corbyn has previously spoken out against companies that discriminate against women by promoting after-work drinking, highlighting the need for more family-friendly policies.

Children's author Alan Gibbons has expressed his support for the program, emphasizing the importance of creative activities in a child's development. "As young people grow, they need stories, poems, songs, drama and play to develop as complete human beings," he said.

The launch of Momentum Kids comes as the Labour party prepares for its leadership election on Saturday, with Corbyn facing a challenge from Owen Smith. Despite the controversy surrounding his leadership, Corbyn remains committed to his vision for Labour, and Momentum Kids is just one example of the group's efforts to engage new audiences and build a more inclusive movement. With its focus on childcare and youth engagement, Momentum Kids has the potential to make a positive impact on the lives of families and young people across the country.

Chris Gayle Set to Return to Somerset Despite Recent Controversy

West Indian cricket star Chris Gayle is set to return to Somerset for a six-game stint in the T20 Blast, despite recent controversy surrounding his behavior. Earlier this month, Gayle was fined £4,900 after asking a TV reporter for a date in a live interview while playing for Melbourne Renegades in Australia's Big Bash League. The incident sparked a backlash, with many criticizing Gayle's actions as unprofessional and disrespectful.

However, Gayle has apologized for his actions, although he believes the reaction was "out of proportion." The 36-year-old is now looking forward to putting the controversy behind him and focusing on his cricket. He will join Somerset on June 1 and will play his first game against Sussex. His six-game stint will come to an end on June 19 against Hampshire.

Gayle has a strong affinity for Somerset, having played for the club in 2015. During his previous stint, he scored 328 runs in just three appearances, making a significant impact on the team. The left-hander's impressive form included a 12-ball half-century, which equalled the record for the fastest fifty in Twenty20 cricket.

Somerset's director of cricket, Matt Maynard, has described Gayle as "box office," suggesting that his presence was a major factor in the club selling out their seven T20 Blast games last year. Maynard has also backed Gayle despite recent criticism from the club's newly-appointed County Championship skipper, Chris Rogers.

Rogers, who played alongside Gayle in the Big Bash League three years ago, has made it clear that he is not a fan of the West Indian's attitude and behavior. However, Maynard believes that Gayle got on well with everyone during his time with Somerset last summer and expects him to make a positive impact once again.

Gayle's return to Somerset has been welcomed by the club's chief executive, Guy Lavender, who has hinted that the club may be able to bring him back to Taunton if they qualify from the group stage. With Gayle's impressive form and experience, Somerset will be hoping that he can help the club make it through to the later stages of the competition.

Despite the controversy surrounding his recent behavior, Gayle remains a fan favorite, and his return to Somerset is likely to generate significant excitement among supporters. With his explosive batting style and charismatic personality, Gayle is sure to be a major draw for the club, and his presence will undoubtedly add to the excitement of the T20 Blast.

Gayle's schedule with Somerset includes matches against Sussex, Essex, Surrey, Glamorgan, Gloucestershire, and Hampshire. With his first game just around the corner, fans will be eagerly awaiting his return to the pitch, hoping that he can recapture the form that made him such a success during his previous stint with the club. As one of the most talented and entertaining cricketers in the world, Chris Gayle is sure to make a significant impact on the T20 Blast, and his return to Somerset is a major coup for the club.

**Outrage in China as CCTV Footage Shows Woman Being Dragged Across Hotel Corridor**

A disturbing video has sparked widespread outrage in China, showing a woman being grabbed and dragged across a hotel corridor in full view of bystanders. The incident, which occurred at the Yitel Hotel, has prompted millions of posts on social media, with the hashtag "Girl attacked at Yitei hotel" being used over two million times and viewed by two billion users.

According to the victim, who uploaded the video on Sina Weibo under the username "Wanwan", the incident began when a man approached her in the hotel corridor and asked which room she was in. When she refused to answer, the man started to drag her away, clutching her neck and face, making it difficult for her to breathe. The woman attempted to run downstairs, but the man grabbed her by the hair and dragged her towards the stairway.

The CCTV footage shows the staff member and other hotel guests watching the scuffle, but most did not intervene, assuming it was a couple's quarrel. It was only when a bystander appeared to help the woman leave the scene that the situation was brought under control.

The incident has raised concerns about the lack of intervention from bystanders in China, where there have been several high-profile cases in recent years of people refusing to help those in need. In one notable case in 2011, a two-year-old girl was knocked over in a hit-and-run accident, and 18 people passed by before someone came to her rescue. She later died from her injuries.

The Yitel Hotel's parent company, Homeinns, has issued an apology to the victim and the public, stating that the incident showed "insufficient security management and customer service". Beijing police are investigating the incident, and the hotel has promised to take steps to improve its security measures.

The video has sparked a heated debate on social media, with many expressing their anger at the hotel and calling for greater awareness about the importance of intervening in such situations. Some have circulated a video campaign called "#WhoWillYouHelp", produced by the Ontario government last year to combat sexual harassment. Others have shared tips on self-defence for women, while some have urged people to stop turning a blind eye to such incidents.

Weibo user Winston commented, "If people stop being indifferent and calling it a 'domestic incident' when husbands/boyfriends beat, drag or abuse their wives/girlfriends in public, wouldn't there be fewer of these dangerous situations?" The incident has highlighted the need for greater awareness and education about the importance of intervening in situations where someone is in need of help.

The reluctance of bystanders to intervene in China is often attributed to the fear of being blamed or sued by the injured person. However, this incident has sparked a renewed call for people to take action and help those in need, rather than standing by and doing nothing. As the investigation into the incident continues, it is hoped that it will lead to greater awareness and a change in attitude towards intervening in such situations.

A search operation for three missing climbers on New Zealand's Mt Cook has been suspended after aerial searches yielded no results. The climbers, Sydney doctor Michael Bishop, 53, German national Yohann Viellehner, 58, and his son Raphael, 27, were last seen on Monday as they attempted to reach the summit. The men, who were roped together, failed to return to their hut, prompting a search effort.

Despite the suspension of the search, police say they will re-evaluate their plans if new information or sightings come to light. The families of the missing men, who are from Australia and Germany, are understandably upset but aware of the reasons behind the decision. Mt Cook, also known as Aoraki, is a challenging climb that has claimed over 230 lives since it was first conquered in 1894. The search team is disappointed with the outcome, and their thoughts are with the families of the missing climbers.

Birmingham's 21-year-old midfielder, Arthur, will leave the club at season's end. He made his debut in 2013 but hasn't featured since 2015. Arthur had a loan stint with Cheltenham, making seven appearances. Republic of Ireland's Noe Baba and goalkeeper Josh Tibbetts will also depart St Andrew's.

Outrage has erupted in Tunisia after a video emerged of a DJ playing a dance version of the Muslim call to prayer at a festival in the north-eastern town of Nabeul. The incident occurred on Friday at the Orbit Festival, where two European DJs were performing near the popular seaside resort of Hammamet. The footage, shared on social media on Sunday, sparked widespread outrage and condemnation.

As a result, the governor of Nabeul, Mnaouar Ouertani, has announced that the nightclub where the incident took place will "remain closed" until further notice. An investigation has been launched, and the club's manager has been detained for "violation against good morals and public outrage against modesty." Governor Ouertani stated that the authorities "will not allow attacks against religious feelings and the sacred."

The organisers of the Orbit Festival have since apologised on Facebook, although they claim not to accept responsibility for the playing of the offensive music. The DJ responsible, Dax J, has also offered his "sincere apologies" for any offense caused, stating that it was never his intention to upset or cause offense to anybody. The incident has highlighted the importance of cultural sensitivity and respect for religious traditions. The investigation is ongoing, and it remains to be seen what further action will be taken.

A fatal accident inquiry into the death of 12-year-old Keane Wallis-Bennett has begun, nearly nine years after she was killed when a modesty wall in her school's PE changing room collapsed on top of her. The incident occurred on April 1, 2014, at Liberton High School in Edinburgh, and a police investigation at the time found that no one would face criminal charges.

The inquiry, which is expected to last for two weeks, aims to establish the full circumstances surrounding Keane's death. Sheriff Principal Mhairi Stephen, who is leading the inquiry, said that the hearing comes at a poignant time, as many of Keane's former classmates have recently been taking exams and are preparing to start their lives.

The inquiry heard that pupils had been leaning on the wall while changing their shoes when it suddenly collapsed, trapping Keane underneath. Witnesses described the efforts of fellow pupils to lift the wall, but it was too heavy. Det Ch Insp Keith Hardie, who investigated the incident, told the inquiry that he still cannot say why the wall fell on that particular day.

The court also heard statements from Keane's classmates, who described the moments leading up to the tragedy. One girl said that PE teacher Nicole Christie must have heard the bang as the wall fell and told the pupils to leave the area. Christie then went over to Keane and reassured her that an ambulance was on the way.

Other witnesses described how pupils would often push or shove against the wall, and one girl said that she had seen a gap at the bottom of the wall on previous occasions. Another pupil said that she had seen a girl try to climb up the wall, but had stopped when she saw it move.

The inquiry will focus on why the wall collapsed, why it collapsed when it did, and the property maintenance regime at the school. Sheriff Principal Stephen said that the whole community was shocked by Keane's death, and that school should be a safe place for all pupils. The inquiry will continue to hear evidence over the coming days, in an effort to provide answers for Keane's family and to prevent such a tragedy from happening again in the future.

New Study Reveals Bats as Primary Carriers of Potential Viral Threats to Humans

A groundbreaking study conducted by the EcoHealth Alliance in New York has shed light on the mammals that pose the greatest risk of transmitting viruses to humans. The research, published in the journal Nature, analyzed 586 viruses known to infect 754 species of mammals, with a focus on identifying potential zoonotic infections that could make the jump from animals to people. The findings suggest that bats are the primary carriers of viral threats, with an estimated 17 zoonotic infections per species.

The study's lead researcher, Dr. Kevin Olival, explained that the team used existing data to fill gaps in knowledge and estimate which species were likely to harbor viruses with the potential to infect humans. The results revealed that bats, primates, and rodents are among the top carriers of zoonotic infections, with bats posing the greatest threat. The researchers mapped the ranges of these species and the infections they carry, identifying global hotspots where the risk of viral transmission is highest.

The study's findings have significant implications for global health, as some of the most devastating outbreaks in recent history, including Ebola and HIV, are believed to have originated from animals. Dr. Olival emphasized that the key to preventing future pandemics lies in minimizing human contact with wildlife, including through hunting and habitat destruction. "Our take-home message is that these diseases are emerging because of the human impact on the environment," he said.

While the study's predictions are not intended to drive specific policy decisions, they can be used to prioritize research and viral surveillance efforts. James Lloyd-Smith, a researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles, noted that "although most pandemics are zoonoses, most zoonoses do not cause pandemics." The EcoHealth Alliance's next project will focus on birds, which are another significant source of zoonotic infections, including avian flu.

The study's findings serve as a reminder of the importance of proactive measures to prevent the spread of viral diseases. By understanding the risks posed by different species and geographic regions, researchers and policymakers can work together to develop strategies for mitigating the threat of zoonotic infections and protecting global health. As Dr. Olival emphasized, "it's not the bat's fault" – rather, it is human activity that drives the emergence of these diseases. By taking a proactive and informed approach, we can reduce the risk of future pandemics and promote a healthier, more sustainable relationship between humans and the environment.

**Gorse Fires Continue to Ravage Northern Ireland, Fire Service Appeals for Public's Help**

A staggering 498 gorse fires have been reported across Northern Ireland since the start of May, with the latest incident forcing the closure of the Cuilcagh Mountain trail in County Fermanagh. The Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service (NIFRS) has condemned the deliberate starting of these fires, warning that they put not only firefighters but also the public and property at risk.

Group Commander Brian Stanfield of the NIFRS described the phenomenon as "complete madness" and "reckless anti-social behaviour". He appealed to the public to come forward with any information about individuals who may be starting these fires, urging them to report such incidents to the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI). "We're appealing to the public, if you do know people who are fire setting, let the PSNI know so we can put them through the courts because this is absolutely ridiculous," he said.

Fire crews have been working tirelessly since Sunday to bring a massive gorse fire near Fivemiletown, County Tyrone, under control. The fire, which covers an extensive area at Mullaghfad forest on the Tyrone and Fermanagh border, has required the deployment of eight fire appliances and specialist equipment, including tanker lorries bringing water to the site. Dozens of personnel are involved in the effort, which has been ongoing for two days.

The fire is believed to have started in multiple locations, and the NIFRS is working with the forestry service and the Southern fire service to bring it under control. The area is part of a large forest that includes Crocknagrally, Jenkin, and Fardross forests, and is located within a Special Protection Area for hen harriers and the Slieve Beagh Area of special scientific interest.

The NIFRS has warned that gorse fires are "resource intensive" and that crews are prepared to deal with any further incidents this week. However, with the countryside being "like a tinder box", the service is concerned that its resources will be stretched to the limit if the fires continue at the current rate. Mr Stanfield cautioned that people are unaware of the personal risks they take when starting these fires, saying that "when the ground is that dry and there's a change in wind direction, the fire will move faster than the person can run, and it's only a matter of time until someone is seriously injured or killed at one of these fires".

The public is urged to remain vigilant and to report any suspicious activity to the authorities. The NIFRS is moving its engines around the country to keep the public safe and is appealing for the public's help in preventing these devastating fires. As the situation continues to unfold, one thing is clear: the reckless starting of gorse fires must be stopped to prevent further damage to the environment and to protect the lives of those who live and work in the affected areas.

Last night's televised debate on The Good Friday Agreement Generation sparked a frenzy of discussion on social media, with the hashtag #GFAGen trending across the UK. The debate, which featured representatives from the DUP, Sinn Féin, Ulster Unionists, SDLP, and Alliance, among others, was watched by thousands and generated a significant amount of buzz on Twitter.

The young audience members who posed questions to the panel were widely praised on social media for their thought-provoking queries and confident demeanor. In contrast, some of the politicians on the panel received criticism from viewers, who were unimpressed with their responses. Veteran political commentator Eamonn Mallie was among those who expressed his admiration for the young questioners, while also expressing his disappointment with some of the politicians' answers.

The debate was attended by representatives from various parties, including Alastair Ross of the DUP, Chris Hazzard of Sinn Féin, and Naomi Long of the Alliance. Other parties, such as the TUV, Green Party, and UKIP, were also represented. As the election approaches on May 5, it remains to be seen whether the debate has swayed the opinions of first-time voters. The next major televised election debate will take place on May 3, when the BBC will host a leaders debate.

A teenager was attacked on Dunkeld Road near the Stagecoach building on Wednesday at 16:40. Two men, aged 20-25 and slim, were involved. One was 5ft 11in with brown hair, wearing a dark red tracksuit and blue jeans. The other was 5ft 9in with dark brown hair and dark clothes.

Tragedy Strikes at Disney: Body of Two-Year-Old Boy Found

A devastating discovery was made in the search for Lane Graves, a two-year-old boy from Nebraska who was dragged into the water by an alligator at Disney's Seven Seas Lagoon. Divers found a body, believed to be Lane's, intact in the water on Wednesday. Orange County Sheriff Jerry Demings confirmed that the body has not been formally identified, but authorities are confident it is the missing boy.

The incident occurred on Tuesday evening when Lane was wading in shallow water near the shore of the lagoon, despite a "no swimming" sign in the area. His father attempted to retrieve him, sustaining minor lacerations to his arm. A massive search effort ensued, with 50 people using sonar equipment to scour the lakes and ponds linked to the lagoon. Five alligators were seized and killed in the hopes of finding Lane's remains.

The absence of warning signs about alligators in the area has raised questions, with a Disney spokesperson stating that the situation would be reviewed. The tragic incident has left the community in shock, and an investigation is underway to determine the circumstances surrounding Lane's death. The Graves family, from Elkhorn, Nebraska, was on vacation with their three children when the incident occurred.

Ravi Shastri, 55, has been named India's new cricket coach, replacing Anil Kumble. Shastri brings significant experience as a player and coach. Zaheer Khan and Rahul Dravid will support as bowling and overseas batting consultants, respectively. The change comes after Kumble's resignation due to an "untenable" partnership with captain Virat Kohli. Shastri previously served as India's team director before Kumble's appointment.

Princess Anne Reveals Wild Boar Attack on Her Farm

A recent farming conference was shocked to hear that Princess Anne's farm had been visited by a wild boar, resulting in the death of one of her prized Gloucestershire Old Spot boars. The Princess Royal, who is patron of the Gloucestershire Old Spots Pig Breeders' Club, revealed the incident to delegates, stating that the wild boar had killed her boar after being introduced to her two sows in season.

The princess, who lives at Gatcombe Park in Gloucestershire, has kept pigs for many years and is known for her passion for farming and conservation. She expressed her concerns about the origins of the wild boar and the potential for further incidents, saying "So far, we haven't found the origins of this particular invader and I'm hoping I'm not going to see him again for a bit."

The incident has highlighted the growing issue of wild boar sightings in the area, with a large population of the animals living in the nearby Forest of Dean, just 17 miles away from Gatcombe Park. In a separate incident, a wild boar wandered onto the M4 in Wiltshire, causing a fatal crash that killed 47-year-old Raymond Green.

The two incidents have prompted North Wiltshire MP James Gray to write to Natural England, expressing his concerns about the wild boar population and seeking advice on how to address the issue. Gray stated that his constituents are increasingly worried about the growing number of wild boar sightings, with recent spottings in Box and Corsham.

The Gloucestershire Old Spot breed, which Princess Anne is so passionate about, is listed as a minority breed on the Rare Breeds Survival Trust watchlist, with only between 500 and 1,000 breeding females believed to be in the country. The princess's loss is not only a personal one but also a blow to the conservation efforts of this rare breed. As the issue of wild boar sightings continues to grow, it remains to be seen how authorities will address the problem and prevent further incidents.

Teachers in Belfast and Newtownabbey are set to go on strike on Wednesday, as part of a long-running dispute over pay. The NASUWT union, one of the largest teaching unions in Northern Ireland, has announced that its members in the two areas will be taking industrial action, with other areas to follow in the coming months.

The strike is the first to be called by the NASUWT since 2011, and comes after all teaching unions in Northern Ireland rejected an offer that would have seen their pay frozen last year and a rise of 1% for 2016-17. While some schools have written to parents to inform them which classes will go ahead as normal on the day, the NASUWT has warned that this could potentially breach the Data Protection Act.

The union claims that by revealing which classes will be affected, some schools may be inadvertently disclosing the identity of NASUWT members, which could be seen as intimidation. As a result, some principals have been warned that they could face legal action if they are found to be in breach of the law. In a letter to one principal, the NASUWT stated that there may be grounds for a complaint to the Information Commissioner and for seeking compensation for distress through the courts.

However, the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) has criticized the warnings, describing them as "shocking". Paul McClenaghan, the president of the NAHT in Northern Ireland, said that school leaders were being "threatened" for simply carrying out their duties and informing parents about the impact of the strike. He argued that school leaders have always put the needs of children first and supported their colleagues, often at a high personal cost.

Justin McCamphill from the NASUWT defended the union's position, saying that it had a duty to ensure that the law was being upheld. He stated that it would be wrong for the union not to inform principals of potential breaches of the law, and that the warnings were simply a matter of informing them of their legal obligations. The strike is set to go ahead on Wednesday, with further action planned for January and February 2017. Other teaching unions are currently engaged in industrial action short of a strike, and it remains to be seen how the dispute will be resolved.

Bangladesh Vows to Stop Deadly Attacks as Opposition Accuses Government of Targeting Political Opponents

Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to do whatever it takes to stop the wave of deadly attacks that have plagued the country in recent years. Her comments came a day after police launched a massive crackdown on Islamist militants, arresting over 3,000 people. However, the opposition has accused the government of using the operation to target political opponents, sparking concerns about the true motives behind the campaign.

Speaking at a meeting of her ruling Awami League party on Saturday, Ms. Hasina said, "It may take time, but God willing, we will be able to bring [the perpetrators] under control. Where will the criminals hide? Each and every killer will be brought to book." The police campaign, which began on Friday, is set to last for a week and has been focused on arresting Islamist militants. However, critics argue that many ordinary criminals have been caught up in the sweep, and that the government is using the operation to silence opposition voices.

Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, the leader of the opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party, claimed that "hundreds of opposition activists have been arrested in the police drive." He told the AFP news agency, "In the name of the crackdown against Islamist militants, many ordinary and innocent people are being detained." The government has denied targeting opposition activists, with Nadeem Qadir, a government spokesman at the Bangladesh High Commission in London, telling the BBC, "There's no targeted political elements in this case, it's an operation...to stop this targeted killing, it's as simple as that."

The crackdown comes amid a surge in deadly attacks in Bangladesh, which have claimed the lives of over 40 people, including secular bloggers, academics, gay rights activists, and members of religious minorities. The latest victim was a Hindu monastery worker who was hacked to death in Pabna district on Friday. In the past week alone, a Hindu priest, a Christian grocer, and the wife of an anti-terror police officer were all killed in attacks by suspected Islamist militants.

Analysts believe that the killing of a police officer's wife last Sunday may have triggered the crackdown. The attacks have been claimed by so-called Islamic State (IS) or al-Qaeda-linked groups, but the government has disputed these claims, with some members blaming opposition parties and local Islamist groups. Bangladesh's home minister has even suggested an Israeli link to the killings, describing an "international conspiracy" against Bangladesh. However, both the opposition and the Israeli government have denied any involvement, with Israel describing the accusations as "utter drivel."

As the government struggles to contain the violence, it faces accusations of not doing enough to protect minorities in the Sunni-dominated nation. The killings have sparked widespread concern, both at home and abroad, and have raised questions about the rise of extremism in Bangladesh. The country has a long history of secularism, but in recent years, there has been a growing trend towards sectarianism and terrorism.

Until the killings stop, the government will face mounting pressure to take decisive action to protect its citizens and restore stability to the country. With the police campaign underway, it remains to be seen whether the government's efforts will be enough to bring the perpetrators to justice and put an end to the bloodshed. One thing is certain, however: the people of Bangladesh deserve peace and security, and it is the government's responsibility to ensure that they receive it.

Belgian Minister Refuses to Back Down on Asylum Case, Despite Fines and Criticism

A high-profile asylum case in Belgium has sparked a heated debate over the country's immigration policies, with the Minister for Asylum and Migration, Theo Francken, refusing to back down despite facing fines and criticism. The case involves a Syrian family of four, including two children aged five and eight, who have been granted visas by a Belgian tribunal but are being denied entry by Minister Francken.

The family, who live in the war-torn city of Aleppo, have been offered food and lodging by friends in Namur, but Minister Francken argues that their links to Belgium are weak and that granting them asylum would open the door to "asylum chaos". The minister has refused to pay fines of €4,000 per day, which have now surpassed €30,000, and has even joked about seeking political asylum in the office of his colleague, Interior Minister Jan Jambon.

In a dramatic turn of events, Minister Francken posted a picture of an empty party office on Facebook, claiming that bailiffs had seized the furniture. However, it later emerged that no furniture had been taken, although the threat still exists. The ministry is appealing against both the fine and the ruling, with a spokeswoman stating that they will continue to work despite the challenges.

The Syrian family's lawyer, Mieke Van den Broeck, has accused Minister Francken of trampling on Belgium's separation of judicial and government powers, saying that he is "playing with our clients' lives and with Belgian tax money". The lawyer argues that the family's situation is exceptional and urgent, given the ongoing conflict in Aleppo and the fact that their home has been destroyed.

Minister Francken, a member of the centre-right New Flemish Alliance, has countered that the family should have applied for refuge in Lebanon, where the father initially applied for asylum at the Belgian consulate. He argues that courts should not set asylum policy and that Belgium has already welcomed refugees, but cannot grant a home to every Syrian who applies.

The case has sparked a wider debate over Belgium's asylum policies, with many criticizing Minister Francken's stance as inhumane and overly rigid. The Belgian family who have offered to support the Syrian family have promised to pay for all their costs, but Minister Francken remains unmoved, insisting that he is elected to serve the public interest and will continue to do so. As the case continues to unfold, it remains to be seen whether Minister Francken will ultimately be forced to back down and grant the family asylum, or whether he will continue to resist the pressure and criticism.

Judd Trump has claimed his seventh ranking title after a thrilling 10-8 victory over Marco Fu in the Llandudno final. The 27-year-old from Bristol staged an impressive comeback, making three centuries in four frames to turn the match around. Trump had found himself 5-2 down early on, but he responded with consecutive century breaks of 136 and 115 to close the gap.

Trump's momentum continued into the final session, with further breaks of 110 and 76 putting him within reach of victory. Although Fu fought back to win the next two frames, Trump held his nerve to secure the title with a fourth century break of 102. Fu reduced the deficit to 9-8 with a 58, but Trump was able to hold on and atone for three defeats in finals this season.

The victory sees Trump move up to second in the rankings, adding to his European Masters title won in October. Fu, who won the Scottish Open in December, had started strongly with runs of 67, 48, 39, and 83 to establish his early lead. However, Trump's superior form in the end proved too much for the world number nine, as he claimed a hard-fought victory. The win marks a significant milestone for Trump, who has now won seven ranking titles in his career.

Eagles of Death Metal Dropped from Festivals After Singer Reiterates Bataclan Attack Conspiracy Theories

The rock band Eagles of Death Metal has been dropped from two French music festivals after lead singer Jesse Hughes repeated conspiracy theories surrounding the 2015 Bataclan attack. Ninety people were killed when gunmen opened fire during the band's set at the venue in November 2015. Hughes had previously suggested that some security guards may have known about the attack in advance, sparking outrage and condemnation from the Bataclan and others.

Despite apologizing for his earlier remarks, Hughes reiterated his claims in a recent interview with Taki's Magazine, stating that the terrorists must have had inside help to carry out the attack. "There's no denying the terrorists were already inside, and they had to get in somehow," he said. "During the shooting I went outside and the backstage door was propped open. How did that happen?" These comments have been widely criticized, with many accusing Hughes of spreading baseless and hurtful conspiracy theories.

The Bataclan venue has condemned Hughes' comments as "grave and defamatory," and has called for speculation about the tragedy to be kept to a minimum while a judicial investigation is underway. The venue has praised the professionalism and courage of the security agents who were on the ground during the attack, saying that hundreds of people were saved thanks to their intervention.

As a result of Hughes' comments, the band has been dropped from the line-up of the Rock En Seine and Cabaret Vert festivals. Organizers of the festivals said they are "in total disagreement with Jesse Hughes' recent allegations" and do not want to be associated with his conspiracy theories. Hughes has apologized for his earlier comments, saying they were "unfounded and baseless" and expressing his "humble beg[ging] for forgiveness" from those hurt or offended by his words.

However, it is unclear why Hughes has chosen to revisit these comments now, despite the harm and offense they have caused. The singer has said he is suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from the Bataclan tragedy, which also took the life of the band's merchandise manager Nick Alexander. An inquest into Alexander's death closed on Thursday, with the coroner ruling that he was unlawfully killed. The court heard that Alexander's former girlfriend tried to save him after he had been shot in the stomach and abdomen.

The decision to drop Eagles of Death Metal from the festivals is a clear indication that Hughes' conspiracy theories will not be tolerated. The Bataclan and others are still trying to come to terms with the trauma and loss caused by the attack, and Hughes' comments have only served to reopen old wounds. As the judicial investigation into the attack continues, it is essential that speculation and conspiracy theories are kept to a minimum, and that those affected by the tragedy are treated with respect and dignity.

Rangers Sign Midfielder Ryan Jack on Three-Year Deal

Rangers Football Club has announced the signing of midfielder Ryan Jack on a three-year deal under freedom of contract. The 25-year-old joins the team after leaving Aberdeen, where he spent seven years and became captain in 2015. Jack's signing is seen as a significant boost to Rangers' midfield, which has been weakened by the departure of loan players Jon Toral and Emerson Hyndman.

St Johnstone defender Richard Foster, a former teammate of Jack's at Aberdeen, has praised the midfielder's skills, describing him as "very much underrated." Foster, who has also played for Rangers, told BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound that Jack is a talented player who excels at tackling and winning the ball. He also believes that Jack has more quality on the ball than he was often given credit for during his time at Aberdeen.

Rangers, who finished third in the 2016-17 Scottish Premiership, have been looking to strengthen their squad ahead of the new season. The signing of Jack, combined with the earlier acquisition of Portuguese defender Bruno Alves, suggests that the team is building a strong foundation for the upcoming campaign. Foster believes that Jack will provide much-needed protection for Rangers' center-backs, who were often under pressure last season due to the team's high-pressing style of play. With his experience and skills, Ryan Jack is expected to make a significant contribution to Rangers' success in the seasons to come.

A debate on granting Welsh Labour more autonomy from the UK party has sparked division at the party's conference. Matthew van Rooyen, a delegate from Bridgend, expressed frustration at attempts to delay a vote on the proposals, saying "We have got Jeremy Corbyn as leader, whether we like it or not." The plans include a seat on Labour's national executive committee, but supporters of Mr Corbyn want the Welsh representative to be elected by party members, rather than nominated by Welsh Labour leader Carwyn Jones. The conference chairman intervened, rebuking delegates for booing a speaker and urging them to be respectful. Mike Payne from GMB Wales called for an end to "prevarication" and for the party to "get on with it." Delegates will vote on the changes later on Tuesday, amid ongoing divisions within the party. The outcome is expected to shape the future of Welsh Labour's relationship with the UK party.

A 49-year-old man from Belfast has been granted bail after being charged with possessing cocaine with intent to supply. Hugh Brady, of Molyneaux Street, was stopped by police on the Sydenham bypass on Wednesday night, where officers seized 3kg of drugs from his car.

According to the court, Brady had been driving around Bangor, County Down, for at least 90 minutes before giving up and heading back towards Belfast. During this time, he stopped at a garage to ask for directions and purchased a mobile phone from a Tesco store, but was unable to buy credit for it.

A detective opposing bail told the court that Brady had alleged he was approached by individuals who he "couldn't say no to" and was asked to deliver a package to another location. However, Brady failed to find the intended address and eventually gave up, leading to his arrest.

Brady's defence solicitor argued that he was at the "very bottom" of any operation to move the drugs and was simply following instructions. The lawyer said that Brady's inability to find the address and his decision to give up and drive back to Belfast demonstrated his ineptness and lack of involvement in the drugs gang.

The detective acknowledged that Brady's actions suggested he was not a major player in the drugs trade, but rather someone who had been entrusted with a consignment due to his trusted position. Despite this, the judge granted Brady bail, ordering him and his wife to lodge a £3,000 cash surety, which represents their life savings.

Brady is due to appear in court again on June 26. The case has raised questions about the involvement of ordinary citizens in the drugs trade and the extent to which they are coerced or intimidated into participating. Brady's apology and apparent remorse during interview suggest that he may have been a reluctant participant in the operation.

A mother has testified in court about the moment she discovered her son had traveled to Syria to join the so-called Islamic State. Sue Boyce told the Old Bailey that her son, Thomas Petty, had kept his plans a secret until after he had left their home in the summer of 2014. Tragically, Mr. Petty, 25, was killed in battle later that year.

Ms. Boyce recounted how her son had converted to Islam at the age of 15, but she had no idea he was considering traveling to Syria to fight. She described how, in July 2014, Mr. Petty flew to Athens and then to Cairo, initially maintaining contact with his family before suddenly going quiet. It wasn't until late August that he called to inform his family that he was on the border of Syria and intended to enter the country as an aid worker.

Ms. Boyce expressed her horror and concern, urging her son not to go through with his plans. However, Mr. Petty was resolute in his decision, sending an email to his family entitled "New Life" in which he explained his desire to live in a "proper Islamic state" where he could freely practice his faith. He wrote that he had been unhappy living in the UK since his conversion to Islam and felt compelled to join his "brothers and sisters" in Syria.

The email also revealed that Mr. Petty had been training to become a "soldier" and believed it was necessary to defend himself in a world that was "uniting to destroy" Muslims. He emphasized that no one had brainwashed or tricked him into making this decision, but rather it was a choice he had made of his own free will.

Ms. Boyce's testimony came during the trial of Lorna Moore and Ayman Shaukat, both from Walsall, who deny terror-related offenses. The court heard that Mr. Petty was one of a group of friends from Walsall who had left Britain in 2014 to join the Islamic State. Ms. Boyce eventually identified her son's body from video footage, which was shown to her by police 10 months after his death.

The trial has also heard that others had sought to follow in Mr. Petty's footsteps, with some receiving assistance from Mr. Shaukat, 27. Trainee maths teacher Lorna Moore, 33, denies failing to disclose information about acts of terrorism, while Mr. Shaukat is accused of helping two men, Sajid Aslam and Alex Nash, on their way to Syria. He denies two counts of preparing for terrorist acts and one charge of possession of a terrorist document.

The case highlights the complexities and challenges faced by families and authorities in preventing and responding to radicalization and terrorism. As the trial continues, it is likely to shed further light on the circumstances surrounding Mr. Petty's decision to join the Islamic State and the roles that others may have played in supporting or facilitating his actions.

US Faces Surge in Child Migrants, Seeks $1.4bn in Aid

The United States is bracing for a massive influx of unaccompanied child migrants, with estimates suggesting up to 60,000 children will cross the border illegally this year. The majority of these children are from Central America and Mexico, fleeing domestic abuse, violent gangs, and poverty in their home countries. Many hope to reunite with parents or relatives already living in the US.

In response to the crisis, the White House has requested an additional $1.4 billion from Congress to provide temporary housing and care for the children. Two military bases have been designated as temporary shelters. According to Cecilia Munoz, Director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, the number of children traveling alone has been increasing since 2009, with a notable rise in girls and children under 13.

The situation is dire, with many children unaware of the dangers they face on their journey, including sexual assaults, forced labor, and hunger. The US government predicts that the number of unaccompanied child migrants could soar to nearly 130,000 next year. This represents a significant increase from previous years, with 24,668 children apprehended by border agents in 2013, nearly double the number from the previous year. The White House is urging Congress to act swiftly to address the crisis and provide the necessary resources to support these vulnerable children.

A 78-year-old man from west Belfast has appeared in court charged with aiding and abetting the murder of Jean McConville, a mother-of-10 who was abducted and killed by the IRA in 1972. Ivor Bell, of Ramoan Gardens, was charged in connection with the high-profile case, which has been adjourned several times since he was first charged in March 2014.

Mrs McConville, 37, was taken from her flat in front of her children after being wrongly accused of being an informer. Her body was not recovered until 2003, when it was found on a beach in County Louth. The Public Prosecution Service had been given a final deadline to proceed with the case, and Bell's appearance at Belfast Magistrates Court was the last chance for the service to decide if the case would go ahead.

Bell is also charged with membership of the IRA. He is due to return to court in six weeks, when a date will be set for a preliminary inquiry to determine if the case will proceed to trial in the Crown Court. Despite a call from the defence to discontinue the case, the prosecution is moving forward, seeking justice for the McConville family over 40 years after her tragic death.

Tensions Escalate in South China Sea as US and China Trade Accusations

A recent incident in the South China Sea has sparked a war of words between the United States and China, with both nations accusing each other of engaging in reckless behavior. On May 17, a US maritime reconnaissance aircraft was carrying out a routine patrol in international airspace when it was intercepted by two Chinese aircraft. According to US officials, the Chinese planes engaged in "dangerous maneuvers," forcing the US pilot to descend approximately 200 feet to avoid a collision.

However, China has vehemently denied these allegations, with a foreign ministry spokesperson, Hong Lei, stating that the US plane had flown too close to Hainan Island and that the Chinese aircraft had followed and monitored it at a safe distance. Lei claimed that the actions of the Chinese pilots were "completely professional and safe." The US Defense Department has addressed the issue through military and diplomatic channels, acknowledging that China has made improvements in its actions over the past year, flying in a safe and professional manner.

The incident highlights the growing tensions in the South China Sea, a region rich in resources and claimed by several nations, including Taiwan, China, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, and Brunei. The US has accused China of militarizing the area, while China has criticized increased US naval patrols and exercises in Asia. The frictions between the two nations have sparked concern that the area is becoming a flashpoint with possible global consequences. As the situation continues to unfold, the US has reaffirmed its commitment to opposing restrictions on freedom of navigation and unlawful sovereignty claims by all sides.

India has successfully launched a record-breaking 20 satellites into space from its Sriharikota space centre off the east coast. The satellites belong to various countries including the United States, Canada, Germany, and Indonesia. This achievement marks a significant milestone for India's space program, solidifying its position as a major player in the multi-billion dollar space market.

The launch, which was closely monitored by Indian scientists and government ministers, saw a rocket carrying the 20 satellites blast off from the launch facility in Andhra Pradesh state. The payload included a range of devices, from a 700kg Indian cartographic satellite to smaller satellites weighing as little as 1.5kg. Notably, 13 of the satellites were from the US, including one made by a Google-owned company.

This launch surpasses the previous records held by the US space agency Nasa, which launched 29 satellites, and Russia, which holds the record for the most number of satellites launched in a single mission with 37 in 2014. According to the chairman of the Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro), Kiran Kumar, launching multiple satellites in a single mission reduces costs and showcases India's capabilities as a low-cost operator in the international commercial space market.

India's space program has recorded several achievements in recent years, including sending probes to the Moon and Mars. With this latest launch, India is poised to become a key player in the global space industry, offering affordable and efficient launch services to international customers. As Kumar aptly put it, "Each of these small objects that you are putting into space will carry out their own activity, which is independent of the other, and each of them will live a wonderful life for the finite period for which they have been designed."

Glencore Shares Plummet 30% as Analysts Warn of "Severe Problems"

In a shocking turn of events, mining giant Glencore's shares dove 30% on Monday, sparking concerns over the company's financial stability. The drastic decline came after a note from analysts at Investec warned that Glencore's equity value could be "eliminated" if the company fails to cut its debt and commodity prices do not recover.

According to Investec's Laura Lambie, Glencore faces "severe problems" due to its significant debt burden and the slump in commodity prices. "Miners grew hugely to meet the demand from China and they borrowed heavily to find it, and the cost of servicing that debt and the schedule of repayments are really putting companies such as Glencore under the spotlight," Lambie told the BBC. "The risk is if commodities don't recover, then companies like Glencore will be in trouble trying to repay its debt."

Glencore's debt pile, which stands at approximately £20 billion, has been a major concern for investors. Despite efforts by chief executive Ivan Glasenberg to reduce debt through share sales, asset disposals, and dividend cancellations, the company's shares have continued to plummet. In recent weeks, Glencore has announced plans to sell its grains business, hoping to generate up to $12 billion to alleviate its debt burden. However, Investec has questioned the valuation of the agriculture division, citing the volatility of the business.

The mining company's stock has fallen by a staggering 85% since its initial public offering in 2011, when shares were priced at £5.30. On Tuesday, Glencore's shares rallied, closing up nearly 17% at 80.24p, but the company still has a long way to go to recover its losses.

Nigel Wilson, chief executive of Legal and General, a significant shareholder in Glencore, warned that the company is facing a "quasi-Lehman moment," referencing the collapse of the US investment bank during the 2008 financial crisis. Wilson called on Glencore's management to provide clarity on the company's viability to stem further stock declines. "There's a lot of noise, and there's not enough signaling. That lack of information causes a huge amount of uncertainty at Glencore, which is having a massive contagion effect across the world," Wilson said.

In response to the concerns, a Glencore spokesperson assured that the company has no solvency issues. "Glencore has taken proactive steps to position our company to withstand current commodity market conditions," the spokesperson said. "Our business remains operationally and financially robust. We have positive cash flow, good liquidity, and absolutely no solvency issues."

Not all analysts share the same pessimistic outlook, however. Citigroup analysts believe that the sell-off in Glencore shares has been overdone and that there is still value in the business. The firm even suggested that Glencore should consider going private via a management buyout if the market rout continues. "In the event the equity market continues to express its unwillingness to value the business fairly, the company management should take the company private, whereby restructuring measures can be taken easily and quickly," Citigroup said.

As the commodity market continues to slump, Glencore's future remains uncertain. While some analysts warn of severe problems, others see value in the business. One thing is clear, however: Glencore must take drastic measures to address its debt burden and restore investor confidence to avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome.

Iranian Vice-President Eshaq Jahangiri has withdrawn from the country's presidential election, set to take place on Friday. The move was widely expected and is seen as a strategic decision to consolidate support for incumbent President Hassan Rouhani, who is seeking a second term. Jahangiri, a key ally of Rouhani, announced his withdrawal in a speech to thousands of people in the southern city of Shiraz, urging his supporters to back the president.

The withdrawal of Jahangiri and Tehran's hardline mayor Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who dropped out of the race on Monday, has cleared the path for a showdown between Rouhani and conservative cleric Ebrahim Raisi. Raisi, a close ally of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, is now seen as the main threat to Rouhani's re-election bid. Recent polls have put support for Raisi and other hardliners at around 52%, with Rouhani trailing at 42%.

Jahangiri played a crucial role in defending Rouhani's record during heated televised debates, criticizing his conservative rivals and highlighting the president's achievements. However, Rouhani's economic record has been a significant challenge, as the landmark nuclear deal he negotiated in 2015 has not triggered the expected economic recovery. Raisi, on the other hand, has promised to build a self-sufficient "resistance economy", create millions of jobs, and triple cash handouts to the poor.

With four candidates remaining in the race, a run-off election may be necessary if none of them secure more than 50% of the vote. The outcome of the election will have significant implications for Iran's future, with Rouhani's re-election seen as crucial for the country's continued engagement with the international community. As Iranians head to the polls on Friday, the contest between Rouhani and Raisi is expected to be closely watched, both domestically and internationally.

Glamorgan Cricket Club has announced the signing of a new long-term contract with 21-year-old Ruaidhri Smith. The Glasgow-born bowler, who has come through the Welsh development system, expressed his delight at committing to the club he has supported since childhood. Despite missing much of the 2015 season due to injury and university studies, Smith has shown promise with a highest first-class score of 57 not out and best bowling figures of 3-23. Glamorgan chief executive Hugh Morris praised Smith as a "very talented young bowler" with real potential. The contract extension is part of the club's efforts to develop young talent, with Smith joining Andrew Salter and David Lloyd as emerging players. Salter recently signed a three-year contract extension, while Mark Wallace agreed to a one-year deal. Smith's signing is a positive move for the club, and fans will be eager to see him make an impact in the first team.

"Between Worlds", the latest English National Opera production at the Barbican in London, has garnered mixed reviews from critics. The opera, which reflects on the events of 11 September 2001, has been praised for its "awesome power" and "crazy courage" by some, with the Daily Telegraph's Ivan Hewett stating that it "tears at the heart". However, others have found it to be "not as affecting as it ought to be", with The Guardian's Andrew Clements noting a lack of "sheer chaotic terror" in the production.

Despite this, composer Tansy Davies and librettist Nick Drake's work has been hailed as a "meditative lament on this human tragedy". The production, directed by Deborah Warner, has been criticized for its "lack of clarity" and "monochrome pace". "Between Worlds" is Davies' first opera and runs until April 25. As the second ENO production to be co-commissioned by the Barbican, it is a notable addition to the opera scene, and its success is being closely watched. With its thought-provoking themes and powerful music, "Between Worlds" is sure to spark important discussions and reflections on the tragic events that inspired it.

The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum has launched a Kickstarter campaign to raise $500,000 to preserve and display the iconic spacesuit worn by Neil Armstrong during the Apollo 11 mission in 1969. The suit, which has been in storage for nine years, is deteriorating due to the materials used in its construction, which were only intended for short-term use.

According to Cathy Lewis, the museum's spacesuit curator, the suit is a complex machine made of 12 different types of textiles and fabrics. Preserving each material individually would be possible, but it would require taking the suit apart, which is not an option. Instead, the museum plans to build a climate-controlled display case to safeguard the suit and slow down its deterioration.

The museum also plans to digitize the suit using 3D scanning technology. The goal is to have the suit ready for display by the 50th anniversary of the first lunar landing. Later, it will be the centerpiece of a new gallery called Destination Moon, set to open in 2020. The Kickstarter campaign aims to raise funds to support the conservation and display of this historic artifact, ensuring its preservation for future generations.

Tragedy struck on the football pitch in Omagh on Saturday when a player broke his leg in three places during a match. Mark O'Sullivan, a player for Omagh Hospitals, suffered the severe injury 40 minutes into the game against Glebe United. An ambulance was quickly called to the scene, which was located off Retreat Close near the Tyrone County Hospital.

However, the emergency vehicle's response was hindered by the lack of a proper path or road to the pitch. The team's manager, Paul McCabe, has been vocal about the need for improved access to the field, citing the danger it poses to players and spectators. "People could end up having a life-threatening problem and an ambulance may not be able to reach them," he warned.

 McCabe expressed relief that the ambulance was able to reach the injured player without getting stuck, but emphasized that this was a lucky exception. He has been urging the council to install a path or road to ensure that emergency vehicles can reach the pitch quickly and safely. O'Sullivan was taken to Altnagelvin Hospital in Londonderry for treatment, and his team is hoping for a speedy recovery. The incident has highlighted the need for improved infrastructure at the football field to prevent similar incidents in the future.

Former UN Secretary General Kofi Annan has spoken out against the handling of the International Criminal Court (ICC) cases against Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta and his deputy William Ruto. In an interview with the Financial Times, Annan stated that the two leaders should not have been allowed to remain free during their trials for crimes against humanity. The ICC ultimately dropped the charges against them, citing witness intimidation.

The cases stemmed from the violent aftermath of Kenya's disputed 2007 elections, which left 1,500 people dead and 600,000 displaced. Annan, who mediated Kenya's post-election crisis in 2007-08, accused the Kenyan government of using state resources to undermine the ICC's efforts. He believes that Africans should seek justice abroad if they cannot get it domestically, and rejects accusations that the ICC is biased against Africa.

Annan pointed to the successful prosecution of war crimes in the former Yugoslavia as evidence of the ICC's impartiality. He also praised the recent conviction of former Chadian President Hissene Habre, who was tried in an African Union-backed court in Senegal. The African Union has been critical of the ICC, with some member states threatening to withdraw from the court. Kenya has already announced its intention to withdraw from the ICC, a move that Annan's comments are likely to do little to reverse.

Tragedy struck in Kildysart village on Wednesday evening, resulting in the deaths of a 27-year-old woman and a 44-year-old man. Officers responding to the scene on Main St at approximately 19:30 local time found the injured woman and immediately called for emergency medical assistance. They also discovered an injured man at a nearby house. Despite efforts to save them, both individuals were pronounced dead at the scene by a local doctor.

The Garda have sealed off the area for a technical examination and notified the state pathologist. Authorities have confirmed that they are not seeking any additional suspects in connection with the incident. The police are now appealing for witnesses, particularly those who were in the vicinity of Main St between 18:00 and 19:30 local time, to come forward and contact them. The investigation is ongoing, with the Garda working to determine the circumstances surrounding the tragic events.

UK Experiences Hottest Day of the Year as Heatwave Continues
