The UK has witnessed its hottest day of the year so far, with temperatures soaring to 30.2C (86.36F) in Teddington, south-west London, according to the Met Office. Forecaster Charles Powell has predicted that Sunday and Monday will be just as scorching, with "dry, sunny, warm, humid weather with high UV, high pollen" dominating the forecast.

The high temperatures are attributed to warm, humid air from the tropical Atlantic, which is expected to bring highs of 32C (89.6F) on Sunday and 33C (91.4F) on Monday to the south and south-east of England and Greater London. This is approximately 10C (18F) above the average temperature for this time of year. However, northern parts of Scotland have experienced some respite from the heat, with rain falling on Sunday and more expected on Monday.

The Met Office has warned that a "wedge of really hot air" will blow in from France on Thursday, pushing temperatures in eastern and southern England up to 34C. The UV strength in some areas has been recorded as high as that in Cyprus and Gibraltar, prompting Public Health England (PHE) to issue a heat health warning.

Dr Thomas Waite, a spokesman for PHE, urged people to look out for vulnerable individuals, such as older people, those with underlying health conditions, and young children, who may be at risk from the heat. "The summer heat can bring real health risks, and we're urging everyone to keep an eye on those you know who may be at risk this summer," he said.

Despite the heat, the weather is expected to remain dry in the lead-up to the Glastonbury Festival next weekend, with only a 20% chance of isolated showers on Wednesday and Thursday. However, the Met Office predicts cooler and fresher temperatures on Saturday and Sunday, with a mixture of sunny spells and showers. As the heatwave continues, people are advised to take necessary precautions to stay safe and healthy.

The Welsh Rugby Union's (WRU) senior player selection policy (SPSP) has sparked controversy, with former dual-code international Hadley labeling it "ridiculous". The policy, aimed at keeping top players in Wales, restricts the number of players who can be selected for the national team while playing outside of the country to just three. Hadley believes that Taulupe Faletau, George North, and Jamie Roberts will be the three wildcard selections, leaving Rhys Priestland facing the end of his Test career.

Priestland, who plays for Bath, has been affected by the policy, which Hadley thinks will ultimately lead to his exclusion from the team. With Dan Biggar, Sam Davies, Rhys Patchell, and Gareth Anscombe all playing in Wales, Priestland's chances of selection appear slim. "Unless one of the others gets injured and cannot be picked, then there's a possibility he becomes the third wildcard choice," Hadley said. Priestland had previously taken an 18-month break from playing for Wales but reversed his decision in 2015. He has 48 caps for Wales and featured in all five games of the 2016 Six Nations.

The WRU has revealed its seven-man list of players affected by the policy, including lock Dominic Day, flanker Nicky Thomas, and scrum-half Rhodri Williams. However, players who signed contracts with clubs outside Wales before the policy was introduced, such as Leigh Halfpenny and Tomas Francis, are exempt from the rule. Hadley argues that the policy should be scrapped, allowing the coach to pick the best players regardless of where they play their club rugby. "For Wales, you want to be playing your best players, whether they're playing in Wales or not," he said. "You want to try and keep them in Wales if you can, but if you can't, then surely you want them still playing for Wales." The policy has sparked debate, with many questioning its effectiveness in keeping top players in Wales.

Avram Grant has announced that he will be stepping down as the head coach of Ghana's national football team. The Israeli coach's contract is set to expire, and he revealed at the Africa Cup of Nations that he would not be renewing it. Grant informed Ghana FA president Kwesi Nyantakyi of his decision, stating that "the time is right for me to move on to a new challenge."

During his tenure, Grant led Ghana to the Nations Cup final in 2015 and the semi-finals this year. Although he was unable to secure Ghana's fifth title, he successfully rebuilt the team after a tumultuous World Cup campaign in 2014. Grant took over the role in November 2014, when Ghana was still reeling from a disastrous World Cup performance. He expressed his gratitude for the experience, citing the passion and loyalty of the supporters as something he will always remember. Grant's departure marks the end of an era for Ghanaian football, and his legacy will be remembered as one of rebuilding and revitalization. His decision to move on has sparked speculation about his next coaching destination.

The FTSE 100 share index experienced a significant decline on Tuesday, dropping 106.72 points to 7,220.38 by the close of trading. The index was already trading lower, but the pound's sudden strengthening led to a further decline. A stronger pound has a negative impact on multinational firms listed on the FTSE 100, as it reduces the value of their overseas profits when converted back into sterling.

The pound surged above the $1.23 mark following a speech by Prime Minister Theresa May, ending the day up nearly 2.9% against the dollar at $1.2392. It also gained 1.83% against the euro, closing at 1.157 euros. The currency's rally was driven by optimism about the UK's economic prospects.

Despite the overall decline in the FTSE 100, some individual stocks performed well. Rolls-Royce shares jumped nearly 7% after the company agreed to pay £671m to settle bribery and corruption cases with UK and US authorities. However, the gain was later trimmed to 694.50p. Hargreaves Lansdown and Greggs also saw their shares rise, by 4% and 1.2% respectively. In contrast, British American Tobacco shares slipped 3.83% to £45.80 after the company announced a $49.4bn deal to acquire US rival Reynolds.

A brazen attempt to steal a statistics exam at a university took a dramatic turn when the instructor, John Cain, surprised two students, Henry Lynch II and Troy Kiphuth, in his office. The incident occurred at approximately 02:00 on Wednesday, according to university spokesman Jay Blanton. Lynch, a 21-year-old biosystems engineering student, had crawled through the campus building's ceiling ducts to gain access to Cain's office.

Once inside, Lynch opened the door for his accomplice, Kiphuth, and the pair began searching for the exam while blocking the door. However, their plan was foiled when Cain returned to his office after a meal and found the door blocked. When Cain threatened to call the police, the two students fled the scene. Lynch later confessed to the crime, revealing that he had attempted to steal the exam earlier that day as well.

This is not the first time Lynch has been involved in exam theft. He admitted to stealing an exam earlier in the semester, although he claimed not to have shared it with other students. The university has referred the matter to its internal discipline system, taking a strong stance against cheating and theft. "Cheating and theft of this kind is very serious in an academic institution," Blanton emphasized. Lynch and Kiphuth are set to appear before a judge next month to face charges related to the incident.

Chris Coleman, the renowned Welsh football manager, has been awarded the Freedom of the City of Swansea. The 46-year-old, who guided Wales to the semi-finals of Euro 2016, received the honour at a ceremony held at the city's Guildhall on Thursday. This prestigious award is a testament to Coleman's outstanding achievements in the world of football and his dedication to his home city.

In an interview with BBC Wales, Coleman expressed his pride and gratitude, stating that it is "important" for him to remain connected to his roots in Swansea. He attributed his success to the values instilled in him from a young age, which have served him well throughout his career. Coleman also expressed his pride in being associated with the Welsh team and his pride in being a Welshman.

The Lord Mayor of Swansea, David Hopkins, praised Coleman as a "proud Swansea boy" and a "terrific ambassador" for the city, making him a deserving recipient of the honour. Other notable individuals who have received the Freedom of the City include Prince Charles, President Jimmy Carter, and football legends John Charles and Mel Nurse. A celebration was held at Brangwyn Hall, featuring a performance by James Dean Bradfield of the Manic Street Preachers, to mark the occasion. Coleman's achievements have truly captured the hearts of the nation, and his legacy in Welsh football will be remembered for years to come.

A jury at the Old Bailey has delivered a verdict of not guilty in the case of a lorry driver accused of causing the death of a 26-year-old cyclist in London. Janina Gehlau, a German postgraduate student from Dusseldorf, was killed in October 2014 when the lorry turned left at Ludgate Circus, pulling her under its wheels.

The driver, Vincent Doyle, 45, had overtaken Gehlau 200 meters before the junction and had waited at a red light for 23 seconds. However, he failed to spot her in the cycle lane, despite claiming to have made safety checks and looked in his mirrors "five or six times" before the green light. The court heard that if his mirrors had been correctly positioned, he would have had Gehlau in his sights for three to five seconds before the accident.

Doyle told the jury that he never saw Gehlau waving her arms or heard her shouting before she fell under the lorry. He described how he felt a "bump" and looked in his mirror to see her head sticking out, and then held her hand and pleaded with her to "hold on" as he waited for the ambulance to arrive. Tragically, Gehlau died just as the paramedics got to the scene.

The verdict has left Gehlau's family devastated, with her mother Andrea Tasic stating that they do not feel they have got justice for Janina. Tasic expressed her hope that her daughter's death would serve as a warning to others, saying "My only hope is that this makes people think twice before cycling in London." Doyle, who has been affected by the accident, revealed that he had a nervous breakdown last year and spent eight months in a psychiatric hospital. The case highlights the dangers of cycling in London and the importance of road safety awareness.

Supreme Court Rejects Appeal by Former MPs in Expenses Scandal

The Supreme Court has rejected an appeal by three former Labour MPs, David Chaytor, Elliot Morley, and Jim Devine, who argued that their cases should be heard by Parliament rather than the courts. The three men, who deny theft by false accounting, will now face separate trials at Southwark Crown Court.

The decision upholds a ruling by the Court of Appeal in July, which stated that the three were not protected by parliamentary privilege in relation to their expenses claims. Parliamentary privilege is an ancient right that protects MPs from legal action arising from proceedings in Parliament. However, the Court of Appeal ruled that this privilege had never been attached to allegations of "crimes of dishonesty" such as theft by false accounting.

The three former MPs had argued that the expenses scheme was created and administered by Parliament, and therefore, any allegations related to it should be dealt with by Parliament. However, the Supreme Court disagreed, with President Lord Phillips stating that "each of these appeals is dismissed" and that the reasons for the decision would be given at a later date.

The trials of the three men are expected to begin soon, with Mr. Morley's trial scheduled to start on November 22. All three men are on unconditional bail and have been barred by their party from standing again as Labour MPs. The charges against them followed a nine-month police investigation triggered by the leak of MPs' expenses claims to a national newspaper.

The case has raised important questions about the accountability of MPs and the role of parliamentary privilege in protecting them from prosecution. The Supreme Court's decision is seen as a significant milestone in the ongoing expenses scandal, which has led to widespread criticism of MPs and calls for greater transparency and accountability. The trials of the three former MPs are expected to be closely watched, and the outcome will likely have significant implications for the future of parliamentary privilege and the regulation of MPs' expenses.

Game of Thrones star Maisie Williams has opened up about her own experiences with online bullying, revealing that she was subjected to cruel messages and harassment during her teenage years. The 17-year-old actress, who plays Arya Stark in the hit HBO series, said that she would often sit in her bedroom crying, with her brother attributing her mood to typical teenage behavior.

However, Maisie explained that there was more to her emotional state than just adolescence. She felt unable to confide in anyone about the bullying, which led to feelings of isolation and sadness. The situation became so unbearable that she would scroll through hurtful messages on her phone, even when sitting next to her mother on the train, trying to hold back tears.

The bullying eventually stopped when Maisie deleted her online profiles and left school, but she acknowledges that this is not a viable solution for most people. Instead, she advises young people to be mindful of their online behavior, urging them to think before posting anything that they wouldn't say or do in person.

Maisie's experiences have given her a unique perspective on the issue of online bullying, and she is now speaking out to help others who may be going through similar struggles. Her story will be featured on Radio 1 Stories: Anti-Social Media on Tuesday night, and she hopes that by sharing her experiences, she can help raise awareness and provide support to those affected by online harassment.

UK Defence Secretary Sir Michael Fallon has announced the sale of three military sites in County Down as part of a long-term strategy to reduce costs and improve efficiency. The sites, which include Abercorn Barracks in Ballykinler, Kinnegar Logistics Base in Holywood, and the Volunteer Gliding School at Newtownards Airfield, are among 56 across the UK slated for sale.

The move is expected to save the Ministry of Defence approximately £140m over the next decade, which will be reinvested in creating "areas of military expertise" across the country. The sale of these sites will also release enough land to build around 55,000 homes. However, not everyone is pleased with the decision. Strangford MP Jim Shannon has described the move as "backwards" and "illogical", particularly with regards to the potential demolition of 200 houses at Abercorn Barracks, which he believes could be used as social housing.

The Kinnegar base is expected to relocate to nearby Palace Barracks, although it is unclear whether any jobs will be lost as a result. The decision to sell two hangars at Newtownards Airfield has also been met with criticism, with Shannon stating that there is no potential for housing development at the site and that the decision has not been well thought out, especially given recent funding for the air cadets. The sale of these sites is part of a larger effort to streamline the UK's military operations and reduce costs.

Saudi Arabia Cracks Down on Controversial Fatwas with Website Blocks

In a move aimed at reducing the influence of ultra-conservative clerics, King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia has issued a decree restricting the right to issue fatwas to members of an officially approved council of Islamic scholars. The decree has resulted in the blocking of several websites that offered fatwas, which are religious edicts or advice.

The decision comes after a series of controversial fatwas sparked embarrassment for the Saudi authorities. Some clerics have used fatwas to publicly oppose attempts to modernize and Westernize Saudi society, while others have issued bizarre and outdated rulings. For example, one fatwa suggested that a man could symbolically become a woman's child by sucking on her breast or drinking her breast milk, thereby circumventing the prohibition on mixing of the sexes.

In response to the decree, the popular website Islam Today has closed its fatwa pages to avoid being shut down by the authorities. The website, which is run by influential cleric Salman al-Awdah, has a large following in Saudi Arabia and is known for its moderate interpretations of Islam. Al-Awdah, a former hardline cleric who was imprisoned in the 1990s, has reinvented himself as a moderate figure and has become a prominent voice in Saudi Arabia's religious landscape.

The blocking of websites and restriction on fatwas is seen as an attempt by King Abdullah to promote reform and reduce the influence of conservative clerics. However, the move is likely to face opposition from some members of the Saudi ruling family and the religious establishment. As the Saudi government continues to navigate the complex balance between tradition and modernity, the issue of fatwas is likely to remain a contentious one.

US-based Liberty Media is set to finalize its purchase of a controlling interest in Formula 1 after receiving approval from the FIA, the sport's governing body. The deal, which will see Liberty take over from CVC Capital Partners, is expected to be completed within weeks. Liberty has already acquired 18% of Delta Topco, the holding company of the F1 Group, and will increase its stake to 35.3% in the coming weeks. The company has outlined its vision for the sport, including protecting historic European races and establishing new events in the USA and Latin America. Liberty also plans to grow the sport through digital media, expanding its global reach and fan base. The FIA has welcomed the partnership, believing it will "ensure the continued success and development" of F1. With regulatory hurdles cleared, Liberty's shareholders have approved the buy-out, paving the way for a new era in Formula 1.

Ukraine has secured a major investment deal with US-based Cargill and Ukraine's M.V. Cargo to build a grain terminal on the Black Sea. The terminal, expected to be completed by spring 2018, will enable Ukrainian farmers to export an additional five million tons of grain. This move is seen as a significant step in boosting the country's agricultural exports. Despite ongoing conflicts with Russia and corruption concerns, Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk believes this deal will demonstrate Ukraine's reliability as an investment destination. US Ambassador Geoffrey Pyatt echoed this sentiment, stating that Ukraine has the potential to become an "agricultural superpower." The investment is a notable vote of confidence in Ukraine's economy, with the country expecting to export a record 37 million tons of grain between July 2015 and June 2016. The new terminal will play a key role in achieving this goal, solidifying Ukraine's position as a major player in the global agricultural market.

Leicestershire County Cricket Club has announced the return of overseas players Umar Akmal and Kevin O'Brien. Akmal, 25, scored 133 T20 runs in four matches this season. O'Brien, 31, will participate in both the T20 Blast and One-Day Cup. According to chief executive Wasim Khan, both players had a positive influence on the club and are match-winners. They made an immediate impact, with O'Brien batting well at Lancashire and Akmal playing a standout innings at Nottinghamshire. The club is excited to welcome them back to Grace Road, and fans are eagerly anticipating their return.

Mexico's Popocatepetl volcano has prompted the closure of several nearby schools as a precautionary measure. The National Disaster Prevention Centre raised the alert to "yellow stage three," the third-highest level, due to increased activity. The 5,450m volcano, located 70km from Mexico City, has been rumbling, with locals reporting they can hear its roar and feel its force. Concepcion Perez, from the town of Xalitzintla, described the experience to Agence France-Presse. Evacuation shelters have been prepared, and officials warn the alert could remain in place for weeks or months. Popocatepetl, meaning "Smoking Mountain," is Mexico's second-highest peak and has a history of major eruptions, including one in 2000 that forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people. Residents are bracing for potential further activity.

Scotland's Six Nations Championship Hopes Dented by Injury to Key Player

The Scottish rugby team has been dealt a significant blow ahead of the upcoming Six Nations Championship, with the news that prop forward WP Nel will miss the tournament due to a neck injury. The 30-year-old Edinburgh tight-head, who has won 15 caps for Scotland, suffered the injury during a Challenge Cup tie against Harlequins and a subsequent scan revealed damage to an intervertebral disc in his neck.

Nel's injury is a devastating blow to Scotland's chances in the championship, which gets underway on February 4 when they host Ireland at Murrayfield. The Scots will then travel to France on February 12, before facing Wales, England, and Italy in the following weeks. Head coach Vern Cotter, who will be leading the team for the last time before taking charge of Montpellier, had included Nel in his 37-man squad for the tournament.

The injury to Nel is not only a setback for Scotland, but also a personal blow to the player himself. The South Africa-born prop, who qualifies to play for Scotland on residency rules, was considered one of the country's few guaranteed Lions for the summer tour to New Zealand. However, with the uncertainty surrounding his neck injury, particularly serious for a prop forward, he must now be considered a major doubt for the Lions.

Nel's absence will be felt by Scotland, who played well in the autumn without him but are undoubtedly a better team with him in the lineup. He brings experience and solidity to the scrum, as well as carrying hard in the loose, and his loss will be deeply felt. As BBC Scotland's Tom English noted, "This is devastating news... Nel is a world-class tight-head and was, until this latest injury, one of Scotland's very few guaranteed Lions for the summer tour to New Zealand."

The Scottish Rugby Union has announced that Nel will be assessed to determine whether he requires corrective surgery. In the meantime, Edinburgh, his club team, has stated that they have had "positive conversations" about keeping him in the Scottish capital, despite reported interest from French Top 14 sides Toulon and Clermont Auvergne.

Scotland's squad for the Six Nations Championship includes a number of experienced players, including Greig Laidlaw, Richie Gray, and Stuart Hogg. Controversy Surrounds Indian Businessman Vijay Mallya's Whereabouts

Speculation has risen regarding the whereabouts of Indian businessman Vijay Mallya, following a Supreme Court case involving unpaid debts of $1.4 billion. A consortium of banks and creditors had demanded that Mallya's passport be impounded and his $75 million severance pay from Diageo be blocked to repay debts. Although the payout was blocked, it emerged that Mallya had already left India, sparking an uproar among opposition MPs who accused the government of allowing him to flee.

Mallya, known for his lavish lifestyle and dubbed "India's Richard Branson," has denied fleeing the country and criticized his "media trial." Reports suggest he is currently residing in London. Opposition MPs are now demanding that the government bring Mallya back to face the law. The businessman, who sold a significant portion of United Spirits to Diageo in 2014, was set to receive the $75 million payout after being ousted from the firm. Mallya also owns a stake in the Formula One team Force India. The Indian government is under pressure to take action and bring Mallya to justice.
